Le Clerc: Defective Handwriting
Le Clerc was a practised writer, both as author or letter-writer and as penman. His spelling is good; his handwriting, fluent, neat, and clear. Failures are rare, but sometimes he formed the letter 'a' without a tail, so that it is indistinguishable from 'o'. In the case of most writers it would be proper to regard the letter as an error in spelling and to print it as 'o'; in Le Clerc's case it is to be regarded as an imperfect correct letter, analogous to the printer's broken letters; I have accordingly printed the letter as 'a' without critical note.
As specimens: in this volume, p. 354, l. 4: Françoises (MS. Fronçoises); p. 472, l. 11: mais (MS. mois); p. 528, l. 5 of letter: au (MS. ou ou moins); p. 530, l. 12: j'aie (MS. j'oie); p. 698, l. 6: l'état (MS. l'étot); l. 8: au (MS. ou); p. 724, l. 21: circonstances (MS. circonstonces); p. 725, l. 22: extraits (MS. extroits).

The Molyneux Correspondence
The Molyneux correspondence begins with no. 1515. The letters from Locke to William Molyneux and E. Burridge, and most of those to Dr. Thomas Molyneux, are here reprinted from Some Familiar Letters between Mr. Locke, and Several of his Friends, 1708. Most of those from the brothers to him are printed from photostats of the original manuscripts in the Carl H. Pforzheimer Library.
In accordance with the usage of his time the compositor of Some Familiar Letters italicized many proper names, words, and passages, which were not underlined in the manuscripts: this is shown by comparison with the facsimiles of the letters to Locke, and of the text of no. 1593 with the independent printing in the Dublin University Magazine. Some words and passages in the manuscripts were underlined for the compositor's guidance, but there is also some underlining that appears to be the work of the writers of the letters. As the facsimiles do not permit of certain distinction I have generally cancelled the italics and disregarded the underlining throughout the correspondence with the Molyneux brothers except where the writers of the letters seem to be responsible.
Passages in the manuscripts were marked for omission; it is clear from the letters to Locke that passages in his letters were omitted; I have printed all the passages omitted from the letters to him, noting their omission from Some Familiar Letters. Where Some Familiar Letters prints 'Dr. S—', etc., I have printed the names in full in the texts. I have ignored other markings in the manuscripts which were evidently directives for the compositor.
― ix ―
Locke's Life: Principal Dates for this Volume
This table is planned to provide dates that should be serviceable to readers of the correspondence. It is not a chronological framework for Locke's life.
The principal difficulty in its compilation is that for many incidents in his life precise dates do not exist. Thus, if the mention is accurate, Locke was acquainted with Robert Boyle on 20 May 1660; there is nothing to show how much earlier the acquaintance was made. Unsatisfactory as many of them are, the dates are the best available.
In the dates a. (for ante) is to be taken to imply shortly before. In the dates for books when a precise date accompanies the word 'published' it is to be taken as the date of the earliest notice that the book had been, was, or was about to be, published, and not necessarily as the day of publication.
      
1690 	24 June. A Second Letter concerning Toleration licensed for publication. In July Locke went to Oates; he returned to London on 17 September, revisited Oates from 14 to 27 October, and returned on 13 December. He kept his London lodgings, but from this time Oates is to be regarded as his home. He visited London frequently and spent some months there every summer and autumn from 1696 to 1699. He paid shorter visits in 1700 and 1701, and his final visit in 1702. 
1691 	8 August-9 September. Locke visits Somerset, etc. 
	27 November. Some Considerations of the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest and Raising the Value of Moneylicensed for publication. 
1692 	16 July. Locke writes his first letter to William Molyneux. 
	23 November? A Third Letter for Toleration published. 
1693 	10 July. Some Thoughts concerning Education advertised.

1242. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 2 February 1690 (1233, 1262)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256r. Printed in Ollion, pp. 195-7. Answers no. 1233; answered by no. 1262.
(English) 
London 2 Feb. 90
Vir Amplissime
Nescio quâ tabellarii negligentiâ actum est ut literæ meæ eâdem nocte cum Franci literis scriptæ toto octiduo tardiores ad Te perferrentur, gaudeo tamen meas illustrissimo Consuli†1 et reliquis Sladi amicis sollicitudinem de mortis genere et modo exemisse. Nullam Slado nostro relictam auri vim quando Oxonium appulit ex eo constat quod a me mutuò petiit argentum ut suppleretur illi ad necessaria illic expensa et in itinere Oxonio Londinum. Quorsum notarius saniei mentionem in commentarios suos inseruerit plane nescio. Ego indusium non vidi, sed cum apertâ cistâ nec <pecunia>†a nec literæ cambii nec aliquid alicujus momenti inveniretur, decessi, non operæ pretium <ducens>,†b nec me vel teste vel inspectore opus fuisse dum induciorum et: fieret catalogus præsertim relicto illic Furleio et alio honesto viro Anglo una cum Franco. De indusio a me
― 2 ―

rogatus Furleius respondit statim fuisse sanguinem nec se dubitare fuisse ex hæmorrhoidibus. male igitur notarius ille saniem appellavit quod cruor fuit, sed cum indusium maculis fœdatum esset ut isti homines solent fœdo nomine appellare voluit. Si vero aliquid sanguinis esset quod Teste Furleio constat id malevolis omnem calumniandi ansam prorsus aufferet. nec si morbo nimis honesto infectus huc accessisset credi possit virum medicinæ peritissimum neglectâ valetudine in hujusmodi itinera (qualia apud nos fecit) gravi malo laborantem se conjecisset, nec me clam habuisset malum quod sciret recessum et otium et medicam†a opem statim postulasse. Nullus igitur sinistris suspicionibus locus est. De <funeris>†b cura et expensis Illustrissimo Domino Hudde et hæredibus per Francum satisfactum iri non dubito. Dominus Tyrrell nepos Magni Usserii ut ex rationibus video omnia curavit diligenter. Non est ille Doctor sed Generosus et amicus meus qui tunc forte fortuna Oxonio erat, et cum mihi notum et familiarem cognoverat Sladum illum humaniter et amice (ut meruit) dum in vivis erat tractavit, et honestam prout res ferebat defuncti sepulturam curavit. In suis ad me nuper datis literis†1hæc habet
― 3 ―

'Dominus Wood qui ante aliquot annos edidit†a historiam et antiquitates Universitatis Oxoniensis jam scripturus historiam virorum illustrium in eâ accademiâ educatorum scire avet annum et diem obitus, locum sepulturæ et epitaphium, si quod sit, celeberrimi Matthæi Sladi qui contra Vorstium tam doctè scripsit, munera etiam sibi indicari rogat quibus ille Matthæus cohonestatus fuerat et an Avus vel quo modo sanguine attingebat hunc Matthæum Sladum qui nuper prope Oxonium mortuus est'†1
(English) De his et aliis quibuscunque memorabilibus ad istum virum pertinentibus si me certiorem facient Sladi nostri Amici ego curabo ut inserantur Domini Wood historiæ, qua etiam occasione hujus nostri Matthæi memoria etiam possit posteritati commendari eum in finem stemma ejus quod inter illius chartas reperi mihi tradi a Franco postulavi antiquæ prosapiæ illustre monumentum et quod his viris eorumque cineribus decori erit
(English) Jam tandem ad vos redit Furleius noster†2 et spero illo impellente brevi editionem voluminis Sancti officii aggredietur Wetstenius.†b Furleius noster una cum his tibi tradet Usserii Armachani historiam
― 4 ―

dogmaticam de Scripturis et Sacris vernaculis nuper apud nos editam, quam ut a me accipere digneris rogo et excuses quod nihil vel majoris momenti, vel maturius miserim. verùm scias oportet his temporibus prælum apud nos aliquid gravioris literaturæ rarò parturire. Scriptores semipolitici, vel disputantes Theologastri†1 toto pene abutuntur typographorum labore. Hunc quem mitto librum nomen authoris et doctrina mihi commendavit, nondum enim legi, nec jam quicquam legere pene mihi vacat, sed spero brevi me rediturum in gratiam cum Musis et me iterum tradam otio literario, illic solum quies, si ad alia <respicis>,†a quanti ubique fluctus quam incerta rerum humanorum jactatio. Vale et fruere otio quo bearis et me ama
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
(English) Salutes quæso meo nomine uxorem liberosque tuos Veenios Guenellonos collegas omnes et eximium virum Verenium†2 cujus humanitati plurimum debeo. Si qua iterum apud illustrissimum
― 5 ―

consulem mei fiat mentio, sciat me nimio honore illius gratiarum actione affici, nec ea præstiti defuncto amico quæ speraveram et destinaveram si fata longiorem moram apud nos permisissent. Illius enim virtuti et mutuæ nostræ amicitiæ plurimum debebam
(Latin) 
London 2 Feb. 90
Excellent Sir,
It must have been through some carelessness in the post that my letter, which was written the same night as Francke's, reached you a whole week later; still, I am glad that it has relieved the burgomaster†1 and the rest of Sladus's friends of any anxiety about the nature and manner of his death. It is certain that our friend had no appreciable sum in gold left when he arrived in Oxford, since he asked me for a loan with which to provide for his necessary expenses there and for his journey from Oxford to London. I do not know with what object the notary inserted a mention of 'bloody matter' in his statement. I did not see the shirt myself; since no money or letter of exchange or anything of any importance was found in the box when it was opened I went away, not thinking it worth while to wait; I did not suppose I was needed as a witness or inspector while the list of shirts, etc., was being drawn up, especially as Furly and another respectable Englishman along with Francke remained there. When I asked Furly about the shirt he replied at once that it was blood, in his opinion undoubtedly from haemorrhoids. So that notary was wrong in describing as bloody matter what was really blood; but since the shirt had ugly stains he thought fit, as those people do, to give an ugly name to them. If, however, it was simply some blood, as is certain on Furly's evidence, then this will deprive malicious people of any pretext for making false accusations. Besides, if Sladus had come here infected by some discreditable disease, it is unbelievable that he, as a highly skilled physician, would have so far neglected his health as to dash off on the sort of journeys he made in this country, when he was suffering from a serious complaint; nor would he have concealed his trouble from me, when he knew that it called for immediate retirement and rest and medical assistance. There is therefore no room for sinister suspicions. I have no doubt that Mr. Hudde and the heirs will be satisfactorily informed through Francke about the management and expenses of the funeral; Mr. Tyrrell, grandson of the great Ussher, attended carefully to everything, as I see from the accounts. He is not a doctor of the University, but he is a gentleman and a friend of mine; he was fortunately in Oxford at the time, and as he was aware that I knew Sladus and was intimate with him, he treated him while still alive with kindness and friendliness, as he deserved, and after his death arranged for his respectable burial, as demanded by the occasion. In a recent letter to me†1 he has these words: 'Mr. Wood, who some years ago published his Historia et Antiquitates Universitatis Oxoniensis, and who is now about to compose an account of the eminent men who have been educated in that university, desires to know the year and day of the death, place of burial, and epitaph, if any, of the celebrated Matthæus Sladus who wrote so ably against Vorstius; he also asks for information regarding the appointments held by that Matthæus, and whether he was the grandfather or in what way a blood-relation of the Matthaeus Sladus who recently died near Oxford.'†1
(Latin) If our Sladus's friends will let me know about these or any other noteworthy matters concerning that man I will see to it that they are inserted in Mr. Wood's history; this may also serve as an opportunity for preserving our own Matthæus's memory for posterity. With that object I asked Francke to let me have Sladus's pedigree, which I found among his papers, a notable record of an ancient stock, and one which will shed lustre on these two men and on their ashes.
(Latin) Our friend Furly is now at last returning to you,†2 and I hope that under pressure from him Wetstein will shortly set to work on publishing the book of the Holy Office. Together with this letter Furly will deliver to you Usserii Armachani Historia Dogmatica de Scripturis et Sacris Vernaculis, recently published here, which I beg you will kindly accept from me, and that you will excuse me for not sending you anything of greater importance or sending it sooner; but you must know that in these days the press in our country is rarely in labour with any serious works of learning. Semipolitical writers or petty theologians with their disputations engross nearly all the work of the printers. As for this book I am sending you, it was the name and learning of the author that commended it to me; I have not read it yet; I scarcely have time to read anything nowadays; but I hope soon to return to favour with the Muses and once more to give myself over to learned leisure; there only is there peace, if one looks elsewhere how uncertain are human affairs, how mighty the billows on which they are everywhere tossed. Good-bye; enjoy the peace you are blessed with, and love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please remember me to your wife and family, to the Veens and the Guenellons, to all our Collegians, and to the excellent Verrijn,†2 to whose kindness I owe so much. If my name should be mentioned again in the presence of [p. 5] the burgomaster, please let him know that I feel myself all too honoured by his expressions of thanks; I did not in fact do all I had hoped for our deceased friend, or all I had intended to do if the fates had allowed him a longer stay among us; for I owed much to his high character and to our mutual friendship.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bij de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graft t'Amsterdam.
1243. Benjamin Furly to Locke, [February 1690] (1151, 1254)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 31. Date from Locke's endorsement. Furly may have set out for the United Provinces by 2 February; he was there by 19 February, O.S., and probably some days earlier: pp. 3-4, 14.
12 aClock Just parting
Deare friend
I thought I should have seen you this morning—I want now 2 days for my self, to take a Catalogue of, and remove my books. I have spoken with Mr. Popple about them, who possibly may find place in his house, for I feare Mr. Pawlin†1 being at a days warning I shalbe forced to be at double charge with them, before I can resolve what to do with them—I must entreat you two to consider of this for me, and to do what may be most convenient. So wishing you all prosperity, I rest in hast, and confusion
Your Affectionate friend
B F.
Address: For Doctor Locke These
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furley Feb. 89

1244. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 7/17 February 1690 (1212, 1245)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 20-1.
Monsieur, je vien de recevoir vostre agreable, et heureusement quoy qu'a l'instant du Sabbath des Juifs Monsieur Pinto†1 accepte le payement, et je garderay la lettre jusqu'a vostre ordre, ou jusqu'a ce quelle echet et auray alors soin de recevoir l'argent, si vous le souhaittez. toute la famille vous salue. Ma femme voudroit vous renouveller ses prieres touchant ce quelle vous doibt, jugeant que c'est dune fort mauvaise grace pour elle de se servir si librement d'un bien qui ne luy appartient pas. elle en trouve la commodité fort grande et il ne tient qu'a vous Monsieur de la rendre parfaitte en la tirant de debte. Nostre pierot se sent fort obligé du souvenir de Mademoiselle le Clarc.†2
Monsieur Thomas†3 se porte presentement tres bien, et prend grand goust aux estudes. Monsieur adriaensh†4 le loue fort, je ne doubte qui ne satisfasse ses amis entierement a son retour. j'ay entamé un college de practique depuis quelque temps auquel il est assidu, et je feray tout <m>on†a possible pour luy. vous scavez sans <d>oubte†a le demeslé de cette ville avec les deputez des autres villes aux estats d'hollande, sur l'Election de nos eschevins et de la seance du Conte de portlant a la ditte assemblée. hier cette ville a deputé 5 Messieurs de la Magistrature pour se tenir a la haye dans leur logement aux escoutes de ce que les autres villes voudront faire. quelques uns esperent que cela poura donner pied a quelque accommodement et†b le regarde comme une demarche favorable de cette ville.†5 tousjours on tient pour certain que le conte de Portlant
― 7 ―

partira la sepmaine prochaine pour l'Engleterre.†1 je mamuse a conter des nouvelles a vous Monsieur qui en scavez l'interieur.†a
je suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON
Amst. ce 17 feb 1690

1245. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 11/21 February 1690 (1244, 1247)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 22-3.
Monsieur,
j'espere que vous aurez receu mon avis de l'acceptation de vostre premiere lettre de change par Messieurs Pinto. aujourdhuy je recoy vostre lettre du 4e. courant avec les deux incloses, dont l'une est formellement signée acceptée par Monsieur louis Serrurier,†2 mais celle de cent livres sterlingh sur Monsieur Hendrik Hermans†3 luy a esté monstrée, mais il vouloit la garder chez luy jusqu'a demain pour quand, il a promis de l'accepter. mon neveu jan locquet quil la luy a presentée, ne la voulut pas laisser n'en sachant pas la consequence. on me dit que cela n'importeroit de rien. et quoy quil en sort il y retournera demain matin et je vous informeray par la prochaine poste de ce quil en sera arrivé. en cas de protest j'aurois soin de faire les choses dans les formes. quand les lettres seront prestes a eschoir je reprendray un folio, en banque sans que cela m'incommode. on est icy extremement surpris de la
― 8 ―

dissolution du parlement†1 et du voyage du Roy pour l'Irlande dans une conjonctur<e si>†a delicate. la dissention de Cette Ville avec le<s estats d'Ho>lland<e>†a est tousjours dans un mesme <estat.>†a ny l'un ny l'autre se relasche de la moindre chose. ce qui retarde extremement l'Equipage et les autres preparatifs necessaires pour la campagne prochaine. de maniere Monsieur quil y aura beaucoup a debrouiller dans les affaires de l'Europe. Je suis affligé de la mort de Monsieur Sydenham†2 et je vous prie de me mander si nous avons encore quelque chose a esperer de ses œuvres posthumes. Ma femme vous conjure de ne luy plus envoyer de chemises accablée de vos bienfaits outre que veritablement elle n'en prend pas le vray usage car elle les porte pardessus une chemise de toile. toute la famille vous salue, et Monsieur limburgh quina et bernagie ont disné hier chez mon beau pere ou nous avons bu solemnellement a vostre santé. adieu monsieur je suis autant que je le doibts
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON
Amsterdam ce 21 feb. 1690.

1246. William Stratton to Locke, 12 February 1690 (1208, 1258)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 43-4.
Sutton the 12th feb 89/90
Dear Cosin
I Received yours whearin you desire to know what mony I have of yours in my hands. I have cast up your Account and theare is in my hands if I mistake not 75l̷: 14s: 4d which mony I shall be redy to pay when you draw a bill uppon me I suppose I paid but 100l̷ since I sent you an account Robert Horals hay is all sould there is near 3l̷ In a suffisient mans hands I think, that will pay me at Lady day next but thear will be sum los about the hay, notwithstanding
― 9 ―

Mr Clarks great care In securing all to you, he binding Robert Horrall to asist In disposeing of it to make the most of it, he hath sould two parsells of it that cums to about fowr pound and hath fingered the mony and I cannot get it he hath but one hors left and thear was a report that he had allmost drowned him selfe but that he was pulled out of the water he looketh badly and I Really fear that If I shold pres hard for his hors and Indore goods that he will destroy him selfe, and I will doe but littell unles I have further orders from you, Abraham Barns is still In your Debt sumthing above 4l̷ I have weighted soe long uppon him that I am loth to weight any longer if you and Mr Clarke send a writ or order any other efecktuall way for the getting of your mony I†a- will <Indever>†b for it,-†a for he is soe great a knave that I am loth you should be cheated you may demand as I conceive mutch more and let him prove how he hath paid it weare he not a very bad man and likewise his wife a bad Woman I should not be soe desireous but would be content to stay sum thing longer soe I mite <be>†c shure at last but he will cum to noe acount and it is hie time to bring him to one
my Wife present her humble servis to you
I am Dear Cosin
your Humble servant
WILLIAM STRATTON
Address: For Mr: John Locke At Mrs: Smithsbys in Dorset Court in Chanell row Westminster London

1248. James Tyrrell to Locke, 18 February [1690] (1239, 1256)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 82-3. Year from Locke's note.
Oxford Feb: 18†a
Dear Sir
I acknowledg the receipt of both yours, as allso the bookes; and I must beg your pardon: if my being out of Towne; 2, or 3 dayes; and the businesse I have now upon my hands: made me interprete,†b your first in that sense as if I should hear from you so suddenly concerning the money; that I needed not write to you again till I received it: but since you did not meane it so; I beg your pardon; and must tell you that since I heard not of you againe; I was resolved to have writ this post to have thanked you for the booke, which I have began to read over with great satisfaction: and to refresh those old Notions;†c which I had from your Manuscript†d copy concerneing that matter:†1 and I must tell you that your booke is received here with much greater applause: then I find it is at London; the persons here being most addicted to contemplation, as there to action: only Dr: F: wishes you had rather writ my Lord S:s life.†2 but you must not be concernd at these things, you know
― 11 ―

the old saying pro captu Lectoris habent sua fata Libelli:†1 I find the divines much scandalized that so sweet and easy a part of their sermons: as that of the Law written in the heart is rendred false and uselesse:†2 but you know the narrownesse of most of their principles. If in reading any thing occurr that shocks me I will observe it. and either acquaint you with it by letter or reserve it till our next meeting which I hope may not be long first: as for the Doctors stick and sword†3 I thanke you; and the Agent on my mans behalf: as for your Quere who were particularly kind to the Doctor whilst liveing etc. all I can say to it is; that upon discourse with Dr: B.†4 I find many Doctors and others very civil to him by inviteing him to dinner etc: but none remarkably kind, except Dr: Musgrave:†5 and the man, (one Mr: Parker†a and his wife) where he lodged. She allso tooke care to bespeake†b- the coffin and-†b provide the shrowd; and divers other things necessary for his funerall. there is one Dr: Baccio an Italian who dissected his braine: and lyes in the house with me. you may make what use you please of these advertisements for I'le assure you nothing is expected. I spoke with Mr: Wood†6 lately; and he thankes you kindly for writeing into Holland, concerning his queryes; and in the meane time desires much to see the pedigree you mention; if the Agent is willing to spare it for a few days; if you please to send it me I will see it safely returned. I am glad to find you like my Lord Primates booke†7 so well, which makes me the better pleased that I sent it you: if you thinke it worth while to read over the volume of letters againe you may freely command another; since you gave away that I sent you;†8 pray let me know your mind concerning this: and I will order my bookseller at the Kings Armes in Pauls Church yard†9 to furnish you with one. as for the booke for Mr: Pococke†10 I deliverd it my self to the good old man, and read your postscript to him; he
― 12 ―

tooke it very kindly: and presents his service to you; and thankes on his sons behalfe; and so does his Lady; who desired me to put you in mind to doe somewhat for her son if it lye in your way: who hath but a small liveing and 11 children to provide for. I have nothing more to trouble you in but to desire you to returne this small summe as soon as you can conveniently; for the coffin and some odde things are still to be payed for: and I would not have them stay so long for their money: I am
your reall Freind: and Servant
J T.
I thanke you for your kind inquiry concerneing my children who are all well: I heard from James the last post; he was then at Hanover: at the Carnival; which he tells me hath bin kept there very splendidly with danceing: and operas: he is I hope gone by this Time into the Academy at Wolfenboutle. Sir William†1 gives him a very good character.
Your old Freind Mr: Wall†2 is well at Hanover with Sir William Colt: and I hope will come over this spring into England. Here is lately publisht a new booke calld the naked Gospel: supposed to be Dr Bs: of Exceter;†3 its intent is to shew the intent of Christian Religion; and the innovations that have bin made in it. by those who would multiply articles of faith.

1251. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 20 February/2 March 1690 (1247, 1260)

Monsieur,
je receu hier au soir vostre agreable par le canal de Monsieur furley et le Pacquet dont il vous plaist nous honorer. je vous assure Monsieur, que vous nous mettez dans la derniere confusion, ne sachant pas le moyen de reconnoistre tant de bien faits. Ma mere†2 et ma femme reservent a vous faire leur compliment en forme. Monsieur Cyprianus vient de me dire quil part inopinement ce soir pour vos quartiers et par son moyen je vous envoye deux dissertations†3 qui veritablement ne meritent pas de vous estre envoyé, mais il faut vous obeir puis que vous le desirez ainsy. vous me mandez que vous m'envoyez outre vostre traitté†4 et le livre de pthisi†5 un traitté de Morbis infantum†6 que je ne trouve pas dans
― 15 ―

mon pacquet, lequel pourtant estoit bien sellé et adjusté, le livre de pthisi estoit couché ouvert dans son milieu pour mieux adjuster le pacquet, de sorte que je ne vois pas quil puisse avoir esté contenu dans cette enveloppe. je m'informeray chez monsieur Limburgh, Le Clerc, ou Wetsteÿn, si par mesprise il ne se sera pas glissé dans leur pacquet. je ne doubte, que vous n'ayez receu mes advis sur l'acceptation des lettres de changes, dont j'auray soin pour l'adve<nir.>†a les affaires de cette ville sont au point que les estats ont interdit la justice pour n'avoir point envoyé la nomination a sa Majesté. cepandant tout est en repos en cette ville. et la bourgoisie en general approuve la conduitte du magistrat, ce qui fait croire quil en sortiront a leur honneur. Toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects, et pierot armé d'une si belle ecritoire, pretend bien tost vous escrire son compliment, et a Mademoiselle Clark pour un si beau present qui luy servira dans son voyage quand il sera en estat de l'aller remercier de bouche. les actions et les obligations†1 ont haussé notablement le jour mesme de l'interdit de la justice qui fut hier. Nos tres humbles respects sil vous plaist a Monsieur et madame Clarq. je suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obligé serviteur

1252. Locke to Charles Mordaunt, earl of Monmouth, later third earl of Peterborough, [February-March 1690?] (1150, 1411)
King, pp. 4-5. Excerpt, probably from a draft. Date: Locke was concerned about a 'Preceptor' for Monmouth's son in February 1690: N. Fatio de Duillier (p. 378) to Newton, 24 February 1690, in Sir Isaac Newton, Correspondence, ed. H. W. Turnbull, etc., 1959- , iii. 390. This date suits the draft, which appears to precede the publication of Some Thoughts Concerning Education.
― 16 ―

Monmouth's son was John Mordaunt, c. 1680-1710; styled Lord Mordaunt from 1689; matriculated from Christ Church 1699; M.P. for Chippenham 1701-8: G. E. C.
I must beg leave to own that I differ a little from your Lordship in what you propose; your Lordship would have a thorough scholar, and I think it not much matter whether he be any great scholar or no; if he but understand Latin well, and have a general scheme of the sciences, I think that enough: but I would have him well-bred, well-tempered; a man that having been conversant with the world and amongst men, would have great application in observing the humour and genius of my Lord your son; and omit nothing that might help to form his mind, and dispose him to virtue, knowledge, and industry. This I look upon as the great business of a tutor;†1 this is putting life into his pupil, which when he has got, masters of all kinds are easily to be had; for when a young gentleman has got a relish of knowledge, the love and credit of doing well spurs him on; he will with or without teachers, make great advances in whatever he has a mind to. Mr. Newton†2 learned his mathematics only of himself; and another friend of mine, Greek†3(wherein he is very well skilled) without a master; though both these studies seem more to require the help of a tutor than almost any other.
March
1253. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, 3 March 1690 (1220, 1271)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 183-4. Printed in Rand, pp. 297-8.
March the 3d. 1689:
Dearest Sir
Your Letter to Mr. Clarke came safe to his hand but he is not in a Condision as yett to answare it though he every day finds himselfe better and I hope in a short time will be perfectly recovered of
― 17 ―

his Rheumatisme, we are both oblidged to you for your derecttions as to his taking the Jesuetts powder which I am resould to see punctually performed theare being nothing more a Greeable to me then to have your Commands in every thing I doe, being then sure of suckcess haveing soe Latly had the Experiance of it in what you ordered for mr. Clarkes man†1 who has bin very Carefull to follow your advice and is for the present perfecttly Cured and I hope soe as it will not returne a Gen. the only inconvenience he finds now is that he has a Great heaveness in his head and some times has a dimness before his sight soe much that when he is wrighting for a small time is faine to Lay by his penn, Sir the Great favor you have done him in adviseing him and the Good he has found by following it has incoraged him to begg of me, to desire to know of you, whether it is not his best way to be Bleeded or to doe any thing Else as you shall thinke Fitt, Sir I have nothing of newes from hence to aquaint you with more then that the Electtion for thiss County is not yett determened and that theare has bin all the fowle Practtiscess Emaginable in the mannagement theareof and tiss thought theare will be afalls Returne att Last a Gainst Sir John Sydenham and Mr Speake in order to sett up Sir Edward Phelipps being the Great piller of the westren Church,†2Bridgwater has the same members as they had Last parlement, and as for the Taunton people they have not made theyr Choyce as yett, but it is now thought that Portman and Clarke will carry it If theare is noe trikes played by the first mentioned,†3 I am
Sir yours: M: C:
my service to you and the Ladys and our†a masters alsoe
betty is wholey yours,

1254. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 4/14 [March 1690] (1243, 1268)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 40-1. The postmark shows that Furly's date is new style. Month and year from Locke's endorsement.
14.
Sir
Since my last last post we have no Letters come in from England, so I shal have the lesse to say, being onely to inform you that being in the Hague yesterday, I there understood, that the differences betwixt Amsterdam and the rest of the members of the State, were adjusted the day before, On this wise. They presented their Nomination, to the States as their Sovereign, requesting them to make the Election or to appoint the Court of Holland to do it, Or otherwise as their wisdoms shal think fit. Upon it the Notes are to be razed out of the Registers. And this day I suppose they sit again, with the Earl of Portland, under the reserv of their Right, by vertu of their Protest.†1
Of this affair men judg variosly, some that they have don wel, and wisely to postpone their own Interest to that of the Public Interest of Europe. Others that they have prostituted themselves, by doing that which they in print testifyed that they could not in honour and Conscience do. It is a most certain truth that the 2 packets I mentiond in my Last are missing. The Postmaster Vander Poel, having given a receit for them, and in the Assembly of States, solemnly sworn that he sent them forward.†2
I hope the Jacht will be arrived and that you have received mine, I was told in the Hague, that the P—†3 is like to be as giddy a one as ever you had, and that there wilbe no hopes of conserving your Liberties, but from the Honor, and Wisedom of the King, that will never desire it of them, but otherwise that they will give all that his Majesty should ask. I beleeve truly there are those that would be glad if they could prevail with him to desire as much power as ever King James used, that so the people finding no difference betwixt the one and the other, save in point of Taxes, might long again for a Captain to lead them back to Egypt,†4 But K.W. sees and knows better, and will prevent them.
― 19 ―

I have since my return, a great Correspondence from Italy, and do receive a great number of Bales of silk by land to send for England, and so do much want my Italian Dictionary, as also my Spanish, which I could be glad Sil. could send me by the return of the jacht, and with them my Bacons History of the English Goverment in 4°.†1 and Wingate abridgment of the statutes in force in 8°.†2
Address: To Mr. John Locke at Mrs. Smithsbys in Dorset Court in Channel Rowe In Westminster
Postmark: MR 10
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 14 Mar 90 Answered 25
1255. Sir John Somers, later Baron Somers, to Locke, 5 March [1690] (1186, 1946)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 153-4. Year from Locke's endorsement. Printed in King, p. 234.
Oxon. Wedn. 5. Mar.
Dear Sir
Since you have wished so kindly to my Election, I cannot but think it my Duty to give you an account that yesterday morning my old partner Mr Bromley†3 and myself were chosen at Worcester without any Opposition. I know you will be pleased to hear that my Lord Bellomont†4 has all the reason in the World to be assured of being Elected at Droytwich and I hope the Next post will bring you a certain account that it is so; to Morrow being his Day. This day was the Election for the County of Worcester and I doubt not but Mr Foley and Sir Fr: Winnington were chosen, which may be lookd upon as good Fortune for there would have bin danger from any pretenders, as far as I can find by the sense of the Country.†5 I was
― 20 ―

very willing to get out of the Town as soon as my Election was over and so got into the Circuit at this Place, from whence I shall go back to Worcester where I hope you will make mee so happy as to let mee receive another Letter from you in which I will beg your Advice (for by this time you have an account of the bulk of the Elections)†1 whether you think I may go on in the Circuit or not. What you write shall be my rule in this Point. If I could hope to be usefull I would not fail to be at the Opening of the Session, but if there be no hopes of it (and that the Gazette inclines mee to beleive) I would take the Advantage of the whole Circuit since I am now engaged in it.†2 This Letter I beg from you by Saturday post†3 And when I have the Satisfaction of seeing you I will beg your pardon for this Freedom, which Nothing but your Kindness to mee upon all occasions as well as my Dependance upon your Judgement could have drawn mee to. I am earnest in expectation of Your thoughts in this and greater matters and shall be often Wishing for the coming of the Post to Worcester on Munday next. I am
Sir
Your most faithfull humble servant
J. SOMMERS.
I am so unfortunate as to have forgot the name of the Gentlewoman at whose house you Lodge and therefore direct this to the E. of Ms.†4

1256. James Tyrrell to Locke, 5 March [1690] (1248, 1266)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 84-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxford March 5th:
Dear Sir
I have received yours, and have according to your desire evend all that was due for the Doctors funerall charges; and I thanke you for geting this money for me, which I might without your asistance either never have had; or at least not so soon: and had you sooner told me your mind, that you had desired that this money might remaine in your hands upon the account between us: I would have discharged those reckonings at first, before I had bin asked for them: for I had rather straiten my self, then that you should not have your owne, as fast as I can raise it: I must likewise returne you my owne and Dr: Bs:†1 thankes for the funeral rings intended us. if you meet with any safe hand comeing downe suddenly you may send them downe together with the pedigree;†2which you thinke not fit to venture by the Carrier; but if you can light of none you know that are comeing downe; if you please to send them to one Dr: Goulds lodging†3 at the signe of the golden ball in hind Court in Fleetstreet; he is a Freind of mine; and one that will be sure to see them safe deliverd to me; at his comeing downe; which I hear will be about a fortnight hence: I pray write a note to him, and if he send you word he will not come downe so soon let your man bring them back againe: I have writ to him about them, but have received no answere from him as yet. I have here sent you a note to my bookseller in Pauls church yard, whereby you may receive the volume of letters I desire to present you. I must now desire you, to inquire whether the King is like to give any money or grant any pentions to any of those Irish Ladyes who have had the misfortune to loose their husbands in his service the last Autumne: for if you thinke it feasible I would beg the favour of you as to present a petition, on the behalf of my Lady Jones the widdow of my Kinsman Sir Arthur Jones;†4 whom you were pleased to be kind
― 22 ―

to, upon my account; and who died in Ireland; of the Flux, or Feaver: and hath left his Lady a person of quality and 3 children in great straits: here in England, and†a is†a above the applying her self to the Commissioners for the common breif money;†1 I pray will you discourse with My Lord M.†2 about it, and if you thinke it feazible pray let me know it, and I will send you up a petition from her: which I desire you would give either to my Lord M. or Lord S.†3 to be deliverd to his Majesty. I was this day with Dr: P.†4 and deliverd your message, and service to him and his Lady; who take it very kindly; but Mr: P: their son is not yet returned from Salisbury; so that he hath not given him your booke as yet. as for the places in the Almes house they should be given onely to old; or maimed souldiers: they are in the Kings gift; and worth 6l: per annum: besides a chamber; but most of them (which are 20 in all) liveing at London, and but 6 here; I cannot tell how to inquire whether any of them are vacant: perhaps the Threasurer of Christ Church can tell, but I have no acquaintance with him: nor doe I know wher els to inquire: but if you please to give me any farther directions in it: they shall be obeyed.†5 as for the booke I mentiond viz: the naked gospel it is supposed to be written by Dr: Bury Rector of Exceter Colledge: I have read it; and it is ingeniously written. but it is not to be had; for it was never sold; and now I hear upon some of the Clergyes muttering against it, he has supprest the whole Edition. I have no more but to thanke you for your kind remembrance of my son who is now in the Academy <at>†bWolfenboutle: and I heard lately from him. And I am sure he <is like his>†b Father
Your humble servant
J T
My service to worthy Mr: C.†6 if still in Towne. I saw Dr: Fs: son†7 yesterday who is newly returnd to Oxford; and tells me he left
― 23 ―

his Father and Mother well. I am glad your booke takes so much among the inquisitive and ingenious. as for the Gentleman that writ me that advertisement he was a disciple of Wills Coffe house†1 and you <know>†a how capeable those sort of sparkes are of Judging of such thinges: here is come from London: a very pernicious booke against the Goverment now establisht called vindiciæ Juris Regii.†2 it is pretended to be writte<n>†b in answere to Dr: Burnets measures of obedience but it hath done a great deal of mischeif here.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at his Lodgings at Mrs: Smythesbyes house in Dorset Court in Cannon Row. Westminster.†c
Postmark: MR 7
Endorsed by Locke: J. Tyrrell 5 Mar 89/90
1257. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 7/17 March 1690 (1234, 1284)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 41-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 42-3.
A Amsterdam le 17 de Mars 1690.
Je vous suis bien obligé, Monsieur, de l'honneur que vous m'avez fait de m'envoier vôtre Livre, je voudrois avoir quelque ouvrage de cette force à vous offrir. Mais je suis obligé <à>†d faire l'échange de Diomede avec Glaucus χάλκεα χρυσείων etc.†e †3que vous accepterez, s'il vous plait, sans quoi je ne saurois vous témoigner ma reconnoissance. Au commencement du Mois prochain, je vous envoierai les XIV, XV et XVI volumes de la Bibliotheque Universelle,†4 avec l'histoire du Jansenisme.†5 Je dois encore vous remercier des Livres, que vous avez joints au vôtre. Lors qu'il paroîtra quelque chose ici, que vous jugerez de vôtre goût, vous n'aurez qu'à m'ordonner de vous l'envoier. J'aurai soin d'executer avec ponctualité toutes vos commissions. Il ne paroit rien présentement ici, de curieux, qu'un
― 24 ―

livre de la lumiére de M. Huygens,†1 mais que je n'ai pas encore vu.
Pour vous parler de la version du vôtre, celui qui y travaille m'a promis quil pourroit être achevé vers le milieu de cet Eté. Dès que cela sera fait, je vous l'enverrai par quelque commodité assurée. Il me dit qu'au commencement qu'il travailloit à cette Version, il avoit de la peine en quelques endroits, mais que présentement il travaille avec assez de facilité. Comme c'est un homme qui a du bien, et qui fait cela pour s'exercer, sans avoir aucune occupation qui demande de l'attache, j'espere que cela ira bien; et en tout cas vous en serez le maître. Je ne doutes pas que le Sieur de la Crose†2 ne soit très-miserable, mais je ne croi pas que la misere soit capable de le faire revenir à lui, parce qu'il la éprouvée plusieurs fois en sa vie sans devenir plus sage. Je lui souhaite de la prudence, et du repos. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J. LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Loke A Londres
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 17 Mars 90
1258. William Stratton to Locke, 8 March 1690 (1246, 1275)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 45.
Sutton Mar: the 8th: 89/90
Dear Cosin
I Rec: your sharp loyns dated the 20th of feb and am sorry that you should make such a use of what I wright to you, as to think that I should be the ocation of your losing your mony dew from that unjust man Robert Horrall for I would not leave a stone unturned for your gaining your Just dew and If I should Indever to get the mony of those that had the hay and should take such meshures that the lawe should eate up the debt you would not be pleased and it would be a troble to me. ― 25 ―

in selling of the hay to Make the most of it, as for this mony of the hay that was sould to John Knight and John Veale, I knew not till it was to late. I spake to John Knight about it and I perceive he intends not to pay it againe, theare is a pease of ground that Rob: Horrall is to pay 20s yearly I hope it is worth more to help pay the debt. If you advise I will take to†1 it and let it if I can get a tenant, I have Rob: Horrals lease in my keeping if that be suffisient to take to it I think it is he being a poor knave, as for Abraham Barns I gave you an account how it was that he ran in arears to you at the end of his account that I gave Mr Clarke and I supposed It would have satisfied you that it was noe negligence in me If I knew how to doe better I would, I cannot give you that satisfacktion as I should If I spake with you. I am In hopes to se you this spring in our Countery and then I hope you will have better satisfacktion. Mr Day†2 cannot return your mony but I hope this bearer Mr Dando will Return all or most of it
my Wife presents her humble service to you I take leave
your Faithfull Kinsman and Humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON

― 26 ―

1262. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 11/21 March 1690 (1242, 1283)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 42-3. Answers no. 1242.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Ingentes merito Tibi gratias ago, pro egregio munere, quo me honorare voluisti, eximio nempe Doctissimi Archiepiscopi Armachani de Sacris Vernaculis tractatu. In illo, sicut in aliis Archiepiscopi illius operibus, indefessum antiquitatis studium relucet, et multijuga lectio autorum, qui non omnes alliciunt, quibusque
― 29 ―

non est is genius, ut omnibus placere possint. Quare non possum non exosculari laborem illorum, qui amore veritatis indagandæ, tædium, quod alios ab illorum autorum lectione deterret, devorare solent, ut omnibus prosint. Ego talium labore fruor libens, sed alio studiorum genere delector. Cum voluptate excerpta eorum ex quibusvis autoribus lego, gratumque mihi est, illis, qui semper antiquitatem crepant, illud telum quo omnes adversarios unico ictu se conficere posse putant, e manibus extorqueri. Isti labori Archiepiscopus hic par erat, in eoque multum præstitit. Utile autem est Ecclesiæ, non omnes eodem studiorum genere delectari, sed unumquemque occupari eo, ad quod naturæ suæ genio ducitur: ut dum unusquisque præstat ad quod valet, omnium laboribus, pro cujuscunque genio diversis, Ecclesia fruatur, et unusquisque quod potest in Ecclesiæ bonum conferat: Quemadmodum singula corporis membra juxta functiones ad quas a natura destinata sunt, operationibus admodum diversis totius corporis incolumitati inserviunt. Literas tuas nondum Illustrissimo D.Consuli prælegi: quia politicos negotiis quibusdam molestis et difficilibus ita occupatos vidi, ut ea interpellare, intempestivum mihi visum fuerit.†1 Cum jam brevi illarum molestiarum aliqualem prævidemus finem,
― 30 ―

paucos intra diës literas tuas illi ostendam. Consanguineos D. Sladi conveni; illis adeo ignotus est suus proavus, ut nihil aliud de eo norint, nisi quod omnibus notum est, scripsisse eum contra Vorstium: ipsum sepulturæ locum ignorant. Ut itaque paucis dicam; Matthæus ille Sladus, de quo quæris, fuit Sladi nostri avus paternus, rector Scholæ trivialis in hac civitate,†1 zelo religionis puritanissimus, et propter illum tempore Elisabethæ ex Anglia profugus. Nullum illius hic exstat epitaphium. An a libro contra Vorstium magnis celebrari encomiis mereatur, malo ab aliis dijudicari. Non magnam in eo ostendit doctrinam, sed zelum immoderatum: talis hic liber ille æstimator. Noster nuper defunctus igneum illum avi sui zelum neutiquam imitatus est, sed de dissentientibus moderatiorem ferebat sententiam. Stemma inter chartas ejus repertum hæredes sibi remitti orant, quia est autographum, nullumque ipsis est apographum. Si D. Wood mittatur apographum, inde æque omnia potest depromere, quibus in descriptione Sladi opus habet. Vidi hic Epistolas Vossii, nuper in Anglia editas,†2 quibus multa præclara continentur. Verum præposteram illam editorum diligentiam minime probare possum, qui omnia a viris doctis scripta maxima
― 31 ―

cura conquirere†a solent, et in lucem edere. Sic enim multa luce minime digna eduntur. Hic innumeræ occurrunt epistolæ de rebus privatis et domesticis, etiam quædam quas premi satius fuisset. Idem nuper vidimus in Epistolis Grotianis.†1 Hactenus Furlæum non vidi, nec ullas ab ipso habeo literas: Ego Sancti Officii Gestorum editionem non urgeo, quia video Wetstenium cunctari, et fœlicius eum a Furlæo quam a me urgeri posse. Omnes Collegæ jam bene valent, excepto D.Quina, quem περιπνευμονία nuper ferme exstinxerat. Nunc convalescere incipit. Reliqui omnes optime valent. D. Cyprianus, ut audio, in Angliam denuo abiit. D. Venius, Guenellonus, integraque eorum familia, uti et uxor mea et liberi, mecum, plurimam tibi salutem precantur. Vale Vir Amplissime, et, uti facis, nos ama.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 21 Martii
 
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I thank you most warmly, as indeed I ought, for the fine present with which you have been kind enough to honour me, the learned Archbishop of Armagh's valuable treatise De Sacris Vernaculis. This, like the archbishop's other works, gives clear evidence of his indefatigable devotion to the study of antiquity and of his multifarious reading of authors who do not attract [p. 29] everybody and whose bent is not such as to be appreciated by all. Hence I cannot but feel the greatest admiration for the labours of those who are moved by the love of searching out truth to endure the tedium which deters others from the reading of such authors, and this for the benefit of all. I am glad to profit by the labours of such scholars, though I find my pleasure in studies of another kind. I enjoy reading their extracts from various writers, and it pleases me when those who are always prating of antiquity are deprived of that weapon with which they think they can dispose of all their opponents at a single blow. The archbishop was equal to that task and was pre-eminent in it. It is of service to the Church that all should not find their pleasure in the same sort of studies, but that each should occupy himself with what he is led to by his natural inclination, that so, while each one gives what suits his powers, the Church may enjoy the labours of all, diverse as they may be according to each man's nature, and that each may contribute what he can to the good of the Church, just as the individual members of the body, fulfilling the functions for which nature has designed them, minister by their widely differing operations to the health and preservation of the whole body. I have not yet read your letter to the most excellent Burgomaster; I found that the public men were so occupied with certain troublesome and difficult affairs that I thought it an inopportune moment for interrupting them.†1 As we now foresee an end of these annoyances before [p. 30] long I will show him your letter in a few days' time. I have seen Sladus's relations; they are so ignorant about their great-grandfather that they know only what everybody knows about him, that is, that he wrote against Vorstius; they do not even know where he is buried. To tell you in a few words, then: the Matthæus Sladus you ask about was our Sladus's paternal grandfather, rector of a grammar school in this city,†1 and by religion a perfervid Puritan, for which reason he came here from England as a refugee in the time of Elizabeth. No epitaph of him exists here. Whether his book against Vorstius deserves any great praise I prefer that others should judge. He does not show much learning in it, but rather an inordinate fervour; let that suffice here for an estimate of the book. Our late friend was far from imitating his grandfather's fiery zeal; his judgement of those who differed from him was more restrained. His heirs request that the pedigree that was found among his papers may be returned to them, as it is written in his own hand and they have no copy of it. If a copy may be sent to Mr. Wood he can obtain from it equally well all that he requires for his written account of Sladus. I have seen a copy of Vossius's letters here;†2 they were recently published in England, and there is much that is excellent in them. What I cannot at all approve of, however, is the absurd industry of editors whose way it is to collect with the greatest care everything that learned men have [p. 31] written and to give it to the world. Thus a great deal is published that little deserves to be. In this case one comes upon innumerable letters about private and domestic affairs, some even that it would have been better to suppress. We saw the same thing recently in the case of Grotius's letters.†1 I have not seen Furly so far, nor have I any letters from him; I am not pressing for the publication of the acts of the Holy Office as I see that Wetstein is hesitant about it, and I feel that Furly is better able than I to hurry him on. All our Collegians are now quite well, except Mr. Quina, who almost met his end recently with inflammation of the lungs. He is now beginning to recover. Everyone else is in the best of health. Mr. Cyprianus, I hear, has left for England once again. Mr. Veen, Guenellon, and their whole family, as also my wife and children, join me in sending you their best wishes. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 21 March
1690

1263. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 12 March 1690 (1230, 1311)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 43-4.
Otterton March 12th. 89.
My Dear Friend
I have deluded my self lately with Hopes, that the happy Time was come, which would bring me again to you; and that I should once more be Bless'd in the enjoyment of your Neibourhood, and most Excellent Conversation; but Heaven will have it otherwise, and I must yet wayt with patience. our Old Gentleman was so fond of being chosen himself for this Parliament, that his son durst not appear to oppose him, and so both are laid aside; and a third person come in at their Borough;†1 However I hope to see you in the Month of May, my Master having promised me a Journey to Tunbridge this Year if we live till the season. which I cannot promise my self, unless you help us with your speedy advice. for my Master has lately been attacqued with some Touches of a Sleeppy disease, or rather some obstructions in the Brain, which seems often Clouded, and opprest to that degree that once he lost his senses for a Minute, about three Weeks since; he was then Bleeded, and purged twice; which did him Good; but the Symptons return upon him again, and he has been often ill, this last three dayes, and is worst when he sits, Walks, or Rides in the Sun. I cannot prevayle with him to apply himself to any Phisitian in this Country; and Sydenham being Dead, he has no opinion of any in London, But your Self, whose assistance he earnestly begs; and would have done it with his own Hand, but that the present disorder of his Head makes him afraid to Write. I beg your Speedy Answer, and that whatever Medicines you think necessary for him, you would order to be prepared by Mr Malthus†2 in the Pelle Melle; he is our Apothecary, and knowes how to send them to us, in four dayes by the Exeter Coach. Dear Sir the infinite importance of this kindness to me, make me assure my self, that I shall without difficulty obtain it, since I know you are the best of Friends, and full of Compassions to the afflicted and
― 33 ―

distressed; help me I beseech you in this Exigency, and delay not to Oblige
Your faithfull humble Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Address: For Mr John Lock at his Lodging in Dorset Court in Channell Rowe in Westminster
Postmark: MR 14

1265. —— Passebon to Locke, 14 March 1690 (1232, 1496)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 196-7.
Monsieur
Je ne fai point de doute qu'un peu de temps, et un peu du monde ne corrige dans mon Pupille toutes les manieres enfantines, et tous les autres petits défauts que l'on y remarque aujourd'huy. L'affaire la plus importante comme vous le dites si bien Monsieur, dans la derniere lettre que j'ay eu l'honneur de recevoir de vous est de s'attacher principalement a le défaire des vices de l'ame. Je ne luy pardonne rien la dessus et je luy en fay connoitre les facheuses consequences aussy fortement qu'il m'est possible. Il vous rend conte dans sa lettre de l'estat de ses études. Je ne vous en diray rien dans la mienne. ce que je trouve de bon en luy c'est qu'il ne se rebute point de tout le temps qu'il passe dans la chambre. cela me fait juger qu'aussy tost qu'il en pourra faire un bon employ il fera des progrés assez considerables.
Je ne luy ay rien enseigné de la Chronologie n'ayant point de livre qui en traite. Si vous jugez que la traduction du Sieur Maucroix du Rationarium temporum du Jesuite Petau†1 soit un bon livre pour cela, je vous supplie, Monsieur, de dire a Monsieur son Pere de le luy acheter, avec quelque petit traité de la sphere tel que vous le trouverez a propos.
Je fais des voeus a Dieu Monsieur pour le retablissment de votre santé.
Je vous suis trop obligé du soin que vous prenez de mon manuscrit. Je reconnois qu'en tout vous m'estes un tres illustre Patron,
― 35 ―

aussy regardes-je comme une chose infiniment heureuse pour moy l'honneur de votre connoissance.
Votre petite Maitresse fait un progrés plus sensible que son frere et sa soeur, elle merite fort tout le soin qu'on en peut prendre. Souffrez Monsieur que je vous fasse encore icy la méme priere que dans mes precedantes, de vouloir assurer les Dames de mes tres humbles respects. Je suis avec un zele tout particulier
Monsieur
Votre tres humble tres obeissant et tres obligé Serviteur
PASSEBON
Chipley ce 14e Mars 89/90

1266. James Tyrrell to Locke, 18 March [1690] (1256, 1273)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 86-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxford: March 18
Dear Sir
I writ to you about a fortnight agoe, wherein I desired you to send downe the Pedigree; and the rings you mentiond in your last by one Dr: Gould who I thought then was comeing to Oxford speedily: but I have since heard from him, and he now tells me that he shall not come downe till some time after Lady day; about which time I shall come up God willing my self; and therefore if you thinke it worth while to have the rings presented whilst I am here; I thinke it were better you sent them downe by the Oxford waggoners or Coachmen;†a in a little box; with a line or two by way of advice where to send them for them; and they will not I beleive fail to be deliverd for they bring downe things every weeke of much greater value: and you may allso write if you please by the Post: and let me know by whom you send them: but as for the Pedigree I advise nothing; since they put so high a value upon it: that may be sent downe by a private hand at any time; when you light of a fit oppertunity. Since I writ last Mr: Pocock hath bin with me and desires me to present his humble service to you, with many thankes for your booke; and all your kind intentions towards his Father;
― 36 ―

and himself: I desired him likewise to inquire of the Threasurers Clerke of Christchurch whether there was ever a place voyde in that hospital:†1 and Mr: P. tells me; his answere was that he does not know of any: but that it hath bin usual for the King to write letters to the Deane; and Cannons ordering them to admit such a Person to the next vaccancy that shall happen in that hospital: this is all the account I can give you of it, of which you may make what use you please. and now for want of somewhat to fill up this paper I will let you know what, the good nature of some people of this place, have invented to disparage your booke: a Freind told me the other day that he had it from one who pretends to be a great Judge of bookes: that you had taken all that was good in it; from†a divers moderne†b French Authours. not only as to the notions but the manner of connexion of them;†2 my answer againe was. that as long as I enjoyd your conversation in England: which was when the maine body of the booke was written:†3 to my knowledg you utterly refused to reade any bookes upon that subject: that you might not take any other mens notions: and that you have taken another course since that time I did not beleive: therefore that if you have fallen upon the notions of others, it was by a necessary traine of thoughts: since truth being but one thing hath commonly but one way to prove it: if you have any better defence then this to make; pray let me know it; and I will make it for you; if you thinke it worth while: I pray likewise tell me what I shall say to those that make you here, the Authour of three new Treatises: the first a Treatise of Goverment. (which I writ to you about in my first) the second of Toleration, (a pamphlet) and the third lesse then that of humane reason in Religion:†4 which they will need<s>†c have
― 37 ―

to be yours or els one of your disciples for the notions a<re>†a the same at the end. I have no more but hopeing that I sha<ll he>ar†aquickly from you I remaine
your most faithfull <Frein>d:†a and humble servant
J T.
I writ to you in my Last about my Lady Jones. if you could doe her any good in that businesse it would be not onely a high peice of charity but a perticular favour to my self.

1267. Edward Pococke jnr. to Locke, 18 March 1690
Dr. Paul Mellon's collection. Transcribed from photograph. For the writer see no. 542, etc.
Steventon March 18th. 1689
Honoured Sir
Being by my present circumstances confin'd alltogether to a retired life, I was so unhappy as not to receive your book till the fourteenth; which made me so backward in time, for the acknowlegement of your favour, and the return of my thanks for it. And now, that I want an apology for my own not writing sooner, I am commanded by my Father to beg your pardon for his not writing at all. I doubt not but his age and infirmitys will be a good plea to you, who are so well acquainted with them; yet he is heartily sorry that he cannot let you know what value he has for your present, but by anothers hand.
For my self Sir, I own it as the greatest obligation, that you are pleas'd†b- at any-†b time to have me in your thoughts; but shall not be able to understand how far I am indebted to you for your book, till I have perused it. But I do allready promise myself an
― 38 ―

extraordinary satisfaction and benefit, from so noble a subject handled by a person of your abilitys; of the greatness of which, though all Europe be sensible, none has a greater esteem then
Sir
Your most humble and most obliged servant
EDW: POCOCKE

1268. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 18/28 [March 1690] (1254, 1269)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 42-3. Month and year from postmark and Locke's endorsement.
28.
Deare Sir.
I perceive when I wrote you last, or rather first, I thought myself in London, but my wife would not have had it true for any mony. I did assuredly deliver your token to your friend†1 and that to John from the young lady,†2 which your squire seing askt very orderly, if there were not another kleyne Joufvrow there that would be his vryster;†3 that might send him such a present. his mother said if you will knit your friend a payre of stockins he will perhaps find one for you. Which with great joy he said he would do, for he is Arch†4 at it. Yesterday, again, as this time twelve month,†a he went to church with the mayd. When he came home we askt him what he had seen, he said een man in een grote Kackstoel,†5 we askt him what he did, he said he spake. we askt him what he said, he said he dopt†6 down in his Caekstoale and said onse Vader, so you see the first Idea he had sticks by him, and I beleeve will never be forgotten—Indeed it is shitten work, and I hope hele learn it to be such. And so much for
― 39 ―

that. next for my shitten marchant,†1 truly he is well eased, for how have I seen him come home discomposed, and crying out of those assemblyes and saying he would never stand another time. So that I suppose he was not waved for want of understanding, but for want of standing for it, tho a company of forward hot headed whigs would needs be putting him upon the trouble again, whether he would or no. But what will become of the whole gangh now? God preserve K.W. and Qu.M. from church bogs. We have strange news here of the fr: being landed in Ireland.†2 A week agoe my Lord P.†3 was coming away. But what has stayd him we know not, but in the hague he is still. Amsterdam mutters still, and alls not well, is the public discourse in the cuntry, every where save in Amsterdam it self, where they wil not suffer any man to speak about it. If you have occasion for seven thousand Swedes to your Danes, you may have them soone, there are talks of other Germans to, but how many, or whence I can heare no Certainty.†4 I am informed all the Gentlemen of the treasury goe off and others come in.†5 Dos my Lord†6 go for Ireland. There is a pernicious letter come abroad the Title, and conclusion of which seems to signify that the malitious author of it, or publisher, would have people think it mine.†7 There are divers things in it which I never thought, or spake; I am afraid the man is as angry with me, as with the goverment and ows me a mischief, as wel as the goverment and so would make to asperse it, and thereby expose me to the lash of both goverments there, as wel as here, and here as well as there, I now make the same request to you, as I have to all my Correspondents this post, that if you hear anybody lay that letter at my doore, or any other paper reflecting upon the goverment, that you wildo me the justice as to tell all men I never saw, wrote, nor heard of any such letter till I was advertisd of it this post from England and that I never wrote any paper reflecting upon the present goverment. For tho there be in that letter things said, that if they be true, I wish it were not so, yet, as I contributed
― 40 ―

nothing to it, so I cannot help it, if it be so. But must be content, and leave things to the care of those who are called to govern, onely I cannot cease to wish wel to K.W. and Q.M. and to my native cuntrye, and that seing the last Parliament so little to setle the nation, this may do it effectually, and provided it be but done I matter not who does it. my wife, and our old Gentleman†1 salute you. mr. Barker is here from Weenen;†2 coming over, Salute me to the Ladyes in your house.†3 And present my most humble service to my Lord and Lady.†4 If you do go for Germany next summer I hope youle take holland in your way and call and see us here—
Address: To Mr. John Locke at Mrs. Smithsbyes in Dorset court channel Rowe Westminster
Postmark: MR 22

1269. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 20/30 March 1690 (1268, 1270)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 44.
Rotterdam 30 March 1690
Dear Sir,
I hope you have received mine of the 28th. however having then forgot to mention some thing about Thomas Davies, and having this opportunity by Mr. Barker who raises me out of my bed; I cannot let it slip without this salutation; I have of the £30 paid me for Dr. Thomas yet f 81†a —in hands, having onely paid according to thy order ½ a years dyet f 200- and f 40 to Dr. Guenellon; His master pieter Adriaansz writes he has been forced to disburse him monies for necessaries, and to pay his french master and now he wants a new suit of clothes—And him ½ a yeare more dyet etc—so I told him I would write to thee about it. I find among my books here one folio belonging to Jeromes works which I have there—I wish it were with the rest or the rest here—Tho I know not where to wish them indeed. We are emptying our magazines apace here of all our Artillery, to help you, which makes people wonder
― 41 ―

that England should be destitute of such things,†1 and we take more care for you, then for our selves. As if we had no enemy to feare. Whereas tho, if possible England must this summer be the seat of war, yet we know not but the common enemy will press us here to. I hope the business of Amsterdam is over because my Lord P.†2 is now in good earnest going—The stories we have had of forces to go to your assistance evanish, and now its said severall have profferd, but the K: refuses to pay any more so that unless, they maybe sent on their own account you are like to have none—I dare not transgress too long on the Gentlemans patience, so must break off, with deare Lo: to your self etc
Yours
B F

1270. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 21/31 [March 1690] (1269, 1325)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 45. Month and year from Locke's endorsement.
Rotterdam 31
Dear Sir
Yesterday I was surprized with Mr Barkers calling so suddenly. after I had wrote sealed and delivered him my Letter, he desired £10 upon his bill upon his Aunt which I let him have, and have this post sent it to mr. Popple, I hope I am not deceivd in the man. He told me that all things were now well with Amsterdam and they and the Earl†2 had sit very friendly together, But the Leyden Gazette†3 tells an od story, That the Earl, understanding the Amsterdammers were in the Assembly, came to take his final leave of the<m>†a whereupon the Amsterdammers rose, and wishing him a good Voyage departed.
Just as this Gentleman was gone, in came the English post, which
― 42 ―

brought me one from that Ingenious minister of Corke,†1 how it got thence I cannot imagine, he makes a sad and lamentable complaint of the Insolencies of the french and Irish, sais they are eat up with quartering. The Rich fled, and their Estates seizd, the poore starved, and all of them like to be so. That he is now reduced from £200 to 10£ a year, and not able now, to his grief to buy any more books, and therefore must leave that Cuntry not being able to subsist there.—He sent me inclosed, which I send this post forward a Letter To Dr. Tho: Gale, Chief Master of St. Pauls School London, who he says was his Tutour in Cambridge. It is to see if he can procure him some settlement in London, or near it, where he may have the benefit of a public Library, and learned, Company.
Knowing how much kindness you have for the man I could not but mention this to you, desiring you if possible to procure him some settlement, for really he is a deserving man; I am confident you will not take it amisse that I give you the charge of this Letter upon this occasion, Mr. Barker told me yesterday that we had a new Consul†2 —whose character in part you know, but if you would have it to the full repayre to my Lodgings. The marchants seeme resolved, if they cannot finally stop it here, to keep it bearing, till they complain in Parliament of imposing or exacting taxes of free English men without Act of Parliament. But they scarce know how to begin it. I think they should first Petition the K: and Councill, and if they have no redress there, then the Parliament. But perhaps thats the way to have it concluded upon us here, by the States, pray a word—Never was consul made but at the request of the marchants that wanted them, and their salary was always allotted by the Marchants.
Address: For mr. John Locke at mrs Smithsbyes in Dorset Court channel Row Westminster
Postmark: MR 24
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 11 Mar 90

[Spreat:]
Honoured Sir
I had in the first place severall Hard Nobbs that did arise some on the Right side of my necke and one under my Right Arme, and after that, in some little distance off those Nobbs severall Clusters of little pimples full of Cleer water, the places on which those pimples arose were very Red and fiery, and very troublesome, like to the stinging of Nettles, But (all humble thankes be to your favourable directions) they with the Nobbs are all long since dissipated and Gone, And now what Remaines is a Giddinesse in my head that frequently surprizes me without the least paine and soone leaves me againe, and alsoe a trembling mist that very often comes before
― 44 ―

my eyes like as when one hath gazed on the fervent sunshine soe that I cannot distinctly discerne for some time; And I doe very often bleed at the Nose. Sir Your former prescription for me was a dyett drinke with 4 Handfulls of Ellder flowers one pound of Common Docke Roots and ½l of Dandelyon Roots put into it, which I have carefully made use of, and find it the most agreeable to me of any thing I drinke; And if you please to give your selfe the trouble of affording me your further directions touching my present case, it shalbe carefully observed and thankfully Acknowledged as the greatest of favours to your most obliged Humble servant
JO SPREAT

1276. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 4/14 April 1690 (1260, 1279)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 30-1.
Monsieur,
Vos lettres de changes sont payées et portent Cinq mille et cent livres:†1 dont je vous tiendray Compte. nous receusmes hier la belle estoffe pour ma femme, cette une nouvelle obligation dont vous la chargez, et je ne scay vrayment comment elle s'en tirera. la moindre reconnoissance qu'on tesmoigne a vos bontez, semble vous exciter a en faire davantage. et comme dans le passé jay travaillé inutilement pour vous dédommager des fraits, je luy laisseray le soin pour voir si elle tirera mieux raison de vous. Vous me faitte trop d'honneur Monsieur de me vouloir procurer un nouveau disciple. je vous ay desja dit que ce n'estoit que pour le bien de mon neveu que je m'estois engagé dans ce nouveau college medicinæ universæ, que je suis obligé de tenir en flamend pour l'amour de quelques uns qui n'entendent pas le latin. ce ne sera que cet hyver prochain que je seray au point de traitter la chirurgie, et comme la pluspart des choses sy demonstrent manuellement, si Monsieur vostre Amy est icy il me fera bien de l'honneur de s'y trouver, et je luy expliqueray ce qu'il faudra en latin. Graces a Dieu, ma practique a tellement augment<ee>†a depuis vostre depart, que ce n'est qu'avec bien de la peine que je peu donner quelques heures a ces exercices et je fais conte que ce sera pour la derniere fois. toute la famille se porte bien et vous salue. Peirot vous presente ses tres humbles respects et il na pas besoin qu'on l'excite par l'object d'une belle maistresse pour l'attirer. le souvenir quil a de vous et de tous les presents quil vous doibt luy sont assez d'engagements pour vouloir vous aller faire la reverence. nous avons mesme peine a le retenir voyant partir mon valet qui a son frere dans les gardes du corps de la Reine.†2 je le chargeray d'un mot de lettre pour vous
― 48 ―

et a fin qu'il vous dise de bouche combien nous parlons de vous. et pour vous assurer que nous sommes inviolablement
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON.
Amsterd. ce 14. Avril 1690.

1277. James Tyrrell to Locke, 6 April [1690] (1273, 1281, 1301)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 88-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.

Dear Sir
I have received both yours with the pedigree; and the rings: for which I returne you many thankes: and have given them, as I told you I would. one to Dr: B. 1. to the woeman where Dr: S. Lay. 1. to the Doctor who dissected his braine.†1 and 1. I have yet to give Dr: Musgrave an ingenious and honest yong Physitian of New Colledg who was extreme kind to Dr: S: and this I likewise dispose of by Dr: Bs: advice: but this I have not yet given because the Doctor is at present out of Towne. as for the Pedigree I not yet deliverd it because Mr: Wood is not a person to be spoke with at his chamber being allways allmost lockt up; but I have sent him a note to come and fetch it, and have allso enclosed in it as much of your last, as was neccessary†a concerneing the Doctors Grandfather;†2 whom he desired to be satisfyed about. ― 49 ―

rings nor this Ped:, whilst I stayed here. nor I beleive had you sent them; had you not met with so good an oppertunity as the hand that brought them. Dear Sir
Your most humble servant

I am glad you have received the booke.
My humble service to the Ladyes where you lye. and to worthy Mr: Clarke.

1281. Anthony Wood to James Tyrrell, 11 April [1690]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 100-1. Letter and presumed enclosure. Year from Locke's endorsements. Written in answer to a letter from Tyrrell, 10 April, no year, in which Tyrrell apologized for the scantiness of Locke's information: B.L., MS. Wood F45, ff. 63-4. Wood appears to have obtained little further information; he used the pedigree and added notices of the grandfather's education and writing, both probably from materials in Oxford; he also added a short account of the grandson: Athenæ, ed. Bliss, ii. 154-5.
[The letter:]
Ap. XI
Sir
Tis pitie that such a learned man as Mathew Slade should be lost, and therefore I desire you again to be sollicitous with mr Lock to send after him againe, when he returnes the pedigree— I am confident that he lived to the year 1628,†a when then his son Cornelius succeeded him in the rectory of the Gymnasium at Amsterdam—
Why cannot his relations search the Register of that parish, wherein the said Gymnasium stood, which is now as they say turn'd into tenements?—without doubt they have registers at Amsterdam, as in other christian countries, and it may therefore be easily knowne—
I set all writers downe accordinge to the time of their death, and unless I can meet with his, I cannot tell well where to place him.†1
Remember me to mr Lock and desire him to let me have a Catalogue of all such things whether little or great, that he hath published. If he hath seen my printed book,†2 he may know the method that I follow, and therefore he need not plead ignorance what to say of himself—
You have written somthing at the end of Archb Ushers life which you have forgot in your last to tell me†3 —
― 54 ―

I wish you a good journey, and remaine
your humble servant
A WOOD
Carry up this note with you for a memorandum.
Address: For James Tyrrell Esq.
Endorsed by Locke: A. Wood 90†a
[Enclosure. Written by Wood:]
The day and yeare of death and place of burial of the famous Mathew Slade who wrot learned books against Vorstius, with a copie of his epitaph if there be any, and names of those employments which he successively enjoyed.
qu. whether he was great uncle or grandfather to Dr Mathew Slade who died lately neare Oxon.
[Note by Tyrrell in margin of enclosure:]
Mr: Anth: Wood the Antiquary of Merton Colledg being about to write a booke of the famous men bred in this university desires you to write to Amsterdam about these queryes since he intends to insert the answere into his worke.
Endorsed by Locke: A Wood 90
1282. William Stratton to Locke, 12 April 1690 (1275, 1296)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 48.
