Dear Cosin
I did the begining of this Weake pay seventy pound to Mr Tho: Edwards of Bristoll hoe this day gave me a bill for you to Receive on ten days sight of Mr John Lilley in Cliffords Inne London, I have heare Inclosed the bill I desire that as sone as you have Rec the mony I may know it that soe I may charg it to your account, I was At Pensford thursday last hearing the widdow Shatter was theare and she hath delevered the cay to me she hath unhanged the doors within that weare hanged on hocks fowr, those that wear with Jemmalls†1 she hath left and will leave the other fowr If I will alow her 6s or 8s: now what the lawe will alow in that case I cannot tell
― 55 ―

I desire a word from you the next post and allsoe how I shall sell three lives in the House I cannot well expres the Inconveniencyes of letting a house in St Thomas Parish: ly voyd or Indeade to keep it in hand and let it at a yearly Rent, I am not without sum hops of selling it to the widdow Sanders If you will sell it for a small matter She Talkes of 20l̷: I have alowed it for 35l̷ I should be glad to sell thre lives for 30l̷ and Continew 4s Chef Rent†1 yearly but doe think she will not give 30l̷ it may be she may cum to 26l̷ or 27l̷. She will advise with her freind that lives at sum distant from her, I have given her time till penford faire then I suppose she expeckts her freind the other that ofered hoe is Mr Briddyes sonn is a littell cold in the buisnes pensford faire†2 is the 27th of this Instant, I suppose you Rec mine by my neighbour Mr: Shirborn whear I gave you sum account of the buisnes about the house, I long to see you in this Countery, it is not plesant for me to cumplaine nor for you to hear it but it is soe bad with tenants that mony can hardly be Raised I hope you continew your thoughts of cuming this summer pray let me have a loyne or two next post of direcktions about the house being all at presant I shall troble you with. I take leave
your kinsman and Humble serv:

1283. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 15/25 April 1690 (1262, 1285)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 44-5. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 306-10. Answered by no. 1285.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Postquam tuis postremis respondi, D.Consuli Hudde communicavi, quæ de Slado nostro scripsisti, quæ gratissima ipsi erant,
― 56 ―

omnemque simplici quam exhibes narratione sinistram suspicionem nullo negotio dilui posse videt. De epitaphio Virum Illustrem interpellare ausus non fui: res est hic admodum rara, et a nostris negligi solita: omnes quos consului amici dissuadent de re apud nostros exigui admodum momenti compellare Consulem, neque credunt eum hâc in re quicquam suasurum aut dissuasurum hæredibus Sladi. Quare pro more apud nos recepto epitaphio carebit, nisi amici ac consanguinei sponte eò propendeant. Verum id non tam imputandum amicis aliis, quam sorori, mulieri fatuæ, quæ, quoniam Sladus absque testamento mortuus est, ex asse hæres est; liberi itaque ejus jam nihil possunt. Male hac in parte Sladus, cui sororis indoles notissima erat, liberis illius consuluit. Verum hoc jam mutari nequit. Accessit me nuperrime Cognatus Guenellon, dixitque se ex D.d'Aranda intellexisse, amicum quendam meum tractatus cujusdam valde hic laudati autorem esse, idque fratrem D. d'Aranda ex Anglia scripsisse, quasi rem illic notissimam. Ego mirabar admodum: ille me urgebat, primo an ego autor essem? negavi. Tum porro, an nescirem amicum illum meum esse autorem? Volui quidem dissimulare: verum ita ab homine amicissimo pressus negare non potui. Hactenus autor in patria nostra nulli,
― 57 ―

nisi mihi uni cognitus fuit; imo nulla, ne levissima quidem, de ipso suspicio fuit. Nunc coram homine amicissimo, et quidem tot indiciis instructo, negare non potui; qui si postea rescivisset, merito succensere potuisset, quod hoc de viro etiam ipsi amicissimo, tam pertinaciter dissimulare, nedum negare, voluerim: Considerans ergo et intimam illius cum autore familiaritatem coram ipso ac socero ipsius autorem me scire fassus sum: obtestans maximopere, ut eadem fide, qua alia ipsis ab autore credita, etiam hoc sibi solis concreditum servent, neque ulli divulgent. Ita, quod hactenus uni cognitum fuit, tribus commune factum est. Unitas omnis multiplicationis est expers: sed quamprimum ab eâ receditur, divisæ fieri possunt multiplicationes. Ego arcanum mihi creditum, quantum possum, servabo; quod a me propalatum non est: Verum quod nunc inter tres dispersum est, facile inter plures divulgari potest; idque præcavere jam meæ potestatis non est. Verum quid si expediat autorem non latere? Nomen illius et plures lectores alliciet, et tractatui autoritatem conciliabit. Duo illi, quos memoravi, viri, audito autoris nomine, majore cum voluptate ejus lectionem repetere voluerunt: Ego singulis exemplar dedi, quod hactenus ausus non fueram; typographus mihi pauca dederat, quia correctioni
― 58 ―

præfueram. Idem pluribus eventurum præsagio: Non enim credo, licet ego fidem datam sanctissime servem, nunc celari posse, quod pluribus innotuit; et duobus amicis indicavi, quia eos Metaphysicâ meâ circumducere non potui, neque veritatem rogatus negare. Verum de hisce satis. Hactenus nullum a D.Decano Petroburgensi†1 accepi responsum: Sed nec a D.Allix, cui prolixiorem de Albigensium et Valdensium dogmatibus ac ritibus, unde illos duas fuisse diversas sectas constat, scripsi historiam, quam se accepisse ad D. Clericum scripsit: Verum verbis ita tectis, ut nomen meum exprimere non fuisse ausus videri debeat: Commendat quippe D.Clerico, ut scriptori historiæ Albigensium et Valdensium salutem dicat et gratias agat. Nescio quæ tanti timoris causa. An simili metu cohibeatur D.Decanus, cujus mihi amicitiam conciliavit D.Allix, ignoro. Hoc scio, Anglorum amicorum neminem ad literas meas declinare responsum. Nuperrime literas a D.Decano Sarisburiensi†2 accepi, eadem qua antea libertate scriptas. Quis viros hosce eruditos scrupulus urgeat ignoro. Cum hasce huc usque scripsissem, convenit me amicus noster Cyprianus, qui mihi salutem a Te dixit, prosperamque tuam valetudinem nuntiavit. Nihil mihi hoc nuntio
― 59 ―

gratius: Cum de Te tuoque statu ex illis qui Tibi adfuerunt audio, quodammodo Tibi præsens videor, suavissimamque tuam conversationem ac familiaritatem in memoriam revoco, nihilque magis mihi displicet, quam quod Oceano ab invicem dividamur. Si nunc Clivæ hæreres, ad Te incurrerem, ut eruditissimis tuis sermonibus eadem qua solitus sum voluptate fruerer: nunc grata eorum recordatione me oblecto. Interim summo cum gaudio te bene valere intellexi: Deus valetudinem hanc velit esse diuturnam. Furlæum nostrum ex quo ex Anglia rediit, non vidi. Dedit mihi præterita hebdomade D.Helmontius literas illius, quibus respondi. Opus Sancti Officii adhuc apud me est. Wetstenius adhuc cunctatur, credo ob summam chartæ caritatem. Recepit a Te Wetstenius exemplar Actorum Eruditorum anni 1688. quare summæ quam mihi debuisti detrahendi sunt tres floreni nostrates, ita ut solummodo restent f 35:8:— de quibus me brevi post Pentecostes festum, quando mihi Roterodamum excurrendum erit, cum Furlæo transacturum spero. De negotio pacificationis Ecclesiasticæ nihil jam audimus: Videtur tota illa transactio sufflaminata, et penitus abiisse in fumum. Ecclesiæ facili negotio scinduntur; scissæ vero ægerrime coalescunt. Omnes causam Christi et Ecclesiæ prætexunt: sed nisi propriam agerent, iniquas pacis conditiones non præscriberent
― 60 ―

aliis, nec æquas sibi oblatas respuerent. Deus pacis orandus, ut omnibus eam inspiret mentem, quam sibi quisque vindicat, et in alio requirit. Vale Vir Amplissime. Uxor mea liberique plurimam Tibi precantur salutem.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 25 Aprilis
 
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
After replying to your last letter I let Mr. Burgomaster Hudde know what you had written about our friend Sladus, and it gave him great satisfaction; [p. 56] he sees that the simple story as you give it is sufficient to dispel any unpleasant suspicions without difficulty. As to the epitaph, I did not venture to put the matter to the gentleman; it is a rather uncommon thing in this country, and our people do not usually trouble about it; all the friends I have consulted advise me against speaking to the burgomaster about a matter which is of very little consequence among our people, nor do they believe that he would offer Sladus's heirs any advice either for or against the suggestion. By our received custom, then, he will have no epitaph, unless his friends and relations show any inclination for it of their own accord. But the responsibility for this lies not so much on his other friends as on his sister, a silly woman, who is his sole heir, since he died intestate; so her children can now do nothing. In this respect Sladus, who knew his sister's character perfectly well, showed little consideration for her children. But that cannot be altered now. My relative Guenellon called on me the other day and told me that he had understood from Mr. D'Aranda that a certain friend of mine was the author of a certain treatise which is highly praised in this country; he said that Mr. D'Aranda's brother had mentioned this in a letter from England, as if it were a matter of common knowledge there. I was not a little surprised; he began to press me with questions: first, was I the author? I said no. He then went on to ask whether I did not know that that friend of mine was the author? I tried to prevaricate; but under such pressure from one who is a close friend I was unable to deny it. So far no one in our country [p. 57]except myself had known who the author is; indeed there was no suspicion, not even the slightest, about his identity. Now that I was confronted by such a great friend, and one furnished with so much evidence, I could make no denial; if he had come to know it later he might have been justifiably angry with me, seeing that the person concerned was also a great friend of his own, if I had persisted in evading the question, much more if I had denied my knowledge. Taking into account, then, his own familiarity with the author, I admitted before him and his father-in-law that I knew who the author is; at the same time I besought them most earnestly to keep this information strictly to themselves, as scrupulously as other matters confided to them by the author, and to divulge it to no one. So it has come about that what was hitherto known only to one person is now the common property of three. Unity can never partake of multiplicity; but as soon as unity is lost by division multiplicity may result. I for my part will preserve the secret entrusted to me to the best of my power; I have never made it public; but what is now shared by three people may easily spread to more; and to guard against that is no longer in my power. May it not be a good thing, however, that the author should not remain hidden? His name will attract more readers and will also lend greater authority to the treatise. When the two gentlemen I have mentioned heard the author's name they were eager to read the treatise once more with the increased pleasure it would give them; I gave them each a copy, which I had not presumed to do until now; the printer had given me a few because I had supervised the correction. I have a [p. 58] feeling that this will be the experience of a large number; for however conscientiously I myself may keep my given word I cannot believe that it is now possible to keep hidden what has become known to more; I may add that my reason for telling even these two friends was that my metaphysic was not equal to the task of deceiving them, and because I could not deny the truth when asked. Enough of this, however. So far I have had no answer from the dean of Peterborough;†1 nor have I heard from Mr. Allix, to whom I sent a rather lengthy account of the beliefs and practices of the Albigenses and Waldenses, from which it is evident that they formed two distinct sects; he told Mr. Le Clerc in a letter that he had received it, but in such veiled language that he must appear not to have dared to put my name on paper; thus he requests Mr. Le Clerc to give his respects to the writer of the account of the Albigenses and Waldenses and to express his thanks. I do not know what can be his reason for such timidity. For all I know the reverend dean, to whom Mr. Allix gave me an introduction, may be deterred by similar qualms. This I know, that no one of my English friends avoids answering me. I recently received a letter from the dean of Salisbury,†2 written with the same frankness as before. I do not know what the scruple can be that weighs so heavily upon these learned men. When I had written this much our friend Cyprianus came to see me; he gave me your greetings and a good account of your health. Nothing could please me more than such news. When I hear [p. 59] about you and how things are with you from people who have been with you I seem in a way to be present with you; I recall your delightful conversation and our familiar intercourse, and nothing distresses me more than the fact that we are separated from each other by the ocean. If you were now lingering at Cleves I would break in upon you, in order to take my accustomed pleasure in your scholarly talk; as it is, I comfort myself with the pleasant recollection of it. Meanwhile I am delighted to hear that you are well; God grant that your good health may long continue. I have not seen our friend Furly since he returned from England. Last week Mr. van Helmont gave me a letter from him, to which I replied. The work on the Holy Office is still in my hands. Wetstein is still delaying, I believe on account of the high price of paper. He has received from you a copy of the Acta Eruditorum for the year 1688; accordingly three Dutch gulden must be deducted from the amount you owed me, leaving only f.35:8; I hope to arrange about this with Furly shortly after Whitsun, when I have to pay a visit to Rotterdam. We hear nothing now about the business of ecclesiastical peacemaking; it seems as if the whole of that work has been brought to a halt and has utterly vanished in smoke. Churches are easily split apart; once they are split, however, it is very difficult for them to come together. All make the cause of Christ and the Church their pretext; but if they were not seeking to further their own interests they would not impose unfair conditions of peace upon others or [p. 60] reject fair ones when offered to themselves. We must pray the God of peace to inspire all alike with that mind which each one claims as his own and looks for in another. Good-bye, excellent Sir. My wife and children send you their best wishes.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 25 April
1690

(Latin) 
London April 22
Learned Sir, I received your letter of the 25th yesterday, and I was shocked on reading what you tell me had passed between you and Mr. Guenellon. I was surprised, I confess, to find that you spoke so easily, and that some here who [p. 62] have a not too friendly curiosity about me were able to fish out of you what I had hoped was deposited in safe keeping. When certain irresponsible reports, originating from those same people, were being spread in this country I was not troubled about them, as they were likely to die down soon of their own accord; you may learn from my last letter to Guenellon what I told him in answer to his inquiries about those rumours. But now that you have disclosed the writer's name they have got hold of it for certain. I will only say this: if you had entrusted me with such a secret in confidence I would never have divulged it either to a relation or to a friend, or indeed to anyone on earth, on any condition. You do not know what trouble you have got me into. All you can do now is to manage, if you can, that what you could not keep dark for yourself may now be kept dark by those other two. I have little hope of that, though; for I do not doubt that Dr. Guenellon, who was not prying so outrageously into another person's business of his own accord but at the prompting of D'Aranda, will have told D'Aranda before this letter reaches you. If you find that that is so you may spare your efforts, for you will have laboured in vain. The thing is done, and there is no remedy for it. Good-bye.
Your most obedient servant.
Endorsed in nineteenth-century hand: JL April 22 (OS) 1690

Vir Doctissime et Amplissime
Siquid in me in scribendo tardiorem tuum ullatenus peccare poterat silentium, id in novissimis tuis et elegantissimis et amicissimis literis cumulatè resarcitum est. Cave autem credas me in te adeo iniquum esse ut te vel levissimæ culpæ hac in parte insimulem. Ullas a te mihi deberi literas non sum tam vanus officii mei æstimator ut unquam agnoscam. Siquid temporis occupationibus vel studiis vel amicis tuis debitum mihi aliquando impendas, et epistolâ beas, id lucro apponam, et quas referre non potero semper habebo gratias. Laudes quibus me ornas tuâ quidem dignæ sunt eloquentiâ quæ in laudando, non tam ipsarum pretio sed suo ingenio res metiri solet, si in me eadem esset facultas amplissimam in tuis meritis reperirem materiem, quam semper suspiciam et mirabor etiamsi satis prædicare nunquam potero. Librum quem desiderasti Cave nostratis de Scriptoribus ecclesiasticis simul cum his ad te mitto. necdum honorario tuo satisfactum est, restat adhuc aliqua pars, verum cum in republica nostra literaria tam segne sit otium
― 64 ―

ut nihil plane prodeat, quod elimatum tuum non <fastidiret>†a ingenium, non ausus fui aliquem alium tractatum nuper apud nos editum huic quem petiisti adjicere, siquid autem sit quod oculis tuis dignum judicas quæso moneas, quod si non feceris quod reliquum est pecuniæ tibi numerabitur. Invenies hic inclusum fragmentum diarii antiqui Romani nuper mihi communicatum a viro illustrissimo et doctissimo Comite de Carbury.†1 quod tibi eo lubentius transmitto quod non meminerim me aliquid hujusmodi uspiam reperiisse. Quænam ex his duabus præstantior sit editio quæso mihi indices.†2 Vale vir Doctissime et ut facis me ama tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
Grævium nostrum meo nomine quæso quam officiosissime salutes et amplissimum virum Dominum Hubert†3
(Latin) 
London 25 Apr. 90
Learned and excellent Sir,
Had it been possible for your silence to be any sort of offence against me, who am the tardier correspondent, this has been abundantly made good by the grace and friendliness of your last letter. Beware, however, of imagining that I am so unjust towards you as to charge you with even the slightest fault in this respect. I have no such vain conceit of the way I fulfil my own duty as ever to admit that any letters are owing to me from you. If only you expend on me now and then some part of the time due to your affairs or studies or friends and gladden me with a letter, I shall count it as gain, and shall always be grateful even if I can make no adequate return. The praises you bestow on me are worthy indeed of your eloquence, which is accustomed to measure its objects not so much by their intrinsic worth as by its own nature; if I possessed the same gift I should find ample scope for it in your own deserts, which I shall always look up to and admire, although I could never praise them sufficiently. The book you wanted, our countryman Cave's Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Historia, I am sending you together with this letter; nor is your honorarium yet made good; there is still some of it to be paid; but such is the slothful ease now obtaining in our learned world that [p. 64] nothing at all appears that your cultivated genius would not disdain; so I have not risked adding any other treatise recently published with us to the one you asked for; if however there should be anything that you consider worth looking at, please let me know; if you do not, the balance owing shall be paid you in cash. You will find enclosed herein a fragment of an ancient Roman journal, which was recently communicated to me by that distinguished and learned man the earl of Carbery.†1 I have the greater pleasure in sending it to you because I do not remember having come across anything of the sort anywhere. Two editions of Livy in duodecimo have appeared from the Elsevier press, one of them based on Heinsius's recension of 1634 and the other on that of Gronovius of 1645. Please tell me which of these two editions is the better.†2 Good-bye, learned Sir, and continue to love me
your most affectionate
J LOCKE
Please give my kindest regards to our friend de Greve and to the excellent Mr. Hubert.†3
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Grævius professeur á Utrecht

1287. Dr. William Cole to Locke, 30 April 1690 (1290)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 195-6. William Cole, 1635-1716; M.D., Oxford, 1666; F.R.C.P. 1694; physician and medical author: D.N.B.
Worcest. Apr 30. 90
Though, Sir, I have not the good fortune to be personally known to you, yet the obligation, my honored Lord Bellomont is pleased to let me know I have to you, for your encouragement to me to remove to London, would make me inexcusable both to his Lordship and your selfe, should I not pay my acknowledgments for so undeserved a favour: and I must be no lesse should I not pay all respects to a person so much in the esteeme of my very worthy friend Dr Sydenham, whose memory I am obliged ever to honour. I wish, Sir, I durst presume to hope for the favour of a letter from you to signify when you thinke best for me to take a journey to London, in order to forming a resolution concerning such a remove: The only scruple concerning which, and which gives me the most despondency, is (and has beene for some number of yeeres) the fixed Interest of so many very great men of the Faculty; among whom I am conscious I can scarce be visible, unlesse by a reflex ray from persons in whom a more than ordinary splendor is inherent, such as is generally owned to be in you, and therfore must be beleeved by,
Sir,
Your most humble, though unknowne, servant,
WILLIAM COLE.

1288. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 2/12 May 1690 (1285, 1317)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 46-7. Answers no. 1285.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Antehac per jocum mihi minatus es, nunc vero serio te iratum video. Doleo tantum te inani indulgere suspicioni, ut rem innoxie
― 66 ―

ab amicissimis tibi hominibus gestam, dolo adscribas. Medicum a mercatore subornatum putas, ut arcanum mihi ab amico concreditum expiscaretur. In quo gravissime erras. Ut ergo scrupulum qui te misere cruciat eximam, distinctius rem prout gesta est narrabo. Medicus forte fortuna obvium sibi habuit mercatorem cum uxore†1 ambulantem: inter alios sermones familiares etiam mercator narrat, quid sibi a fratre suo scriptum sit: alter respondet, se id minime credere, quoniam nihil tale ex amico suo audiverat: Mercator asseverare, tanquam rem in Anglia notam et pervulgatam. Sic discessum est, nulla mei mentione factâ. Elapsis ab eo sermone plus quam duabus hebdomadibus medicus me accedit, occasione cujusdam a te scriptæ epistolæ, quâ me salutari jusseras, teque ad me scripturum ais. Tum inter alios sermones mihi ut rem novam narrat, quid a mercatore audiverit. Obstupui, fateor, cum id expresso nomine ex improviso narrari audirem, et admirationem simulavi. An ille aliquam in me perturbationem deprehenderit, ignoro; credo tamen: quæsivit enim, an ego autor essem? negavi. Quæsivit de amico meo: an ego non scirem illum esse autorem? hic ego eludere illum volui, sed cum eludendo satisfacere non possem, et aut aperte negandum,
― 67 ―

aut fatendum esset, hæsi aliquatenus; et cum ille adderet, mercatoris fratrem scripsisse, esse id in Anglia pervulgatum, fassus sum, tanquam homini utrique nostrum amicissimo; obtestans interim, ut inter nos contineatur, donec ad amicum meum scripsissem, ut cognoscerem, an pateretur, id quod nunc in Anglia vulgatum erat, etiam hic patefieri. Cum ædibus meis exiret, accessit socer, cui hac occasione idem innotuit. Scripsi ego quamprimum ad amicum meum, ignarus ullius quod metuebat ex evulgatione rei jam vulgatæ periculi: Sed et interea medicus scripserat, quid ex mercatore audiverat: responsum quod nactus est mihi communicat: inde vidimus amicum rem, quæ jam vulgata dicebatur, occultam velle. Itaque ille mercatorem, quem interea temporis non viderat, adit; dicit, rumorem illum esse falsum, se ad amicum suum scripsisse, illum vero hunc suum fœtum minime agnoscere. Nihil exinde cum mercatore actum. Quantæ facilitatis accusandus sum, tuo permitto judicio. Cum res esset recens, et a pluribus auctor quæreretur, plus quam centies, imo ausim dicere ducenties, amicos et familiares meos elusi, qui me præsente de autore inquisiverunt, meque de autore interrogarunt, præsertim cum mei ordinis aliquis esse crederetur:
― 68 ―

Neque hactenus ullus fuit, cui vel levissima suspicio oborta fuerit de autore. Quod nunc eum fassus sim coram duobus amicissimis, merum fuit infortunium, quod subita illa narratione obstupefactus, ita me continere non potuerim, quin aliqua perturbationis indicia in me deprehensa sint, et sic tergiversatione eludere non potuerim. Aliud est, quando ab absente per epistolam quid quæritur, et deliberandi ac meditandi spatium est; aliud quando præsenti subito est respondendum, et quando ex responsione alia enascitur quæstio, cui denuo est satisfaciendum. Doleo hunc incidisse casum; præsertim cum audiam, ex evulgatione amico aliquod imminere periculum, cujus incommoda meo damno, si possem, redimere cuperem. Sed si negassem, quod salva sinceritate ac veritate Christianâ non potui, quo ore compellassem eos, qui id jam vulgatum mecum credebant, et quibus responsione illa elusoria, quæ epistola continetur, minime satisfactum fuisset, quique ex perturbatione mea aliquid colligebant, quod rem aliis vulgatam, coram se utrique amicissimis aperte negarem, meque mendacio obstringerem? Attamen si omnia prævidissem et præmeditari potuissem, ut omnem ab amico meo suspicionem amoverem, potius me autorem nec fassus fuissem, nec
― 69 ―

negassem, ut sic ego creditus autor omnem quæ de amico concepta erat suspicionem, in me derivassem. Vides, Vir Amplissime, nihil hic factum dolo, sed curiositate innoxiâ, quâ medicus sibi plaudebat, id, quod maxime probabat, ab amicissimo sibi homine profectum. Interim non est quod metuat amicus noster, medicos id vulgaturos, præsertim lecta postrema amici mei jurgatrice epistola: nec etiam nunc, prout in initio, illius vulgandi occasio est: quia nunc vix ulli amplius de ea re hic sermones sunt; nec hi sermones nunc incidissent, nisi vir ille, cujus res agitur, nobis amicissimus fuisset. Quod circa alios locum non habet. Et si forte aliquis ex eodem rumore quid audiat, et nos roget, dicemus, rumores illos etiam nobis auditos, sed amicum nostrum a nobis ea de re consultum, eum minime pro suo agnoscere. Interim culpam deprecor, et doleo hoc inopinato casu aliquid viro mihi amicissimo contigisse ingratum. Adeo me affecit epistola tua, ut noctem insomnem duxerim, nec nisi amicum meum placatum noverim quietus esse possim. Narravi jam candide rem prout gesta est; quicquid amicus meus a me exegerit præstabo: illud unum effice, ne ob rem adeo ex incidenti et præter opinionem imprudentius tractatam, frigus aliquod in amicitia oboriatur. Cogitet, arcani conscios esse homines ipsi amicissimos,
― 70 ―

quorum pluribus documentis ipsi probata amicitia et fidelitas, quibusque amici sui salus cordi est. Plura non addam, ne candidissimi amici amori diffidere videar. Hæc per primum tabellarium mox ad te scribere volui, ut omnem, quo gravissime angitur amicus meus, metum animo ejiciat suo. Vale Vir Amplissime et amicissime, meque crede eundem esse qui semper fui
Tui sincero cordis affectu amantissimum
PHILIPPUM A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 12 Maji
 
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
You have previously threatened me in jest; now, however, I perceive that you are seriously angry. I am sorry that you should indulge so far in groundless [p. 66] suspicion as to find guile in what was done in all innocence by some of your greatest friends. You suppose that the doctor was put up by the merchant to fish out of me a secret entrusted to me by a friend. In that you are seriously mistaken. In order, then, to relieve your mind of the trouble that is distressing you I will give you the story of the affair just as it happened in clearer terms. The doctor happened by chance to meet the merchant as he was taking a walk with his wife;†1 in the course of familiar talk about various things the merchant also mentioned what his brother had said in his letter; the other replied that he could not believe it, as he had heard nothing of the sort from his friend; the merchant asserted it positively as a matter of common knowledge in England. With that they parted, my name not having been mentioned. More than a fortnight after this conversation the doctor came to see me on account of a letter of yours, in which you had sent me your greetings and said that you would be writing to me. Then amongst other things we talked about he told me, as a piece of news, what he had heard from the merchant. I was dumbfounded, I confess, at hearing this so unexpectedly with the name given outright, and I pretended surprise. Whether he noticed any signs of perturbation in me I cannot say; but I think he did; for he asked me whether I was the author; I said I was not. He then asked about my friend: did I not know that he was the author? I wanted to evade his question; but having no success in that way, and being faced with the necessity of either [p. 67] denying it outright or admitting it, I was baffled for the moment; and when he added that the merchant's brother had said in his letter that the thing was generally known in England I admitted it, considering that he was a close friend of us both; meanwhile I begged that the information might be kept to ourselves until I had written to my friend to know whether he would allow what was now common knowledge in England to be disclosed here as well. As he was leaving my house his father-in-law joined us, and so he came to know it too. I wrote to my friend as soon as possible, having no idea what danger he could fear from the disclosure of a matter that was already well known; but in the mean time the doctor had also written to tell him what he had heard from the merchant; he gave me the contents of the answer he received, from which we realized that our friend wished that the matter which was said to be now generally known should be kept secret. Accordingly he went to the merchant, whom he had not seen in the intervening time, and told him that the report was false; he had, he said, written to his friend; but that friend was by no means willing to acknowledge the production as his own. The matter has not been discussed with the merchant since then. How far I am to be accused of pliability I must leave to you to judge. When the matter was still fresh, and when many people were seeking to know who the author was, on more than a hundred, I might say two hundred occasions I eluded the inquiries of friends and relations who raised the question in my presence and asked me about the author, especially as he was believed to be some one of my own calling; nor so far was there anyone [p. 68] who had even the slightest suspicion about the author. That I have now admitted it in the presence of two close friends was a simple misfortune; I was so dumbfounded by the story being suddenly sprung upon me that I could not control myself sufficiently to avoid giving some signs of confusion, so that I could not escape by subterfuge or evasion. It is one thing when one is asked a question in a letter by someone who is not there, so that there is time for thought and consideration; it is quite another when one has to give an answer to someone face to face on the spur of the moment, and when that answer gives rise to another question, which must be satisfied by yet another answer. I am sorry that this accident should have happened, especially when I hear that my friend is threatened with some danger as a result of the disclosure; I should be only too glad, if I could, to relieve him of such trouble at any cost to myself. But if I had said 'no', which I could not have done except at the cost of sincerity and a Christian regard for truth, how could I have looked those people in the face who believed, as I did, that the knowledge was now common property, and who would never have been satisfied with the sort of evasive answer that might be given in a letter; and who would have inferred from my confusion that in thus openly denying knowledge of a thing generally known to others, and denying it before themselves who were good friends of us both, I was guilty of a falsehood? All the same, however, if I had foreseen everything and been able to take thought, in order to remove all suspicion from my friend I would have chosen rather to say neither 'yes' nor 'no' when asked whether I was the author, that so I might be [p. 69] believed to be the author and thus divert to myself any suspicion that had been formed about my friend. You see, excellent Sir, that there was no question of guile in what took place, but only of innocent curiosity on the part of the doctor, who was delighted to think that a work he approved of so highly was the product of one who was a great friend of his own. Meanwhile our friend has no reason to fear that the doctors will spread the information abroad, especially after reading my friend's last objurgatory letter; and in fact there is no such occasion to do so now as there was at the beginning, because there is now hardly any more talk about the matter, nor would there have been any on the present occasion if the person concerned had not been our closest friend. There is not the same reason for others. And if anyone should by chance hear anything of the report and should ask us about it we will say that we too have heard those reports, but that we have consulted our friend on the matter and he definitely does not acknowledge the work as his own. Meanwhile I beg forgiveness for my fault, and I am sorry that this unforeseen accident should have given such a friend any cause for displeasure. I was so powerfully affected by your letter that I passed a sleepless night, nor can I enjoy any peace of mind till I know that my friend is pacified. I have now frankly told the story of the affair just as it happened; I will make whatever amends my friend may demand of me; this one thing I beg: do not let there be any cooling of our friendship as a result of my somewhat imprudent behaviour in so sudden and unexpected an emergency. Let him reflect that the persons sharing the secret are his warmest friends, who had given him [p. 70] many proofs of their friendship and loyalty, and who have the well-being of their friend at heart. I will say no more, lest I should seem to doubt the affection of my open-hearted friend. I have hastened to send you these lines by the first post, that so my friend's mind may be entirely relieved of the fears that so grievously distress him. Good-bye, excellent Sir and my very good friend, and believe me to be the same that I have always been
In all sincerity of heart your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 12 May
1690

1289. R. Vincent to Locke, 10 May 1690
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 27-8. I cannot identify the writer.
May 10 1690
Sir,
I am one of those, who have read over more then once your Incomparable Book, with extraordinary Satisfaction and Improvement. I wish, I had the happiness to be as well acquainted with The Author. I should thereby find a means to draw greater advantage to my selfe and others, from the favor I am going to ask of you, in their behalfe as well as my own. A favor, Sir, which if I am not much mistaken in your Book, you your selfe will not deny me. In
― 71 ―

short, I have an unhappy freind or two, who have plung'd themselves into Deism, and even into Atheism it selfe; you may remember, how invincibly you have proved, even equall to Demonstration, The <Ex>istence†a of God; lib. 4. cap. 10. You have also <sh>ewn,†a how reasonable and secure it is, to give the Highest assent to Divine Revelation. ibid. cap. 16. But I cannot find, that you have any where found it in your way to prove, that there is a Divine Revelation.†1 This They deny; and call upon me to prove. I have by your help beaten them off from Their Innate Ideas, and their Universal principles, borrowd from my Lord Herbert,†2 etc. I have also endeavord at a positive proof of Divine Revelation which to me seems Conclusive, and which I will (with your permission) submit to your Judgment; and do humbly intreat you, for charity's sake, to let me know, if it be sufficient. Tis This. 1 There is a God (this they Grant)
2. He ought to be Worshipt. (this they also grant)
3. He is Obliged to shew, How he will be Worshipt. (because of our Distance and Incapacity to find out what should please him)
4. Therefore, he has Done it; I mean He has shewn, how. (Else he would be Wanting to himselfe, which he Cannot be)
5. This shewing How, is what we mean by, Divine Revelation.
This, Sir, is The proof which I offer, after I have taken away theyr refuge of Idéas and results of reasoning; which they would make to be all The Revelation there is. Now, That of Ideas being but Imaginary, that other of my Lord Herberts, being uncertain, and far from Universal, we must look further for such a Revelation; and then, it will not be hard to give the precedency to The Christian, against all other pretenders.
This, Sir, I desire you to tell me, if it be sufficient, or wherein you think it faulty.
But I should be more Obliged, if you Could awhile to give me one of Your Own. That would do the Deed. You need not be long about it; I should take the strength of it, from a very few hints or stroaks. Only, Bring it in, with telling me, What kind of p<roof>†a You think it Capable of; and let yours be an Inst<ance>†a of it.
― 72 ―

Sir, If you shall please to Oblige us, in this matter; you may make the paper up like a letter, and send it by the penny poast, with This Direction, for Mr Vincent, to be left with Mr Green, a Goldsmith, at The Three Blew Bals, in S. Martins lane, And it will Come most acceptable to,
Sir, Your most obliged and most obedient servant.
R.V.
Address: For Mr Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: Vincent 10 May 90
1290. Dr. William Cole to Locke, 18 May 1690 (1287, 1299)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 197-200. In view of the technical nature of a large part of the letter I have not tried to explain most of Cole's obsolete or unusual words.
Worcest. May 18. 90.
Sir,
I am sorry the indispensable occasions of my profession should have kept me abroad so long as they have done, to hinder me from receiving, and consequently sooner returning thanks for, and an answer to, your very obliging letter (having not beene three whole dayes at home these three weekes till this) and that they rob me of the satisfaction of paying my acknowledgments personally so soone as I would, these countries growing more sickly than they have a good while beene, and therfore hindring me a while from pursuing your advice of a more speedy repaire to London. Indeed I doubt the reason you please to urge for the sodainness of it can have but little influence on my affaire, viz. the Session of Parliament;†1 since there are very few of the members of it that I have so great an Interest in, that I can eyther take the confidence to addresse to for their mention of me upon a removall, or hope for an effectuall recommendation from: But there are severall that, having beene my Patients in the Country, now live in London, whose kindnesse in that particular I thinke I could more rely on; severall of whom have heretofore urged my removall thither; and kindnesse frequently flowing more from extrinsick and accidentall motives than desert, I may perhaps hope the more for it, since I am conscious I have a very small pretence to the latter.
― 73 ―

To come to the latter part of your letter: first, I am very sorry, Sir, you are under the indisposition and apprehensions it intimates; and next that my acquaintance with you should commence so late. But the honour you doe me in vouchsafing to aske my thoughts is too great, when you are in a place where are so many great men of the Faculty, from whom you cannot faile to receive much more ample satisfaction; though, give me leave to say, I cannot thinke you need it: for I have beene informed that your owne studyes in Physick have beene such, as to make you as great a Judge in it as any man. However, to shew my deference (if you'll please to pardon the tediousnesse, and perhaps impertinency, of my answer) I adventure to obey you.
To the first of your questions. Though I have not perhaps made so narrow a scrutiny into the Expectorations of most of my phthisicall patients, as to determine accurately whether they were truly purulent, yet some I can be positive I have had under my care who have so voided perfect Pus and yet recovered. To Instance; There is a Gentleman, who most Termes goes to London, an Attorney living at Tewxbury, by name Mr Bulstrode (sonne to Sir Richard Bulstrode I thinke)†1 of Clement's Inne so farr as I remember; who severall yeeres since was in a Phthisis, judged (by his usuall Physitian, as well as my selfe who was called in) deplorable; but, after a long discharge of perfectly purulent matter, recovered, and has for many yeeres since had no touch of it. And being accidentally two dayes agoe at a place where lives a laborious man that above five yeeres since consulted me on a like score, I (to refresh my bad memory, that I might answer your question the more satisfactorily) discoursed him againe particularly. He had for about four yeeres before that time had great symptoms of a confirmed Phthisis; but at the time he, as I said, consulted me, his expectoration was perfectly purulent, and so fœtid, that twas very offensive both to himselfe and others. Expectorating thus for above three moneths, he by degrees at last recovered and againe followed his busynesse well (being by profession a Tanner) as he does still; only to this time he has, he tells me, every night one great fit of coughing, and expectorating, but what he brings up now is more like (by his description) mucus narium, than pus.
To trouble you with no more Instances, but come to your
― 74 ―

second question concerning the remedy, or method, I rely on for curing those who expectorate true Pus,
First. I thinke tis too like a pretender to the Philosophers stone, or a Mountebanke to talke of one Medcine to cure almost any disease, much more such a one as a Phthisis: Since as there is none but may be so circumstantiated (by different constitutions of persons, age, seasons of the yeere, time of the distemper, etc.) as to make it necessary to respect several indications, not to be satisfyed by one medcine, so particularly this has those difficulties above most others, that tis impossible but that one medcine, though appropriated to heale the Ulcer, must be interrupted in its designe. Therfore in the second place
I conceive a due method is that which ought to be insisted on†1 to remedy it: And that which I propose to my selfe may be the following, and upon such grounds as these which at present occurre to my thoughts.
I suppose the Phthisis pulmonaris (the case under consideration) to begin from a too great inteneration of the habit of the Lungs (made up of numerous vesiculæ, and exceeding small glandules, to all parts of which the sanguiferous vessells reach) whether this proceed from the ill crasis†2 of the bloud, or nervous liquor, moving continually eyther through or to them, to which the detained effluvia (the effect of what wee call taking Cold) usually conduces; or from inevitable outward injuries of the aire, as tis known some countries are more subject to them than others, as well as to severall other determinate distempers. This inteneration must, after some time, occasion a congestion in them; both the bloud and nervous juyce (from which last I conceive all parts have even the matter of their nourishment, though perhaps you'll looke on this notion as very paradoxicall) being continually, though each with a much different degree of motion, and to different ends, carried to them. Afterwards the tone of them, or such part of them where the congestion happens, comes to be so weakned, that not only they cannot assimilate what they ought for their proper nourishment, but moreover from the hence acquired opennesse of their secretory vessells or proper pores, and the indesinent motion of the bloud, they come to discharge much more than what is by natures designation (of which the due proportion of all the vessells
― 75 ―

is both the measure and the signe) fit, wherby tis evident a contabescence of the whole body must follow. Hence in time these parts may come to have the texture of their constituent stamina so loosned at their extremities, as no longer to be able to resist the continuall appulse of their contents, but be at length dissolved: And thence these liquids (otherwise good and fit for nourishment) must passe forth into the cavities of the vesiculæ, destined only for the reception of ayre, and extromission of the continually expiring halitus, where it comes to be digested into that substance we call Pus; which perhaps, by the admixture of the fermenting particles of the Ayre, continually brought to it, grows so acrimonious, as, continuing to disorder the tone of those parts, totally to corrupt them. Though much of the matter of the excretion before Exulceration be the same with this purulent (though not all; for I suppose that the greatest part of the grosse excerned pituita is immediately secerned from the bloud in the glandillæ pulmonares, distended on the forementioned score, by their secretory ducts, which without doubt all glandules have; and even in the most purulent discharge much of this still comes away too) yet as tis obvious it differs afterwards much in Forme, so I consider (pardon the excursion, which yet helpes me, by conceiving a modus fiendi, to forme a notion in my selfe towards the cure) that it may be on this score it does so; viz. That one of these substances, the difference betweene which consists only in the contexture of their particles, has a Colature to make it what it is, and to separate it from some other which must diversify it; wheras the other is, upon erosion or laceration of the vessells, effused through free and patulous passages, in its whole substance; The one has no admixture (perhaps) of the aire (at least of but a small quantity of it) except by the usuall course of its admission, viz. by the way of distribution of the nourishment from the stomack into the lactealls, then into the bloud, and afterwards through the braine into the nerves, and thence into their ramifications which I take to be all Tubuli, and to make up the whole habit of the body, except some parenchyma which must necessarily goe to fill up the triangular interstices of them; the other has it immediately and copiously admixed with it in the Lungs, and thence must become much altered. Withall I conceive the intentions toward a cure must be different; The parts, in the former case, needing only a contraction to exclude what is congested in them, and thence to returne to their due tone; but in the
― 76 ―

latter, the losse of the substance of the part being to be repaired before a stop (at least a full and effectuall one) can be put to the production of the purulent matter; which indeed must be very hard to be effected since all that is to doe it must fetch so vast a circuit, and, let the medcines be ever so fitted for it, be much refracted in passing so long a tract, and mixing with so many active as well as very differing substances in the liquors that are to be their vehicle: adde, that a very small part of what is taken can reach the part, passing to it through so comparatively few (upon my alledged supposition of nutrition by the nerves and their productions) and very strait vessells.
So that as there is little ground for a very safe prognostick in such indispositions, even when they are but newly begun, so tis, I conceive, only a good method that is to be relyed on to effect the cure; which though difficult yet I account not impossible. For though the continuall motion of the Lungs and the rapid one of the bloud through them (which is the usuall suggestion toward a fatall prognostick) make the consolidation†a the more difficult, especially upon violent coughing; yet, if my notion (which one time or other perhaps I may farther consider) concerning nutrition, and consequently reparation of exulcerated parts, be true, I am not (at present) convinced that this (provided the sanguiferous vessells be not so broken or eroded as to let out quantities of bloud in specie) must have the supposed fatall influence upon those (more properly perhaps to be called) constituent parts of the Lungs; since that motion belongs not to them as such, but collectively as a great Organ; and the motion of each of these ultimate vessells seems but a kind of moderate vibration (if the coughing be not very violent) though not very likely indeed to corroborate their tone, yet scarce (necessarily) to destroy it.
But, not to trouble you, Sir, longer with these too confused speculations, which the frequent intervention of unavoidable busynesse will not permit me at present better to digest; and which indeed I should dread to offer to you, who (unlesse I am much misinformed) are so accurate a Master of Notion, and in Physick as well as other Sciences; The Method I propose to my selfe for rectifying, when possible, these disorders, consists in a Due adaptation of medicall administrations, and Diet.
As to the Former; First, If there be any feaverish indisposition,
― 77 ―

as there usually is, or the bloud be acrimonious, I conceive moderate Phlebotomy must be usefull, both to correct that, and allay the too briske motion of it through the Lungs, and withall to give the distended parts, by that diminution of the quantity, opportunity to contract themselves, and so to extrude what was oppressive to them: all parts of our body having naturally a tention, and thence a tendency to contraction, but more upon some morbifick occasions. Which evacuation might therfore be now and then repeated. And the argument of the timorous against it, from a debilitation like to ensue, cannot influence me, unlesse I could be convinced that the taking away so small a proportion as 12 or 16 ounces out of (perhaps) 18 or 20 pound of bloud could much depresse the sanguifying power in the rest, when I thinke tis obvious that every thing we eat and drinke wants but little of the perfection of bloud before it gets into the stomack, or at least into the veines; all being highly fermented eyther by nature or art, and may be supplyed ad libitum; and the observation of those, who have recovered after excessive profusions of it, may convince that a smaller remainder than can be heere objected, is sufficient.
Next if the first concoction be not good, and the stomack appeare oppressed, twill, I conceive, be necessary gently to cleanse it eyther with some such puke as oxymel scyllit, or sal vitrioli, etc. to be repeated after there is a signe of a fresh congestion (which the opening of the secretory ducts in the stomack by one vomit must, I conceive, occasion; though the effect may be good, viz. the draining the bloud in some measure by that meanes) and if this were done now and then (without too great a concussion of the Lungs) it might possibly be very available; or else by some gentle cathartick of which authors have variety. But if there be no, or not much, disaffection at the stomack, I see not what great indication there is of such administrations, which may possibly in such case both disorder the tone of it, and, by being farther admitted, put the bloud or other juyces into greater disorder than before they had.
But then for more appropriate medcines, respecting more particularly the Ulcer, and other symptoms; First I am afraid the great (however authenticated) use of relaxing ones, as the usuall pectorall drinks, lambitives. etc. does commonly more hurt than good in the degree of the Phthis<is>†a (at least) your question relates
― 78 ―

to. For by that effect they seeme likely to hinder the closing of the Ulcer, which requires drying administrations. Indeed in a marasmus, in which the body is beyond natures designation too dry, they may be necessary, since their influence may be greater on the rest of the body than the Lungs, to which (however it must be owned that the bloud, and with it all admitted substances, passes through them in circulation) a small part only reaches effectually, i.e. by the vessells designed for their nutrition, and other proper functions. And withall perhaps they may be somtimes usefull to helpe expectoration, where much glutinous matter sticks in the vesiculæ: not, that I can imagine by sliding downe the Trachæa, nature forbidding any thing but ayre or substances admixed with it to passe that way, but by being brought by the course of circulation to them: and my Tanner (before mentioned) found much reliefe by Lucatellus's balsame,†1 which he long insisted on every night; though perhaps that effect may be accounted for from the abstersive and sanative operation of the Turpentine in it.
But in their stead I conceive that decoctions of (the heavy) China,†2 or the santala,†3 (made gratefull, but not clogging, by the addition perhaps of raysins or the like) may be insisted on, which having some stypticity, not easily destructible by cocture, but rather extricable only by it, may inter circulandum, by continuance, possibly be presumed to reach the parts needing that assistance: on which score the Vulneraries, as sanicle, hedera terrest. bugula, etc. may be supposed to act; but these, I conceive, should be rather used in infusion like Tea (or fermented with small ale) than decoction, since the texture of their chiefly operative parts being more tender may be presumed easily dissipable, wheras the compactnesse of the roots and woods requires cocture.
On the same score I lay much stresse on the Cortex Peruvianus, and have for severall yeeres past seene considerable effects of it in Phthisicall persons: For I conceive it to produce its effect (and as well here as on agues) by a kind of Stypticity (and I hope I may one time or other have the good fortune to aske your opinion concerning some papers I have drawn up concerning the reason of its effects in agues) and I lately find Dr Morton†4 relyes much upon it. I give it to ʒi (plus, minùs) twice or thrice a day, and after it decoctions of
― 79 ―

China, or infusions of some of the vulneraries sweetned (but not more than needs) with syr. balsami Tolutani, or other gratefull edulcorants, or other liquids that the stomack will beare, particularly to some a fermented infusion of absynt. centaur. agrimon. and pass. solis add. flor. cerevisiæ in water.
But besides, I conceive that Balsamicks may be very usefull to the proposed intention; since the particles of them being of a gummous nature (on which score decoctions of guaiacum, celebrated by some Authors, may produce their effect) may prove in some degree emplastick as they reach the part; and as they circulate with the bloud through the Lungs may possibly deposite some of their particles into the vesiculæ, where, even by an external application they may contribute to close the ulcerated parts, as well as others of them may get into the very tracts of them the usuall way of their admitting their juyces. And heere is one phthisicall patient of mine in towne, who though farre gone (though I cannot be positive his expectoration was purulent) and irregular ynough, was first managed with the cortex P. a good while twice a day, and opiats at night to give rest; but now (tired with them though he mended upon them) takes only, and has done for severall weeks, at bedtime a spoonfull of a mixture of balme of Gilead ℥ss with syr. bals. Tol. ℥iiij, which agrees, facilitates his expectoration, and lengthens his breath, and he seemes neere recovered beyond my expectation.
Opiats you'll owne, Sir, necessary to be taken, at bedtime at least, if the cough be, as you know it generally is, in the night troublesome, or the patients are subject to a diarrhœa; upon the reason of which I need not expatiate. And I had a few yeers agoe a Gentleman to my patient, whose grand support for 3 or 4 yeeres, as I remember (togither with a milke dyet and bochet)†1 was a good dose, (somtimes the quantity of a nutmeg somtimes two or more) of the following Electuary (prescribed him I thinke by Dr Short)†2 usually at bedtime when he needed it, but indeed at any other time when much inclined to coughing. ℞ cons ros. rub. ℥iij. diascord ℥iij. Laud. Lond. gr. x. syr. symphiti, q.s. F.Elect. His expectorations were evidently purulent, and he told me they had beene so for severall yeers before he became my patient, which he was by
― 80 ―

intervalls about 2 yeers before he dyed. I give frequently (for change) pil. Mathæi, e styrace, or laud. liq.
The great Mr Boyle mentions, I remember, a Physitian who cured many phthisicall patients with the fume of flos sulphuris:†1and though I can light on few or none that will use it, at least regularly, yet it seemes to me one of the most proper administrations, in regard fumes only act immediately on the part heere affected, which needing exiccation†2 and constriction, this and one seems most likely to prove effectuall, the person accustoming himselfe to it by degrees that it prove not too irritating, which perhaps at first it may if that caution be not observed. The time of the day for using it I propose to be in the morning, after the free anacatharsis, the disaffected parts being then most empty and so best yielding to the energy of the medcine. If the fumes of sulphur agree not, at least that of succinum may probably be usefull. Bals. sulph. terebinthi nat. mixed with sacch. candum (gut. xx. bals circiter ad ℥i sacch) I oblige many to hold in their mouths frequently letting it gently dissolve for the sake of the odour.
More administrations to this end I suppose superfluous to urge to you, Sir, who know where to find them all. Only give me leave to remark on one very celebrated. viz. Fontanells, which I seldome urge; since I cannot see what good such loopholes in the skin, which discharge nothing Electively, can doe, and are rather too like the ulcer they are proposed to heale than a remedy for it, and may perhaps helpe a man faster toward his journeys end by contributing to discharge more of the alible juyce, when too much still goes off at the lungs. Indeed those who find advantage (upon cleere and distinct reasoning) should continue them, and may speculate upon it.
As to Dyet: I conceive, Flesh, and even the broth of it, keepe up febricitation in the bloud; but if any, you will allow me, Sir, to like to propose that of the youngest sort, and tenderest substance; but particularly calves feet seeme to me some of the fittest, as being least stored with active and exagitating parts (as the muscular flesh is) but most adhæsive, as snailes likewise are supposed to be. But I rather think a whole milke dyet, or at least for the greatest part, (grewell, milk-porridge, flummery, or the like being somtimes
― 81 ―

allowed) if twill agree, to be the best; which besides that it leaves least of excrement, and gives the ferment of the stomack little or no trouble to digest it, and by reason of its softnesse may readily be admitted into any vessells; may also convey in many of the sanative particles of the herbs (and perhaps more now in the spring and summer than at other times of the yeere) and so prove both meate and medcine.
I am sure, Sir, you expected not so long an answer to your letter, (which had come at least one Post sooner, but for a fresh interruption then) neyther did I designe to have beene a quarter so tedious when I began to put pen to paper, and am very much to beg your pardon that I trouble you with so many speculations, which I doubt you'll thinke rather shew my ignorance than true judgment upon the questions. However since you have beene pleased to ask my thoughts, I conceive you are obliged in some degree to excuse the impertinence of the answer. But I beseech you believe me,
Sir,
Your most humble, and faithfull servant
WILLIAM COLE

1292. Dr. Charles Goodall to Locke, 21 May 1690 (1137, 2055)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 27-8. Printed by K. Dewhurst in Review of the History of Medicine, xvii (1962), 497.
London May 21. 1690
Deare Sir
I heartily begge your pardon that I have not long since returned my thanks and answer to your last; the truth is, my wife hath been so ill lately, and now being at Hogsden,†2 I have been so engaged that I wanted an oppertunity to do it, till now. I know that you are so much Master of our profession, that I can offer litle which may be more servicable to you, then what you already know; Neither can I pretend any thing extraordinary in your case, I thinke that Countrey aire, diet, and attending symptoms are of greatest use, though I know some particular medicines are not a litle recommended by Authors, whether deservedly or no, I cannot tell. Bals. [sulphuris] Anisat. Terebinth. Syrup. Dyasulp etc are good medicines, if not contraindicated by the Fever which generally accompanies this distemper, and perhaps indicate<s>†a now and then gentle bleeding, and the frequent use of the cortex. Dr Morton doth highly commend the following pills.
℞. pulv. Milleped. prep.†b ʒiij. Gum Ammoniac optime depurat. ʒiss flor. Benzoin ʒj. Extract croc. bals. Peruv. an   ss. Bals
― 83 ―

[sulphuris] Terebinth. vel Anisat q.s.m. f. pil.mediocr. deaurand. vel pulvere glycyrrh. involvend. cap. iij ter in die e cochl. Syr. vel linctus alicujus convenientis superbibend. haust. Apozematis†a pectoral. calidè†1
The Doctor hath wrote an admirable book de phthisi, which if you have not read, tis highly worth your reading and considering. and if you will appoint any day when you will dine with me about 2 of the clock, you may have a<n>†b oppertunity to discourse the Doctor after dinner.
Be pleased to write me word where I may wait upo<n>†b Mr Furly, or how I may settle a correspondency with him about the Iron spaw waters,†2 you will herein very much oblige
your faithfull Freind and servant
CH: GOODALL

1293. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [25 May/4 June 1690?] (1235, 1294)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 67. Toinard apparently wrote to Locke three letters about the same time, one addressed to Leers for forwarding, one to Wetstein for forwarding, and one, dated 25 May/4 June 1690, direct to Awnsham Churchill: no. 1295, the Churchill letter. From its contents and the remains of its date no. 1294 is the Wetstein letter. The contents of no. 1293 suggest that it is the Leers letter. It appears to be slightly earlier than the others. It is possible, however, that there were only two letters, no. 1293 being enclosed in no. 1295, which would have been sent to Leers to forward to Churchill.

Comme je scay que vous vous interessez dans tout cequi me regarde, je vous diray que je me dispose à partir dans peu pour

Paris,†1 quoique malheureusement je puisse dire avec feu mr ciceron: Credas velim mihi majori offensioni esse quàm delectationi, possessiunculas meas.†2 Ad Attic. Lib. XIII. avec cete diference qu'au lieu de delectationi, je metrois commodo; car pour avoir un peu plus de bien que je n'en avois otrefois, je suis devenu de pire condition.
J'ecris à l'ocasion de cet in 4°†3 à mssrs Leers et Westin, etant rezolu de traiter de mon ouvrage†4 avec quelque Imprimeur etranger, si une tentative que je dois faire à Paris ne me reüssit pas. Il y a desja du tems que vous m'ofrites de vous emploier pour cela envers l'un ou l'otre de ces messieurs, mais je vous diray qu'ordinerement ils ne donnent que des exemplaires, et que du papier ne m'acommode pas. Le tout est bien rectifié dans une seule copie.

1296. William Stratton to Locke, 29 May 1690 (1282, 1297)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 49.
Sutton the 29th May 1690
Dear Cosin
I have hear Inclosed sent you a lease which I desire you would seale and return it by Mr Thomas Edwards hoes lodgings are at Cliffords In his wife expeckts him home whitson eve†2 I have sent it by the carrier that soe it may cum Back safe and spedylie, I dout not but my worthy freind will bring it, the lease will be In London twesday I hope he will not cum from London till Wednesday I am willing to have it back as spedy as may bee not knowing how the lives may stand that soe there may be noe diference, the Widdow sanders is substanciall I dout not, she and her sonn is to be securyty for the mony and to pay it all about the 24th of June but I gave her liberty to stay till micalmas for one halfe if she would pay the other halfe At sealing Ither way I dout not but is safe, I had sumthing to doe to bring it to the price and had she not feared whear noe fear was I should not have had soe mutch, I have brought her to a herriot which I did not understand that ever any was paid before
― 87 ―

it was the best terms that I cold make I hope you will accept it my Wife presents her servise to you I take leave
Your Faithfull Kinsman and Humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
Endorsed by Locke: Stratton 29° May 90
1297. William Stratton to Locke, 30 May 1690 (1296, 1343)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 50.
Sutton the 30th: may 90
Dear Cosin
the same hand that Carried a lease to the london carrier for you to seale which is a grant to the widdow sanders of Shatters house as you will find by the contence hath brought me back your letter,†1 for I was In expecktation of the mesenger to bring me direcktions that soe I might direckt you wheare to send for the lease, two resons why I was desireous why the lease should be dispatched back was first that mr Thomas Edwards of Bristoll might bring the lease hoe I hope will not be cum forth of london before you seale it he is my worthy freind and will bring it for nothing his Chamber is at cliffords Inne In London his wife expeckts him home Whitson Eave the second reson is when the lease is sealed and the widdow hath given securyty or the mony then it is firm and then noe troble will be if Ither of the lives should fall, the Carriers name is Samuell Whibben he lodgeth at the three cups In Bredstreate†2and will be in London about two aclock twesday next the agrement for the carriage is 9d: I desire you would send for the lease and seale it and send it to Mr Edwards chamber for me I hope he will not be gon if you send twesday night
there is noe mention in your letter of your Receipt of the 70l that I returned by Mr Edwards my sonns name is Peter he presents his humble service to you and soe doe my wife and daughters I
― 88 ―

suppose you desire noe farther account at presant of the widdow shatters house becaws it is sould I take leave
your Faithfull Kinsman and humble servant
WILLIAM STRATTON
I have not paid the carrier for the letter that soe there might be the more care taken of the lease If Mr Edwards be cum from london I know noe better way then to return it by the same Carrier

1298. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 10/20 June 1690 (1279, 1302)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 34-5.
Monsieur,
Jay tousjours dilayé a vous escrire pour vous mander en mesme temps la reception de la lettre de change sur Monsieur Jan van Oosterwijck de deux milles et cinquante cinq livres argent de ce pays. si vous aviez dautres lettres a remettre je vous conseillerois d'eviter cet homme qui s'est fait tirer l'oreille jusqu'a l'extremité, il ne vient que de payer, au moment que j'allois faire contre luy un acte de protest, il ne delaisse pourtant pas de passer pour un homme accommodé et c'est pourquoy que jay attendu le dernier moment de vostre droit pour obliger d'autant plus vostre amis de dela. vous trouverez peut estre apropos de n'en rien dire a son correspondant pour luy conserver son credit. quoy qu'il en soit vous este payé, et vous avez sur moy par cette reception avec ce que jay receu auparavant la somme de sept milles cent et cinquante cinq florins argent de banque†1 —f7155. jay esté fasché de vous avoir donné occasion de vous allarmer dans une affaire pourtant ou assurement vous ne courez aucun risque. l'inquisition de Monsieur D.†2 n'a pas esté assurement par aucune induction mais par incident.
― 89 ―

et il est tellement dissuadé que je suis assuré quil jureroit que cela est faux. Ma femme ayant desja fait une petite emplette pour vous envoyer, avoit cru vous escrire aujourdhuy, mais elle est tellement prise depuis quelques jours de son asthme quelle ne peut bouger du lict, vous aurez donc la bonté de l'excuser encore pour cette fois. Maistre pieter adriaens mavoit prié de vo<u>s†a toucher un mot sur le different quil a pour la pension de lannée suivante a<vec>†b Monsieur le docteur Thomas, qui apres avoir donn<é>†b quatre cent livres par an,†1 voudroit a cette troisiesme année luy donner que cent florins, dans la pensée quil peut meriter la plus grande partie de sa pension par son service, qui a la verité ne scauroit estre consideré a ce point dans un pais ou la Chirurgie ne se fait presque que par le maistre mesme. il ma dit quil en escriroit aussi a monsieur thomas mesme, et quil ne le feroit pas a moins de deux cent livres outre quil nauroit pas voulu s'en charger une autre année qu'a la consideration que le jeune thomas†2 le souhaitte ardemment et quil est persuadé que cela achevera de le perfectioner, puisquil est fort diligent et retenu. toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects, et je suis comme je le doibs,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres Obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON.
Amst. ce 20 juin 1690.

Postmark: IV 13
