1299. Dr. William Cole to Locke, 11 June 1690 (1290, 1321)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 201-4. As with no. 1290, I have not tried to explain most of Cole's obsolete or unusual words.
It has beene againe, Sir, my misfortune to be kept so long from home since your letter came, that I am forced againe to beg your pardon for the delay of an answer to it. Indeed I am concerned,
― 90 ―

busynesse should keepe me from the satisfaction of a personall knowledge of one for whom I have that great respect, and of whom I have heard severall speake so advantageously; But a certaine proverbe advising to strike while the Iron is hot, which it has beene more with me alate†1 than a good while before, I am confident your consideration will rather justify me, than impute the delaying a while my designe of a London-journey to a levity in resolution: Though I'm satisfyed, a moderate London Practise for a Physitian must be, as more easy, so more advantageous than the best Country-one can be.
From the accurate account you are pleased to give of your symptoms, and the progresse of them, I am much inclined to beleeve your apprehensions of your condition in relation to your present distemper, are but the same which the most of thinking men (Physitians not excepted) have of themselves when indisposed; viz. They make too close reflection on their owne diseases, eyther magnifying them, or not so distinctly perceiving them through their immediate and great concerne which generally makes men forme dreadfull Ideas of things; as the Eye does an Object brought too neare it. Not but that all Phthises, though ever so recent, carry danger; and what at first is but a slight Catarrh (as they call it) may in a little time, especially if neglected, give the Lungs such an atony (if not perhaps in time exulcerate them) as must be fatall. But I hope what you take for a purulent discharge may be only a pituita better ripened than ordinary, and thence may be a signe your cough is taking leave of you. For I beleeve we are apt ynough to mistake such for Pus, from the apparent likenesse it has to it when more throughly digested: And yours may very well be such; since, if you please to consult the aforesaid Dr Morton (who, so farre as I have read in him, seemes to have taken a great deale of very commendable paines in observing the distemper) in pag. 127. perhaps you may find never a one of his three signes of a purulent anacatharsis agrees with yours. But those who read Hippocrates much (part of whom I chanced not long since to looke over) who speakes much of the Exulceration of the Lungs (particularly 1° De Morbis),†2 may perhaps, from the reverence they have for that great man, be apt to thinke most phthises have such an
― 91 ―

exulceration; wheras I am of opinion (but with all deference to better judgments) that the structure of this part seemes not very fit for it (unlesse, as I intimated in my slender Hypothesis t'other day, at some of the fibrillæ, which yet can never discharge such great quantities, as wee thinke to be purulent matter from the Lungs) as being nothing muscular; and it may be suspected that upon an exulceration, if considerable, as must be to give a copious discharge, the sanguiferous vessells would soone be eroded, and thence great effusions of bloud happen, which yet rarely doe. And what you relate of the great alleviation of your symptoms since your being out of Towne,†1makes me hope the better of your condition; it being, to me, hard to be conceived, that an ulcer in such a part, through which the bloud continually runnes so impetuously, and which the necessary reciprocations upon respiration keepe continually in motion, can give such a truce as you find. This in order to induce you to suspend the ill Prognostick, you seeme too prone to make, of your danger.
And now to looke back a little to the former part of your letter. As I thinke no Hypothesis allowable which goes not upon such [mechanicall]†a grounds as the subject is, without straining, in an easy and obvious chaine of thoughts, capable to beare; so all ought, as much as is possible, to be eyther built on Experiment, or be tryed by it; and if that confirme them not, when it can come in to be consulted, they ought to be slighted. But, since every thing has a reason of its being so or so, I thinke that Physitian is very much to blame who will content himselfe, without particularly enquiring into it (so farre as the matter will beare, and his Talent goes) to advise medcines upon generall rules, which can never square to all cases, the circumstances and complication of diseases and symptoms being so various, and thence a variation of Indications so necessary; so that tis requisite a man dig deepe to lay a good foundation to build a judgment on; and, according to the Maxim, Dolus latet in Universalibus.†2 Which Notion though my friend Dr Sydenham was used, suo more,†3 to scout, yet any man may find by reading him twas his principle; and I am most confident, Sir, (from the height of reason shewn in the Translation of a Discourse of yours, on another kind of subject, my Lord Bellomont was pleased to let
― 92 ―

me see)†1 tis yours. For my owne part, though I must repeate I beleeve my selfe very unable to give you a solid satisfaction in any of my speculations relating to your indisposition, yet since you are pleased to oblige me with your friendship in the roome of our worthy deceased friend,†2 and, as a specimen of it, require my thoughts, I would at least endeavour at it by rendring [my]†a reasons of them, that I may not pretend to the favour gratis (your candor will pardon the seeming pride of the expression, if you thinke it so) but make such a retribution as I can, since I perceive my deductions are not altogither unacceptable to you. On which score too I wish I had time to draw up a scheme of my notion of nutrition by the nerves, for your censure: but that requires more time and thoughts than I have now to employ, or perhaps may a good while, being only as yet in thought; and (I owne) may perhaps be thought only a πάρεργον†3 to that of a Phthisis, but may heerafter come as an illustration of an hypothesis I have long conceived (but is yet but in Embryo) of intermitting feavers,†4 which I found in the nervosum genus.
I must assent to your exception against composition of active medcines, especially before we are satisfyed by experience that they have no destructive operation one upon another. Tis true, Experience has been found to give suffrage to the great effects of som, as your Theriaca Andromachi,†5 Mithridate, etc. But I doe not take my selfe for that great man to thinke I have warrant ynough to imitate those who made such compositions: and I have somewhere or other met with a severe sarcasticall censure of the first inventors of them, That a wise man may make use of what none but one that is otherwise would compose. And indeed in them the vertue of any one simple, except the opium, cannot, I thinke be discovered, but the medcine must be looked on as a new concrete, the effects wherof are owing to the resulting crasis, not any particular Ingredients, as such, of the Composition, except that mentioned. Tis possible they designed such medcines for Panacea's by the Jumble-of-Altogither in them: But if they had not lit upon Opium to adde
― 93 ―

to them, tis likely yet, for all that Crasis, they would scarce have kept their reputation any thing more entire than many of their fellowes of those ages, which we only read in this but seldome or never use. And had the admirable Cortex Peruvianus beene given always blended with other, however promising, Ingredients to the same purpose, perhaps we should have beene yet as much to seeke for a good Febrifuge as before its discovery.
As to the use of it in such cases as yours, I generally give it, to those who like it so, as Dr Sydenham did in Agues, with Cons. Ros. p. ij to p. j of the Cortex or in equall quantityes, made up with syr. papav. or any other that has no repugnant operation; but somtimes made into pills with a solution of Gum. tragacanth (as you like it) but not stiffe, least they cannot be dissolved time ynough in the stomack; whence if they get first, the peristaltick motion of the Intestines may well be presumed to carry too farre before they can be so in them: and I remember once or twice to have met with such an accident; the pills (I doe not remember of what Ingredients) made up with this gumme hard, having come away whole. But, for the effect of it in Phthisicall cases, I assure you, Sir, I have now under my prescription two or three of that distemper, who owne them selves much advantaged, and I have reason to beleeve by the use of it; for I cannot ascribe very much of the effect to the other medcines (used withall) except in one of them, to whom (in hopes to correct the flaccidity of the Lungs the more) I direct Limat. Martis with it, in the proportion of p. j. of the limature to p. ij. of the Cort. and after them decoc. Chinæ: and Milke, grewell, flummery, milke-porridge, etc. have beene his dyet for above this moneth; from which method he is sensibly better hitherto: Only when his nocturnall sweats seyze him (which most are subject to) they weaken him more, which yet opiats in a great measure usually represse (particularly laudanum liquidum cydoniatum more than others) given at bedtime. I doe not remember to have found any ill effect of a mixture of Cortex and Chalybs, though I have given it often in this and other cases, particularly Hypochondricall ones.
It seems, Sir, all Opiats disagree not with you, if you can beare Ther. Andromachi, and Laud. liquid. But I have found Syr. de meconio would disagree with some in the Small-pox (in which, you know, Dr Sydenham so much recommends it) and procure a diarrhœa, with whom yet Laudanum liquidum would very well agree.
― 94 ―

As to your question about Guaiacum, etc. As we contract acquaintances, as well in Medcines as common life, not always from merit, but many times (and perhaps somtimes unaccountable) kindnesse; so it has beene my luck to have this for China; the Woods and this, you know, being reckoned in the same Classe as to their effects. But that which most determined my inclination to it (pardon the excursion) was, That happening about 14 or 15 yeeres since, as I remember, to have contracted a large Aposteme about, or just below, the region of my Stomack, by inadvertently using to leane against the edge of a low Table in writing, and that at last (very advantageously for me) discharging itselfe into the Intestines, I chanced to have a present of a parcell of excellent Jamaica China made me, fresh brought over to one heere who had a plantation there: Which decocting in water (I thinke in no greater proportion than of ʒij to l̷l̷ ij) ad medias,†1 it gave a very deepe Tincture, and such a consistence, as made it tast, to my palate, (adding sugar ad gratiam,†2 and slicing into each dish a litle Nutmeg) like a good broth, dranke hot like Tea. The continued use of which contributing, I thinke, much to the healing of the Ulcer (though indeed I had before drank the Chalybeate waters, and used many other medcines, gave me (who always think my selfe obliged to retaine a gratefull sense of benefits) the kindnesse I have for it. But I thinke the East India light and carious China has little more vertue than a rotten Post; though much dearer than this, was used to be at least.
But though I have this reason to esteeme China, yet I cannot upon more deliberate thoughts preferre it at least to Guaiacum. For though the celebrated stories Ingrassias†3 and others tell of its effects are the best arguments to recommend it, yet the reason that appeares to me (who can never content my selfe without some Theory, however jejune) for it may perhaps sway me to give the preference, indeed, to it before China.
The reason therfore of this effect of these woods and rootes I deduce (according to the slendernesse of my notions) from a Gummosity which I suppose is in them all, but so evidently in some that tis not to be controverted, particularly in guaiacum: and the grosser consistence the China upon decoction yields to the
― 95 ―

water induces me to beleeve, That, as well as Guaiacum, abounds with gummous substances, whose gumme, so called, is (as I remember they tell us) nothing else but the decoction in water inspissated by evaporation: though my lazy temper has not allowed me to try it.
These Gummes (as well all others, among which yet there is known to be a considerable difference, some being much more resinous than others) I imagine to be at first abstersive where any substances abound which need that operation; their concretion, according to Dr Grew's experiments about the production of them,†1 being from a combination of Acid and Oleaginous substances: And though perhaps the acid, if at liberty, would prove too lancinating, and so rather contract the tone of the Vessells into which tis admitted, than exert such an effect, as I suppose, upon the contents of them; yet by that association, and the disterminating of their particles, their points, from the variation of the texture of the resulting concrete, may be so blunted (or rather sheathed) as to have that faculty suspended, but, I conceive, not so much as to loose totally their inciding one: so that whilest any of the parts of our bodyes (which I take to be all made up of vessells except a small parenchyma betweene them) especially toward their extremities, are under any atony, or obstructed by a grosse matter which frequently gives it, they may exert that operation. But then, this being effectually done, and no obstacle remaining in their way, of moment (some considerable time being required I conceive, for first productions of that kind) partly the other softer particles may apply themselves to the weakned or exulcerated parts, and perhaps stick there some while; but especially the alible juyces (by the organicall direction of nature; all nutrition being certainly performed mechanically, as well as all other bodily operations, and by a due organization of vessells) come regularly and placidly to be apposed, the atony being in a degree corrected. On this score (if you will allow the Hypothesis) Guaiacum may possibly be the best of these medcines, as abounding with this gummous substance most of any known (To the farther discovery of which, by the by, perhaps the consideration of Ponderousnesse may somwhat conduce; such gummous substances by reason of their plicablenesse being apt ynough to insinuate themselves into all the intercepted spatiola of the fibres of the concrete, and so to give a greater weight
― 96 ―

by the extrusion of the ayre out of them) and withall being found by experience to be agreeable to our bodies in generall, may therfore be fittest to be used; especially since some mens experience has recommended it in our case.
You may, Sir, perhaps aske why the Gumme it selfe, separated from it, should not then be rather used than the decoction: To which I answer, first, by granting that severall Gummes are by Authors commended, as Mastick, Olibanum, Myrrh, Ammoniacum, Benzoin, etc. at least for redressing some of the symptoms: But, secondly, I conceive that decoctions of these gummous substances must needs be more effectuall, because in them the gummous particles are more disterminated, and thence fittest, both to mix with the bloud and secondary juyces, and also to be carryed to, and deposited in, the parts where they are to exert their effect. And on such a score as this possibly the syrup of Balsam of Tolu (another of your enquiries) or rather, perhaps, the bare decoction without the lushious clog of Sugar (the syrup being made usually by a decoction of that Gumme, for by a little farther drying it becomes so, in barley water, and then sugar added) may deserve to be esteemed: And the great fragrancy of it shews it (to me) to abound with finer and more agreeable volatill particles than most gummes, except perhaps to hystericall persons, or those the texture of whose braine is too lax, or whose spirits are too apt to be exagitated, which experience tells us such fragrant substances are apt too much to excite.
As to your scruple about the Milke-dyet: Give me leave to suggest, that I see nothing but that the bloud that is made of milke may be as good, and fit to supply a lasting nourishment, as that from any other Aliment. For since tis evident the food of severall persons uses to be very various; some men feeding dayly on flesh, some others (at least in forreigne countreys) seldome eating any, nay feeding on herbs and fruit and roots, which must yield a much more flabby nourishment than milke (which comes a well digested aliment into our stomacks though made out of herbs) and yet all enjoying equall degrees (as to appearance) of health, I conceive we are not to deduce the reason of it so much from the matter of our Aliments, as the Sanguifying power (wherin soever it resides). This power in valetudinary persons is low and weake, and consequently indicates, that supplyes are to be had from such substances as both agree, and withall give least trouble to it till it growes
― 97 ―

stronger; which experience is to determine, and of which the Appetite, in convalescent persons, gives, I conceive, a great indicium: Indeed you will owne emaciated bodies necessarily require such aliments as are generally of a very humecting and soft nature; which quality though it may appeare to symbolize†1 too much with the disaffection of the Lungs, which in your case may require exiccation, yet the medcines and other administrations respecting that, may, from the sutablenesse of some particles in them to these parts, perhaps produce that effect with a prevalency over these, all parts admitting only what is agreeable to them; and so there may be no interfering of indications. But when eyther by secret changes of the Constitution, which we can only know a posteriori, or the use of due administrations to that end, this sanguifying power comes to be mended, I conceive those very substances which were before of that tender and flabby nature must (by the action of the particles of the ferment which causes it, being now exalted) be so altered in their Texture, as to acquire the same congruity to the parts to be nourished, which those have which are primarily made out of more compact matter. And there seemes no great difference, as to the reason of the thing, betweene Our nutrition and that of Plants; many of which of the same species grow much alike in different earths, and from supplyes of waters of differing qualities. For I conceive the specification of nourishment depends not so much upon the antecedent matter of it, as this Sanguifick Ferment, and the Texture of the parts into whose exhausted porosities tis to be deposited. As therfore the constitution of the body alters, so that of the bloud must likewise, as indeed concurring to denominate, as well as make it. And it may be considered that, as the Aire growes colder, it confirmes the Tone of the parts the more, and must likewise the Crasis of the bloud: nay growing toward winter more Nitrous (as is at least generally presumed) may therfore exalt the nutritive substances the bloud carries (as tis supposed to doe all fluid, at least heterogeneous, bodies besides) and fit it to yield matter to the nerves (in my Hypothesis) for an agreeable nourishment more at such time, aswell as strengthen, on that score likewise, the tone of the parts. Adde, that nothing of the appelling nourishment continuing long, but there being an incessant absumption of some parts of it, aswell as a supply of more, the sanguifying ferment still selects (I meane, only Mechanically) or makes, out of
― 98 ―

the new brought Chyle what is most congenerous to it. But when the indisposition ceases, the Diet is to be altered, according to the indigences of nature, of which perhaps the Appetite may then be the best Judge.
But upon the whole, I must needs, Sir, propose to you, that, if upon the method of living, etc. you are under you find your symptoms abate and your strength returne, you persist in that: or, if it should come hereafter to agree lesse, that you take away Bloud moderately, and perhaps more than once, before you goe upon another, to observe whether it be not (though perhaps not the luxuriancy, yet) the pravity of that which causes the alteration, and is best, perhaps, corrected by repeated emissions of it. Which administration I take to be the most advantageous both for prevention and cure of most diseases of any that belongs to Physick; and thinke that generally a frequent in some, and in others a plentifull emission of bloud positively weakens lesse, and accidentally strengthens more (however paradoxicall the position may seeme, and even to some Physicians) than any other forced evacuation.
And now, Sir, I beleeve you will thinke tis time to send this letter; for the length of which I shall make little other apology (since you seeme to disallow it) than by urging your commands to have my thoughts concerning your enquiries; which though others might have couched much more significantly in fewer words, yet since I pretend not to their abilities, I am sure your knowledge of the different genii of men, will excuse my thin-spread Notions. I have only to assure you, that tis my earnest wish to be esteemed,
Sir
Your friend, as I am your most humble servant,
WILLIAM COLE.
Worcest. Jun. 11. 90.
My most humble service to my Lord and Lady Bellomont.
I gave orders last weeke that Mr Wild, at the Map of the World, in Pauls-Church-yard, should present you a trifle of mine concerning Apoplexies,†1 more to have it honoured to stand in your study, than that I can thinke it to deserve your reading.
― 99 ―

You will oblige me in letting me know whether you receive this, since I lately had a letter miscarryed that I sent by the Post.
My papers of the Cort. Per. are not at present in my hands but lent to a friend: but I hope ere long to shew you them, being designed as an appendix to my notion of intermitting feavers.

Yarmouth in the Isle of Weight

I came hither out of Curiosity to see, or hear of ours, and the French Fleets, who have been within A League and are now within 3 Leagues one of another: the french consists of about 80 Men of War, 30 fire ships, besides tenders; and had not the Wind turned to the NE, Sunday in the afternoon they had certainly†a surprized us. our fleet consists of above 70 men of War, 48 of which are the best Vessells that we have, and of 16, or 18 fire ships, very well manned and A great desire in the seamen to fight, and tis expected that they will dayly increase, and therefor delay fighting, for the delay is supposed to be on our side, we having the Wind and can fall downe upon them when we please.†1 Sir Robert Holmes†2 is incamped on the Hills in sight of the fleets, with what Number of men the Island can afford.

1301. James Tyrrell to Locke, 30 June [1690] (1277, 1281, 1307)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 90-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Okeley June. 30th.
Dear Sir
I hope the good air you drew in at Parsons green,†2 together with the late warme weather hath quite taken away, (or at least much mended your cough) and that you are now restored to the same degree of health you enjoyed before your late relapse, and I should be glad to see it under your owne hand before I remove from this place; which if you please to take in your way into the West would be a fresh token of the continuation of your Freindship to the owner: For I suppose Mr: Clarke, and his Lady are not yet gone out of Towne, in whose company if you doe not goe downe, but follow them; I hope the trouble of goeing a little out of the direct road may not be great. however if I may not be so happy as to see you now, I shall (next to that) be content with hearing from you, and receiveing your commands, if you have any for me: and I should be likewise glad to know where <you>†b intend to spend the rest of the summer, and how I may direct a letter to you; I thanke you for your asistance in drawing the petition tho' there hath bin
― 101 ―
no need to deliver it. because my Lord M.C.†1 hath promised to give us all satisfaction without it; and besides it seems he does not thinke fit to proceed in passeing his†a Patent as yet: however wee keep the Caveat still on foot. but to talke a little of somewhat more pleasant, and usefull, since I came into the Countrey I have began again to read over your excellent Essay; with great satisfaction; and discourseing with some thinkeing men at Oxford, not long since; I found them dissatisfyed with what you have sayed concerning the Law of nature, (or reason,) whereby wee distinguish moral good, from evil and vertue, from vice. for tho' I confesse in your third chap: p. 21.†2 you thinke they equally forsake the truth, who runing into the contrary extremes, either affirme an innate Law; or deny that there is a Law knowable by the light of nature; i.e. without the help of positive revelation. yet they thinke you have in your second Chap: p. 15.8. 159. 160.†3 destroyed this reasonable concession, and resolved all vertue and vice, and†b- the Law by which it is establisht,-†b out of a commonwealth, and abstracted from divine Revelation; into the praise, or dispraise that men give to certaine actions in several clubs or societyes, by which hypothesis. if Drunkennesse, and sodomy, and cruelty to Enemyes (for example) (which are not vices directly contrary to the peace of civil society) should be in any Countrey (as I thinke I can shew some examples of that kind: out of the Spanish and other relations of America) thought praise worthy; and that those that could drinke most; or enjoy most boys and be most cruel (not only) should be counted the gallantest, and most vertuous, but allso be so indeed: and so would really become subjects of that which you call the philosophical Law of vertue, since it had all that you suppose was requisite thereunto, viz: the tacite and general consent of that whole nation where such wicked customes are establisht: and this you farther confirme by these words, p. 160. These three then, first
― 102 ―
the Law of God. secondly the Law of politick societyes. thirdly the Law of fashion, or private censure, are those to which men variously compare their actions:†1 which seems to come very near what is so much cryed out upon in Mr: Hobs; when he asserts that in the state of nature and out of a commonwealth, there is no moral good or evil: vertue, or vice but in respect of those persons, that practice i<t o>r†a thinke it so.†2 if you please to tell me what I shall say to those that <ma>ke†a this objection you will doe your self right, and allsoe adde to the fa<vours y>ou†a have already bestowed on
Your humble servant
J T.
I pray present my humble service to Mr: C.†3 and his Lady if still in Towne. as allso to the 2 sisters where you lay,†4 and to Mr. Pawleing.†5
I shall stay here till the begining of August
Address: For John Lock Esqr. at Mrs: Smithesbyes house in Dorset Court in Canon Row. Westminster.
Endorsed by Locke: J. Tyrrell 3° Jun 90

1305. Lady (Mary) Calverley to Locke, 12 July [1690] (1164, 1438)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 3-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Escrick†a †1 12 July
Sir
I hear you are got to town again. I hope you have gott quitt of your retirement at a cheaper rate, then I shall of mine, for I am taken with such a violent aversion to it, that I question whether I shall ever make such another sally, were I once with you again, Judg then how nearly your reproaches touch me, upon this subject, you ought not to have laid any stress there, but to be serious with you, wou'd you not have blam'd me, if I wou'd have livd upon the brink of a precipice, to gain Honnour by the steadiness of my Conduct, for there was no Safety there abouts, that woud have bin such a vain way of tempting danger, it wou'd have bin like the foolish pride of the Vitturini†2 in Italy, who tho they have room enough, will drive you, within an Inch of a Precipice, meerly to show their address, If I have committed a fault in this matter, it is something sweetned to me by the Honnour you doe me to write to me, and I hope you are assurd that there is no price I woud not give for such a good, as are your letters to me, and tho I have a great prejudice against all that you who are so mighty in Oratory say, when you will seem gallant, yet to Know I have the Honnour to be in the memory of the greatest man in the world, I can dispence with your complements, I must tell you, that how mortifyd soever you may think me, to ambition, the marks of your freindship affect me sencibly, and we're not I at such a distance from everything that is excellent, my pleasure wou'd be too great—for when you tell me you esteem me, that gives a Joy, that ought to be Ballanc'd with a chagrine, or it could not be supported. Ma Petite†3 salutes you affectionately, she is under no small discontent to be confin'd to the foggs of Yorkshire. pray give my Humble service to all our friends.

I rejoyce to hear that your health is confirm'd. may you spin out a long succession of happy dayes is the hearty wishes of your most humble servant
M C

1307. James Tyrrell to Locke, 27 July [1690] (1301, 1309)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 92-3. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 1309.
Okeley July 27th
Dear Sir
I am glad to receive from your owne hand, the good news of the great amendment of your health, and I wish I could be so happy not onely to read it, but see it my self at this place. And I had sooner told you this, had I beleived my answere required hast. but I am sorry any thing I sayed in my last should make you beleive the conclusions which some had drawne from that passage in your booke should proceed from my self, for I did intend no more then to give you an account not†a- of my owne but-†a other mens censures: and therefore desired your meaneing of that place; that I may know how to answere them, or any others upon occasion: Tho I must tell you as for the passage you quote in your vindication, I tooke notice of it to them, when wee discoursed about it, but their answere was, that by a divine, Law, and a Law given by God to Mankind, and likewise a Law, whose only enforcements where the rewards, and punishments, of another life,†2 you could meane no other then the divine, or reveald, Law given by Moses, and Reinforced by Jesus Christ with higher, rewards and greater punishments in the world to come, then were expressely promised, or denounced either by the Law of nature or that of Moses: I must confesse I could not tell positively what replye to make; because you doe not expressely tell us, where to find, this Law, unlesse in the SS.†3 and since it is likewise much doubted by some whether the Rewards
― 108 ―
and punishments you mention can be demonstrated as established by your divine Law, which I am satisfyed is the same with that which others call the Law of nature. tho I must freely tell you that you your self have bin in great part the occasion of this mistake; since you there take no notice at all of Gods reveald will, or Law, given in the SS: which certainly were not intended only to discover Gospel mysteryes, but cheifly as a Rule whereby men might more plainly and easily know their duty towards God, and their neighbours, and Judge of the moral good and evil of their actions, then they could by the Law of nature or meer reason alone; so that if some have mistooke your meaneing it was not out of ill will, but because you did not more clearly expresse what you meant by a divine Law: since it had bin easy for you to have added, in a Parenthesis, which others call the Law of nature,†1 or els to have allso expressely mentiond the reveald Law of God: as†a- distinct from that,-†a to have taken away all ambiguity; and so I should have advised you to have worded it, if I had had the honour of haveing it communicated to me before it had bin made publick. for in those notes you left in my hand, there is nothing sayed of these three Laws.†2 But now I am satisfyed of your meaneing I fully agree with you in your definition both of moral good, and evil, as allso of this divine, or natural Law; since did it not proceed from God as a Lawgiver I am satisfyed it could not properly be called a Law; and the not takeing God into this Hypothesis has bin the great reason of Mr: Hobs mistake that the Laws of nature are not properly Laws nor doe oblige mankind to their observation when out of a civil state, or commonwealth.†3 but I conceive men for the most part lye under sufficient obligations to observe the Laws of nature from those natural rewards to Duty, and punishments for sin, which God hath by the natures of the things themselves appointed in this life; and where those fall short, that God will make it up in the life to come, as Dr: Cumberland hath very fully proved in his booke of
― 109 ―
the Laws of nature against Mr: Hobs.†1 and Dr: Parker as to the necessity of a future state hath more fully made out in his Demonstration of the Law of nature according to Mr: Cum: Principles.†2 and I could wish you would publish your owne thoughts upon this excellent; and material subject; since I know you have made long since a Treatise or Lectures upon the†a Law of nature which I could wish you would revise, and make publick, since I know none more able, then your self to doe it. and which would likewise make a second part to the former worke: and I have heard you say more then once that you intended it: I have no more but if you doe not like that I should tell you what objections the world make against what you write I shall for the future be more reserved; tho however not lesse your humble servant. JT.
Endorsed by Locke: J Tyrrell 27° Jul 90

1309. Locke to James Tyrrell, 4 August 1690 (1307, 1312)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 277-8. Copy, written by an amanuensis (Sylvester Brounower?). Printed in King, pp. 197-200 (King identifies the addressee). The letter as sent was accompanied by a covering letter: p. 116. Answers no. 1307; answered by no. 1312.
Oates†1 4 Aug 90
Dear Sir
I see you or your freinds are so far from understanding me yet rightly that I shall give you the trouble of a few lines to make my meaning clearer, if possible, then it is, though I am apt to thinke that to any unprejudiced Reader, who will consider what I there ought to say, and not what he will phansy I should say besides my purpose, it is as plain as any thing can well be—L.1. c 3. § 13, where it was proper for me to speake my opinion of the Law of nature, I affirme in as direct words as can ordinarily be made use of to Expresse ones thoughts that there is a Law of Nature Knowable by the light of nature—Booke 2d: c.27. §. 7 and 8.,†2 where I have occasion to speake indefinetly of the divine law, 'tis objected I could meane none other But the divine revealed law, Exclusive of the law of nature and†a- that for two reason.-†a The first is because I call it a law given by God to mankinde—The law of nature then, in these mens opinions, had not God for its author, for if it had, he gave it to mankinde, and if he did I thinke it is no derogation to it to say he gave it to mankinde—I fear some body on the other side will from this very sentence argue that I could not meane the Mosaical or Evangelical law of God—I am sure they may with more reason, For neither of those, as I take it, was given to mankinde, which is a terme which in my sense includes all men. Tis plain the Mosaical laws was not given to mankinde, for it was 'Hear Ô Israel' and I never met yet with any one that said the laws of Moses was the laws of mankinde. And as for the revealed will of God in the New testament, which was a revelation made to the children of men 2000 Years after Moses law, and 4000 years after the Creation,†3 how
― 111 ―
that can be cald a law given to mankinde is hard to conceive, unlesse that men borne before the times of the Gospel were no part of mankinde, or the Gospel were <reveald>†a before it was reveald.
The other reason I finde in your Letter why I could not there meane the law of nature is because the divine law I there speake of has inforcements of rewards and punishments in another life—your Letter indeed says whose only inforcements; But only is of your putting in and not mine as you will perceive if you read that passage in my book again, and that I suppose would have as well Excluded the law of Moses as well as that of Nature, and I imagin the law of the Gospel too. But if those Gentlemen thinke that it is a denyall of that branch of the divine law which is cald the law of nature to speake of a divine law, whose inforcements are the rewards and punishments of another life which is as much as to say the law of nature has no such inforcements, And if they are of that opinion they cannot but be very sincere and Zealous stiklers for a divine law of Morality only upon rewards and punishments of this life 'tis easy to see what a kinde of Morality they intend to make of it. You tell me you could not tell me how to answer them. I am sorry for it not being able to see any difficulty. The reason you give in these words I must confesse I could not tell possitively what reply to make because you do not Expressly tell us where to finde this law unlesse in the SS. And since it is likewise much doubted by some whether the rewards and punishments you mention can be demonstrated as established by your divine law. This reason or reasons seems very admirable to me that I could not meane the law of nature because I did not Expressly tell you where to finde this law unlesse in the SS. I do not remember I any where tell you it is to be found in SS. cannot I tell you in matter of fact that some men many men do compare their actions to a divine law and thereby forme the Ideas of their Moral rectitude or pravity without telling where that law is to be found? Another thing that stumbles you is that it is much doubted by some whether the rewards and punishments I mention can be demonstrated as established by my divine law. Will nothing then passe with you in Religion or Morality but what you can demonstrate? If you are of so nice a stomach I am afraid If I should now Examine how much of your religion or Morality you could demonstrate how much you would have left, not but that I thinke that demonstration in those matters may be carried a great deale farther then it is But there are many perhaps millions
― 112 ―
of propositions in Mathematiques which are demonstrable which neither you nor I can demonstrate and which perhaps no man has yet demonstrated or will do before the end of the world. The probability of rewards and punishments in another life I should thinke might serve for an inforcement of the Divine law if that were the businesse in hand But in the present case demonstration of future rewards and punishments was no more my businesse then whether the Squaring of the circle could be demonstrated or no. But I know not how you would still have me besides my purpose and against all rules of method run out into a discourse of the divine law shew how and when it was promulgated to mankinde demonstrate its inforcement by rewards and punishments in another life in a place where I had nothing to do with all this and in a case where some mens bare supposition of such a law whether true or false servd my turne. 'Twas my businesse there to shew how men came by moral Ideas or Notions and that I thought they did by comparing their actions to a rule. The next thing I endeavour to shew is what rules men take to be the standards to which they compare their actions to frame moral Ideas and those I take to be the divine law, the Municipal law and the law of reputation or fashon. If this be so in matter of fact I am in the right in all that I pretended and was proper in that place. If I am out in either of these propositions I must confesse I am in an error but cannot be accused for not haveing treated more amply of those rules in that place or enterd into a just disquisition of their nature force or obligation when if you will looke into the end of that chapter you will finde 'tis not of concernment to my purpose in that chapter whether they be as much as true or noe but only that they be considerd in the mindes of men as rules to which they compare their actions and judg of their morality. But yet you thinke me guilty of other mens mistakes because I did not write plainer and I thinke they might have considerd better what I writ. I imagin what I was there to make out I have done very plainly And if readers will not allow so much attention to the books they read as to minde what the Author is upon and whether he directly pursues the argument in hand, they must blame themselves if they raise doubts and scruples to themselves where the Author gave no occasion for any. And if they be ill naturd as well as groundlesse objections one may suspect that they meant not over well to the Author or the argument they are so scrupulous about. You say that to shew what I meant I should after divine
― 113 ―
law have added in a parenthesis which others call the law of nature which had been so far from what I meant that it had been contrary to it For I meant the Divine law indeffinetly and in general how ever made known or supposd; and if ever any men referd their actions to the law of nature as to a Divine law 'twas plain I meant that if any judgd of their actions by the law of Moses or Jesus christ as by a divine law 'twas plain I meant that also.†1 Nay the Alcoran of the Mahumetans and the Hanscrit†a of the Bramins†2 could not be in this case Excluded (though perhaps you or your freinds would have thought it more worth their censure if I had put them in and then I had lain open to I know not what interpretations) or any other supposd divine revelation whether true or false. For it being taken for a divine law it would have served men who made use of it and judgd of their actions by it to have given them notions of morality or Moral Ideas and that was all I was to shew. Indeed if you can tell of any other rule but 1°. Divine laws or the law of God 2°. Civil laws or the laws of the Magistrate 3°. the law of fashon and reputation where by men judg of the goodnesse of their actions I have then faild in giveing a full account whence men get their moral Ideas but that is all I can be accusd to have faild in here. For I did not designe here to treat of the grounds of true morality which is necessary to true and perfect happinesse and 'thad been impertinent if I had so designed: my businesse was only to shew whence men had moral Ideas and what they were and that I suppose is sufficiently don in that chapter. I†b am
Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE
Endorsed by Locke: J Locke to J.T 4 Aug. 90

1311. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 28 August 1690 (1263, 1341)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 45-6.
Tunbridge Wells August 28th. 90
Dear Sir
I have all the Obligation to you imaginable for the Favour of yours and have been answering it ever since by following your Good Advice, in casting of all care and Solicitude of any Nature whatsoever, and banishing all Thoughts that could hinder the kindly operation of the Sweetning Element, or pleasant Conversation which makes this place so desirable; where nothing is wanting (now my Brother is come to me,) but Your most desirable presence; which could I obtain it would perfect my Cure. I must own I am very much better then when I wrote to you last, and do every day find good effects of the Course I am in, which I would pursue a little longer, had not the good Weather forsaken us, and my Brothers affairs made his speedy return necessary; he has been here but two dayes, and 'tis resolv'd that Tuesday next†1 we all leave this place, and adjourn to London, where we shall tarry 'till the Monday following, and no longer. by all I mean Mr Freke, Mr Beal,†2 and my Dearest Mrs Hunt,†3 who has perform'd her promise of giving me a Visit for one ten dayes; they all tender you their best services especially my Brother, who would fain see you, and levell accounts with you, if our good fortune would bring you to London, or to Chiply, Otterton, and Escott, which you have sometimes talked of; when will that happy time come, is there any hopes of it this Autum, if Travelling be as beneficial to you, as it uses to be to me, the Journey it self will be some inducement; pray consider of it Seriously, 'tis an Obligation you have laid upon your Self, and must some time or other be acquitted; Mrs Hunt Talks of a ramble to the Bath, why should we not all go that way; 'tis now truly and propperly the long vacation, there is no King, Parliament,

1312. James Tyrrell to Locke, 30 August [1690] (1309, 1378)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 94-6. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 1309.
Rolleston†2 Aug: 30
Dear Sir
Had I not bin allwayes upon the remove for near this fortnight, I had sooner returned an answere to yours; for I would not lye long under your misapprehension of me, concerneing what I spoke in private to Mr: P.†3 concerneing the booke. and therefore I shall first answere your encloseing paper which is of greater concernement to me then the letter it self, for whether I, or my Freinds (as you are pleased to call them) have mistaken Mr: L. in a philosophical disquisition is of no great moment, and If I am in the wrong, am as glad to be convinced of my mistake, as if I had allwayes bin in the right: but whether or no Mr: L. doe rightly collect that Mr: T.
― 117 ―
hath not carryed himself as becomes a Freind is a thing not of that indifference to him. and therefore I shall endeavour to clear this mistake in the first place; for I did not (I confesse) understand before, what it was I had concluded too quick: and therefore I shall only represent the matter of fact, and then leave it to your self either to excuse or condemne me. therefore in the first place I must tell yow, that when I writ to you to know if you could informe me who was the Authour of that†a booke. you returned no answere at all, as I can shew you by the letter it self, which I have still by me:†1 'tis true in another when I writ you word that the People at Oxford had now found out a better Authour then I, for it: viz: your self, your answere was to this effect, that since they would not have you to be the Authour of a booke that you owned, you did not thinke it worth while to give them any satisfaction in those that you did not owne at all: but you farther sayed that you would convince me of their mistake both about that, and another called humane reason (which they allso layed to you) when wee next met:†2 so you may remember, that when I first waited of you at your Lodging as soon as I came to Towne, I fell purposely in talk of that booke, and sayed that whoever had writ it, whether your self, or another, I thought him very much in the right in most things: and that he agreed perfectly with my conceptions in Patriarcha non Mon: (which he had quoted)†3 which I spoke on purpose that you might then take occasion to deny it if I were mistaken, which since I found you did not, but rather declined, the discourse, and turned it off to another subject; I must confesse I did then (as I doe still) entertaine some suspicions of your being the Authour of it, as I must doe till your pleased positively to averr the contrary: but for my uttering this suspition to another, and not to your self; I must tell you I thought it not good manners to urge you any farther upon that point: which if it 'twere true, perhaps you had no mind I should know. but I assure you I never utterd this suspition to any body but Mr: P. nor had I done it to him, but that I knew
― 118 ―
him to be a very good Freind of yours, and that would not doe you any prejudice by my discourse: but he might likewise have told you, that I then gave him some reasons why he might gather, that the booke was not yours; and then†a I then told him; that I was not confident of it (and therefore did not conclude etc)†b but only had such a suspition, for the reasons I have now given you, in which if I am mistaken, you must thanke your owne reservednesse. So that I hope when you consider better of it, you will find that you have no reason to take my uttering my private opinion ill, unlesse it be, because you will take it amisse, that is, not by the right handle; for Ile assure you whether you owne or disowne it; you shall never find that I publish this suspition to your prejudice, or ever speake so much againe of it. and if I sayed too much to him I beg your pardon. as for the letter it self,†1 all I shall answere to it (since I have unfortunatly left it behind me) shall be very short: I am now satisfyed that your meaning, by a divine Law, was to include all divine Laws either natural,†c- or supposed reveald-†c in that generall definition, but how the hanscrit of the Indians, or the Alcoran of Mahomet, could be therin included as given to mankind any more then the law of Moses I am still to seeke: and therefore either the Law of Moses must be given (that is intended)†d for Mankind or els these supposed divine Laws, cannot be included in your definition a divine Law given to Mankind: but to let you see that my Freinds mistake is not so grosse as you would make it: it will I suppose appear plaine enough that the Law of Christ and consequently the moral part of that of Moses, tho not actually reveald, yet was given for all mankind to be in due time the better for it. appears by our Saviours command to his Apostles, and their sucessors in preaching the Gospel, vi: Mat: 28.19. Mark. 16.15. Luke 24.47. and tho it is not yet†e that actually done, yet this no more an objection against Gods designe, than†f that Fools and Madmen are not (tho parts†g of Mankind) subject to the Laws of nature. So that I am not yet satisfyed, but that you had better have confined your definition wholy to the Law of nature knowne by reason; and that exprest in common words. since no man but your self (as I know of) ever called
― 119 ―
the Law of nature; or the false Laws of some particular nations; or Religions, a Divine Law: which had taken away all occasion of doubt or mistake: and Horace says well, brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio.†1 and therefore I hope you will be so charitable as to beleive that if either; or my Freinds mistooke your meaneing it was <neither>†a out of prejudice or ill nature: for as my owne part I am as†b well†b satisfyed in haveing my mistake rectifyed then if I had bin allwayes in the right; I have no more but to beg your pardon for this tedious scribble: and to wish you all health, and beg you to beleive that these small differences in Judgment doe not make me lesse your faithfull; and humble small†c servant
J T.
My brother Blount (at whose house I am whilst I write this), desires to have his service remembred to you: and since I suppose you are often at my Lady. Ms:†2 (from whose house I guesse your last was dated. you would due us both a favour to inquire whether Dr: C. her Father did not leave the second part of his Systeme of the Universe in Manuscript,†d and whether there be any designe to publish it, if it be fit for it.†3
If you doe me the favour as to answere this whilst I continue in these parts, which will be till after Michaelmasse. you may direct yours For me at the house of Mr: Henry Cavendish†4 at Dovebridge: to be left at the Post house at Utoxater Staffordshire. Stone bag.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at his Lodgings at Mrs: Smithesbyes house in Dorset Court in Cannon Row Westminster.
Postmark: SE 5

1313. Locke to Edward Clarke, 1 September 1690 (1174, 1326)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 34. Printed in Rand, pp. 299-301.
Oates 1° Sept. 90
Dear Sir
I was very glad to receive the news of your health and quiet by yours of the 20th Aug: and the continuance of the same by an other of 23d. The inclosed from Monsieur of your sons proficiency not answering his expectation I hope is rather from his great care and concerne than any just cause of complaint and I am the more encouraged to hope soe because I finde he complains also of the litle progresse my wife had made in French, which yet I found when she was in town was beyond what I could have expected. He names both childishnesse and obstinacy in your son, if it be the first though it be not now to be indulged, yet we are not to hope quite to cure it that must be the worke of age. But obstinacy is a dangerous point and must at any rate be masterd or else all will be spoild. I have writ to him soe and pressed him again to be sure to make himself obeyd. I know not whether Monsieurs†a temper be capable of that austerity and rigor†b which may be necessary. I must desire you to examine and looke to that and if there be any obstinacy in the case see it masterd. To dispose your son to it perhaps it may be enough to represent to him with a serious brow that it is absolutely your will that he should perfectly obey Mr Passebon and that if he make any difficulty to doe it, or that you finde he does not you will send him to schoole where he shall be hardly used, whipd often and be under your displeasure to boot. This said in few words and your countenance kept may perhaps be enough to produce all we desire if not you must both order Mr Passebon when he is obstinate to correct him severly and goe on in the correction till he finde him subdued or else you must see it don your self but it were better he did it by himself and if all this will not doe we must looke for a new Tutor rather than have your son spoild, though if this man can gain an authority over him perhaps we may not easily finde a better for I thinke him one of the best and honestest Frenchmen I have met with and let me tell you there is this good in his temper that the lesse he is inclind to severity and the lesse he depends: on whiping the more pains he will take and if it can be
― 121 ―
brought to doe, the milder is certainly the better way. When I say your son must not be spoild we must not thinke that childishnesse or a neglect in him of his improvements is presently that, you must allow him to be a child and be like other children averse to study and carlesse of what is for his future advantage. But an obstinate prevalency in haveing his will against the direction of his tutor or an habituall idlenesse must not be indulged and†a the later I am confident by the advances he makes it is not and the former I guesse consists more in a cunning elusion of Mr Passebons orders than an open refusall or opposition to them. I have writ something to Mr Passebon for a farther advance in his studys and I begin to thinke it time now to enter upon Latin which I advise Mr Passebon may be by reading the Latin Testament and explaining it in French
I am not sorry that Madam has for some time stopd your journy towards sutton. The ill weather we have had here togeather with the intreaties of Sir Francis†1 and my Lady joynd to my cough which with the ill weather began a litle to returne have kept me here longer than I intended else perhaps I had been by this time at Bath if my Lady Monmouth be (as Mrs Lockhart writ me word she intended) gon thither But haveing heard noe thing of it since I know not but the constant rain we have had here ever since may have kept her as well as me from travelling. As soon as I get to town if the weather favour travelling I intend for the West if noe thing else upon the place which I cannot foresee hinder me for I long to see Madam at Chipley pray tell her soe and assurer of my respects I am
your J L
Sir Francis and my Lady present their service to you. the corne here is pittifully in the suds. My love to my dear wife and all the yonge ones and my thanks to Master for his Kinde letter which I shall in a short time thank him for my self
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Chipley near Taunton Frank†2
Postmark: SE 3
Endorsed by Clarke: J: L: touching my sonn Received the 5th: September 1690.

1314. Martha Lockhart to Locke, [1 September 1690] (1315)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 3-4. Date from Locke's endorsement and no. 1315. 1 September 1690 fell on a Monday.
The writer was a daughter of Sir William Lockhart of Lee and his second wife Robina, daughter of John Sewster of Weston, Huntingdonshire, by his wife Anne, a sister of Oliver Cromwell. Sir William was a soldier and diplomatist, serving Cromwell and the succeeding governments as representative in France from 1656 to 1659, and Charles II as envoy and later as ambassador to Louis XIV from 1672 until his death in 1675. Martha was one of Queen Mary's six Bed-chamber Women probably from the queen's accession in 1689; her salary was £200 per annum. After the queen's death in 1694 she was granted a pension. She was still living at the time of her brother James Lockhart's death in 1718: Noble, Protectoral-house of Cromwell, ii. 267; etc. She was, through her Cromwell descent, a third cousin of Sir Francis Masham. She appears to have maintained her connection with her Cromwell relations.
Munday night
I begine realy to belive Mr Locke has not only forgot the way to london but that ther is any here has Concern for you at least I may reasonably suspect you have left me out of the number for in your last you told me of your Coming to town in a day or two which I thought was a very good reason not to writ expecting every day to se you and never since to hear from you make's me belive you wear resolved by this Contrivance to rid your self of my troublsome letter's but if this hapen to be true you se by this disapointment that it is not easy to hinder a women to doe what she has a mind to but all this rallery a part I doe asure you I am in some paine to kno' what has made you allter your resolution of Comeing to town and tho I doe very much wish to se you, yet I shall†a be sattisfied if noe other reason but your good Company has deffered your comeing to town. I had been much more Constant in my writing to Dear Lady Masham had wee had the newes one might have thought so much time might reasonably have produce'd but since the 14 of last month I doe assure you wee have not on word from Ierland, which sillance putts the inventtors of both parttyes to work from whom wee have dayly acounts but I did not think the dull insipid lys of the town worth the troubling my lady but upon the wholl I find the Considering people of all sides amazed; her Majesty not at all I never saw her merreyer nor more semeingly unconcerne'd in my life notwithstanding all things go's admirably ill perticuliarly in
― 123 ―
soctland where the Rebells of latte have seem'd much more formidable then ever severall men of notte are gone in to 'em amongest other Sir Petter Fraser who went in to 'em with some 16 hors. the rebells at first suspecting them to be some party of our Forcess fierd upon 'em and Killed 2 or 3 of his men before the wear understood they have Come done so Low that Eddinburgh†a was not thought secure for the prisoners by order of Counsell was removed to the Bass and the towns men hiding all ther tresour's†1 My lady Southerland†b †2 has been some part of her way to scotland and is returned. I am so very sleepy I know not what I writ and shall only add that I hope youle doe me the favour to excuse me to my lady for not writing she has not answered my two last about Coss Same.†3 I just now receive a letter from Mr Clarke who tell's me of a wonderfull motion of the earth that has happned about him, which so apparintly shoke all the houses for nigh 20 milles round and without any noyse, by which the in habitants was so terified, ran out of ther beds and quited ther houses with out Clothes he tells me the doges and Cattles of all kinds manifested ther fear, and sence of it by very unuesuall Howlings and Bellowing and extrordinary Motions that wear amongest them.†4 pray send me word what you think of it and when we may expecte to se you hear where you are sure to be wellcom to many but to none more then
Sir
Your very obliged and ever Faithfull Servant
M L
Service to Sir Fra: Mrs Codworth†5 and all my Cosen's perticularly my husband.†6 I send my L:M the Book I promised her and the Choc: but for tea we have now noe stock in our Family
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Lockhart 1 Sept 90

1317. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 12/22 September 1690 (1288, 1330)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 48-9. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., III D 16, ff. 198-9. Short quotation from the copy in Ollion, p. 197 n.
The Reformed Church in the United Provinces, the Public Church (p. 295, etc.), Calvinist in doctrine, was Presbyterian in organization. The lowest assembly was the Consistory (consistorium, kerkeraad, kirk-session), consisting of the minister and elders of each particular church. Next came the Presbytery or Classis, the ministers and representative elders of the churches within a prescribed area. Above the presbyteries were the Provincial Synods, one each for North and South Holland and one for each of the other six provinces. Ranking with them was the Walloon Synod, which was at the head of the French-speaking churches throughout the country; it met twice a year but had no fixed place of assembly. Above these synods was the National Synod; it had not met since the Synod of Dort in 1618-19.
The various bodies and their functions are described in the course of the account of religion in the Netherlands in F. M. Janiçon, État présent de la république des Provinces-unies, 1729-30, i. 14-37.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Jam dudum ad Te scribere gestii, verum scribendi materia oppido rara fuit. Ex epistola tua ad D. Guenellonem jam ante plures hebdomadas scripta Te graviter decubuisse, et ex morbo convaluisse intellexi. Gratulor Tibi restitutam sanitatem, eamque solidam ac
― 126 ―
perpetuam precor. Totus jam sum in adornanda Inquisitionis historia, quæ volumini Sententiarum præmittatur. Materia hæc admodum fœcunda est; et cum jam labore meo defunctus videor, nova se uberrime offert. Velim illius officii sanctitatem vivis suis coloribus depingere, illudque integre repræsentare. Non exigui laboris est, omnia ex tam diffusis autoribus, velut in ingenti Oceano dispersa, colligere; sed non minoris, molem adeo informem apte digerere. Dum materiam hanc quotidie verso, ecce in patria nostra illi, quos id minime decuit, qui vix persecutorum manus effugerunt, S. Officii ideam nobis repræsentare voluerunt. Juriæus Ministro cuidam Hamburgensi, nomine Consilario, antehac sibi (uti ait) amico, ob privatas quasdam causas infensus, pro sua mansuetudine Theologica exitium, per fas per nefas, struere conatus est.†1 Nulla id perficiendi aptior ac promtior via quam hæreseos diro ac horrendo crimine inimicum adspergere. Quare edita epistola pastorali eum ut Socinianum traducit, amicitiam cum Papino et Auberto, du Versé objicit.†2 Alter injuria ista provocatus Hollandiam petit, adversarium
― 127 ―
coram Synedrio Roterodamensi†1 citat, criminaque sibi objecta probari cupit. Juriæus indigne ferens se a judicum subsellio removeri, distinctione ex sancto officio mutuata, se non accusatorem sed denuntiatorem haberi cupit:†2 et hoc nomine sibi inter [[sic]]judices locum dari postulat. Verum hæc distinctio admissa non fuit. Dati illi sunt tres menses, ut testimonia, quibus accusationem suam probet, producat. Tempus illud in longius extractum est: Omnem movit lapidem ut undique testimonia conquirat; quæ tamen ex voto obtinere non potuit. Ipse nonnunquam tanquam commissarius testium depositioni præsidere voluit. Instante Synodo†3 edidit Factum contra Consiliarium, in quo inter alia hæc leguntur.

― 128 ―
Rem paucis dicam. Tandem controversia hæc delata est ad Synodum Gallicam, nuperrime in civitate nostra celebratam. Hic Juriæus inter judices sedere voluit; et cum argueretur esse adversarius, respondit, Gomarum etiam Remonstrantium fuisse adversarium, scriptis editis eos oppugnasse, et nihilominus in Synodo Dordracena sedisse judicem.†1 Regessit alter: hic non esse quæstionem de fide, sed de facto; non, quæ sententia vera sit; sed an ipse docuerit sententiam, quæ communi utriusque consensu damnatur ut falsa. Hic cum Juriæus accusatoris partes assumpserit, inter judices sedere non posse. Itaque e judicum numero remotus accusatoris partes sustinere debuit. Res calidis satis animis per aliquot dies in Synodo disceptata est. Crimen Socinianismi neutiquam probare potuit Juriæus: nihil in amicitia cum Papino crimini verti potuit: Verum Aubertum du Versé commendasse (quod negaverat) Consiliarius convictus fuit. Cum rogarentur suffragia, quinque ex junioribus eum plane exautorare voluerunt; tredecim, in ministerii functione ad tempus suspendere; Viginti autem aliorum suffragiis absolutus est, et renuntiatus orthodoxus; addita tamen censura, quod imprudenti sua Auberti du Versé commendatione justam Juriæo causam præbuerit eum Socinianismi suspectum habendi:
― 129 ―
Juriæo gratiæ actæ pro zelo ac vigilantia pro Ecclesiæ orthodoxia; additum autem, desiderasse Synodum, ut servata Euangelii lege, primo privatim monuisset Consiliarium, deinde coram Ecclesia sua; non autem publice edito scripto accusasset. Hisce peractis decretum fuit ut fraternitatis dexteras sibi invicem darent; quod diu recusavit Juriæus: tandem post multas Synodi intercessiones manum suam a Consiliario tangi ægre permisit: Actisque Synodi insertum fuit, ipsos esse reconciliatos: Verum cum postridie Synodi Acta relegerentur, Juriæus non destitit, donec ea verba delerentur, neque ullum reconciliationis monumentum in Actis Synodi exstare voluit. Sed et aliud est. Ministri Gallorum in Anglia profugi datis ad Synodum Gallicam Amstelodamensem literis conqueruntur de Socinianismo inter suos grassante rogantque et adjurant Synodum, ut remedia convenientia illi malo sistendo adhibeat.†1 Ita transmarinæ appellationes placere denuo incipiunt. Hos a Juriæo subornatos, ut tanto facilius Consiliarium opprimeret, nemo fere ambigit. Synodus ex miseris exulibus magnam partem constans, non aliter ac si ἀνυπευθύνᾳ polleret autoritate, quasdam positiones damnat
― 130 ―
ut falsas, scandalosas et perniciosas; quarum prima est, quod Socinianismus sit doctrina tolerabilis, in qua quis possit salvari. Sequuntur aliæ contra tolerantiam: Tandem addunt. Defendant sous les dernieres censures a toutes personnes ecclesiastiques et seculiers de les debiter ni dans les chaires, ni dans les conversations particulieres: etc. Mox addit. Enfin pour ne rien oublier dans une occasion si importante, la Compaignie ordonne tres expressement a tous les Consistoires qui dependent d'elle, de redoubler leur soins et leur vigilance pastorale, a proportion du danger, qui menace leur troupeaux, de reprimer sans distinction et sans complaisance tous ceux, qui se trouveront coupables, en suspendant les particuliers de la Saint Cene, <et>†a a l'egard des Ministres, ils les suspendront de leur charge, jusques au prochain Synode, en apellant a ce jugement deux pasteurs des Eglises voisines, sans que les denunciateurs puissent estre pris a partie, etc.
(English) Et porro mandant et præcipiunt, non aliter ac si audires Romanos rerum dominos in augustissimis suis Conciliis decreta sua Apostolica autoritate pronuntiantes.
(English) Si illis sceptra ac fasces submittere velint reges, brevi novum habebimus S. Officium, quod antiquo nec astutia nec crudelitate cedat. Multis mirum fuit, cum Synodus censuram strinxerit in Consiliarium ob commendatum Aubertum du Versé, quod animum Juriæi ἂσπονδον et a reconciliatione alienum nulla censura notaverit: quodque zelus ille orthodoxiæ, quo in privatorum sermones
― 131 ―
inquirere cupit, ne ulla Socinianismi labes impunita relinquatur, adeo languidus sit ac remissus erga Juriæum, quem Consiliarius in Facto suo, quod Juriæi Facto opposuit, variarum erronearum opinionum, allatis ipsius Juriæi verbis, reum egit, ut ne levissima quidem censura notatus sit. Verum in sancta hac congregatione, non minus quam alibi, Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas.†1 Quidam sunt albæ gallinæ filii,†2 quibus impotens in quoscunque hæreticos debacchatio contra quasvis censuras clypeus est impenetrabilis. Verum hæc hactenus. Nisi fasciculus in nimiam molem excrevisset ipsum Synodi decretum misissem. Tractatus tuus de Intellectu humano ferme totus jam in linguam Latinam est versus. Verum id rectius ex ipsius interpretis literis cognosces. Vale Vir Amplissime, Amice mihi præ omnibus dilecte. Uxor et liberi plurimam Tibi precantur salutem.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 22 Septenbris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have been longing to write to you for some time, but there has been very little to write about. I learnt from your letter to Mr. Guenellon some weeks ago that you had had a serious illness, and that you had recovered from it. I congratulate you on your restoration to health, and I pray that it may be [p. 126] thorough and permanent. At the moment I am entirely taken up with adding the finishing touches to my account of the Inquisition, which is to serve as a preface to the book of the Sententiae. The material for this is very plentiful; when I seem to have finished my task new matter offers itself in abundance. It is my wish to depict the holiness of that office in the lively colours that are proper to it, and to present a complete picture of it. Collecting all the notices from so many separate writers, scattered, as it were, over a vast expanse of ocean, is a matter of no small labour; nor is the due arrangement of such a formless mass any lighter task. While this subject is my own daily occupation, lo and behold in this country of ours those whom it least behoved, people who themselves have barely escaped the hands of persecutors, have decided to show us an exemplar of the Holy Office. Jurieu, such is his theological clemency, has set himself by fair means or foul to work the ruin of a certain Hamburg minister, la Conseillère by name, previously (so he says) a friend of his, with whom he is at enmity for certain private reasons.†1 He found no fitter and readier way of effecting this than by besmirching his enemy with the dire and awful charge of heresy. He therefore published a pastoral letter holding him up to reprobation as a Socinian, and accusing him of friendship with Papin and Aubert de Versé.†2 The other, provoked by this affront, proceeds to Holland, cites his adversary before the Council of [p. 127] Rotterdam,†1 and desires that the charges preferred against him may be proved. Jurieu, indignant at being removed from the judges' bench and borrowing a distinction from Holy Office procedure, desires to be counted not as a prosecutor but as a denunciator,†2 and accordingly demands to be given a place among the judges. But this distinction was not admitted. He was given three months in which to produce the evidence to prove his accusation. This period was further protracted; he spared no pains to scrape together evidence from all sources, but was unable to obtain enough to satisfy his requirements. He sometimes wanted to preside in person like a commissary at the taking of witnesses' depositions. When the Synod†3 was about to assemble he issued a Factum against la Conseillère, in which amongst other things the following words occur:
(Latin) Do you not seem to be listening to the Holy Office pronouncing sentence on a heretic 'convicted on denial'?†4 The unjust proceedings were long drawn out, and there were endless twists and turns. I will put the matter [p. 128] shortly. The controversy was at length referred to the Walloon Synod, recently held in our city. Here Jurieu wished to sit among the judges; and when it was contended that he was an opponent of the accused he replied that Gomarus too had been an opponent of the Remonstrants and had attacked them in his published works, and that he had nevertheless sat as a judge at the Synod of Dort.†1 The other rejoined that in this case the issue was not one of faith but of fact; it was not a question of what opinion was true, but whether he himself had taught an opinion which was condemned as false by the common consent of both parties; as Jurieu had assumed the role of accuser in the case, he could not sit among the judges. He ought accordingly to be removed from their number and to act as accuser. The matter was debated in the Synod for several days with considerable warmth. Jurieu failed entirely to prove the charge of Socinianism; there was nothing in la Conseillère's friendship with Papin that could be used against him; he was, however, convicted of having expressed approval of Aubert de Versé, which he had denied. When the votes were called for five of the junior members were for summarily dismissing him from the ministry; thirteen for temporary suspension in his ministerial functions; while twenty others voted for his acquittal and reported him as orthodox, with a rider, however, censuring him for his imprudent commendation of Aubert de Versé, by which he had given Jurieu just cause to suspect him of Socinianism; Jurieu was thanked for his [p. 129] zeal and vigilance on behalf of orthodoxy in the Church, a note being added expressing the regret of the Synod that he had not observed the rule of the Gospel by first admonishing la Conseillère in private and then before his church; but he should not have accused him in a published document. When these proceedings were over it was decreed that they should give each other the right hand of brotherhood; for a long time Jurieu refused to do so; at last after many attempts at mediation by the Synod he reluctantly allowed his hand to be touched by la Conseillère, and it was noted in the proceedings of the Synod that they had been reconciled. But when the proceedings were read over on the following day Jurieu would not rest until these words were deleted, nor was he willing that any record of reconciliation should stand in the proceedings of the Synod. But there is one other thing. Some French ministers who are refugees in England have addressed a letter to the Walloon Synod in Amsterdam in which they complain that Socinianism is threatening to spread amongst their people; they accordingly beg and implore the Synod to apply suitable remedies for the checking of that evil.†1 So overseas citations are beginning to be in favour once more. Hardly anyone doubts that these ministers were suborned by Jurieu, who hoped to crush la Conseillère the more easily thereby. The Synod, which consists for the most part of unfortunate exiles, behaving just as if it enjoyed irresponsible authority, condemns certain positions as false, scandalous, and pernicious, [p. 130] the first of these being the assertion that Socinianism is a doctrine to be tolerated as one in which one may find salvation. This is followed by other clauses directed against toleration, and finally one
(Latin) They add:
And so they proceed with their commands and instructions, just as if one were listening to the Roman lords of the earth met in their most august Councils and pronouncing their decrees with Apostolic authority.
(Latin) If kings are prepared to lower their sceptres and fasces to these people we shall soon have a new Holy Office, yielding nothing to the old in cunning or cruelty. Many were astonished that, though the Synod had resorted to censure against la Conseillère for his commendation of Aubert de Versé, yet the implacable and irreconcilable spirit of Jurieu was visited with no mark of its disapproval; it was observed that that zeal for orthodoxy which makes the [p. 131] Synod fain to inquire into private conversations, lest any taint of Socinianism should be left unpunished, is so very faint and remiss in dealing with Jurieu; for la Conseillère, in the Factum which he issued in opposition to that of Jurieu, had in fact arraigned him for holding various erroneous opinions, adducing his own words as evidence; yet Jurieu received not the slightest reprimand for this. However, in this holy congregation no less than elsewhere it is true that 'censure spares the crows, but harries the doves'.†1 There are certain persons, 'chicks of the white hen',†2 whose insensate fury in attacking heresy of any sort provides them with a sure shield against all criticism. But enough of this; I would have sent you the actual decree of the Synod, if it had not meant swelling this packet to an inordinate size. Your treatise on the Human Understanding has now been almost completely translated into Latin. But you will be better informed about that by the translator's own letter. Good-bye, Excellent Sir and my best-loved friend. My wife and children send you their best wishes.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 22 September

B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 38-9.
d'Amsterdam ce 22 Sept. 1690
Monsieur,
je vous doibs depuis longtemps un mot de lettre. j'attendois le moment de vous pouvoir mander a mon tour quelque nouvelle surprenante. n'attendez pas pourtant que ce soit quelque nouvelle d'estat, il semble qu'on n'en vous scauroit mander cette année que des meschantes. non Monsieur, je ne passeray celles de ma famille, qui se prepare a une belle conqueste, ma petite femme toute languissante quelle paroit, espere de mettre bien tost un autre enfant au monde, et si on en croit son courage, et quon aye esgard a la grosseur de son corps, elle pouroit faire au dela, et nous donner deux bezons.†1 elle croiroit sa joie parfaitte, si vous vous trouviez a ce beau moment, Je vous assure Monsieur, quelle vous feroit chaire entiere, sa passion de vous y voir va au dela de ce que vous pouvez imaginer. Mais comment vous y convier vu la saison avancée et fascheuse, et qu'a tout bien prendre il y auroit de l'impertinence de vouloir troubler vostre repos pour estre a la naissance d'un miserable enfant, et qui peutestre ne verra pas le jour. ce sont <de>†a passions qui luy naissent dans l'idée que nous vous reverrons encore un jour, et que vous nous dite que vostre despart a desja esté tout prest. Ma seur De Wilde est encore grosse pour une autre fois; mais pour elle ce n'est pas miracle. jay soigné le mois passé, de collationer vostre Compte qui s'est trouvé exact. la ...†a Vous aurez receu apparemment la bagatelle que ma femme vous a envoyé par Monsieur Daranda. toute la famille vous presente ses tres humble respects. et je suis comme je le doibs
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant Serviteur
P GUENELLON.
