1319. Gisbertus Verrijn to Locke, 13/23 September [1690] (1339)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, f. 18. Year from Locke's endorsement. For the writer see no. 1179 n.
(English) Vir Eruditissime, Acutissime et Expertissime.
Annus est, et quod excurrit, a quo elaboratissimum Cogitationum Tuarum de Intellectu Humano Specimen†1 Latinum facere sum aggressus Hortatu clarissimi Domini Joh: Clerici; ex quo cùm te percupere Cogitationes Tuas Romano expressas idiomate†2 rescivissem, id oneris in me suscepi, impar ipse licèt tunc præsertim temporis, utpote qui vixdum prima Linguæ Anglicæ Fundamenta jeceram. Nunc verò tandem aliquando integro operi impositurus ultimam manum, accuratioremque singulis ejus partibus limam adhibiturus e re meâ duxi Te primùm consulere, quid de meâ tractatûs Tui versione agendum videatur. Tibi priùs non visam publico dare haud sustineo, quâ commodissimâ ratione videnda tibi queat exhiberi, nullus equidem scio. Haud inconsultum fortassè foret, si per vices frustulatim Tibi mitteretur, revidenda, emendanda, corrigenda. Quippe non is sum, qui imaginer in omnibus
― 134 ―
Mentem me Tuam accuratissimè cepisse. In longè plurimis <non>†a hallucinatum me mihi†b persuadeo. In nonnullis Tua mediocriter expressisse parum abest ut sperem, in omnibus operam pro virili navâsse certus sum. Nîl itaque superest, quàm ut impedimenta remoræque omnes, quæ editionem Latinè forsan ab ignaris Linguæ Anglicæ jam exspectati diu Voluminis protelare queunt longius amoveantur, in quo nullus ego defuero, si per humanitatem Tuam liceat, ut a Te, quos commisi in vertendis Tuis cogitatis errores, ostendantur, expungantur, potioraque reponuntur. Quî tutò maximè et commodè ad Te folia nonnulla repetitis vicibus appellere queant, Te quàm optimè scire non dubitaverim. Quare Te obnixè rogatum cupio, ut quantocyus Tuam hac de re Mentem aperire non dedigneris Tuis consiliis summâ cùm curâ obsecuturo. Interim Te incolumem diu studiorum, præcipuè Metaphysicorum, bono servare velit, Summum Numen supplex oro, veneror, obsecro,
Humillimus Tui Cliens
GISBERTUS VERRŸN.
Dabam Amstelædami ad diem Septembris 23.
(Latin) Most learned, acute, and accomplished Sir,
It is a year and more since I set about turning into Latin the highly wrought essay†1 of your reflections on the Human Understanding, which I did at the instigation of the distinguished M. Jean le Clerc; it was on learning from him that you were desirous of having your thoughts expressed in the Roman language†2 that I undertook the task, though personally unequal to it, especially at that time, when I had hardly laid the first foundations of my acquaintance with the English language. Now, however, that I am at last about to finish off the whole work and to polish particular parts of it more carefully, I thought it would be to my advantage if I first consulted you as to what you think should be done about my translation of your treatise. I cannot think of publishing it unless it has first been seen by you; but I do not know how it can most conveniently be submitted to you for your inspection. Perhaps the wisest course would be if it were sent back and forth between us in instalments for you to look through, emend, and correct. I suggest this as I am not the man to imagine that I have grasped your meaning in everything [p. 134] with complete accuracy. In by far the most cases I feel sure that I have <not> been mistaken; in some I may almost hope that I have expressed your thoughts fairly well; whilst in everything I am certain that I have done my best. Nothing therefore remains but to secure the removal of all obstacles and delays which might further defer the publication in Latin of a book that has now been long awaited by those who are possibly unacquainted with the English language; to which task I shall not be found wanting if you are kind enough to permit that the mistakes I have made in rendering your thoughts may be pointed out, removed, and replaced with something better by yourself. I do not doubt that you know best what is the safest and most convenient way in which some sheets can reach you from time to time; I therefore beg you most earnestly to be kind enough to let me know what you think about this as soon as possible; you may be sure that I shall scrupulously follow your advice. Meanwhile that Almighty God may long preserve you safe and sound for the good of studies, especially the metaphysical, is the earnest prayer and supplication of
Your most humble servant
GISBERT VERRIJN.
Amsterdam 23 September.
Address: Viro Doctissimo, Eruditissimo, Clarissimo Domino Johanni Locke M.D.
Endorsed by Locke: Verryn 23 Sept. 90 Answered 23

1320. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 16 September [1690] (1315, 1353)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 7-8. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Sept. 16
I was at last very agreeably surprise'd with mr Lock's letter. who I did Conclued had with as much ease as I own you had reason forgott that you ever had made so troublsome an acqantance, but passing that I am by this to excuse my self both to my good Lady Masham and you Sir for not haveing soner answered your letter's if being obliged to double waiting (Mrs Windham†1 being gone home sicke) and to this the trouble of removeing be a just excuse I doe assure you tis a very true one and to have this occasion to tell you so I was Forcet aske leave to stay in town affter My Misstriss,†2 I had writ to My lady M: but in her last she forbid me till I sent her a ceartin paper which is not yet in My power I am very glad to find that My knowing you writ to My L: P.†3 has made My lord M:†4 equall with him in your Favour as to this, but why you should imagin me so vaine as to brage how I cam to know it I cant imagin. I now Can satisfie you My lady†5 is safely returned from bath but what injury this newes may doe My lady Masham I am not suer. only I desier if it should perswaed you to leave her that you will not doe me the ill office to let her know it came from me, but upon the wholl to doe justice to all I cant think you can wish more to se my Lady Mon: then she express her disier of seing you so that if you doe not Come youle Chang my opinion of you as to this I give you many thankes for your Concern for My sister†6 who is not yet Come from Tunbridg but will be here on fryday and is I fear Condemed to goe imidiatly in to scotland with L. Southerland who has more then enouffe lost her self in this Cort since you went out of town, I cant pretend to tell you any publick newes all partes are strogling for the Mastery more then ever. My Lord Portland is Come home they say noe frind to our faire Marquiss but a might servant to the Black,†7 so that with some reason Changes are
― 136 ―
expected, but none to the advantage of poor England since in all probability it must be one of thes two ill's; C: Cutts†1 has been very dangerously wonded but is now in likly way to recover, my lady Mon: dos me just now the honour to Call me to Cary me home which is a good reason for My not adding more to this short letter or rather that I doe not add to the length an excuse for so intolerable a trouble which if pardonable on any acount it must be your belife that it Comes from one that is most syncerly to you
a most obliged frend and very Faithfull servant.
I must not forgit to tell you my Cosen Cuts†2 could scarss make more inquieryes affter her lover then she do's in every letter affter you I dare not let her know you doe not return it. My service to Sir F My La and all the good family. I wonder I have noe answer of two letter's I writ about 3 weekes agoe Concerning My Cosen Sam:

1322. Locke to Lady Masham, 30 September 1690 (1040, 2280)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 189-92. Draft, with many erasures and alterations, here mainly ignored. Some reconstruction and supplied punctuation in transcript. Locke was in London from 17 September until 14 October, when he returned to Oates: Journal.
It is possible Madam that I haveing very litle satisfaction in the place I am but what I have from your letters should yet be in danger to want them out of your neglect of me? and must I owe it to your quarrell with Mrs Lockhart rather than to your freindship to me that I yesterday received the honour of one from you? When I consider you I†a- know anger is not the genuine temper of your minde,-†a and when I reflect on my self methinks that unfreindly passion ought not to have any thing to doe with what comes from you to me, and yet I know not how it soe falls out that that is the only advocate I had lately with you and prevaild on you to write
― 138 ―
to me at a time when all the interest I had in your calmer thoughts should not it seems have procurd one word from you.†a
pardon me if I complain a litle on this occasion which soe nearly concernes me espetialy since the same true and long establishd freindship which has made me soe tender and sensible in this part bids me assure you that for all this complaint it makes me noe lesse sensible of the great obligations I <have>†b to you for your writeing soe often and can you blame me if throughy seasond by that freindship I am loath it should be lesse frequent. But however reasonable it may be to allow your Ladyship to disperse your owne Kindenesse in what measure you shall thinke fit yet I cannot bear it that you should deale soe hardly with mine and tell me that I am weary of writeing to you at the same time that you professe your resolution to have let the post have gon without bringing me any news from you. I have not omitted one post since I came to town. I plead it not as merit but looke on it as a priviledg and thanke you for allowing me when I doe not see you and when I doe not hear from you the next great pleasure I have to those which is to talke to you. I am soe much a flatterer of my self that I can finde severall excuses for you if you should sonetimes forbeare to write, but I leave it to you to consider whether you can finde in your heart to let any excuses stop these necessary effects of your freindship and I thinke it enough that you know that I have such an esteeme and respect for you that I cannot but be always much more happy for hearing from you though the same esteeme and respect will hinder me from being angry or quarrelling with you when I doe not
I told Mrs Lockhart I had received a letter lately from you wherein you bid me assure her you had writt to her twice and thankd her for the care she tooke of your things which you was satisfied was noe lesse than what you did of your owne she sais she received neither of those letters but that she would write to you the next post her self she came yesterday <to>†c town and sent for me to advise about her soar eyes which she has very much complaind of these 5 or 6 days. she was to have been bleeded to day and purgd to morrow but I knowing not whether if you had been here your self
― 139 ―
you would have said to her at this time any thing more of what was in your letter concerning that matter I forbore the rest till farther order
I know not whether I have don well or noe, but this I am sure had I not interested my self for you as for a sister or a daughter, or something nearer than those relations, I had never mentiond it to you at first. I am not ignorant how touchy those things are to medle with and tis with the same sincerity and freedome which I thinke you expect from me I tell you that if you were my daughter I should say My dear Child, they who are least faulty have advantage enough to make the greater allowance to others, and what boots it soe to maintain ones innocence as to loose or disobleige a friend. But I doe not soe far forget my self or you as to talke thus to your Ladyship only I thought it not well for me to tell her that seeing in the begining of your letter that the things were receivd she read not the remainder where in were your thanks for her care in sending them. you can assure her you writ her two letters in acknowledgment and you can freindly allow her not to have received them. you seeme to have reason to be angry with me for beleiveing that you had neglected to returne her thanks
I will always be answerable to all the world for your civility to every†a <one>†b and for your gratitude to your freinds. this I faild not to assure her of in respect to her self in that particular case. But what should I say to you when she told me positively more than once that in the same letter wherein you acknowledgd the receit of them you said not one word whether you were pleasd with them or noe. Will you make a serious businesse of it and urge it on her again that you did and expect that she should unsay what she had said and excuse her self to you for it. Consider what will that produce, or will you write lesse kindely to her than you intended before the receit of my letter and then what a happy instrument shall I have been between you by sending you that notice on purpose to prevent any misunderstanding. Consider too she has really don you the service you desired of her, but imagins she has received noe thanks from you for it, will you not take care that she shall be as sure that you thank her for it as that she did anything for you, rather than expect she should excuse her self to you for not acknowledging those thanks which she beleives she never receivd, If she has taken any care or pains about your things (according or
― 140 ―
contrary to your directions it matters not unlesse you will owne to her that it was soe negligently that you are not obleiged to her for it) and you doe not disowne that you owe her thanks for it will you not make her sensible that you doe thank her and if once doing it doe not satisfie her will you not repeat it twice or ten times or oftener rather then enter into a dispute that you have don it already. for this there is noe necessity of acknowledging a fault it is impossible you should ever be guilty of which is designedly to neglect returning your thanks but cannot the slip be laid on your scribe or be charged on those letters she says she never received and for your satisfaction if you thinke fit I will endeavour to get a sight of the letter wherein she says you mentiond the receit of your things. when you are obleiged by any one there is noe remedy but you must convince them that you acknowledg it unlesse you will have a quarrell or a coolnesse the forerunner of one, and give them the advantage in it. Whether if you finde any one too capritious†a or unreasonable in punctillios you will thinke them worth the continuance of your familiarity or fit to be imploid an other time is an other question, where of you are at liberty to be judg, but are not at liberty not to doe what is your part what ever others doe on their side. except but†b me†b and if in coole bloud you resolve it fit to have any misunderstanding to fall out or breake with any one else you have my cosent on condition you manage it soe as to keepe the advantage and right on your side and leave all the just blame or regret to the other. You may perhaps thinke I have dwelt too long and too seriously on a subject not weighty enough to deserve it. I had rather erre on that hand than appear negligent in any thing where in your Ladyship is concernd. And since you require it of me as a duty of freindship mine is soe sincere and soe obedient that It makes me discover my naked thoughts though they chance to differ from yours and that in a case very nicely to be medled in and wherein I perceive your anger is a litle up and has already put you not in the best humor towards me. But were it not that you are yet in this mortal state where in some†c- degree <of> passion-†c perhaps once in 7 years may a litle disturb you I in dischargeing this difficult duty of freindship should have noething to doe, for your owne reason will never mislead you and therefor when you have sedately consulted that I shall not be concernd if you condemne my opinion
― 141 ―
in the case and follow the contrary. I shall only take care that you shall never have reason to blame my want of zeale or concerne for you, for I am sure I am an infallible freind to you though I thinke my self very far from an infallible adviser
After you could finde in your heart to put soe unjust a supposition <into your letter>†a if†b- you are weary of writeing-†b tis noe wonder you should reproach me for not haveing given you a particular account of my cough which I thought I had don in a way to let you see how well you had by your care of me disarmed it. But since your kindenesse and care of my <person>†c will not be satisfied without a more particular account I must owne that though it be a litle increased since I came to towne yet the retreat and security Sir Francis and you have soe favourably given me at Oates†1 against it which I desire always to acknowledg to you both makes me now not looke on it with that apprehension and aversion I was wont to doe. If my cough trouble me not I shall have the satisfaction of comeing to oates as soon as I can disintangle my self heare without being driven thither by the necessity of my health and if it grow stronger upon me it will soon breake the ties and appearances of businesse that severall expect should hold me here and it will with pleasure hasten me to a place where I desire to be when ever I can without the reproach of those whom either gratitude or good manners obleige me to pay some deference to. But be not Madam I beseech you too hastily thus severe upon me. if you saw all my thoughts since I left oates I am sure you would pitty me and a litle mollifie your stile into an other more suited to the condition of one who sufficently feels the uneasinesse of being here without any addition to it from your hand. I am very glad your cold is gon and troubled that masters†2 cough is not if it continues pray†d the syrop here in directed and let him take that a spoonfull mornings or at nights either by it self or in cowslip water
Judg by this unmeasurable letter which is likely first to be weary I writeing or you reading what I write. Though I must confesse I was never lesse satisfied with any letter I ever writ to you in my life. I have some thing within tells me this is not the conversation I ought to have with you. The perfection and goodnesse of your
― 142 ―
inlightend and enlarged minde had given me the view and tast of one of an other kinde. Why would you without any occasion soe soon interrupt it. If freindship too must be made use of to imbitter those few happy howers are to be expected in this world tis time to give up this foolish†a game of life with all its vaine hopes and retire. Pardon this melancholy reflection which I cannot help though I distrust not your goodnesse I cannot suspect your freindship though <anger>†b or I know not what has a litle usurped the place of it. but yet I have some parts in my soule very tender and when I am in pain I can not avoid feeling it. If I am as I thinke rich in your freindship let me be the better for it, be at ease in it and rejoyce suitable to such a state, it will else be a strange management to allow my title to a great treasure and yet let me pine for want enterteine not any hard or unkinde thoughts you know not why of a man who will never deserve any other from you but what are due to the higest esteeme and sincerest friendship. I am
Endorsed by Locke: JL to L Masham 30 Sept 90

1325. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 16/26 October 1690 (1270, 1328)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 46-7.
Rotterdam 26 October 1690
Dear Sir
The bearer hereof Wetsteyns brother,†1 telling me he was bound for London this packet, and enquiring If I had nothing to you, made me resolve to send you by him, these 2 pieces, which I had else kept to send by Captain Robinson;†2 I received them from Monsieur Le Clerc in sheets, and looking into the Index of his work, I found something about le Peché Philosophique, which made me get them sticht, in hopes to understand what that is, but I am never a whit the wiser for what's there said of it: Unless it be an opinion maintaind by all the Casuists of the Jesuits (and then its no new thing) and is this that care of a mans salvation, of informing himself any thing about it, is no ways necessary to Salvation. This or some such defence of a brutish ignorance and carelessness in men of once knowing, muchless, doing their duties seems to be it. If you know particularly pray inform me.†3
I thank you heartily for the 2 prints,†4 but I am deprived of the benefit of your Letter about them; which I presume you sent by that packet that was cast overboard for feare the Letters should be carryed up to Dunkerk.†5 I hope you will however be pleasd to take the same pains again, and give me the same Informations.
― 145 ―
At the same time, and by the same hand, I received from mr. Popple. The Answer to the Letter of Toleration, whose Author is a Ninny, or he writes booty, if the worthy Gentleman be known, I would gladly know his name. I presume he printed it, at his own charges, the paper being so good, and the stuff so singular.†1 With it I received the Ingenious reply to him,†2 in which he is as ingeniously corrected, as Sir R:F:†3 in the Treatises of Goverment; I wish he may be the better for it. I received besides Dr. Sherlocks Vindication of the Doctrine of the Trinity, I hope the Noter upon the Athanasian Creed, will now pull in his hornes, or push them further out, and shew the contradictions he so confidently talks of.†4
But what I expected more while my friend thought upon Dr. Sherlock, was, the account of his Conversion; for I suppose he has taken more care of his reputation than to leave the world to think it to be in expectation of a Bishopric, or to be the more capable of serving his Jure Divino masters:†5
The next piece I received was mr. Norrises christian blessedness, and cursory reflexions upon your Essay Sir.†6
And I hope by this time that you are sufficiently convinc'd that you had's good not have writ at all, if the understanding takes no notice of it self. That you are yet to tell the world what you mean
― 146 ―
by the word Idea. That there are Principles to which all mankind give an universall assent, because there are Propositions self evident. Tho all men assent not to them, till they think upon them, or are brought so to do. That there maybe truths imprinted upon the soule, tho she nor perceivs nor understands them; because the soule may have lost the view of many Ideas she once had, and yet has dormant in her memory, that is because she cant view and think upon all things at once. That as there is a certain time for thinking. or when children begin to think. so there is for such and such thoughts: and that (tho there are no innate Ideas propositions, or principles Imprinted upon any soule or mind) yet those which are not perceived till after a long time of thinking may as wel be innate, as any other perceivd long before.
That you have contradicted yourself, in denying that there is any practical truth universally received when this Proposition is (tho not perhaps universally received or thought on) as certain as any demonstration in Euclid, and as plain too—which you have assignd p: 274. sect. 18.†1 viz. That there is no injustice where there is no propriety. And because you own as incontestable principles, in morality, as in any other science. That Innate truths maybe deduced from Reason; and conclusions as wel Innate as propositions: tho indeed neither be so. That an Innate law (if there were any such) may as welbe transgressed, as a written and otherway known one. That 'tis not so easy a matter, as you imagind, to distinguish between innate, and other Impressions. Because Caiaphas could not distinguish his Inspired impression, from his own thoughts.†2
Nay I hope by this time you are satisfyed that there are no mental impressions at all; and that al your labours lost, as well in shewing how the mind comes to have any thing impressd upon it, as that it has nothing so innately, tho your book (pray be not proud) be so excellent, that the Gentleman would not part with it for half a Vatican;†3 pray how much mony is that?
And finally I hope he has given you and the world, if not there, in his Reason and Religion; a clearer Idea, and account of the presentialness of his λόγος or Ideal world, what it is, and how we see in it all things.†4
― 147 ―
The gentleman being come for this, I must break off; and onely tell you, I expect satisfaction from you, nothing but confession or explication, or what you please, that may satisfy an impartiall man as I am.
I shall ad that monsieur Le Clerc desireing me to get him if possible, the naked Gospell,†1 and in the meantime to lend him mine that he maybe upon the bones of Jurieu, that fals foule upon the Author. I have lent him mine, and all the other books above mentioned.
My thief†2 and I are now pretty nigh an end, I shall lose the best part of £100 by him, I hope by the Capt.†3 to send your account.
My Lord Bellomont, will have acquainted you of the uproar here and raseing of our Bailljus house.†4 The rabble has been at that work at haarlem, at the Bailljus there, and 3 Burgermasters but were suppressed.†5 Theres one that rules and overrules and dos what he lists.†6 Its thought those of Leyden will avenge Sir Tho: Armstrong.†7
If it goes no further than to fright here and there a bashaw, the harm will not be much—
I am
Sir
Yours—
Endorsed by Locke: B: Furly 26 Oct 90 Answered 4° Nov:
― 148 ―
1326. Locke to Edward Clarke, 17 October 1690 (1313, 1347)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 35. Printed in Rand, pp. 301-2. The addressee from Clarke's endorsement and the contents.
Oates 17 Oct 90
Dear Sir
Things goeing soe easy soe smooth and soe right in your house,†1 I know you will excuse me that I went into the country to enjoy there an uninterrupted satisfaction and quiet in the contemplation of them.†2 I hope they continue on in the same course since my comeing away, and the zeale and forwardnesse of you your selves makes it needlesse for us without dores soe much as to thinke of the publique which is the happyest state a country can be in, when those whose businesse it is, take such care of affairs that all others quietly and with resignation acquisce and thinke it superfluous and impertinent to medle or beat their heads about them. You will see what I say in the inclosed which I desire you to seale and deliver and discourse accordingly if you see occasion. You have a right to doe it because in truth you were the first who suggested that thought to me and the more I have reflected on it the more I am convincd you were in the right. You may from me consult my Lady†3 about it whom you will finde of our side. However I will be sure to come to town either to prevent or prepare for the journy whenever I am sent for and therefor pray let me not faile to hear from you if either the house be like to rise or any preparations be made or orders given concerning the Ks journy.†4 but I would willingly finish what I came for before I returne if I may, but that still shall give way to any commands from my Lord†5 your self or any of my friends in town. My humble service to them all particularly the gent were with you at my chamber the day before I came away. I am
perfectly yours
J L
you are kindly rememberd here

B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 53. Approximate dates for nos. 1328 and 1331 can be worked out from statements in nos. 1331 and 1336 and from the endorsement of no. 1331. Six days before receiving Locke's letter Furly wrote to him by the captain (sc. Robinson): p. 161. 1329. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 22 October/1 November 1690 (1284, 1381)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 44-5. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 44-5.
A Amsterdam le 1 de Novembre 1690.
J'ai envoié, Monsieur, depuis quelques jours deux Livres à M. Furly, qui m'a promis de vous les faire tenir: C'est le dernier Tome de la Bibliotheque et ma version de la Philosophie des Chaldéens.†4 Il m'a prêté quelques livres Anglois, entre lesquels sont les Cursory Reflexions de M. Norris. Quand il n'auroit pas mis ce titre à son livre, il ne seroit pas difficile de voir qu'il l'a fait en courant. Au moins les trois ou quatre premiéres pages m'ont paru d'un homme qui n'entendoit rien en ce qu'il criticoit. J'en parlerai dans la Bibliotheque, et je ne manquerai pas d'insinuer ce qu'on en peut croire.†5 J'ai aussi quelques livres Anglois de la Tolerance, que je ferai valoir comme il faut contre nos†a Persecuteurs.†6 Je ne doute pas que vous n'aiez recu
― 151 ―
mon Specimen de la Version du V.T.†1 Faites moi la grace de me dire ce que vous en pensez. S'il en paroit néanmoins quelques nouveaux de consequence, vous m'obligerez de m'en avertir, parce qu'il faut que j'aide autant que je pourrai celui qui me succedera.†2 Mr. Furly ma aussi prêté l'Evangelium naked, et la Vindication de M. Sherlok. Le paradis n'est néanmoins pas si fort en leur disposition qu'ils se l'imaginent, et j'aurois peur pour moi que si je le fermois ainsi aux autres, je n'en fusse exclus moi même. Hoc θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται†3 et tout le secret est de ne faire tort à personne. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant Serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Celui qui vous rendra cette Lettre est un Marchand Libraire de Geneve de mes Amis nommé M. de Tournes. Il a dessein de voir M. Boyle, et vous m'obligerez de le lui recommender. C'est un honête homme, et qui a fait imprimer les Oeuvres Latines de M. Boyle. Si ce dernier s'en plaint, il est prêt de lui donner toute sorte de satisfaction.†4

1330. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 24 October/3 November 1690 (1317, 1335)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, f. 50. Answered by no. 1335.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Mensis jam est, et quod excurrit, ex quo literas ad Te dedi, quibus suas junxerunt duo cognati, Guenellonus et Verrinus. Hactenus autem nemo nostrum ullum a Te accepit responsum; quare veremur ne adversa utaris valetudine. Fateor meas nullum flagitare responsum, verum D. Guenellonus ait, suas illius esse argumenti, quod responsum omnino flagitare videatur. Verrinus de versione tractatus tui de Intellectu humano scripsit. Neutiquam credimus literas nostras aberrasse, quia per ordinarium tabellarium missæ sunt. Retulit mihi D. Clericus, accepisse se duos tractatus Anglicos: prior est refutatio Epistolæ de Tolerantia, ante sesqui annum hic editæ, cujus, quia mihi mirifice placuit, exemplar me Tibi misisse memini, ut et tu eam legeres et expenderes; alter illius Epistolæ est defensio: hanc dicit D. Clericus admodum esse accuratam ac solidam, et dignam quæ Epistolæ jungatur. Doleo me non gnarum linguæ Anglicæ, ut librum istiusmodi legere et intelligere possim: Ipse vero ait, se illius argumentum velle exhibere in bibliotheca universali, quæ finiente hoc anno proditura est. D. Venius, amicissimus nobis, Tibi per me nuntiari voluit, uxorem suam nocte ea,
― 153 ―
quæ inter vigesimum octavum et vigesimum nonum Octobris, seu inter diem Saturni et Solis proxime elapsum media fuit, correptam passione iliacâ, quæ quotidie ingravescens omnia remedia respuit; donec tandem heri mane, seu dië Jovis, qui fuit secundus diës Novembris, circa horam quintam morbi violentiâ extincta est, ac marito et liberis triste sui desiderium reliquit. Scio Te Viri amicissimi doloris expertem esse nolle: non enim prospera tantum et læta, sed et adversa ac tristia amicorum communia sunt. Ita et nos admonemur mortalitatis nostræ, nobisque nil nisi breve vitæ spatium esse concessum: cum sæpe miseri hic nobis æternitatem promittamus. Plurimam Tibi Dominus Venius scribi jussit salutem: Salutant Te generi ipsius filiæque, uxor mea ac liberi, omniaque Tibi prospera ac fausta a Patre luminum precantur: Imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 3 Novembris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
It is now a month and more since I wrote to you; two kinsmen, Guenellon and Verrijn, enclosed letters of their own with mine. So far none of us has received any reply from you, which makes us fear that you may be suffering from ill health. I admit that my own letter calls for no answer; but Mr. Guenellon says that the contents of his certainly seem to demand one. Verrijn wrote about the translation of your treatise on the Human Understanding. We cannot possibly suppose that our letters have gone astray, as they were sent by the regular post. Mr. Le Clerc has told me that he has received two English treatises. The first is a refutation of the Epistola de Toleratione, which was published here a year and a half ago; I remember that I sent you a copy, as I was wonderfully pleased with it, so that you too might read and judge of it. The other is a defence of that Letter, which Mr. Le Clerc says is a very careful and sound piece of work and deserves to be attached to the Letter. I am sorry that I have no knowledge of English, so that I cannot read and understand a book of that kind; but Mr. Le Clerc says that he means to publish the gist of it in the issue of the Bibliotheque universelle which is due to appear at the end of this year. Mr. Veen, our very close friend, wished me to let you know that in the night [p. 153] between 28 and 29 October, that is between Saturday and Sunday last, his wife was seized with an attack of colic, which grew daily worse and refused all remedies, until at last yesterday morning, Thursday the second of November, about five o'clock, she expired under the stress of the malady, leaving her husband and children to lament their heavy loss. I know that you would not wish to have no part in the grief of so dear a friend; for it is not only joy and prosperity but sorrow and adversity that friends have in common. So we too are reminded that we are mortal and that only a brief space of life is granted us, though often, poor souls, we may promise ourselves endless life here below. Mr. Veen has told me to send you his warmest greetings; his sons-in-law and his daughters send you theirs, as do my wife and children; they pray you may have all prosperity and happiness from the Father of lights, as I do myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 3 November
1690
Address: For Doctor John Locke at Mrs. Smithsbijs in Dorset Coort in Chanell row Westminster
Postmark: NO 6

1331. Benjamin Furly to Locke, [c. 27 October/6 November 1690] (1328, 1336)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 48. For the proposed date see no. 1328 n.
Deare Sir
It is now past 3 in the morning and so you must not expect long preambles. I see I guessed right, that that Letter went to the bottom of the Deep, I hope the Enditer received mine by yong Wetstein, in which I condoled the Losse of it,†1 but now you assure me I am like to have the originall, I long, and think every day 7 till I see it, and him that brings it.†2 comes he over to see, be, or assist at the new creation so much talkt of?†3 or what, pray if he be not come away desire him to call at mr. Popples and bring me Dr. Cudworth,†4 and let him not forget to bring with him my accounts, for my rascall is run away and I cannot find where he has layd my copies of them; I understand this post by Joseph Wright†5 that he has now at last receivd of mr. Foche the £23:7:6 that I was to pay in the hague for my Lord, but as for the £10 which I lent his brother Osmond, I understand, Foche says he dyed in Ireland, yet outlived his quarter day, and so Foche confesses he has so much in his hands. But can not pay it, without my Lords order; Pray be so kind as to speak to my Lord about it: In a time when we get little and live upon the Expence, to retrieve 10£ If a man can fairly and honestly, I think my duty.†6 My Grand Debtor Swinton is now in full possession of his fathers Estate of £1000 per Annum. And being turnd, or rather declared A Calvinist, he is become a member of Parliament,†7
― 155 ―
If Madam Lockhart, when she has securd her own debt, could get me any part of mine, she would do an act of charity to a man, and family abused by every body. I will neither detain you, nor my self longer, but conclude with my humble service to her, to your good self and Landlady†1 and her sisters, as also that of my wife, not forgetting Mr†a Clark Sir Walter and honest J.F.†2 I am told that mr Kick is like to return C— hither, but I cannot beleeve it.
I am
Sir
Entirely yours
B.F.—
Apples

1332. Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton, to Locke, 28 [October] 1690 (1338)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 137 Printed in King, pp. 216-17 (with month as September); Newton, Correspondence, iii. 79 (no. 355). The correct month from the postmark.
The writer is the author of the Principia (1687); born in 1642; F.R.S. 1672; president of the Royal Society from 1703 until his death in 1727; knighted 1705: D.N.B. The earliest extant evidence for his acquaintance with Locke is contained in a letter from Nicolas Fatio de Duillier (p. 378) to Newton, 24 February of this year; Locke was to make an application to Monmouth on Newton's behalf; Newton was also concerned in finding a tutor for Lord Mordaunt: Newton, Corr. iii. 390; see also no. 1252.
Sir
I had answered your letter sooner but that I staid to revise and send you the papers which you desire.†3 But the consulting of Authors proving more tedious then I expected so as to make me defer sending them till the next week, I could not forbear sending this letter alone to let you know extreamly glad I was to hear from you. For tho your letter brought me the first news of your having been so dangerously ill, yet by your undertaking a journey into Holland†4 I hope you are well recovered. I am extremely much obliged to my Lord and Lady Monmoth for their kind remembrance of me and
― 156 ―
whether their designe succeed or not must ever think my self obliged to be their humble servant.†1 I suppose Mr Fatio is in Holland for I have heard nothing from him the half year. Sir I am
Your most humble servant
IS. NEWTON.
Cambridge Sept 28. 1690
Address: For Mr Lock at his lodgings in Dorset Court in Channel Row in Westminster
Postmark: OC 29

1334. Elizabeth Yonge to Locke, 3 November 1690 (857, 1337)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 136-7.
Escott Nov. 3d. 1690
Sir
I could not with any confidence give you this trouble, especially at this time when soe many things of greater moment require your thoughts, and which indeed only deserve them, had I not by experience found you to be the most indulgent father, and the most Obliging of all men; which encourages me to hope for your Pardon, and once more beg your advice, that has always been successfull to me, and which I am sure I vallue above all the worlds beside. the occasion of it is this, a bout a month since I perceived a little swelling in my left cheek, Just underneath the Jaw bone, and is now grown to the bignes of a small Walnut, it seems to be of a hard substance, and soe loose in the flesh that twill slip under my finger. it is not at all sore, or tender, but I sometimes feel a little pain in it, but tis very little and is soon over, there is nothing of rednes appears but the flesh looks as it uses to doe, but it being in a place which is usual for swellings of the Kings-evil it makes me the more concerned at it, tho I am willing to flatter my self its nothing of that nature, our Family having never been subject to it, and for my own particular have always been of a healthy constitution and never had any swelling of this nature before, and am at this time in other respects extreamly well. however I am a little causeous how I tamper with it for fear of the worst, therefore beg you to give me your opinion in it at your first leasure, whither a dissolving plaister will be proper, or inward medicins pray freely advise me what I ought to doe in this case, which I promis my self you will doe, it being so much your inclination to doe good, and having been
― 158 ―
always ready to oblige me, for which I am more indebted to you then I can express. besides pray remember your Daughter is not yet past her preferment, that moderate share of beauty which she posseses will be much eclips'd, and I believe will doe little execution for the future, noe Englishman will soe much as break their sheens for her unless you help her to get rid of this blemish, but to be more serious, I shall look on it as a new Obligation upon me to esteem and honnour you, and as a fresh instance of your Friendship which I shall always cherrish, and endevour to deserve in the best manner I am able. I know not where this will find you, either in London or in the country, therefore must inclose it to Sir Walter to convey to you; my Bro: and Sis: Duke was here last week, and desir'd me to give you their humble service, he finds himself extreamly well since the waters, and has now none of his old complaints. but I was much troubled to see my Sister return in soe low a condition, and without the usual benifitt of the waters. I think I never saw her soe thin, but she is something better now, which she imputes to her constant drinking of water in persuance of your advice and design's to continue it. I think its now time to release you, when I have once more begg'd Pardon for thus presuming on your time and patience, and hasten to assure you I am in great Sincerity
Sir
Your most affectionate Dutyfull Daughter
and humble servant ELIZ: YONGE
Address: For Mr John Lock These
Endorsed by Locke: E: Yonge 9° Nov. 90.
1335. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 7 November 1690 (1330, 1368)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256 s. Printed in Ollion, pp. 197-8. Answers no. 1330.
(English)
London 7 Nov. 90
Vir Amplissime
Heri accepi tuas 3° hujus mensis datas quibus me silentii accusas et justò quamvis innocentem accusas, respondi enim et tuis et
― 159 ―
Verrini humanissimis literis eodem quo accepi tempore et copiose quidem tuis respondi, amplam enim nostri ecclesiastici rescribendi suppeditarunt materiam nec vester <Synodicus>†a fervor nostrum de rebus theologicis orthodoxum zelum longe superat. Hæc scripsi sed ut jam video omnia absorpsit mare, Navis enim tabellaria à Gallis pene capta <epistolarum>†b sarcinam, ne in hostium manus venirent, effudit in mare, has inter meam ad Te et ad Verrinum alteram.†1 Id in nuperis ad Guenellonem dubitans monui a te jam certior factus rem ita accidisse, quod doleo, Nam licet tua me humanitas securum reddat, nollem tamen cum et illius urbanitas et res ipsa festinationem exigeret in respondendo tardus Verrino videri. Te igitur apud illum patronum paro. Epistolæ defensio quam laudat D Clericus illius esse creditur ad quem tu olim ipsam epistolam uti scribis misisti. Gratulor patriæ nostræ, si, quæ a vobis Latinè eduntur, nos sermone Anglicano possimus defendere, sed causæ bonitas minus dificile reddit patrocinium. Uxorem tam prudentem juventæ suæ socium senectutis solatium Veenio nostro avelli sine maximo suo†c mærore non posse satis certo scio, et an
― 160 ―
quid crudi adhuc vulneris dolorem lenire possit dubito. Non tamen deero amici officio. Utrumque amavi, defunctam lugens desidero, superstitem colo et veneror, nec beneficiorum quæ ab utroque accepi ulla vetustas minuet memoriam. Quam D Verrino scripsi tuæ inclusi epistolæ, nam vicum in quo Amstelodami habitat ignoro, ignoscas rogo. Si versionem ad me suam transmittendam cogitet, quod forsan non abs re fuerit Furleio nostro tradendam suadeo Is enim diligenter curabit ut recte ad me mittatur. Ego quamprimum accepero perlegam et mutatis si qua sint quæ a mente mea aberraverint restituam. Veenio nostro hac nocte scripsi. eum Guenellonios reliquosque amicos meos præsertim eos qui in tua sunt domo meo nomine quam officiosissime salutes. vale et ut facis me ama tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin) London 7 Nov. 90
Excellent Sir, Yesterday I received your letter dated the 3rd of this month, in which you accuse me of silence, and with reason, though you are accusing an innocent [p. 159] man, for I replied to your own and to Verrijn's very kind letters at the same time as I received them; yours, indeed, I replied to at some length, for our ecclesiastics supplied me with ample material for writing back; your synodical fervour does not greatly surpass our orthodox zeal in theological matters. I wrote about these things; but, as I now see, the sea has swallowed up everything, for the packet-boat was almost captured by the French and the bag of letters was thrown overboard to avoid their falling into enemy hands, amongst them mine to you and the other to Verrijn.†1 I told Guenellon so in a recent letter, though I was doubtful about it; I now know for certain from you that that is what happened. I am sorry for it; for although your own kindness sets my mind at rest, yet I should not wish to seem to Verrijn to be slow in answering, when both his courtesy and the matter itself called for haste. I therefore provide you to plead my case with him. The defence of the letter which Mr. Le Clerc approves of is believed to be the work of the person to whom, as you tell me, you sent the letter itself some time ago. I congratulate our country if we are able to defend in English works that are published by your people in Latin; but the excellence of the cause renders advocacy by no means difficult. Our friend Veen, I am sure, cannot have suffered the sudden loss of so sagacious a wife, the companion of his youth and the solace of his age, without the deepest grief, and I doubt [p. 160] whether anything can assuage the pain of the wound while it is still fresh. I shall not fail, however, in a friend's duty. I loved them both; I mourn the dead and feel her loss, whilst I cherish and honour him who survives her; nor will any length of time obscure the memory of the kindnesses I have received from them both. I have enclosed a letter to Mr. Verrijn in yours, as I do not know what street of Amsterdam he lives in; please excuse this. If he should be thinking of sending me his translation, which perhaps may not be useless, I advise that it be delivered to our friend Furly; he will take care that it is properly dispatched to me. As soon as I get it I will read it and return it after making alterations if there are any places where it may have missed my meaning. I have written to our friend Veen this evening. Please remember me very kindly to him and to the Guenellons and the rest of my friends, especially those of your household. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
LOCKE
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graaft t'Amsterdam
Postmark: LV
Noted by Limborch (beneath date): Recepta 25 Novembris.

1336. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 11/21 November [1690] (1331, 1344)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 49. Year from Locke's endorsement.
21th Nov.
Sir
Yours of the 4/14†1 I have, and am glad this finds you in safe harbour, I am glad you have mine by the Captain, and dou'bt not but you understand me, In answer I thinke safe enough at present, and will so remain while it keeps that forme, I have found the Jesuits Peché Philosophique, I doubt not but you have received mine in answer to yours which I received not till 6 days after the Captain went away,†2 in which I desired your friend†3 to bring with him, if not come away Dr. Cudworths booke, that we began once to read together, I suppose he intends over by the Captain and should be glad to receive Rushworths,†4 and Burnets Historyes†5 which make I think 6 parts†a and a smal folio of William Penns called the Christian Quaker.†6 I am of that Ladyes†7 mind that William Ames†8 is a man whose memory deserves as much to be preserved as any mans among us, and that may be one Reason why he is so much neglected, and his Writings not collected; as others among them when they dye. Robert Barclay†9 is lately dead and one Robert Lodge†10 and John Burnyeat†11 two of the best speakers that ever I heard, the first tho a butcher one of the meekest men living of a very chearfull spirit full of love, and sweetness, and when
― 162 ―
he spake a heavenly magick and melody as Dr. Foot†1 use to phrase it attended him. Pray recommend me to the Doctor when you see and tell him his Angelical melodious man Robert Lodge is dead. I long to see your friend,†2 that we may have some winterchat. Pray learn and let me know, if it may be who was author of that smart piece intituled, The True cause of the present Scarcity of mony, and the proper Remedies for it.†3 I perceive there some think as well as I, that a shilling, by being carried into Pennsylvania, and there called 15d, is not a farthing the more worth, for its new name. Whether are we rambling? Do we think we can hinder the carrying out of Bullion, or coin either by Laws? We laugh at your politics; If your parliaments would never trouble their heads about 2 things, thats Religion and Trade, we should grow both Religious and rich. Provided the Laws might be rigorously executed against immorality and debauchery, which I plead not for. I told your small friend†4 that I was to write to you, and would know what I should say of him. his answer was that he begins to read and write, and so he dos archly, hele soone or'etop John; he has perpetually his Esop Dutch and french,†5 In his hands, to learne Wysdom. But he wants the pictures in his booke.
This Evening his mother asking John, what he would do with his brother if she and I should dy, he answerd he would buy a chamber or Cellar to dwell in. The younker tooke him short up, and told him he never found chambers or cellars to be bought, (he is no Templer†6 you must know) but onely to be hired. which is true, here, but I thought far enough from his observation, but it seems he has learnd this from the bills he reads as he goes along. —we are making Triumphal Arches in the Hague, and all things fit for reception of our Stadholder and your king, God bless him, tho Van Beuningen†7 t'other day when they drank that health to him, turnd it and said heres a health to the K: of H. and Stadholder of E. He is in state, as Peganius†8 said approaching to that of a
― 163 ―
prophet and prints comments upon the Revelations that vex those that say he is made.†1 Tho he is pretty near the matter—my service
to Sir—and my Lady Masham—
Address: To mr. John Locke at Madame Smithsbyes in Channel Row— Dorset Court Westminster
Postmark: NO 20
Endorsed by Locke: B: Furly 21 Nov. 90 Answered 21
1337. Elizabeth Yonge to Locke, 12 November [1690] (1334, 1349)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 138-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Escott Nov. 12
Sir
I beg you to accept my utmost thanks for the favour of yours, in which you express that care and concern for me as has extreamly Obliged me, and you are much in the right when you imagin I will easily forgive your prescribing me a London Journey, for had I noe other inducement then the seeing you, and the rest of my Friends, that would be sufficient should I follow my inclinations; but I was much surprised to find you thought it necessary for me, I confess I did not apprehend it to be of that consequence, but thought that in the beginning you might have prevented any ill effects, tho I were at a distance from you, but I have always had that regard to your opinion and advice, that I shall most redily dispose my self to follow it. but I cannot soe suddenly as I might have don had I had my Bro: letter sooner, which came not to my hands till tuesday, soe that fryday was the first day that I could with any conveniency, begin my Journey; but my Brother and Sister Duke have desired me to defer it till wensday in the next week, for some particular reasons of theirs, and tis but 4 days odds, which they Imagin cannot be Injurious to me, the swelling not being at all increased, since I writt you last, but I fancy tis rather a little abated, but I know
― 164 ―
not whither it may be the nature of these swellings to rise and fall, with the increase or decrease of the Moon, however it be, I resolve to be absolutely disposed of by you, and shall without fail set forwards on that day if you approve it, which pray let me know by the next Post. I omitted to tell you one thing in my last, which is, that when I first perceived this swelling, before I thought of troubling you with it, I annointed it 4 or 5 nights following, with a warm dispersing ointment, which I have formerly used with success for swellings occasioned by the tooth-ache. but I sensibly found it grew bigger, which made me resolve to medle noe more with it; but then I was perswaded to wear a gold chain about my neck, and a piece of double flannell on my cheek, and to drink a glass of white wine every morning in which Rue had been infused, which I did accordingly, but till then I never felt any thing of pain in it, but I have every since more or less felt a pricking pain which I know not how to discribe, but its somtimes like the motion of a pulse; perhaps I have been to blame in what I have don; but I think I ought to conceal nothing, from you, since you are soe kind as to undertake the care of me, which is an Obligation I am extreamly sensible of, and shall be ever gratefully acknolidg'd, by
Your most obliged humble servant
ELIZ: YONGE.
My Brother and sister Duke with the rest of my sisters present you their humble service.
Address: For Mr John Lock These
Endorsed by Locke: E. Tonge 12 Nov 90 Answered 20
1338. Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton to Locke, 14 November 1690 (1332, 1357)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 138. Printed in King, pp. 215-16; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 82-3 (no. 357).
Novemb. 14th. 1690.
Sir
I send you now by the Carrier Martin, the papers I promised. I fear I have not only made you stay too long for them, but also made them too long by an addition. For upon the receipt of your letter, reviewing what I had by me concerning the text of 1 John 5.7, and
― 165 ―
examining authors a little further about it, I mett with something new concerning that other of 1 Tim. 3.16, which I thought would be as acceptable to inquisitive men, and might be set down in a little room; but by searching further into authors to find out the bottom of it is swelled to the bignesse you see. I fear the length of what I say on both texts may occasion you too much trouble, and therefore if at present you get only what concerns the first done into French, that of the other may stay till we see what successe the first will have. I have no entire copy besides that I send you, and therefore would not have it lost, because I may perhaps after it has gone abroad long enough in French put it forth in English. What charge you are at about it (for I am sure it will put you to some) you must let me know: for the trouble alone is enough for you.†1 Pray present my most humble service and thanks to my Lord and Lady Monmouth for their so kind remembrance of me. For their favour is such that I can never sufficiently acknowledge it. If your voyage hold I wish you a prosperous one and a happy return. I should be glad of a line from you to know that you have these papers, and how far you have recovered your health: for you told me nothing of that. I am
Sir
Your most faithful and most humble servant
IS. NEWTON.
Endorsed by Locke: I: Newton 14 Nov. 90 Answered 15

1339. Gisbertus Verrijn to Locke, 14/24 November 1690 (1319, 1391)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, f. 19. Apparently enclosed in no. 1340.
(English)
Viro Acutissimo, Doctissimo, Expertissimo Johanni Locke
S.P.D. Gisbertus Verrÿn
Tardior <Litterarum>†a Tuarum adventus hactenus nihil boni fuerat <ominatus>†b imò suspicionem injecerat de adversâ Valetudine, cum ex doctiss. D. Guenellon, cujus humanitate in hisce ad Te perfruor, rescirem, tandem aliquid responsi allatum Tuumque consilium de Versione meâ communicatum, scilicet cupere Te ut pars quædam quantocyus ad D. Furly Roterodamum mittatur inde ad Te deferenda. Hac in re Menti Tuæ jam fuissem obsecutus, nisi quæ commaculatiùs ob hîc et alibi crebriores emendationes scripta, quò distinctè legi possent, forent describenda denuò. Id nunc operam dabo, ut proximâ septimanâ primus speciminis†1 Tui Liber Roterodamum perferatur, rogans et obsecrans quàm obnixissimè, ut simulac ad Te appulerit, humanitati Tuæ lubeat, perlegere, corrigere, addere, expungere, prout visum fuerit, necnon quantâ poterit festinatione huc denuò, ut adferatur, curare. In reliquis Editioni, saltem Tuo conspectui adornandis non ego cunctabor. Interim dum
― 167 ―
hæc fiunt, Valetudinem Tibi exopto illibatam, integram, quæ perpetua ad extremum Vitæ Terminum ut sit, summus faxit rerum Arbiter. Vale et me Tui cultorem obsequentissimum ne diffide.
Daba<m>†a Amstelæd: Novembris xxiv. Anni MDCXC.
(Latin) To the most acute, learned, and accomplished John Locke from Gisbert Verrijn, greeting.
The delay in the arrival of any letter from you had up till now augured no good, indeed it had occasioned a suspicion that you might be unwell, when I learnt from the learned Mr. Guenellon, whose good offices I enjoy in sending you this letter, that a reply had at last been received and that you had stated your plan in regard to my translation; you desired, that is, that a part of it should be sent as soon as possible to Mr. Furly at Rotterdam, to be forwarded to you from there. I would now have complied with your wishes in this matter, except that some passages, which were rather defaced by the numerous corrections I have made here and there, had to be copied afresh in order to be clearly legible. I will now set to work on this, so that the first book of your essay may be sent to Rotterdam next week; I earnestly beg that as soon as it reaches you you will have the kindness to read it through and correct it, making what additions and deletions you may think fit, and that you will have it sent back here again as quickly as possible. I shall lose no time in preparing the remainder of the work for publication, or at [p. 167] least for your inspection. Meanwhile while all this is proceeding I pray that the supreme disposer of all things may grant you unimpaired and perfect health to last till your life's end. Farewell, and be assured that I am your most obedient servant.
Amsterdam 24 November 1690
Address: Viro Ornatissimo, Acutissimo, Expertissimo D. Johanni Locke MD. Londini.
Endorsed by Locke: G. Verryn 24° Nov. 90

Monsieur,
Vous verrez par l'incluse†1 que jay soigné a vostre commission; mais l'esgarement de vos lettres nous a tellement donné l'alarme, que nous vous <croyions>†b mort ou extremement malade, et la triste experience que <nous>†c venons de faire de la fragilité de la vie en perdant nostre bonne mere†2 en moins de cinq jour augmentoit nostre crainte pour vous. mais graces a Dieu vous vivez encore et ce nous est un gain qui adoucit aucunement†3 la perte irreparable d'une personne qui nous estoit si chere a tous et si necessaire a nostre pauvre pere dans son haut age et a ma petite femme, quelle aimoit si tendrement, et qui attend l'heure de son accouchement.

1341. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 21 November 1690 (1311, 1387)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 47-8.
Escott Nov: 21st. 90.
Dear Sir
I was lately made Happy by the receit of yours of 13th: instant, which brought me new assurances of your Friendship, and that I have still a place in your Memory and affections, which is necessary to my wellbeing. You have highly Obliged me also by the Present you have made me, which I Vallue more then I can express, nothing in the World could be so acceptable to me; and afford me so much pleasure, and improvement too; as the frequent reading of it, which is secured by its being put into my possession; I esteem it above all riches, and can never enough thank you for it. But Sir, how could you conclude your letter without saying something to me of my sister Betty's concern, since you know how nearly I am related to her both by Kindred, and Friendship; and that I cannot but be solicitous for her, you cannot escape me so; give me leave therfore to tell you that I have been in great pain for it, fearing it might prove the Evill,†1 it being a loose Glandule, without any pain, and in a suspitious place; how long it has been there we know not, but she never took notice of it till since my Brother went to London, 'twas at first about the bigness of a small Nutmeg, but with the anointing (of which she has given you an account) it grew
― 169 ―
sensibly; which made her afraid what it would grow to, and advising with a Lady in the Neibourhood, she perswaded her to wear Gold, and use the other things she mention'd to you; and in a day or two, she felt a small pricking, which at first was scarsely sensible, but has since been more considerable, and more frequent, so that she could not be satisfied till she had consulted you about it; and would have hasten'd to you, upon your first letter, but that it began to lessen, and is now but little bigger then when she first perceiv'd it. and she being fat it appears very little to the Eye, though it may easily be felt. she purposed to have determin'd her Journey as your second letter should advise, and summoned me over to meet it, and we were not a little disappointed that the two last Posts brought us none from You. pray do us the favour to write us by the next, your Opinion in full; and whither this pricking in it be a good or ill sign, and whither she does well to cover it so very warm, or it be better to leave it open to the Aire, as at other times when nothing is amiss; also whither the swelling call'd the Evill do usually increase, and abate with the Moon, and whither you do not think it necessary for her to enter speedily upon an alterative course, to rectify her blood, and prevent the increase, or worse consequences of this Humour; in which respect I fear delay may be injurious to her, though I can see no hast as to the swelling, there not appearing any tendency either to gathering or breaking; but she now tels me that this last Year she has felt a heat and itching in her Eyes, whenever she sate up, late or read much by Candle; which was troublesome to her, though not Visible to others; and for which she caused her self to be let blood in the Arm this Spring, which gave her relief, but has not wholly freed her from it. I hope you will think of some propper Course to set her right in all respects, which will be done with the more Ease if taken in the beginning; she depends upon your kindness and care of her; and will quickly hasten to you, or follow your directions here, as you shall think best. The tender of her Humble Duty, shall conclude this, with that of
Sir
Your Most affectionat Daughter
ISABELLA DUKE
Address: For Mr John Lock at his Lodging in London
Endorsed by Locke: I: Duke 21 Nov. 90

Dear Cosin
I was this day with David Horrall to speake with him about further time in your teniment at Belton†1 he was not willing to cum to me becaws he could not get in mony to pay his Rent I suppose him to be suffisient but thus it is he will not Rent it longer then Ladyday next unles he shall have it for 18l̷: pr Anum: and have that ground that was his Brother Roberts in with it for I profered that with the rest that he had before and he will give but 18l̷: for one year or for 3 years and if times doe mend he will give sum thing more for the two last years to make up the three years, if himself must be Judg I dout you will have but littell, I am very loath to

let it without your Aprobation for If onc an estate is doun it is a hard matter to raise it againe and if a man keep an estate in hand unles his ey be over it dayly he wear better let it for halfe to doe and he did aprove of it Robert Horrall is Content that I should take to†1 the ground becaws he cant help it, I did this day goe over it and I cannot but conceive it is better worth then 40s p 1345. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 2/12 December 1690 (1344, 1346)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 51-2. Excerpt copied by Locke, on rates of interest, etc., in the United Provinces, in MS. Locke b. 3, f. 28.
Rotterdam. 12 December 1690
Dear Sir
I receive with admiration yours of the 28th past, to see Captain Robinson come away, and to heare that our friend†5 is not come with him, and which is more, that he cannot spare me his skinner,†6 as little as his skin. I see he loves to sleep in a whole skin, and not to venture his carcase through the cold, and uncertain Element. When the cask of Apples arrive I shall send it to Dr. Guenellon; But mr. Popple tels me of 4 cask are the other 3 for my wife.
I shall not faile, God willing to gratify that worthy Lady with the story of W.A.†7 and with those seeds and plants she desires, in the mean while pray tender her my humble service. As to our Legal
― 174 ―
interest it was 5 a 6 per Cent till J de W—†1 brought it down to 4, and so it remayns, and upon security may be had for 3 a 3½ per Cent. Our ducatons have been about ½ per Cent any time this 3 years above the ordinary value, since the coyning of the f3 pieces which are not of so good alloy.†2
I shall write to Thomas Davies and enquire how affairs stand. But as for me, I have, according to the Doctors order paid all the mony I had, and so we are even—when the Capt. comes and pays me £5—I shall pay it Thomas. D. I perceive my answere, as to that Gentleman†3 is not so informing as you would have it, I now then speake more positive I judge his security good, I should now trust him for my all, which to me is as much as anothers all to him, I was Jealous, but I am now satisfyed, and I hope upon good grounds that that cloud he seemd in danger of is over, now all our Exeter ships come safe into Amsterdam (I mean all the goods, for one of the ships is dasht in pieces) save one who after many days storm has got into safe harbor at Holy Island, a happy place to him. So that I should make no difficulty of trusting him, to all intents and purposes, he will keep his old form, and rank among his neighbours, but when I last wrote I was afraid from a square he might by beating of his corners have become a round, and then he would rowld god knows whether—If those Latin papers come to hand†4 I shall take care to send them you, tho I had rather you would come and read them here, when the King comes—my wife and self salute you, and your family, and Sir W. Mr. Cl. and mr. Fr.†5 whom thank for my wives apples—I am Dear Sir
Yours
B F

1347. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 December [1690] (1326, 1369)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 36. Water-stained and torn. Printed in Rand, pp. 302-3. Year from Clarke's endorsement.
Oates 22 Dec
Dear Sir
You who doe your freinds businesses soe carefully and soe exactly have noe need to excuse your self for want of time when you write your letters: I returne you my thanks And am desired by my Lady†1 to doe the same for her who is extreamly obleiged to you for your care in her businesse. She says that she concludes whatever hast you are in that the Parliament†a will not sit in the Holydays contrary to the priviledges of the Church which has a right to make people idle at some time as well as eat fish at others and she says what ever sort of recesse you have you cannot now keep your Christmas at Chipley, and however great a lover of the town you may be she guesses that you may <fai>rly†b by this time have your bellyfull of it. This being soe she <mak>es†b it her request to you that you would come and spend a few days here.†2 She shall take this she says as kindely as any thing else you have don for her. She desires me to inclose this letter to you which is to the same purpose as she says, but orders me to excuse the shortnesse of it to the weaknesse of her eyes which seldom permits her to write at all. I need not tell you
― 176 ―
how glad I shall be to see you. My service to Madam when you write and thanks for her letter and my love to my wife and the rest. If you goe to the house after the receit of this pray in your way deliver it to Mr Fox†1 if not it will be well <enough>†a to send it to Mr Pawling by the penny post and he will <deliver>†a it. It is to put an end to his †b pray tell me his name and <where he lives, and>†c †d the top of those he sends to Sir Francis as you will see on the top of this†2
Pray if you come hither doe me the favour to bring me a pair of drawers of swans skin†3 which I have writ to your neighbour clarke†4 to make for me. if you weare them down on your owne they will doe you noe harm this cold weather. and if it be not too much trouble to you I would beg you to bring me two peices of Lightfoot†5 which D. Thomas sent me and which Mr Pawling promised to call for at Richards Coffee house†6 where D. Thomas orderd <them>†e to be left for me. And pray also take out of the garret where my books <are>†e the XIV Vol of the Bibliotheque Universelle†7 it is a booke in 12° bound in Velom as all that whole set is, and bring it with you.
Give my service and speake all things fit to shew my respect and preserve†f my interest in the Stone gallery.†g †8
Endorsed by Clarke: Mr Lock and Lady Masham's Letters Received the 24th December 1690.

1348. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 26 December 1690/5 January 1691 (1346, 1350)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 56-7. Excerpt copied by Locke, on rates of interest, etc., in the United Provinces, in MS. Locke b. 3, f. 28.
R. 5 Jan 90/91
Deare Friend
You will easily excuse a man that hath kept his bed for a fortnight, from writing long letters; and especially that I wrote not last post, but to Mad. Popple, to speake to you to spare our friend†1 the View of the furnace the Baron†2 gave you, or if that cannot be the draught of it, which request I now renew, on his behalf to your self. Capt. R:s†3 lighter lyes yet frozen up in the old mase.†4 So I cannot come at any of the things, I feare the apples will be all frozen —I was wondring what book it was had received 4 and might 14 answers. But mr. Spademan†5 who has visited me twice I thank him —tells me Dr. Sherlocks has received 10 already so that may be it.†6 The £10 has been some weeks received. And I doubt not but by your mentioning it, for which I thank you. Tho' the relation he had to my Lord was the motive, yet I never was so senseless as to imagine my Lord any way obliged. Onely I perswaded myself that he stood in aw of my Lord: and upon his command would pay me.†7 I am now with yours of the 9th past. I expected Skin and Skinner together, when first I desired mr. Popple to speak to you, by your Best friend†8 to send me Skinner with the other books. But when I saw Skinner must stay there: I concluded the Skin and Skinner would not be separated.
Where to get Skinner in these parts I know not, I find him in no Auction exposed, had I, I had certainly had him. The yong man I expected, is come without any books, at all. But there's no such hast. I have books enough to stay my stomach at any time—My distemper, a great looseness, without gripes, was once stopt 48 houres, and I had 2 very orderly stooles, but then it returned with
― 178 ―
gripes for one day. now I have been 5 days without a stoole, except 2 this day, the last looser than the first and that with gripes. So that I cannot be confident that the worst is over tho I hope it. Your Little friend†1 values himself not a little upon the news I have given him that you intend him a brave booke. But if I dye of this sickness, if my wife can spare, him, I intend if I make a will to bequeath him to you, not doubting but you'll educate him well—
I was mistaken to take the Interest the State gives of 4 per Cent for the Legal interest. I am informd there's no limit to interest by law—fooles may give as much as knaves will exact of them: Judgments or precedents there are in our hooghen Raad†2 when 7 per Cent has been allowed without, and 6¼ per Cent upon a mortgage. And I remember a certayne Collegiant†3 of this Town, did shew me a bond (upon Pawn in his hand) by which he had indented for 1 per Cent per month Interest, which he called a Gospell Interest, saying the man profferd him 2 per Cent per month or 24 per Cent per Annum, but he would onely take een Evangelisch Interest, giving me to understand how good a Gospeller he was.
I cannot yet learn when the States who first paid themselves 6¼ per Cent reduced it to 5. and afterwards to 4 per Cent as it continues. I shall enquire particularly when I go abroad. But I have been always told, it was since 1650. Bank mony here (to be paid as they wilbe in bank by ducatons) was 10. October, 5f and in schellings —5¼ per Cent and in 12 Nov. 4½ and 4¾ per Cent now 47/8; and 53/8; per Cent. the common difference betwixt such current mony as the bank receives here, and smaller mony as to f 3. 30 st. 28 st. 6 st. pieces is ¼ per Cent but shirks†4 that ly upon the bench,†a and will not produce the bills till the last day, and than peremptorily require it to be paid in bank, or 3/8 and sometimes ½ per Cent more than in Ducatons get their wills, because men can't get bank mony at an houres warning.
Now as to the difference betwixt Gold and silver, thus it stands. The finest silver is called 12 pence; or penningen.†5 And the finest
― 179 ―
gold is called 24 Caraat.†1 And the price for silver and gold, is made at the fineness of the standard. If the Essayers†2 find them courser the seller has in proportion less for it. The finest silver that ever was yet seen they say was but 11 pen 22 graines (24 make a penny-weight) And the finest gold that is our Rose nobles†3 23 carat 10 pen. (12 makes a carat)
This is further observable If you bring gold in the bar to the mint the mintmaster is bound to deliver you; for every mark of 24 carat 70 Ducats. now because the mintmaster can't buy Ducats for f 5 (as in the mint they are esteemd, but must pay sometimes 4½, 4¾ 5 per Cent for them, he is forced to sell the gold again. This I confess I understand not.
But a mark of fine silver is worth at present f25. sometimes 4 5 or 6 stivers more—as its more plentiful or scarce.—
And an ounce of fine gold f 47—sometimes 8 or 10 stivers more that is 8 ounces or a mark—f 276.†a
Or an ounce of such fine silver 1 Ducaton, and of fine gold 15 ducatons, so that 15 graines of fine silver is circumcirca the value of 1 grain of fine gold. If I have not miscounted.
The exportation of bullion has never been stopt, but every man may openly carry out what he pleases silver or gold.
Nor has our Interest been reduced by Laws, but had its free course when mony has been plentifull our Interest has been and is low, when scarce higher—a few years agoe our solicitors gave 7 per Cent and gave in Pawne ordinances of the state†4 —If in any thing I am short of understanding what you would be informd of let me know it, and I shall do my best to get you the best information I can. I pray remember me to mr. Pawlin, dos his patience last yet,
― 180 ―
I'm glad my did not—my service to mr. and mrs Popple to whom I send forward a letter this night—but my back akes not a little with writing this letter, therefore I turne me now to my beloved bed— And remayne
Yours
B F
since I rose I have had a very loose stoole so that this humour I fear is going again, as I am to take Laudanum†a
Address: To mr. John Locke at mr Robert Pawlins in Dorset court in Channelrow Westminster
Postmark: IA 13
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 5 Jan 90/1
1349. Elizabeth Yonge to Locke, 27 December [1690] (1337, 1362)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 140-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Escott, December 27
Dear Sir,
It has been contrary to my Inclinations, to have thus defer'd my thanks to you for your last Obliging letter, and alsoe for the directions and assistance you have been pleased to give me, of which I have a due resentment, and have forborn hitherto only to avoid being troublesome to you, but that can noe longer prevail with me to omit my Duty, being impatient to assure you, your kindness is not thrown away upon an ungratefull creature, but on one that has a real esteem and affection for you, and the deepest sense Imaginable of her Obligations to you, which are such as can never be forgotten. and were it possible I could ever be in a capacity of serving you, I should with great pleasure demonstrate by my actions that which I can only now doe in verball expressions. and I must own my self very defective in that respect too, which I beg you to supply, by imagining what naturally flows from a heart full of grattitude, and believe it to be the true sense of mine. the swelling in my Cheek is not yet removed, but I hope it still lessens, I
― 181 ―
think tis not bigger then when I first observed it; you may assure your self I shall not venture on any outward applications, nor any thing else but what you shall advise me, in whoes Judgment and care too, I have an entire confidence, therefore shall be noe further solicitous about it then to observe your directions, which I shall doe with all the exactnes I am able, I am still using the drink, but have been much disapointed about the Diacarthamum. I could not get it ready made, and having order'd it to be prepared for me, and I expected to receive it, they sent me word they could not get the ingredients, but I have sent to London for it and hope I shall have it in 2 or 3 days, but least it might be injurious to me to neglect purging soe long, at one of the changes of the Moon I took a gentle infusion which I have formally used. I have been carefull of my dyet ever since your caution, and my being in your hands has secured it from troubling my thoughts, which otherwise I could not easily have don. but I am much troubled to hear your illnes has driven you once more into the Country, I hope the free air will soon give you relief, which shall be my prayer to heaven for you, and that god almighty would bless and reward you for the care you have taken of
Dear Sir
your most Obedient Daughter
ELIZ: YONGE
my Sisters are your humble servants
