1350. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 2/12 January 1691 (1348, 1351)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 54-5.
2/12 January 1690/91
Dear Friend
I had wrote you last post to supply the defect of my last this day sennight, but that my distemper hindred me, For tho, I had not had a stoole from Saturday to Tuesday, I found myself so wearyed with writing one, necessary letter, that I could not set up to write to you which I thought would come as well now. And Just as I was taking pen in hand, I thought I should now have been
― 182 ―
prevented, by a qualm came over my stomach and discharged it of the little birds I eat at dinner—But that being gone I find myself the fresher, yet must make it short—my looseness till yesterday was the third time stopt again from Saturday to Thursday noone; and then began as water again, so that I tooke again laudanum last night, and this afternoone, which may have been the occasion of my discharging my stomack so—
Munday last†1 I was visited by a Gentleman who gave me a more perfect account of the Interest and reduction. The Reduction from 5 to 4 made by the State was in the yeare 1655. And ever since If any man lends another mony at Interest without expressing the tantum, 4 per Cent onely is allowed. But If a man sell another goods and doth not trust, but expect ready mony, abating 1 per Cent, and afterwards can't get his mony, nor find his goods to revindicat them, If such a one sues for his mony and Interest, under the name of marchants Interest, The Judges always allow 8 per Cent per Annum; because there was no intent of trusting the goods upon Interest, but a force put upon a man, that is supposed to know a better way to imploy his mony in. This he assures me de certaine science, as having Judged such cases himself when he partooke of the goverment. I enquired of him the difference between fine silver and fine gold; as well knowing that he had made his remarks upon such things also. And he confirmd what I wrote you that the proportion was as 1 to 15—Thene we talkt about the reall, intrinsic worth of those mettalls—And he said there was no such, but that was arbitrary and depended upon the will of any soverain In his own dominions to set what value he would upon a ld of Gold or Silver—And if he sit a greater value upon it in his than in any other Cuntry, the marchants finding it, he should certainly, for his comodities draw in a short time all the silver and Gold into his kingdom. And added that by this Trick the french King had within 40 or 50 years last past drawn all the gold out of these parts into his K. and the K: of England into his—Now this I know to be true, that when I came first to dwell in Amsterdam Anno 1655 we could not go any where to receive monyes without gold scales, all payments being made in Gold. And he sayd his wives father did weekly (with divers other marchants) buy up all the gold they could get to send for france and England; because they raisd the value of gold, and of their Coynes. And that it was a great oversight in
― 183 ―
their neighbours that, they did not follow his example. He added that this is an infallible token to a state When they may without prejudice to their subjects or trade, raise their coynes—to wit, when the people begin to marchandise with the coyne, and to make one among another an advantage of it beyond the standard, or first value set upon it. For that advantage reasonably belongs to the soverain, and thereby hele keep the coyn in his cuntry. This brings to my memory a Jeweller of Antwerp, that about 6 or 7 year agoe came over, big with a project of bringing great advantage to the State, provided they would ingage, if they thought fit after his discovery of it to allow him a tantum out of it, but he would not discover it, till he had that assurance. He consulted me about it— and discovered it to me. I gave him address to the Pensioner Fagel.†1 But he would not listen to him, And so it was never discovered— After his repulse, I brought him to the Gentleman here mentiond, where he largely discoursed the policy of france, in that point.
But there occurs to my mind a late Instance that makes this Gentlemans axiome, not so certain. As I take it for a whole yeare or more 28 stuyvers pieces were bought up at 28½ 29 Stuyvers, Some marchants having found a way to passe them in Turkey as 30 stuyvers pieces.†a If the State should have gone to raise that specie in any measure; upon that occation, they would have been sufficiently abused, by having multitudes of those pieces poured in upon them from other Provinces. As I was interrupted in the beginning by vomiting, so I have now again been so by purging and vomiting both, The vomiting I beleeve came from a luscious Wine Tent†2 I took my laudanum in with. my purging I feare comes from my drinking beere in my sickness. tho, all men condemn me for drinking water, yet I scarce think it will now cease wholly till I return to water again. But I have found now and then a glasse of Canary and a tost during my sickness has been good—
You will doubtless have seen the extract out of the memoriall of our Rear Admirall Schey concerning passages in the councell of war, publisht in last Satturdays corant. In which he agrees in all things with the E. of N.s Letter to my Lord D. save in one point. His Lordship says all the officers and seamen were inraged at the
― 184 ―
Ad: for his conduct. Schey says but one Captain of them all appeared against him, and he had not much to say against his Admirall. Sure his Lordship was then mistaken, or their rage is turned into love, finding themselves mistaken, or the Councill of war†1 —Vast are the Preparations in, and flockings of people to the Hague, Lodgings deare, bread and beere scarce to be baked fast enough. The expence of particulars as well as of the publick will be great.†2 Capt. R.†3 —is going tomorrow to fetch some things over the Ice. I am
Yours
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Lock at Mr. Robert Pawlins living in dorset-Court in Channel Row, Westminster neat London
Postmark: IA 13
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 2/12 Jan 90/1
1351. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 6/16 January 1691 (1350, 1354)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 58.
Rotterdam 16 January 1691
Dear friend
Since mine Last post I have yours of the 21 November†4 which explains the mystery of the Eyder Downe, my wife says she promisd it you here, come, and sheel be as good as her word, I assure you, for she would fain see you here, especially now I am ill, yet since my last last friday I have not had a stoole, tho I am not free from gripes, which, in barbados, is worse and mortal in 3 days, after the looseness is stopt. I desired not to borrow your Skinner unless yourself brought it, as I then expected, I know thats not a book to be separated from the owner—The true cause of the present scarcity of mony,†5 I made no doubt but you did know the
― 185 ―
author of, there is one sent me, without any letter, you are almost a prophet with respect to the Apples, could you have foreseen they would have lain afreezing in The old mase you had not sent them. Pray present my service to the Triplicity†1 (I will not use the Athanasian word because I intend no offence to their long ears) that were with you when you wrote. This post brings us great news, if true, that will revive us all and make us all looke big. The Royal†a eyes are opened and opening (in fieri)†2 Maj: Bourne†3 has been graciously received and is like to receive marks of favour, no less than 40 officers like to be reformd, begining with the wise Mr. Gr—who askt our blundering Dutchman, if he would swear that if my Lord T. had come up, they should have beat the Enemy (Dos this Gentleman make any part in the wisedome of the Nation, as his father in the upper chambers?).†4 As it is written in the Amsterdam currant of saturday last was a week, see the Translation at Bridges Coffeehouse—†5
But this is not that alone that dos us good; But my Lord Preston,†6 and some others are taken in a smack embarkt for france, and so surprized (by one sent by the marquis of C— (whose son†7 they say appeard before the councel of war a great penitent, begging the Admirals Pardon for being mislead to beleeve any ill of his innocent personage) that tho they had their papers fastned to leads, they had not time to cast them overboard. They had, it seems great store of gold with them, profferd much to have leave to cast away their papers—assured the Capt. of a revolution at hand, and promisd him a great station in it, if he would but consent to casting
― 186 ―
away their papers. A brave fellow that could withstand the sight of gold, and prospect of preferment, in the next turne—But will not this prove the second part of my Lord Griffiths bottles?†1
In good earnest if this be true It may force strange visions upon a man whether he will or no, at†a lest†a I must remember my weakness I find, whether I will or no and so I must break off. and remayn
Your affectionate friend
B F
I find I have very few of these books to send to monsieur Le Clerc he having them of mine already for the most part.†2 He that has wrote his Thoughts upon his vindication of the Trinity; is a cunning chapman.†3
I thank you for your acco: sent, but that part I have intire, and do onely want that part that goes to 3 June 1688, by balance of which next account Credits you f3243: 03: 12—that part from July 1687. to 3 June 1688 is missing, or torn off from the rest, I know not wherefore.—
Address: To mr. John Locke at Mr. R. Pawlins in Dorset Court in Channel Row Westminster
Postmark: IA 10
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 16° Jan. 91
1352. Richard Old to Locke, 8 January 1691 (749, 1361)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 176-7.
Ch: Ch: Oxon
Jan. 8.90.
Sir

1353. Martha Lockhart to Locke, [14 January 1691] (1320, 1359)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 9-10. Date from Locke's endorsement, contents, and Mrs. Lockhart's date.
Kensington Wedensday
I am in reall concern to hear You are goeing out of town, so soon;†1 that t'will not be in my power to se you. t'was indeed my Chieff earant to london this affternoon, tho I was very much indispos'd, and have been so ever since I saw you, and I am not with out fear's that my Cold will turn to a fevour, which makes me more then ordinary Carefull of my person; and for this reason, I durst not stay latte in town, besidess eight aclock being struck I gave over all hopes of seing you, and hearing you goe to morow I Cou'd not forbear to send this to wish you a good journey, and all the good success you expect from change of aire, and that it may so farr make so perfect <a cure>†a upon you, that without danger to your health, you may at least some times be able to oblige your frendes in the town, as well as those in the Countrey, how ever all envey aparte, I give my most humble service to my lady Masham; who Cant be more at her ease then I would allwayes have her to be. we do belive if the wether doe not againe change, the King will goe to morow,
― 188 ―
if so we shall soon be in town.†1 and so in telling you I am your ever Faithfull Servant
I bid you
Adieu
I should be glad to know if your Journey hold's to morow and if you doe not I shall give you the trouble of a letter on the subject we talk't of when I saw you last

1353A. Hendrik Wetstein to Locke, 23 January 1691 (1060A, 1831)

1354. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 23 January/2 February 1691 (1351, 1355)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 59-60.
Rotterdam 2 february 1691 N.S.
Dear Friend
I have yours of the 12 December and 13 January both together come to hand this day, where the one has been so long I cannot imagine. I am beholden to you for your great concern for me, and good advice. I am so far advanced that both my Doctors have quitted me (for I had no less than 2) and left me to the Kitchin, and my Nurse. Kohlhans is this day gone to Amsterdam, upon a friday, a sad thing that a man should be forced to travail upon so unlucky a day, he bewaild himself sadly, till I laught at him for his superstition; But go he must—V. Helmont did so drive him, worse than when he was in Germany to come down to him here, when he was making that furnace.†2 I fancyed it to be about some such business. But it seems it is to write for him something that he pretends might not be intrusted to this Town, because the author would not let it go from him. My Distemper was no Disenteria, but a Diarrhœa. But had it continued I should never have been able to follow your first remedy to ride. Not onely for the scandal I should
― 189 ―
have given my neighbours who would have thought me mad, and turning Ranter, to rant it about the Cuntry a horse back—But for the torment of it, (worse than riding the woodden horse) to ride 30 miles a day upon these Cuntry trotting Jades, when I was so mauld last yeare with riding a soft paced english horse. But besides the season has been so cold that I could not beare the ayre. Which, together with my aversion to Rhubarb, with which I was so plagued, when a lad, that my stomach turns to heare it but named, as the Gentlewoman, or man uses to be at the sight of a Pothecarys shop, or sound of his mortar, was the reason of their not purging me with Rhubarb, tho they sometimes spake of it, but said I was too weak, and the season too cold to purge. I used nothing but Tincture of Steel, Laudanum and powder of red Coral—Sometimes they talkt of giving rhubarb tosted, and sometimes of giving me a Clyster; but did not. The looseness seems stopt, was so for 8 or 10 days till I eat some golden pippins which tinged†1 (as well as any stone ever I see) and gave 3 stooles last tuesday, and the 2 last loose, which made me write to mr. Popple that I feared my looseness returned. But I have not had a stoole since, and been freed from Gripes—But I am now much troubled with a pain in my back, as my wife uses to have in the Case she is in expecting her houre dayly, But she being free, I tell her, I have got her pains, now I have layn in for my self, I must ly in for her. As to that furnace the old Gentleman, is so far from what you suppose that, the Gentleman that desires it,†2 visiting him in Amsterdam, complaind he wanted a portable furnace, and askt him, if he could not tell where he might get one—Fell into a passion, raving at all that used them, as cheats and what not. As if (quoth the Gentleman to me) we had not known one another etc—so that I continue my suit on his behalf.
The first thing I savoured in my sickness was a Tost and beer with Edams cheese. Then because the Doctor said I must drink a little wine, I got first Rhenish wine, then canary, of which I have ever since drank a glasse Dinner and supper. I have for some time eat all things flesh and fish, first birds, then mutton, but I durst not meddle with water grewell or any other liquid meat. And to confesse the truth I have so feared a looseness that I have never abstaynd from Laudanum 3 nights together. Ile now begin and try,
― 190 ―
but if my looseness returns, I must keep that bridle over it. I have never had the least feaver—in all my sickness—Dr. Guenellons apples are here till the waters open, and I hope will doe well, both my cask are well—
Pray present my service to mr. and mrs Popple, and those other my friends—and tell her I have hers and her husbands of the 16th And do hope to heare of Churchill†1 and my books soone,†2 the K. arriving yesterday†3 at the Hague, the Bishop of L— came first hither,†4 and is this day gone thither, I presume mr. Brochman†5 and mr. Stevens and mr. Wilmore†6 there, who came over last week— my humble service—to Sir Fr: and his Lady, I shall so soone as I am able seek up some papers and answer her desire—and so I rest
Your most affectionate friend and servant
B F
Dr. Lock
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Locke at Mr. Robert Pawling living in dorset court channel row In West-minster

1355. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 27 January/6 February 1691 (1354, 1356)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 61-3. Answered by no. 1356.
Rotterdam 6 February 1691
Dear Friend
After my Letter was gone last post, I began to think that I had forgot one thing to wit, the Eyder down, and to let you know that there was nothing earnest in that expression but to let you see how much in good earnest my wife, and self did desire your company: For the thing is ready to be given Captain Robinson when he can goe.
As I wrote you I would begin to try if I could passe 3 nights without being necessitated to recur to the succours of my beloved Laudanum, I began that night, and was well enough both with
― 191 ―
respect to my rest, and looseness, and the next night, but on Sunday night I was so allarmd, that I lay in no smal payn, to keep all fast till morning, that I could see what I did, and then the floodgates burst open at such a rate, that I was constrained to take sanctuary there again, within an houre, having had stoole upon stoole in that time. And glad I was I had it to run to. This immediately stopt it, and, tho I tooke none last night, has to this houre, being about noone, that I rose to write this, but if I be incommoded while I set up, I shall use it again at night. Tho it seems a demonstration to me, that it alone, as you write will no more cure me, than eating and drinking will cure that disease of hunger and thirst, but that in spight of the strongest potions and fittest doses, it will after the revolution of a few houres return again. Yet, for as much as there intervened a visible cause of its return, it does contribute to the shocking of my confidence that Laudanum alone will not cure. when I seem to have been so oft, in this time cured. Till new occasions of raising (as upon every turn we have seen one thing or other) it again. And this time, the Doctor having so commended veal, as a nourishing food, and so convinced my wife that I was wel, my stomach wel, because it savoured and digested anything I eat, very wel, and that I wanted now nothing but good nourishing food, to ad strength, to my wel disposed stomach, my wife bought a breast of veal (the more because I can eat that flesh dry roast, and that she Judgd such dry meat now better for me, than mutton, which I must have green)†1 of which I did eat well, But we Judg this the occasion of my looseness again at this time, because when I am wel and bound, if I eat once or twice of veal, it certainly opens and loosens my belly, and sometimes makes me throughly loose—This she takes to be full as good an experiment, as the Doctor that first wrote Bacon a present remedy for An Ague, and then corrected it to present death, to an English, but present restoration, to a westphalian. And so she will give me no more veale.
But supposing this to have been no new cause, nay no occasion of my looseness. But that it proceeded from the old cause unremoved. Seing you confess purging with Rhubarb, in this season, very dangerous, more dangerous than to ride 30 miles a day. We think it the safest way to keep the old enemy in chaines, as oft as he rebels and gets loose, so long as we have so Certain and effectuall chaines to lay him in for a day 2 or 3—as bread and cheese will allay
― 192 ―
hunger, and good drink thirst for some houres; rather than to hazard the whole fabrick, by indeavouring to eject him by force; in this winter season. We apprehend ourselves to reason well and right in this case, I mean my Doctor, as well as my self and wife. For tho Laudanum should be admitted never to cure, alone, yet we cannot conceive that it does any harm, nor what harm it can do in this case. I intreat your Judgment upon this our reasoning. And do assure you that I oppose not in crosseness, as I was lately out of England rudely told, because I refused some to be sent of a fooles errand; they said I called them fooles and was grown very cross: because I wrote I was the worst in the world to be sent of a fooles errand. Whereas I meant, not an errand that a foole would send me about (For a foole may send a man of a very wise errand), but an errand, that none but a foole, would be sent of; which cunning men often put such men upon. I assure you I speak as I think, and tho when I have Laudanum in, I am mightily not onely at ease, but well pleased, for I do mighty things I make the Jacobites wise, I help the Gulonites.†1 I break down Tyranny in church and state, I destroy all sects from the first to the last and erect a Church universall, and so do things that never were done below the moone, yet of this fooles paradice I am not so fond, but I can easily quit it, if I can apprehend it to be perillous to my health, which men prefer before their wealth, as the Doctor sais in the Triple plea for the superiority.†2
I have just now received a Letter from my Lord†3 from the Hague, in which he kindly promises me a visit, if my sickness will not permit me to wayt upon him there; of which I see at present little probability (for one while) having been so long kept in a warm chamber: which last Saturday and sunday I quitted, and went down; and so that may have been some small occasion of the return of my distemper.
Last Saturday brought to this place from Amsterdam by the post, and doubtless to all the towns in holland, multitudes of papers, in print, giving a sample of our late High sherrifs pranks to stop the mouths of his adorers, that boast in print, by a mercenary pen,†4 that the Commissioners of the Court of Holland had found nothing of moment against him, and that therefore, when the Court of
― 193 ―
Holland, had received their report, and made report to the Assembly of States, the States found the matters so frivolous that they were discontented, and expressly forbad them to commence any process against him. Whereas, saith this Author, The Court had not made any report at all. Nay not so much as to the Committee, whom the States appointed to heare their report, and make report to them. And that because the Deputies for Rotterdam were present in the Committee, whom the Lords desired might be ordred to go forth, because some of the magistrates of Rotterdam were concernd in some of the Informations. But they refusing to go forth, The report was not made. But report of the reason of the obstruction, whereupon, it was resolved the 2d of November that the Committee should examine the reasons of the Court for requiring the Deputies of Rotterdam to go forth. And so the thing stands.†1
Having thus refuted this Ly; He proceeds to give us part of the Oath of Purge, which every Vroedschap†2 is bound to take before the High-Sherif, at his entrance upon his office.
By which they swear, that they neither have by themselvs nor any others, directly nor indirectly given or promised anything to any man, nor ever wil, for his recommendation to the Nomination or election to that office, and that if at any time he shall ever come to know of any thing promised or given by any person, without his privity he will discover the persons by and to whom—
Then he produces to acts of 2 brothers immediately succeeding each other in the Vroedschap, the first in the yeare 1687—the other (by his death) the last year. In which they both promise, and sweare solemly, with lift up fingers, that if it shall please his Ro: High. then, and now Maj: of Eng: to chuse them, they shall and wil, Correspond with him, and his faction in matters of Goverment of church and state, giving or recommending to offices, blindly follow his sentiments. If he change party change with him. Maintain and defend the Goverment by Stadholder, and the maximes thereof in the State, and the maximes of the Voetians†3 in the Church. That they never shall or will at any time sollicit for any man, Relation or no Relation, for any office in the magistracy, but by his
― 194 ―
previos consent. That in all cases they shall and will comply with his maximes, and for confirmation, and performance of the promises, they not onely swear, but do bind all their goods. And submitt their office of Vroedschap to be declared Vacant, if he shall Judge that they shall in any thing have been unfaithfull, they desire the Vroedschap, at his request, to proceed to a new nomination, and his Ro: High. and Maj. thereupon to elect another in their stead. And to demand this, they do authorise the Baylif, by that their grant and resignation—And—finally they declare upon their oaths, in the presence of god, that all this they have done, sworn and promised of their own accord proper will, and motion, without being thereunto induced or perswaded by any man. In these things they both agree. But, the first, the Oldest brother, who, by this meanes, got in, in the year 1687 particularly besides all his goods, specially bound a bond of f 4000, which he lent into the Treasury of his Ro: H: which if the Baylif Judgd he had in any thing faild, was (forsooth) to be forfeited to the poore of Rotterdam and he impowred to see it. And this obligation was to endure his whole life time, in so much that after the loss, or forfeiture of this f 4000 he was to remain obliged as much as ever to the performance of all those Articles. And he was never to correspond with his own brother in Law and his faction, but as well to oppose him as anybody else that should at any time oppose him (the Baylif) in his person, or good designs. This was the 14 Nov. 1687—upon the same instrument is found a postscript of the same date, in which he saith, that for further security he gives him and a Burgermaster since dead, full power, as they shall think fit, either to deposit this Instrument in the hands of his Royal Highness or to keep it safe in their own hands. And the 21 detto is another postscript found, in the Hague. By which he submits his Vroedschaps place, as above said.
It seems, they were cruel Jealous and afraid of him, and as the last and strongest bond of all, this last act of resignation, was devised for him to sign. And after they had got that example it proved a coppy for his brother readily to write after. And 'tis suspected others since have done the same, and that it would have been a thing of course ere long, for this man, under pretence of the name, Authority and Interest of his maj: to have made him self master of this city to all intents and purposes, and as well to have kept the magistrates, as people in aw, according to his beloved saying Better be feared, than loved.
― 195 ―
These 2 Acts they say, were found in the rubbish of his house with other papers of concernment. It has been by his creatures said that he wilbe restored, and advanced higher than ever. But I presume those persons either had not heard of these Acts or did not beleeve that there were any such. For 'tis not to be beleeved that his Maj: will see a man so notoriously make use of his name and Authority, for such Villanies, and not shew his indignation against him, in terror of others for the future. For, tho, they both swear that they did promise all these things, of their own proper will and motion without being thereunto induced by any one. Yet who can beleeve it? When the whole tenor of it shews it to be a formal contract, and condition, without which they could not obtain the Nomination, much lesse election. This is at least evident,†a that it was deposited in his hands, in order to the procuring his favourable recommandation.
But what Geese, were these Wise-heads (as the word imports Vroet†1 being sage, wise, prudence. and schap. a termination answering to ship in English as of Vriend—friend—Vriendschap—friendship) to be kept in aw by such bugbears, which he never durst have produced to put in execution, because he would have exposed himself to the Law, and to the Indignation of the K.
You that know not the men may think them the Cunning Knaves and the B. the goose. That would easily promise him those things, which they knew he could never execute. But they that knew the deceased, know he was a f— in folio. and that that was as Remarkably Visible, as the nose on his face. I have done.
Sir
The Inclosed†b gives you an account of my present†c condition, It is now evening and I have not yet had a stoole. Who would not then make use of Laudanum in my case, at least till the frost breaks and the weather be more moderate. I forgot to inform you that Father Simons critical history of the Versions of the N.T. is abroad: and therein he promises a history of the Commentators; I have now a request to you in behalf of a friend†d of mine, who earnestly desires me to get information, where the papers and
― 196 ―
manuscripts of the famous Isaac Vossius are. Whether in hands of either of his wives,†1 for it seems he was (in this cuntry) marryed to 2, to shew, as he said, that he was a man as wel of the old, as N.T. Or whether did leave them to any learned person. If they be in his wives hands he supposes they may be had for a small matter, or part of them, there are things he has promised in some things of his, with respect to this Cuntry, which my friend would fain have. I have now this 2 days observd your rules and nor eat flesh, drank wine, nor beare, but barly water, and milk and water boyld, and eaten nothing but milk and water thicknd with flower, and now my wife comes and asks me what Ile eat, and would give a tost and cheese—I tell her that's good, but a shoulder of mutton would be better and I could pay it off, if I had it. But I shall yet a while forbeare, I intreat you to procure some account if it can be, so long after his death, of Vossius's his manuscripts; and so with kind salutations I rest
Yours
D. Lock

Oates, 3 Feb. 91.
Dear Friend,
* * * *
I bear the winter pretty well here; but, going to London at Christmas, I wanted breath presently, and was almost dead in a fortnight.†2
I have received the Latin translation of the first booke of my Essay. I know not by whom, but you say noething of it in yours either of the 2d or 6th.
― 197 ―
When you see the gentleman from whom you received a letter from the Hague just as you were writeing to me yours of the 6th, pray present my most humble service to him, and tell him that I was extrem glad to hear that, after his fourteen howers adventure, he got at last safe on shore, whoever it was that has the credit by good advice to have saved the cargo.†1
Pray send by Robinson P. Simon's Critical <Hist>†a of the Versions of the New Testament. Vossius his books I thinke were left to his brother. If I mistake not, I have been told the Universitie of Oxford was like to have bought them of him, and offerd, as I have heard, a good round sum for them; but what is become of them now, I cannot tell, but will endeavour to informe. My kinde love to your wife; I wish her an happy hower. Remember me to my litle friend.†2 I am yours,
J. L.

(English)
Amstelodami 19 februarii 1691
Vir Doctissime
Mutua cum sit nostra amicitia dubitare non potui quin <mutuus>†a sit noster Luctus: et cum mollitiam meam cognoveris facile judicare potes, quam profunde penetraverit vulnus, quod ex improviso cor meum passum fuerit amissione dilectissimæ meæ uxoris, quæ ut benevola plurimis, ita mihi triginta trium Annorum Amplexu et Amore coalita citra sensum ad intima viscera penetrantem tristissimum avelli non potuit, qui mihi non ita minuitur, ut potius
― 199 ―
augeri videatur et <accrescere>†a indies: in hoc autem me consolor quod luctus mei socios habeam, quos inter tu imprimis amicissime Domine sinceræ virtutis æstimator. Quo invido morbo ileo mihi trium quatuorve dierum spatio erepta sit, ut non juvat scire, ita animus meus exhorrescit referre; quare humanissime vir ad gratiarum actionem me converto potius, quod tam amice dolorem tuum in novissimis tuis testeris, quas tibi illo solatii officio debere me confiteor, majores vero promitto, si id aliquando coram facias, invenies non quidem hospitem solitam, solitum habebis, qui te ambabus manibus amplexurus erit: quod futurum aliquando D Helmontius sperare jussit. quo casu rogo obnixe hospitium capere velis apud Venium qui
Totus est Tuus.
(Latin)
Amsterdam 19 February 1691
Learned Sir, As our friendship is mutual, so I could not doubt but that our grief is mutual; and as you know my tenderness you can easily tell how deeply the wound penetrated that my heart unexpectedly suffered by the loss of my beloved wife. As to many by her kindness, so to me she was united by the conjugal love of thirty-three years, and she could not be torn from me without the saddest feelings penetrating my inmost bowels; and this, so far from diminishing, seems rather to grow and increase daily. In this, however, I [p. 199] console myself, that I have companions in my grief, amongst them especially yourself, my dearest friend, who esteem true virtue. As it does not avail to know by what cruel intestinal illness she was snatched from me in the space of three or four days, so my spirit shudders to relate it; wherefore, most kind Sir, I turn rather to thanking you for the most friendly expression of sympathy contained in your last letter. I acknowledge my debt of gratitude to you for that service of consolation, but I promise to thank you more adequately should you ever give me the opportunity of doing so in person; if so, you will find, not indeed your accustomed hostess, but your accustomed host, who will welcome you with open arms. Mr. van Helmont led us to hope that this might happen sooner or later; in that case I earnestly beg you to accept the hospitality of Veen, who is
Entirely yours.
Address: Doctissimo spectatissimoque Viro Domino J. Lock Londini

1360. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 12/22 and 13/23 February 1691 (1356, 1363)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 64.
22 february
Deare Sir
I have now of a long time received none from you, nor wrote to you, since mine of the ; with me it continues, I dare not trust my self three nights without Laudanum, 2 days I am wel, but the third day it breaks out again: I sent Dr. Guenellon your booke,†1 and took occasion to let him know my distemper, and crave his advice, whether my continuing to use Laudanum, till the sharpness of the weather abates, could do me any harm. To that he answers not, but saith that his father in Law Dr. Veen, (from whom is the Inclosed)†2 and he both Judge, since I do keep my chamber, that its needfull I should take the Rhubarb, to remove the sharp matter that is in my guts, and to preserv against new humours, And thinke the safest way to be, thus

I began this, and got up on purpose, expecting one to call for it, but my servant coms now, and tells me he is gone. so I lay it by till tomorrow. Our magistrates have here forbidden the printing of anything about the Tryall of the Lord Preston,†3 in the mean while the Amsterdam Courant tells us they are about it there, these Amsterdammers, will never be obedient, in small things—and this year again would not send their nomination out of the Cuntry, but lodgd it with the States, desiring them to order the Judges to elect, But the king arrived Just in time to do it.†4 They are a crosse graind people.

1361. Richard Old to Locke, 14 February 1691 (1352)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 178-9.
Ch: Ch: Oxon Feb. 14. 1690/1
Sir
Mr Wall†3 in his passage through Oxford into Worcestershire acquainted me, that you had bin pleased very frankly to promise one of your Essay's of Humane Understanding to Ch: Ch: Library, and that if I sent any person in London to your Lodgings, the book was ready and should be delivered to him. Immediately after that (which is now some time since) I requested by letter the favor of Dr Wake†4 that he would send his own servant on that errand; he returned me answer that he had so don, but that his servant was not so lucky as to find you within. I have no other acquaintance in London, and cannot reasonably presume to put Dr Wake to any farther trouble in this buisness, and therefore desire that you would be pleased to send the booke to Dr Wake's house in the Red-Lion-square in Holborn, from whom it will be safely conveyed to me with some other things now in his hands, which are shortly to be sent to me. This will add to the kindness of the guift you are
― 203 ―
pleased to designe for the Colledg, and double the obligation that will thereby be laid on
Sir
your most faithfull freind and humble servant
RICHARD OLD.
Dr. Ferrars†1 the Master of University Coll. died here on Friday last. it is not yet known who is most likely to succeed him.

1362. Elizabeth Yonge to Locke, 14 February [1691] (1349)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 142-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Escott Febru: 14th
Dear Sir
I find 'tis in vain to make any resolutions long before one puts them in execution, something or other almost always disapoints them; I have pleased my self a good while with the thoughts of seeing you in London by this time at farthest, but now I find I must deny my self that sattisfaction a little longer, haveing by the last Post received a letter from my Brother, which tells me tis necessary for him to hasten into the country for a short time, but shall return again the latter end of March or beginning of Aprill, and that he hopes if I deferr my Journey till then 'twill not be Injurious to me; I cannot but be a little troubled at soe long an adjourment, but I hope nothing will prevent my accompanying him at that time; which I am sure will seem long to your Daughter Betty, who is not only desireous to discourse you more fully about her indisposition, but alsoe to thank you in person for those many favours you heaped on her. which she cannot pretend in any sort to have merited. the buisness of this is to desire you would let me know whither I ought to continue the method I am in, in the mean time, I have taken the drink 12 weeks without intermission and the
― 204 ―
Purging draught constantly since your last direction. it agree's very well with me in all respects, and I find noe inconvenience by it, unless that I am a little thinner then I was before, but tis noe more then I can well enough spare. there is still some remains of the swelling, and I sometimes fancy it has been at a stay this last month or 5 weeks, at least the abatement has not been soe sencible to me as before, but I may easily be mistaken, for tis now soe little in it self and ly's soe in the hollow of the Jaw bone, that tis hard to make any Judgment of it. I beg a line or two from you at your next leasure, and that you will Pardon the frequent troubles given you by
Your affectionate humble servant
ELIZ: YONGE
my Sisters are your humble servants.
Address: For Mr John Locke These
Endorsed by Locke: E Yonge 14 Feb 1690/1
1363. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 17/27 February 1691 (i) (1360, 1364)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 65.
Rotterdam 27 February 1691
Deare Friend
I have but Just time to let you know that my wife was God be thanked safely delivered yesterday of a daughter†1 who with herself are reasonable for the time: she has understood that your old Quarters are broke up,†2 and having heard a good character of their mayd, I think her name is mary she earnestly desires you, by silvester, to enquire if she be clear,†a and free to come over and serve us, I'le pay her charges to and fro, if she like not, we have long wanted an English mayd to speak english among our children. she shall chuse whether she will be childrens mayd, or cooke mayd. In this you will doe my wife a singular service to get her timely answer, if she can come or no—because the time draws nigh to hire here, if she come not. I have now taken twice Rhubarb inline image ii (tho some considering my weakness would have persuaded me but to
― 205 ―
one at a time) I tooke it in a wafer with broth, and never tasted it; but swallowed it quick.—It wrought the first time more then the last, I had 7 stooles—and yesterday but 3. I rest to day, and repeat it tomorrow God willing. I imployed Churchil†1 the bearer, to seek a Skinner, who found one but would†a not have less then f 11 —wheras Vandervelde†2 sold one for f 4—The bearer wayts for this, so I must break of and rest
Yours
B F
Inclosed one from Dr Veen

1364. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 17/27 February 1691 (ii) (1363, 1367)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 66-7. Answers no. 1356.
Rotterdam 27 February 1691
Sir
I wrote you in great hast, a few lines today by mr. A. Churchils Brother,†4 since which I have received your large and painfull letter, and am mightily ingaged to you, as also my wife, for the great care you shew of me; In that letter, I did, in the name of my wife request a kindness of you; Viz to let her know, if Mary, your old Landladyes mayd, be out of service (for we hear that family is almost dissolved) and whether she could resolve to come over and serve us, I have given the mayd so good a character that my wife is very desirous to have her, if it may be, and leavs it to her to be Cooke, or Kinder mayd.†5 This afternoon my wife has had a fit of an Ague, that her teeth chattered in her head, and now is hot. I have sent
― 206 ―
for a Doctor, tho she knows it not, and makes light of it, and says 'tis a good thing.
Now as to myself, I continue weak, but properly I am not sick, nor have been this 6/w. The beginning of my distemper, people will have, to be drinking so long water, but that I laugh at, I know not what to ascribe it to, I had in the great flood about 4000 els of Linnen, of my Nephews,†1 wetted, I had ingaged our bleacher, to take and dry them for me, he neglected to fetch them, 4 days after finding his wife with my wife, and that they came not for the Linnen but let it by, I chid heartily, being very angry at their neglect, Kohlhans being by, he ascribes it to that. The next day I ate eels, and they sate not well in my stomack, and that night my looseness insued, and the next day such a weakness that I could not sit up. Kolhans thinks my water drinking (and so many others) ruined my stomach, gathered the materia peccans, the passion I was in excited it, and the eeles did that which Hobbes his act of Volition does in his animals.†2 This is all the account I can give you of it: I have taken my Rhubarb without any aversion in the world, and do wonder that the Doctors never told me that I would take it so—I fell into the thought by Dr. Guenellons saying misce fiat pulvis.†3 I never had any shivering, nor fever, till last friday,†a- as I then wrote you.-†a
Our old Friend†4 I beleeve has quitted Rotterdam almost for a full doe,†5 but he is since, a wandring Hermit, he is now in his fourth Lodging. He soone quitted Galenus'es,†6 then went to another mennists; fell in with a censured minister of the Calvinist party, who I presume has received his Doctrine, He is to translate him a N.T. into Dutch, Interlinear as Arias Montanus's in Latin,†7 O Monstrum Horrendum! but because this will be a monster to the common people there shall be another version in good Dutch, with the Variis Lectionibus, and giving in margin the various senses of the greek words, that every body may chuse for himself—This I
― 207 ―
presume is it—they are about, if it be not somewhat else, which I suspect because of his shifting Lodgings so oft, his first lodging was very convenient for his writing work. Then he removed to a mennist preachers, on the New Dyck, where Galenus kept shop. Now he and Kolhans are at one Doctor Buchius's†1 on the Keysers gracht neare the white fox. What they are about I know not, but Kolhans wishes himself here again.
I observ your remedy against galling, but don't beleeve I shall ever want it in this Cuntry; I hope I shall after tomorrows purging, be able to use my Laudanum safely. But I cannot imagin, seing you recommend me so much to have a care of cold taking, How you can talk of Rideing for me, after having kept my chamber above 2 months: and for ought I know, I shall do so, In my own defence, against the cold all this next month.
Pray present my humble to Sir F. and his Lady; I hope to come out of her debt, that is to discharge my promise—
The Gentleman that translated the first booke, is a Lawyer, a friend of mine, Monsieur Verryn, an able and well disposed man,†2 he last week wrote to me to intreat me, if it came back to my hand, to send it him without loss of time.
That Gentleman, whose 14 hours adventure you mention,†3 his Gentleman was just now with me, with a letter to follow mr. Churchill, and he is this evening gone by waggon after him—
What that story is of which you desire to know the issue, which is so admirable I know not.†4 But I'le tell you an Admirable thing, they say our Baillju is indeavoured by divers, In our Counsell to be restored, which has occasiond a Libel to be affixt, warning the people of it, and mentioning their names, and qualifyeing one of them by the title of perjured, appealing to an Instrument by him signd and crept out in print. But its said the K. will not, or at lest has not yet seen him.†5
Robinson went away as I told you in my Last, so I could send nothing by him. Will you have Simon in quires, or frenchband?†6
― 208 ―
If you can, my friend intreats a certain account of Vossius's manuscripts.
I have not else to ad, but that a friend of yours had a mind to steale some thing abroad to make that people wiser, that he has most converst with, in a few dialogues exhorting to unity, in those things that are indisputably true and evident, and not to keep up divisions about smaller matters much less about singularityes,†1 could you, or would you, peruse†a and get it abroad—hele send you a coppy, by some safe hand. I am
Sir
Yours
B F
P:S. I have wrote madam Popple to enquire about the mayd, pray inform her where she is to be found.
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Lock at Mr. Robert Pawlings in Dorset court Channel Row West-minster.
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 27 Feb 90/1
ROBERT PAWLING
Robert Pawling was probably a kinsman and perhaps a son of Thomas Pawling of Oxford, a mercer and a member of the city council from 1634 until about 1642. Robert was also a mercer. The poll-tax return in 1667 describes him as a gentleman; he has £200 in money; in the house with him are his wife Christian, their three children, two apprentices, two women servants, and Mr. George Pawling, who has £300. The house, which had six hearths, was probably at no. 126 High Street. He was prosperous. He was still in trade as a mercer until 1681 and probably for some time longer.
He had already been a member of the city council, having been made a Chamberlain in 1658 (there were about thirty members of this rank). He was discharged in 1663 by order of the commissioners appointed under the Corporation Act of 1661. No reason is given for the order, but he was said later to have been brought up as a Puritan. In 1676 he was given a Bailiff's place (there were about thirty or forty men of this standing; they ranked higher than the Chamberlains). He did not take it up at this time. He was again given a Bailiff's place on 25 August 1679. He now took it up, was promoted to the mayor's council a week later, and on 15 September was chosen
― 209 ―
mayor for the coming year. His term of office started on 30 September. This was a time of tension. The perennial dispute between town and gown was exacerbated by divergences in religion and politics. Pawling was reputed to consider the university ill disciplined and to advise gentlemen not to send their sons to it. Among the townsmen he was second to Alderman William Wright (no. 615), who was to provide lodgings for Monmouth during the Oxford Parliament; his principal supporter in the university was Dr. John Wallis, who was to lend Shaftesbury his house (no. 620). Regardless of his interests as a trader he kept proper order in the town. This led to some petty annoyances for members of the university. He was responsible for the reception of Buckingham and Monmouth when they visited Oxford in August and September 1680 and for the conferment of civic honours on some of Monmouth's followers. He was said to have attacked some members of the university by name in his outgoing speech on 29 September; the speech appears to have been sharp but not unduly offensive in that way. A few months later he refused to sign an address to the king thanking him for holding the Parliament in Oxford. He continued as a member of the mayor's council until the surrender of the city charter in August 1683.
His son Thomas (p. 229) matriculated from Lincoln College on 19 May 1682. One of the fellows of the college was James Parkinson (p. 150, n. 6), who after the discovery of the Rye-House Plot was accused of holding anti-monarchical and anti-Anglican views; when on 3 September he was bound over to appear at the next assizes Pawling was one of the two men who stood bail for him. He apparently moved to Headington some time after this; he was living there in June 1685 when, during the alarm caused by Monmouth's rebellion, he was arrested and sent to Oxford Castle. He was reported a few weeks later to have been found guilty of defaming Lord Abingdon (no. 715) in a letter written in 1683. Early in 1688 James II appointed him an alderman; Pawling refused to serve. On 23 October, after the city's old charter was restored, he was again elected a member of the mayor's council.†1 There is nothing to show whether he attended any meetings; in August 1689 he was summoned to attend and in September he was superseded. At that time he wrote that he had business in London to be dispatched.
He occupied a house in Dorset Court, a square adjoining Channel Row in Westminster, from September 1690 or earlier. Locke lodged with him from September onwards, and kept his rooms continuously; when he was at Oates Pawling looked after some of his affairs. Pawling's sources of income at this time are unknown. He was interested in the projects for the foundation of Greenwich Hospital; he may have hoped for some employment in connection with it.†2 In 1694 when duties were imposed on all legal documents Pawling was appointed comptroller of the Stamp Office. His salary, originally £150 per annum, was soon raised to £200 and later to £300 (there may have been perquisites also). He moved house to Carey Street near Lincoln's Inn, and Locke transferred with him. He was superseded about September 1707.†3
― 210 ―
It is regrettable that no letters from Pawling to Locke survive for his Oxford period, but the sixty-four survivors, ranging in date from 1691 to 1704, display to a remarkable degree the character and ability that are deducible from his earlier activities.
Authorities: Surveys and tokens, ed. H. E. Salter, 1923; Oxford Council Acts, 1626-1665, ed. M. G. Hobson and H. E. Salter, 1933; Oxford Council Acts, 1665-1701, ed. M. G. Hobson, 1939 (Oxford Hist. Soc., vols. 75, 95; new ser., vol. 2); account of the city council in R. Fasnacht, A history of the City of Oxford, 1954; Wood, L. and T.; Prideaux, Letters; Pawling's letters below and notes to them. Wood and Prideaux as gownsmen and Tories disapproved of and disliked Pawling.
1365. Robert Pawling to Locke, 25 February 1691 (1372)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 211.
London Feb: 25 1690
Sir
I have called on your Watchmaker severall times for a Watch somewhat smaller than this I have; but he cant send one as yet. he finds you be very curious therfore he must take more time to provide one to your mind; this which you had he tells me is an extraordinary good one if you had found that it went too slow or too fast you should have nickt†1 him to it and if you expect that a good watch will go true with a good sundiall you wilbe mistaken for an exact Watch will many times vary 10 12 or 14 minutes from the Sundiall some times twilbe faster some times slower, yet at the years end they will agree; as is demonstrated by a printed paper he gives out and presumes that you have one of them.†2 I have discoursed an hour or two with him on that subject and am become very knowing in that mistery when a Watch that is true set and hath gon well in his box when it comes into the pocket it may vary and he expects the owner should have skill to regulate that, but youl reply as a gentleman to one of our profession†3 when he comended his Scarlet Cloth for as good a colour as any in England when twas shewed in his Shop; that he did not intend to wear it there. but the case varyes.
― 211 ―
the ribon, Orange butter, and bottle of water are directed to mrs Cudworth
the 15 tome†1 is sent and directed to you
Madam Lockhart cannot as yet tell me what the things come to, as soon as I know Ile pay her; mr Foxes bill is inclosed; mr Clarke†2 is sick I have been twice for it but cant have it
I have received the £20 and thank you for your care of me lest I might be out of stock. I delivered mr Hatter†3 his letter he promised to send an answer to me but tis not yet come unles this that came by the penny post be from him
I brought home with me this morning the book for mr Old and will deliver it as you direct and I will write to him†4
The Writings†5 are don but how well I shall leave you to judge; when you first wrot to me about them and desired it might be don with as much privacy as might be; I did resolve to undertake them myself and went presently and bought parchments and by mistaking you about the insignicant lynes I thought to leave out all that had strokes under them but being gravelled with them and not being able to make sence of it I shewed them to mr Freke who was of my mind presuming those lynes to be left out. afterwards shewing them to mr Starky†6 and intending to put him on doing what I thought too difficult a task for me; he found out my mistake which you confirmed in your next letter. after that upon a review I thought fit to go on with the work having provided my tackling I finished them at last and I hope have don them to your mind. I omitted one lyne, for I had written so far before I found my error which I have not only interlyned in the Indenture but have taken notice of it on the back side when they are witnessed; which I hope is as good in law as the other though it be a blemish to my work, seting that a side I have committed very few mistakes and those very small. I was once in the mind to have bought an other parchment and have written it over again but I feared I might commit some other mistake so let it pass having often times seen greater Clerks guilty of greater faults. they cost me 4s with the halfpound of wax that I sent with them. I should have spent my time worse if I had not
― 212 ―
been so employed and twas to me a good divertion, so I troubled not mr Starky any more and for that reason I have not delivered him your letter neither shall I till I hear again from you. I spake to mr Solicitor†1 a second time early this morning; he hath written but could not compleat his letter till tomorrow morning; so I have appoynted the messenger to meet me tomorrow morning at Richards.†2 I will send him away as soon as I can. mr Popple tells me mr Furley is better, it may be this Forrain letter may be from him which came this day; your other letter went by Oxford post. I think this is all at present from
Your humble servant
ROB PAWLING

1366. Martha Lockhart to Locke, [26 February 1691], with postscript by Joanna Cutts (1359, 1520; 1359)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 13-16. The date is about 1 a.m. on the Thursday following Wildman's dismissal.
Wedensday night
I have not time to answer the Merry parte of your letter which was very deverting, but haveing this occasion of a sure hand, I cant forbear tho it be allmost one aclock, and I extreemly harass't with waiteing, to let you know, that to the great amaze of all people, this day Major Willdman is turned out;†3 I was with him yesterday, allmost all day, he had not the least suspition of it, nor to day at seaven aclock at night, tho t'was all over the house†4 at noon. I met him at lady Mo.†5 in the evening, he then would not belive ther was any thing in it; but the minitt he left us, we had the ceartinty of it. And to show you how very unjust it must seem to the world, tho it
― 213 ―
was resolved in Mundays Cabinet Counsell; yet because, yesterday was the day the Citty was to subscribe their perticular†a sums to be advanced on this new lone,†1 which he did most vigorously advance, and him self subscribe a 1000 ll too: yet, till this was over, t'was keep't secrett, and the very next day declared. his office is in Commission, two allready declared, a very Tory Sir Robort Cotten, and Thom Franklin.†2 the first was sent for post out of the Countrey, and arived to the secretarys office this night; but if I had First told you, that for Ceartin the K: has been all over whige in holland; you would have with lese ease beleved this storry, the reason given for it, is he thinking that party his Enemies, as much therr as the Church is here,†3 I am so very sleepy I can add noe more, but service to all with you; assure my lady from me I shall obey all desier's in her letter, and answer it very soon; poor Cosen Same†4 has been ill with a feverish Cold, but he is now much better; I durst not goe to him my self, fearing the Q: who is fearfull; but I have Constantly sent, and seen he wanted nothing. I have power to say no more but that I am
Your very Faithfull and affectionat Servant
M L.
[Postscript by Joanna Cutts:]
My Cousen Lockhart ha's been since You Went out of town Extreamly Vext with the Clamour of Mrs Leigh who has spread Coppys of the rediculious affidavit You saw all about town and with a great many Lyes too tedious to mention has made a horrid noise reporting to ev'ryone the Certainty of her being ingadged in a plot for King James. and is indeavoring with her usial noise and violence to doe her all the injury she Can: we Want Your advice very much what to doe with her for she ha's made it past a jest and it must now be a triall of skill between them whose intrest is
― 214 ―
strongest. Mrs Leigh makes her patience hitherto one argument of her guilt pray Sir 'till we Can se You send us your opinion of this affair.†1 my very humble service I beg you to give to my Lady Masham and that my next to her may not be fill'd with tedious apollogy's <tell>†a her that I hope when she Consider's the many vexations I've been under since I wrote last both in the affair of my neece†2 and since in this last 3 weeks my Brothers illness I hope shee'l have the goodness to pitty and forgive one that has really not been in humour one day this 3 months to Entertain her with any thing that Could be a deversion, or rather not being troublesome. I am
Sir
Very much Your
servant

1368. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 6/16 March 1691 (1335, 1375)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 51-2. Answered by no. 1375.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Acri hac ac diuturna hyeme omne literarum commercium interruptum videtur, ac immodico hoc frigore digiti obriguisse. Soluta cum nunc sit acris hyems grata vice veris ac favoni,†1 ad scribendi intermissum officium redeo. Ego tuis 7 Novembris anni proxime elapsi scriptis eodem mense respondi: meis suas adjunxerat Verrinus, cum versione primi libri tractatus tui de intellectu humano.†2 Literas nostras cum prima libri parte ad D. Furlæum, prout jusseras, misimus: Nullum hactenus a Te responsum tulimus, eas tibi esse redditas, licet jam ad D. Guenellonem et D. Clericum plures literas dederis. Non spero versionem illam libri tui periisse. Si ad Te pervenerit, tu facile judicabis, an eam edi oporteat. Velim quidem eam Tibi placere, ut cogitata tua sermone Latino commode expressa legere possim. Sed quoniam nullam plane in tuis ad D. Clericum literis illius mentionem facis, aut nondum ad Te pervenisse colligo, aut fortasse minus esse exactam: quod dolerem: quoniam fructum quem speraveram inde percipere non possem. Interim
― 216 ―
tu jure tuo tanquam autor in proprium tuum opus uti potes. Wetstenius jam tandem serio de editione Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ cogitare videtur: ad finem jam properat editio Diogenis Laërtii:†1 spero intra duos menses operis tam diu desiderati editionem inchoandam: Interea quæcunque ego præmittere constitui parata erunt, Deo mihi valetudinem conservante. Verum quæ ego commentatus sum in majorem excreverunt molem: Statueram primo quædam de Inquisitione præfari: sed tam copiosa mihi sese obtulit materia, ut pleniorem Inquisitionis historiam conscripserim. Illa divisa est in quatuor libros. Primus ostendit persecutionem religionis causa repugnare genio Religionis Christianæ, ac doctrinæ primorum Patrum: ostendit porro, quantum a tempore Synodi Nicænæ Christiani mutati fuerint: hic recenseo varia Patrum testimonia, et præterea leges Imperatorias: tandem devenio ad tempora Papatus, et ostendo quomodo Inquisitio introducta et passim porro propagata sit, et quomodo tandem in Hispaniam et Lusitaniam sit introducta. Secundus describit omnes Inquisitionis ministros, quæ singulorum officia, potestas, ac privilegia, ac qualis eorum carcer. Tertius ostendit, qui judicio ac tribunali Inquisitorum subjecti sint. Hic dissero de hæreticis
― 217 ―
eorumque poenis: tum exhibeo varias hæreticorum distributiones in hæreticos manifestos et occultos, affirmativos et negativos, poenitentes et impoenitentes, hæresiarchas, credentes, defensores, receptatores et fautores hæreticorum, suspectos de hæresi, impedientes officium Inquisitionis, relapsos, blasphemos, divinatores, magos, Judæos et redeuntes ad ritum Judæorum. Multa hic occurrent curiosa. Tandem liber quartus repræsentat modum procedendi coram tribunali Inquisitionis. Hic ostendo, qua ratione munus suum inchoet Inquisitor, quomodo processum contra delatum de hæresi inchoet, quomodo eum continuet. Prolixe hic explico, quid doceant de testibus, et qualium testimonium in causa hæresis admittatur: quæ est materia admodum fœcunda. Si reus crimen neget, qua ratione processus contra eum instruatur, donec tandem ad sententiæ pronuntiationem deveniatur. Quomodo processus finiantur, 1. quando reus est absolvendus. 2. Quando est diffamatus, et illi imponitur purgatio canonica. 3. Quando tantum est semiplena criminis probatio: Hic dissero de tortura, et rationem torquendi in Inquisitione explico, narratione tormentorum Don Balthasaris.†1 4. Quando reus est de hæresi suspectus. 5. Quando est diffamatus et suspectus. 6. Quando est convictus seu confessus, et poenitens.
― 218 ―
Hic prolixe explico poenas poenitentiales, vestem Sanbenito, perpetuum carcerem. etc. et quousque rei ad poenitentiam admittantur. 7. Quando est relapsus et poenitens. 8. Quando est impoenitens, non relapsus. 9. Quando est impoenitens relapsus. 10. Quando est negativus.†1 Hi quatuor posteriores traduntur curiæ sæculari: et si sunt clerici prius degradantur: Modum degradationis describo. 11. Quando est fugitivus. Tandem processus sequitur contra mortuos, ac contra domos. Integrum tractatum claudo narratione actionis de fide. Habes brevem totius operis ideam; spero nec lectu injucundum nec ingratum fore. Omnes nos hactenus recte valemus. De tua valetudine nihil adversi mihi nuntiatur: precor eam Tibi diuturnam, ut plura quibus publico inservias elucubrare possis. Venius noster satis bene valet, nec non omnis illius familia. Salutat Te officiosissime uxor mea, liberique, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 16 Martii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
By this keen and lasting winter weather all correspondence seems to be interrupted, and our fingers to have been stiffened by the excessive cold. Now that 'sharp winter thaws and welcome spring returns with western breeze',†1 I return to my neglected duty of letter-writing. I answered yours of 7 November of last year the same month; Verrijn added a letter of his to mine, together with the translation of the first book of your treatise on the human understanding.†2 We sent our letters along with the first part of the book to Mr. Furly, as you had bidden; so far we have had no reply from you that they have been delivered to you, although you have already written several letters to Mr. Guenellon and Mr. Le Clerc. I do not suppose that that translation of your book has been lost. If it has reached you you will easily judge whether it ought to be published. I should like it to be acceptable to you, so that I may be able to read your thoughts suitably expressed in Latin. But since you make no mention whatever of it in your letters to Mr. Le Clerc I must conclude either that it has not yet reached you, or perhaps that it is not sufficiently accurate; I should regret that, as I should not be able to get the profit from it that I had promised myself. Meanwhile it is your [p. 216] right as the author to do as you wish with your own work. Wetstein seems at last to be thinking seriously about the publication of the Sententiae of the Toulouse Inquisition; the publication of Diogenes Laertius is rapidly approaching its end;†1 so I hope that a start will be made within two months on the publication of a work so long felt to be wanted; meanwhile whatever I have decided to set before it will be made ready, God keeping me in health. But in fact what I have written has grown to a considerable mass; I had originally intended to make some prefatory remarks about the Inquisition; but the material that offered itself to me was so abundant that I have written a rather full account of the Inquisition. This is divided into four books. The first of these demonstrates that persecution for the sake of religion is repugnant to the spirit of the Christian religion and to the teaching of the first Fathers; it shows further how greatly Christians have changed since the time of the Council of Nicaea; here I cite various pieces of evidence from the Fathers and further the laws of the Empire; at length I come down to the times of the Papacy, and show how the Inquisition was introduced and afterwards was spread to all parts, and finally how it was introduced into Spain and Portugal. The second book describes all the servants of the Inquisition, what are the duties of each, their power, their privileges, and the character of their prison. The third shows what persons are subject to the [p. 217] examination and tribunal of the Inquisition. Here I have some remarks on heretics and their punishments; I then make clear the distribution of heretics into various categories: into heretics manifest and secret, affirmative and negative, penitent and impenitent; heresiarchs; those who give credence to heretics; who defend, harbour, or support them; persons suspected of heresy or who impede the Inquisition in the performance of its office; relapsed persons, blasphemers, diviners, magicians, Jews and those reverting to the practice of Judaism. Many curious matters will be found here. Finally, the fourth book portrays the manner of procedure before the tribunal of the Inquisition. Here I describe the way in which the Inquisitor sets about his task; how he initiates a proceeding against one reported as guilty of heresy and how he continues it. I here set out at length what they teach regarding witnesses and the kinds of persons whose evidence is admitted in a case of heresy; this subject provides a good deal of material. If the accused denies the charge, how the proceeding against him is conducted; until at last we come to the pronouncement of the sentence. How the proceedings are concluded: 1. When the accused is to be acquitted. 2. When he is in bad repute and a canonical purgation is imposed. 3. When the charge is only partially proved; here I make some remarks on torture and set out the way of inflicting it in the Inquisition, with an account of the torture of Don Balthasar.†1 4. When the accused is suspected of heresy. 5. When he is in bad repute and suspect. [p. 218] 6. When he is convicted or has confessed, and is penitent. Here I give a full account of penitential punishments, the Sanbenito garment, perpetual imprisonment, etc., and how far accused persons are admitted to penitence. 7. When he is relapsed and penitent. 8. When he is impenitent and not relapsed. 9. When he is impenitent and relapsed. 10. When he is negative.†1 These last four are handed over to the secular court, and if they are clerics they are first degraded; I describe the method of degradation. 11. When he is a fugitive. At length there follows the proceeding against the dead, and that against houses. I conclude the whole treatise with an account of the auto-da-fé. There you have a short conspectus of the whole work; I hope you will not find it unpleasant or unwelcome reading. We are all well up to now. I have had no adverse reports of your own health, I pray that it may long continue, so that you may be able to contribute further results of your labours to the public. Our friend Veen is quite well and his whole family also. My wife sends you her kindest regards, as do my children, and first and foremost myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 16 March 1691

1369. Edward Clarke to Locke, 7 March 1691 (1347, 1370)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 59-60. Printed in Rand, pp. 303-6. Answered by no. 1376.
Chipley March the 7th. 1690/1
Deare Sir,
After about 12. dayes absence being now gott home againe I hold my selfe obleiged to acquaint you that I spent some part of my time with Mr Stratton in your Affayres about Sutton, and not to mention other Particulars of lesser moment, I only acquaint you at present, that I have at last obtain'd an actuall Entry to bee made on the Parcell of Ground next Robert Haroll's house which you formerly Leased to Him, and is I feare all the satisfaction you are ever like to have for the Remainder of the Debt due from Him, Hee being now much more likely to stand in need of Releife from the Parish, then ever to bee in a possibility of Paying what remaines due to you, had this Entry been made sooner, as I Advised, there might have been more of your Debt satisfied thereby, but lett that Passe, 'Tis now disposed of (tho not without difficulty) with the rest of the Grounds to David Haroll for 20l. for one yeare from Lady Day next, and more then this Wee could not possibly Advance it to, and I feare another yeare, if the Price of Corn, Cattle, and Wooll etc: does not Advance, there must bee further Abatements, but more of this with other particulars when next I see you, In the meane time I cannot omitt to acquaint you, That Mr. Stratton hath lately Marryed his Eldest daughter to James Hazell,†1 to whome the House and Landes that Mr. Stratton Liv'd in at Sutton are Assigned, but upon what Terms or Conditions I know not, only that Mr. Stratton and his Wife and the rest of his Family are to remove speedily to Bristoll, where Hee has taken a House, and sayes Hee intends to spend the rest of his dayes, soe that I thinke it will bee necessary for you to have a New-Steward for the mannagement of your Concern's in those parts, but of this likewise I shall discourse you more fully hereafter; Mr. Stratton tells mee that Hee has about 60. or 80l. of your money in his handes, for which I indeavour'd to gett a Return,†2 but could not doe it at this time from Bristoll, without losse, which I declyn'd, knowing that
― 220 ―
your occasions were noe wayes Pressing for it; The money due to you from Abraham Barnes upon the Writt I sent down against Him at your suite, is well secured, and Mr. Stratton tells mee will bee speedily paid; There's one thing more I thinke materiall to acquaint you with, and that is the Agents for your Landlord Mr. Popham†1 have lately began a Coale-Worke on the Landes call'd the New-Tynings which you hold by Lease for your Life, which is and will bee to your Dammage And I know not what remedy to Advise untill I see your Lease and can have opportunity to consider with you upon it; There's nothing else of Moment that occurrs at present, but if there happens any thing wherein I can bee any wayes further serviceable, you may depend upon it, it shall bee carefully performed: And Now methinks I would fayne Answer that Part of your last Letter to mee which relates to the present state my eldest sonn†2 is in both in respect to his Mind and Learning, but indeed the Taske is soe hard, that I know not well how to answer your Expectations therein, and therefore can only acquaint you that as to His Mind, upon the strictest observation I can make, there's noe manner of Disposition to any thing that's ill, neither can I find any inclination in Him towards any sort of Learning whatsoever, nor any Pleasure that Hee takes therein, however Hee goes on, tho slowly, and with a verie great Indifferency; Monsieur†3 complaynes much against Him for want of Application to his Businesse, and tells mee Hee is capable, but too Carelesse and Indifferent in all things, and verie apt to forgett what Hee Learn's tho never soe perfectly, which I attribute more to the badnesse of Memory then Neglect in Him; I am satisfied Hee hath made some Progresse in Geographie, but haveing soe little Knowlidge therein my selfe, am altogather unable to give you any particular Account thereof; Hee allsoe understands perfectly, Addition, Substraction, Multiplication, and Division, And a little use will I presume make Him verie ready in those parts of Arithmatick; Hee allsoe proceeds (tho but slowly) in the methods proposed by you for learning the Latin-Tongue, and I hope will in time bee made Master of that as well as of French; Monsieur certainely takes greate Care and Paynes with him, and the only discernable fault is, that Hee hath all along, and still does suffer Himselfe to have too little Authority over Him, by which means the Childe stands in little or noe Awe at all of Him,
― 221 ―
the consequence whereof is so ill, that thereby the Childe has not that Esteem and value for His instruction, as I beleive Hee would otherwise have, frequent instances whereof I have seen in the Childs haveing a greater regard to, and minding much more what I or my Clerke say to Him, then what His Tutor instructs Him in, And if wee could but find an effectuall Cure in this Particular, (and soe as not to disobleige Monsieur neither, for that I would carefully avoyd) I fancy our Businesse would goe on much the Easier and pleasanter for the future; Monsieur Writt to you about 3. weeks since, which I hope you Received, and since that the Eldest Boye has been ill of the Meazells, but is now well recovered againe, only his Eyes are something weaken'd thereby, and there remaines a Cough, which I hope will weare off in a little time after being gently Purg'd, which is intended to morrow; All the rest of the younge-Fry continue as yett well, your Wife makes the greatest Progresse in French of any of the Children, but I find it verie difficult to gett them to speake French when they are out of my sight, But the greate Misfortune of All is that neither my Wife nor I can speake the Language, for I am satisfied that if either of us could doe that, the Children would Learn it, with much lesse difficulty, and in halfe the time; but this I take to bee a Dissease without a Remedy, the Hurry of Businesse I am constantly in not permitting mee opportunityes to Learn it, and the naturall Aversenesse there is in my Wife to all sorts of Learning and Bookes, tho of verie good Naturall-parts, keepes Her from attempting it; Upon the whole matter I fancy there's hardly any thing but your presence with us here will mend any of our faults, and therefore, as well as for many other Reasons, I hope you will beare being importun'd to visitt your own Native Countrey, and make us happy with your company here, without which I hardly thinke it possible to grow Fatt here as formerly I have done, the generall complaints of others, and my own frequent disappoyntments and losses by the Breakeing of Tennants and otherwise, are Preventives suffitient against increaseing either in Body or Purse: I thinke I have suffitiently tyred you, but however I am desiered by my Wife, and Yours, all the Children, and Monsieur, to present you with theire services, before I tell you how much I am,
Your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:
Endorsed by Locke: E Clarke 7 Mar 90/1
