1370. Locke to Edward Clarke, 9 March 1691 (1369, 1376)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 31. Printed in Rand, pp. 306-10. The letter is apparently a later addition to the Education letters: ii. 624 n.
Oates 9° Mar 90/1
Dear Sir
Though by your way of writeing and the litle tampering I presume would be used in the case made me hope your son would not suffer much by the measels you told me he had in your letter of 23d Feb: before you went to Sutton yet I could not forbear to write to Madam about it and send her some generall rules concerning that disease which perhaps might be of use in some other cases though I hope master needed†a not any. Supposeing him therefor recoverd of the measels and quite well again I desire we may enquire a litle into his studys and temper of minde. I†1- suspect he trifles away in his chamber a good part of his time and does not by a diligent application of his minde dispatch it soe soon as he might that soe he might goe to his recreation or any thing else. An†2- habit of this sauntering humor I looke on as one of the worst things that can befall him as well as one of the hardest matters to be cured.-†2 But with all pray consider it is very apt to be mistaken and therefor we must use great care and warinesse to get a true knowledg of it, and not mistake one thing for an other. I know he has a great respect for you and stands in much awe of you. The first caution therefor to be used is that the enquirys you make concerning this matter be made with all the gentlenesse and softnesse imaginable and be soe managed that even his Tutor suspect not that any intimation concerning this matter comes from me but that you thinke it convenient of your self to enquire what your son does, what progresse he has made and how he spends his time, and therefor before you come to this enquiry examin him in Geographie and other parts of his study and let it be some time after the receit of my letter before you begin it-†1
2° if†3- you doe finde that he does loitre at his booke and let a
― 223 ―
good deale of the time he spends in his chamber run idly away doe not presently conclude that this is from a sauntering humor in his temper. It may be childishnesse and a prefering something to his booke which his thoughts run on, and he dislikes his booke,†a as†a is naturall because it is forced upon him as a taske. To know this perfectly you must observe him out of his chamber and at play or following his owne inclinations, and see there whether he vigerously sets him self about any thing, designes any thing, and with labour and eagernesse pursues it till he has accomplished it, or whether he lazily and listlesly dreams away his time. If this lazynesse be only when he is about his booke I thinke it may be easily cured. If it be in his temper it will require a litle more pains and attention to remedie it. If you are satisfied by his earnestnesse at play or any thing else he sets his minde on in the intervalls between his times of study that he is not of himself inclinde to sauntering, but only want of relish of his booke makes him negligent and sluggish in his application to it. The first remedie is to trie by talkeing to him kindely of the folly and inconvenience of it whereby he looses a good part of his time which he might have for his diversion. But be sure to talke calmely and kindely and not much at first but only these plain reasons in short. If this prevails you have gaind the point by the most desirable remedye which is reason and kindenesse. If it prevails not trie to shame him out of it by you and your mothers laughing at him for it askeing every day if there be noe strangers there when he comes downe with his tutor how long he was that day about his businesse and if he has not don it in the time he might be well supposd to have don expose and turn him into ridicule for it, but mix noe chideing with it, only put on a pretty cold brow towards him and keep it till he reforme and let his mother doe soe too. If this worke not the effect you desire Then tell him he shall be noe longer troubled with a Tutor to take care of his Education you will not be at that charge to have him spend his time Idly with him in a chamber But since he prefers this or that [whatever play it be he delights in]†b to his booke that only he shall doe and soe in earnest set him on worke on his beloved play and keepe him steadily and in earnest to it Morning and afternoon till he be fully surfeted and dog weary of it and would at any rate change it for some houers at his booke again. But when you thus set him a taske of his play you must be sure to looke after him your self or set some body else
― 224 ―
to doe it that you may constantly see him imploid in it and that he be not permitted to be idle at that too. I say your self looke after him for it is worth your while whatever businesse you have to bestow two or three days upon your son to cure soe great a mischeif as is sauntering at ones businesse.
This is that I propose if it be idlenesse not from his generall temper but a peculiar or acquired aversion to learning, which you must be carefull to examine and distinguish, and which you shall certainly know by this if you in good humor give him a playday once or twice and observe then whether he spends it lazily, or actively about some project of his owne; But though you have your eye upon him to observe what he does with the time he has at his owne disposal, yet you must not let him perceive you doe soe, for that may restrain him from following his owne inclination, and that being the thing his head or heart is upon and not dareing to prosecute it for fear of you he may forbear doeing other things and soe seeme to be idle and negligent when in truth it is noe thing but being intent on something which the fear of your eye or knowledg keeps him from executeing. You must therefor when you would trie him give him full liberty, but let somebody whom you can trust observe what he does and it will be best he should have his playday of liberty when you goe from home and if Madam and Monsieur too went abroad at the same time it would not be amisse. For if you are in doubt whether†1- sauntering be only a lazynesse at†a his booke or a listlesnesse in his temper-†1 this is the first thing to be don that you may come to a certainty.
If†2- there be any thing of sauntering and lazynesse in his naturall disposition-†2 as it is one of the most unpromiseing tempers I know soe it is also one of the hardest to be dealt with, For it generally carrying with it a kinde of indifferency for future things may be attributed to want of foresight and want of desire, and how to plant or increase either of these where nature has given a cold or contrary temper is not I thinke very easy. In our present case if there be any thing of it you must first finde out his most predominant
― 225 ―
passion and carefully examin what it is to which the greatest bent of his minde has the most steady and earnest tendency, and when you have found that you must set that on worke to excite his industry to any thing else. If he loves praise or play or fine clothes etc or on the other side dreads shame and disgrace, your displeasure etc what ever it be that he loves most except it be sloth, (for that will never set him on worke) let that be made use of to excite him to activity. For in this listlesse temper you are not to fear an excesse of appetite (as in all other cases) by cherishing it, for tis that which you want and therefor must labour to stir up and increase for where there is noe desire there will be noe industry. If you have not hold enough upon him this way to excite vigor and activity in him, you must imploy him in some constant bodily labour whereby he may get a habit of doeing something, It were better to imploy him constantly in some study to get him a habit of exerciseing and applying his minde, but because that is an invisible attention and noe body can tell when he is or is not idle at it, you must finde bodily imployments for him which he must be constantly busied in and kept to, and if they have some litle hardship and shame in them it may not be the worse to make them the sooner weary him and make him desire to return to his booke the†1- sooner it may not be amisse,-†1 but be sure when you exchange his booke for his other labours set him such a taske to be don in such a time as may allow him noe time to be idle only after you have by this way brought him to be attentive and industrious at his booke you may upon his dispatching his study in the time set him as a reward give him some respit from his other labour which you may increase†2 as you finde him grow more and more steady in his application and at last wholy take of when his sauntering at his booke is cured.†-3 But if I mistake not mightily your sons temper we shall not need this remedie. My service to Madam my wife and the rest I am
yours
J L
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Chiply near Taunton Frank
Postmark: MR 11
Endorsed (not by Clarke and probably not by Mrs. Clarke): Mr. Lock about Master Edward.

1371. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 10/20 March 1691 (1367, 1379)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 69-70.
Rotterdam 20 March 1691
Dear Friend
I was in hopes to have had time by my Lord†1 to have answerd yours of the 26th past; but the wind coming about on Sunday last,†2 he scarce allowed himself time to dine, nor me to write 6 lines. So that the Seeds and Trees†3 could not be got. But what was in house, the bag with Down, markt IL and Pere Simons last treatise or Critique des Versions du Nouveau T. in Quires in a Roll. I put abord, and, desiring the Captain to take care to keep the bag clean, being a new bag made by my wife, for another use, tho never yet used, my Lord ordred him to put it into his Cabin.
My Lord being gone, and the weather inticeing I walkt round the boomtjes:†4 yesterday I was at the Exchange and afternoon an express coming up from my Lord from the Briel, to signify, that the Convoy, which should have been ready a week agoe had not yet half his men, and to press, that he might be ordred to take men out of another ship, that he might be gone as this day. I went with his Lordships Letter, and after wayting an houre betwixt 2 doores, to speak with one of the Lords,†5 at last he came out and told me, he could do nothing, but said if I presented the Letter tomorrow, the Captain would receive a sharp reprimand, having muster'd to them some days ago, 110 men, and my Lord wrote that he had but 50 on board.
This day the letter was given in, and seconded by an Express from the Hague, and all that could be obtaind was, that there was a Snaauw†6 expected in every houre, and he should be supplyed with men from on board her. The other ship, having 50 marchant-men†a ready to—(I was about to tell you that these ships being ready to) saile for Scotland, they could not yield to a thing so prejudicial to their trade. And that on the Exchange we had news that the
― 227 ―
yachts with my Lord M— Dorset mr Wharton†1 and others, were saild out with 2 privateers—
And behold my Lord at the doore, and coming upstairs—I have now been up and down with him, to get an order for that friggot, but find an order sent to the other assigning him people in their service upon their ships, and commanding him to sea, upon his peril to morrow morning, so my Lord is Just now about 10, at night gone down in an open boat rowing, it being a dead calm, having bought a blanket to lap himself in. I wish him safe over.
The french Dauphin, is with 60 000 men before Mons, and a body of 40 000 to turn any force that may come against them; as letters from Brabant say. So the K. and Duke of Bavaria†2 are expected to morrow to pass through this town, in all hast to the Army. This Summer is like to be a Summer of great Action, I wish it have the Same, or better Success, if it maybe, than last campaign in Ireland. Having done now with anything that is publick, I return to entertain you with my own condition. I took such cold yesterday, wayting between those doores, that I am this day as loose in the hilts†3 as ever—And had I not this evening taken in Laudanum, I should not be able to sit and write this, which I took 3 hours agoe, to ease the pain in my back. Which, before my wives delivery I conceiv'd I should be delivered from when she was delivered. But it continues still. I have never yet been able to forbear 3 nights together, Laudanum, but my looseness has returned, I intend now to take it 8 or 10 nights together, and see if that wil bind me up. But I think, this fine weather, to take Rhubarb, once more first.
I bought not Skinner at that extravagant rate: I am in love with the book, as a curiosity, but I like not to buy it so dear: tho I have known the time, when that consideration would not have stuck with me.
I perceive that we are not to expect Mary, and so shall accordingly take our measures. I understand now how I may ride, and not catch cold so as to incommode me. But, till this warm weather came on, that the boys that 2 or 3/w agoe rode over the mase upon the Ice, have this day swom in it, I could not have told how to ride without cold feet, for by riding if the weather be any thing cold, my feet are almost mortifyed—
― 228 ―
I am glad you will lend your helping hand to what I have in hand, but cannot yet tell how to get done.†1 Kolhans I cannot perswade to let me know, what they are adoing, nor his wife neither, she concludes if it succeeds not we shall never know, and I the quite contrary.
Your little friend,†2 being askt what I should say to you in his name said, tell him I would fain he would come and be with us, that I might see him, how he is now clad. When mr. Brockman came, they would perswade him, that that was his friend. His coulour went and came, and he could not beleeve it, and he came to me, and askt me if that were so; and said if it was he did not know him again. He goes now, with John to schoole, and this evening, to our amasement he said and told us, that he had been almost in all the churches in this towne, with his schoole fellows, at the Great church, the french, the Southern, the Arminian, and being askt which he liked best, said the great church, because there was the bravest cack stoole,†3 and pictures, and bras candlesticks. And then, of his own accord, told us he wondred at first how the Predicant could get up into that high cack stoole, but having been there once when they did not preach he found that he went up by staires. And that while he was there looking, he heard a great noise, as if the church were full of people singing, but there being few people, he thought it was in a church hard by, and at last had seen great pipes that spake so loud, so loud, as if it had been many people. We askt him, if he had ever been in the Jews church, he said no, but coming to describe another church where he had been, we found it was the synagogue, he saw a man there, with a white thing upon his hat, and other men with white things on their hatts carryed him an Apple upon a stick and put it to his nose, and he bowed, as if he bowed his head to the Apple. I askt him who he saw there, he said drunken Moses, and that the boy that carryed him said he must not laugh, or they would cutt off his head, so you may conceive he was very grave for he has no mind to part with his head yett, tho yesterday being askt which he would rather should dy his brother Benjohan or he, said, he, And†a gave for reason that he was little, and his brother would be soon fit to serve his father.
― 229 ―
I never heard of any such thing among the Jews, but my servants say that once a yeare they do represent Eves, or the serpents Apple.†1
These are childish things, but shew a great curiosity in the boy to see things, and observation upon them as well as memory. And while he is telling his story theres no parson has more action with his hand and whole body to induce you to take notice of what he would tell you.
I have writ to Wetstein for your account and shall pay it. I know nothing that I have now to add, save my and my wives best respects to your self and my service to Sir Francis and his Lady and so I rest nigh midnight
Yours
B F
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Lock at mr. Robert Pawlings living in Dorsetcourt Channel Row in Westminster

1372. Robert Pawling to Locke, 12 March 1691 (1365, 1385)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 212.
London March 12th. 1690
Sir
I wrot you an answer to severall particulars of your letter the day before I received it; if it were proper so to speak or write but tis no bull. Tom†2 hath been this day to enquire for Cicero's Ep: he finds they are not easily to be met with but amongst the french booksellers at one place he met with them†a translated by P: Du Ryer†3 Paris 1650 in 12° only French in 3 vol: at an other place†b by Godowin†4 Lecteur et Professeur du Roy Paris 1663 in Octavo french and
― 230 ―
Latin at 7s 6d in 2 vol: and the other at 2s. 6d each so they are just as dear only in french as tother in Latin and french. he intends to try again tomorrow and will look out mr Boyles works†1 and I will send them you direct. I will wait on mr Boyle tomorrow. mr Brockman is returned with mr Stephens†2 he presents his service to you and tells me the Earl of Monmoth wilbe at home very speedily and then I hope we shall see you here. I was with Dr Welwood†3 this day to visit him where I met with mr Sheaphard†4 who enquired how you did, therupon Dr Welwood took occasion to oblige me to present his humble service to you which I promised to do. I beleiv Dr Hutton your friend wilbe in a capacity to assist me in my affair.†5 I hope you wilbe here at the Kings return†6 at which time the Doctor is expected. our Neighbour Mr Vander Hoven†7 is verry ill of a fever he hath only a Dutch Doctor to take care of him. I fear he will dy. I would have had his Wife have sent for an able Phisitian but mr Jones†8 and his Wife and children too I was going to say opposed me saying some able Apoth.†a are as good as Doctors.†9 these two letters came since I wrot last, one came by mr Brockman. by my next I will acquaint you what the drawing of the writings come to if it must be so twas not because I was ashamed but because I never did use to demand any thing for what I do for friends that cost me nothing: when I was in trade I alwayes confined my profits to the busines of trade what I did for friends out of that I alwayes did it gratis and have refused many gratuitys and
― 231 ―
now and then bribes. I have not Madam Lockharts account yet of what she laid out. I am
Sir
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
Address: For Mr Locke

1374. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 13/23 March 1691 (1340, 1390)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 41-2.
Monsieur
Il y a long temps que je n'ay eu l'honneur de vous escrire, attendant tousjours vostre responce sur celle que j'escrivis a Noel sur l'accouchement de ma femme.†2 depuis nous nous flattions de jour a Autre de recevoir vostre beau present de pommes. Comme j'ayme passionement ce fruit j'ay beaucoup regretté le malheur de leur retardement et de ce que la pluspart sont fondues par le degel. mais Monsieur si vous en aviez envoyez moins, nous les aurions sauvez toutes. deux grands barils font plustost monstre de marchandise que de present. vostre liberalité va au dela de ce qu'on oseroit esperer et que vous deviez faire, quoy que plustost vous ne deviez rien, et que nous sommes beaucoup endebté aupres de vous. Vous aurez peut estre desja appris que Monsieur le Clerk et Monsieur Verrijn le traducteur de vostre livre ont epousé depuis peu, ce qui n'est guerre propre a des philosophes, tousjours plusieurs auroient souhaitté que Monsieur le Clerq s'en fust abstenu craignants que cela le detournera de ses occupations serieuses. il a epousé la fille de Monsieur l'historien Leti.†3 vostre argent en b.†4 est tousjours dans la mesme
― 233 ―
assiette. Monsieur charleton m'a fait l'honneur de me faire present de quelques medailles que Monsieur Daranda ma apportez. je vous prie de luy faire tenir l'incluse. Monsieur furly m'a envoyé la responce aux obj. contre le livre de la t.†1 que jay lu avec beaucoup de plaisir croyant que l'autheur n'a pas besoin de craindre de nouvelles obj. toute la famille vous presente ses tres humble respects. Mon beau Pere particulierement et je suis avec un profond respect
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
d'Amst. ce 23 Mars. 1691.

1375. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 13 March 1691 (1368, 1393)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256 t. Printed in Ollion, pp. 198-201. For transmission see pp. 254-5. Answers no. 1368; answered by no. 1393.
(English)
Oates 13 Mar 90/1
Vir Eruditissime
Has ego chartas tibi in manus tradendas curavi ut iis, si libet, perlectis Interpreti reddas et simul gratias quod tantum laborem meis scriptis impendere dignatus sit. Optassem sane ut initio operis sui antequam tam longe esset progressus mihi unam vel alteram paginam suâ Latinitate donatam misisset, Tunc forte liberiùs de versione ejus judicium meum interposuissem. Tu ex iis quæ
― 234 ―
tribus primis capitibus manu meâ adscripsi, (ubi tamen multa emendanda non attigi,) facile judicabis quod minus laboriosum mihi foret novam instituere versionem quam hanc corrigere. Interpres non mihi videtur ubique satis callere Linguam Anglicanam. Inde <forsan>†a evenit ut dum verbum verbo fidus nimis reddit et voces sequatur sensum meum aliquando non ita assequatur et Latine exprimat ut facile capiant lectores. Hoc tibi legenti abunde constabit nec dubito quin in Latinâ hac versione Latinitatem subinde desiderabis. Ego nihilominus docti et amici Interpretis laudo industriam, an vero hoc in opere eum habuerit successum ut erudito hoc sæculo commendari possit et cum laude scriptoris in publicum prodire penes te amicosque ejus sit judicium. Ego verborum plane negligentissimus, et forsan plusquam par est elegantiarum contemptor si modo Lectoribus stilus non fastiditus sensum meum clarè et perspicuè exhibeat nec res per se satis obscuras magis involvat cætera non curo. Ex nuperis a Furleio nostro acceptis literis intelligo jam desiderari has Chartas ut quam citissime remittantur. Ideo primam jam nactus occasionem illas Londinum mitto, ut illic quæratur fida manus cui credantur ut maturè si fieri
― 235 ―
possit restituantur. Ego cum primum illas accepi valetudine et jam alio opere quod præ manibus habeo impeditus illis <perlegendis>†a corrigendisque satis vacare non potui. Ultimum hujus primi libri caput prorsus intactum reliqui aliis curis avocatus ne diutius apud me hæreret jam (ut video) Amstelodami expectatus libellus. Hoc non incommode accidit ex quarto enim capite nullis lituris contaminato facile <dijudicare>†b possis de reliquâ versione et inde interpreti prout visum fuerit consilium super totâ re dare.
(English) <Inchoatas>†c hasce nondum finiveram literas cum tuæ 16° Martis datæ mihi redditæ sunt tanto acceptiores quod post diuturnum et inusitatum silentium male ominantem animi ægritudinem mihi levarent. Versio de qua agitur sero admodum mihi hic rure reddita est nullis adjunctis nec a te nec a Verrino literis quod miratus sum. Postquam hic aliquamdiu commoratus essem monuit me per Epistolam Hospes meus Londinensis se accepisse fasciculum chartarum ex altera parte urbis ad me domum suam missum per bajulum, quid vero essent vel a quo venerint se plane nescire. Suspicatus quid esse possit, rescripsi ut fasciculum aperiret et in eo si reperiret aliquam partem libri mei Latinè versam complicaret rursum et quamprimum daretur occasio fidi internuncii ad me mitteret, si
― 236 ―
aliud quid contineret†a mihi indicaret quid esset et apud se retineret. res accidit ut conjeceram et aliquanto post famulus hujus in qua versor familia Londinum petens mihi versionem asportavit. Literæ ubi interciderint plane nescio sed cum diu expectatum†b de his chartis per epistolam ne verbum acceperim credidi fido alicui amico huc proficiscenti festinatò sine literis commissas ab eo Verrinum de iis certiorem†c factum†c quievisse. Quid de ipsa versione sentiendum sit vobis prorsus relinquo. Multum me Eruditi Verrini, studio benevolentiæ humanitati imo et labori debere libens agnosco, nec tantum mihi arrogo ut de alieno opere multis lucubrationibus jam ad umbelicum perducto aliquid statuem. Hoc vobis integrum sit, Vos amici ingenuo et industrio juveni consulite. Operam quam meis cogitatis impenderit ego semper agnoscam, quid alii in erudito et critico hoc sæculo facturi sint vos videte. Hoc eo libentius dico quia non mea res agitur. De meo opere jam factum est judicium et cum jam prodiit non <amplius>†d mei juris est. Quicquid de versione judices rogo ut authorem quam officiocissime salutes meo nomine, eique promittas meo nomine omnem meam operam studium
― 237 ―
industriam si qua in re ipsi utilis esse potuerim. interim æstimo maxime et amplector una cum fratre†1 cujus humanitati multum debeo.
(English) Gratissima mihi sunt quæ de Sancto officio scribis. Tua prolegomena multum ponderis et gratiæ addent operi et erit doctior simul et utilior pars libri. Plurimum tuæ eruditioni tuisque hoc in argumento lucubrationibus debebit orbis Christianus qui tantâ fide et industriâ eruisti e tenebris occulta hæc et sedulo celata iniquitatis simul et crudelitatis mysteria et palam fecisti. Editionem avidè expecto et mecum filia Doctoris Cudworth, quam tibi olim ut miri ingenii fæminam inter familiares mihi notam nominavi. Ea nupsit Baronetto qui in hoc parlamento hujus provinciæ Deputatus est.†2 Hi me hospitem in domum suum acceperunt et commodissimum valetudini meæ asylum præbuerunt. Domina ipsa ita in Theologis philosophisque studiis et contemplationibus versata est ut paucos invenias homines quibuscum majore cum fructu et jucunditate verseris: Limatissimi inprimis est judicii. paucosque novi qui tanta cum perspicuitate de rebus abstrusissimis et a captu non dico fæminarum sed etiam plerorumque literatorum remotis <disserant>†a et difficultates <solvant>.†b Lectionem cui olim multum
― 238 ―
erat dedita jam impedit oculorum imbecillitas, cui abunde supplet mentis acies. Tuum nomen Tuaque merita ex commercio quam cum patre habuisti olim†1 illi nota, et cum sciret te mihi notum Amstelodami et familiarem fuisse multa de te subinde rogavit de tuis rebus prosperis nostrâque amicitia plurimum gavisa. Cum tuæ mihi heri ad cænam vocato redditæ essent, rogavit unde, cum a Te responderem, et aliqua de re literaria continere suspicata esset, rogavit insuper si ejusmodi essent quæ communicari possint, quæ contineret epistola tua illi explicarem, quod haud invitus feci, ratus tibi non displiciturum. valde illi placuit idea operis quam exhibuisti, et properam sperat editionem, nam etsi Linguam non intelligit Latinam ex me tamen præcipua tuæ præfationis argumenta se intellecturam non dubitat. Interim mea manu tibi plurimam salutem dicit. Uxorem tuam optimam liberosque Venios, Guenelonos reliquosque nostros inter quos Verrinum utrumque officiocissime saluto, Vale Vir Amplissime et ut facis me ama Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin)
Oates 13 Mar 90/1
Learned Sir,
I arranged for these papers to be put into your hands so that you may, if you will, read through them and return them to the translator, giving him at the same time my thanks for deigning to expend so much labour on my writings. I could have wished, to be sure, that at the commencement of his work and before he had proceeded so far with it he had sent me one or two pages as presented in his Latinity; then perhaps I would have intervened more freely with my opinion of his translation. You, from the notes inserted in [p. 234] my hand in the first three chapters (where, however, I have not touched on many points where correction is needed) will readily judge that it would be less laborious for me to undertake a new translation than to correct this one. The translator does not seem to me to be everywhere familiar enough with the English language. Hence perhaps it comes that while translating word for word too faithfully and adhering too closely to verbal expressions he sometimes does not grasp my meaning and express it in Latin in such a way that readers may easily understand it. This will be abundantly clear to you as you read, nor do I doubt that in this Latin translation you will from time to time feel a want of Latinity. Nevertheless I commend the industry of the learned and friendly translator; though whether he has succeeded well enough in this work to enable it to be commended to this erudite age and to be published with praise to its author is a matter for you and his friends to decide. I myself am very negligent about words, and a contemner of literary graces perhaps more than is proper; so long as my style is not distasteful to readers and exhibits my meaning clearly and perspicuously, and does not further conceal matters that are obscure enough in themselves, I am not concerned for anything else. I understand from a recent letter that I have received from Furly that the return of these papers is now desired as quickly as possible. I have therefore taken the first opportunity of sending them to London, in order that some reliable hand may there be sought to which to [p. 235] entrust them, so that they may if possible be returned in good time. When I first received them I was prevented by my health and by other work that I now have on hand from finding sufficient leisure for reading and correcting them. Being called away by other business, I have left the last chapter of this first book entirely untouched, so that the manuscript should not be detained with me any longer, now that, as I see, it is awaited in Amsterdam. This has happened not inopportunely; for as the fourth chapter is not blurred by any of my markings you can easily form an opinion from it about the rest of the translation, and may accordingly give the translator what advice you see fit on the whole matter.
(Latin) I had begun this letter and not yet finished it when yours dated 16 March was delivered to me; it was all the more welcome as it relieved the sickness of my mind which was presaging evil after your long and unwonted silence. The translation in question was very late in reaching me here in the country, and there was no letter with it from you or Verrijn, which surprised me. After I had stayed here for some time my London host informed me by letter that he had received a parcel of papers, which had been sent to me at his house by a porter from another part of the city, but that he did not know what they were or whom they came from. Suspecting what it might be, I wrote back telling him to open the parcel, and if he found it to contain any part of my book in a Latin translation to wrap it up again and send it to me at the first opportunity of a trustworthy messenger; if it contained anything else [p. 236] he was to let me know what it was and to keep it with him. It turned out to be as I had surmised, and some time after a servant of the family I am staying with went to London and brought me the translation. I do not know where the letter was lost; but since I had received not a word in writing, as I had long expected, about these papers, I supposed that they had been hurriedly entrusted, without an accompanying letter, to some trustworthy friend who was travelling to this country, and that on being informed by him about them Verrijn had done nothing further. What is to be thought of the translation itself I leave entirely to you and those with you. I freely acknowledge my great debt to the attention, goodwill, kindness, and, what is more, the labour of the learned Verrijn, nor do I take upon myself to pronounce any judgement on another man's work which has now been brought to completion with many lucubrations. Consider yourselves perfectly free in the matter; you, as his friends, must do what is best for that open-hearted and industrious young man. I myself shall always acknowledge the work he has expended on my thoughts; what others in this learned and critical age may think of it is for you to consider. I say this the more readily because I am not concerned. Judgement has already been passed on my own work, and as it has now been made public it is no longer under my control. Whatever opinion you may form of the translation, I beg that you will give the author my kindest regards and promise him in my name all my care, goodwill, and assiduity in any matter in which I can be of use to him. Meanwhile I highly esteem and embrace [p. 237] him together with his brother,†1 to whose kindness I owe so much.
(Latin) I am very pleased with what you write to me about the Holy Office. Your prolegomena will add much weight and attractiveness to the work, and will be at the same time the more learned and more profitable part of the book. The Christian world will owe a great deal to your scholarship and to your lucubrations on this theme; by them with fidelity and industry you have dragged forth from the darkness and made known to the world these secret mysteries alike of iniquity and cruelty that have been so sedulously concealed. I eagerly await the publication of the book, as also does Dr. Cudworth's daughter, whose name I mentioned to you some time ago as that of a remarkably gifted woman and one of my familiar friends. She is married to a baronet who is a representative of this county in the present parliament.†2 These two have taken me into their house as a guest and have provided a most opportune refuge for my present state of health. The lady herself is so much occupied with study and reflection on theological and philosophical matters, that you could find few men with whom you might associate with greater profit and pleasure. Her judgement is singularly keen, and I know few men capable of discussing with such insight the most abstruse subjects, such as are beyond the grasp, I do not say of women, but even of most educated men, and of resolving the difficulties they present. She was formerly much [p. 238] given to reading, which the weakness of her eyes now hampers; but her mental acumen amply makes up for this. Your name and your merits have long been known to her from the intercourse you had with her father,†1 and when she knew that I had made your acquaintance in Amsterdam and that we were on familiar terms she asked me many questions about you from time to time, being delighted that things were going well with you and about our friendship. Your letter was delivered to me yesterday just as I was called to supper; she inquired whom it was from; when I replied that it was from you, as she surmised that it contained something relating to learning she asked me further to disclose its contents to her, if they were such as could be communicated; I was glad enough to do so, thinking you would not disapprove. The general plan of the work as set forth by you pleased her greatly, and she hopes it will soon be published; for although she does not understand Latin she has no doubt that with my help she will understand the principal arguments in your preliminary discourse. Meanwhile she sends you her best wishes through me. Please give my kindest regards to your excellent wife and children, to the Veens, to the Guenellons, and to the rest of our friends, especially the two Verrijns. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch op de Kaÿsers Graft bij de Remonstrantse Kerck t'Amsterdam
Noted by van Limborch (beneath date): Recepta 17 Maji 1691.

1376. Locke to Edward Clarke, 16 March 1691 (1370, 1406)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 32. Printed in Rand, pp. 310-12. Answers no. 1369. Most of the letter concerns the young Edward Clarke specifically. One or two sentences are echoed in Some Thoughts concerning Education, but there is no general reproduction.
Oates 16 Mar. 90/1
Dear Sir
By mine to you the post before I received your kinde letter of the 7th you will perceive that Monsieur†1 letter came to my hand. Had I then had the view of your sons state soe well as I have now by your letter I should have either spared you that longue trouble or writ otherwise than I did. I beleive matters stand with him just as you apprehend them. Monsieur haveing by his lenity at first failed to establish that awe which is soe very necessary in a Tutor will noe doubt now have great difficulty to recover it. The want of this does noe doubt not a litle clog our progresse. I foresaw it from the begining and more than once talked to Monsieur of it, but whether it were good nature in him or any thing else I fear he never put on that austerity which haveing once establishd an ascendent over the childs minde he might afterwards have safely been as familiar and gentle as he would. Another thing that you suspect makes master goe on slowly is want of pleasure in learning to which you adde the badnesse of his memory, To cure what is curable in this case I thinke we ought diligently and carefully to enquire into the root and bottom as far as we can and see from whence any of this inconveniencys spring.
1° As to his cariage to his Tutor it should be carefully examind, whether it be contempt of his person; an opinion of his ignorance; presumeing on his lenity; or an aversion to learning that makes him have soe litle a regard to him, when you have by your owne observation as well as talkeing with Monsieur and the child made a certain and clear judgment in this point I doubt not but if you and monsieur joyn your forces this will be cured well enough, for I understand he stands mightily in awe of you.
2° As to his not very much likeing his booke pray consider what I writ in my last and observe whether he who is a litle coole in his studys be warme intent and vigorous at other things where he has the freedome to follow his owne inclinations and whether he will
― 240 ―
play heartily and with all his might. And next if you can pray informe your self whether he more dislikes his Tutor because of his booke or his booke because of his Tutor. When we know these things I cannot but thinke the remedie easilie atteinable. The hardest part is that of his memory. How to mend that naturall faculty if it be any way weake I confesse I scarce know Though I doubt not but time and health will by degrees restore it in him for I looke on it as an effect of his dangerous fever.†1 How to assist it I know ways but they lyeing more in order and method of thought than any thing else I doubt whether a childe be capable of any advantage by them.
Two things mightily please me in your letter one is that you finde in him noe inclination at all to anything that is ill. This carys with it the promises of a great deale of satisfaction from your son a good man will bring you much more comfort than a great scholler, and very ordinary parts with a good disposition will make a better and more usefull man, than great abilitys with vitious inclinations,†2 the only oddes would be if that were the case that he imbibes knowledg slowly, that there should be chosen out for him only the most necessary and the rest be let alone. But by the other thing you tell me I doe not see that is like to be our case. I am mightily pleased to heare he understands Arithmatique soe well not only as it is a part of knowledg that will be very usefull to him all his life, but as a marke of the goodnesse of his parts, for that is a science not to be gotten without memory and reason.†3 I would have him by constant exercise more or lesse every day be well confirmd in it. When at your leisure you have been able to satisfie your self of those other things we will then bethinke our selves what is to be don. In the meane time let him proceed in Latin and if he knows Longitude and latitude perfectly upon the globe†a and how to apply it to particular maps and thereby finde their situation on the globe I mean the countrys those maps are of he will have Geographie enough by lookeing in the maps or globe
― 241 ―
for those countrys and places he reads of in history or the gazets. To which if Monsieur can adde a generall view of Chronologie if it be but of those two Epochs the Julian period and the year of Christ it will be enough but of this I shall write to him and hope this sommer will be soe favourable to me as to let me see you at Chipley. I am much indebted to you for your great care in my affairs. I am at a losse where to finde one to looke after my concernes at Pensford if my Cosin Stratton give it up but I will not now tire you any longer. My service to your Lady. I hope she received the letter I writ her in your absence. I am
Dear Sir
your most faithfull humble servant
J LOCKE
My kindest love to my wife and master and the rest
All here are well My Lady herself writes today to Mrs Clarke and sends her owne complements. If you take any notice of any thing to your son pray doe it very spareingly and very gently till we have resolvd togeather what course to take only observe as much as you can which you will doe the more the lesse you interpose
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire member of Parliament at Chipley near Taunton Frank
Postmark: MR 18
Endorsed by Clarke: J:L: touching my Son and his Tutor etc: Received the 22th March 1690/1

1378. James Tyrrell to Locke, 19 March [1691] (1312, 1394)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 115-16. By Locke's endorsement the year could be 1692, but the passage relating to Tyrrell's Brief Disquisition shows that it belongs to 1691. The book was licensed for publication on 14 March 1691/2; the passage was obviously written before that. The address also points to 1691; in the autumn Tyrrell addressed his letters to Pawling's house: nos. 1424, 1430.
Oxford March 19th:
Dear Sir
I have received both yours. and as for the former, I must beg your pardon that I have not returned a more speedy answere to it, but indeed when I received it I intended to have bin in Towne my self before this time, tho I have since altered my resolutions, and shall not now be there before Easter:†1 but the maine reason why I did not answere it was, because being hindered by a long season of ill weather, as well as businesse I could not goe to Okeley to looke your gilt spoon etc: but now I went thither on monday, and I am sorry I can give you no better an account of them, for I doe not remember that I ever saw them among your things that came from Oxford, if they were, they were sent you with your writeings in the little hair trunke: for I have now carefully lookt over all your bookes; and other things that are lockt up in the two Trunks, and I cannot find them there: so that either they were sent you in that Trunk, or els they were stollen out of the chamber when they had broke open the door, both of that and the bedchamber, before ever John Clarke†2 who was then in the Countrey (I being at London) could goe over to remove the bookes and other things: therefore pray doe you, and Syl: call to mind if you can, where you left the spoon etc. and then I can Judg whether it were stollen out of the room; before John, came; or els by them
― 243 ―
that removed the things: for If I thought it were lost by my owne carelessenesse, or dishonesty of my servants I would give you another with all my heart. as for what you write in your last letter of sending you, or bringing up along with me what you have of Mr:Boyles workes shall be done, when I come up, since I perceive you are not in hast; and that this way they may come up with my things without any charge to you: but pray let me know whether you will have the 2 parts of the usefullnesse of experimental philosophy†1 sent up with the rest; since they are onely an introduction to it: and I must now commend your designe of againe resumeing the study of natural things; which as Dr:More very well observed doe afford perpetual variety, and the highest reasons to admire the wisedome and Goodnesse of their Creator;†2 whereas few civil historyes shew one any more then the great corruption; and pravity of humane nature, whose unreasonable lusts, and passions have,†a- and will-†a produce the same effects in all ages past, and to come: and as for your censure of the world as commonly governed, and mannaged, I perfectly agree with you: there is but one objection against natural experimental philosophy that I know of, and that you have given us in your booke, when you shew us, the reasons why it can never arrive to the perfection of a science:†3 yet however even the very guesses at truth, are certainly the best and most instructive of all Romances, but since you are pleased to inquire what I doe; I shall now tell you that I am about to publish my Epitome of Dr:Cumberlands Law of nature: with his Answere to Mr: Hobss Principles: placed by themselves by way of Prolegomena:†4 I have had it writ fair, and sent to the Authour for his last hand and approbation:†5 and when I come up I beleive shall receive
― 244 ―
it againe and will put it to the presse; but if you please first to peruse it I shall take it as a Favour: however it may provoke you to publish somewhat more perfect: which will be a great satisfaction not only to the lea<rned>†a world, but in particular to your <aff>ectionat†a servant.
J.T.
I should be glad to hear from you in answere to this before I come up: as allso whether you will have your Telescope brought up with me, the glasse of which I have now found: or whether you have your velvete rideing cap linnen, or any thing else I have of yours in my keeping.
I have allmost done my 6†b dialogues,†1 and when they <are>†c finisht shall bring them up with me. I should be glad your affaires would bring you to Towne whilst I am there: the weather will be then Temperate; and the air not much infected with smoke.
Address: For John Locke Esqr. at Mrs: Smythesbyes house in Dorset Court in Cannon Row Westminster to be sent with speed.
Postmark: MA 23
Endorsed by Locke: 19 Mar. 91
1379. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 18/28 and 20/30 March 1691 (1371, 1386)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 71-2.
Rotterdam 28 March 1691
Deare friend
I was last night prevented for want of time to write you by the post, and I know not but I maybe too late with this, by a passenger, to let you know the afflicting news of the losse of our dearest Babe,†2 our little Philosophus Autodidactus,†3 whom it pleasd divine Providence, to remove from this visible world, the 26 Instant about 3 in the morning, after 8 days sickness of the mazles, which, with
― 245 ―
an extraordinary, and almost intollerable pain, in my wives right thigh, keeps her very low: That night Just as I was going into bed I was also seizd with a Violent fit of Vomiting, and Purging, after I had tooke in Laudanum, which I have continued now every night, for this 9 nights, and do intend to continue—I cannot tell what to attribute it to, but the sudden great change of weather from midsummer to Christmas, and eating a piece of those superstitious pyes†1 received from England. But I am now again fresh. The K: passed this Town the 26. to lye at Bredah that night, and so thence to Mons, to whisk of Monsieur who is their with his Brother Allye,†2 and the Dauphin. This town†3 thought they should have had some respit by that Accident, but he has taken care that their matters shall not hang in suspence. The 7 prisoners men and women that were hurryed in the night from their ordinary Judges to the Court of Holland, that are not their ordinary and proper Judges, are left there. And the Bailif is delivered from the feare of the Court, who are his proper Judges Ratione Officii, and the schepens†4 of the Towns, and put under the power of other pickt Judges, as his peticion desired. To three Commissioners, he has delegated the Power inquisitory, that, the States, I had like to said, but more properly the 18 cities†5 —have given him to Inquire into the sedition, to summon before them all men in order to find out the bottom of it, to examine them upon their oaths, to which every man is bound to answer, even against himself, as the Civil Law exacts in all criminal cases. They have actually summoned our Burgermasters, who have made their appearance, and they will, they say, summon all the Captains of our Trainbands. And any other they see fit. And have Power as the see cause, in order to the future peace of the city to keep in, turn out, and put in whom they please into the magistracy, our swearers and promisers themselves not excepted. They say there is a Letter come forth, shewing the perniciousness of such oaths to the state. The villany of those that could give, and did Administer them. Presupposing them true, because nobody purges himself of the scandal, which every man can do, by addressing to the Court of Holland, for a mandamus
― 246 ―
of purge. But if the originall acts should be found there, it will be made ill work—
Peter†1 comes now in, tells me the passenger is gone—
Now we are come to the 30th Inst. and with it news from Brabant†a that the french had 7 Times stormd a mill a quarter of an houre from the towne, and at Last with losse of 2000 men have gaind it. They continue battering with 150 cannon, and 20 mortars, so that people are here wondrously afraid that it wilbe lost before we can be ready, But the K: is at Bruxels and will neglect no oportunity to raise the siege, of which, for all the discouragement of our Populace, the more prudent, expect to have a good account. They say that the french having drawn off the water, from a Quagmire to raise upon it a battery of 30 Guns, they from the town have sent them water against, and sunk their Guns. Time will shew us the issue of this Campaign, which is like to be a bloody one; unless the french carry this Town, and then decline fighting†2 —I am, with hearty salutations to yourself, and Sir F: and his Lady
Yours—
B F
I received yesterday a Letter from Monsieur Verryn, who I thought had been the Advocate, but tis his Brother the Doctor.†3 He says he wonders you should say, you knew not who had done it, seing there were letters had past betwixt you, about the Translation, This makes me think I misunderstood your letter, and that you did not speak it with respect of the Translator but the transferrer —and of the last I thought you could not doubt, you haveing directed it to pass through my hands.
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Lock at Mr. Robert Pawlins in Dorset court, channel row Westminster
Postmark: (G.P.O., indecipherable)
Endorsed by Locke: B: Furly 28° Mar. 91

1381. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 1/11 April 1691 (1329, 1388)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 46-7. A paragraph printed in King, p. 230; the whole in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 45-6. The letter was carried by N. Fatio de Duillier (p. 378 n.): p. 302; and did not reach Locke for some time: pp. 256, 277, 299.
A Amsterdam le 11 d'Avril 1691
Il y a long-temps, Monsieur, que je devrois vous avoir fait réponse, et vous avoir remercié des livres, que vous m'avez envoié.†2 Voici un livre beaucoup plus petit, en attendant que je puisse vous envoier quelque chose de meilleure.†3 Je n'en ai fait que le Mois de
― 248 ―
Fevrier et le dernier article, étant dans le dessein de quitter entierement cet Ouvrage, pour m'appliquer au Pentateuque, que j'ai déja commence.†1 J'espere de dire bien des choses, ou qui n'ont point été dites, ou qui ne l'ont pas été comme il faloit. La Societé des Rémontrans m'a donné, pour trois ans, cinq cent francs de plus qu'elle ne me donnoit; à condition que le Pentateuque seroit achevé, dans ce terme.†2 Il le sera, sans doute, si Dieu me donne de la santé, comme j'en ai eu jusqu'à présent. Mais comme tout dépend ici de Marchands, qui croient que l'on ne sauroit rendre de plus grand service à l'Eglise, que d'épargner autant qu'il est possible, je ne sai si cela aura de suite, quoi qu'on m'en ait donné quelque esperance. Il semble à ces sortes de gens que la vie d'un homme de Lettres doit être comme celle d'un valet, et le peu de bien qu'il font à ceux, par qui leur Societé subsiste, se fait de si mauvaise grace, qu'il est impossible de n'en être pas dégouté. Si je trouvois ailleurs quelque liberté et de quoi vivre, sans me dissiper l'esprit en travaux inutiles, je pourrois faire bien des choses qu'apparemment je ne ferai pas. Dès que j'aurai quelque loisir, je traduirai ou en Latin, ou en François le petit historical account etc†3 qui mérite de voir le jour. Je croi pourtant qu'il pourroit être meilleur, si l'Auteur avoit lu avec soin ce que M. Simon a dit du sujet, dont il parle, dans la Critique du N.T. P.I. Plusieurs personnes qui ont sû que l'on préparoit une version Latine de vôtre Essai, m'ont demandé si elle ne paroîtroit pas bientôt, et il y a un libraire de cette ville qui voudroit déja l'avoir pour l'imprimer.
Je ne dois pas oublier de vous remercier de la peine que vous avez prise de me faire savoir les jugemens de divers savans hommes de vôtre île.†4 Ils sont assurément trop favorables, aussi bien que le vôtre; mais ils m'exciteront à faire tout ce qui me sera possible, pour ne tromper pas leur attente. Je ferai même en sorte de ne choquer personne, par des sentimens éloignez des communs, en les proposant, si j'y suis obligé, avec tant de précaution qu'on ne pourra pas voir s'ils sont au goût de l'Auteur, ou non. Vous savez les vers de Lucrece
― 249 ―
—pueris ut crustula blandi
Doctores elementa velint ut discere prima etc.†1
Autrement on se nuit, sans faire du bien à personne. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre tres-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J Le Clerc.
La principale raison, qui a fait que je ne vous ai pas répondu si tôt que je l'aurois dû, c'est que je me suis marié, il y a environ deux mois. Une vie retirée et studieuse, dans un lieu comme celui-ci, demandoit nécessairement une Compagne. Celle que j'ai, qui est fille de Mr. Leti, dont vous avez vû le Sisto V.†2 a une très-grande estime pour vous, qu'elle avoit conçuë sur la lecture de l'Abregé de vôtre Essai, et qui est devenuë plus grande encore par ce que je lui ai dit de l'Ouvrage même. Elle m'a chargé de vous assurer ici de ses respects.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Londres
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 11° Apr. 91
1382. Thomas Day, junior, to Locke, 2 April 1691 (2887)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 200. The writer was perhaps a son of the writer of no. 1221. The attribution of nos. 1382 and 2887 to a single writer is based on the hand-writing.
Sir
My father having been very much indisposd commanded me to write to you, to desire your advice, in his case; sometime since he took cold which hath causd such a defluxion, that he spits very much and coughs much in the night, rather by his own inclination then the Phisiciens advice, he took away 5 ounces of bloud which much easd him, and since that took a gentle purge, but notwithstanding he spits much still; by my perswasion he hath tak'n for some nights some Diacodium, which I am very well satisfid does him good, but doth not put a stop to it, he takes but a small quantity, if it was in any bodys case but my fathers,
― 250 ―
I would prescribe 3 times the dose, (having by my own experience found it the best remedy ever I took) and have prescribd Tisane generally tak'n in such cases. I give you this trouble to satisfie my father, to whom 2 or 3 lines from you will be a very great obligation as well as to my self. Hopeing in a little time to kisse your hand in London and excuse this trouble I subscribe
your faithfull friend and humble servant
THO: DAY Junior.

1386. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 28 April [1691] (1379, 1389)
Forster, pp. 43-7. The year there is '90'. The correct year from Mrs. Furly's death and from Furly's answer, no. 1392.
Oates, 28 Ap. 90.†1
Dear Friend,
Though I am very much concerned and troubled for your great losse, yet your sorrow being of that kinde which time and not arguments is wont to cure, I know not whether I should say any thing to you to abate your grief, but that, it serveing to no purpose at all but makeing you thereby the more unfit to supply the losse of their mother to your remaining children, (who now more need your care, help, and comfort,) the sooner you get rid of it, the better it will be both for them and you. If you are convinced this is fit to be don, I need not make use to you of the common though yet reasonable topicks of consolation. I know you expect not to have the common and unalterable law of mortality which reaches the greatest, be dispensed with for your sake. Our friends and relations are but borrowed advantages lent us dureing pleasure, and must be given back when ever cald for; we receive them upon these termes, and why should we repine? or, if we doe, what profits it us? But I see my affection is runing me into reasoning, which you need not, and can thinke of without any suggestions of mine. I wonder not at the greatnesse of your grief, but I shall wonder if you let it prevaile on you; your thinkeing of retireing some whither from businesse was very naturall upon the first stroake of it, but here I must interpose to advise you the contrary. It is to give yourself up to all the ills that grief and melancholy can produce, which are some of the worst we suffer in this life: want of health, want of spirit, want of usefull thought, is the state of those who abandon themselves to griefs, whereof businesse is the best, the safest, and the quickest cure. I say not this in favour of your doubt whether you should be acceptable to any of your friends: I know none of them you named that I doe not thinke you would be acceptable to. And I can assure you of it from some whom you did not then thinke of; my Lady Masham, alwayes enquireing very kindely after you, when I told her by the outside that the letter I had then received was from you, was impatient to know
― 254 ―
how you did, and when I had told her of your losse and sadnesse, was mightily concerned, and desired me so tell you that if you would come and spend some time here with her you should be very wellcome. You do not doubt, but I should be exceeding glad of your company; I know no man's I would sooner have or should be more pleasd with; were I setled in an house of my owne, I should tell you how welcome you should be to me a litle more at large, but I suppose you doubt it not. But, for all this kinde and sincere invitation from my Lady Masham (the like wherof I doubt not but you would receive from your other friends if they knew your state and present thoughts) I advise you to thinke of none of them. You would be presently sick of, and constantly uneasy in such a course of life. Keep in your imployment; increase it, and be as busy in it as you can now more than ever. This is best for you and for your children. And when your thoughts are a litle come to themselves and the discomposure over, then calmely consider what will be the best way for you to dispose of them and yourself; but at present lay by none of your businesse, nor neglect it in the least. I know there is little roome for reasoning in the first disorder of grief; what that proposes is alone hearkend to. I must therfor desire you to trust me on this occasion. I am truly your friend, and love you; and therefor you may doe it. I am unbiassed, and not under the prevalency of any passion in the <case>†a and therefor am in a state to judge better, and I will be answerable to you for it you will hereafter thank me for this advice, and for your children we will hereafter, when you are in a better state to doe it, consider what will be best for you to resolve.
I have writ to you twice concerning your <debtor>†b in Scotland†1 but have never heard a word from you. I told you in my last that Mrs. Lockhart tells me he offers to pay the principal in five years, bating the use. She thinkes not fit to abate the use. This is the state of the case; by it take your measurs. She will be ready to serve you by the same hands she manages her owne concernment with him. I sent to Mr. Wright's lately for your Skinner,†2 which is for Arent when you have don with it. I sent also to Mr. Wright the translation of the first book of my Essay, with a letter to Mr.
― 255 ―
Limborch,†1 to whom I desired the translation might be conveyd. I suppose he has sent them by Robinson, who told me he had such a role directed to you. I also desired Capt. Robinson to pay you the five pounds for Tho. Davis. Pray have a care of your health, and believe that I am sincerely yours,
J. L.
I writ you word by Capt. Robinson that I had received the Down, but not P. Simon's books,†2 which Robinson says he received not, nor can hear of. Remember me to my litle friend†3 and his brothers. Send me word in your next what you have laid out for Syl, for his letters, etc. that I may take it of him here.
Address: For Mr. Benjamin Furley, an English Merchant in Rotterdam.
May
1387. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 1 May 1691 (1341, 1399)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 49-50.
Escott May 1st. 91.
My Dear Friend
I did not know but that I might have been so fortunate as to accompany my Brother and Sisters to Town, which made me spare you the trouble of a letter, this last Month, or two. but now it is otherwise determin'd, and they are upon the Road towards you; Your Daughter Betty will tell you that I long to see you, as much as she can do; and need your assistance, and care, as much or more then Ever. drinking Water kept me quiet and well; though extream low both in flesh and strength, till near Crissmass; but then I could hold it no longer; I could neither sleep, nor digest well; perhaps for want of good wine, but so it fell out. then I return'd to Small Beer, and have once a day taken Dr Sydenhams Steel Pils, till the latter End of March, when I was seiz'd with a Terrible defluxion of Rhuem, and Violent Cough; which has tormented me ever since, and I thought would have cured me of all diseases, but this week of warm Weather has greatly reliev'd me, and my poor Girle too, who has been in the same condition, as well as many of our Neibours. my sisters will inform you more at large how it is with us, Tuesday next they will be at their Lodgings at Sir Will:
― 256 ―
Scroggs House in Essex Buildings,†1 where you will be the welcomest Man in the World to your Daughter Betty, who will beg your Charitable assistance, and advice both for me and my Child; our Coughs ripen, and are past the worst, but perhaps something may be necessary for us both to Sweeten the blood, and help us to nourish; I am sure I need it being more wasted and declined then you can imagin. pardon me that I am thus troublesome to you, but Bidgood†2 is dead, and Sydenham too, and 'tis too late for me to begin with a new man, that is an absolute stranger to my constistution, therefore if you can, forgive my importunity, and pitty, and help me; if you do not come into the West this Summer, I shall despair of sharing in that blessing, or seeing the happy day; but I shall live, and dye, deeply sensible of my Obligations to you, being most affectionatly yours
ISABELLA DUKE
Address: For Mr John Lock at his Lodgings in London
Endorsed by Locke: I: Duke 1 May 91
1388. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 7/17 May 1691 (1381, 1410)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 48-9. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, p. 47. The letter was not delivered until after 18 June: pp. 276-7.
A Amsterdam le 17 de Mai 1691.
Il n'y a pas long-temps, Monsieur, que je me donnai l'honneur de vous écrire par un de mes Amis qui alloit à Londres, mais comme je soupçonnois que vous n'y seriez pas j'addressai le paquet que je lui donnai à M. Boyle, à qui il en devoit rendre un autre.†3 J'espere qu'il aura eu soin de vous envoier celui qui étoit pour vous. Je ne me souviens pas si je vous marquois que Mr. Limbourg étoit en peine de savoir de vos nouvelles, et que M. Veryn attendoit avec impatience vôtre jugement touchant sa Version. Ils sont encore dans la même attente.†4 Celui qui vous rendra cette
― 257 ―
Lettre se nomme Monsieur Chamier, et est descendu d'un célebre Ministre de France qui a fait quatre gros Tomes de Controverse contre les Catholiques Romains.†1 C'est un fort honête homme, qui va à Londres à dessein de s'établir dans un Meeting François; mais comme ceux qui forment les Assemblées n'ont pas de quoi donner à leurs Ministres de quoi bien subsister, il a dessein d'instruire de la jeunesse dans les Humanitez, dans l'Histoire, dans la Geographie et autres sciences nécessaires aux jeunes gens. S'étant déja aquité de cet emploi en Suisse, je ne doute pas qu'il n'y rëussisse fort bien. Ainsi si quelcun de vos Amis cherchoit un personne, chez qui envoier un Enfant, j'oserois vous prier de leur adresser M. Chamier, qui est assurément digne de l'estime des honêtes gens. Je prie Dieu qu'il vous conserve en parfaite santé, si vous l'avez entierement recouvrée, comme je le crois, ou de vous la rendre, si vous ne l'avez pas encore aussi parfaite que je la souhaite. Je suis, Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble et tres-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke near Westminster, in Dorset court, in channel row A Londres.
Endorsed by Locke: le Clerc 17 May 91
1389. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 8/18 May 1691 (1386, 1392)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 73.
I feare I shall have tired you, as well as myself, by that time you have read the Inclosed.†2 The Captain†3 comes not, nor for the hams, nor with the mony. Peter†4 is going abord, with them—Pray forget not to send back the new bag in which the Downe was. (Latin) Illustrious Sir,
What may be the reason why I have had no letter from you since I had my papers sent to you I cannot so much as guess, unless the blame is to be laid on your health, which I heard not so long ago from Mr. Guenellon had not been good. Mr. Furly kindly wrote to say that those I sent had reached England safely. I have been hoping for some time that they have been read, revised, and corrected, and I am surprised and distressed that they have not come back yet, as it is my earnest wish to have them back. If, then, your health is sufficiently restored to permit of it (though I almost fear that you may still be unwell) I urgently beg you to be kind enough to give your attention to the matter and to let me have back as soon as possible the first part of your book, which I sent you, to be sent to press forthwith, if you consider it advisable. If you will comply with this request I shall be most grateful to you for your kindness and shall ever be ready to meet your wishes in all things
Your most obedient servant
GISBERT VERRIJN
Amsterdam 24 May 1691

1392. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 15/25 May 1691 (1389, 1396)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 74-5. Answers no. 1386.
Rotterdam 25 May 1691
Dear Sir.
My Last to you was the 18th Instant by Captain Robinson; who had promisd to Call for certain goods of one of his owners in my warehouse, but sent downe his Jacht without calling for them, or giving me warning, in so much that when I saw he came not and hired a boat to carry them abord, the Jacht was gone and that charge lost, and a greater occasiond, for I was forced next day to send a boat down to the Briel with the goods. This I mention because it hindred, what I mentiond, should be done to find what became of Pere Simons booke sent you the last time, which Peter Sonmans gave into the same hand, at the same time, I saw it, with the bag of Down: Peter, went in order to speak with, and convince the man he gave it, but the Jacht was gone. Afterwards the Captain came and left mony here for the £5, which, by your order, I payd for Dr. Thomas's account to Thomas Davies. But tooke nothing of Peter for it, not so much as a receit. So that, in deed, he may redemand the mony, as onely left with me. But it was onely because he was in so great a hurry that he had not time to stay till a receit was writ. So if he calls upon you for the £5. you may pay it him; but first, to teach him better, demand my bill, or receit. By him I sent you from Dr. Guenellon, a small maund with 4 westphalia hamms in it. The Captain was very difficult to take them, but at last yielded. All the Doctors Golden pippins, he writes, were utterly spoyld, the other not so. And so much for that. Now as to your Letter of the 28th past since come to hand—I approve of it in every part of it, your advice is good, sound, and solid, and exactly quadrats with that of mr. Popple. I resolve at lest this yeare to continue in this house, and see how it will fadge†1 to keep house with Sytje.†2 If ever man stood in need of a wife, or
― 261 ―
some solid, trusty, prudent body, to manage the affaires of the family, I am he, for I have no more understanding, or knowledge, than one that never kept house, but has always been a sojourner. This consideration, made my sister,†1 and her eldest son John Furly,†2 advise me to break up house keeping immediately, to place my 2 children some where at schoole in England, continue Benjohan at Noortwyck,†3 and betake myself to boarding, with my servant, But by no means to quit my business, because by that time a yong lads time wilbe out which I have for 6 years, besides Peter Sonmans, Benjohan wilbe fit to enter upon busines. They tell me, for me to keep house, will expose me to ruine, I shalbe cheated on all hands, being utterly unfit for it. It will retrench my charges. I shall not be so exposed to entertainments etc. All which I am sensible is very true, and good advice, but considering that I am faln into this years hire, I should not be able to put off my house, for which I pay f 500 per annum, at least not till the half yeare. In that time we may possibly see a great way into the issue of this war, for this Campaign, must one way or Other, give a great stroake towards the bringing it to an end, except the officers on both sides can play the tricks they use to do, alternately in flanders etc to spin out a war, because they live upon it. But I see not but the French K. looks so wel to his business, and pushes so strenuously that, as they cannot easily play him such tricks, so he is in earnest to make short work of it. The K: is gone to Loo, where they say he is to meet the Dukes of Hanover and Zell;†4
I am extreamly obliged to that Good Lady where you are, for her great, and to me altogether undeserved favours. and wish I could in any measure do her, or hers any acceptable service in these parts. I am now settled, as above, in my mind to stay in my business, till some other kind of providence calls me, or drives me from it. But this was (I am glad I can speak of it in that tense) so terrible a shock to me for some days, that it cast me out of all measures, I knew not which way to turn my self. I could divert my
― 262 ―
self for the present, all the day long with variety of things, but a nights I could not rest for the multitude of thoughts. Till I came at last to a resolution to prosecute my business.
I am now going to write a letter to Swinton and one to Mrs Lockhart, to intreat her to get it delivered and to procure of him an answer, If it can be. But I profess I am almost at a losse how to begin it. I am one of the lefthandedst men in the world, for my self, when I undertake anything for others, I am vigorous, expedit, and overlook all difficulties, when my own Interest is at stake, dilatory, easy, can hardly tell what to say, write or doe, I fancy so many difficulties, promise myself so little success, by the untowardness of men, that I can scarce set pen to paper about it. and thus I find my self, in the case of Swinton, my wife was troubled I did defer writing. I think there is scarce such an other od piece of flesh as I am, for myself, to be found again amongst men —
This crosses the sea by a yong Gentleman that I have placed at schoole at Noortwyck to fit him for a marchant. If I have time to write to mr. Swinton I intend to send it to you to peruse, as not trusting my own Judgment, in my own concern I may as well do myself harm as good. And therefore I shall desire you to peruse it, and send it to Madam Lockhart, If you approve it, or return it to me with your remarks.
I have payd for letters for Sil. f 02:11:— for which be pleased to receive of him, st which I pass to your account.
I find my wives cast†a †1 over stockt with a great quantity of Table Linnen, both Damask and Diaper, pure fine and good, strong and as good as new, some of her own spinning, weaving, bleaching etc. so strong and handsome (for dayly use) that theres scarce any wearing of it out, perhaps my Lady masham, mrs Clark, or some or your acquaintance, might be as well accomodated to have it, for the worth of it, as I to be rid of it, for if I keep 3 or 4 dozen of Napkins and 5 a 6 Tablecloths, it wilbe enough, and I beleeve there are 25 dozen of Napkins. Perhaps Mrs Hunt,†2 or my Lady Cawerly†3 might desire some of them —
My friend†4 despairing of recovering this packet, I have had time to write the inclosed Letter to Mr. Swinton; which, with the account
― 263 ―
which with the Interest amounts to f 18885:17:12. I wish I had my mony, or good security for it, without Interest, nay I would abate 30 per Cent of the Capitall, to any man that would immediately pay me, and wait his 4 or 5 years. But this is not to be hoped for. Nay could he raise and pay me immediately but £600 I would discharge him†1 —But how far it may be fit to tell him or any body else this I know not; Times are ticklish, he mortal, who'l come next I know not. It may be one that will pay no debts but by Law, which one of their Judges, they say told my Lord Bacon, was, Shew me the man, and I'l show you the Law:†2 and whether it be better now I know not, but this I know I have no great mind to try. I intreat you send this for him sealed to the Lady Lockhart, and you will oblige, him who is
Your most affectionate friend and servant
