(English) Vir Amplissime
Literae tuae 13 Martii scriptae demum 17 Maji ad me perlatae sunt, cum parte versionis doctissimi tui de intellectu humano tractatus. Ubi tam diu haeserint incertus sum. Furleius noster, qui ante paucos (ut audio) diës uxorem suam amisit, eas se pridie accepisse scribit. Interim conspectis tuis maxime gavisus sum,
― 264 ―
quoniam ob diuturnum tuum ac inusitatum silentium mens mihi nescio quid mali præsagiebat: nunc me omni sollicitudine de Te ac tua valetudine tuæ liberarunt. Quid prioribus meis et Verrini literis, quas ipse Verrinus fasciculo chartarum alligavit, acciderit, nescio. Doleo ego versionem non felicius successisse, meâ causâ, qui jam uberrimo fructu, quem ex libri tui lectione sperabam, spoliatus sum. Non autem (ut ingenue ac rotunde tecum agam) id plane præter exspectationem meam evenit: quia semper non satis linguæ Anglicanæ peritum credidi, ut tractatum de materiis philosophicis subtiliter disserentem ita Latine posset exhibere, ut†a- et sensum autoris, et argumentorum vim ac ἐνέργειαν perspicue repræsentet.-†a Nondum ego interpretem conveni; cupio enim integrum scriptum, antequam ipsi reddam, perlegere. Sed licet non ederetur, non periit ipsi penitus suus labor: Tractatum enim tuum cum attentione legit, plurima non vulgaria (quæ utinam et ego Latine legere possem) ex eo didicit, et horas suas, quæ forte alias ipsi periissent, studio sibi utilissimo impendit. Ambiebat nuptias, quas nuper consummavit:†1 erant impedimenta quædam, quæ eas ad tempus aliquod differre coëgerunt: ille ut tempus istud,
― 265 ―
amantibus valde tædiosum, honesto labore transigeret, versionem hanc suscepit et perfecit. Interim doleo versionem illam non melius successisse, tum mea, tum et omnium eorum qui linguam Anglicanam non intelligunt, causâ. Cum D. Clerico, qui nunc etiam uxoratus est, aliisque amicis consulam, et interpreti consilium dabimus, quod quale sit futurum, facile vides. Speraveram ego Volumen sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ hoc mense prælo subjiciendum; Verum Wetstenius causatur, Diogenis Laërtii editionem nondum esse ad finem perductam; nullius autem novi operis editionem inchoare cupit, nisi hac prius plene ad finem perducta: Denuo itaque quatuor aut quinque mensibus editionem differt. Ego meum quem præmittam tractatum, constitui ab initio ad finem relegere, si quid desit supplere, et ita perficere, ut editioni paratus sit, ut, quamprimum Wetstenius se paratum dicit, in me ne minima quidem sit mora: Quamquam jam per me inchoare posset. Præmitto ego brevem narrationem antiquiorum sæculorum, et sententiæ Patrum (uti vocantur) de hæreticorum persecutione. Non possum quin edicta Imperatorum quædam reprehendam, et maxime doctrinam Augustini, qui omnium apertissime Donatistarum persecutiones propugnavit: Singulorum testimonia, tam qui persecutiones impugnarunt, quam propugnarunt, adscribam: atque
― 266 ―
ita transibo ad sæcula, quibus Papæ Romani se Ecclesiæ dominos constituerunt, et Imperatorum ac regum sceptra sibi subjecerunt. Proxima occasione mittam Tibi indicem capitum, ut pleniorem totius operis ideam conspicias. Hæc jam præcedente hebdomade scripta erant: Verum subito Harlemum evocatus ob funus neptis cujusdam ex fratre uxoris meæ,†1 hanc non potui nisi jam absolvere et ad Te mittere. Ego interim tractatus tui interpretem conveni, inspexit correctiones tuas, salutem a Te plurimam dixi: non se ausum dixit ea libertate in alieno opere uti: an suæ versionis correctionem tentaturus sit, ignoro: puto tamen eum literas ad Te daturum, quas si mittat meis includam; in iis plenius se explicabit: Ego nondum ipsi scriptum reddidi, sed hac hebdomade, postquam perlegero, redditurus sum; tum uberius cum ipso loquar.
(English) Maxime gratum fuit ex tuis cognoscere, Dominam Cudwortham honestam mei memoriam servare. Inter amicos Anglos maxime semper D. Doctorem Cudworthum colui; spirabant ejus epistolæ eruditionem non vulgarem; unicum doleo, quod occupatior rariores ad me dederit. Nunc Illustri adeo fœminæ gratulor, quod non tam opum paternarum, quam ingenii ac eruditionis paternæ
― 267 ―
hæres sit, patremque ea parte, qua proprie homines sumus, animo ac mente, referat. Gaudeo illi institutum meum ac scribendi methodum probari: spero ipsum opus quando prodierit ipsi placiturum, quando te interprete in eo totum illud iniquitatis mysterium revelatum videbit, quod verbis vix exprimi potest quam atrox ac detestandum sit. Rogo humillima mea servitia illi offeras, illique dicas, me ardentibus votis precari, ut quicquid honesto lectionis assiduæ exercitio oculorum aciëi deperiit, Deus judicii acumine, aliisque gratiæ suæ donis compenset, ut sic mente contempletur ea, ad quæ oculorum acies, etiam acutissima, penetrare nequit. Ipsam ego colere ac venerari non desinam, ejusque dotes minime vulgares semper suspiciam. Antequam finiam memorabile quid, et quid miraculi instar est, hic adjiciam. Novi ego Harlemi puellam, quæ jam octavum annum explevit, et nonum ingressa est: Nata est penitus surda, ita ut nec clamorem, licet vehementem, nec campanarum sonitum, nec quemcunque alium sonum unquam audiverit. Hoc narro non ex relatu aliorum, sed ipse testis sum ocularis, qui a prima infantia puellam illam sæpius vidi, et ipsam auditu penitus destitutam deprehendi. Surda cum esset, nullum sermonem discere potuit, neque ullorum verborum significationem comprehendere; nutibus et gestibus omnia percipiebat et exprimebat;
― 268 ―
et in hisce admodum se solertem ostendit. Nunc tamen paucos intra menses arte et industriâ loqui didicit. Est hic quidam Helvetius, Medicus,†a juvenis viginti quinque circiter annorum, qui artem excogitavit, surdis motu oris labiorum ac linguæ monstrandi, qua ratione voces formare et pronuntiare possint.†1 Hic intra spatium quinque mensium, nam decimo quarto dië Decembris institutionem puellæ inchoavit, eam plurima non tantum verba, sed et integras sententias eloqui, et apte satis pronuntiare, et, quod mireris, legere docuit. Ipse dië adscensionis experimentum cepi: cum uxore mea in parentum ædibus diverti: hospites mei humanissimi coram me producunt filiam, quam anno elapso plane mutam videram: gratulatur illa mihi et uxori adventum: scribo in charta, verum literis majusculis, nomen meum et uxoris; illa distincte legit: offertur ipsi schedula, qua hic in funus homines invitari solent, in qua exstabant non tantum literæ majusculæ, sed et romanæ et cursivæ, uti vocantur; omnes distincte legit, et, quod miratus sum, singularum totius alphabeti literarum vim distincte novit, et unamquamque literam primo intra labia formabat, mox totam syllabam pronuntiabat, atque ita pergens totam formabat vocem:
― 269 ―
peccabat quidem aliquatenus contra accentum; quia enim auditu caret necesse est ut aliquoties in accentu erret; sed distincte tamen quicquid legebat et loquebatur intelligebamus: quin et numeros, seu cifras legebat;†a idque didicerat puella octo annorum intra tam breve temporis spatium: recitabat coram nobis integram precationem dominicam; verba percipiebat ex motu oris paterni; si quid vero minus perciperet, innuebat patri ut scriberet, et mox legebat. Cum abirem, et mihi et uxori meæ valedixit, expressis nominibus nostris, quæ ex lectione bis tantum repetitâ memoriæ ipsius inhæserant. Plurima jam noverat verba, et eorum significationem, et quotidie plura addiscit. Ita vidimus et mutos jam loqui in patria nostra, magno parentum, quibus unica hæc est soboles, gaudio. Non potui, quin rem adeo miram tibi indicarem: ad certum quendam patris gestum, quem intelligebat, mihi dixit verbis Belgicis, Ego sum surda, verum ego non sum muta. Omnes non sine admiratione puellam aspiciunt, et quotidie ex aliis civitatibus plures adveniunt in ædes viri illius, ut puellam videant. Tu mecum miraberis, et agnosces benignitatem divinam, quæ ea homines solertia instruxit, ut et surdos verba, quæ audire nequeunt, pronuntiare doceant. Verum ego nimia prolixitate jam pecco. Vale Vir Amplissime, et mei memor vive. Salutant te amici omnes,†a
― 270 ―
Venius, Guenellonus, Grevius advocatus ultrajectinus,†1 præcipue vero uxor mea ac liberi, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus

(English) Hodie archithalassus noster Trompius in hac civitate diem suum obiit, lento morbo consumtus.†a †2
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Your letter written on 13 March reached me at last on 17 May, together with the part of the translation of your scholarly treatise on the human understanding. I am uncertain where it can have been sticking all that time. Our friend Furly who, I hear, lost his wife a few days ago, writes that he had received them the previous day. Meanwhile I have been gladdened by [p. 264] the sight of your letter, as my mind foreboded I know not what evil on account of your long and unwonted silence; it has now relieved me of all anxiety about you and your health. I do not know what can have happened to my previous letter and to Verrijn's, which he attached to the packet of papers with his own hands. I am sorry that the translation has not proved more successful, and that for my own sake, as I am now robbed of the abundant profit I promised myself from reading your book. However, to be frank and forthright with you, this does not exceed my expectations; for I always believed that he was not sufficiently expert in English to be able to present in Latin a treatise subtly discussing philosophical matters in such a way as to represent clearly the author's meaning and the strength and energy of his arguments. I have not yet seen the translator, as I desire to read the work through as a whole before giving it back to him. But even if it should not be published his labour has not been altogether wasted: he has read your treatise with attention and has learnt from it much that is out of the common (which I only wish that I too could read in Latin), and so has expended on most profitable study the hours that might otherwise have been lost to him. He was seeking a marriage, which he has recently achieved;†1 there were certain obstacles which compelled him to put it off for a while; so in order to spend [p. 265] that interval, so tedious for lovers, in doing some commendable work, he took up and finished this translation. Meanwhile I am sorry that it has not turned out better, both for my own sake and for that of all those who do not understand English. I shall consult Mr. Le Clerc, who also is now married, and some other friends, and we shall give the translator some advice; you can easily see of what sort it will be. I had hoped that the volume of the Sententiæ of the Toulouse Inquisition would go to the press this month; but Wetstein gives as his excuse that the publication of Diogenes Laertius is not yet finished, and he does not wish to start the publication of any new work until this first is finished; so once more he is putting off the publication for four or five months. I have decided to read my preliminary treatise again from beginning to end, to make good any deficiencies, and so to complete it as to be ready for publication, so that as soon as Wetstein says that he is ready there may be not even the smallest delay on my side, though as far as I am concerned he could begin now. I put first a short account of earlier times and of the opinion of the Fathers (as they are called) as to the persecution of heretics. I cannot but find fault with certain edicts of the emperors, and most of all with the teaching of Augustine, who contended most openly of all for the persecutions of the Donatists; I shall cite the evidence of particular persons, as well those who impugned as those who contended for the persecutions; and so I shall pass to the ages in which the Roman popes constituted [p. 266] themselves masters of the Church and subjected the sceptres of emperors and kings to themselves. I shall take the first opportunity of sending you a list of the chapters, so that you may consider a fuller plan of the whole work. I had already written this much last week; but as I was suddenly called to Haarlem for the funeral of a niece, the child of my wife's brother,†1 I was not able to finish and dispatch this letter to you until now. Meanwhile I have seen the translator of your treatise; he examined your corrections, and I gave him your greetings; he said that he had not dared to take such a liberty with another man's work. I do not know whether he will try to correct his translation; I think, however, that he will write to you; if so I shall enclose his letter with mine; he will explain himself more fully in it. I have not yet returned the manuscript to him, but I shall do so this week after I have read it through; then I shall talk more largely with him.
(Latin) I was most gratified to learn from your letter that Mrs. Cudworth remembers me with approval. Among my English friends I always esteemed Dr. Cudworth most highly; his letters exhaled learning not of the common sort; my one regret is that he was so occupied that he could write to me only rarely. I now congratulate that illustrious lady on being heiress not so much to her father's possessions as to his talents and learning, and so recalling him in that part by virtue of which we are properly men, the spirit and the mind. [p. 267] I am glad that she approves of my design and the arrangement of the work; I hope that when the book itself appears it will please her, when with you as interpreter she will see revealed in it that whole mystery of iniquity, whose atrocious and detestable character words can hardly express. I beg that you will offer her my most humble service, and tell her that it is my heartfelt prayer that, whatever the keenness of her eyesight may have lost in the praiseworthy exercise of constant reading, God may make amends for it by fineness in judgement and by other gifts of His grace, that so she may contemplate with the mind those objects to which keenness of eyesight, however acute, cannot penetrate. I shall not cease to esteem and honour her, and shall always admire her most uncommon gifts. Before I close let me add here a note of a remarkable thing and one that seems like a miracle. I know a girl at Haarlem who has just completed her eighth year and entered on her ninth; she was born completely deaf, so that she never heard even the loudest cry or the ringing of bells or any other sound. I tell you this not from hearsay but from the evidence of my own eyes; I have often seen this girl from her earliest infancy, and have found her to be absolutely devoid of hearing. Owing to her deafness she was unable to learn any language or to grasp the meaning of any words; she understood and expressed herself entirely by nods and gestures, and in this she showed considerable adroitness. Now, however, within the last few months she has learnt to speak, thanks to [p. 268] method and application. There is here a certain Swiss, a doctor, a young man of about twenty-five, who has devised a method of showing deaf people by movements of the lips and tongue how they can form and pronounce words.†1 Within the space of five months—for he commenced the instruction of the girl on 14 December—he has taught her to utter not only a number of words but complete sentences too, and to pronounce them sufficiently well; also, what may surprise you, he has taught her to read. I got proof of this myself on Ascension Day; I was staying in her parents' house with my wife; my kind hosts bring me their daughter, who had been absolutely dumb when I saw her the previous year; she told me and my wife how pleased she was with out visit; I wrote my own name and my wife's on a sheet of paper, but in capital letters; she read them distinctly; she was given a card of the sort that is commonly used in this country for invitations to funerals, which contained not only capital letters but also roman and italic, as they are called; she read them all distinctly, and, to my surprise, was clearly acquainted with the value of each particular letter of the whole alphabet. She first formed each letter in her mouth, then pronounced a whole syllable, and so proceeding formed a whole word; she occasionally made mistakes in accentuation, for being devoid of hearing she is bound to make such mistakes from time to [p. 269] time; nevertheless we understood clearly whatever she read and said; she could also read numbers, that is the arabic figures; and all this an eight-year-old girl had learnt in such a short time. She recited the whole of the Lord's Prayer in our presence; she made out words from the movement of her father's mouth; if there was anything she did not quite follow she signed to her father to write it down, and then she read it. When I was leaving she said good-bye to me and my wife, pronouncing our names, which had cleaved to her memory after reading them only twice. She already knew a good number of words and their meaning, and she learns more every day. So we have now seen even the dumb speak in this country, to the great joy of her parents, whose only child she is. I cannot help telling you of one remarkable thing: at a certain sign from her father, which she understood, she said to me in Dutch, 'I am deaf, but I am not dumb'. Every one is astonished when they see the girl, and many come every day from other towns to this gentleman's house to see her. You will share my wonder, and you will acknowledge the Divine mercy, which has endowed men with the skill to teach even the deaf to pronounce words which they cannot hear. But I am becoming guilty of long-windedness. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and do not forget me. All our friends send you their greetings, Veen, Guenellon, de Greve the Utrecht [p. 270] advocate,†1 but in particular my wife and children, and first and foremost myself
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 29 May

1395. Robert Pawling to Locke, 4 June 1691 (1385, 1444)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 214.
London 4th June 1691
Sir
I have not sent to you since I wrot by Sir Francis. the two books†2 were delivered to the Lady Carverley and mr Delone:†3 the french Parson calling to give you a visit had his book.†4 I went on Sturday to mr Shermer†5 for the £50 but he had heard nothing then from mr Cheswell. I called again as I went that way on Monday and Tuesday but could not meet with mr Shermer but this day I called again and he said he had orders so as I returned from the City I received the money. I delivered Mr Haiters†6 letter at the Shop he not being at home I shall wait on him for his answer. so all is don according to my paper of Memoranda. the patterns of Cloth are inclosed they are all very good please your self as to the colours and send word which you like best. the letter to Madam Lockhart was delivered according to directions. I have made a little progress in her affair and will endevour to end it. I presume she thinks me a fit man to be employed because you do. mr Clarks pain in his head ended in a great swelling in his face; after it was launced within side his cheek, it abated, but it kep him in town longer than
― 272 ―
he intended; whether he be gon yet I know not, but it may be you have heard from him. I thank god my son is very well recovered and walks abroad every day and his stomach is very good. here is a letter for Sil but none for you. mr Brockman since dinner received a letter from mr Furley who presents his service to you. I am very glad you got well down whether it was in the Coach box, or behinde, or on horseback, Ile not enquire; tis none of my busines as the good woman said that saw Colonel Birch riding his horse in the Stable;†1 but perhaps the Ladyes at Whitehall†2 may make enquiry into it. when I have told you I received the papers you inclosed of Education, which I will coppy out as I have leasure†3 I think I have said as much as is needfull at present. I am
Sir
Your humble servant
ROB PAWLING
Madam Lockhart fears she shall not get the Lady Mashams things time enough to send this Saturday the holy dayes†4 have the people idle that should have don the work.

Oates 12° Jun 91
I litle expected two Ladys should confer notes about me to finde out whether I were not bestowing my self upon a third twas an
― 274 ―
honour which if ever I had been capable of I thought my self now past. But since your Ladyship who knows soe well the irresistible power of your sex concludes that neither philosophie the artificial nor age the natural fence against it is sufficiently armor of proof tis better to passe for a Jesuit or any thing rather than owne my self capable of noething but flat insensibility when your Ladyship thinks me worth the Lookeing after. I will not therefor goe about to justifie my self against that accusation but conclude with my self that had the K of Fr but your Ladyships art in persecuteing noe thing could stand him and he might by a sure and effectuall way make whom ever he pleased forward and willing slaves. the infinite worth that all the world acknowledges in your Ladyship and the infinite obligations I in particular have to you I thought left noe roome for any addition to the ties your Ladyship had upon me till I received the honour of your last letter where in I finde railery too and persecution in your hands when you please to make use of them that way are noe lesse effectuall to make one highly sensible of your favour and goodnesse than those which are cald real benefits. I shall always prefer that night I was misseing†a in to the fairest of all my days since it hath drawn from your Ladyship those rebukes wherein you doe me the honour to use the names of Jealousy and freind. One who had the boldnesse to professe him self in love at first sight might perhaps not soe much wonder that your Ladyship should divert your self with one of them at a time when there is litle other matter to be merry with But the other is a title soe seriously weighty and glorious that if I were not before wholy devoted to your service this would ingage all the future care and service of my life to preserve it. As to the time of the journey†1 though you know your country men better than I I am not yet fully satisfied I was mistaken though I shall not be sorry if I were for I never value my opinion by the event espetially where I had as I had now others of my minde whose judgment and freindship you cannot but allow, and when your Ladyship condemns me on this account I shall not want the consolation to have very good company and such as your Ladyship esteems. when your Ladyship considers who are now there it will not be
― 275 ―
easy to thinke this the fitest time though I owne that were not the cheif of my reasons, If the sommer passe merily in other places (as I wish it may though I am censurd) the autumn will not be the lesse pleasant nor lesse effectuall there and I resolve with my self when the next time comes to enjoy the honour and advantages of the journey without examining signes or seasons and goe blindefold without any reasoning which as ill suits with our world as with diversion. If what I and others apprehend happen not I am apt to be of your Ladyships minde that as one man is like another soe one year will be like another. Who ever cary the links or rather the darke lanterns of the fashon now set up in the streets which glare more than light†1 I desire to be in the darke with the dreamers of dreams and seers of visions†2 and take it a litle amisse that Sir J: should be thought†a- worthy to be amongst them-†a who is more to blame than I that he makes soe ill a use of the priviledg of being in town and near. 1398. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 18 June 1691 (1393, 1409)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256 u. Printed in part in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 332-3; opening passage and address in Ollion, pp. 201-2. Answers no. 1393; answered by no. 1409.
(English)
Oates 18° Jun. 91
Vir Amplissime
Priores tuas una cum Verrini literis intercidisse valde doleo, nihil enim a te proficisci potest quod mihi, uti convenit, non sit valde charum. Novissimas tuas 29 Maji datas amore et benevolentiâ usitatâ plenas accepisse lætor tum quod tuæ tuorumque valetudinis et redditæ versionis me certiorem faciunt. Quicquid vos illic Verrini amici de versione illâ statueritis illius erga me animum semper mihi perhonorificum existimabo et agnoscam, et optarem sane ut si quid tractatus ille meus utile habet et lectu dignum (quod mihi assumere nimis esset fastuosum) id illius cum laude Latinè prodiret et doctorum virorum judicio subjiceretur tuo inprimis, cujus opinionem amoto tum odio tum favore de istis meis lucubrationibus libentissime audirem. Doctissimum Verrinum tantum suæ versioni laborem frustrà impendisse valdè dolerem. Salutes illum quæso fratremque ejus quam officiosissime meo nomine, Gratulor illi uti Clerico nostro conjugales tædas, et omnia fausta et fælicia utrique opto. Nuptiæ et amatoriæ simul et maritales
― 277 ―
curæ causa ut videtur fuerunt quod a Domino Clerico nullas jam diu acceperim literas,†1 et satis gravis causa quæ solet et debet totum occupare amantis animum.
(English) Misi ad illum circa Natalitias una cum epistolâ alias quasdam chartas,†2 redditas speraveram cùm amico minime negligenti Amstelodamum proficiscenti portandas tradiderim, verum ab eo tempore a Doctissimo Clerico ne verbum quidem. quod miror et me sollicitum habet. De amicitiâ illius nihil dubito: vir ipse ad scribendum impiger, et responsum efflagitaveram, apud me igitur tabellariorum accuso incuriam per quam illius literas aberrasse autumo. Interim aveo scire an fasciculum a me missum a Domino Churchill acceperit.†3 hoc quæso a me cum plurimâ salute ipsi et uxori ejus dicas et quid respondeat renuncies.
(English) Sancti Officii historiam oscitantia Bibliopolæ in ipso partu ita hærere doleo. Prolegomena tua Domina Cudwortha et ego valde probamus et capitum indicem quam tam amicè promittis avide expectamus ut ista sciographiâ†4 operis tui structuram prælibemus,
― 278 ―
interim optantes ut quam citissime integrum volumen christiano orbi maxime proficuum et pene dixeram hoc tempore necessarium prodeat, Illic enim fons omnis persecutionis sub prætextu religionis, illic fundamentum tyrannidis ecclesiasticæ, quam minores sectæ eo exemplo animatæ prædicant affectantque. Sed quo tendat, quas tragœdias ubique, quando parum adoleverit, editura sit eo in speculo qui sibi oculos non eruunt facile videbunt. Ejus lectionem sibi et utilissimam et jucundissimam fore spondet Domina Cudwortha, quæ paternæ benignitatis hæres omnem de rebus religionis persecutionem maximè aversatur. Gratulatur sibi se in partem amicitiæ qua patrem amplexus es successisse. Te officiosissime salutat, plurimum æstimat et veneratur, unumque hoc dolet quod non utatur linguâ utrique communi ut ex commercio literarum amicitiæ et eruditionis tuæ quem optaret fructum perciperet.
(English) Historiam tuam de Surda Loquente duplici exemplo hic apud nos confirmare possum. Duo Juvenes utrique surdi quorum alter a Doctore Wallis celebri illo Oxonii Matheseos professore, alter a Doctore Holder theologo edoctus loquelae usum didicit. Utrumque Juvenem novi, et verba proferentem audivi, destincte satis et articulate, tonus solùm vocis parum erat ingratus et inharmonicus.
― 279 ―
De altero quid factum sit nescio: alter adhuc vivit legendi scribendique peritus et a quo illum primo loquentem audivi (viginti enim et plures sunt anni) uxorem duxit paterfamilias. Vir est ex generosâ prosapiâ nec diu est a quo illum viderim.†1 Uxori liberisque tuis. Veniis Geneloniis et Collegis nostris plurimam salutem meo nomine dicas. Vale Vir Amplissime et me ut facis ama
Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin)
Oates 18th Jun. 91
Excellent Sir,
I am very sorry that your previous letter was lost together with Verrijn's, for nothing can come from you that is not very dear to me, as indeed it should be. I am happy to have received your last, dated 29 May, full as it is of your accustomed affection and goodwill, and to be assured by it that you and your family are well and that the translation has been returned. Whatever you in Holland who are Verrijn's friends may decide about that translation, I shall always recognize and feel highly honoured by his goodwill towards me, and I should certainly wish that if that treatise of mine contains anything useful and worth reading, which it would be too presumptuous in me to assume, it might appear in Latin with praise of him and be submitted to the judgement of scholars, notably your own, whose impartial opinion on those lucubrations of mine I should very gladly hear. I should be most sorry for the very learned Verrijn to have expended so much labour on his translation to no purpose. Please give him and his brother my kindest regards. I congratulate him as well as our friend Le Clerc on getting married, and I wish them both all prosperity and happiness. Marriage and the cares at once [p. 276] of a lover and a husband have, it seems, been the reason why I have now for a long time had no letter from Le Clerc,†1 and a sufficiently weighty reason that usually and properly occupies the whole mind of one in love.
(Latin) About Christmas-time I sent him, together with a letter, some other papers,†2 and hoped they had been delivered as I had entrusted them to the hand of a very careful friend who was travelling to Amsterdam; but I have not had a word from him since then, which surprises and worries me. I have no doubts about his friendship; he himself is a diligent correspondent, and I had asked particularly for an answer; so I suppose I must blame the carelessness of the letter-carriers on this side for his letter having gone astray. Meanwhile I should like to know whether he has received the packet I sent by Mr. Churchill.†3 Please tell him this, with my best wishes for himself and his wife, and let me know what he says.
(Latin) I am sorry that the account of the Holy Office sticks in this way at the very moment of its birth through the sluggishness of the bookseller. Mrs. Cudworth and I are very pleased with your prolegomena, and we are eagerly looking forward to the list of the chapters which you are kind enough to promise us, so that by that draft we may have a foretaste of the general plan of your work. We wish meanwhile that the complete volume may appear [p. 278] as soon as possible, one most profitable, I had almost said necessary, at this time for the Christian world; for there we have the fountain-head of all persecution carried on under the cloak of religion; there is the foundation of that ecclesiastical tyranny which lesser sects preach and strive after, inspired by that example. But whither this spirit is tending, what tragedies it will bring about everywhere when it has attained some growth, those who do not tear their own eyes out will readily see in this mirror. Mrs. Cudworth is confident that reading it will be most useful and pleasing to herself; as heiress to her father's kindliness she has the greatest aversion to all persecution on account of religious matters. She thinks herself fortunate to have succeeded to a part in the friendship with which you embraced her father, and she sends you her warmest greetings. She has the greatest esteem and respect for you, and is only sorry that she is not conversant with a language common to you both, so that through intercourse by letter she might get the profit she would wish from your friendship and learning.
(Latin) I can confirm your account of the deaf girl speaking by a twofold example in our country. Two young men, both deaf, learnt the use of speech, one of them being taught by Dr. Wallis, the celebrated Oxford professor of mathematics, and the other by Dr. Holder a theologian. I came to know both of them and have heard them pronounce words, which they did quite distinctly and articulately, only their tone of voice was somewhat harsh and unmusical. I do not know what has become of one of them; the other is still living; he is [p. 279] proficient in reading and writing, and since the time when I first heard him speak, which is twenty and more years ago, he has married and is the father of a family. He is a gentleman by birth, and it is not long since I saw him.†1 Give my best wishes to your wife and family, also to the Veens, the Guenellons, and our Collegians. Goodbye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE

Escot June 18th. 91
Dearest Sir
I Blush that I have not sooner paid you my Thanks for your last Favour, of the 16th. of May; in which according to your wonted Goodness you express a tender Compassion, and solicitude for me, which shews you the best of Friends, and has made deep impressions on me, and powerfully revived the sense of all my former obligations to you, for which I can never enough Love and Thank you. I hope to make a good Use of the advice and directions you therin bestow upon me, Though hitherto I have been otherwayes
― 280 ―
engaged, which is the only reason I have deferr'd writing to you till I could say somthing of the Success of my New Docter. my ilnes was so pressing about that time, my Cough especially, that for Decencies sake I applyed my self to a phisitian, one Dr Musgrave†1 who is newly come to Exon, a Gentile ingenious Man; he encouraged my bleeding a Second Time, and approv'd my taking Milk and order'd me to swallow pils of Gum Ammoniacum with every draught, which I did to noe purpose several days, for they never digested but pas<t>†a thorough me like so many Bullets, (perhaps tis the nature of that gum to do so.) Since that he has Essayed a Method of steel, but my Stomach could not bear his preparations of it. However my Cough which I so much apprehended is gone, and I am now much as I were before it seized me, extream low in flesh, and strength, and subject to a Cough on the least accident or disorder. he proposes my drinking the Bath Waters; which since you approve, I would try again, (though formerly they purged me so that I could not bear them.) if I could hope to Meet you there; being†b- near you-†b perhaps would work the cure without them, 'tis a cruel hardship to be always at a distance from the best of Friends; have you laid aside all thoughts of comming thither this Year; and must I go out of the World without seeing you once more, let me know my Fate; and I will bear it as well as I can, yet while I breath, I shall wish and hope that some happy providence may Oblige you to steer your course westward. you were most affectionatly remembred, and passionately wish'd here yesterday, by Mr Clark, Mr Stringer, his Lady etc whom I came hither to meet; and within a fortnight we expect my Brother, who was Married yesterday;†2 when I have paid my duty to him, his Lady, Mrs Hunt and such Friends as come with him, I will observe any Commands you shall send me, nothing sha<ll>†a turn me from the Obedience that becomes
your most Dutifull Daughter I. D.

1400. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 19/29 June 1691 (1396, 1402)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 78.
Rotterdam 29 June 1691
Deare Sir
I have at last per post yours of the 18th past, which was intended by captain Robinson; but came to Joseph wrights hand too late, to send by him, and to mine to return answer the same way. I am glad to understand, that I was not mistaken in my friend Joseph as to the liberty I used. The five pounds of Dr. Thomas, which you payd Captain Robinson, I received of him, and I doubt not but Thomas Davies has acquainted the Doctor that I have paid it him. As for Pere Simons booke which was given with the feathers to the same person, he sayd he knows nothing of it, dos not remember it—and so I beleeve it will never come to light. I have written to the professor Grævius as you desire, and to wetstein for those books. I had long since given my Lady an account of William Ames, but that I expect some information from Bristol concerning him, first. I shall observe your directions in teaching my small fellow†1 Latine. But I have some thoughts of bringing him into England with me, this summer; being almost perswaded by a neighbour of mine that my presence in Scotland will (perhaps) prevaile more than letters: concerning which I request your thoughts. I have an inclination, if I should not go for Scotland, to go into the West, to Exon and Plymouth, and see if I cannot being there prevaile with some to give me their commissions.†2 I can never go from home, better than, while I have so substantiall, and solid a person as Peter Sonmans to looke after my business in my absence, for after his other 2 years are expired, I shalbe miserably tyed by the heeles at home, and not be able to stir out; upon what ever occasion it should be, tho it should be to seek a wife, or stay to my family. I hope I shall prevail with Coolhans and his wife to come and stay so long at my house, and take care of all in my absence, and perhaps after my returne. I have formerly advised you, that I cannot perfect your account in my books without a coppy of the 2 first accounts given you, which my Rogue†3 has lost or made away
― 282 ―
for I cannot find them. I have not else, but my dearest L.†1 to you, and all that can receive it, among my acquaintance. We have no news at all, but are from post to post expecting to heare great things that our armies will do against the french, but the cowardly rogues will not suffer us to come near them, we are marching towards Dinant, to get that way to Paris, and the Inhabitants are removing their best goods to Charlemont, when any happens worth notice you shall have it among you from
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate friend and servant
BENJAMIN FURLY†a

Okeley June 29th
Dear Sir
I know not whether there will be any need to beg your pardon for not sending you sooner your bookes you trusted me to transmit to you. with those you last writ for; since if you went to the Bath, you can have no need of them as yet, and if you went againe to my Lady Ms.†1 (for you sayed only you were goeing out of Towne) I hope they will come time enough to answere your occasions; but be it as it will, I hope my pardon will not be very difficult to obtaine with so reasonable a Judge when you know the reasons why I could not send them you sooner, for in the first place it is not yet a fortnight agone since I came hither to stay, haveing bin at Shotover till then, that my Father, and Mother went a journey into Derbyshire:†2 so that I could not have time to looke out the bookes and send them till I came hither to stay: but that which made it more impossible to doe it was, that I found that to be true, which I feared before, that I should find no catalogue of your bookes amongst your Manuscripts.†a for I have looked over them all with great care, never thelesse to give you all the satisfaction I am able, I have taken the paines to make you a new catalogue of all the bookes I have in my hands of yours: which I have here sent you in the box; makeing bold to write it in a paper booke of yours which had little writeing in it. and I hope you will rest satisfyed with my paines: for I doe assure you on the word of an honest man that I never saw the Catalogue you mention since I saw it once at London; (if I rightly remember.) so that whether it never came to Oxford, or was lost there in the removeal of your things I know not. but this†b- much I can-†b assure you with the same protestation; that I have here sent you a true catalogue of all I have.†3 as likewise a note of what
― 285 ―
I have deliverd†a- to Dr: T.-†a†1 by your order, and allso to your self: I have allso here sent you not onely those bookes you desired,†2 but allso 2 other volumes of Mr: Boyles workes, with†b his treatise of Formes both which I found upon†c this second review. I have allso sent you 2 other treatises of his which came out when you were abroad viz: of the true notion of nature and of fineal causes since I know not whether you have them or not;†3 and if you have not. I thought it my duty to send them you considering how many more of your bookes I dayly make use of: I have allso besides the booke of verses you mentiond bound in pastboard;†4 sent you another booke conteining the verses against Sir William Davenants Gondibert,†5 which I find,†d you desired, but are not in the booke you writ for. I have allso sent you a locked leather writeing box, since I hope your knife, spoon and forke may yet be there: however you well may need the box on other accounts: I have allso sent you your two little Treatises of my Lord Bacon:†6 to help fill up the box, as allso some paper bookes which may be usefull to you: I send you these copyes of the Laws of Carolina:†7 because you may have occasion to bestow them on Freinds: and you have four†e copyes still
― 286 ―
left here: one of them seald with the seals of the Proprietors: I sent you the second part of the State of France because I gave you the first part at London before;†1 I have here allso sent you enclosed a true inventory of all the things you have here; and as for such of them as will not answere the charge of removeal such as the chairs, and cupboards I am willing to give you as much for them as they shall be prised at, by any indifferent person: I would have sent you your telescope if the box had bin long enough: but you may have it when you please: So hopeing you will take what I have done in thes matters in good part I am. Your faithfull humble servant.
J TYRRELL.

1404. Thomas Herbert, eighth earl of Pembroke, to Locke, 30 June [1691] (1170, 1497)

London June, 30
Sir
I am sorry I must express my self in a different stile from that I writt out of Holland,†5 for I would not have you think I now take any pleasure in writing to you, there is now no Sea between us; I dare not trust my self to say any more being so much dissatisfyed att the length of your three dayes that nothing but seeing you will make me forget it, in the hopes of which I shall still subscribe my self
Your Friend and servant
Pembroke.

1405. Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton to Locke, 30 June 1691 (1357, 1437)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 142-3. Printed in King, pp. 217-19; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 152-4 (no. 365).
Cambridge June 30 1691
Sir
Your deferring to answer my letter is what you needed not make an apology for because I use to be guilty of the same fault as often as I have nothing of moment to write and therefore cannot in justice complain. If the scheme you have laid of managing the Controulers place of the M.†1 will not give you the trouble of too large a letter, you will oblige me by it. I thank you heartily for your being so mindfull of me and ready to assist me with your interest. Concerning the Ancient of days Dan. 7, there seems to be a mistake either in my last letter or in your's because you wrote in your former letter that the Ancient of Days is Christ, and in my last I either did or should have asked how you knew that.†2 But these discourses may be done with more freedome at our next meeting. I am indebted to my Sollicitor Mr Starkey.†3 If you please to let me have your opinion what I should send him I will send it with a letter by the Carrier. My Lady Masham and you have done me much honour in looking into my Book†4 and I am very glad to have the approbation of such judicious persons.
The observation you mention in Mr Boyles book of colours†5 I once made upon my self with the hazzard of my eyes. The manner was this. I looked a very little while upon the sun in a looking-glass with my right eye and then turned my eyes into a dark corner of my chamber and winked to observe the impression made and the circles of colours which encompassed it and how they decayed by degrees and at last vanished. This I repeated†a a second and a third time. At
― 289 ―
the third time when the phantasm of light and colours about it were almost vanished, intending†1 my phansy†2 upon them to see their last appearance I found to my amazement that they began to return and by little and little to become as lively and vivid as when I had newly looked upon the sun. But when I ceased to intend my phansy upon them they vanished again. After this I found that as often as I went into the dark and intended my mind upon them as when a man looks earnestly to see any thing which is difficult to be seen, I could make the phantasm return without looking any more upon the sun. And the oftener I made it†a return, the more easily I could make it return†b again. And at length by repeating this without looking any more upon the sun I†c made such an impression on my eye that if I looked upon the clouds or a book or any bright object I saw upon it a round bright spot of light like the sun. And which is still stranger, tho I looked upon the sun with my right eye only and not with my left, yet my phansy began to make the impression upon my left eye as well as upon my right. For if I shut my right eye and looked upon a book or†d- the clouds-†d with my left eye I could see the spectrum†b of†b the sun almost as plain as with my right eye, if I did but intend my phansy a little while upon it. For at first if I shut my right eye and looked with my left, the spectrum of the sun did not appear till I intended my phansy upon it; but by repeating this, appeared every time more easily. And now in†d- a few hours time-†d I had brought my eys to such a pass that I could look upon no bright object with either eye but I saw the sun before me, so that I durst neither write nor read, but to recover the use of my eyes shut my self up in my chamber made dark for three days together and used all means to divert my imagination from the Sun. For if I thought upon him I presently saw his picture though I was in the dark. But by keeping in the dark and imploying my mind about other things I began in three or four days to have some use of my eyes again and by forbearing a few days longer to look upon bright objects recovered them pretty well, though not so well but that for some months after the spectrum of the sun began to return as often as I began to meditate upon the phænomenon, even†b though I lay in
― 290 ―
bed at midnight with my curtains drawn. But now I have been very well for many years, tho I am apt to think that if I durst venture my eyes I could still make the phantasm return by the power of my fansy. This story I tell you to let you understand that in the observation related by Mr Boyle, the man's phansy probably†a concurred with the impression made by the sun's light to produce that phantasm of the Sun which he constantly saw in bright objects. And so your question about the cause of this phantasm involves another about the power of phansy which I must confess is too hard a knot for me to untye. To place this effect in a constant motion is hard because the Sun ought then to appeare perpetually. It seems rather to consist in a disposition of the sensorium to move the imagination strongly and to be easily moved both by the imagination and by the light as often as bright objects are looked upon.
If the papers you mention come not out I will tell you at our next meeting what shall be done with them.†1
My humble service to Sir Francis, my Lady and Mrs Cudworth. I am
Your most humble servant
IS. NEWTON.
Address: For Mr John Lock at Sir Francis Masham's Baronet at Oates neare Bishop Stafford in Essex.
Endorsed by Locke: I: Newton 30 Jun 91

1406. Edward Clarke to Locke, 8 July 1691 (1376, 1415)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 61. Printed in Rand, pp. 313-14.
Chipley the 8th. July 1691.
Deare Sir
By the last post I answered your Letter of the 22th. of June, which, by reason of my Absence from home for about a fortnight past, came but then newly to my handes; I have therein fully Answered my Lady's Question stated in your Letter,†2 and hope it
― 291 ―
will goe safe to your handes, And because I had not then time to acquaint you, what Discourse I had with Mr. Stratton, and what other inquieryes I made into your Concern's in that Neighbourhood, I take this first opportunity to tell you, That tho Mr. Stratton bee actually removed to Bristoll, with his Wife and Family, and become a settled Inhabitant there, yett Hee hath hitherto, and promises mee to continue, to take the same Care of your Concern's as formerly, untill Hee can have an opportunity of settling his Accompts with you, Which Hee is now soe hotly bent upon, That all that I could say to Him was but barely suffitient to prevent his putting Himselfe to the Charge and Trouble of makeing a Journey to Oates on purpose to passe his Accompts with you; By which, and by his leaveing his Trade of Tanning, and Quitting his other Countrey Affayres, And retireing into the City where Hee hath noe Imployment, I guesse Hee hath now soe much time upon his handes That Hee doth not well know how to dispose of Himselfe; If in hindring Him from this unnecessary, chargeable, and Troublesome Journey, (The Expence of which would I presume one way or other have been expected from you)†a I have done amisse, pray correct mee in your next as for an Error in Judgment, not in Wyll; The Repayres most absolutely necessary about the House at Belton are finished, And I find upon Inquiery that the Agents for Mr. Popham have for several moneths past forborn to digg any more Cole on your tenement, and as I am informed They pretend a readynesse to make reasonable satisfaction for any Dammage you or your Tennants have sustained by the Cole-Workes there, Therefore I have now againe desiered and press'd Mr. Stratton to informe Himselfe of the Particular Dammages allready sustayned by you, And bee in a Condition to make the same appeare by Proofe, in case there shall bee occasion for it; This is all materiall that at present occurrs to my memory touching your Affayres in those Parts; And now give mee leave to observe to you, That Madam's humor for the Boarding-Schoole continues, and I beleive nothing but the conversation of her Freinds and acquaintance in London will change her Opinion, or Resolutions in that matter, 'tis an affayre that I am as much sylent in as possible I can, but dare not contradict nor Argue against it; Monsieur†1 I hope is verie
― 292 ―
industriouse to improve my son, and with care hath amended in a greate measure, what in my last discourse with you I complayn'd of, Hee, and the Childe, and your Wife, and all the rest of the younge Fry, with Madam and my selfe, are as much your servants as you can Wishe, and doe all passionately desire your Company here. In every one of your Letters pray give us repeated assureances of your Intentions of seeing Chipley this summer, That if we should bee soe unfortunate to Misse that Reall happynesse, yett we may not want the Good Effects, That the expectation of your Company will certainely produce in the Government of the Family here; I am
your Faithfull Freind and servant
EDW: CLARKE:
Pray give our hearty services to my Lady and all at Oates etc.
Endorsed by Locke: E Clarke 8° Jul. 91

1409. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 17/27 and 21/31 July 1691 (1398, 1429)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 55-6. Answers no. 1398; answered by no. 1429.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Quid de Versione tractatus tui statuendum erit, adhuc incertus sum. Vellem quidem Verrino suum non periisse laborem: mallem
― 295 ―
cogitationes tuas doctissimas mihi sermone quem intelligo exhibitas et clare expressas, ut ex illis fructum, quo nunc frustratus sum, percipiam. Quæ in illo legi, magis desiderium meum et reliqua legendi excitant. Credo ego summa cum utilitate eum legendum, ab illis præsertim, qui conceptui alicui non satis pleno neque distincto, tanquam pleno distincto et adæquato, integrum systema inædificant. Hunc non minimum erroris fontem credo, quod homines se plene et adæquate rem percepisse credant; cum imperfectum solummodo illius rei habeant conceptum: qui porro ipsis unicum, cui reliqua cogitata inædificent est fundamentum. Hujus rei jam vivum in civitate nostra habemus documentum. Minister Ecclesiæ publicæ†1 hujus civitatis, cui nomen Balthasar Bekker, Theologiæ Doctor, librum edidit de existentia spirituum.†2 In eo ostendere conatur, malos dæmones, seu, ut vocamus, diabolos, nunquam homines tentare aut tentasse, nec corpora eorum infestasse, non
― 296 ―
seduxisse primos homines, nec tentasse D. Jesum, aliaque plura, quæ communi Christianorum sententiæ adversantur. Nec bonis angelis ea adscribit, quæ Christianismus unanimiter illis in Scriptura adscribi credit. Loca illa plurima Scripturæ quæ de angelis tam bonis, quam malis, loquuntur, longe aliter explicat. Tractatus lingua Belgica est conscriptus; si Latine exstaret eum tibi per nostrum Furlæum mitterem. Fundamentum hujus opinionis unicum ipsi est, conceptus de spiritu, ex Philosophia Cartesiana haustus, quod nimirum spiritus sit cogitatio, prætereaque nihil. Cogitatio autem extra se nihil operari potest, sed omnis ejus operatio est immanens. Hinc colligit, angelos nec in animam, nec in corpus nostrum quicquam operari posse: Animam quidem operari posse in corpus cui unita est, non vero in aliud. Ego vero credo, illum conceptum de anima inadæquatum sibi assumere tanquam adæquatum, atque ita rem non plene perceptam sibi repræsentare tanquam plene et distincte perceptam. Cogitationem spiritui esse essentialem in dubium minime revoco: an vero spiritus natura requirat, ut actu semper cogitet, non definio: multum minus, in spiritu aliud nihil esse, præter nudam ac solam cogitationem. Animam in corpus nostrum agere, et vicissim corpus in animam nostram, experientiâ constat. Illam reciprocam actionem per nudas cogitationis et
― 297 ―
extensionis ideas explicari posse, nondum Cartesii sequaces nos docuerunt. Quod mihi evidentissimum argumentum est, ideam illam mentis, quod sit cogitatio, non esse plenam neque adæquatam; saltem in ea obscuritatis quid esse: ac proinde, qui illi, tanquam perfectæ, adæquatæ, ac distinctæ integrum systema superædificat, facile in varios posse abduci errores. Ab imprudentia sane neutiquam excusare possum, ex tali idea argumenta petere, quæ prævaleant claris Scripturæ verbis, et ne in illa idea aliquam agnoscamus imperfectionem aut obscuritatem, in verbis Scripturæ sensum quærere, qui sine maxima quæ clarissimis verbis affertur violentia, exinde hauriri nequit, per quem etiam variæ historiæ in dubium vocantur, quibus tamen quid Sacri Scriptores designare voluerint non explicatur. Facile viro illi concedo, diaboli eam non esse potentiam, quæ vulgo illi adscribi solet: neque eum promiscue quoscunque homines ad malum sollicitare, sed ordinarie propria concupiscentia homines ad peccandum abduci: non tamen illam de spirituum natura ideam mihi normam ac regulam certam esse velim, ad quam Scripturæ Sacræ verba exigenda esse cupiam. Doleo viri illius, et eruditi, et pii, et æqui ac moderati, imprudentiam. Hujus enim libelli editione Collegarum in se provocavit judicia immitia, quorum aliqui eum tanquam atheismi patronum proscindere non verentur; ac male metuo illi, ne prorsus, nisi palinodiam
― 298 ―
canet, ministerio et functione ecclesiastica spolietur. Adeo receptæ Theologorum opinioni contradicere periculosum est. Putem hunc, aliosque illi similes, tui tractatus lectione instrui posse, ne facile sibi blandiantur, nec plene se ea scire credant, quorum ideam se habere claram putant; sed ubi accurato ideæ illius examine instituto deprehenderint, omnia quæ ad rei illius essentiam spectant per illam explicare se minime posse, illi aliquid deësse agnoscant, ac proinde, ne temere, quicquam per eam explicari nequit, rejiciant. In aliis autem eam æquitatem desidero, ut non statim, quicquid a sua recedit opinione, tanquam impium damnent. Non quivis error impietatem sibi habet conjunctam. Quamvis enim a gravi imprudentia illum minime excusem, præsertim quando et scribendi rationem, et varia illius libri contenta considero; Theologorum tamen esse credo, solidis rationibus, benevolentia ac mansuetudine, erroribus occurrere, non vero errantes præpropere damnare, et sola autoritate ecclesiastica ad palinodiam cogere. Verum antiquus hic morbus est, cujus medicinam frustra speramus. Vides hic indicem librorum ac capitum historiæ S. Officii Inquisitionis. Omnia in capitum titulis distincte exprimere non potui; verum tu ex hisce facile judicabis, quid ipsis capitibus contineatur. Si aliquid Tu, vel D. Cudwortha, deësse credatis, me moneri velim, ut ea in
― 299 ―
tempore addam: jam enim typographum urgere constitui, ut editionem maturet. Oblatam a tam insigni matrona amicitiam avidissime amplector: Non minus ego doleo me non posse uti lingua utrique nostrum communi. Reverentiam et obsequium quod ipsi debeo ultro testarer; damno sæpe negligentiam meam, qui mihi linguæ Anglicanæ, quæ maximam cum nostra habet communionem, non comparaverim notitiam; nunc vero senescenti jam linguam novam addiscere, molestius est. Rogo illam quam officiosissime a me salutes, nihilque illius amicitia mihi esse gratius, dicas, quod utinam documento aliquo testari possim. Interim semper illius virtutes colam, ipsamque, ut tanti patris dignam sobolem, venerabor. D. Clericus fasciculum tuum a D. Churchill accepit, et jam ante plures menses tibi responsum misit, suumque responsum Tibi non exhibitum valde miratur. Juveni cuidam,†1 qui commendatitias ad doctissimum D. Boyle petebat, tradidit fasciculum, qui continebat ultimam, quæ mense Aprili prodiit, bibliothecæ universalis partem, cum literis ad D. Boyle: illis aliud exemplar cum literis ad Te inclusit. Aut ergo oportet juvenem illum non reddidisse fasciculum D. Boyle, quod minime credit, quia illius colloquium ambiebat; aut exemplar Tibi destinatum cum literis adhuc apud
― 300 ―
D. Boyle hærere; aut postquam e manibus D. Boyle exiit aberrasse. Ipse D. Clericus suas literas meis se additurum promisit, et jam rescripsissemus†a- ante octiduum, verum summus æstus,-†a qui integris duabus hebdomadis tanquam sub zona torrida nos adussit, tarditatem scribendi produxit, cum nullus in ædibus reperiri posset locus, qui nos contra insolitum hunc æstum tutaretur. Ipsum monebo, me jam scripsisse, et hodie literas ad Te missurum, ut suas meis jungere possit. Venius, Guenellonus, aliique Collegæ hactenus bene valent, omnesque Tibi plurimam dicunt salutem: præsertim vero ego cum uxore ac liberis. Vale, Vir Amplissime, et me, ut facis, ama
Tui Amantissimum
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 27 Julii

(English) Hasce jam dië Veneris scripseram; verum non potui illo die D. Clericum monere; itaque satius credidi sequenti tabellario eas committere. Nunc mihi suas tradidit D. Clericus, quas meis includo. Audio Theologos admodum D. Bekkero infensos, ob libri de dæmonibus editionem. Jam congregata est Synodus Hollandiæ Borealis:
― 301 ―
multi credunt, illum, nisi quæ scripsit, revocet, exauctorandum. Mira errores exstirpandi ratio. Argumentis animus convincendus est, non terrore nec minis. Lingua ac calamus cogi possunt, animus autem ut credat, quod falsum esse sibi persuadet, nequaquam. Et quid, si reluctante animo condemnet suum tractatum (quod minime facturum credo) eritne aptior ministerio, postquam se improbare mentitus est quod non improbat, quam cum sincere quod animo credit profitetur? Plura jam non addo †a Ecclesia <Chri>stiana,†a et quæ sibi soli Reformatæ ti<tul>um†a vindicat, geri. Vale iterum Vir Amplissime, et Generosam tuam Hospitam quam officiosissime a me saluta.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I am still uncertain what will have to be decided about the translation of your treatise. I should wish Verrijn's labour not to have been wasted; I should [p. 295] prefer to have your profound thoughts presented to me in a language that I understand, and clearly expressed, so that I may get from them the profit that I am now disappointed of. What I have read of the book makes me the more eager to read the rest. I believe that it would be most profitable reading, especially for those people who build an entire system on some concept that is not sufficiently full and distinct, as if it were full, distinct, and adequate. I believe this to be not the smallest source of error, that men suppose that they have apprehended a thing fully and adequately, whereas they have only an imperfect concept of it; this then becomes the sole foundation on which they build the rest of their thoughts. We have a living proof of this at the present moment in our city. A minister of the Public Church†1 of this city, by name Balthasar Bekker, a doctor of theology, has published a book concerning the existence of spirits.†2 In it he attempts to show that evil daemons, or devils as we call them, never assail or have assailed men or infested their bodies; that they did not lead the first of mankind astray or tempt the [p. 296] Lord Jesus, and much else that is contrary to the common opinion of Christians. Nor does he ascribe to good angels what the Christian world unanimously believes is ascribed to them in Scripture. Of those many passages of Scripture which speak of angels good as well as bad he has a widely different explanation. The treatise is written in Dutch; if there were a Latin version available I would send it you through our friend Furly. The one foundation for this opinion of his is a concept of spirit derived from Cartesian philosophy, which certainly identifies spirit with thought, but goes no further. As for thought, it cannot operate in any way outside itself; its operation is wholly immanent. Hence he concludes that angels cannot operate in any way either on our soul or on our body; the soul can, indeed, operate upon the body with which it is united, but on nothing else. I, however, believe that he is taking for himself an inadequate concept of soul as if it were adequate, and so is representing to himself a thing not fully apprehended as fully and distinctly apprehended. That thought is essential to spirit I would certainly not call in question; whether, however, the nature of spirit requires that it should always be thinking in action I do not determine; much less, that there is nothing in spirit except thought pure and simple. That our soul acts upon our body and in turn our body upon our soul is evident from experience; that this reciprocal action can be explained through the bare ideas of thought and extension is something that the followers of [p. 297] Descartes have not yet taught us. This for me is evident proof that that idea of mind that it is thought, is neither full nor adequate; at least that there is some obscurity in it, and accordingly that he who erects an entire system upon it as if it were perfect, adequate, and distinct, may easily be led into various errors. I cannot clear from a charge of imprudence the seeking from such an idea arguments that should be stronger than the clear words of Scripture, and, lest we should recognize any imperfection or obscurity in that idea, the requiring from the words of Scripture a meaning which cannot be extracted from them without doing the greatest violence to the clearest words; furthermore various narratives are called in question, yet without; explaining what meaning the sacred writers intended in them. I readily concede to this man that the devil has not the sort of power which is commonly attributed to him; that he does not promiscuously solicit all and sundry to evil, but that ordinarily men are led into sin by their own concupiscence; I would not, however, be willing to accept his idea of the nature of spirits as a sure and certain rule by which I should wish to measure the words of Holy Scripture. I am sorry for the imprudence of the man, one so scholarly, devout, fair-minded, and moderate. By the publication of this book he has provoked harsh judgements on the part of his fellows, some of whom do not hesitate to decry him as an advocate of atheism; indeed, I seriously fear that unless he makes a recantation he may be deprived of his ministry and [p. 298] functions in the church. So dangerous is it to contradict a received opinion of theologians. I should think that he and others like him might be taught by reading your treatise not to flatter themselves lightly, or to suppose that they fully understand those things of which they consider they have a clear idea; but when, after making a careful examination, they perceive that they cannot explain everything relating to the essence of that thing, they should acknowledge that something is lacking from the idea, and accordingly not reject hastily whatever cannot be explained by it. As for others, I desire such fairness in them as not to condemn out of hand as impious whatever recedes from their opinion. Not every error is associated with impiety. For although I cannot by any means clear that man of serious imprudence, especially when I consider his way of writing and various items in his book; nevertheless I believe that it is the duty of theologians to meet errors with solid reasoning, kindliness, and meekness, and not over-hastily to condemn the erring, or to force them to recant by ecclesiastical authority alone. But this is an ancient malady, for which we may vainly hope to find a remedy. You see here a list of the books and chapters of my account of the Holy Office. I could not express everything clearly in the titles of the chapters; but you will readily judge from them what are the contents of the chapters. If you or Mrs. Cudworth should think that there is anything wanting I should like you to let me know, so that I can add the things in time; for I have now [p. 299] decided to urge the printer to make haste with the publication. I embrace most eagerly the friendship offered by that illustrious lady; nor am I less sorry that I am not conversant with a language common to us both. Of my own accord I would have borne witness to the respect and service which I owe her; I often blame my negligence in not having acquainted myself with the English tongue, which is so closely akin to ours; now, however, as I grow older it is more troublesome to learn a new language. I beg you to give her my most dutiful respects, and to tell her that nothing is more pleasing to me than her friendship, and that I only wish I could show it by some proof. Meanwhile I shall always esteem her qualities and shall honour her as the worthy issue of so great a father. Mr. Le Clerc received your packet from Mr. Churchill; he sent you an answer some months ago, and he is much surprised that his answer was not delivered to you. He gave the packet to a certain young man†1 who was asking for a letter of introduction to the learned Mr. Boyle; it contained the latest part of the Bibliotheque universelle, which came out in April, together with a letter to Mr. Boyle; he enclosed another copy with a letter to you. It must be, then, either that this young man has not delivered the packet to Mr. Boyle, which Mr. Le Clerc can hardly believe, as he was eager to have some conversation with him; or that the copy he designed for you with his letter is still sticking with Mr. Boyle; or else that it has gone astray after leaving Mr. Boyle's hands. Mr. Le Clerc [p. 300] promised to add a letter of his own to mine, and we would have written a week ago by now, but the extreme heat which has been scorching us for a whole fortnight as if in the torrid zone has made writing slow work, as no place can be found in the house to protect one against this unaccustomed heat. I shall tell him that I have now written and am sending you the letter today, so that he may add his own to mine. Veen, Guenellon, and our other Collegians are all well so far and they all send you their best wishes, as I do myself together with my wife and children. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 27 July
1691
(Latin) I had already written the above on Friday, but I was unable to let Mr. Le Clerc know that day; so I thought it better to send my letter by the following post. Mr. Le Clerc has now given me his, which I enclose with mine. I hear the theologians are very wroth with Mr. Bekker for publishing the book on [p. 301] daemons. The Synod of North Holland has now assembled; many believe that unless he retracts what he has written he ought to be discharged from the ministry. A strange way of rooting out errors. The mind must be convinced by arguments, not by intimidation or threats. The tongue and the pen can be compelled, but the mind by no means, to believe what it convinces itself is false. And were he to condemn his own treatise against his inner convictions (which I do not for a moment believe he will), will he be fitter for the ministry after falsely professing to disapprove what he does not disapprove than when he sincerely avows what he believes in his heart? I will add nothing more now should be done in a Christian church, and one that claims for itself alone the title of Reformed. Good-bye once again, excellent Sir, and give my deepest respects to your well-born hostess.
(Latin) Amsterdam 31 July

1410. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 21/31 July 1691 (1388, 1446)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 50-1. On this and on some of Le Clerc's later letters there are pencil marks; they were made probably by or for Lord King, and are ignored here. An excerpt printed in King, pp. 230-1; the whole in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 47-8. Enclosed in no. 1409.
A Amsterdam le 31 de Juillet 1691.
Ce n'est pas entierement, par ma faute, Monsieur, que vous n'avez pas reçu de mes nouvelles, depuis si long-temps, quoique j'eusse sujet de vous remercier de la bonté que vous aviez euë de m'envoier des livres, que j'ai lûs avec plaisir, et que Mr. Churchill me remit fidélement entre les mains. Six semaines, ou deux mois après, un nommé Mr. Fatio de Geneve allant à Londres, il se chargea d'un paquet, que j'adressai à Mr. Boyle, où il y avoit le dernier Tome de la Bibliotheque de l'année passée, avec un billet pour vous, dans une enveloppe particuliére. Je n'ai pas vû Mr. Fatio depuis, mais je ne puis croire qu'il n'ait rendu le paquet.†1 Je vous y disois quelque chose du MS. sur le passage corrompu.†2 Je n'en ai encore rien fait, à cause de diverses occupations que j'ai euës, mais j'espere d'avoir occasion de le publier avec quelques autres Dissertations, étant trop petit pour paroître tout seul. Un trop petit livre se perd, il faut tâcher de le grossir un peu, si on veut qu'il subsiste. Je suis présentement tout à fait occupé de mon travail sur le Pentateuque. J'espere qu'il ne déplaira pas aux connoisseurs; quoi que j'aie résolu de me ménager en sorte que personne ne se trouve blessé. Peutêtre que dans quelque temps, j'en envoierai en Angleterre les deux ou trois premiers chapitres pour avoir le sentiment de ceux qui entendent ces sortes de choses, et je vous prierai alors de me marquer ce que vous en pensez. Le jugement des personnes comme vous et de ceux qui ne <sont>†a pas pleins de préjugez theologiques, est d'un beaucoup plus grand poids chez moi, que celui des Docteurs. Il y a quelques mois que Mr. Allix m'écrivit que quelcun avoit entrepris en Anglois un nouveau commentaire sur le V.T.†3 mais que cela ne feroit pas tort à mon dessein, à cause de la diversité de la méthode. Lui aiant demandé quelque éclaircissement la
― 303 ―
dessus, il ne m'a rien répondu. Si vous en aviez ouï parler, vous m'obligerez extrêmement de m'apprendre ce que c'est. Je vous remercie des souhaits que vous faites en ma faveur et en celle de ma femme, dans la Lettre que vous avez écrite à Mr Limbourg. Elle m'a chargé de vous assurer de ses respects, et je vous supplie de croire que je suis toûjours, de tout mon cœur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Londres.

1411. Charles Mordaunt, earl of Monmouth, later third earl of Peterborough, to Locke, [30 July 1691?] (1252, 1535)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 107-8. The letter is here associated with Monmouth's visit to Bath in 1691. His exact movements are unknown but he was there probably in August: no. 1414, address. Locke was at Oates from 28 May to 13 July; in London from 13 to Saturday 25 July; at Oates from 25 to Friday 31 July. He returned on the 31st to London, and was there still on 6 August. On Saturday 8 August he came to Daunsey (Dauntsey), Wiltshire, where Monmouth had a seat (it is about 90 miles from London and about 20 from Bath): Journal. Locke was presumably in company with Lord and Lady Monmouth on this journey (it is probably the ramble mentioned in no. 3373). In that case the likeliest date for the letter is Thursday in the preceding week, when Locke was at Oates, 30 July.
Mr Lock.
I hope the direction writt by a Ladys hand will quicken the messenger. I feare that I writt to you Munday night was not well directed, we goe a munday to the Bath, and my Damsell†1 hopes the watters will entice the watter Drinker. Mrs Cutts gives me paper and her pen, which I must restore to her and so only desire your answer, we will stay Two or three days for you it being indifferent any time the begginning of next week.
Sir
Yours
MONMOUTH.
Thirsday.

1412. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 10 August 1691 (1203, 1443)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 93-4.
St Giles's Aug the 10th 91
Dear Sir
I should say much to You on the Favour You have done Mee with my Lord Pembrook: for besides the Kindness You have done my Brother;†1 I am to Reckon on the Esteem of so Knowing and Learn'd a Man, as Your Purchase for Mee, and what I could have done so little towards, upon my own Bottom; that I should not have dar'd, with the whole Wealth of all my Stock, to have so much as Bidd for itt: Bee itt how itt will; as itt is, I am sure I find my self sensible of this, as of a very Great Obligation: Whether You yourself are sensible of itt as you should bee; or whether You think that I am so, or by any thing I say, may bee made to think so; is what I very much doubt of: for, to acknowledg the first, were to Yeild that You yourself Judg allways advantageously enough of what you doe for Mee; which I positively deny You ever did: neither can I expect that You, who are not so your self; Should beleive mee sensible as I ought: and therefore, as to the last Point, to think that by saying any thing, or by what ever I could write, I Could really Cause You to be sensible of something that before You were not; Would be to Imagine that by meer Reasoning (not by Matter of Fact, onely or Representation) I could be able to give You some New Idea, or Correct what You had before; which Power I wholly disavow in myself; Unless I could define my self so a Part of your own Reason or a Creature of your Reason's; that from Mee as from a sort of By-memory or Memory of reserve, You might att
― 305 ―
some times receive some of your own Ideas reflected thence, instead of having them from their First Immediate Repository. Therefore as matters stand I have but little subject of writing though there appears to be so much Cause: And as for this present Favour; I resolve to say no more of itt: for however considerable itt be in its Self; Yet now, that it is thus over and past with mee and thrown in with all the Huge Arrear behind; It appears nothing almost, and is quite lost in Such a Sum: for the Sum it self is not so much as perceptably increas'd by itt and I am afraid You will find itt but as the Odd Money sett att the foot of the Account which vertually does not make the Bill the greater and is never minded in the Payment, when it comes ... I was going to have Run on more in the same Strain and have told You; how that I was as one who being in for more then the real Valew of what he has and already Indebted more then the worth of his own head; grows desperate and Cares not how deeper he Engages, nor how lavishly he receives from the Person whome already he depends upon; and that this way You might resolve to yourself the meaning of my Easy Negligent and Slight Reception of all Benifitts from your Hands. Much of this and the Like I was going on to have said: But I perceive from the beginning of my Letter hetherto, I am hedg'd in with a Style meerly Clownish Rude and Barberouse; infected with the Practice of Life and Objects I have continually before mee Here, where I have now been a longer time, to my sorrow, then ever since I knew my self. It is impossible for mee to write any thing pleasant or to pretend to Politeness: for if itt be but a Phrase or a Term of Buisness, or Art, belonging to that Brutal state, call'd a Country-Life; that upon any occasion, as itt will doe, thrusts it self in; It is enough to Spoyl the best sentence in the World, or make the best Thought of but Insipid relish. I cannot chuse indeed but be exceeding lusciouse: for I find a sort of a naturall, Illitterate Chimistry here, that has extracted all my Salt. This makes mee out of all Patience to see how meer Mechanicall our Frames are, and gives me a shrewd longing to renew the Dispute again with You, of our Absolute materiallity: But that I am but too sensible, that in the Condition my Spirit or Immateriall Substance is att present, and in the manner that itt hangs togather, I am very Unfitt for Disputation. If the Filling Matter of my Present Life were not of a Nature to drown'd all Reflections, especially such nicer ones on the Loss of some Particular more refin'd Pleasure; And if the Universall and
― 306 ―
Immediate Loss of all sort of Tollerable Divertion in a present Life, did not make mee disregard the Losses of Other more distant Enjoyments of Time Past, or Future; I should here certainly express a great deal of Regrett for what I have been forc'd to loose in Essex, and what I am now, as itt were, loosing, and still to loose on, att the Bath, of your Company, and the Conducing Advantages of Both Places. As for the Charachter You give mee of the latter; It is to Mee the most inviting in the world: for the Different Foppery You describe there, is but an Exuberancy, or Excrescence of Civiliz'd Society, The sure Sign of Good Soyl, and Growing allways out of the most Green and Flourishing Parts, as doe our Mushrooms: which (as I suppose) but You may correct mee) are but an excrement thrown out from the most oyly and fattest of the Ground. I imagine It to bee as those Scurfs and Crusts which grow round the Oar of all Rich mines,†1 which is what they are discover'd first by, and allways found in. I look upon such Matter, (and I look on Itt Hence with Envy) as that necessary Ferment which I would never have the World or the Seat of my divertion without. I would not (could I help it) ever Venture on Unleaven'd Company. I should be apt to loose my Tast in itt. This is the Spirit, the Salt, and every Thing. 'Tis the Rough whetstone that Sharpens and Polishes the Conversation of all those near Itt, who are of a Mettle fitt to receive an even Impression and admitt a Smooth Surface and Lovely Form. All this, att an other time, would have rais'd in mee Strong Ideas, and have made mee Impatient of any Stay from You: But now, that I am Where I am; By this time (Thank God) I am reduc'd to a Perfect State of insensibility. I am affected with nothing: and of what I am, or what I say I scearce feel any thing, besides this, that I am Your Obliged Freind and Humble Servant
A ASHLEY
Good Mr Lock forgive mee this long letter I knew not really what I was doing.
Endorsed by Locke: L. Ashley 10° Aug. 91
