1413. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 17 August 1691 (1399, 1602)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 53-4. The letter was apparently sent to Yonge in London to be forwarded.
Otterton Aug: 17th. 91.
Dearest Sir
I have with an impatient desire expected to hear of your being come to the Bath all this Summer, Coveting nothing more then to drink those Waters in your Company, from which I promised my self all manner of advantages, as being the most probable Method of restoring me to a better state of Health, and making me once more happy in the most agreable, and valluable conversation in the World. I receiv'd the Notice of your being going thither, with a great deal of Joy; though it was much allayed by my present incapacity of hastening to you. for dispairing of your comming I gave Betty Brown leave to go 50 Miles to see her Friends, and to Tarry a fortnight; 'twill be Saturday next†1 before she is expected here again; and I cannot Travell without a Servant, tho I make a bad shift to be without her here at Home. I know not how short your stay may be at Bathe, by that time she is returned perhaps you may be comming towards Chipley, where I may wayt on you, and shorten my Journey, since I dare not drink the Bath Waters so late in the Year, as the end of August and September, being naturally inclined to Violent purgings in the Autumn; but I will not fail to make my appearance at Chiply assoon as I can learn you are there, of which I beg the earliest notice; that I may not lose one day of your Company whilest you are in the Rowe. Sir Walter Yonge his Lady and Sisters who are all here, (and Just riding out to see the Royal Fleet who lye at Anchor in Torbay;) send you their best services, and bid me tell you that they expect a good share of your company, my Lady sa'yes she has a promise of it under your hand, and we all with a pleasing impatience expect your making it good; but none can receive you with that Joy, and Satisfaction as Dear Sir
Your most Obliged Friend and Obedient Daughter.
Is: DUKE
Mr Duke is most affectionately yours.
I thank god I am recover'd much beyond my hopes, and shall be able to ride to meet you at Chiply with Ease and pleasure.

1414. Dr. William Cole to Locke, 20 August 1691 (1321, 3299)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 207-8.
Sir,
Tis so long since I saw Mrs Walwyns son of Helen's†1 that some circumstances of his indisposition may possibly have slipped out of my memory. Twas on the occasion of a violent convulsive distemper I was first consulted; since the abatement of which I more than once, I remember, at distances prescribed him medcines both to prevent returnes of those fits and also otherwise to secure his health: which methods I conceive ought to be repeated now and then both to carry off humours, which not being fit for exercise But eating freely (as I remember) he cannot but congest and†a- to corroborate.-†a But I doe not remember I positively declared for his going to the Bath, though perhaps, revolving many things in my thoughts, I might mention it incidentally as one meanes of answering both those intentions. But at this time of the yeere I should hardly propose it, the season being late to begin, and must be the later by the preparation of bleeding and purging which ought to precede the use of it; least otherwise the humors, rarifyed by the warmth of the bath, should more impetuously flow to his head, too weake and susceptible of them naturally. I should rather at present advise he had the last method repeated about the equinox which is so neare, the heates being then likely to be over; unlesse any new symptoms or indications perswade to the altering of it. The prescripts were made at Mr Harris's an Apothecary in Worcester, about 12 miles from Helens, where I suppose he is. My most humble

service to his Lordship,†1 though unknown; and be pleased to beleeve I shall esteeme all opportunities very fortunate which can expresse me,
Sir,
Your most humble servant
W. COLE.
Great Queenstreet.

Deare Sir
At the importunity of my sonn I have Promised Him the Liberty of waiteing on my Lady Masham and your selfe at Oates, and therefore begg the Favour of you by a Lyne or two to lett mee know what stay you are like to make there before your next Return hither, to the end Hee may bee certaine to find you there when I send Him, And if you please to informe mee by what Coach I may best send Him, and at what place Hee may bee sett down to bee afterwards conveyed to Oates most conveniently, and where the Coaches stand here in Town, you will therein lay a further obligation upon,

1416. Edward Clarke to Lady Masham, 15 September 1691
The Houghton Library, Harvard. Draft. See no. 1415 n. Printed in Rand, pp. 314-15.
London September the 15th. 1691.
I Presume Mr. Lock hath acquainted your Ladyship that my Wife and I and our three eldest Children are now in Town, and hath done us the Right to present our humble services to Sir Francis and your Ladyship, and hath alsoe inform'd you of my intentions to have waited on you, but the constant indisposition Mrs. Clarke Labours under will not I find (at least untill after shee is Delivered)†1 permitt mee that happynesse, and indeed tis that which putts mee under a necessity of Begging that by Letter which otherwise I should have done in Person, Tis for your Ladyships leave That my sonn may waite upon you, and spend a few dayes at Oates now whilst Mr. Lock is in the Countrey with you, and herein lett mee deale playnly and like an Old Freind with you, my Designe being to give Mr. Locke an opportunity of observeing what Improvements the Child hath made under his Tutor,†2 and allsoe the Tutors Conduct in the mannagement and Education of Him, in all which I am wholly incapable of makeing any Judgment, being altogather a stranger to the French Language, And therefore begg your permission to make use of this opportunity for my satisfaction in this Particular. And doe allsoe earnestly request you to bee my Advocate to Mr. Locke, and soe to Represent my Desires to Him (which are of greate Concern to mee) That Hee may not bee uneasy in the Gratifying mee therein nor thinke mee incroaching on his Frindship by Desireing such a Trouble of Him, espetially since I doe it by you for whom I know Hee has soe Greate a Respect; If you can Pardon mee for this Freedome and at any time give mee an opportunity to serve you, it will bee a greate Addition to all the former obligations you have layd on,
Your most humble servant
EDW: CL
Pray accept mine and my Wifes humble services, and present the same to Sir Francis, your mother, Mr. Locke and the rest of the good Family at Oates etc.

1419. William Stratton to Locke, 10 October 1691 (1343, 1426)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 65-6.
Bristoll the 10th: Octo 1691
Dear Cosin
David Horrall Leaveing your estate the same day meting with John Veale have let it for ten years as will apeare by the Inclosed lease which I desire you to seale and send back as spedyly as you can John Veale Is the tenant that I have Indevered for sum years to provide for you, he is soe good a tenant that his landlord is trobled at the los of him and I doe not know a better, he hath leave from david Horrall to put soyle on it in heaps and hath all Redy put
― 313 ―
severall loads brought from pensford and Intends to put mutch more next weake I doe not dout by gods blesing but he will prove as good a tenant as ever you had he is very likely, he hath sealed the Counter part allredy I have sent this by Mr: Dando whoe will not stay In London more then 4 or 5 days, I have desired him to delever it as sone as he cums to toun that soe your freind may with the first opertunyty convey it to you and you likewise return it back that it may be sent to him to the three Cups In Bredstreate for Mr: Dando Will not have time to se whether it be returned but If you cannot return it by Mr Dando I doe not at presant mind any better way then the Bristoll Carrier you may have sum other way by sum acksidentall person that I know not of, If you remember David Horrall would give but 18l̷ p year and If I had not let it befor they had spoken to gether I might not have had more then 20l̷ p year I have given this Incoragement that his rent shall not be Raised nither turned out of his Bargaine and I thought good Reson It being soe neare the former Rent and soe dificult to raise rent I hope that 22l̷ pr year will please you as well as my selfe for I am pleased becaws I did not know wheare to have the like I spake to Mr Dando to return the mony In my hands of yours but he was taken up before but If you have any way befor I can Return it I am redy to pay your bill on sight with advice from you my Wife presents her service to you I take leave In hast
Your Faithfull Kinsman and humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
the word Rack Rent in the Lease is mentioned becaws he hath a lease for old doun
Endorsed by Locke: W. Stratton 10° Oct. 91
1420. James Tyrrell to Locke, 15 October [1691] (1403, 1424)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 102-3. Year from Locke's endorsement, etc.
Oxon Oct: 15th.†a
Dear Sir
I have received yours, which was very satisfactory to me, since it assured me not onely of the continueance, but increase of your
― 314 ―
health, by drinkeing the Bathe waters, and it was the more gratefull as <comeing>†a at a Time, when by reason of your long silence, I feared you were either not well, or at least that I was not so in your esteem; either of which would have bin a great disturbance to me, but since you give me so good reasons for your silence; I am satisfyed; and if I have not bin so quick as I might have bin in performeing your commands, I know your candour will excuse it; since haveing some businesse here I could not well goe over to pack up your bookes, and other things sooner then I did, yet they might have come, quicker, but that John could not get a Cart before last weeke to bring them hither, nor was there ever a barge ready to carry them till to day; but I hope, they are gone; or if not, will goe in a day, or 2: and therefore I thought fit to write now to give you notice of it: But to tell you more particularly what I have put up and sent you. First I have (as you desired) sent all your bookes, except those Physic bookes and cleane paper bookes that are left out of your note; and such bookes as I have made bold to borrow of you for some longer time; and for which I here send you a note of my hand: but as for all the bookes you mention as omitted in your Catalogue; you are in the right; they were either by the carelessenesse of the party that tooke downe the bookes and brought them me to be catalogued, or else by my owne neglect haveing so many at a time before me forgot to be written downe; but when you please to examine your bookes you will find all, viz: Fletchers plays†1 with the rest you want (even to the little greek Testament) all there. I must likewise beg your pardon if thorogh hast, or forgetfullnesse I omitted, to put downe. your cane chair; and Table to it; with the quillt,†b in the Inventory; but they are all now sent up, and I hope will come safe to your hands for I have given the bargeman a great charge of your chair: but pray remember there is but one quilt, and 1 pair of blankets, which are now sent up; which I know not whether they were in the Inventory or not, all your other goods are put up even to your velvet Cap: except the carpets; and the Cushion for the chair; and 2 locks with the Keys to them which could not be well sent now; for as to the Carpets, they could not be put up in the Cloath, that holds the rest of the things,
― 315 ―
because it was not big enough to cover them, and besides Nan†1 affirmes, that you gave my wife all three Carpets; but for my part, I doe not remember you gave her more then one; but it is left to you to be Chancellour in this case; and if you please to say they are all yours, they shall be sent you up by the next oppertunity, when your other bookes goe up: but for the Cushion John tells me, it was forgot to be put up in the bundle; not being seen, but coverd up with some other things: but I desire you to take notice, that your napkins and other linnen are in the Trunk; and that the bundle contains no more then the quilt, and blankets; with Taverniers Travels,†2 which I orderd to be put up in the middle of those things; because all the boxes were so full, that there was no room for it; your Telescope is in one of the boxes on Top of the bookes: and your hammer behind them. but your small terrestrial Globe (for there was but one) and your Barometer are left behind; for another oppertunity when the rest of your bookes; and boxes shall come; your Barometer is at Shotover; but†a- I have-†a put 2 pound†b of fresh quicksilver to it; the old being growne very fowl; and naught: so that it would not move right: as for your Manuscript†c collections in Physick and†d- other things-†d etc since you did not write particularly for them; I have not sent them up now, but will doe it whenever you desire it, or els will bring them up with me when I come next month; there are two pair†d- of†d cases of boxes still left behind; in which the rest of your Physic and paper bookes; (which are not many) shall be put up, when you desire to have them sent you: But I must now returne you my thankes for your kind present of the Chairs and cupboards; which is more then I could expect for so little trouble as your things have been to me: but as for the greater Cupboard to which is fitted, a case with divisions for papers; you may freely command it; whenever you have the like occasion for it as you had before, and I should be very glad to part with it upon that account. I must allso beg your pardon for not sending you up your box with the lock, for haveing taken the bookes; and other things out of it, and put them in the trunk; I lent my wife the box to put some Linnen in, and since that my daughter (who is now in wales) haveing the Key of it in her keeping; I could not send it
― 316 ―
without breakeing it open, which I was loath to doe; but I will write to her, to let me know where she hath put the Key that I may send you up that box, as†a- allso your little hair trunk,-†a when I send the rest of your things.
I should be glad to know what you will have done with all your glasse bottles, and the things in them; and the seeds which are in†b- little boxes. I-†b have here sent you back the note of your Physic bookes you writ for, that you may see I have sent them all, except two, or three little ones; which I could not find, and du Hamels de affectionibus Corporum: which I am now a readeing over; and will bring up with me when I come: I have herewith sent your Key of the trunke; and pins for the Table: to your chair. I forgot to tell you there is allso an old Table with a drawer; which was in your study at oxford; and which you may have sent if you please to command, it. Otherwise I shall take it as a favour if may be left at Shotover where at present it is, in my closet there: But I thinke I have sufficiently tired you with this tedious account I have given†c- you of your things;-†c which I could not well contract into lesse compasse; but it is high time to conclude assureing you that I shall ever be
Your most faithfull, and humble Servant
J TYRRELL
My Father and Mother are pretty well, and much your servants. James is not yet returned from his Journey but I expect him this weeke.

1421. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 15/25 October 1691 (1408, 1469)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 83-4.
Rotterdam 25 October 1691
Deare Friend
I was glad after so long intermission to see a line from you and to hear of your good health, tho not where you are. your books are nothing lesse than lost. They were in a maund of sleevs etc. sent to mr. Mol, quansuys†9 for saving charges. But the knaves at the custom house would not pass them, but made them pay custom, and Sir P.†10 was so generous that he would not patronize his servant in so sneaking a matter. His worship wrote me the 16 August
― 318 ―
That the papers should be <delivered>†a for Dr Lock, whom he had not seen of a very long time, they (of the custome house) would not deliver them to mr. Moll, I must give a more express order, saith he.
So now you know where your books are. Be pleasd to speak to Joseph Wright, (when you are at Rachels wedding,†1 for I presume you will honour her, as well as her sister, with your presence) and inquire if that more express order, has been given, for the papers were directed to him, for you. And if not given, to procure it. There is a worthy Gentleman, that has dwelt abroad in the late Ks days, who now returns to England, in a Trunk under his conduct, I send you Furetiers Dictionary, the ordinary paper, because I found it to open well enough, as I thought, in Reading.
Your letter with the copy of Swintons I received, but found so little comfort in it, that I nere minded it. I have placed all my children at school at Noortwyck, where your little friend,†2 is the Darling of the master and mistress and all his fellow schollars who call him their little king.
I thank you for your intentions to speak to your friends the Bankers, but that trade is, in a manner, at an end, the States finding themselvs, (as well as England will) abused, by coining a vast quantity of their base schellingh mony, (made of their own Ducatons and your mill'd mony and plate, melted down to that purpose) have put a stop to the minting of any but fine silver coyne, till They should setle their mint upon a new foote.†3
One cashier in Amsterdam has received from 3 bankers in London about 29 millions sterling, by which they have gaind 20 per Cent. (and consequently above 5 millions sterling). This I am told by a Gentleman, who hearing it, would not beleev it, till he had it, out of the Cashiers own mouth—If then 3 Bankers sent to one man 29 millions it may easily be thought that the Jews, and all the rest sent double, 58 millions. which makes 87 millions. And for the service of the nation, not less than 1/20 41/2 millions must needs have been sent out to pay for raysing and transporting forces; the charge of the expedition; for allyes; to pay the Armies; etc—I have seen thus a Computation of above 91 Millions sterling brought out
― 319 ―

of England within this 3 years. And all the coin that came, was of your weighty milld mony,†1 so that you have, they say, nothing left you but clipt mony, which also had been, a great part of it, conveyed away, if it had not been too light to get by. So that it were a question fit to be sent to your Athenian mercurist,†2 to resolve; which are the best patriots, the clippers, or the Bankers. The remarks this calculator makes upon this fact—are melancholy. That this mony is utterly lost to England (and in a great degree to holland too, being cheated 20 per Cent thereby) for that of it, which was coynd here, can never return; and what was not coynd, has, in all probability, for the most part, been conveyed into france, as all the German, and holland fine mony is, of which not a penny is to be seen, in ordinary payments. every doller (having received a new mark at Lisle or Paris etc) passing there currantly for 10 stivers more than here, or in Germany. a Gold Louis yields there, 12 livers 10 ss. and here but f 9:9. (10 or 11 stivers at present) a crown there 70 ss. here but 50 (a 51 stivers at present)†3 So that whatever mony comes into france no man is so mad as to bring thence again, to lose by it. English mony, unstampt, goes there for 1d in the shilling more then in England. Out of france it can't return, by trade, because thats prohibited, nor in specie, for the reason above. Thus you are more than christians, who are bound onely to furnish their enemy with bread, if he hunger, and drink if he thirsts. But these men furnish theirs with money to war against us. When I first came to live here 36 years agoe I could not receive £50 without carrying a payre of gold scales in my pocket, The french have long since eased us of that trouble, by raising the price of gold in their quarters. In the years 1676. and 1677—we received little else but Ducatons for the corn we sold, now we cannot get a Ducaton for our bills of Exchange, they drayning us of all our fine silver mony, and leaving us nothing but our base coyne.
So that I am now convinc'd of a necessity of raising the Value of a pound of silver and gold, if we intend to keep any in our cuntry
― 320 ―
or to get any back, and if so we must raise those lesser pieces that we mint. For at this rate you'l have no mony left you to war with. I hope the parliament will look into this affair, and take some effectuall course for stopping it, for (as this Computator saith) 'tis impossible that all this Treasure should be the Bankers alone, Jacobites must send over their estates, to secure them, or worse, for no body could gain by it but the bankers, alone—
I send you herewith your account to this day by which is due to me, if no mistake, of which I amnot certain, (having no time to examine it, nor read this) f 234:15:12 which concludes this—from
your humble servant
B F
my most humble service to my Lord and Lady,†1 to mr. Freak, etc—
I was lately at Noortwyck, and the children came with me in the waggon to Delf, but would not be perswaded to come home, for a day or, and Arent lest of all, lest he should have stayd.
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Mr. John Locke at Mr. Robert Pawlins in Dorset court Channel Row West-minster per P. Sonmans
Endorsed by Locke: B:Furly 25° Oct 91
1422. Locke to Robert Boyle, 21 October 1691 (1001)
Boyle, Works, ed. Birch, 1744, v. 571.
Oates, Oct. 21, 1691.
Honoured Sir,
By this bearer, my servant, who comes to town on purpose, you will receive your papers concerning the titles of the air.†2 I have read them all over very carefully, numbered them according to the titles they belong to, and laid them in that order, the best I could, according to the state they are in. I have besides corrected many of the mistakes of your amanuenses; but yet, for all this, they are not in a condition to be sent to the printer, or put into a bookseller's
― 321 ―
hand, in order to publishing. For besides that they are not all laid in the order of the titles they belong to, it often happening, that those of different titles are writ in the same paper, which I would not venture to cut in pieces, without your direct order; and some of them being writ on both sides the leaf, cannot be cut; and therefore I have contented myself only to mark in the margin the title each belongs to: besides this, I say, there are some faults in the writing, which, without consulting you, I durst not correct; and in other places defects and omissions, which I could not supply; and many things, which suggest queries, which I think fit to advise with you about. I know not whether you think it necessary to hasten the edition of them. If upon that or any other account you desire my coming to town, I shall not fail, upon the first summons, to wait upon you. I have with them sent a copy of my register of the air, and in some few places made some little additions to the observations of your papers, as you will see; and I doubt not, but, if one had time, one might find many more. Besides the many strange and pleasant remarks your papers contain, and uncommon experiments you have made yourself about the air, your design opens a large and useful field, and I must confess gives me a larger view than I had before of this subject, which yet I have a long time thought deserved as much to be considered, as any part of nature; and which your discoveries had so much recommended to the study of all inquisitive men. But enough of the air on this occasion. Give me leave now to tell you, that I have water, and I have vessels, I only want soap to be at work. Whatsoever you shall give this bearer for me will be safely brought me. I hope he will bring me good news of your health, and I shall be glad to receive the honour of your commands by him. I am,
Honoured Sir,
your most humble, and most obliged servant,
J. LOCKE.
I had forgot to mention above, that I have a little altered some of your titles, the better, as I think, to accommodate them to the papers are to be ranged under them. You will find the alterations I propose writ on the backside of the printed titles, and I know you will pardon this presumption, since I should not make a right use of the freedom you expect from me, should I not without reserve offer my thoughts to you.
― 322 ―
At the end of all you will find some papers which I am in some doubt about, whether they ought to have any room at all amongst the other.
Whenever you have any commands for me, a letter left at my lodging in Dorset-Court in Channel-row will be conveyed to me.
1423. Locke to Edward Clarke, 21 October 1691 (1418, 1431)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 47. Printed in Rand, pp. 316-17.
Oates 21 Oct. 91
Dear Sir
I presume Madam and the children are all well or else I should have heard from you by Saturdays post though I should have been better satisfied had I received it from your owne hand.
My papers have now all that I at present can thinke of on those subjects they only want transcribeing.†1 If I can have time enough I would willingly examine two or three litle treatises I have here concerning these matters and answer any objections in them that may deserve it. I am sure some of them have a good deale of nonsense in them. I writ to you the last weeke for the two things you suggested to me in my chamber which I can not recollect
I here with send you a lease sent me by my Cosin Stratton to execute. If I mistake not it is very sillyly drawn and needs mending. for I thinke for all there sayd he may shroud†2 all my trees and plough what he pleases of my land. I desire you there for if it needs to amend the draught and then give it to Mr Pawling to ingrosse for me desireing him to dispatch it as soon as he can
My Lady presents her service to you and soe doe all the good company here. you are desired to minde Mr Andrews†3 again not to deliver up the mortgage but to give back the counterpart if it be mentiond to him
I have also a question to aske you viz whether the person that has an action of waste can sue the person against whom the action lies without aresting him
― 323 ―
Pray present my humble service to Madam my wife and the yonge folke. I hope you and they are very well. I am
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
My service to Mr S: to Sir W. Y. and J F†1
Endorsed by Clarke: J:L: about the Lease sent from Mr. Stratton Received by Syll the 21th. October 1691. Answered by Syll the 22th.
1424. James Tyrrell to Locke, 22 October [1691] (1420, 1430)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 104. Year from Locke's note and endorsement.
Oxon: Oct 22.†a
Dear Sir
These had come to you above a weeke; or 10 dayes sooner, had not your boxes layn here this fortnight waiting for a passage, for the locks†2 being at fault the barges could not passe till they were mended; but I hope they will now come safe to your hands there are in all 6 great boxes. 2 smaller ones, with one Trunke, a great bundle, and a cane chair with the board to it; I herewith allso send you the pins for the chair, and the Key of the trunke, which I hope will arrive before the things which they tell me will not be till Munday†3 at the soonest: I hope this may find you in Towne ready to receive them and that you have bin well; and without any cough this Autumne; I should be glad to receive a few lines from you of the receipt of them as soon as please. I have one thing more to <tr>ouble†b with; I have now finisht my abridgment of Dr: Cumberlands Law of nature and have added his confutations of Mr: Hobs at the end of it; and have allso made a long preface to it:†4 all which I shall send up to London next weeke; and I should take it as a favour if you would take the paines to peruse it; and give me your opinion of it; if you doe not designe to publish any thing your self upon the same subject;†5 and allso if you please to marke what you dislike; and to write your reasons of it either on the blanck page; or in a peice of paper by it self; I would allso the rather have
― 324 ―
you see it because I have quoted divers things in it out of your booke†1 the papers, will be within these 10 dayes in the hands of one Mr: Cooke, a Barrister, who lives in the lower end of plough yard in Fetter lane, and who will have orders to deliver them to Syl: if you please to send for them. no more but am.
your most faithfull, servant
JT.
Address: For John Locke Esqr at Mr: Pawleings house in Dorset Court in Cannon Row Westminster.
this with a Key; and other things.

1425. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 28 October/7 November 1691 (1390, 1453)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 45.
d'amsterd. ce 7 nov. 1691
Monsieur
Je ne puis voir partir Monsieur thomas†2 sans vous escrire quoy que nous soyons presentement dans un accablement terrible de malades attaquees d'une fievre epidemique double tierce. Monsieur veen a quitte la practique par un accident facheux d'une hemoptose qui le menace de phtysie. nostre Cousine trompers†3 est morte phtysique depuis trois jours. nostre pierot est malade d'une double tierce et n'est pas hors de danger. le reste de la famille se porte assez bien. esperant ainsy de vous. Monsieur Thomas a fort bien profité de son temps et sort tres bien davec ses maistres. on peut esperer quelque chose de bon luy. il vous dira quil m'est resté redevable de dix ducatons pour un college de practique quil a frequenté chez moy ce dernier hyver. il est minuict, jarrive au logis et le soupé m'attend. je m'en vay boire a vostre santé et suis, avec le dernier respect
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
GUENELLON
Endorsed by Locke: P. Guenellon 7° Nov 91 Answered 1 Jan.92

1426. William Stratton to Locke, 31 October 1691 (1419, 1427)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 67. In the date Stratton wrote the year badly; hence Locke's endorsement. That the year is 1691 is shown by the payment to Edwards and by Veale's lease.
Bristoll the Last of Octo 1691
Dear Cosin
as sone as I Received your letter†a- I was-†a with Mr: Edwards†1 and have paid him 81l:2s:5d It being the Just Ballanc of the Aaccount that we made when you was At Bathe and I have a note from Mr Edwards to pay you At his Chamber In Elive or Eline Court†2 In the middle Temple he Intends to set for London next Wednesday I intend to send the noate in a letter by his oun hand I know noe saffer way and think it best to acquaint you with it befor that soe you may send for it I suppose he will be In London by saterday at farthest If he doe not stop by the way to keepe any Court pray when you have Received the mony let me have a loyne from you of your Receipt of it which will be my satisfacktion I know not when Mr Edwards Returns or whether his Grome doeth return back suddenly If he doe he will bring John Veales lease safe to my hand I suppose I take leave
your Faithfull kinsman and humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
I doe not desire you shold send the lease by post if you doe it will cost dear for they charg me with 5d for the last letter I shold be glad to have it as spedy as may be not knowing what may fall out but I think Jo Veale is honest

1427. William Stratton to Locke, 2 November 1691 (1426, 1448)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 68-9.
Bristoll the 2th: Nov: 91
Dear Cosin
I have hear inclosed sent you my Cosin Edwards Bill for 81l:2s: 5d: which I hope will cum safe to your hands I this day saw John Veale hoe told me that John Mills denied him a way thorow one of his Grounds In to yours It is by the wayside that goeth doun to Stanton I doe not mind the name of the Ground I suppose John Mills was a littell trobled to see what a provedent neighbour he was like to have for John Veale was haleing with a plow erth out of the way into your ground the washing†1 of Belton streate, and that disturbed John Mills, he hath formerly spoken of it but I know noe othe way and I satisfied John Veale that if it wear your way I would bear him out in it as I remember the Ground cums up to the way: but there is a hollow way and I thinke noe convenient goeing into your ground and I never knew any other way then thorow his Into yours I have spoken great words about it but had rather doe soe ten times the put you to the charge and my selfe to the troble wonce to goe to lawe I take leave and remaine
your Faithfull kinsman and humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
Address: For Mr: John Locke At Mr: Pawlings In Dorset Court in Chanell row Westminster
Endorsed by Locke: W. Stratton, 2° Nov. 91
1428. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 4 November 1691 (1380, 1463)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, f. 107.
Sarum Nov 4. 91
Deare Freind
I have sent this to you to desire your advice concerneing my sonne John whom I designed for the lawe to which I find he hath no inclination but on the contrary to goe to sea and to be a seaman
― 327 ―
which if the warre were over might parhaps be the more adviseable And in truth though I am not willing to crosse his inclinations yet I must consider that his life is in 300l̷ per annum†1 and also if it prove adviseable that he follow his owne inclination I would endeavor to set him out in that way may be most advantagious which as I thinke if a now East India company be erected by act of Parliament†2 may be best to send him thither but in this case I desire to be well advised and therefore desire your opinion I am
your affectionate Freind and servant D Thomas
all my familly present their services to you My wife is now pretty well recovered of the yellow Jaundice.
†a I thinke I shalbe at London the later end of the next weeke but am not certeine.
Endorsed by Locke: D Thomas 4° Nov 91
1429. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 14 November 1691 (1409, 1447)
Amsterdam University Library. MS. R.K., Ba 256 v. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 334-6; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 202. Answers no. 1409; answered by no. 1447.
(English)
London 14° Nov.91
Vir Amplissime
Quod grandem tibi jam diu destinaveram Epistolam ideo accepisti nullam. Quæsivi vacuum aliquod mihi tempus dari ut tecum liberius et fusius colloqui possem et gratias agere pro ultimâ tuâ et amicissimâ epistolâ cui jam dudum responsum oportuit. sed nescio
― 328 ―
quam rerum etiam non mearum importunitate ita mihi omne otium sublatum est ut ne propriis quidem et domesticis negotiis vacare licuerit. Cave autem credas me publicis negotiis implicitum, nec valetudo nec vires, nec rerum agendarum imperitia id patiuntur. Et cum mecum repetem quid a tribus jam mensibus adeo impeditus egerim incantamenti instar videtur ut quisque dies secum afferret negotiorum onus aliorum ex aliis nascentium quæ nec sciens prævideram nec cupiens evitare poteram.
(English) Indicem librorum et capitum historiæ Sancti officii Domina Cudworth et ego legimus simul magna cum voluptate. Hæc prælibatio magnum excitavit in utroque integri operis desiderium, quod jam sub prælo esse cum gaudio a quodam Scoto non ita pridem ex vestra Batavia rediunte accepi.†1 Bonis cum avibus procedat opus Christiano orbi inprimis utile. Hospes mea Tyrannidi Ecclesiasticæ inimicissima sæpe mihi laudat ingenium et consilium tuum laboremque huic operi tam oportunè impensum. Creditque frustrà de Religionis reformatione et Evangelii <propagatione>†a tantum undique strepitum moveri dum Tyrannis in Ecclesia, vis in rebus religionis
― 329 ―
(uti passim mos est) aliis sub nominibus utcunque speciosis obtinet et laudatur. Quid tandem factum <est>†a cum Doctore isto Theologo qui tam mira docuit de angelis in libro suo de Spirituum existentia. Annon expertus est fratrum suorum pro religione pro veritate pro Orthodoxiâ Zelum? Mirum si impune evadat. Apud nos prælum quod video nihil pene parturit quod alieni cives scire aut legere multum desiderabunt. Ita obstrepunt undique arma ut Musarum voces vix audiantur. Imo lis†b Theologica†b jam consopita magnam in partem conquiescit, utinam cum animarum et partium concordia. Sed ea spes vana est, nec tam facile componuntur Theologorum controversiæ. Bene est si incertas aliquando ferant inducias ut mutuâ charitate sanentur penitus quis expectabit? Magnâ mihi apud te excusatione opus est ut tam diuturno ignoscas silentio. Id Tibi persuadeas velim, hoc non alicui voluntatis alienationi. non decrescenti et minus fervidæ amicitiæ tribuendum, Te ut semper maxime æstimo, amo, amplector, semperque amabo. Fac itidem ut facis et me ama Tui Studiosissimum

(Latin) London 14 Nov. 91
Excellent Sir,
That I had some time since resolved on a long letter to you is why you have received none. I have been trying to get some spare time in which I could talk with you more freely and fully and thank you for your last very [p. 328] friendly letter, which should have been answered long ago; but somehow or other the importunity of business, and of business that is not my own, has so deprived me of all leisure that I have had no spare time even for my private and domestic affairs. Do not imagine, however, that I am involved in public affairs; neither my health nor my strength nor my inexperience in the conduct of such business permit of it. And when I think of what I have been doing for the last three months amid such hindrances it seems like an enchantment, each day bringing with it a load of affairs, one arising from another, which I had neither the knowledge to foresee nor the power, had I wished, to avoid.
(Latin) Mrs. Cudworth and I have read together with great pleasure the list of the books and chapters of your account of the Holy Office. This foretaste has aroused in us both a strong desire for the complete work; I learnt with delight from a certain Scotsman on his recent return from your Netherlands†1 that it is now in the press. May this work, which is so eminently useful for the Christian world, go forward prosperously. My hostess is a determined foe to ecclesiastical tyranny; she often tells me of her admiration for your talents and purpose, and for the labour you have so opportunely expended on this work. It is in vain, she believes, that so much noise is made everywhere about the reform of religion and the spreading of the Gospel so long as tyranny in the Church—force in matters of religion—as is generally the [p. 329] custom prevails under other names however specious and is commended. What was done in the end with that doctor of theology who taught such marvellous things about angels in his book on the existence of spirits? Has he not experienced his brethren's zeal for religion, truth, and orthodoxy? It would be a marvel if he gets off unscathed. With us the press is in labour with hardly anything, so far as I can see, that people of other countries will wish to know of or to read. There is such a clatter of arms everywhere that the voices of the Muses are scarcely heard. Even theological strife is lulled asleep and for the most part ceases; would that it were with harmony of souls and parties. But that is a vain hope; nor are theologians' controversies so easily settled. It is well enough if they observe an uncertain truce from time to time; who will expect them to be perfectly cured by mutual charity? I am certainly much in need of excuses to obtain your forgiveness for such prolonged silence. I would have you be sure of this, that it is not chargeable to any withdrawal of affection or to decreasing or less warm friendship; as always I value you very highly, I love, embrace, and shall always love you. Do likewise, as you always do, and love me
Your most devoted
J. LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my best wishes to your excellent wife and children, as also to [p. 330] our friends Veen and Guenellon and the whole family. I hope you are all well and that you keep me in mind.

1430. James Tyrrell to Locke, 22 November [1691] (1424, 1461)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 105-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Nov: 22d:
Dear Sir
I hope you have re<c>eived†a all your things safe, tho' I have as yet received no account from you of it, Since my son returned from his Journey, I find he had borrowed some of your bookes; and put them in his chamber in a drawer where I could not find them, and so they were forgot to be catalogued; and allso sent you with the rest; but I have now put them all in a box together with some of his, and have sent them up to London; where as soon as he receives them; he will not fail to deliver them safe to you; I have allso sent you up the 2 first Tomes of your French Herodotus; and the last which I lent my daughter, is come as far as Oxford, but I cannot have it to send up this returne but you shall have it the next weeke; when I send up some other things to James: I desired Mr: Thomas†1 who I suppose is now in Towne to tell you the reasons why I did not send up your Manuscripts: the one was because they were not particularly mentioned; and the other because, the little hair Trunke in which I use to keep them I had lent to my daughter, who is in wales; and so wanted a fit case for them; but if you will have them I will buy such another; and either send, or bring them along with me: James had likewise borrowed your Ogiilbyes†b Japan Embassy†2

which being too big to goe in this box; shall be sent you with the Africa which my Father hath borrowed. there is allso left behind, and which I forgot to mention in my last a little old terrestrial Globe; which shall be sent you up if you please, but it hath never a fellow. all the rest of your bookes shall be safely returned you as soon as I have perused them: Mr: Thomas tells me you have given him those Physic bookes in my hands; I expect your order for the delivery of them, and then he shall have them, pray send me word what you will have done with the 2 pair of deal Cases they are in, for he says he does not desire them; and they will be empty when the bookes are taken out. I have orderd James to wait of you with this, and to follow your advice in the Course of life he is about to take; I should take it as a favour if you would recommend him to my Lord Ashleys acquaintance; I have no more but hopeing this will find you in health I remaine

1432. Locke to Robina Douglas, countess of Forfar, 29 November 1691
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 37. Draft. Robina, c. 1661-1741, a sister of Martha Lockhart; married, 1679, Archibald Douglas, 1653-1712, first earl of Forfar (Scotland) 1661: G.E.C.; D.N.B. for Forfar.
Though I have more than ordinary encouragements to write to your Ladyship yet I finde it is not without difficulty that I bring my self to it. Tis not I am sure for want of a due respect of your ranke and quality. Tis not that I doe not joyn with all the world in a just admiration and esteem of your wit and virtue.†a Nor tis not for want of a more particular inclination to doe any thing that I could flatter my self might be acceptable to your Ladyship. But Madam haveing by my good fortune got a litle share in the good opinion of a person whose judgment has the publique allowance would it not be madnesse to venture the losse of what the great and the learned would purchase at any rate only out of an unseasonable vanity which could only importune your Ladyship and hurt me. I have noe businesse to sollicit you about. I have noe good news to tell you and though I have all the good wishes for you that one can have for a person of the highest worth in herself, extreamly valued by her freinds and particularly obleigeing to me yet there are none of them but might be more respectfully made in silence without a letter. I know my owne defects in writeing which my concerne to continue your Ladyships good thoughts will but increase. I know your Ladyships quicknesse and penetration and how ill consequence it may have to put these two things togeather and yet after all your Ladyships sees I am silly enough to doe it. My Lord Farfar has been pleased more than once to tell me I must write to your Ladyship, a good commission had I but wit and Gallantry enough. Mrs Lockhart assures twill be acceptable to your Ladyship, and you know she makes me beleive what she pleases. Tis certain I have obeyd and your Ladyship has the trouble of it. But I beseech you be not revengd on me. I had noe mallice mixed with my deference, though perhaps if I might reveal†b it†b was not without some secret satisfaction in haveing once the oportunity to tell the finest lady†c in Scotland the veneration I have for her under the shelter of soe good an excuse as she her self must allow.
― 334 ―
I am extremly sorry to hear of your Ladyships sicknesse but apprehend it the lesse as being only the concomitant of a great belly†1 and I make noe doubt but that haveing now don sufficient penance for begining soe late you will every day increase in ease and strength. Whilst you are breeding you have the power to change the worth and relish of things and may without the censure of a depraved pallate prefer crabs and blackberrys to Apricots and peaches and tis noe ill manners to offer such trash to your Ladyship if you have but cast a looke towards them. Madam you see I make use of this priviledgd season and†a- venture to present you with docks and daysies upon a confiden of what my Lord and your sister assure me that your good likeing now will turne them into roses and myrtell.†b doe soe I beseech you Madam at least let your opinion joynd to my earnest wishes put virtue in them to be medicinall and that from the time You receive this paper all your languishing and indisposition may leave you. Tis in your power to doe this you have a soule able to doe any thing you will set it to and you need only raise your minde a litle-†a me thinkes I have some right to demand this of you that since I for your sake by writeing as I doe hasard being thought a†c wofull†c scribler. You for my sake by makeing your self well should gain me the reputation of an wonderfull physitian This is all that is wanting to compleat our joy here in the hopes you give
― 335 ―
us of a young Lord in a few months†a I share very particularly in it. And am

1433. Locke to Edward Clarke, 3 December [1691] (1431, 1434)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 49. Printed in Rand, pp. 319-20. Year from Clarke's endorsement.
Oates Dec. 3
Dear Sir
I came safe hither yesterday†1 where I found Master and every body well and I phansie my self a litle better already though I feele my lungs yet cruelly oppressed. Though I finde every body here in love with Master and particularly my Lady who makes account of keeping him till Mrs Clarke comes to fetch him now that Syl has told her that Madam intends to make her a visit, yet I thinke it convenient you should send for them away as soon as conveniently you can. Doe not perplex your self to finde out the reason why I have soe much changed my opinion since I parted with you. You will not guesse at it and I promise you to explain it to you hereafter. only I assure you in the mean time that the child has behaved himself very well and there is noe thing in it that will when you know it trouble you in the least. And therefor pray be sure not to Alarme Madam, but finde some reasons to satisfie her why you send for him away sooner than perhaps she understood you intended. If you can finde noe better you may tell her you hear there is company comeing sodainly hither and that they will here be streightend in room, but if you can finde other reasons of your owne it will perhaps be better. You may if you thinke fit to morrow in the evening take places for them for Monday next in London in the Bishop Startford Coach at the Pewter pot in Leadenhall street,†2 and by the
― 336 ―
same coachman send a letter to me with one inclosed to Master, directed to be left with Mr Harison at the crown in Harloe to be sent to Oates from thence by an Expresse.†1 You may also (for fear that should miscary) write by Saturdays post and inclose it in one to Mr Jocelin to tell him you have taken two places for your son and his Tutor who are at Oates in the Bishop Startford coach and desire him to speake with the master†a- of the coach-†a and let him know they shall be ready to meet the coach at Harloe on Monday next by nine of the clock and desire him to send away by an expresse the letter inclosed to me or your son.
You must present my Ladys service to Madam and excuse her that she returnes not an answer by Sir Francis now to Madams kinde letter. Sir Francis only cald here this morning in his returne but staid soe litle while that she could not possibly get any time to write by him and soe is forced to defer it till to morrow. She presents her service to you. Pray give my service to Madam and the children and be assured I am
Dear Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE
Who ever goes to take places for them at the Pewter pott must speake with the Bishop Startford coachman him self and set down their names and tell him that comeing from Oates they shall be taken up at Harloe on Monday morning. But if this be too much trouble and you have noe body you can send to morrow night to the Pewter pott who will doe it right. You may doe all as well by Mr Jocelin at Bishop Startford, who may take the places there and send word of it to me hither by the same messenger that comes expresse to bring your letter from Bishop Startford hither.

1434. Locke to Edward Clarke, 4 December [1691] (1433, 1435)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 178. Printed in Rand, pp. 320-1. Year from contents.
Oates 4 Dec
Dear Sir
I suspect I surprised you yesterday by the letter Sir Francis brought you and I fear I shall draw a quarrell on me from my Lady, who designeing to keep master here till his mother came downe (for she and every body else here are mightily pleased with the child) will certainly be very angry with me if she imagin I had any hand in his removeall soe soon. We must therefor manage the two women in this case that there be noe suspition of unkindenesse on either side and you must finde out reasons to satisfie my Lady for sending for your son as well as to satisfie Mrs Clarke. And you must take it wholy upon you as the sole cause of takeing him away soe soon Though I owne to you that I am it. And I know noe body but my self who would not be very glad to have him here much longer, And yet I hope you doe not thinke me weary of him. Rest satisfied till I see you that there is noe thing in the case that ought any way to give you the least thought. And I should not like it soe well if I did not thinke it conduced to the end you proposd when we talked togeather in the Speakers chamber.†1 Pray send the inclosed sealed when you have read it to mend your owne by†2 My Lady and every body here present their service to you. Master is very well and presents his duty. My service to your Lady my love to my wife and remember me to all my friends. I am perfectly yours
J LOCKE
1435. Locke to Edward Clarke, 7 December 1691 (1434, 1436)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 50. Printed in Rand, pp. 321-3.
Oates 7° Dec. 91
Dear Sir
Your orders concerning your son have been obeyd though to the great dissatisfaction of my Lady who is not well pleased
― 338 ―
that you have sent for him away soe soon. I have told her the reasons you writ but that does not content her, She was really pleased with the childs company and would fain have had it longer: and thinkes besides, that she haveing such obligations to you she might have presumd on you for a greater stay than this and I thinke Madam is doubly bound to make her amends.
Upon examination of your son I cannot owne that he has made all the proficiency I could have wishd or you might justly have expected. Mr Passebon himself is of the same minde. Where the fault is I cannot certainly say. Mr Passebon lays it wholy on the childs negligence and obstinacy and unconquerable aversion to him. He professes his great pains about him and indeavours to be advantageous to him, and I beleive he speaks truth. But with all he addes that it is not reasonable that you should be any longer at the charge to keep about your son a man that is not like to doe him good, and who despairs to answer the expence by a suitable successe. Though when he quits this imployment he has noe thing to subsist till he can finde an other, yet he cannot consent you should be deceived in your expectation concerning your son but advises you either to get an Englishman that speaks French who possibly may have more authority with him or else put him to your French maids brother to schoole where emulation might excite his industry. The poore man spoke this with tears in his eyes and this way of proceeding has soe much of fairnesse and ingenuity in it in his circumstances that it extreamly moved me and if I had wanted any inclination before to doe him any kindenesse it would certainly have forced it upon me. He spoke to me also to represent this soe to you that you and Mrs Clarke should not take amisse of him the giveing up the conduct of your son not being able to satisfie himself in the want of that successe which he has in vain labourd for and which has made him very uneasy. And the triall being now caried as far as he can he has given up his hopes. I undertooke to him for your favourable interpretation and acceptance of this his soe open and direct a way of dealeing with you. and for the continuation of your freindship, and I doubt not but you will be ready (as I shall always be) to doe him all the good offices you can upon any occasion. I know not what you will thinke of him for a Tutor but this I dare say you will joyn with me in thinkeing him one of the fairest men you have met with of his nation, and one that deserves best to be kindely treated and taken care of. He has spoken to me
― 339 ―
again about his Marine Manuscripts.†1 if you or J.F:†2 can help him with Churchill. Basset†3 or any other bookseller who will give him mony for them I know you will to which I will help all I can. Tis more to be wishd than hoped that Mrs Lockhart could help him to any litle place to make him subsist at Court. There is one Mr Cuningham†4 of her acquaintance who speaks French well if I mistake not, whom I have heard severall people speake very well of. I know him but not long enough to give his character but I judg him above the ordinary size. He is a Scotch man and newly returnd from travelling with a yonge Gent who as I thinke died beyond sea. I know not what he would undertake nor his rate But I am sure it is worth your enquireing after and by Mrs Lockhart I thinke you may doe it. My humble service to Madam whom I hope to see here speedily let me know when, my Love to my wife and mis Nany. I am
Dear Sir
yours
J LOCKE
I had forgot to tell you that Mr Passebon spoke very respectfully of you and Mrs Clarke and expressed a great sense of your civility to him
Every body here present their service to you and Madam.
I mentiond above Mr Passebons manuscripts but askeing of Syl what part of the roome they lay in, where my books are, that I might direct Mr Pawling where to finde them and deliver them to him he tels me he does not remember to have seen them there lately and that he remembers I bound and sealed them up and thinkes I locked them up too. if it be soe Mr Passebon must blame him self if he cannot have them till I come to town for if he had spoke to me when I was there he had then been sure of them however I have writ to Mr Pawling to looke for them among my books and if he can finde them to deliver them to you. Dear Sir
Your Kinde letter of 8th gives me litle satisfaction in the news it brings me of your toileing to noe purpose doe your endeavours cheerfully and they not being your faults vex not your self with disappointments. 1437. Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton to Locke, 13 December 1691 (1405, 1457)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 144-5. Printed in King, p. 222; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 185-6 (no. 378); a probable draft for it, ibid. iii. 184-5 (no. 377).
Cambridge. Dec. 13. 1691
Sir
When I received your former letter I was engaged here by the Term†1 and could not stirr. I thank you for putting me in mind of Charterhouse,†2 but I see nothing in it worth making a bustle for. Besides a Coach which I consider not, it's but £200 per annum with a confinement to the London air and to such a way of living as I am not in love with. Neither do I think it advisable to enter into such a competition as that would be for a better place. Dr Spencer the Dean of Ely†3 has perused the specimen of Le Clerk's latin version of the old Testament†4 and likes the designe very well but gives me no remarks upon it. Pray return my most humble service and hearty thanks to my Lady Masham for her Ladyships kind invitation and accept of mine to your self for so frankly offering the assistance of your friends if there should be occasion. Mr Green called on me last Tuesday and I designed to have answered your letter sooner and beg your pardon that I did not. I am
Your most humble servant
IS. NEWTON.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Sir Francis Masham's Baronet at Oates in Essex. To be sent from Bishop Stafford.
Endorsed by Locke: I: Newton 13 Dec. 91

1439. Edward Clarke to Locke, 15 December 1691 (1436, 1440)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 62. Printed in Rand, pp. 324-5. Answers no. 1436; answered by no. 1440.
London December the 15th. 1691.
Deare Sir,
Your letter of the 11th. with those inclosed for Mr. Pawling and Mr. Churchill came safe to mee, which I sealed and left them at theire Houses they being both abroad when I went to speake with them, And I will make use of the first opportunity I can gett to take the Note of Him which Hee Promised to give after this Edition touching the Copy etc, I have given Sir Francis one and have disposed of 4. or 5. more soe Advantagiousely in the House, That it is allready a doubt whither the Byll for Lowering the Interest of money will ever bee read a second time or not, And all that have read the Considerations are cleerely of opinion, the Arguments therein are abundantly suffitient to distroy that Byll and all future Attempts of the like Kind;†1 I heare the whole Treatise generally much approved of and Commended, for the many usefull Notions therein touching Money, Trade, and Taxing, And there have been verie particular Inquieryes to Know the Author, And I must tell you that there have been many that have shrodely guessed at Him, And some I beleive there are, who mightily commend the ingenuity of the Author, yett I beleive will hardly forgive Him for some Parts of His Booke were Hee known; And soe much for That:
Monsieur has hitherto carefully avoyded all opportunity of talkeing with mee since his Return from Oates, and has not said one Word to mee touching any discourse you had with Him in the Country about my sonn, nor hath Hee mentioned any thing of the Proposeall Hee made the Citizen of Cambridge etc; nor have I as yett thought fitt to begin any Discourse with Him upon the subject of the Childes Education, being not as yett provided with a Conveniency to dispose of Him to my satisfaction in the manner I mentioned to you before you went last out of Town; in which Resolution I shall still continue, unlesse you give mee Reason to alter my Opinion in that matter, therefore pray lett mee know
― 344 ―
what 'tis that (you say) you have to propose to mee, And therein you will lay a further obligation upon,
Your most affectionate and Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:
Pray give and take Madams and mine and all the younge folkes humble services to my Lady and your selfe, and the rest of the Good Company at Oates, And lett my Lady Know that the true reason why my Wife hath not as yett performed her Promise, is because the Girles are not yett plac'd out by reason of the Frenchwomans indisposition where they were to goe, etc:
Not a word of the Parliament etc:
Address: These, For Mr. John Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Franke: Edw: Clarke:
Postmark: DE 15
Endorsed by Locke: E. Clarke 15 Dec 91

Dear Sir

1441. Lady (Mary) Calverley to Locke, 20 December [1691] (1438, 1749)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
I dare not pretend to enter into the first part of your letter, what interpretation soever it bears, I will take it in the sence you will have me, and upon all occasions own my self the person in the world the most obliged to you, for, any favour of yours bestowed Upon so little meritt as I have, raises a debt to him that bestowes to a Huge bulk; but to our business I take the mark you have given me of your remembrance of me, as I ought to doe, and must take leave to tell you, that I desire no shorter way, than you can manage for me, nor indeed no other way, your measures are what I have preferd to those of all other men, and therefore since you give me incouragement to hope you will undertake this matter, I will consult no other man, nor prescribe any other rules to you than your own, I recommend it wholly to your care, and what you think good for me, I shall whilst I live say Amen too,
Adieu I am as in duty bound with all the respect possible
Your most obliged Humble servant
M C

1442. Locke to Edward Clarke, 27 December [1691] (1440, 1445)
Rand, pp. 327-8. Rand notes 'This letter is in fragments.' Words in square brackets are supplied by him. Year from the contents.
Oates, 27th December [1691].
Dear Sir,
<My Lord Ash>ley†a †1 is here, and returning to town again .... He mentioned to me Monsieur Soveraigne†2 as the person with
― 347 ―
whom you were like to place your son, and told me at his coming hither that you desired my opinion of it. The man I have heard well spoken of formerly, and if he will undertake the conduct of him, you know I like that way much better than a public school. If you be satisfied about the character of the man, which I suppose you may have from Mr. Popple, <who>†a as I remember I have formerly heard speak of him. Whether he go to Soveraigne or anybody else, I would be glad we might preserve as much of our method of education as could be, and at least not perplex him with grammar, much less with themes, declamations, and making of verses, but only reading and translating prose authors, beginning with those of the [easier sort, and] so proceeding to harder. This I think you would do well to discourse beforehand with the person you have under consideration, to see whether he be not superstitiously wedded to the methods he himself was educated in, for from such a man I should not expect much. And this, if he speak no English, you may do by Mr. Popple or my Lord Ashley. I shall be very glad to have him here with me some time before he [begins with his tutor]†1 to see as much as I can of his parts and temper....†b
My Lord Ashley has afforded us the honour of his company. ... I know not how Madam will answer it to my Lady, if she make not [an effort to keep] her promise. I wish her, and you, and all your flock a happy new year, and withal an increase of the advantages of this life. My service to her, and my wife, Master and Miss Nanny. I thank you for the resolution of the case I sent you, and am,
Dear Sir,
perfectly yours,
J. LOCKE.
My service to Sir Walter [Yonge] and the family, to Mr. Sov., to Mr. Popple and his, and J[ohn] F[reke]. I admire your opinion concerning the clause added by the Lords to the Bill of Treason.†2 I wish myself with you for an hour, but desire you to consider that
― 348 ―
what they propose (if I am rightly informed in it) is what is of great advantage to the Commons of England....

1443. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 31 December [1691] (1412, 1451)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 95-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London. Decem: the 31
I needed not your Letter, nor the Adventure of the Coat, nor yet so much as any farther Shew of Favour from My Lady,†1 your pretended Enemy, to have Set me a writing: You had given mee cause enough 'ere You let me goe from You; but which I perceiv'd nothing of, 'ere I got hither, and had been some time in Town. Indeed You are a Pleasant Man to talk as you doe of a Confederacy; as if there were such a One really form'd against You by Mee, in conjunction with One of the Most Powerfull Persons I know living; (If I judg by what I have found in my self) when att the same time You actually still persue what you have been doing with such Extrordinary Execution already, in a quite contrary Confederacy; I mean One against Mee, and Joyn'd even with that very Person who bears such Power. Some Ignorant Body now, and that had state-affairs much in their Head (which may sometimes happen togather wee know) might Imagine, here, that It were Armys, or Huge Provinces or Kingdomes that are meant in this Place; and that You had got on your Side, according to my way of talking, Some Mighty one of the Earthly Potentates. But they would be far out by being far short: for the Power that I mean is favourable to You, is yet more considerable then all of that Kind. It begins where Reason does, and gains the Mind first. It Extends it self whither the Power of Princes, as Princes meerly, cannot attain, and works in a Manner which that other cannot Imitate: Besides that there is there a Kind of Rule which I know not how a Man can be suppos'd to bear: for I am not able to Explain any such forcible Dominion over the heart in the Person of One of our Sex. This looks
― 349 ―
terrible against mee: But I comfort my self that this is a season of time not so very Lucky to Confederacys:†1 for It seems to bee but a very Scurvey Plannet that hangs over that mighty one on which the Eye of the world is so fix'd. Thus if I must conclude my self to be injur'd att all in one respect; I may hope to be repair'd in an other; upon this ground, that these two wondrouse Confederacys are to Stand and fall togather: but no more of that ...
Though yet, again, I am sure I have felt more from a Confederacy than that Monarch†2 that has been now so long Baited with so formidable a One: for I would fain know, besides what Countrys or Parts of his Kingdome, what Divertions or Pleasures has he lost? whether or noe he may not bee att perfect Ease and Repose for any Enemys he has, or any Shrewdness that appears amongst'em? If he has not all his Pleasures still about him, or (as they assure) Increas'd in their Number and Magnificence: and that too really without any affectation more then is naturall to that Genius:
Whilst I, here, have lost by the Bargain, for my share, as good almost as one half of all the Pleasures of a Former Life, by a moderate computation. I know not indeed how to Define precisely what It is that You have done to Mee. But I am sure of this, that in the main It ought to be reckon'd a Diskindness to anybody to put 'em out of Conceit with what us'd to be most diverting and satisfactory to em in their Particular Life. and this I owe to You. Though to say truth you never seem'd all the while to have any malice or spleen against mee; but rather so much the contrary that It appears Strang how any such thing should have been brought about by You. But You appear least to be what you are, and can disguise so well that You can describe your self sometimes as you really are and yett Blind those about you with a seeming Raillerie and a particular Tone and Accent that serves you on such occasions. Aussi, ma foy, quand vous avouez, comme pour badiner, que vous etes Sorcier et que de la mesme maniere on le dit apres vous; Je croy qu'il n'y a rien de plus vray que cela, et Je vous prens au pied de la Lettre.
Je tiens pour assuré tout ce que la Fille de Chambre a trouvé dans vôtre appartement. Ces Empoisonnements. Ces Figures et ces
― 350 ―
Instruments effroyables, et tout cet Attiraille Diabolique. Je croy que tout cela vous appartenoit et que vous vous en serviez a des telles Usages.
Je m'etois bien douté l'autre soir, comme vous sçavez, qu'a la verité j'etois Enchanté, et que Cet agreable Palais, et ces Augustes Personnages qui sembloient m'y entretenir, avec touts ces Discours merveillieux et charmants qu'on y tenoit, ces Choses Spirituelles et ces Sentences Divines que J'entendois a touts moments D'une Dame; a quoy on auroit jamais pû s'attendre; que tout cela, dis je, qui me paroissoit tel, n'etoit autre chose que les Effets ordinaires de la Magie, et que c'etoit là un Chateau Enchanté.
Si ainsi dont il en est; O sage et Puissant Enchanteur! Je vous conjure de ne me plus tenir dans vos Enchantements a present que je suis dehors de vôtre Chateau, et ne Souffrez plus que Je me vois Tyrrannizé par ce Degout que J'ay presentement pour le monde ou Je suis rentré et pour touts mes anciens Plaisirs: Ce qui ne me vient que de L'Idée imparfaite de ces Plaisirs surnaturelles que vous m'aves fait eprouvé dans ce Chateau, et qui mesme presentement que J'en suis si Eloigné me Suit Incessamment et ne me laisse jamais en repos a Jouir paisiblement de ces Divertissements du monde qui Jadis faisoient presque tout mon Bonheur, et qui à cette heure sont toujours corrompues par cette fatale Memoire qui me reste de ces Plaisirs Enchantées qui ne servent a present qu'a ternir touts les autres par leurs Eclat: ce qui m'empeche de me rejouir comme auparavant, ou d'être satisfait d'aucune Chose qui se presente. Voyez dont a quel Etat vous m'avez reduit!
In Good Earnest, though; Considering I was not to stay with Yee long; but according to your own Will and appointment was to live again in the same world afterwards; Both my Lady and You, Mee-thinks, might have deny'd your selves a little of that pleasure you take in ruining of People and Unsorting of 'em to the world, and might have <afforded>†a to have spoylt mee a little less then You have done. For I am now Just at that Pass that without Love to Mankind, and Zeal for the Publick, an Impartiallity to Truth, an Industriouse application towards the Promoting of Letters and Knowledg in the world, and without the Plain Appearance of disintressedness in these and all such Actions and Professions, I can scearce but with pain support the Presence of a Man: and without as much almost as all this; att least without an absolute
― 351 ―
freedome from Pride even in the Things that may seem most to Justifie It, without Real Vertue and Piety free from Superstition, in fine, without some Indifferent Portion att least of that same Knowledg and worth that I have lately Experienc'd in One of that other Sex; neither can I make the acquaintance of a Woman satisfactory or her Company so much as tollerable. Now, doe but Consider the world as It is, and then say if I am not in a fine Case, and If I am not likely to have A pretty Time of Itt, if this goes on. Thus You see what your Confederacy has done. and I have given you the occasion to applaud your selves for this success. and you may after this Triumph over mee att your Pleasure.
I say nothing to my Lady for fear of farther obligations to her, which Shee most unjustly has lay'd on mee beyond what I deserv'd, or Can well bear. I can onely say more that I am Yours
A ASHLEY
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 31 Dec. 91 Answered 15 Jan.

1445. Locke to Edward Clarke, 6 January 1692 (1442, 1452)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 37. Printed in Rand, pp. 328-9.
Oates 6 Jan 91
Dear Sir
I steal soe much time from a housefull of people who are keeping Christmas here today as to thank you for your kinde letter of the 2d and to tell Madam that I shall be very glad to see her here as soon as her businesse will let her as I know my Lady will be. Master also will be very welcome to her and to me you know more
― 353 ―
than upon one account because I hope it may give me an oportunity to doe you or him or both some litle service. I know you will never need any justification to me or any body else in what you doe haveing I am satisfied noe other aime than the publique good, but I mistake very much if I could not convince you that the thing in question between us and that you are against is very much soe even granting the designe to be such as it appears to you, for I aske you who are those who ever did and ever shall be aptest to fall under the prosecution of that law even in this reigne and all those we can foresee.†1 When you have resolved your self that question then doe what you thinke fit. I wish you a happy new year and am
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE
Pray send the inclosed by Tuesdays post and excuse me for giveing you the trouble
My most humble service to Madam my wife and the rest to all whom I wish a happy new year
