1446. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 10/20 January 1692 (1410, 1486)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 52-3. Passage printed in King, p. 231; the whole in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 49-50.
A Amsterdam le 20 de Janvier 1692
J'ai reçu, Monsieur, le paquet, que vous m'aviez envoié, depuis quelques semaines, avec un livre où il y a plusieurs Traitez περὶ τῆς T .†2 L'Auteur a écrit sur le papier blanc, qui est au devant du livre, son nom et sa demeure, avec quelques civilitez pour moi. Si vous le connoissez, je vous prie de me marquer ce que vous en savez. Il y a tel zelateur, pour et contre, avec qui il est dangereux d'avoir quelque commerce. J'aurai soin d'inserer dans la Dissertation sur le passage de S.J. l'addition que vous m'avez
― 354 ―
envoiée, et de traduire l'autre, pour les publier toutes deux ensemble en Latin.†1 Si je n'étois pas engagé dans un autre travail, qui demande tout mon temps, j'entreprendrois de composer, ou de traduire en Latin quantité de Dissertations Angloises, ou Françoises, ou Italiennes, sur des sujets de Literature, qui sont peu connuës, et que leur petitesse fait perdre. Je les donnerois de temps en temps au Public, comme la Bibliotheque, ou les Nouvelles de la Rep. des Lettres;†2 et je le ferois à mes dépens, parce que les Libraires sont ici si avares et de si mauvais goût, qu'ils veulent tout avoir pour rien, et méprisent les meilleures choses, lors qu'on les leur offre. Mais je suis à présent trop occupé pour cela. Il est vrai que j'ai sous la presse une Logique, une Ontologie, et une Pneumatologie.†3 J'ai dédié la premiére à feu Mr. Boyle, et j'espere que l'exemplaire que je lui en envoiois sur la fin de l'année passée lui aura été rendu avant sa maladie.†4 J'ai fait dessein, si vous ne le trouvez point mauvais, de vous dédier l'Ontologie et la Pneumatologie, où j'ai infiniment profité de vos lumiéres, comme vous le verrez, et comme je l'ai déja dit dans la Préface de ma Logique, où j'ai marqué vôtre Ouvrage, comme l'un de ceux qui m'ont le plus servi.†5 J'espere que dans quelque semaines le tout sera imprimé, et pour lors je l'envoierai à Mr. Furly, qui aura la bonté de vous le faire tenir, par la plus sûre commodité. On en trouve plus fréquemment à Roterdam qu'ici, où il faut se fier à des gens, qui sont souvent peu exacts. Je vous suis bien obligé de la bonté que vous avez pour moi, et je voudrois pouvoir vous en marquer ma reconnoissance.†6 La liberté que je demanderois n'iroit qu'à n'être point obligé à faire une confession de foi en particulier, ni à aucune espece de rétractation. Pour m'accommoder aux sentimens et aux céremonies, cela ne me feroit pas de peine, parce que ces sortes d'accommodemens doivent être regardez en gros, sans quoi on ne pourroit vivre avec personne, puis qu'il n'y a personne, dans les sentimens de qui on se
― 355 ―
trouve parfaitement. Pourvu qu'on ne soit obligé de faire aucun acte opposé à la charité et à la tolerance chrétienne cela suffit. Ainsi si j'avois une occasion d'entrer dans l'Eg. Ang. et d'y subsister honêtement, je n'en ferois pas de scrupule. Je vous ouvre, Monsieur, mon coeur là dessus, quoi que je ne fusse pas bien aise qu'on le sût, si je demeure toûjours ici. Vous connoissez les gens de ce païs. Il n'est pas besoin que j'en dise davantage. Je suis parfaitement, Monsieur, vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Londres.
Endorsed by Locke: le Clerc 20 Jan. 92
1447. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 12/22 January 1692 (1429, 1456)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 57-8. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 319-23. Answers no. 1429; answered by no. 1473.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Acceptis tuis literis non mediocriter gavisus sum, quia anxiam de tua valetudine sollicitudinem mihi exemerunt. Statueram confestim iis respondere, sed impedimento admodum molesto hactenus retentus fui. Cognata quædam mea†1 moriens me liberorum suorum tutorem designavit. Negotium hoc, quod commode declinare non potui, a studiis meis alienum, plures mihi dies abstulit. Jam scribendi opportunitatem nactus, calamum arripio, ut et me omnesque meos valere scias, et per gratiam divinam totam meam familiam hactenus a morbis et febribus admodum in patria nostra grassantibus
― 356 ―
fuisse immunem. Scotus,†1 qui tibi renuntiavit historiam Sancti Officii jam sub prælo esse, erravit. Wetstenius editionem de dië in diem differt: Causatur Diogenem Laërtium nondum in lucem exiisse; nullius autem operis novi editionem se inchoaturum antequam ille prodierit. Cum urgerem, ut semel tandem tot dilationibus finem imponeret, respondit; se circa Pascha editionem inchoaturum, et ante anni finem absoluturum firmissime promisit. Interim ego historiam meam relego; et si quid desit, suppleo; hiantia connecto, superflua reseco, ut nihil editionem a mea parte remorari possit.
(English) Doctor ille Theologus, qui de angelis paradoxa illa docuit, satis fratrum suorum pro puritate zelo experitur. In Synedrio†2 Amstelodamensi liber est condemnatus, aut, ut ipsis Synedrii verbis utar, Synedrium librum illum pronuntiavit abominabilem. Synodus Hollandiæ Borealis non tantum Synedrii sententiam approbavit; sed etiam Synedrio mandavit, ut ante primum Septembris jam elapsi diem scandalum illo libro datum efficaciter repararet: quod si intra constitutum diem non possit, mandatum dedit Classi Amstelodamensi scandalum illud efficaciter reparandi: utque majore cum autoritate Classis procedat, illi adjunxit quatuor Synodi deputatos. Jam multum sudatum est, ut Doctor hic ad
― 357 ―
palinodiam cogatur: plures sunt concepti articuli, quibus ut <subscribat>†a cupiunt: his non tantum continetur rejectio sententiæ ipsius, verum etiam approbatio omnium actorum Synedrii contra ipsum. Ille articulos illos rejecit; primo dati ipsi sunt duo menses ad deliberandum: Magistratus zelum illum Ecclesiasticum temperare conatur: sed ipse nosti, claves regni cælorum, synedrio creditas, non posse committi magistratui, nec judicium ecclesiasticum ullo modo sæculari esse obnoxium. Interim hoc effectum est, ut alterum duorum mensium ad deliberandum spatium ipsi concessum sit: ne vero sine ulla censura ecclesiastica interea vivat, breve scriptum e suggestu Ecclesiæ est prælectum, quo indicatur, processum cum Doctore ipso nondum esse ad finem perductum, ideoque rogatur Ecclesia ut duobus adhuc mensibus illius eventum exspectare velit. Durius erat conceptum decretum, sed Magistratu intercedente mitigatum est: a quibusdam etiam, Doctori illi minus adversis, pronuntiatum est voce adeo submissa, ut vix audiri potuerit. Hæc dilatio ipsi per Amstelodamenses est procurata; Classis enim sententiam pronuntiare voluit. Multi credunt Amstelodamenses jam esse mitiores, quoniam metuunt, ne, si hic exauctoretur, illis denegetur facultas alium in ipsius locum vocandi:
― 358 ―
Ne ergo ministerium ipsorum aliquo onere gravetur, hunc creduntur retinere malle, quam illius exauctorati vices supplere. De quo tamen certi nihil affirmare possum. Nunc alterum deliberandi spatium elapsum est, et propediem exspectatur, quid Classis decretura sit: Illa ubi sententiam pronuntiaverit, quæ tantum interlocutoria est, Synodus Hollandiæ borealis, quæ proxima æstate conveniet, sententiam decretoriam pronuntiatura est. Interea plures adversus illum calamum stringunt; quidam admodum imperite et infeliciter; alii felicius paulum: Verum, quod mireris, nec ipse in toto suo tractatu, nec ullus eorum qui ipsum impugnant, hactenus controversiæ statum rite formarunt; ideoque tota hæc disputatio satis est confusa. Prostat libellus Anglicus, titulo, Doctrina dæmonum probata quod sit magna illa apostasia horum ultimorum temporum: scripta ab N. Orchard ministro in Nova Anglia:†1 illius sententiam noster sequitur, variisque pugnat argumentis ex illo libello depromptis: Sed et alia plura habet de dæmonibus. Negari nequit, multa a Doctore hoc valde imprudenter esse asserta, quæ profanis hominibus Scripturæ historias aliquot cavillandi præbent occasionem;
― 359 ―
quæ tamen salva ipsius sententia abesse potuissent: ipsum etiam absque ulla necessitate quædam obiter dicere, quæ ipsis suspicionem præbent heterodoxias, et quidem ejusmodi in capitibus, quæ si quis vel leviter tangat hæretici infame nomen evadere nequit. Verum de hoc negotio hactenus. Noster D. de Cene†1 hæret Londini: aliquam in Anglia sibi promotionem sperat. Doleo viri illius vicem. Commendatitias ipsi dedi ad Reverendum Episcopum Bathensem et Wellensem nuper electum,†2 qui amicissime mihi rescripsit. Ostendit se in Epistola pacis ecclesiasticæ quam maxime studiosum. Venius noster rus concessit habitatum, valetudine ejus id flagitante: aliquoties sanguinem evomuit; corpus ejus continuas illas fatigationes non fert: Quare rure degit in otio, aut potius, in studiis, sed molesto illo Medicinæ praxeos exercitio non fatigatur. Habes jam epistolam prolixiorem, cui malo brevi epistolio respondeas, quam longam meditando nullam mihi mittas. Salveat plurimum D.Cudwortha, cui indicem librorum et capitum historiæ Sancti Officii probari gaudeo. Spero integram historiam, ubi prodierit, non displicituram. Fortassis jam sedatioribus animis excipientur, quæ in hoc tractatu, qui unice Pontificiis oppositus videtur, de persecutionibus ob
― 360 ―
religionem a me dicentur; quæ, si vel paucula quædam de Reformatis immiscerem, primo statim aspectu a zelotis rejicerentur. Plerumque enim sua vitia in aliis taxari minus gravate ferunt homines: et fortasse quidam meliora docebuntur.†1 Vale Vir Amplissime. Salutat Te Venius, Guenellonus, uxor mea ac liberi: imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 22 Januarii

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I was more than delighted to get your letter, which has relieved me of the great anxiety I felt about your health. I had decided to answer it forthwith, but was kept back until now by a very troublesome obstacle. A certain kinswoman of mine†1 on her death-bed appointed me guardian of her children. This business, which I could not well decline, though it is foreign to my proper pursuits, has deprived me of many days. Now that I have an opportunity of writing I seize my pen to let you know that I and all mine are well, and that by the grace of God my whole family has so far been free from the [p. 356] illnesses and fevers that are raging in our country. The Scot†1 who reported to you that my account of the Holy Office is now in the press was mistaken. Wetstein puts off the publication from day to day; he gives as his excuse that Diogenes Laërtius has not yet seen the light, and he will start the publication of no new work until that comes out. When I pressed him to put an end once for all to so many postponements he replied that he would start the publication about Easter and promised me firmly that he would complete it before the end of the year. Meanwhile I am reading my account again; and I am supplying anything that is lacking, connecting the disunited, and cutting off the superfluous.
(Latin) The doctor of theology who taught those paradoxes about angels is experiencing enough of his brethrens' zeal for purity. The book was condemned in the Consistory†2 of Amsterdam, or, to use its own words, the Consistory pronounced the book abominable. The Synod of North Holland not only approved the opinion of the Consistory but also instructed the Consistory effectually to repair the scandal given by that book before the first day of last September; and in case the Consistory should be unable to do this by the appointed day, it instructed the Presbytery of Amsterdam effectually to repair that scandal; and, in order that the Presbytery might proceed with greater authority, it added four deputies of the Synod to that body. Great efforts have already been made to force the doctor to a recantation; [p. 357] a number of articles have been drawn up to which they desire him to subscribe; these include not only rejection of his opinions but also approval of all the proceedings of the Consistory against him. He has rejected these articles; at first two months were given him for consideration; the magistracy is trying to moderate all this ecclesiastical zeal; but you know yourself that the keys of the kingdom of heaven, which have been entrusted to the Consistory, cannot be committed to the magistracy, nor is the judgement of the church in any way subject to the secular power. Meanwhile this much has been effected, that a further period of two months has been allowed him for consideration; in order, however, that he may not live in the interim without any ecclesiastical censure, a short document has been read from the pulpit, in which notice is given that the proceeding relating to the doctor has not yet been brought to an end, and the church is therefore asked to be willing to wait another two months for the result of it. The decree was originally drawn up in harsher terms, but has been mitigated on the intercession of the magistracy; by some, too, who are less opposed to the doctor it has been read in such a low voice that it could hardly be heard. This postponement was procured for him by the Amsterdammers; for the Presbytery wanted to pronounce sentence. Many believe that the Amsterdammers are now calmer because they fear that if he is discharged they may be denied the power to invite another to fill his place; so, lest their ministry be burdened [p. 358] in any way, it is believed that they prefer to retain this man rather than to fill his place if he is discharged. About that, however, I can say nothing for certain. The second period for consideration has now run out, and what the decree of the Presbytery will be is expected shortly. When that body has pronounced its sentence, which is only interlocutory, the Synod of North Holland, which will meet next summer, will pronounce the decisive sentence. Meanwhile a number of men are taking up the pen against him; some of them unskilfully and ineffectively, others rather more effectively; but so far, what you will wonder at, neither he himself in the whole course of his treatise nor any of those who are attacking him have properly formulated the point at issue in the controversy, and the whole disputation is therefore utterly confused. There is an English pamphlet on sale entitled 'The doctrine of daemons proved to be that great apostasy of these last times', written by 'N. Orchard, minister in New England';†1 our man follows his opinions and contends with various arguments taken from that pamphlet, though he has much else to say about daemons. It cannot be denied that many of this doctor's assertions are exceedingly imprudent, as giving an opportunity to profane men for finding fault with sundry narratives in Scripture, although he might have omitted such statements without prejudice to his own [p. 359] opinion. Quite needlessly, too, he makes certain casual remarks which by themselves arouse suspicion of his heterodoxy, and these indeed on points of a kind on which no one can touch even lightly and escape the infamous name of heretic. But enough of this business. Our friend Mr. de Cene†1 is staying on in London; he is hoping to obtain some advancement in England. I feel sorry for the man. I gave him a letter of introduction to the recently elected reverend bishop of Bath and Wells,†2 who sent me a most friendly reply. He showed himself in his letter to be deeply concerned for peace in the church. Our friend Veen has gone to live in the country, as his health demands it; he has vomited blood several times, and his system does not tolerate those continuous fatigues of his; so he is living in the country in leisure, or rather in his studies, without being fatigued by the troublesome work of medical practice. You have now a rather lengthy letter, which I should prefer you to answer with a short one rather than to send me none while meditating a long one. Give my best wishes to Mrs. Cudworth; I am glad that she approves of the list of the books and chapters in the account of the Holy Office. I hope that the entire account, when it appears, will not displease her. The remarks I shall make on religious persecution in this treatise, which is apparently directed solely against Romanists, will now [p. 360] perhaps be received with calmer spirits; though if I were to intermingle with them even the scantiest allusions to the Reformed they would be rejected at first sight by the zealots. People are usually less offended at seeing their own faults censured in others; and perhaps some of them will be taught better things.†1 Good-bye, excellent Sir; greetings from Veen, Guenellon, and my wife and children, and especially from myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 22 January
1692

1449. Dr. Louis(?) Paul to Locke, 15 January 1692 (2991)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 206-7. Probably forwarded by Lord Ashley with no. 1451. The statements in that letter about Maurice Ashley and Denoun show that the year in Paul's date is new style.
The writer is probably the physician at Montpellier mentioned by Locke in his Journal (1677, p. 60) and by William Charleton in nos. 526, etc. A Louis Paul, M.D., an alien, was elected F.R.S. about 1692; he continued as a fellow until 1707, but then disappeared from the lists. He is probably the Dr. L. Paul who witnessed William Popple's will in 1698: William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser. xxiv (1967), 208, 213. Lewis Paul, the inventor (D.N.B.), was probably a son.
London January the 15th 1692
Sir
My lord Ashly expresseth a great kindness to Mr Denoune†1 his brothers†2 tutor, who indeed deserves it much, when he desires your advice for him, and his lordship lays no smaller obligation on me, by giving me an occasion, to converse and thereby to improve my self, with you. Mr Denoun's case is laid downe in a letter of his I send you, but there are wanting severall circumstances, perhaps necessary enough, which I suppose he hath omitted because he thought I should remember them.
he was taken in juin at Vevay with a double tertian ague, which soon brought him low, made him light headed, and his friends afrayd for his life. they had not been able to persuade him to take Jesuits Powder, till at last brought down by the violence of the distemper, he could not resist. The remedy had it's effect; but not
― 363 ―
so full as if it had been taken sooner, and as some are deaf after such distempers, he had a fluxion and a weakness left in his eye to which indeed he had a disposition before. that indisposition hath proved so stubborn, that hitherto it hath not seemed to yeeld to any remedye. Indeed a journey he took immediately after his recovery, in the midle of the summer, as farr as fideris in the grisons,†1 was not very proper for it. there he took the minerall waters for which that place is famous; by which and some other remedyes his intermitting feaver been stirred, he took Jesuits Powder to appease it and to enable himself to performe his journey through Germany. Then I met him and his company at Lindau and went along with him to Roterdam. he bore the journey pretty well, but his eyes grew rather worse then better. There after a sufficient refreshment I advised him to some few generall remedyes and to a†a blistering†a plaster, not omitting the kin. kin.†2 to hinder the return of his feaver. but this taking no effect I advised him to a purging electuary of Steel, in order to make his blood more lively, even, and free from some matters, that make it apt to cause obstructions and fluxions, particularly after feavers. and for feare this remedyes working should increase the fluxion for the present I advised him to intermix bathing at home, which of it self proves often a good remedy for the eyes. I do'nt know how exactly this hath been done for I did not stay at Roterdam. but Mr Denoune hath recieved no benefit by it, nor by some collyrium's he hath used. At last I advised him to endeavour to root out the distemper with some good antimoniall vomit, which often conquers the stubborn remainings of intermittent feavers and severall distempers of the head. but his present condition, of which you see the account hath hindered him to use it. Althoug I beleeve his loosiness is bad enough. yet his pulse full and slow shows him at least to be free from feaver, and makes me suspect it to be such a disorder as happens often to scorbuticall or melancholick people as he is made by his distemper, more than he was before. But <if>†b he's present condition does not suffer him to make use of vomits. I do'nt know whither you will think fit he should take some tincture <of>†c Rhubarb and some bitter decoction to improve his digestion, and besides hinder the production of raw humours, that are fit to entertain his indisposition in
― 364 ―
the eye which might at last turn to a gutta serena, as he feares it, for he sees but litle with his cleare eye. Jesuits powder may do him also good, for I remember he took it, and cured himself by it upon the journey of a stubborn loosiness. After he hath got some strenght he may trye if you thinke it proper whither a seto.†1 will do him as much good as it hath done to many others. but I refer all to your prudence. It is supported by so vast a knowledge, and so great an exactness of judgement, that I ought at all times to submitt myself to it. My lord Ashley hath a mind to persuade him to come over and here he may be encouraged to do things better, for his indisposition maketh him Lazy, and his being a physitian lessens his faith for remedyes. I durst not have given you so much trouble, although I know your kindness is very great if I had not been countenanced by his lordship. but although I have spoke so long for others I must say one word for myself and desire of you the favour to let me have still a share in your friendship, and to be persuaded, as you may easily be, of the great value I have for you and to beleeve I am truely
Sir
Your most obedient and humble servant
PAUL
Sir I send you Mr Denounes one relation where you see that not only his eye, but part of his head is affected, even inwardly, and that makes me inclined, to use besides inward medicines some owtward remedy that evacuats from near the part affected as the seto. or the percing of the ears or some issue even in the head.
Address: For Mr Lock

I write to you in a Cover, purposely that You may assure I mean not this as a Letter or give itt to You for such; therefore I could find in my heart to take no notice att all that I had receiv'd any letter from you, as I did a Post agoe.

Dear Sir
I am always best pleased when my freinds recover from any inconvenience in their health without the use of my prescriptions. Monsieur Sibelius m'en donnoit l'occasion, estant sur son depart pour vous aller trouver. c'est sans doubte un fort grand bonheur pour luy dans le dessein quil a formé de vous avoir pour amis et ainsy Monsieur il a lieu aussi bien que nous de prier pour vostre longue vie et prosperité et mon fils pierot contant desja la dessus se forme le project de vous aller

(English) Humanissime Vir
diu est quod nullas ad te dedi literas præcipue materiæ defectu, cujus quidem ne nunc quidem copia suppetit, suasit tamen amica tua, quam per Guenellonium aliosque accepi, salutatio, ut vicissim tibi solvam reddamque meam, gratiasque agam, quod meæ valetudinis conscius invitas, ut ibi tecum aqua nescio qua, medicata, cæloque et aere fruar. credo equidem illa multum mihi profutura, sed cum hoc vix possit in mea ætate, jam omnino sponte mea exemplum tuum consiliumque sequtus fui. Nam cum nunc retro aliquot tempus per brevia intervalla infestaret me <hæmoptysis>,†a videremque ex maiori corporis motu illam continuo renovari, tum et mihi tædio esset magis magisque praxis molestia, illam ilico reliqui, deseruique hanc urbem, meque rus suscepi, prope villam quam Velsen†1 vocant, non longe a pago Beverwÿck ultra Harlemum duas circiter horas. ibi ego domum inhabito satis commodam, et hortum colo egregium, ubi et multi alii æstate se recipiunt, qui hic operam meam adhibere solent, ita ut inter illa otia nonnumquam
― 371 ―
sint negotia, ut minus frequentia ita etiam minus incommoda. id autem in hoc meo morbo solatio fuit aut saltim ita mihi blandiebar, sanguinem, quem levissima tussi reddebam rutilum et salsum, non ex profundo pectoris vel ipsis pulmonibus provenire. remedia, medicorum more, fuere paucissima: purgavi aliquando corpus leviter: utebar aliquo <tempore>†a decocto rad: consolid. majore cum syr. lymph: fern: et sæpe sæpius Narcotico vestro, cujus mihi adhuc parum restabat, quod profuit eo magis, quod creberrime noctes totas haberem insomnes, tum præterea molestissimus mei erat non tam quidem dolor dicendus, quam molestia, et tædiosa titillatio in cruribus nonunquam et in brachiis, quæ me sive vigilantem sive dormientem convulsivis quasi motibus non patiebatur membra habere quieta, præsertim cum ad focum vel in lecto calerem, qui dolor si gravior esset, nondum enim desiit, non possum non vocare <rheumatismum>†b , qui nunc tantum rheumatica affectio meretur dici, quamquam satis incommodus sit. Vespertinis horis sæpe sumpsi emulsiones cum diacod: aliquando solum illum syrupum: diætam quod attinet, vix in potestate mea est quin aliquando peccem: a vino abstinere possum, non ita ab omni cibo minus convenienti†c cum appetitus constet. ad aquas spadanas accederem instanti æstate, si non obstaret bellum, in earum defectu videbo num ruri
― 372 ―
serum caprillum, quod in propria villa habeo, prosit: nisi aliter suadeat tua perspicacitas. hæc non potui non apud te referre præstantissime Vir de Valetudinis meæ statu defectuoso; cum et miseriæ solamen aliquod videtur quærelas in amici gremium infundere. precor Deum ut sospitem te servet diu, meque consolari velit, qui nunc altera solatii mei parte, uxore dilectissima, destituor.
(English) Vale Vir et Amice integerrime et amare persevera
Tuum EGB. VEEN.
(English) Quæso, præstantissime Domine, si quæ præter jam diu edita Domini Sydenhami, <prostent>†a participem me facere non graveris, præsertim si quædam reliquerit de morbis chronicis. <profecto>†b illa quæ de podagra et imprimis de hydrope scripsit.†1 talia sunt ut doleam me non prius illa legisse. sequutus omnino sum methodum illam suam cum ægrorum commodo. quæ de morbis epidemicis tradidit, exceptis illis de variolis, non sunt nisi viris exactioris indaginis et ingenii.
(English) Dabam Amstelodami primo februarii 1692.
(Latin) Most kind Sir,
I have not written to you for some time, chiefly for the want of anything to write about, and not even now is there very much; however, your friendly greeting, which I have received through Guenellon and others, has moved me in turn to pay you and return you mine, and to thank you for the invitation that you, knowing the state of my health, give me to enjoy there with you some medicinal water, I do not know what, and the climate and air. I believe that this would be very good for me, but as it is hardly possible at my age I have, entirely of my own accord, followed your example and advice. I have now for some time past been afflicted at short intervals by spitting of blood, and have noticed that this recurred immediately after any considerable bodily movement; at the same time, too, the worry of my practice was becoming more and more irksome; accordingly I gave up the latter there and then, and left this city and betook myself to the country, near the village they call Velsen,†1 not far from the district of Beverwijk, about two hours beyond Haarlem. There I live in a suitable enough house and cultivate an excellent garden; many other people too come to stay there in the summer; they are in the habit of availing themselves of my services while there, so that that repose is sometimes interrupted by business affairs, which as they [p. 371] occur less frequently so are also less troublesome. As for that ailment of mine, there was one consoling thing about it, or so at least I flattered myself, that the blood which I brought up red and saltish with the slightest cough did not come from deep down in my chest or from the lungs themselves. My remedies, as is the way with doctors, were very few; I sometimes took a mild purgative; for a time I used a decoction of rad. consolid. majore cum syr. lymph. fern., and I frequently took a dose of your narcotic, of which I still had a little left; this did me all the more good as I very often had whole nights without sleep. Besides this my greatest trouble was what could not be called a pain so much as an annoyance, a tiresome tickling in the legs and sometimes too in the arms, which, as if by convulsive movements, did not allow me, whether awake or asleep, to keep my limbs still, especially when I got warm at a fire or in bed. If this pain were to become more severe, for it has not ceased yet, I should be bound to call it a rheumatism, though now it only deserves to be called a rheumatic affection, troublesome enough as it is. In the evenings I often took emulsions with diacodium, and sometimes that syrup by itself. As to my diet, it is hardly in my power to avoid making occasional mistakes; I am able to keep off wine, but not so easily to avoid all unsuitable food when I have a good appetite. I would have gone to the waters at Spa this summer if the war had not stood in the way; in default of them [p. 372] I shall see whether goat's whey, which I have at my own house in the country, may do me any good, unless your discernment should advise otherwise. I could not help telling you all this, excellent Sir, about the poor state of my health, since it seems to be some comfort in one's misery to confide one's complaints to a friend's bosom. I pray that God may long preserve you safe and sound, and that He may grant me some consolation, now that I am deprived of that other part of my solace, my most beloved wife.
(Latin) Good-bye, dear Sir and most constant friend, and continue to love
Your EGB. VEEN.
(Latin) If there are any works of Mr. Sydenham on sale apart from those long since published I beg you, excellent Sir, if it will not trouble you, to let me know about them, especially if he has left anything on chronic ailments, certainly anything he has written about gout and especially about dropsy.†1 They are so good that I am sorry I had not read them before. I have followed that method of his exactly with benefit to my patients. His remarks on epidemic diseases, except those on smallpox, are only for exact and intelligent investigators.
(Latin) Amsterdam 1 February 1692.

1455. Edward Clarke to Locke, 23 January 1692 (1452, 1458)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 63. Printed in Rand, pp. 330-1. Answered by no. 1458.
London January the 23th. 1691.
Deare Sir
The inclosed was publiquely Delivered in the Court of Requests,†1 by which you may see to what height that Businesse is carryed, But nothing is suffitient to make some men Wise; For News I can only tell you That the Reasons of my Lord Marleborow's being turn'd out of All are not yett publiquely Known, but the generall Discourse is of a Cock-Pitt-Designe, a little time will I presume discover the secrett, and Experience will convince that there ought to bee noe Medium between Turning Him out and putting Him in the Tower.†2
This day the Byll for Reduceing the Interest of money to 5l. per Cent. Passed the House of Commons; severall Attempts wee had upon the first, second and third Reading of the Byll, to have thrown it out, wherein all imaginable Reasons were used to that End, In which Debates, I was not a little pleas'd, to heare all the Arguments used, that are contain'd in the Considerations upon Lowering the Interest of money, whereby 'twas manifest to mee that the Greatest and best men in our House were obleiged to that Treatise for all the Arguments they used in those Debates, But I am satisfied if an Angell from Heaven had mannaged the Debate, the Votes would have been the same as now, For 'tis not Reason but a supposed Benifit to the Borrower that hath Passed the Byll, and I beleive 'tis that will carry it through the House of Lords likewise;†3 I wish wee may have better successe upon the Byll of Coynage,†4 and soe I Rest,
Your most truly affectionate and Faithfull Servant:
― 374 ―
Madam is Well and soe are the Children, and they all Joyne with mee in theire hearty services to my Lady and your selfe and all the rest of the Good Family at Oates etc.

1456. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 23 January/2 February 1692 (1447, 1473)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 59-60. Probably carried by Dr. Sibelius. Answered by no. 1504.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Amicus tuus D.Caspar Sibelius hinc in Angliam discedens se harum latorem mihi obtulit. Gratulor mihi hanc ad Te scribendi oblatam occasionem. In postremis meis de Doctore illo Theologiæ scripsi. Post missas meas literas in negotio ejus a Classe pronuntiatum est. Ipse scriptum tradidit Classi, in quo plurima scripti sui revocat; solummodo cupit in sententia illa tolerari, qua statuit, diabolum homines non tentare ad peccandum, sed hominem propria concupiscentia ad peccatum seduci: quam tamen sententiam promittit se nec scriptis, nec in concionibus propugnaturum. Classis illi declarationi hactenus acquievisse videtur, ut non exautorandum censeat: interim Ecclesiæ libri illius editione scandalum datum est, quod reparari oportet: quare decem hebdomadibus eum a muneris sui exercitio suspendit. Quid decem illis
― 375 ―
hebdomadibus elapsis futurum sit, et utrum Synodus Hollandiæ Borealis, proxime æstate convocanda, acquietura sit, tempus docebit. Omnes nos bene valere, et hactenus a morbis fuisse immunes, me tibi in proximis scripsisse credo. Sed D.Advocatus van den Ende†1 periculosissime ægrotavit, et quasi ex orci faucibus ereptus est. Doleo tibi sanitatem aliquamdiu fuisse minus confirmatam: gaudeo autem balneorum usu illam tibi restitutam.†2 Quid si terras nostras revisas, quarum aër tibi minime fuit incommodus. Hæc paucis: assidet enim mihi scribenti D.Sibelius, qui coram, si quæ desint, Tibi referre poterit. Vale Vir Amplissime, et me, ut facis, ama. Salutant te uxor mea ac liberi. Plurimam rogo D.Cudworthæ a me dicas salutem.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 2 Februarii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Your friend Dr. Caspar Sibelius, who is leaving here for England, has offered to carry this letter for me. I congratulate myself on getting this opportunity of writing to you. I wrote to you in my last about that doctor of theology. After my letter was sent a pronouncement was made by the Presbytery in his affair. He himself has delivered a document to the Presbytery in which he withdraws most of the points in his book; he only desires that he may be suffered to hold his opinion in affirming that the devil does not tempt men to sin, but that man is led into sin by his own concupiscence; but he promises that he will maintain this opinion neither in writing nor in preaching. The Presbytery seems to have been so far satisfied with this declaration as not to think that he should be discharged; meanwhile by the publication of that book scandal has been given to the Church, and that must be repaired; it therefore suspends him from the exercise of his office for ten weeks. What [p. 375] will happen at the end of those ten weeks, and whether the Synod of North Holland, due to assemble next in the summer, will be satisfied, time will show. I think I wrote to you in my last that we all are well and have so far been free from illnesses. But the advocate Mr. van den Ende†1 has been dangerously ill, and has been snatched as it were from the jaws of death. I am sorry that your health was uncertain for some time; and am glad that it has been restored by the use of baths.†2 What if you were to revisit our country, whose air was not at all injurious to you? This is a short letter; for Dr. Sibelius is sitting by me while I write, and he will be able to tell you anything that is omitted when he sees you. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me. My wife and children send you their greetings. Please give my best wishes to Mrs. Cudworth.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 2 February
1692

1458. Locke to Edward Clarke, 27 January 1692 (1455, 1460)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 55. Printed in Rand, pp. 331-2. Locke's year in the date is shown to be new style by Clarke's endorsement and by the contents of the letter. Carried by Sir Francis Masham: no. 1460. Answers no. 1455.
Oates 27 Jan 92
Dear Sir
Whether the supposd soon riseing of the Parliament with this present sharp weather or any other reason hath changed that resolution, I have reason to conclude the London Journey†1 is quite off for this time Soe that now there is noe manner of hindrance to Madams purpose on this side nor pretence for not keeping her promise. But of this as I cautiond you in my last pray take noe notice to any body. The printed paper you sent me inclosed in yours of 23d vexes me cruelly I meane the whole businesse. I always saw inconvenience in it, and did what I could pray send me word what is like to come of it and present my most humble service on all occasions. Though I felt benefit from the fresh air as soon as I came into it, yet the impressions were made on my lungs when last in town stuck soe hard that I got them off but very slowly and tis but lately that I am got quite free of them. Perhaps I agree with you in thinkeing there ought to be noe medium between the two things you mention. but yet you must needs approve constancy to a methode all of a peice. I cannot (you may imagin) be displeased with what you say about the debates concerning the bill of Interest. Sir Charles Herbord†2 once made a motion in the house, that all who wore Peruks should pay for it in the tax. but after haveing sate still a litle he rose again and told the Speaker he recald that motion, because casting his eye about the house he saw there were more members wore Peruks then there were that did not. But what if those who expect a benefit should finde themselves mistaken! Sure there can be no such mistaken interest for the bill of coynage
I am
Dear Sir
your most faithfull servant
J LOCKE

Honoured Sir

1461. James Tyrrell to Locke, 30 January [1692] (1430, 1464)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 107-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London: Jan: 30
Dear Sir
As soon as I came hither I desired Mr: Pawling to write to you, and Sir Fr: Massam to tell you that I was in Towne, and should be glad to see you here for a few dayes; if your health and occasions would give you leave, since I had brought up all your Manuscript†a bookes, and besides the happynesse of seeing you desired to deliver them into your owne hands; I doubt whether they deliverd my message fairly to you since you answere nothing positively to my request, nor yet have bin informed what it is I have brought up of yours: and therefore now tell you againe that besides your Manuscripts†b I have allso brought 1. or 2 little bookes relateing to Divinity, one of which being at Shotover was forgot to be catalogued: I desire your orders as to these bookes whether you will have them sent you downe immediatly to Oates, or els put in a small box, and sent to Mr: Pawleings, which you command shall be observed; if you cannot come up to receive them your self. and now I must tell you the truth, why I did not send you up your Manuscripts†b with the rest of your bookes: in the first place all the boxes and Trunk were full, and I could put no more into them; and the little hair trunke in which I used to keep them I had lent my daughter into wales; but indeed I was loath to send them up in a box by themselves for fear they might be lost: and I know the value you have for them: and therefore resolved to deferre it till I came my self. but since it seems you have forgot what I writ to you when I sent you up your bookes etc. concerning what things are
― 381 ―
still in my hands:†1 the trouble will not be great to repeat it, since you desire it of me. first I have your 2, Carpets; or all three if you please to accept of them: since you know I offred it you once already since I came over,†2 and doe now againe if you please to accept of it; since I have no need of it, and therefore I hope you will not thinke that what I writ you in Jest (perhaps impertinently) concerneing what my man and maid sayed about them: was out of designe to screw them out of you: I hope you have never found me so mean spirited as to goe about to aske any thing of you more then what you pleased freely to offer: and therefore to tell you the true reason why the Carpets were not sent with the rest of you things, it was because my daughter hath your†a key locke<d>†b up in her Cabinet of the box in which I intended to send them, and I was loath to spoyle the Lock by breakeing it open; and therefore I thought since you stood in no present need of them whilst you lye in Lodgings that they might be sent you up as well another time, when I could get the Key from her, which will be at spring when she returns out of wales; but if you desire them sooner I will write to her againe (as I have done once already) to send her Key up that I may command that of your box in which there is now nothing of yours. besides your Carpets I have an old terrestrial Globe of yours; which would not well goe into the Trunke; and so is left to come up them: as allso the Barometer; which is now at Shotover; and to which I have added 2 pounds of new quicksilver of my owne; the old being growne so fowle, that it would not stir; but I shall not consider that since I am much more obliged to you: then that small matter comes to: as for the rest of your Cases for bookes. I am sorry that I could not send you them up all, for the truth is 2 pair of them were then at Shotover, with some bookes of mine; and I could not prevayle with the Carter to goe out of the way, and take them up as they went to Oxford with the rest of the things: but I will send them up with the rest of your bookes whenever you please to order them; for I have now†c them brought back to Okeley. as for bookes not medicinal James had in his keeping unknowne to me Oglebyes Japan;†3 and my Father had borrowed Africa of the same Authours†4 but they shall both be sent you with the boxes; and
― 382 ―
Carpets: and now with the note of bookes I sent you as borrowed of you, I have truely told you all the things that I have of yours; and I hope you will thinke them as safe as they have bin for these 7 years last past: and tho it is true my dear wife is dead to my great losse; as well your regret; yet I hope you shall never find any want of that kindnesse; and truth in Him that survives her, and whom you have formerly beleived to be your faithfull freind, and servant.
J TYRRELL
Since perhaps I shall not be so happy as to see you whilst I am in Towne: I shall give you some account of my small Family. James is at present at Shotover, as being not returned since he went downe at Christmasse. I have bin trieing to buy an Imployment for him, but cannot yet find one to my mind. I thanke you for your kind thoughts towards him, upon what ever considerations you are pleased to retaine them, and wish he may deserve your Freindship, as for Thom: he is now growne a lusty Lad; and I have bin advised by my Father; and brother the Capt:†1 to put him to Sea, neither his Inclinations nor Genius being for learneing (as I desired:) so I have followed their advice; and have brought him up along with me, and have bound him to one Capt. Dorrell an honest stout man; and a good sea man, who is goeing to the East Indyes Commander of the Berkeley Castle; upon the Companyes account.†2 he is to teach him navigation; and Merchants accounts; I thought this a better way then to bind him to some shop trade in which none of our Family ever succeeded; and for a Merchant I have neither money to give with him at present; nor stock sufficient for his seting up when out of his Time: the poor boy is very willing to goe, and stayes onely for a change of weather; and in the meane time; desires to present his humbl<e>†a service to you, and Love to Sylvester: which <I als>o†a doe.
I suppose D. Thomas is come to Towne for he hath bin expected all this weeke, but I have not seen Mr. Clarke these 3 dayes and
― 383 ―
therefore can not certainly tell. I lye at the signe of the blew perriwig in Catherine street.†1
I shall stay in Towne about a fortnight longer, I am sorry this place agrees no better with your Lungs.

1464. James Tyrrell to Locke, 13 February [1692] (1461, 1477)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 110-12 (f. 112 is an enclosure). Year from Locke's endorsement.
Feb: 13.
Dear Sir
I have received yours, and in obedience to your commands have sent all your Manuscript†a bookes in a little box to Mr: Pawlings: except one viz. your fowle copy of your late Treatise of humane undertstanding:†1 which being too big to goe into it I have tyed it on to the Top; yet so seald up†b- that no-†b body can looke into it: I am sorry the want of your boxes proved so great a trouble to you: but to attone for that fault I will send the rest of your things to Oxford at my owne charge; and then that of their carriage to London by water will not be. I hope I may have the Key of your box by that time I come downe and then you shall have the rest of your things sent up as soon as the weather and wayes will permit: I have here sent you a bill from John Clarke of what the cordage: and Carriage of your bookes etc. cost; which I hope you will not thinke too much. I have allso here sent you a note of what bookes I had of you whilst you were in Holland, which will more then ballance this small account. they are these: Crellius Christian Ethics.†2 Capellus s notes on the new Testament†3 Witssii Ægyptiaca contra Johan. Marsham:†4 all in 4°. bound in vellum.†c Clarks letters against Pere Simons histoire Critique 2. vol: smal. octav: 1. bound the other not: more in sheets.†5 Jonass Historia Islandiæ. unbound†6 Pere Simons Reply to Clarks letters. 4°.†7 I have either lost or
― 386 ―
mislayed the letter where the price of them was set downe: therefore pray see if you have it not in some notes of yours: when you have done this and will likewise tell me whether the money I layed out upon Dr: Sladus funeral shall goe for the interest of your 31l: I had in my hands; or whether it shall goe towards the discharge of the 10l: I owe you upon a†a note of my hand; I shall know what I am more to pay you; all which if you please I will discharge before midsummer. since even reckonings make long Freindships;†1 and for the continuance of which I hope there shall never be wanting on the part of
Your faithfull and humble servant
J TYRRELL.
I am sorry I cannot be so happy as to see you whilst I am here, yet I hope I may hear from you againe whilst I stay: for I know not yet when I shall goe downe; more then that I intend it as soon as the weather breakes and that I can send my son away: who is much your servant and is very well pleased you approve of his goeing to sea. James is still in the Countrey. I saw Dr: Thomas last night. He goes out of Towne about the middle of <nex>t†b weeke.
I have still of yours a Manuscript†c Treatise written by the late Bishop of Lincolne concerneing Excommunication.†2 besides some papers of Dr: Gibbons†3 and Mr: Grebyes.†4 which I desire I may have leave to transcribe.
The Manuscripts†d at Mr: Pawlings are besides the booke without the box. are in it. an interleaved booke partly printed: and partly written Collections. bound in vellum. 4°. besides which there are 3 thin bookes of Collections, and other things bound in vellum and about 12 little bookes more of collections bound in leather and two small printed bookes.

1465. Issac (later Sir Isaac) Newton to Locke, 16 February 1692 (1457, 1499)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 148a, b. Printed in King, pp. 219-20; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 195-6 (no. 384).
Cambridge Feb. 16. 1691/2.
Sir
Your former letter came not to my hands but this I have. I was of opinion my papers†1 had lain still and am sorry to heare there is news about them. Let me entreat you to stop their translation and impression as soon as you can for I designe to suppress them. If your friend hath been at any pains and charge I will repay it and gratify him. I am very glad my Lord Monmouth is still my friend but intend not to give his Lordship and you any further trouble. My inclinations are to sit still. I am to beg his Lordships pardon for pressing into his company the last time I saw him. I had not done it but that Mr Paulin prest me into the room. Miracles of good credit continued in the Church for about two or three hundred years.†2 Gregorius Thaumaturgus†3 had his name from thence and was one of the latest who was eminent for that guift. But of their number
― 388 ―
and frequency I am not able to give a just account. The history of those ages is very imperfect.†a Mr Paulin told me you had writ for some of Mr Boyles red earth and by that I knew you had the receipt.
Your most affectionate and humble Servant
Is. NEWTON

1466. Robert Pawling to Locke, 18 February 1692 (1450, 1487)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 3-4.
London Feb: 18 1691
Sir
Mr Tyrrell hath sent in a box naild up and a parcell of papers sealed which I presume are the writings that have been so long talked of;
I hope you will have satisfaction of the Carier, tis pity so good wine should be spilt but I hope the Carier took more care of it than so, and perhaps could tell before you could, that it was very good; mr Clement is so kind as to let you have it at the old price the bottles are 2s per doz and the Hamper etc cost 22d and the cariage to the cariers 12d.
I was again at Mr Boyles but I fear you will have no more earth; though mr Santlow†1 told me, who was not then at home, that he hoped to get some more for you. I have not sent mr Newtons letter not written to him as yet that I cant have any either pounded or unpounded for him.
I hope my affair†2 will move well; the Lords of the Ad: moved it to his Majestie last Sunday he approves well of it, Secretary Nothingham was present and approved, the Lord Godolphin†3 made a little objection but received a satisfactory answer from
― 389 ―
Coll. Austin†1 or Sir Robert Rich.†2 the King asked what would be saved, the Colonel gave him an account according to my paper. the King thought it was a little too remote from the sea; Colonel Austin answered according to a paper that I put into his hands very luckily the night before, that in the Dutch war in Oliver Cromwells time Ely house and the Savoy were made Hospitalls to which all the wounded were immediately brought for cure;†3 wher Sir Tho: Millington then a young Physitian was employd by Dr Barksdale†4 and Trapham of Abington†5 was surgeon; one of the Comissioners for the Sick and wounded came to Colonel Austin in Westminster hall and told him they had spent their Majesties but 40 thousand pounds this year; Dr Hutton assures us that the King hath now a paper in his hands by which it appears there hath been spent every year above 80 thousand pound and in this last year, since Welwood was put in comission, though none were wounded, at lest in battle, and very few sick yet more hath been spent than in either of the former years.
I finde the Lady Monmouth, who complains she had no answer to the letter Madam Cutts delivered Sir Francis's servant, who caried mine, desires to see you here; she bid me write you word that a man of your ceremony cant let Madam Clarke come up without waiting on her. I was glad Madam Cutts, in her presence, ownd she deliverd the letter, because I was charged with it, which troubled me a little, because I received none from thence and so could not send any to you. I am glad to hear by Sir Francis that you have your health very well, I pray god continue it. I told him what I was to write from my Lady Monmouth I finde he hath no minde to see you here he replied he hoped mr Clarke would be so kinde a Husband as to go down to her himself and so save you that complement
I could make this letter as long as my last by writing of Madam Lockhart, but I will not; Ile only let you know she is well, and I presume will take a time to answer yours, but resolves never to tell
― 390 ―
me more that she intends to write to you. I have room enough yet to subscribe my self
Sir Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
the inclosed came this day to me by penny post from mr Winter

1467. Locke to Edward Clarke, 20 February 1692 (1462, 1471)
Rand, pp. 334-5. The words in square brackets are supplied by Rand.
Oates, 20th February, 1691-2.
Dear Sir,
My Lady Masham has this one trouble more to beg of you in her affair, and then she hopes she has quite done. You will in a black box receive by Mrs. Clarke these following writings:
(1) Sir Francis Masham's deeds of mortgage by lease and release to Sir Walter [Yonge], etc., for the raising of £600 for Mrs. Margaret Masham.†1
(2) A bond from Sir Francis Masham....
(3) Assignment of Sir Francis Masham's mortgage ... to Richard Andrews†2 and Samuel Cudworth†3 to protect the Lady ... from encumbrances, dated 5th October, 1691.
(4) Dr. Walker's receipt for £600, dated 5th October, 1691.
(5) Sir Francis Masham's declaration that Dr.... bonds for £600 deposited in Sir Edward Abney's†4 hands were to remain there for his [protection] until the encumbrances on her additional jointure were taken off.
(6) Sir Francis Masham, Damaris Cudworth†5 and John Cudworth's†6 assignment by lease and release of Sir John Barrington's†7
― 391 ―
mortgage for £600 to Rich. Andrews and Samuel Cudworth for securing the old encumbrances dated the 28th February, 1690-1.
These writings, as you will see by the enclosed, she thinks convenient to be [placed] with Sir Paul Whichcote,†1 who is one of her trustees, and has the ... writing of her marriage settlement. And she thinks it best, if you [agree thereto] that these as belonging to the same matter and the other should be kept together. Whether it be fit to have or demand any receipt or memorandum from Sir Paul, that he has these writings, and the other, she leaves to you. She thinks it not so convenient to trouble her brother Andrews, for he having lately brought them hither with him, and left them here, she thought it not of so good [form] to send them back again to him to be conveyed to another. And therefore ...
She bids me tell you that she takes it kindly that your son is left here with her, and hopes he will bear with the inconveniency of the house, and says she hopes the ... a pledge in her hands to draw you down hither before you go into Somerset. I should be very glad it might be so, for I resolve to see you before you go to Chipley, and I had rather it were here, than in London, not for the pains of the journey but the air of the place. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most ... and humble servant,
J. LOCKE.

1468. Nicolas Fatio de Duillier to Locke, 23 February 1692 (1459, 1697)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 95-6.
Honoured Sir
I had been very glad to see You any where, but chiefly in the Country, where I beleeve one might enjoy you better than in Town: but besides my circumstances will not allow me of going from
― 392 ―
London at this time I find our meeting would be but lame, since Mr Newton hath told me he could not possibly join now with us. I give You Sir many thanks for your letters to <My Lord>†a Pembrock and myself. Mr Cuningham hath desired me to express to You very Kindly the sense he hath of the obligation You have laid upon him. I have seen, Sir, Dr Thomas but two or three days ago and he is allready gone for Salsbury. He expressed to me how unwilling he was to live in town because of his lungs, tho I thought there might be found a remedy for them. You had Sir found out the very man I desired to have, and I am sorry his circumstances do tie him so closely to Salsbury. I am with all manner of respect
Honoured Sir
Your most humble and most obedient servant
N. FATIO DE DUILLIER.

1469. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 23 February/4 March 1692 (1421, 1480)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 85.
Rotterdam 4 march 1692
Dear Friend
I hope you received my Letter of the 1/11 of January by the N. york man, in which I told you I could not understand how people could remit mony out of England with an intent not to have it returnd, unless they resolved to follow it hither: I wrote, and caused one to speak to that cashier at Amsterdam, but can get no answer from him—
I understand by mr. Wright that he has a packet from you for me, Which I shall now be dayly expecting. I having now no thoughts of ever seeing England more, have desired mr. Popple, if he can get an opportunity by some body comeing over with the
― 393 ―
King, to send me two or 3 boxes of my bookes; if mr. Wharton†1 should come he would do me the kindness. It being out of mr. Popples way, I have desired him to address to you, for assistance. Wetstein now at last resolves this yeare to have that M.S. printed;†2 pray, if you can; inform me what M:S. greek copy it is that Dr. Hammond designs, in his Annotations, by the name of the Kings M.S. which he says is all in Capital letters;†3 because I find none among all the Various readings of the polyglot†4 designd by that name. I enquire the rather because I want to know the certainty of one upon the 1 Pet. 3.20. the first word of which was ὃ. quod, and Beza†5 changed it into ῷ cui from the complutense Edition;†6 supposing that ὃ was a corruption tho it be better than ὦ of the two, but neither of them are so natural as inline image which Dr. Hammond avers that Kings manus: to have that is to say, by inference, he concludes it, for tho it be there Ὁ. yet being written in Capitals, he tells us that O is oft wrot for inline image .†7 and gives an instance of inline image for διονυςinline image .†8 But what confirms it right down is, that he says there is a ms. in Magd. Colledg†9 that has it inline image —which I admire at and do almost question because I find it not in the Polyglot, nor in the Oxford N.T.†10 The States Translators†11 and Hartsoecker†12 seem to have read it in the Genetive case in their copies. I would be glad if you could get me the certain knowledg of it. Mr. Leers has desired me to get him a list of all that have wrote any thing of the history of our cuntry since Henry the 7th. that might be serviceable to his frenchman that is writing a french History of
― 394 ―
England from that time,†1 that what of them he has not he may get, if to be got. I am,
Yours
B F

1470. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 25 February [1692] (1451, 1474)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 98-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London. Feb: the 25th
Mr Lock
If I have been lyable to reproach for having by my own fault lett fall, for some while, a Commerce so desireable, and to the support of which I am so many ways oblig'd, as this I am now attempting to revive; Itt might seem I had some kind of excuse by being able to say, what would appear naturall and sincere enough, that I have nothing to contribute that's worth of my own and nothing besides Impertinences. But notwithstanding; when I consider and assent fully to this great truth; I am Yet so far from finding my self Justifyable that I am forc'd to confess my self either the most shamefully Idle or the most Ingratefull Creature in the world: For when I consider how well I was us'd for my first Impertinences and what good success I had with a whole Pacquet of that kind that I once sent: I say, when I consider what a Good Return I had, what the Profit was that I made and the satisfaction I procur'd my self; I think, no one ever neglected his Intrest and Duty more then I did, by staying there, and Employing no more of All that Stock that remains since what ever itt be in other respect it is what, by your means, I make to turn to so good account to my self: so much are you Created or Dispos'd to be Benificiall to mee above what can be imagin'd.
But, no more. this is already too much in a Place where I have nothing to doe but to Inquire my Doom and so as to Learn of You,
― 395 ―
if upon the Knowledg of my very worst Guilt You think mee capable of a Pardon; I mean, as one able to Expiate his Crime and unlikely, if forgiven, to fall into the same again: for as to my self I am resolv'd to say nothing in my own defence nor promise any thing though I think I have large subject enough. I Fear I shall soon goe into the Country. I would gladly know of You if You are to be in town in any time. I Expect My Brother and Poor Mr Denoun now with mee. I hear that Mr Fashio†1 will not be Governour to Sir John Barringtons Brother†2 Mr Hill that was my Lord Hides Governour†3 having, as I am told, been employ'd to prevail with him. If this Extrordinary Person be not to come in that Place and that Sir ... Barrington be to have a Governour I cannot but entreat you to remember that Gentleman whome I was speaking of, when att Oates with You: I told you then his Charachter, which is the best I could ever give any man in his station or indeed almost any man whatever. His name is La Treille†4 which I suppose you have heard for he is equally known, and equally esteem'd by Mr Freak and Mr Popple and more of our Freinds as by myself. My Lady†5 is very well, and knowing I have some kind of Correspondance with you enjoyns me to give her service to you when I write and Sir John Cropley the same with much respect and thanks for your Remembrance
Dear Mr Lock
I am Intirely yours
ASHLEY
I am in such hast that I cannot mention my service to My Lady Masham with respect enough. But pray doe for mee something in that kind like what You know to be my sentiment and what I wish to express.
Address: For Mr Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: (G.P.O., indecipherable); GC
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 25 Feb 91/2

1471. Locke to Edward Clarke, 26 February 1692 (1467, 1472)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 40. Printed in Rand, pp. 335-7.
Oates 26 Feb 91/2
Dear Sir
I am satisfied about your son that he wants not parts soe that if he has not made all the progresse we could have desired I lay it wholy upon want of application, which as far as I can guesse is oweing, something to a saunteringnesse that is in his temper; a good deale to an unsteadinesse of minde which is quickly tired with a bookeish attention which he takes noe great pleasure in; and a litle to something of my yonge master. I here mention not any particular aversion he had to Monsieur Passebon, for I can discover noething of that. And I thinke all the quarrels he had with him was from a mixture of lazynesse and contempt and endeavour for mastery assisted possibly by the folly and incouragement of servants, wherein he gaind his point and would noe doubt have a triall of skill with any other that shall succeed him. But yet though indulgeing to his ease tis like will make him weary and resty†1 with any other tutor espetially if he have hopes to tire him out, yet I looke upon it as very far from being unconquerable. For he does what I bid him and has sometimes since he has been here spent several hours in the day by himself and I suppose busy about what I set him. But to obtein this I think it necessary to keep a pretty cold and <constantly>†a severe countenance to him, and when at any time he neglects and makes excuses I shew him gravely and without passion that I see it to be an excuse which signifies noething but that he has had noe minde to doe it. And sometimes I chide him, but still gravely in few words and without any passion by which way of treatment I thinke he is better reconciled to his booke for he comes sometimes of himself to me to shew me what he hath don and to aske what he shall doe next though he has not all the Alacrity towards it I could wish. And I know not whether there be not some cuning in it for fear I should represent matters soe to you that I should incline you to send him to Westminster Schoole, of
― 397 ―
which and the discipline used there I have given him such a representation that I imagin he has noe great likeing to it
I know the question you will be ready to aske me is But what will you have me doe with him? To which I answer I should be still of my first opinion of haveing a Tutor for him at home, But that there are two great Obstacles lye in the way. The one is that Madame if I am not mightily mistaken is utterly averse to it. The other is Where shall we finde a man with discretion and steadynesse enough to manage him right, for he will require a constant attention and a due application to his temper
The next to this were some Frenchmans house where he might be taken in and looked after by the man him self
The last is a French schoole where the master would have a particular eye to him and manage him with such a rain as his temper requires. But which of these three is easiest to be found I can not tell. A French man it must bee that he may not loose the French tongue or else perhaps I might advise you to Westminster or some other very severe schoole, where if he where whipd soundly whilst you are lookeing out an other fit Tutor for him he would perhaps be the more pliant and willing to learne at home afterwards. But for the reasons above mentiond I thinke not of that.
Whose ever hands he is put into, he must be sure to keepe a steady hand upon him for the bias lying on the lazy wayward side he will be ready to slip from him by all the artifices and excuses can be imagind all which he should constantly be beat out of by admiting noething but the thing don. And the first time any thing came in contest to be sure to correct him severely and repeat it on till his tutor perceived it had wrought upon his minde and setled the mastery. that once don and he was become pliant and submissive to orders with all his industry, then not to strain him too hard but give him such imployment, such tasks as his parts may with moderate industry dispatch. Prayseing him when he deserves it and findeing out ingenuous recreations for his vacant times but never leting him be saunteringly idle, but let play of some kinde or other and Exercise as Danceing, Fenseing etc or study take up all his time. If you can any where enquire out a man that will follow this method you will finde your son improve to your great satisfaction. and without this I fear he will have a great many unprofitable and uneasy hours and I wish he make not you have some uneasy ones too. I thinke Madam has not don amisse to leave him here for
― 398 ―
many reasons. I shall have the more time to observe his temper and you will be eased of the feare and trouble of haveing him in town without a Tutor.
Madam I hope will returne to you very well and not a penny the worse for the wearing. Pray remember me kindely to my wife and sister. her mother tels me my wife has a cough looke after it betimes. My humble service to all my freinds that you see in your walks. I am
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
J LOCKE
Give me leave to minde you of your opinion concerning inlargeing my security†1 and of the note I am to have from Mr Churchill†2
Monsieur Passebon desires me earnestly to returne you his thanks for your great kindenesse to him in geting him another place
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire

1472. Locke to Edward Clarke, 29 February 1692 (1471, 1475)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 41. Printed in Rand, p. 338. Answered by no. 1475.
Oates 29 Feb 91/2
Dear Sir
I am very glad Madam came safe my service to her. I like all in your son, except his cough, better than whilst his mother was here. His cough not amending at all I send to day to Bishop Startford for one to let him bloud to morrow, for since his cough abates not I thinke that the properest remedy and which at this time of the year can doe him noe harme. and his mother thought it advisable when we talked of it here. As to any trouble your son is to me you know
― 399 ―
me not as you ought if you doe not beleive that were it ten times more I should take pleasure in it whilst it is what his condition and circumstances require. And as for a trouble to the house I shall be as nice in that as you and if I saw it was thought soe by any body I should take the liberty with you as my freind to put an end to it. For my Lady in particular I can be answerable to you that it was her desire ever since he went from hence to have him here again. And therefor I bid you be at rest about his being here longer than is convenient as long as you heare noe thing of it for me. I am glad of the hopes you give me of seeing you here and am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
My service and love to my wife
By a letter I received from my Lord Ashley but now I finde he talks of goeing into the Country. which makes me again minde you of your opinion concerning enlargeing my security. When you see my Lady Shaftesbury I desire you to aske her whether Mr Cheswell be still to pay me and desire of her an order to him or who else is to pay the mony and if as you formerly intimated you finde she intends to abate any thing for the tax be pleased to let her know that I doe not thinke my Lord her husband would have don soe.

1473. Locke to Philippus van Limborch, 29 February 1692 (1456, 1485)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 257 a. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 336-9; address in Ollion, p. 202. The year in Locke's date is necessarily new style. Answers no. 1447; answered by no. 1485.
(English)
Oates 29 Feb. 92
Vir Amplissime
Si ex literarum tarditate de amicitiâ meâ judicaveris metuo ne me suspiceris ad officia nimis ignavum, a quo me profiteor cum res
― 400 ―
postulat longe alienum. in hoc literarum commercio si qua utor libertate id plerumque evenit cum ad eos scribendum sit, quibus benevolentiam amicitiamque meam re potius quam verbis testatam fore mihi in animo est. Hoc an tu probaveris nescio, ita ego tibi persuasum velim. nemo enim est omnium qui te magis suspicit, æstimat diligit quam ego: id nunc facio et semper faciam. Non placet Wetstenii in edendâ Sancti Officii historiâ Cunctatio, hoc unicum in eâ morâ placet quod te identidem relegente et sub incudem sæpius revocante, limatiorem perfectioremque habebimus. Hoc unum ut te moneam jam occurrit. sc: alterum hujusmodi volumen duodecim circiter ab hinc annis Monspessulis extitisse ab hoc distinctum. duo enim tunc erant illic hujusmodi volumina.†1
(English) Zelus theologicus uti video semper et ubique idem est eodemque modo procedit. quid tandem devenit Paradoxorum ille de Angelis Auctor scire cupio, si evasit mirum est quanquam eò res inclinare videbatur quo tempore scripsisti, favente etiam Amstelodamensium prædicatorum desidiâ vix tamen veniam ei datam credo.
― 401 ―
Hujusmodi orthodoxiæ propugnatores non solent errantibus ignoscere. Presbyteriani in Scotia quid agant mallem ex aliis quam ex me scires. Zelus illic in frigido isto aere per <antiperistasin>†a †1 incalescere videtur. Satis fervide disciplinæ suæ operam <dant>,†b an satis prudentèr an satis modestè ipsi videant.†2 Sed ubi causa dei <agitur>†c ut nosti et ejus ecclesiæ quid sibi Theologici non putant licere autoritatem suam soli deo acceptam referentes.
(English) Dominum de†d Cene semel vidi Londini sed semel tantum idque obiter apud Nobilissimum Boyleum adeo ut sermocinandi locus non esset de rebus illius vel amicis Amstelodamensibus. ab eo tempore parum Londini commoratus sum valetudini rure vacans, pulmones enim non ferunt fumum urbis. Episcopum illum†3 cui Dominum de Cene commendasti credo pacis ecclesiasticæ sincere studiosum. Sollicitus sum de valetudine Veenii nostri angusto est pectore et metuo pulmonibus ejus, metuo etiam ne praxi continuæ jam a multis annis assuetus rure otio intabescat. opto illi diuturnam
― 402 ―

(Latin)
Oates 29 Feb. 92
Excellent Sir,
If you judge of my friendship by the tardiness of my letters I fear you may suspect me of being too lazy in fulfilling my duties, to which I profess [p. 400] myself very averse when occasion demands. If I use some freedom in this traffic of letters it usually happens when I have to write to persons to whom, as I think, my goodwill and friendship will be made known by fact rather than words. I do not know whether you approve of this; I should wish you to feel assured of it; for there is no one in the world who admires, values, loves you more than I; this I do now and always shall do. Wetstein's lingering in publishing your account of the Holy Office is displeasing; the one pleasing thing in this delay is that by your constantly re-reading it and returning it many times to the anvil we shall have it in a more polished and more perfect form. There is one thing about which it now occurs to me to warn you: that is, another volume of this kind was extant at Montpellier about twelve years ago, distinct from this one, for there were two such volumes there at the time.†1
(Latin) Theological zeal, as I see it, is always and everywhere the same and proceeds in the same way. I should like to know what has become in the end of the author of those paradoxes about angels. It would be a marvel if he escaped, though things seemed to be inclining that way when you wrote, what with the further support given him by the inactivity of the Amsterdam preachers; yet I hardly believe he has been forgiven; such champions of orthodoxy are not wont to pardon the erring. I should prefer that you should [p. 401] learn from others rather than from me what the Presbyterians in Scotland are doing. Zeal in that chill atmosphere seems to be growing hotter by force of contrast.†1 They are concerned warmly enough for their own discipline; whether they are using sufficient prudence and discretion in this is for them to consider.†2 But where, as you know, the cause of God and his church is concerned, what do theologians not think is permitted to them, declaring, as they do, that they hold their authority from God alone?
(Latin) I saw Mr. de Cene in London once and once only, and that incidentally at the Honourable Mr. Boyle's, so that there was no opportunity to talk about his affairs or my Amsterdam friends. I have spent little time in London since then, living as I do in the country for the sake of my health, for my lungs do not tolerate the city smoke. I believe that the bishop†3 to whom you gave Mr. de Cene an introduction, is sincerely concerned for peace in the church. I am anxious about our friend Veen's health; he is narrow-chested and I have fears for his lungs; I am also afraid that, having been accustomed now for many years to uninterrupted practice, he may be pining away in leisure in the country. I wish him a long, healthy, and happy old age; I owe him much for which I shall always be grateful. You do rightly [p. 402] in condemning persecution on account of religion in Romanists only. If you should pick out and stigmatize for its cruelty any particular sect among Christians you will be commended by the rest of them, though persecution is the same everywhere and plainly popish; for any church whatsoever lays claim in words to orthodoxy and in practice to infallibility. Mrs. Cudworth sends you in return her kindest and most respectful greetings. Please give my good wishes to your wife and family, and remember me very kindly to Veen and Guenellon and all that kindred. Good-bye, honoured Sir, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
(Latin) I desire information about miracles after the Apostles' times; I am not sufficiently versed in Church history to know what opinion to form about them. I therefore ask urgently, as it concerns me to know, whether any miracles were performed in the Christian Church after the Apostles' times; by what authors and with what trustworthiness they were handed down to memory; how frequent they were, and whether they continued until the reign of Constantine or later? Also, who was that Thaumaturge whose so goodly title has come down to us, and what was done by him? I do not seek a list of the miracles as recorded by ecclesiastical writers; what I ask is [p. 403] whether it is established on the authority of trustworthy historians that there were genuine miracles; whether they were performed rarely or frequently, and for how long that gift was granted to the Church.†1

the 3d:
Doe not expect, Sir, that I should thank You for all your Compliments to mee on my Comeing of Age:†2 Itt was no more then what I needed to make mee relish the Pleasure of that Circumstance, att that time, as I should doe, and so as A Man in reason should be suppos'd to have the means to doe; if he have not hard luck indeed. I tell You, I could not have abated you one ace of a Compliment; since onely those of your fashioning amongst so many others as I have had are onely able to give mee the least liking of my self: The rest as Extrordinary as I can assure You they have been have not yett been able so much as to make mee not repine att the having left behind mee three such Lovely Years as are counted by our Yong men from 18 to this Age and by the Weemen a little under att the same proportion from 16 to the Confines of Twenty which begins to sound sadly and which is a kind of Summer Solstice where motion is stop'd or att least render'd imperceptible for some while. But to tell you a plainer reason yet then this why I doe not think my self oblig'd to You for your Compliments; Itt is because they were due to Mee: and on what score think You? I'll tell you instantly:
― 404 ―
But in the mean time now were I but to know the Truth, what a fine turn should I see here on a suddain in your opinion! What pretty things are you thinking of this Vain Creature that devours Compliments att a rate that never was heard of! Say seriously. doe you not begin to wish you had given 'em slower and with a little more deliberation. I warrant You Yes ... But not to frighten You more then is convenient nor to punish your Rashness too dreadfully; I'le tell you then in what sence itt is that I say all this Compliments were no more then due to mee. and thus itt is. You, forsooth, had forestall'd all my happiness and Anticipated all the Joy that I was to have conceiv'd by Right in the Day of my Manhood
You us'd me like one that should tell mee the Plott of a Play or the latter end of a Romance in the Middle of itt and so spoyl main of the matter against the Conclusion where the Pleasure is to be. You were us'd to treat mee att that Rate, dealt with mee so like a Freind in every strictest Relation, Seem'd to seek my Company for my Company's sake, and conferr'd with mee upon Subjects as though you were really better for not being alone. Now, all this from One like You, from a Man so Unvulgar as You, I leave any Body of good sence to Judg if itt were not enough to put any Young Fellow besides himself, who had his vanity turn'd the way that mine ever was; and if this were nott fully enough to make him miscount himself a man before his time. Thus had You season'd mee so as to leave mee not the least matter to raise Joy out of but enough to have answer'd any of my Congratulations with the least Feature of Gladness or with any mark of satisfaction on my side: But that in Consideration I suppose of the wrong You had done mee; this Letter of yours came most seas'nably, and Just made amends by giving mee some additional pleasure att that time above what was ordinary; which otherwise I could not have had upon my own score and by giving mee some good thoughts of my self that I never had before. For I think I might say that if other People by their Compliments could have made mee apprehend my self something that was above a meer Boy; You by Yours could make mee imagine my self something beyond a Common Man such as now Pass in the world for such. So, Ending with the same continued Air of Vanity with which I began In which, however, You have the Cheif hand; I Rest Just as I was, for If I could be I would be more
Your Constant Freind and Faithfull servant
