1475. Edward Clarke to Locke, 5 March 1692 (1472, 1476)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 64. Printed in Rand, pp. 339-40. Answers no. 1472; answered by no. 1476.
London March the 5th. 1691.
Deare Sir,
I intended to have Written to you by the last Post, but was prevented by a suddain Summons to appeare at Mrs. Eliz: Yonge's Wedding, who was that day Marryed to Mr. Beale, (Mr. Hunt's Relation), Wee all Remembered you Kindly and wish'd you with us, I am concern'd to heare the Childe's cough continues, and that Hee is thereby made soe much the more Troublesome to you, but am infinitely obleiged to my Lady and you to dispence with all for my sake, I am verie glad to understand that you intended to have Him Bleeded, and what ever further you thinke fitt to have done, I shall thankefully acquiesse therein as the best and most proper meanes for His Cure: Pray give my humble service and thankes to Sir Francis and my Lady, and acquaint my Lady That I have Plac'd Her Deeds and Writeings with Sir P. Whichcott and have taken a Receipt from Him of these last, and those formerly Delivered to Him, Which, I shall keepe by mee untill I have an opportunity by a safe hand to convey it to you:
I have this weeke been twice at my Lady Shaftesbury's to have spoken with Her about the Payment of your Annuity, but miss'd Her both times, however that shall not discourage mee from
― 406 ―
Repeateing my visitts untill I can be soe fortunate as to speake with Her, and then you shall not faile to have a further Account from mee, I have allsoe duely considered the proposeall touching the inlargeing of the security for your Annuity, and upon the whole matter doe thinke it most Adviseable for you to Attempt it, being satisfied that should my Lord Ashley dye, you would imediately have the Farme of Kingston turn'd upon your handes for your satisfaction, but as long as my Lord lives, I recon you are safe in His Promise, Which upon another occasion in Discourse my Lord was voluntarily Pleased to Renew to mee; The method for Doeing this, Whither by your Writeing to my Lord, and my Delivery of it, or By my Application to Him on your Behalfe, or by any other Way, you thinke most Proper, I submitt to your better Judgment, And assure you that I shall most heartily and willingly serve you therein, and shall joyfully imbrace every opportunity wherein I may shew how much I am
Deare Sir,
Your most truly affectionate and Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:

Dear Sir
Haveing sent away my second son,†4 and the other being now come to Towne to looke after his owne affaires I am now leaving it my self, but before I goe thinke it my duty to take my leave of you, and assure you that what you command me concerneing your things at okeley shall be punctually performed upon your first orders: and the paper bookes and other bookes that are left behind will goe near to fill your 2 cases of boxes: so that I hope all the prejudice you have had in not haveing them sent sooner will prove no
― 409 ―
more then your being without them one half year, which I hope will not be much: as for your plates I (haveing not your square cap by me to bring it mind) forgot to tell you in my last that my man could not find your old bedmakers house: and so cannot as yet give you any positive answere; what is become of them, but I hope I may in my next; for if they were not stole out of the Room that woeman: had them: as well as all your pots, glasses. etc. for I am sure they were never brought to my house; my Treatis of the Law of nature will be out I beleive by the next Terme:†1 as soon as it comes out, I will order one to be sent you, in the meane time I have bin advised to put out my Dialogues single. once in a month as the onely way to put them well off:†2 the first is come out already and I have ordered one to be left for you with Mr: P:†3 tho I suppose you will not trouble your self to read more then the preface,†4 since, it being upon a subject, which either you or I have written on before you will not find any thing new in it, but what you know already; however it may serve as well as the next (which will be on the divine of succession) to make up the set: which will consist of 8, or 9 discourses on all the subjects: which you may see in the preface to this first Dialogue: I have no more but assure you that the money I have already payed: on the Doctors account;†5 and more too shall goe for the interest of your 10l: I owe you; and for the†a- 31l: from-†a the time you demanded it to be payed in: I pray give me your answere as to this; that I may know what to pay you; as allso the date of that note if you please to accept interest for it: so wishing the continuation of all that health, and happynesse which you now enjoy in the Countrey I remaine
your most humble servant

1478. Locke to Edward Clarke, 11 March 1692 (1476, 1481)

Oates 11 Mar 91/2
Dear Sir
The hopes you gave me in your last of seeing you the next weeke pleased me at first sight extreamly but when I reflected on it again and thought how probable it might be that you intended to take back your son with you I was a litle at a stand, desire to see you urgeing me one way and the consideration of your son weighing on the tother, his cough since his bleeding is better but not quite gon and I should not thinke the town air fit for him till his cough be gon. besides if you are not yet provided of a place for him, what will you doe with him in towne, he will be much better here. With me I hope you will not be nice in the case or thinke I am weary of him, and to everybody else I assure you he is welcome. My Lady when I told her you entended to be here some time the next weeke answerd I hope he does not intend to take master away with him. Soe that if you mean not to take master back with you come as soon as you can the sooner the better, if it be your resolution that he shall returne with you when ever you come,†a let your comeing be as late as you can. This I say (though I long to talke with you) as your freind that advises what he judges right. Let not any scruple of any inconvenience he may be here hasten you. If I perceivd any thing that might be the least reason to you to take him away I should be as forward as you and send you word, you know I have don soe once already and you may trust me in the case. You need not be uneasy I assure you or hasty at all upon that score, and of this rest satisfied and let him be here as is most for your
― 411 ―
convenience. It is good for his health, I hope noe disadvantage to him other wise and†a Noe trouble to the house or any body of it and I am pleased with it.
I have here inclosed writ to my Lord Ashley as you advised. You will there read the true history of that affair, to what is there said you may adde if you finde need that if my Lord had given me this annuity (which has not been a thing unusuall for great men to those who have been faithfull to them) it would be a shame it should not be paid me. But when it was paid for with all that I had got in attending on him ten or a dozen of the best years of my life it will be very hard measure to have the trouble which I designed to avoid in stead of the full annuity I purchased.†1 my lord Halifax never used Strangers soe†2 and shall it be said this is a usage my Lord Shaftesbury provided for his freinds. But I hope there will be noe need of arguments in the case. I desire you would talke with my Lord Ashley and deliver the inclosed before you come out of towne and if he be prevaild with to doe it I beg you to make the security and draw the writeing as you thinke fit. Sir Francis and my Lady present their service to you and Madam. Mine to her and my wife and Nanny. I am
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant

1479. Locke to Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, 11 March 1692 (1474, 1482)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 45. Copy written by Clarke. Printed in Rand, pp. 343-4. Answered by no. 1482.
Oates 11° March 169 1/2
My Lord
Among the things that I have Lov'd best in this world, the two that I allwayes preferr'd to the rest, were, My Lord your Grandfather, and Quiet; Hee was pleas'd to bee soe Favorable to mee, That Hee Himselfe was pleas'd to Contrive Both for mee, and to that purpose when Hee Retired from Businesse into the Countrey, told mee that I should bee in the Countrey with Him, and that Hee would find out somewhere thereabouts an Annuity for mee, knowing that I had little money by mee, But either meeting with none, or none that Hee lik'd, Hee, after some time, told mee Hee would doe it Himselfe, This Pleas'd mee extreamly, knowing my selfe safe in His Lordshipps handes, and soe referring the whole matter to Him both for Price and security, I paid 800 l.,†1 and Kingston-Farme was settled for it, Which, not examineing whither it was†a of a suteable value to such a Charge, I tooke rather as a Declaration of my Lords Intention, than a security for†b my Annuity, not doubting but that (if I should out-Live Him) such a regard to his memory, and Honour, would goe along with the Estate Hee should Leave, That I should never meete with any Difficulty about this little matter in a Family I had the Honour to bee soe long related to; But your Lordship is not ignorant, That it has been under deliberation, and Advice has been given, That instead of receiveing an Annuity, I should bee made a Farmer; I wish my Lord your Grandfather had been by to have hear'd it: If His intention to mee that I should dureing my Life receive the full hundred pounds yearely without trouble has not been yett Crossed, I know how much I owe it to your Lordshipp, whose Justice, and the Assureance you gave mee by Mr. Clarke concerning it, I take for soe good security, That could your Lordship bee but as sure to outlive mee, as I should bee to rest satisfied with your Word, I should desire noe other, But your Lordship knows what will become of
― 413 ―
mee if I should have the Misfortune to fall into the handes of Him that is next, I begg the Favour of you therefore to compleate the Kindnesse and put mee out of those Dangers, That for the small Remainder of my Life, this little support of it may not Wast it in Cares, and the Affayres of a Farme which I understand not, and which my Lord your Grandfather never intended I should purchase of Him; And the little time I have to come, I hope I may imploy to better Advantage: This letter and my Desire I have putt into Mr. Clarkes handes to be delivered to your Lordship, Hee is noe lesse your Lordshipps than my Freind, And tho I thinke there bee nothing unreasonable in my request, or difficult in the Case, yet I am Willing, one whose Advise I know your Lordship thinks well of in other Cases, should bee Privy to it. I begg your Lordships Pardon for the trouble of this Letter, it is of a sort I doe not Love to write, espetially to your Lordship, And this is one Inconvenience I receaved†a from this Businesse already, But I hope I shall have noe occasion to write to your Lordship any more, but about matters and in a Way wherein I may more suiteably to my own Inclination expresse how much I am
your Lordships most humble and most obedient servant
J LOCK.
1480. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 12/22 March 1692 (1469, 1506)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 86-91. Marginal citations of pages in the Histoire abregée are here inserted in the text in square brackets; other square brackets are due to Furly.
Rotterdam 22 march 1692
Dear Friend
Yours of the 14/24 past, I received from mr. Masham,†1 and wonder you have not received any from me since Peter Sonmans return; I have wrote 2 if not 3 to you. In the first I told you. that the Bankiers it was that gaind so considerably by that trade. That I am satisfyed you reason right that 'tis impossible for people to send their effects abroad, but with an intent to have them back again. But when people do things in a pannick fear, they do not
― 414 ―
always think of gayning by the returne, but onely of securing part, in case they be necessitated, by ill success of affairs, to follow. For, to me, that argument is still strong that so much cannot have belongd to the Bankers, and of the sum I doubt not much: nor could others consent to it, in hopes of proffit; what the mystery is I know not, but Sir S. E. and his partner†1 I beleev had no small share in the business.
I desired you in another to get me, for Leers, the most exact information that can be of any pieces extant that may contribute any thing to the information of his frenchman that is writing a french History of England from the Reign of Henry the 7th†2 both great and small Treatises, I received part of an account of such Authors from mr. Popple, which mr. Freak gave him, which Leers desires me to send you, and to intreat you to inform him of any others that may have Come within your cognisance. I told you of a malicious french booke stiled Histoire abregée Du Kouakerisme et de celuy de ses Dogmes.†3 In which not onely the Q. are horribly treated but the English nation in General as fantastick melancholy fooles, and Enthusiasts [p2], made so by their eating their meat half raw [3], and the pestilentiall smoak of their Coals which do so infect the ayre that, that and the crude juice of their bloody meat does so affect their Lungs, that the whole oeconomy of their spirits, is disturbed thereby, and so no wonder, that all england is filld with fooles and fanaticks that for a song do hang and drown themselvs and cut their own throats in coole blood. That they are so proud that, in comparison to all other nations, they look upon themselvs as descended from the Gods [p.10,11], that they have no respect for any strangers whatsoever, receive them after a barbarous, brutish, uncivil manner void of all civility, honneteté, and sweetness, treating them rather like enemies than friends, witness their making them pay tribute at their coming in and going out. And that therefore it was a fit soile for Quakerism†a to grow, and thrive in—which is nothing else but the effect of pride and ignorance and the last effort of the Devill for ruin of the Christian†b
― 415 ―
Religion; meer Deism, and would tolerate absolute Atheism [p.162], and therefore ought to be the object of the hatred of all men, unworthy of all protection, and toleration, tho they have obtaind it under this new goverment upon subscribing a certain profession, against their consciences, witness B.F.s struggle against it [p.142] (who is a meer Deist) but by all his sollicitation, he could not obtain of the Parliament the change of one word.†1 But what was writ was writ, and they must swallow as best they could. Whereas 'twas not a form imposed†a upon them, but sillily given Sir T.C.†2 by two of them—
He says [p.21] they deny that christ ever was a visible man, turn all the scr:†3 into Allegoryes, and that so to doe is accounted amongst those that are let into the knowledg of this mystery of the cabal†4 to eat the Passeover: [p.18] That this he has learnd from some of themselvs, but such as had not yet eat the passeover, that is renouncd J.C. the son of Mary
That to shew their spight to the christian Rel: [p.51] they have rejected his 2 sacraments, which would oblige them to a publick profession, of his person, life, death, Resurrection—All which yet they do profess with their mouths—but do not beleeve.
A doughty Historian—and Reasoner—
This gives me occasion to examin au fond, the foundation of those 2 Ceremonies. And if I mistake not, I prove them, to be no institutions of J.C., (or rather shew that no man can shew them to be such) but old Jewish customs and practises, yea that they are, in their first rise, purely Pagan institutions, hatcht by the Jugling Egyptian priests (among many other Ceremonies) which the Jews having learned in Egypt constraind God himself (as it were) not of choice, (but in condescention to their weakness and indeed madness, after they had made and worshipped the Egyptian God Apis, the calf) to set up amongst them:
But that there never was any true Religion in such things, I prove abundantly, out of all Antiquity (by the help of Marsham,†5
― 416 ―
and Spencer)†1 both Jewish and Christian. And that the True Religion has never been but one, nor can ever be more, and that that is this, To love god above all, and our neighbor as ourselvs. That all that deviats in the lest from this, to teach men to hate God, or their neighbor, for Gods sake, is so far from being the true, that 'tis no, Religion at all, nay the greatest irreligion, and propagater of wickedness, and profaness among men in the world.
This has led me to examin the Varios readings upon all the Texts that speak of these two things and that, to discover things I never thought of, and that will torment the Tradesmen, and, if men were wise spoyl the Trade: Of this Trade—Or mystery of iniquity called Religion; in which I forget not that notable distick†2 —
Naturall Religion was easy, first and plain.
Trade made it mystery, and offerings gain.
Then Ceremonies and sacrifices were prepar'd
The Priests eat Roast meat, and the people star'd.
I prove by stronger arguments than any Beza uses for his challenging the Text in his Annotations. That the words of Command, Do this in remembrance of me,†3 (which is all the shaddow they have of a command) Not onely may be translated this you do, as wel as do this. but that so to do was more answerable to the Jewish Custom in that supper, and breaking of bread, which Christ then fulfilled. And did not institute anew.
That 'tis most likely that christ never spake those words, nor yet that Luke ever wrote them, but that they were since Lukes time added to the Text, And that perhaps Innocently enough, as Beza and many others shew that other passages, have been done.
Because that Matthew who was an eye witness says n'ere a word of it. Nor Mark that followed him, and, as the fathers witness, onely wrote a compendium of his Gospel. And because there is an Ancient copy yet extant, Bezas Cambridge copy†4 that has none of those words in it, nor these—[which is given for you.]†a
That their being found in Paul,†5 is no confirmation, he onely
― 417 ―
quoting Luke—and there being [broken] for [given for you,] its evident that there had been Tampering, for if Christ did speak those words—he either said—[given] or [broken]—but not both—
Therefore in all likelyhood those words—[which is given for you,] Do this (or this ye do) in remembrance of me.] were not in Luke when Paul quoted that description of that nights action from him. But that that passage was added by somebody after Pauls decease, as Beza Judges those words to be—Luke 22.20. [which is shed for you] because its false Greek,†1 and not quoted by Paul—That the Argument is much stronger against this passage in the 1 Cor. 11.25. concerning the cup. [This do ye (or this ye doe) as oft as ye drink it in remembrance of me] For that neither Mathew Mark nor Luke do report that ever christ said any such thing of the cup.
If Bezas argument be of any weight to prove his suggestion, that those words [which is shed for you], were first added as a marginall note, supposing that some such thing was, or might have been said concerning the blood, or ought to be said, as well as it was concerning the body, [which is given for you].
It is of more weight to prove my suggestion, that these words concerning the cup in Paul were so added, because Luke himself (whom (he says) Paul quotes) has them not, nay not to this day.
And if that can be, 'tis easy to think how these 4 words ἄχρις inline image ἄν ἔλθῃ†2 might be added; yea the whole 26 Verse—
And than theres nor ground, from Christ for the Command, nor from Paul for the continuation to the worlds end.
Nay nor then neither, if the words were indisputably Pauls.
For the scripture speaks of comings of Christ before the end of the world, John 14.18.20 and Revel. 3.20
And if they will have it of an outward†a coming as the Son of man they may find that to; Math 10.23. and Matth. 24 V.27.30.34 which last Beza interprets of the Destruction of Jerusalem Anno 71—
And many have Judgd that those things, with the Agapis, were designd onely till the Temple was destroyed—
But by what authority (save that of oral Tradition) they can necessarily conclude that those words, must needs be understood
― 418 ―
of that one coming, exclusive of all other, comings of his mentiond in Scripture, I cannot tell—
I have often wisht for you while I have had this in hand. But I must leave Sir Fr: and My Lady M— in possession, of that felicity. Tho when I came out of England I thought we should have had you here again before this.
Two things I request of you; first (if you can) to procure me an extract out of Bezas Cambridge Venerable old manusc: of the 22 Luke. v. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20.†1 Then to tell me what M:S. that is, that Dr. Hammond in his Annotations, calls the Kings m:s. which he says is written, all in Capitals and in which he finds 1 Pet. 3.21. That reading which the Vulgar had, till Beza chang'd it—from ὃ to ὧ —neither of which make any tolerable good sence. But the Doctor saith O in capitalibus, passes for inline image And than it is an easy, plain, and true sence. the Antitype Whereof Baptism now saves. And thus the States bible has it. Welks Tegenbeelt, But the Doctor to confirm his O to be inline image saith there is a manuscript in Oxford that has it inline image but he decyphers it not,†2 and I find no such thing in the Polyglot, nor in Curcelleus,†3 nor any else. And secondly to weigh my reasonings in this case, and if you can help me to any stronger, or any thing that may tend to move the point better, you will do the next generation a kindness, for I expect not that it will signify much to this—
At first reading the preface,†4 I thought verily that it had been my neighbour Jurieu,†5 tis his very Image. But some of his disciples came and told me that it was assuredly my Neighbor B—†6 I received the information with all the gravity I could be master of— and went and told Monsieur B— what I heard of him—and that I had not expected such things of him—he, supposing me to speak in earnest, began to purge himself, I told him it was needless—I was sufficiently persuaded of the contrary.
A while after, one of them came and told me it was not B— that they had askt Monsieur Jurieu, and he said it could not be B— I told him Monsieur J— could certainly get it out of his printer, in the hague, of whom he had the copy. which he promisd to doe—
― 419 ―
A while after the same man came and told me it was Versé.†1 of whom one writes to Leers from Paris, La bonne ame de Monsieur Versé va publier icy les motifs de son retour dans le sein de l'eglise.
I had in my answer ghest it to be some pauvre fripon that had attempted to borrow mony of some Q.†2 and had been disappointed. And that expected to be well received in England, and was not treated according to his own conceited merits. for which he burst out into such a rage against the Nation in generall and the Quakers in particular.
And these 2 things agree exactly to him. For after my return home I refused him mony, and all converse with him, for reasons. And I know his disappointments in England and how vehemently he rayled at Chr: Vane†3 —who he said, had promisd him entertainment.
Ad to it, strange passages not suiting any protestant. after having chargd the Quakers with being secret papists because they had never declared their Adoration of J.C. in the Sacrament Idolatry [p.94].
Himself avers, it is not [p 157]—charges it on the Parliament as an injustice [158] that they would impose such a profession upon their members, yea saith 'tis no sin, so to do, the Sacrament being an Image instituted by christ to represent him, and that [154] 'tis no sin against the second Commandement to worship J C in the presence of an Image by him instituted to represent him. nay nor yet at the foot of a crucifix nor crosse neither: tho not by him instituted to that purpose [155]
That the second Commandement onely forbids representations of the invisible Deity. and Images of creatures that are not objects of adoration.
That the command not to worship the sun moone etc—was onely given to the hebrews. That the other nations were not Idolaters that did so.
That [p 66] 'tis in the power of every christian to have the faith of miracles if they will, that it depends solely upon them, that 'tis their fault, a voluntary and criminall unbeleef in them, that they have it not. That all such have no faith, not so much as a grain of mustard seed.
― 420 ―
That [p 62] the Devill devised that Doctrine that miracles were ceased, and [p. 63.] onely to continue for a time, on purpose to hinder the propagation of the christian Religion. Which can not be propagated among the Heathens without miracles, nay nor kept up against Atheists and Deists, who, without their fault, dwelling among the christians, do mock at and reject the christian Religion, because they see it not backt by any one miracle, and therefore conclude that there never were any wrought formerly, no more than now.
Hence I conclude this man can be no protestant.
When he sayth, Transubstantiation is a ridiculous Doctrine [p 110], the worship of Images in the Roman church, espetially those of the Virgin, a gross Idolatry etc—
That he is no Papist. And so while sometimes he seems a zealous Protestant sometimes a Papist—and sometimes neither t'one nor t'other—
He gives just ground not to suspect him to be a Deist, for his lying labors added to this prevarication in his pretended Religion, are inconsistent with the Reverence due to the True God, to whom lying lips are an abomination, but to be an Ante Deist or right down Atheist—And there I leave him—
My Lady to whom give my most humble service, as also to Sir Fr. will excuse me that I have not yet performd my promise to her Ladyship or to you for her.
And now I begin to be overwhelmd with noise and hurry; I could have wisht this quiet frost had continued One month longer. But among all the ships arrived that One, which I longd most for in which are your Letters, that was forced back and when I shall have them I know not.
My young ones I heare are very well, and do go forward. And your yong friend the Archest of all—I shall have them here next week against Easter.
Shall we never have your good company more? The Baron, is still at Amsterdam has lately publisht a booke in Dutch,
Aan merckingen van Fr: mer: van Helmont over den mens en desselfs siektens alles op gewisse en onfeilbare gronden, so van de natuurlycke rede, als ervarentheit gevestigd. Het eerste Deel 't Amsterdam, by Pieter Rotterdam Boeckvercooper op de Vygendam 1692—†1
― 421 ―
with an excellent preface, in which he tels his Reader, that he needs not tell him the contents of it, seing he may read it in a short time, onely he thinks it needfull to tell him by whom, and by what occasion, it came to be written: to wit that haveing stayd some time in Amsterdam he there grew acquainted with Paulus Buchius a Physitian there in whom observing a great desire to know whether there were not certain infallible principles to judge of deseases and their causes by, he discoursed with him upon that subject, and the Doctor put it in writing, and then shewed it him. And he was mightily glad to find that he had understood him; whereupon he had discovered to him all that he knew concerning that Art, (that could be advantageous to him in his practice), but on this condition that he should serve the poor with advice, and medicines for nothing. There you have the errand of the preface, if not of the whole booke so far as the Doctor is concerned in it, who has an excellent bargain of it, to have so much knowledge so cheap. But if this pleases them, they shal have a second part.†1 He tels him further that his Paradoxal discourses,†2 is fitter to be read by one that understands his Philosophy beforehand, than by one that never understood his principles, because he finds things there not so wel demonstrated, or exprest as they might have been. So that now you may see the reason of your ignorance Sir. If you have a mind to be better informd, and have so much Dutch still, I may send you one, and then you may again read his Paradoxal discourses with more fruit. I will open no more of this matter to you, till I see how this works with you, and so I bid you good Night Sir.

1481. Edward Clarke to Locke, 19 March 1692 (1478, 1501)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 65. Printed in Rand, p. 345. Answers no. 1478.
London March the 19th 1691.
Deare Sir,
I would have Written to you by the last Post, but was dissabled then in one of my Writeing Fingers, But now I am able to hold a Pen well enough to acquaint you, That I waited on my Lord Ashley with your Letter, Which, after Hee had read, Hee frankly discoursed with mee upon it, And expressed a greate Readines<se>†a fully to Answere your Desires therein, and gave mee all the assureances imaginable That as soon as ever Hee has any thing in His Power to dispose of, Hee will increase the security for your Annuity in any manner that can reasonably bee Desiered, And this Assureance Hee promised mee to give you with the first opportunity under His own Hand, soe that I thinke now the next step that I can make towards your service in this Affayre, must bee to find out (if possible) something whereby my Lord may inlarge your security, But at present I know nothing of that Kind, and therefore shall carefully inquire into it, and imbrace all opportunityes to secure this Poynt to you:
― 423 ―
I am soe unfortunate as not to bee able to waite on you as I fully intended, but am necessitated to visitt Chipley for 10. dayes and then return hither againe, I shall goe hence Fryday next,†1 and bee here againe in Easter-Terme,†2 if I can serve you in any thing here before I goe, or whilst I am in Somersettshire, you need but lett mee know it, and I shall rejoyce in the performeance of it, Pray make my acknowlidgments to my Lady for Her last obleigeing Letter, and Her great Favours to mee, in Her Kindnesse to my sonn, and your Willingnesse to continue my sonn with you yett a longer time is the greatest obligation imaginable upon,
Your most affectionate and Faithfull servant,
EDW: CLARKE:
Mrs. Smithsby understanding I was to have visitted you this weeke, sent mee the inclosed to bee delivered to you, which I convey this way being not able to deliver it my selfe etc:

1482. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 26 March [1692] (1479, 1512)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 91-2. Copy, lacking the postscript, in Shaftesbury's letter-book, London, P.R.O. 30/24, bdle. 22, no. 2. Printed from the original in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 289-91. Year from the copy and contents. Answers no. 1479.
London March the 26th.
Mr Lock,
I am sorry that my Brother's arrivall with poor Mr Denoun should have given mee such Buisness as has hindred mee writing to you the last Post or two upon the subject you wrote mee; and that my suddain Journey into the Country with Him and the Buisness I have now to dispatch should here hinder mee from writing what I would doe and from speaking my sentiments on this head as distinctly as I would doe, had I more time.
I should have done very ill indeed to have left you in suspence ever so little a while; But that I did not: for Mr Clerk assur'd mee he would Inform you again more particularly what were my Thoughts and Resolution, and what my Power was in that Matter.
― 424 ―
All that I shall here say is, that I desire You as to what relates to mee to think that in the Honour (I mean the Fidelity and Justice) of the Family, you have now a Full assurance of what ever you could have assurance of before, and that your security is as Good for what ever my Grandfather in the Name of his Family has signified a Promise of. During my Life therefore and whilst I am master of any Proportion of what was his, You have that to your Intrest that is Equivalent to what you could have; were he (as I wish him) alive: And for what is to come after my Life; I shall take all the Care You can expect and that you now propose that you may have security Yet farther. I can now indeed doe nothing: for I have nothing. and I who hold all by Bounty and Courtesy, cannot Plead or Ask a Stronger Tye for an others Interest then that which I must be contented with for my own.
So that if there be a Danger for You should All Pass into the hands of him that is next mee without stopping ever, any part of itt, in mine; It is a Danger which all my Power cannot divert from You: for I can doe no more hereafter then now or heretofore; if I come never to possess or hold any thing from my Grand-Father more then I doe now or have heretofore.
I need not say I wish for you, after what I have said; because itt is plainly no more then wishing for my self: so much att least, as that, by the order of nature, I may Enjoy a Heritage after those who had Place and were born before mee, and before those who are after and were born since mee. I can say that this Occasion, has taught mee to goe farther in wishing then I us'd to doe: for considering my self onely; those matters are so Indifferent to mee that I never make any wish att all, about 'em.
In Concluding I onely tell you, that I hope you will be so far from doubting of mee in what Honour would Call mee to perform; that you will rather Expect from mee much more Yett in all Concerns then what That meerly would oblige mee to in your Behalf: Since You are sure of such a Place in my Freindship (if I may use such a Big-look'd Phrase) as I think scearce any can have besides your self: which may make you Compute allways with a right Estimate
how much and after what Rate I am
Your Freind and servant
ASHLEY
― 425 ―
In deep Earnest I here warn you that if (as you threaten) you renounce a Certain Office that you some time since assum'd for mee and acquitted your self faithfully of (Viz: that of the Conveyance of my Respects and Services to Lady Masham) I solemly renounce all Freindly offices for You and all the fine things I ever said. Therefore pray doe something extrordinary this time, to attone.
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 26° Mar 91
1483. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke [late March 1692?] (1271, 1490)
Rand, p. 346. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The mentions of Master's cough and Clarke's finger indicate a date about March 1692: pp. 410, 422. The message to 'Master in the country' indicates a date just before or shortly after Clarke's departure for Chipley on 25 March.
[March, 1692.]
...,
It is time to acquit myself of my obligations and return you my thanks for your kind letter, which though I owed to Mr. Clarke's finger a little, the [use of] your hand, yet being pleased when on any occasion you bestow [it] on me I cannot but acknowledge the obligation. The world goes here as it used to do, only that nobody rejoices to find ill, rainy, stormy weather that confines them within doors, when they expected fair sunshine to tempt them abroad into the fields. So that at present, bateing the [severity] of the town air and the kindness it†1 has for [weak] lungs, we have not here much advantage of you, [since we have] no other diversion here but telling of tales by the fireside; for it is both wet and cold, and for that you have more choice of matter and company.
Just here Master comes in to me and tells me he is perfectly well, and that he has not coughed at all this morning, which notwithstanding it has for some time been going with very great abatement, yet I think till now he has generally had some touches of it at his rising. But the amendments of it of late have been to so little a remain of it that I judge it not to be any care or [further trouble] about it. I hope you and my wife, and her sister, are all well in
― 426 ―
[London]†1 We are all so here at present. Our service, love and duty to all there respectively. I am,
Dear Madam,
your most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
My humble service to Master in the country.

1485. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 1/11 April 1692 (1473, 1493)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 61-2. Answers no. 1473.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Tuis ante duodecim circiter diës mihi traditis è vestigio respondere constitueram: verum impetum meum occupationes gravissimæ retardarunt. Wetstenius diu cunctatus, et de die in diem editionem Sententiarum S.Officii differens, tandem, cum dicerem moras illas mihi esse molestas, meque historiam a me conscriptam seorsim editurum, incaluit, et editionem jam maturare cupit; duo præla simul fatigabuntur, ut opus integrum, quod in†a- folio, litera majori-†a quam Augustinam†b †1 vocant, ducentis circiter foliis
― 428 ―
constabit, intra quatuor vel quinque mensium spatium ad finem perduci possit. Sex folia hebdomatim singulis prælis excudentur. Proxima hebdomade operi accingemur. Itaque præparare mihi oportuit mea ad editionem. Verum non sine molesto labore id fieri potuit, quoniam ex autoribus quibusdam recens mihi comparatis varia in meo opere emendanda et supplenda sunt. Ante triduum e Lusitania accepi Ludovicum a Paramo de Origine et Progressu Officii S.Inquisitionis, etc.†1 quem librum magno labore hic frustra quæsivi: Hic mihi novus enatus labor. Si mihi ante biennium hic liber ad manum fuisset, immenso, quem nunc exhausi, parcere potuissem labori: Commodum vero accidit, quod ante inchoatam editionem mihi allatus sit Ulyssipone. Aliquot itaque dierum moram facile occupationibus his, quas te promotas cupere scio, condonabis. Moneri forte posset lector in præfatione, alterum ejusmodi volumen Monspessulis ante decennium esse visum, ut, si hæc editio placeat, alterum illud investigari possit.†2 De tua valetudine valde fui sollicitus, non vero de aliquo, ne minimo quidem, amicitiæ tuæ, quam et sinceram et constantem esse certus sum, frigusculo. Gaudeo te non morbo, sed occupationibus a scribendo
― 429 ―
cohibitum. Zelus Theologicus contra autorem libri paradoxi de natura spirituum quotidie magis incalescit. Classis Amstelodamensis mense Januario ipsum decem circiter hebdomadibus a muneris sui functione suspensum esse voluit: illis elapsis functionem suam repeteret. Verum undique insurgit zelus fratrum pro gloria Dei certantium, perinde uti olim totus Israel, cum duæ tribus cum dimidia altare ultra Jordanem erexissent.†1 Hoc enim exemplum zelo suo prætexunt. Classicum cecinit Consistorium Roterodamense, ad omnium civitatum Consistoria missis literis. Illius exemplum alia <Consistoria>†a et Classes sequuntur, adeo ut nunc quotidie Consistoriales et Classicales literæ ad Consistorium Amstelodamense et Roterodamense prodeant. Omnes librum condemnant, autorem exautorari cupiunt nisi palinodiam canat, et quidam excommunicari. Causam ad Synodos Hollandiæ Australis et Borealis referre cupiunt: quin et in suarum Provinciarum Synodis eam se judicaturos dicunt. Adeo ut Fratrum suorum manus evasurus minime sit. Consistorium Amstelodamense decrevit, ut sententia suspensionis prorogetur ad tempus Synodi Borealis, nisi interea cordata palinodia Ecclesiæ satisfaciat, et scandalum datum reparet. Ita vides unanimem et minime languidum zelum fratrum
― 430 ―
pro honore Dei certantium. Scotorum zelum aliquoties in novellis nostris legi: per antiperistasin non incalescere solum, sed in fulmen converti videtur ille zelus. Miracula post Apostolorum tempora edita fuisse in Ecclesia Christiana plures ex antiquioribus narrant. Verum nullum hactenus vidi, qui se præsente ea facta testetur, aut se a teste oculato ea habere. Narrant quæ ante sua tempora, aut in locis procul a se dissitis gesta sunt, et quorum rumores ad aures suas pervenerunt. Ita ut rectissime scripserit Melchior Canus Dominicanus de Locis Theologicis lib. XI. fol. 657.†1 Negare non possumus, viros aliquando gravissimos, in divorum præsertim prodigiis describendis, sparsos rumores et excepisse, et scriptis etiam ad posteros retulisse. Qua in re, ut mihi quidem videtur, aut nimium illi sibi, aut fidelium certe vulgo indulserunt: quod vulgus sentiebant non tantum ea facile miracula credere, sed impense etiam flagitare. Itaque signa nonnulla et prodigia sancti quoque memoriæ prodiderunt, non quod ea libenter credidissent; sed ne deësse fidelium votis viderentur. Id vero eo magis sibi licere existimarunt, quod intellexerunt, autoribus nobilissimis placuisse, veram historiæ legem esse, ea scribere quæ vulgo vera haberentur. etc. Confirmant hoc Cani judicium
― 431 ―
ipsa quæ narrantur miracula, et occasio quæ illis inserviisse dicitur: miracula enim illa sæpe nullum generi humano præstant usum, et occasio nullum flagitavit miraculum. Possem id variis allatis exemplis ostendere; verum superfluum id foret. Gregorius Thaumaturgus dicitur floruisse tertio sæculo, in persecutione Decii. Varia illius miracula narrat Basilius Magnus†1 libro de Spiritu S. cap.XXIX. et illius frater Gregorius Nyssenus†2 in vita Gregorii; de quo Nysseno Erasmus scribit, quod ipsi placuerit pia simplicitas.†3 Verum si autores hi ad manum non sint, omnia aut pleraque collegit Baronius, tomo 2. præsertim ad annum 253. §130 et seqq.†4 Dicitur precibus suis ingens saxum loco movisse, alii ajunt, montem: inde Thaumaturgus dictus, quod fide suâ montem transtulerit. Verum ego me non admodum in antiquitate ecclesiastica, cujus historia admodum fallax et incerta est, versatum fateor: malo horas meas investigationi Scripturæ sacræ et præceptorum divinorum meditationi impendere. Venius noster jam ruri degit, admodumque ipsi vita hæc rustica placere videtur: Villam habet satis amplam, et vicinos, sibi jam a pluribus annis familiares, ex
― 432 ―
præcipuis hujus urbis familiis. Videtur tamen uxoris obitus senium ejus accelerasse. Statui paucas intra hebdomadas ad ipsum excurrere. Hac æstate occupatissimus ero; prælum quippe typographicum egregie me exercebit. Nam præter opus hoc S.Officii, sub prælo habeo omnes Episcopii conciones, antehac tribus voluminibus in quarto editas, nunc autem cum non exiguo auctario concionum festalium et aliarum nunquam editarum in folio edendas.†1 Maluissem singula sensim edere; verum hunc Wetstenii fervorem arripere placuit, ne forte iterum languescat, et penitus exstinguatur. Rogo D.Cudworthæ humillima mea officia offeras, plurimamque a me salutem dicas. Uxor ac liberi plurimum te salvere jubent, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 11 Aprilis

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I had decided to send an immediate answer to your letter, which was delivered to me some twelve days ago; but very serious employments checked my impulse. Wetstein, who had been lingering all this time and putting off the publication of the Sententiae of the Holy Office from day to day, on my telling him that these delays were irksome to me and that I would publish the account separately, at last grew warm and now wishes to expedite publication; two presses will be kept working simultaneously, so that the whole work, which will consist of about two hundred sheets in folio, in the larger type which they call Augustijn,†1 can be finished within [p. 428] the space of four or five months. Six sheets a week will be printed on each press. We shall be ready for work next week. Accordingly it was necessary for me to prepare my material for publication. This, however, could not be done without troublesome labour, since various passages in my work have to be corrected and supplemented from certain authors whose works I have recently obtained. Three days ago I received from Portugal Luis de Paramo's De Origine et Progressu Officii S. Inquisitionis, etc.,†1 a book which I had with great labour sought for here, but in vain; here is fresh labour arisen for me. If this book had been available for me two years ago I could have been spared an immense labour which I have now performed; still it happened opportunely that it reached me from Lisbon before publication began. So you will readily accept the delay of a few days for the sake of these employments, which I know you wish to be advanced. The reader might perhaps be informed in the preface that another book of the kind was seen at Montpellier ten years ago, so that if this publication is approved the other can be sought for.†2 I have been very anxious about your health, but not about any possible cooling, even the least, in your friendship, which I am certain is sincere and constant. I am glad that you have been prevented from writing not by illness but by employments. Theological zeal against the author of that [p. 429] paradoxical book on the nature of spirits is growing hotter every day. The Presbytery of Amsterdam in January wished him to be suspended from the performance of his office for about ten weeks; at the end of that period he was to resume his functions. But the zeal of brethren striving for the glory of God is mounting on all sides, just like all Israel in old time, when the two and a half tribes had set up an altar beyond Jordan;†1 for this is the example they use as a pretext for their zeal. The call to battle has been sounded by the Consistory of Rotterdam, in letters sent to the Consistories of all the cities. Other Consistories and Presbyteries are following its example, with the result that Consistorial and Presbyterial letters addressed to the Consistories of Amsterdam and Rotterdam are now appearing daily. They all condemn the book; they desire that the author be discharged unless he recants, and some, that he be excommunicated. They wish to refer the case to the Synods of South and North Holland; they even say that they will try it in the Synods of their own Provinces. So he will scarcely be able to escape from the hands of his brethren. The Consistory of Amsterdam has decreed that the sentence of suspension be extended to the date of the Northern Synod, unless in the mean time he satisfies the church by a judicious(?) recantation, and so repairs the scandal he has occasioned. So you see how unanimous and how far from languid is the zeal of the brethren who [p. 430] are striving for the honour of God. I have read from time to time in our newspapers about the zeal of the Scots; it seems that through contrariety that zeal is not only growing hot but turning into a thunderbolt. Many of the older writers tell of miracles performed in the Christian Church after the Apostles' times. So far, however, I have not seen one of them who testifies to such things having been done in his presence, or to having been informed of them by an eye-witness. They tell of things that were done before their own times, or in places far away from them, reports of which have come to their ears. So, as Melchior Cano, a Dominican, says very justly in his work De Locis Theologicis, book II, p. 657:†1 'We cannot deny that sometimes very grave men, especially in describing the wonderful acts of the saints, have not only listened to scattered reports but have even recounted them to posterity in their writings. In this matter, as it seems to me at least, they were overindulgent either to themselves or certainly to the generality of the faithful; for they felt that the generality not only readily believed in such miracles but even eagerly demanded them. Accordingly even saintly men have recorded sundry signs and wonders, not that they willingly believed in them, but lest they should seem to be neglecting the wishes of the faithful. They were indeed the readier to think this practice permissible because they understood that the most eminent authorities were of opinion that it is a right and proper law of history to write what is held to be true by the [p. 431] generality,' etc. This opinion of Cano is confirmed by the miracles themselves that are narrated and by the occasions which are said to have served for them; for those miracles are often of no use to mankind and the occasions demanded no miracles. I could demonstrate this by giving various examples; but that would be superfluous. Gregory the Thaumaturge is said to have flourished in the third century, during the persecution of Decius. Various miracles of his are narrated by Basil the Great†1 in his book De Spiritu Sancto, chap. XXIX, and by his brother Gregory of Nyssa†2 in his life of Gregory; of the Nyssene Erasmus writes that his pious simplicity pleased him.†3 If, however, these authors are not available, all or most of the material has been collected by Baronius, volume 2, especially under the year 253, § 130 and following.†4 He is said to have moved by his prayers a huge rock from its position, or some say a mountain; hence he was called the Miracle-worker, because by his faith he had removed a mountain. But I confess that I am not well versed in ecclesiastical antiquity, of which the history is largely fallacious and uncertain; I prefer to devote my time to searching into Holy Writ and to meditating upon the divine precepts. Our friend Veen is now living in the country, and this rural life seems to please him greatly; he has a large enough country house and for neighbours people belonging to the principal [p. 432] families of this city, and with whom he has been on familiar terms for years past. It seems, however, that the death of his wife has hastened his decline. I intend to run out and see him in a few weeks' time. This summer I shall be very busy, since the printing-press will keep me hard at work. For besides this work on the Holy Office I have in the press all the sermons of Episcopius, previously published in three volumes in quarto, and now to be published in folio with no small supplement of festival sermons and others that have never been published.†1 I should have preferred to publish them at leisure one by one; but it seemed well to seize this ardour of Wetstein's, lest it should perhaps languish once again and be totally extinguished. I beg you to offer my most humble service to Mrs. Cudworth and to give her my best wishes. My wife and children send you their greetings, as do I first and foremost
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 11 April
1692

1486. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 1/11 April 1692 (1446, 1511)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 54-5, 78. An excerpt printed in King, p. 231; the whole in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 50-3.
A Amsterdam le 11 d'Avril 1692.
Il y a, Monsieur, dix ou douze jours, que j'envoiai à Mr. Furly deux exemplaires de mes petits Ouvrages de Philosophie, dont l'un relié en deux Tomes, et en marroquin rouge est pour vous, et l'autre en basane et en un volume pour M.L'Evêque de Salisbury, à qui vous aurez bien la benté de le faire rendre. M. Furly m'a répondu qu'il a remis mon paquet à un maître de vaisseau, qui a promis de le rendre fidelement. Je ne vous ferai pas un nouveau compliment, sur la maniére obligeante dont vous recevez ma dedicace. Vous verrez ce qu'elle dit, et vous comprendrez aisément que j'ai ménagé vôtre modestie. Mr. Furly m'a aussi envoié un paquet de vôtre part, où je trouve Pocok on Joel, un petit livre of the lowering of interest etc.†1 qui me paroît très-joli et très-solide, et le même recueuil de traitez περὶ τῆς T. dont je vous avois écrit. Il m'avoit été envoié par un homme qui m'est inconnu, mais qui se signe Firmin,†2 sur la premiere page. Peut-être le connoitrez vous. Quoi qu'il en soit, je vous suis extrémement obligé. Marquez moi, s'il vous plait, quel Tome de la Bibl.Univ. vous avez reçu le dernier. Quoi que je ne la fasse pas, je m'en suis réservé quelques exemplaires.
Pour répondre à vos Lettres j'avois bien parlé, pendant la vie de M. Boyle de ce dont je vous ai écrit, dans une Lettre qui lui fut renduë tard, et qui étoit dans le paquet, par lequel vous reçutes le dernier Tome de la Bibliotheque Un.†3 Depuis le bon homme a été dans une perpetuelle langueur. Je n'ai pu encore savoir si mon livre lui a été rendu, quoique j'aie bien sû que celui qui le portoit étoit arrivé assez à temps. Je vous serai obligé, si vous voulez bien prendre la peine de vous en informer à quelque occasion. L'exemplaire de ma Logique, que je lui envoiois, étoit relié comme le vôtre.
Je n'ai pas d'autre ami, en qui je me puisse fier, et qui pût m'aider dans ce que je souhaiterois. que M. Burnet Evêque de Sal. qui m'a
― 434 ―
plusieurs fois promis de bouche et dans des Lettres qu'il le feroit. Il a fort approuvé mon dessein sur la Bible, et m'offrit lors que je le lui envoiai dix livres sterling de pension, de sa part, pendant sept ans. Je le remerciai, parce que ces sortes d'offres, dont il faut faire ressouvenir à plusieurs reprises ceux qui les font, si l'on veut en profiter, ne m'ont jamais accommodé. Je croi néanmoins qu'il me veut quelque bien, parce qu'il a parlé plusieurs fois de moi, depuis qu'il est Evêque, en termes obligeans, et que j'ai fait beaucoup valoir <ses>†a ouvrages, en les traduisant.†1 Mais ces Messieurs sont si occupez, qu'à moins d'être sur les lieux, ils oublient tout. Je lui ai envoié de temps en temps diverses petites pieces, sur quoi il m'a remercié dans des Lettres que j'ai reçues de lui, depuis qu'il est dans la fortune. Peut-être qu'il pensera à moi, en voiant le volume que je lui envoie. Je sai les formalitez par ou il faut passer pour entrer dans l'Egl. Anglicane, et comme je ne les établirois pas, si cela dépendoit de moi, je les supporterois, comme une infinité d'autres choses, sur lesquelles il faut passer legerement, ou gronder tout le genre humain, et devenir inutile à soi et aux autres.
C'est dommage que les deux Diss. MSS. que j'ai demeurent supprimées.†2 Je ne croi pas que l'on pût reconnoître qu'elles sont traduites, à moins qu'on ne le dît. Dans une matiére de cette nature, où je ne saurois manquer de prendre le sens de l'Auteur, j'y donne un tour d'Original qui ne sent point du tout la Traduction. Je n'avois pas encore conclu pour cela avec l'Imprimeur, qui faisoit difficulté, à cause de la petitesse de l'ouvrage, et depuis vôtre Lettre, je ne lui en ai plus parlé. Les Dissert. que je vous écrivois, que l'on pourroit donner au public, si j'en avois le temps, se trouveroient assez facilement, quoi que ma mémoire ne m'en fournisse pas à présent un grand nombre. Il y en auroit cinq ou six de M. Dodwell†3 et de J. Smith,†4 celle de M. Cumberland des Mesures des Hebreux.†5 Diverses Dissertations Françoises touchant les
― 435 ―
Medailles et les antiquitez Romaines, comme une fort curieuse de M. Rainssant des jeux séculaires,†1 quelques unes de M. Nicaise,†2 que j'ai vuë depuis peu de temps. Plusieurs de la même matiere écrites en Italien, comme sont celles du Chev. Orsati,†3 quelquesunes de F. Redi,†4 qui n'ont point été traduites. En recherchant, on en trouveroit plus qu'on n'en auroit besoin, et plusieurs Amis en fourniroient de MSS. pourvu qu'on leur en donnât quelques exemplaires imprimez, ce qui seroit très-facile. Mais il faudroit n'avoir autre chose à faire.
Pour vôtre question, touchant les Miracles, qui ont été faits après le temps des Apôtres, vous trouverez un recueuil de ce qu'il y a de plus remarquable là dessus, dans la 2. Dissert. Irenaïque de M. Dodwel.†5 Cet homme, quoi qu'horriblement entêté, et incapable de raisonnement exact et rigoureux, dit mille choses très-remarquables, et dignes d'être luës. On crieroit ici furieusement contre qui en diroit autant.
J'avois envie de faire contre M. Witsius Professeur fanatique d'Utrecht, qui m'a déchiré dans ses Miscellanea S.†6 aussi bien que Mr. Spencer de Cambrige,†7 qu'il maltraite terriblement, un petit traité, dont la matiére est toute prête, intitulé De argumento theologico ab invidia ducto,†8 où je ferois voir par des exemples tirez de l'histoire ancienne et moderne quo pacto invidia moveatur.†9 J'y mettrois divers exemples de Witsius, quoi qu'en passant. Cela seroit assez joli, et pourroit être lû des Réformez un peu raisonnables, sans aucun scandale, car je m'abstiendrois des exemples, qui les pourroient choquer. Vous verri<ez>†a là depuis combien de temps on réfute ceux à qui l'on ne sauroit répondre, en les rendant odieux au peuple. Mais je n'ai pas le temps, à cause de mon grand Ouvrage,
― 436 ―

qui s'avance.†1 Dans un an et demi, j'espere qu'il paroîtra. Il y aura bien des choses nouvelles, et peu de chose dans les Comment. vulgaires, qui soit de quelque usage, que l'on n'y trouve.
Si je n'étois pas distrait, par des Leçons ennuieuses, on verroit le reste bien-tôt après, mais ubi non potes quod vis, hoc velis quod potes.†2 Si j'avois un bénefice, sine cura animarum,†3 comme l'on dit, qui me donnât cent livres sterling en quelque petite ville d'Angleterre, beato otio fruerer, cujus tamen rationem baud illibenter redderem.†4 J'ai à present autant ici, pour cette année et la prochaine, de nos gens, mais la dépense est excessive dans cette ville, comment que l'on puisse faire, et l'humeur des Consistoires est si peu bienfaisante, que je ne sai qu'esperer. Ce qu'on appelle ἀπειροκαλία†5 est un vice si répandu ici, que vous ne sauriez le croire. Quoi qu'il en soit, il faudra faire son devoir. Si vous voyez vous même M. L'Evêque de Salisbury, faites moi la grace de me marquer ce qu'il vous aura dit. Il a un Cousin, nommé Jonston,†6 secretaire pour les affaires d'Ecosse et d'Irlande, qui m'a quelque petite obligation, aussi bien que l'Evêque, quoi que je ne leur en aie aucune. C'est néanmoins un assez galant homme, autant que j'en ai pu juger. Si ces Messieurs vouloient emploier un credit, qu'ils emploient pour bien d'autres, ils pourroient beaucoup. Il faudra louër Dieu de tout. Je le prie de tout mon coeur, Monsieur, de vous conserver la santé, et de repandre sur vous ses bénedictions, comme étant très-sincerement, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: These for Master John Locke at Mrs. Smithsbys in Dorset Coort in Channel row, Westminster. London.
Postmark: AP 9 (?)
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 11 Apr 92 Answered 2° May.

Sir
I thank you for your advice as to the diet drink. I think there is no great need of it, they have good whey. they may drink that.
mr Jones†1 had your letter and I finde he wil restore your linen etc and the other lumber continues in the house. I have nothing more to say as yet about myne own affair; they move very slowly at the Admiralty board because very full of busines. I have received a parcell of books; they came from Sir Patience Ward†2 who sent them by a porter who demanded 18d and would not depart without a shilling; if he would have been so kinde as to have sent me a lyne or two by the penny post of them I would have gon for them. it came as the porter said from the Custom house but is directed to Mr Joseph Wright for you; the letter inclosed, directed on both sides came with it; the other 4 came from severall hands. there is a parcell which I presume may have a doz letters in it, directed to Mr Wright for you as the great parcel, which I think is too big to send by the post; and an other round parcell came this day by the penny post that I take to be a sermon or some book not much bigger. I am
Sir Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

1489. Dr. Caspar Sibelius or Sibly to Locke, 5 April 1692 (961)
B.L., MS. Locke, c. 18, ff. 110-11. The date may be either old or new style.
Monsieur,
Il est si naturel aux grandes ames d'etre sensibles aux moindres honestetez qu'on leur temoigne, que je ne fus nulement surpris d'avoir veu couler de votre plume tant d'expressions de reconnoissance pour ma personne qui meritoit si peu, J'aurois voulu trouver les occasions de vous pouvoir assurer avec plus des marques de respect et d'amitie du desir que j'aurois de contribuer a vos divertissements et de vous étre utile a quelque chose, mais je n'ay pas encore ete assez heureux pour cela, et me voyant dans l'impuissance de me les procurer a moy méme, j'ay cru qu'il me seroit plus honorable de rester dans la silence, que de vous importuner ou par ma presence ou par mes écrits. Ce sont ces sentimens de respect, Monsieur, qui m'ont empeché jusques a present de continuer nostre correspondence des lettres si heureusement en Hollande entretenue, et Dieu sait si je ne fusse pas demeuré eternellement dans ce silence, en cas qu'une yoye et le bonheur, dont toutes nostres Provinces avec l'Angleterre resentissoient, ne m'eut reveillé de l'assoupissement ou j'etois, Il n'y a eu guere des personnes, en qui il' n'ait operé, mais sur tout, je puis dire qu'il a fait en moy un effet inconcevable, lors que j'ay consideré qu'il trainoit apres luy les nouvelles de votre retablissement et dans vos biens et dans vos dignitez, Ouy, Monsieur, je participe tellement a ce bonheur, que quand il nous devroit étre commun je ne le pourrois pas davantage, Cette annee plus heureuse que les precedentes et en la quelle je prie le Ciel de vous combler de ses faveurs, semble ne s'offrir a nous que pour me donner lieu de vous en feliciter, et de vous etrener de tous les voeux dont je suis capable pour votre bonheur et pour votre repos, Mais au moins, Monsieur, que l'eclat de cette grandement, dont vous reyouy de nouveau ne vous empeche
― 441 ―
pas de jetter parfois l'oeil sur ceux de vos amis que vous laissez en nos pays, Vous estez trop genereux pour refuser votre assistance a ceux que vous avez bien daigné honorer de votre amitie, Et puisque vous estez tout puissant dans ce lieu ou vous estez, que la Medicine est en nostre Ville et Province d'Overÿssel peu estimee, et que ceux qui l'exercent en peuvent a peine subsister, j'ay resolu de quiter ma chere patrie et de chercher ma fortune ailleurs. Je ne doute pas, Monsieur, que les lettres de vos Amis par moy vous envoÿees Samedy passe,†1 vous seront donnees, dans les quelles je croy vous avez appris mon Intention. Je souhaiterois fort d'avoir l'honneur de vous voire et aboucher avec vous concernant les moÿens pour m'avancer en ces lieux. Plusieurs des mes Amis icy a Londres m'ont persuade de me transporter en Irlande et aller a Dublin pour de raisons suivantes: parce que a Dublin il n'y a pas tant des Medicins, et Scavans comme icy a Londres; aussi il fait a Dublin non pas si cher vivre: Et pour cela je trouveray plutost la ma fortune dans la Practique qu'icy. Je vous prie, Monsieur, que vous me fassiez la grace de me donner votre avis par une lettre de response aussi tost que vous pourrois, si votre presence ne permetteroit pas de parler de bouche en bouche. Si vous aviez l'occasion de me pouvoir procurer quelque avantage dans mon dessein par lettres des Recommendations a quelque un, ce seroit un bien que ny moy ny les miens n'oublieront jamais, mais pour lequel nous vous aurons une eternelle obligation, Je finirois icy ma lettre, en souhaitant fort de vous voir devant mon depart, J'espere que vous me ferez l'honneur de m'apprendre votre demeuree, et l'etat au quel vous vous trouvez a present, puisque je suis l'homme du Monde qui prend le plus d'interest dans votre conservation, et qui est avec tout le respect imaginable
Monsieur
Vôtre treshumble et tresobeissant Serviteur

1492. John Norris to Locke, 14 April [1692] (1505)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 163-4. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 1505.
The writer, 1657-1711, graduated B.A. of Oxford in 1680 and was a fellow of All Souls College from 1680 to 1689. He graduated M.A. in 1684 and was then ordained. In 1689 he became rector of Newton St. Loe in Somerset. About September of this year he was presented by Pembroke to the rectory of Bemerton, between Wilton and Salisbury in Wiltshire, where he remained for the rest of his life. He studied Plato and corresponded with Dr. Henry More, but is 'chiefly valuable as a solitary representative of Malebranche's theories in England'. He was an able and productive writer: D.N.B.; Thomas Naish, Diary, ed. D. Slatter, 1965, p. 26; R. Acworth, La philosophie de John Norris, 1657-1712, 1975.
Norris addressed The Theory and Regulation of Love, 1688, and Reflections upon the Conduct of Human Life, 1690 (2nd ed., 1691), to Lady Masham. He appended 'Cursory Reflections' on Locke's Essay to his Christian Blessedness, 1690: above, pp. 145-6, 150; there was a second edition this year.
Bemerton April 14
Mr Lock
That which occasions my writing to you now would have made me write to you sooner if I had been sooner inform'd how much I was endebted to your Interest for my Lord Pembroke's late Favour to me. Sir I have a very gratefull sense, of your great generosity towards me, which indeed is of so rare and singular a nature that it surprizes me no lesse than it obliges me, and raises my wonder to
― 444 ―
as high a pitch as it does my gratitude. I am only troubled that I have no other way to expres my thankfull resentment of so uncommon a Kindnes, than that Common one of writing, for methinks I would do something extraordinary in return to a Favour that is so very much so. But Sir I hope your goodnes and my inability will procure acceptance for a verbal Acknowledgement, tho upon all accounts defective but only in that reality whereby I assure you that I am
Your most obliged servant
J. NORRIS.

1493. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 15/25 April 1692, with postscript by A. de Greve (1485, 1504; 1787)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 63-4. Answered by no. 1504. For de Greve see no. 868 n.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Quoniam communis noster amicus D.Cyprianus iter in Angliam meditatur, neque inde ad nos rediturus est, nisi te in Anglia compellaverit, commodissimam hanc ad te scribendi occasionem minime negligere potui. Quamvis enim nihil novi quod scribam habeam, utpote qui nuper prolixiores ad te dederim literas, hoc unum ut ex me audias tibi gratum esse scio, me omnesque meos optime valere. Historiæ S.Officii editionem jam jam inchoabimus, eamque brevi ad finem perducemus. Tres priores libros jam penitus in
― 445 ―
ordinem redegi, et editioni paratos habeo. In quarto quædam sunt supplenda, et paucis in locis ordo aliquatenus <immutandus>:†a quod paucos intra dies a me perfectum erit. Ita tandem opus illud in lucem prodibit: Spero id te etiam hoc anno lecturum. D.Clericus novam Bibliorum Versionem, notis illustratam, adornat: ad instar speciminis in Obadiam quod edidit: jam magnam Pentateuchi partem absolvit. Uxor ejus nuper peperit, verum infans non est vitalis. Processus contra autorem paradoxi de natura spirituum tractatus jam adornari incipit: Omnia illi infausta præsagio. Verum ad finem perduci non poterit, nisi in Synodo, quæ mense Julio ordinarie convocari solet. Hanc scribo in ædibus D. de Greve, Jurisconsulti, cujus uxor nuper filiam peperit: Ipse cum uxore plurimum te salvere jubet. Etiam uxor mea liberique plurimam tibi salutem dicunt.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
As our common friend Mr. Cyprianus intends to travel to England and will not return to us without calling on you in England, I could on no account neglect this very convenient opportunity of writing to you. For although I have nothing new to write to you, seeing that I recently sent you a rather lengthy letter, this one thing I know you will be glad to hear from me, that I and all mine are in the best of health. We are now about to start the publication of the account of the Holy Office, and we shall finish it in a short time. I have already brought the first three books completely into order and have [p. 445] them ready for publication. In the fourth there are some additions to be made, and in a few places the order has to be somewhat altered; I shall finish this in a few days. So at last that work will see the light; I hope that you may even read it this year. Mr. Le Clerc is preparing a new translation of the Bible, illustrated with notes, like the specimen which he published on Obadiah; he has already completed a large part of the Pentateuch. His wife has recently given birth, but the infant is not likely to live. The proceeding against the author of the paradoxical treatise on the nature of spirits is now preparing; I foresee misfortunes of every sort for him. It cannot be finished, however, except in the Synod, which is ordinarily convoked in July. I am writing this in the house of Mr. de Greve, the jurist, whose wife has recently given birth to a daughter; he and his wife send you their greetings. My wife and children also send you theirs.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Utrecht 25 April 1692. In haste.

In haste.

I have reciv'd yours to me and in it another to Mr Tyrrell authorizing him to deliver me the bookes you are soe kind to lend me:†1 Thankes are the least I can returne for soe great a favour, and I shall endeavour by making good use of them to answer the end you have proposed by lending them; I was in this country when your letter's came hither, and have not as yett sent Mr Tyrrell that directed to him, thinking it could be to noe purpose since I shall not be in Oxford till the Act-Term,†2 at which time I shall not be backward in delivering it to him. Sir
Now the churlish weather is almost over I was thinking within a Post or two to put you in mind of my desire to see you here where you shall be as welcome as I can make you. ― 451 ―
'Concerning miracles there is a notable passage or two in Irenaeus l.22, c. 56 recited by Eusebius l.5.c.17. The miraculous refection of the Roman army by rain at the prayers of a Christian Legion (thence called fulminatrix) is mentioned by Ziphiline apud Dionem in Marco Imp. and by Tertullian Apolog. c.5, and ad Scap. c.4 and by Eusebius l.5, c. 5 Hist.Eccl. and in Chronico, and acknowledged by the Emperor Marcus in a letter as Tertullian mentions. The same Tertullian some where challenges the heathens to produce a Demoniack and he will produce a man who shall cast out the Dæmon. For this was the language of the ancients for curing Lunaticks. I am told that Sir Hen. Yelverton in a book about the truth of Christianity†1 has writ well of the ancient miracles, but the book I never saw. Concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus see Gregory Nyssen in ejus vita and Basil de Spiritu sancto c. 29.'†2
My humble service to Sir Francis and his Lady. I am
Your most humble Servant
IS. NEWTON.
Cambridge May 3d 1692.

1501. Locke to Edward Clarke, 13 May 1692 (1481, 1502)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 58-9. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 234; Rand, pp. 346-7.
Bishopstartford 13 May 92
Dear Sir
I am got thus far homewards from Cambridg where I have been for two days drawn thither by businesse that was very necessary to be dispatchd. I staid there lesse time than I could well have spent there and was very much importuned to But I left not Mrs Cudworth soe well restord to her health as to be sure she would need noe more assistance which made my Lady†1 very earnestly presse my speedy returne from Cambridg and twas with much difficulty I got leave to goe thither. I here meet with yours of the 10th instant, which is the first and only one of yours is come to my hands since I saw you.
The consultation you would have me be at about the health of our infirme freind†2 I know not what to say to, You know I wish him very well, but my notions in physick are soe different from the method which now obteins that I am like to doe litle good and not being of the Colledg†3 can make noe other figure there but of an Unskilfull empirick, and noe doubt any thing I should offer would seeme as strange to his physitians as the way you tell me they take with him seems strange to me. But as every ones hypothesis is, soe is his reason disposd to judg both of disease and medicines. But I hope the yonge gent will doe well without me, and that the danger will be over by that time this comes to you. I hope my Lady will not as you say blame my absence considering the necessity cald me away and her son was in soe good hands that I concluded there was noe need of me in that case and I shall never omitt any occasion wherein I may be serviceable. In your next pray doe but name the person of whom I may enquire upon occasion for what belongs to me.†4 you need but name him without troubleing your self to mention again what you informe me in yours that I have now before me, is done. I have also received this post a Letter from

1502. Locke to Edward Clarke, 16 May 1692 (1501, 1526)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 58. Faded. Printed in Rand, pp. 348-9.
Oates 16° May 92
Dear Sir
Yours of the 10th I met at Bishop Startford on friday last in my returne from Cambridg and answerd it from thence and since that I have yours of the 14th. these are all I have received from you since I came out of towne soe that of the 4 you have writ 2 I see are lost. You know any desire of yours or any of my freinds there to bring me to town are not very forwardly resisted by me at any time and therefor I thinke I shall come. But whip me if I can thinke what I shall doe in a crowd†a or a smoake. I finde my head as litle suited to one as my lungs to the other. And I am soe morose grown or moped by a country retirement that all the world appears a bedlam to me and a madnesse to medle with it. Perhaps you will thinke me distracted for writeing thus and possibly you have reason, and we may perhaps have that mutuall compassion to pitty one an other, and that perhaps is the utmost either of us can doe
― 455 ―
Haveing received from John Wheelock a letter wherein my Lady talkes of building a house on Kingston farme and deducting the taxes out of my annuity to help pay for building a house on it for the improvement of the farme. I have writ the inclosed answer. I know not whether the indignation to be soe used has made it a litle too warme. If you thinke not, pray seale it and deliver it and acquaint my Lady that I have writ to John Wheelock and to what I have said there (which I would desire you to bid him shew her) be pleased to adde in your discourse to her that by the condition in the setlement of the annuity I have a right in law to £100 per annum, what ever others may have advised her to. This I thought a great deale better to be said by you to her than be put into my letter wherein I thought it best only to insist on my Lords intention to me in generall, and the pretences I had to be better used, for the other insisted on I suspected would looke more like threatening, though from you it will be an advice to her, when you informer I have a covenant in my grant to be paid £100 per annum. If you thinke the letter not fit to be deliverd I must then beg you to discourse the whole matter with her and represent to her how litle such an usage of <m>e†a will suit my Lords Kindenesse and intention to me or be for the honour of his memory and my Ladys Credit. I would not trouble you again in this affair but that I know you can doe more in it than any body and it is necessary to stop it in the begining. For if I once admit of any abatement I know there will be noe end of it. I thank you for your good news and am
Dear Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE

1503. John Wheelock to Locke, 31 May 1692 (1500, 1642)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 86-7.
May 31:92
Sir,
I received your second Letter—the first I had answerd by Writeing but heareing mr Clarke was goeing downe to you I presumed to Acquaint him with my Ladys answer, to your first, which I suppose he enformd you with—or else I should have been a fraid of Incuring both yours and my Ladys Displeasure
The contents of whose answer was—That she had been often enform'd by severall that she might (I may say she was encouradged to) throwe the Farme into your manadgement—At the Least she might and ought to deduct the Taxes. The first she fully resolved against: and declined the offering of the Latter (by reason she had received severall favours from you and knew noe other way to retalliate them) But seeing the Taxes were Like too continue—And being informed of the Declineing state of the Farme and of the Necessity ther was of Building an house—She thought (if it was your right to pay them) You must take it Kindly, if she applyd them to such an end that you might find and have the Bennifit of—if after her's and Lord Ashleys Deaths it were thrown into your hands (which if theirs should happen before yours I feare you'l finde too true)—And to my Knowledge she designd to have taken but part of the Taxes, Past†a and to have added the rest out of her own Purse) But since you say that you ought not to allow them, she comanded me to assure you she will never offer to deduct them; for she says she has as much reason to rely on your Word as on any Persons; and she has noe knowledge of the Instrument or agreement betwext you and my Lord— Therefore she assures you she'l never throw it into your hands as Long as she's able to pay it; nor deduct the taxes since you say it was my Lords full intent, that you should have a 100 per annum Cleere. This is the full contents of what my Lady said on that subject which I acquainted mr Clark with: soe that I hope none has reason to complayne of me in this affaire besides my Lady whom I have brought into an noose by building an house at her own Charge which might with some small Loss have been Let a Lone for her Life and now it will Cost her a Considerable some.
― 457 ―
I hope this will Learne me to know the trueth of things (and not to trust to others assertions) before I put any Person (by whom I'm Imployd) on a Cirtaine charge or an agrement for the Payment of moneys—Who am Sir the sincerest of your servants
JOHN WHEELOCK
I have not yet acquainted my Lady with your Last Letter—My Lord Ashley had answerd yours but that he daly expected you in London—my Lady is well, as is my Lord and Mrs Percivall, who present their hearty servis to you

Vir Amplissime
Pudet sane duabus tuis unam, eamque vacuam reponere. distuli igitur aliquam diu spe adeundi Londinum, qua in urbe forsan occurreret aliquid in republicâ literariâ quod scire tibi non esset molestum. <Quanquam>†a ut verum fatear intonante per mare per terras Marte Musæ pene obmutescunt hisce in regionibus. Si vero pari successu in continenti pugnabitur quo in mari nuper demicatum est†1 spes erit otium his regionibus restitutum iri, et gaudentes
― 458 ―
eo literas aliquando reviviscere. Spencerum†1 aliquod opus elucubrare audio. <quodnam>†a vero illius sit argumentum haud scio, a priore haud longe alienum suspicor. Prælum interim Wetsteineanum†2 Sancto officio jam operam suam impendere spero, opus sane est, quod impatienter expecto, nec alterum scio orbi christiano magis profiturum, qui enim libertatem Christianam non ut par est amant nec provehunt; ferrum tamen et flammas aversantur et Sancti officii immanem crudelitatem a se longe amotam volunt. Hactenus bibliopolæ cunctationem æquiore tuli animo quod hanc moram historiæ tuæ sub incudem <revocatæ>†b profuisse scripseris. Gavisus sum in novissimis tuis te monuisse vos jamjam editionem inchoaturos et brevi ad finem perducturos. in proximis tuis me certiorem fieri magnam illius partem jam absolutam esse spero. Gaudio Te tuosque tam rectâ usos fuisse valetudine deus vos sanos salvosque diu conservet. Quid Veenius noster agit ut valet, reliquique nostri quorum ego beneficia et in me singularemque benevolentiam semper retinebo semper agnoscam. Grevium qui me ad calcem epistolæ tuæ tam humaniter tam amice salutavit quæso meo nomine quam officiosissime resaluta, Uxorem etiam tuam liberosque,

Guenelonis familiam, Collegasque nostros plurimum salvere jubeo. Vanden Ende ex orci faucibus ereptum valde lætor, illum Clericumque nostrum saluto.
