(Latin)
Oates 2 June 92
Excellent Sir,
I am truly ashamed of answering your two letters with one, and that with nothing in it. I put off writing for some time in the hope of going to London, where perhaps something in the commonwealth of learning might present itself that you would not be sorry to know of. To tell the truth, though, with this thunder of war by sea and land the Muses are almost dumb in these parts. If, however, fighting is as successful on terra firma as it recently was at sea†1 there will be some hope that leisure will be restored in [p. 458] these parts and that learning, rejoicing in it, will some day revive. I hear that Spencer†1 is engaged on some work, but what his subject may be I do not know; I suppose that it is not very different from the previous. Meanwhile I hope that the Wetstein press†2 is now busy with the Holy Office; it is certainly a work that I am impatient to see; nor do I know any other that is likely to be more profitable to the Christian world; for those who do not love and promote Christian liberty as is right nevertheless shrink from fire and sword, and want the monstrous cruelty of the Holy Office to be kept far from themselves. I have so far borne more patiently the bookseller's lingering because, as you wrote, this delay has been for the good of your account when returned to the anvil; I was glad to learn from your last letter that you and he are now about to start publication and that it will shortly be finished. I hope to be told in your next that a large part of it is already completed. I am glad that you and yours have been enjoying such good health; may God long keep you safe and well. What is our friend Veen doing? is he well, and the rest of our friends, whose good offices and singular kindness I shall always remember and acknowledge with gratitude? De Greve sent me very kind and friendly greetings at the end of your letter; please give him my best remembrances in return. My best wishes to your [p. 459] wife and children, to Guenellon's family, and to our Collegians. I am delighted to hear that van den Ende was snatched from the jaws of death; I send my best wishes to him and to our friend Le Clerc. I know of no one who could come with greater scholarship and a less corrupt or biased mind to the translation of the Scriptures than can that friend of ours. I am glad that this work has been undertaken by him; it is arduous enough, but will, as I anticipate, be exceedingly profitable to the Christian world. Mrs. Cudworth sends you her best wishes. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE

Sir
If my interest in my Lord Pembroke has been of any use to you I am glad of it. I am sure when I spoke to him of you it was with that
― 460 ―
intention and I was extreamly pleasd to finde it has had the successe I wishd since as my Lord let me know when I was last in towne, I had herein received from him a favour in the most obleigeing manner that could be and for a person <whose> learning and parts I very much estemd†a and with a Lady†1 I thought deserved a better station in the world. There is soe much pleasure in doeing service to a worthy man even where there are not the usuall motives of relation interest or obligations that I wonder you a philosopher should be surprised at it unlesse it were because you did not expect it from a man whom you might imagin to have lived soe long and soe much in the world as to be governd by the fashons of it. Dear Friend
I had yours of the 26 Ap: in its season, I am so from all parts disswaded from publishing any thing against that Impious Authour,†2 that I have at lest, at present layd aside the thoughts of it, the more
― 461 ―
because I have a matter of greater moment to me in hand, of which more when I see you; of which my Lord M.†1 whom I most unexpectedly met upon the Exchange last post day gives me hopes wilbe shortly, with my Lady M and my Lady Wentworth.†2 I shalbe heartily glad to see it. And if it can with any convenience be, I wish you could bring with you the rest of my books,†3 which I cannot resolve to part with.
I must also further intreat a kindness of you, for a friend of Dr. Kolhanses, who salutes you heartily, that is, by vertue of this note to receive from monsieur Leon Agent of the Prince of Courland,†4 living in Kings street near St James'es square, next doore to the Peacock, a smal Trunk, with the key, if the Gentleman has it, for the owner sent it him out of Germany, but knows not if it be come to his hand or no.
I have yet a further trouble to put you upon and that is to speak with mr. Charleton, to whom give my service, who, I think has a Collection of all our English meddals, if it be so, and he be willing to part with them, or to suffer monsieur Leers to have some cast by them, he would purchase them, or otherwise, as he should think fit, to make use of them in his french history,†5 to wit any that relate to those times from Henry 7th.
If you should not come, I desire you however to get the trunk and send it to mr. Joseph Wright to be sent to me, and to desire mr. Popple to send my bookes well corded by any good conveyance that may present, which is all at present from
Deare friend.
Your most affectionate friend and servant—

1507. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 17/27 June 1692 (1504, 1509)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 65-6. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 324-7. Answers no. 1504; answered by no. 1509.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Prælum Wetstenianum jam fervet. Historiæ Sancti Officii editio ex voto procedit. Jam tertia operis pars excusa est: duo nimirum præla hoc opere occupantur: Alterum historiâ meâ, cujus jam primus liber excusus est: et in secundo jam pervenimus ad caput de Crucesignatis:†1 In indice tibi misso facile videbis, quousque processerimus: Alterum prælum occupat Liber Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ: et illius tertia pars jam impressa est. Spero intra tres menses opus integrum proditurum. Non ero labore meo defunctus ante finem editionis: Nuperrime mihi liber ad manum venit, unde et nonnulla historiæ meæ magis expoliendæ apta depromsi, et quotidie, etiam inter excudendum, depromo.†2 Quando liber prodierit, istiusmodi augmentis et correctionibus non erit amplius locus. Et tamen is sum, qui, dum opus adhuc in manibus meis est, negligere aut contemnere non possum, quæ mihi nova mihique inaudita suppeditantur. Catalogum autorum, e quibus historia mea concinnata est, illi præmittam, ut unusquisque de fide meâ certus
― 463 ―
esse possit. Verum est aliud, in quo operam tuam flagito. Non is sum, qui quæ a me eduntur alteri dedicare gestio; hoc tamen opus, pro conscientiarum libertate, contra persecutionem ob religionem multo labore elucubratum, dedicare cupiam Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi,†1 viro longe præ omnibus, quos novi, Theologis, uti dignitate, ita etiam meritis eminentissimo, si Reverendissimæ illius Dignitati meam dedicationem non ingratam fore nossem. Et scripta et actiones ipsius testantur, favere ipsum doctrinæ, quam mihi propugnandam suscepi: quamvis enim historiam solummodo scribam, ipsa illa historia quod intendo luculentius confirmat, quam si multis ad id probandum uterer argumentis. Utinam tu, qui Rev. illius non es ignotus, captatâ occasione expiscari posses, num dedicationem meam benignè admissura esset. Nescio an mea professio inter Remonstrantes ipsi apud rigidiores zelotas aliquam sit conflatura invidiam aut indignationem. Nolim meâ operâ vel minimam creari molestiam viro quem ex animo colo ac veneror. Tu argumentum et scopum operis mei nosti: capitum historiæ meæ indicem habes, quem ostendere potes, si opportunum duxeris. Nulli rectius opus pro conscientiarum libertate dedicari potest, nisi illi, qui non tantum libertatis illius est patronus, sed et
― 464 ―
inter patronos dignitate præ aliis est conspicuus. Si dedicationem non respuat, velim illam ante illius editionem ad te mittere, ut et a Rev. suâ videri possit, et si quid incautius forte a me dictum sit, resecetur, emendetur, amplietur. Interim titulos quibus compellari debet, ut mihi scribas exspecto. Hoc quicquid sit tuæ prudentiæ committo, et gratissimum mihi feceris, si quamprimum rescribas, quoniam editio velocissime procedit, et spatium ad deliberandum non est amplum. Grevium, cui ante quatriduum Trajecti adfui, tuo nomine salutavi: Ille pro suâ, quâ me complectitur benevolentiâ, suppeditaturus mihi est, historiam cujusdam ex ordine Francisci, qui adulteratis Pontificiis diplomatibus se falso jactavit Episcopum, et postea Trajecti comprehensus post degradationem verbalem et actualem†1 ferventi ollæ fuit immissus; postea tamen inde ereptus et capite truncatus. Historiam ipsam habeo ex Raynaldo; sed sententiam, illius pronuntiationem et executionem, prout exstat in archivis Capituli S.Salvatoris, cujus ille est Canonicus, mihi Grevius est suppeditaturus.†2 Istiusmodi flosculis undique corrasis historiam meam exornatam dabo. Ipse Grevius plurimam tibi salutem rescribi jussit. Venius rure bene valet: inter homines sibi amicissimos ac
― 465 ―
familiarissimos, qui villas illius villæ vicinas incolunt, degit, eorumque quotidianâ consuetudine fruitur. Jam ab aliquot hebdomadibus illum non vidi: recte tamen valere audio. D.Cudworthæ rogo humilissima mea officia offeras, salutemque plurimam a me dicas. Salutat te uxor mea, liberique. Vale, Vir Amplissime, et in amore mei persevera.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 27 Junii

(Latin) Excellent Sir
Wetstein's press is now hard at work. The publication of the account of the Holy Office is proceeding as I could wish. A third of the work is already printed. Two presses, of course, are occupied with this work: the one with my account, the first book of which is now printed; and in the second we have now come to the chapter on the Cruce-signati;†1 you will readily see in the list that I sent you how far we have advanced. The other press is occupied with the Liber Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ, and a third part of that is now printed. I hope that the entire work will appear within three months. I shall not have done with my labour before publication finishes; very recently a book came to hand from which I have made a number of extracts that serve to embellish my account, and I continue to make extracts daily, even while printing is going on.†2 When the book appears there will no longer be any opportunity for such additions and corrections. However I am such a man that I cannot, while the work is still in my hands, neglect or despise anything new and strange to me that is supplied to me. I shall prefix to my account a list of the authors from whom it has been put together, so that everyone may be assured of my trustworthiness. There is another [p. 463] matter, however, in which I entreat your assistance. I am not a man to long to dedicate to another books published by myself; this work, however, prepared with much labour for freedom of consciences, against persecution on account of religion, I should like to dedicate to the Archbishop of Canterbury,†1 a man, as in station, so also in deserts most eminent, by far beyond all theologians with whom I am acquainted, if I knew that my dedication would not be displeasing to his Reverence. Both his writings and his actions bear witness to the fact that he favours the teaching which I have undertaken to maintain; for although I am writing only an account, that account in itself establishes what I am urging more clearly than if I sought to prove it by many arguments. Would that you, who are not a stranger to his Reverence, could seize an opportunity and extract from him whether he would kindly permit my dedication. Possibly my profession of faith as a Remonstrant might kindle some ill will or anger against him among the stricter zealots. I should not wish any activity of mine to cause even the least annoyance to a man whom I heartily respect and venerate. You know the subject and scope of my work; you have the list of the chapters in my account, which you can show him if you think it opportune. To no one can a work on behalf of freedom of consciences more justly be dedicated than to him, who is not only a defender of that freedom, but among the defenders by reason of his exalted [p. 464] position is conspicuous above all the rest. If he does not refuse the dedication I should like to send it to you before it is published, so that it may be seen by his Reverence, and so that, if by chance anything is said by me incautiously, it may be cut away, amended, or amplified. Meanwhile I wait for you to write me the titles by which he should be addressed. This, whatever it may be, I entrust to your prudence, and you will do me a great kindness if you will reply as soon as possible, since publication is proceeding very rapidly and there is not much time for deliberation.
I gave your greetings to de Greve, when I was with him at Utrecht four days ago. He, with the usual kindness with which he embraces me, will supply me with the story of a certain Franciscan, who by means of forged Pontifical diplomas falsely paraded himself as a bishop, and later when arrested at Utrecht, after verbal and factual degradation, was plunged in a boiling cauldron; afterwards, however, he was pulled out and beheaded. I have the story itself from Raynaldus; but de Greve will supply me with the sentence, its pronouncement, and execution, as it is extant in the archives of the Chapter of S. Salvator, of which he is a canon.†1 With suchlike flowerets, raked together from all sides, my account is to be adorned. De Greve bade me to send you his heartiest greetings in reply. Veen is keeping well in the country; he lives among close and familiar friends who occupy country [p. 465] houses near his, and he enjoys their society daily. It is now some weeks since I saw him, but I hear that he is in good health. I beg you to offer my humble service to Mrs. Cudworth and to give her my best wishes. My wife and children send you theirs. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue in your love of me.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 27 June
1692.

(Latin)
To the illustrious John Locke, greeting
A whole year and more has gone by since I saw my Latin translation of the first book of your Essay on the Human Understanding returned by you from England. I was very sorry that it was sent to Mr. van Limborch, passing me [p. 466] by. However, I put this down to the unfortunate accident that had happened to my letter; it was attached to the parcel and by some mishap got lost, or at any rate it never reached you, as I perceived from your letter to Mr. van Limborch at that time. Besides this I was distressed on account of my translation, which displeased you so much that you were not far from pronouncing, if I remember rightly, either that it ought to be condemned to eternal darkness or, unless I was resolved to prejudice the reputation of your treatise or to expose myself to severe punishment by the experts in both languages, that it ought to be refashioned from start to finish. I have approved this latter advice of yours, while wholly rejecting the former, as I could (only) with very great difficulty persuade myself to gather no fruit from so great an effort, so much distasteful labour. Accordingly following Mr. van Limborch's advice I had resolved to cut out all Anglicisms without exception, to correct mistakes pointed out by you, to delete erasures one and all that you had not noticed, and to remove suspect Latinity wherever it occurs, so far as consideration of philosophical study might permit: in short, to put everything in order in such a way as the dignity of so great an author and so great a treatise might require. While engaged in this I went to see the bookseller J. Wolters,†1 who some time ago had greatly desired to print this translation of mine. But he, whether drawn away by other matters or not [p. 467] bearing the costs on account of the dearness of paper and suchlike, is not inclined to set about the work. We are therefore putting it off until such time as we can reach some more satisfactory agreement. Meanwhile the hour speeds by and time is flying beyond recall. Very recently, in fact in June just past, visiting the same bookseller with Mr. Le Clerc, I see that he is by no means averse to publishing it, now that the books that he has in hand, which are almost finished and on the point of being published, have left his workmen's hands free. When therefore I heard yesterday from the distinguished Mr. Le Clerc that you think of abridging your Essay and reducing it as it were to an epitome, I thought the best thing would be to consult you seriously as to whether you think it advantageous that your English treatise, completely translated into Latin, as it is, when it has been reworked by Messrs. van Limborch, Le Clerc, Guenellon, or any others who may be called upon, should see the light in that form; or whether, indeed, it seems better to you that I should wait for the epitome you have in mind sheet by sheet, and that I should turn it into Latin with as much perspicuity and elegance as possible, and so present it to the eyes of the learned world.†1 Consider, decide, pronounce about me, whatever you please, whatever seems to be to your advantage; you will find me compliant with your [p. 468] decrees. I myself could perhaps endure with an easy mind the loss of all fruit of my lucubrations; but the fact is I can no longer withstand the importunate persistence of voices deafening me daily and urging me to keep promises that I made long since. To be brief, then, if you will not refuse to let me know freely your opinion about this business you will be doing a great favour to
Your most obedient servant
GISBERT VERRIJN
(Latin) P.S. The courtesy of Mr. Le Clerc, by whose kind help this letter of mine will I hope reach you, will no doubt do me the same service when I may require it.

1509. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 30 June 1692 (1507, 1516)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 257 c. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 339-41; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 204. Answers no. 1507; answered by no. 1516.
(English)
London 30 June 92
Vir Amplissime
Ab acceptis tuis 27 Junii datis ad urbem accedens†1 hodie primum Archiepiscopum conveni. Quam primum tuum audivit nomen, agnovit acceptam a te Contra Judæum disputationem,†2 excusavit silentium quod ob <valetudinem>,†a oculorum debilitatem, et alia quæ intervenerunt impedimenta integram nondum perlegerat. Laudavit maxime illud opus una cum authore, et gratias quas nondum egit se habere agnovit. Historiam Sancti officií jam valde oportunam judicavit. Capitum indicem summa cum voluptate et approbatione perlegit, et cum tuum de dedicatione consilium aperuissem, ea verborum urbanitate et honore, eo vultu accepit, ut si adfuisses hoc sibi non ingratum fore certus esses. mitte igitur quam primum dedicationem, novi viri modestiam et laudo consilium tuum, quod prælectam ab eo prius velis quam editam. Illi monstrabo, quod scio honori ducet, et si quid mutandum videtur
― 470 ―
indicabo. Interim dixit se habere librum Lusitaniæ editum de quodam actu Inquisitionis in Lusitania, in cujus exordio occurrunt Paparum bullæ aliaque diplomata quibus potestas Sancti officii concessa et stabilita est, accuratius collecta. Nomen authoris non retinebat memoria et liber ipse, illius bibliothecâ nondum in ordinem redactâ ab ipso quæsitus non repertus est. volumen est ut aiunt in octavo. Brevi ipsum iterum revisam, eam curam cuidam domesticorum mandabit ut ante reditum meum præsto sit liber, Tunc tibi nomen authoris perscribam, et si nondum videris ipsum librum tibi mutuo commodabit Reverendissimus Archiepiscopus. Grevium Guenelonem Veeniosque omnes meo nomine saluta. Clerico nostro, quem officiosissime saluto, ante aliquot septimanas an menses dicam scripsi an pervenerint ad illum literæ meæ ignoro nam ab isto tempore nihil ab eo accepi, hoc quæso illi indices ne me tarditatis, si mea interciderit epistola suspicatum†a habeat. Fæminam tuam dilectissimam liberosque summo cum affectu saluto vale vir Dignissime et ut facis me ama
Tui studiosissimum
J LOCKE
Gaudio præli opus ita fervere
(Latin)
London 30 June 92
Excellent Sir,
On receiving your letter of 27 June I came to the city†1 and today for the first time met the Archbishop. As soon as he heard your name he acknowledged the receipt of the disputation against the Jew†2 from you, and excused his own silence on the ground that, on account of his health, weak sight, and other hindrances that had intervened, he had so far not read the whole work through. He commended it highly together with its author, and acknowledged the gratitude which he has not yet expressed to you. He thought that your account of the Holy Office is most opportune at this time. He read through the list of chapters with the greatest pleasure and approval; and when I disclosed what you had in mind about the dedication he accepted it with such courtesy and esteem in words and with such a countenance that if you had been there you would have felt certain that it was not unwelcome to him. Send the dedication, then, as soon as possible; I know the modesty of the man and commend your prudence in wishing it to be read by him before it is published. I shall show it to him, which I know he will take as a compliment, and if anything seems to need altering I shall [p. 470] point it out. Meanwhile he said he has a book, published in Portugal, about a certain act of the Inquisition in Portugal; at the beginning of it are to be found the Papal Bulls and other diplomas by which the authority of the Holy Office is granted and established; these have been carefully collected. He did not remember the name of the author, and the book itself, though he has looked for it, has not been found, as his library has not yet been put in order again. The volume is in octavo, as it is called. I shall visit him again shortly, and he will order one of his household to have the book ready before my return. I shall then write you the author's name, and if you have not yet seen the book the Most Reverend the Archbishop will lend it to you. Give my best wishes to de Greve, Guenellon, and all the Veens. I wrote to our friend Le Clerc, to whom I send my best respects, some weeks, or should I say months, ago; I do not know whether my letter reached him, as I have had nothing from him since then; please tell him this lest, if my letter has been lost, he should suspect me of tardiness. I send my most affectionate greetings to your dear wife and children. Good-bye, honoured Sir, and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J LOCKE
I am glad to hear that the press is so hard at work.

Deare Mr Locke
I long till you come down. I should be very glad to see you for I love you mightyly. I desire you to come and teach me some Longitude. I am afraid you wont be well if you stay in Town. 1511. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 5/15 July 1692 (1486, 1525)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 56-7. The first part of the last paragraph printed in King, pp. 231-2; the whole letter in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 54-5.
A Amsterdam le 15 de Juillet 1692.
Aiant reçu, Monsieur, vôtre Lettre plus d'un mois après la date et aiant été empêché d'ailleurs je n'ai pas pû vous répondre si tôt que je l'aurois souhaité. Je vous suis bien obligé de la bonne volonté, que vous avez pour moi; c'est tout ce qu'on peut demander de ses amis, puisque cette bonne volonté ne manque pas de produire de bons effets, dès que l'on en trouve l'occasion. J'ai écrit depuis quelques semaines à Mr. de Salisbury, par un de mes amis, qui ne manquera pas de lui rendre ma Lettre. Mais au reste, il en usera comme il plaira, je ne l'importunerai jamais. J'envoierai au premier jour à M. Furly les Tomes de la Bibl. Univers. qui vous manquent; et je l'aurois même déja fait, si je n'avois attendu le dernier, qui retarde au delà de son terme, parce que l'Auteur a été incommodé. S'il entendoit l'Anglois, je vous prierois pour lui de m'envoier les Catalogues;†2 mais comme il ne l'entend point, et que
― 472 ―
je n'ai point le loisir de l'aider, cela me seroit inutile. Vous êtes, Monsieur, le premier Auteur, à qui j'ai ouï parler de publier une seconde Edition corrigée et abregée.†1 On met toûjours augmentée. Je croi néanmoins qu'il n'y a pas grande chose à retrancher dans vôtre Ouvrage, et je connois de gens qui soûhaiteroient qu'il y eut divers endroits que vous eussiez étendu, comme celui ou vous dites que la Morale peut être demontrée.†2 Il y a quelques mois que dînant chez un de mes amis avec Mr. de Volder Professeur à Leide, que vous connoissez;†3 il me témoignoit beaucoup d'envie de voir ce qu'on pourroit dire là dessus. Je lui dis que l'on pourroit dire une infinité de choses que tout le monde trouveroit bonnes; mais qu'il y auroit d'autres qui pourroient choquer les Docteurs, si l'on entreprenoit de venir à une précision rigoureuse. Je voudrois que ce que vous me dites (to me alone) fût de cette nature; mais quoi que ce puisse être, je l'attendrai avec impatience. Pour répondre à vôtre question, touchant le fonds que l'on doit faire sur ce que les Peres disent des miracles, qui se faisoient de leur temps; pour moi je croi que quand ils diroient vrai, il ne nous seroit guere possible de nous en assurer.†4 1. L'Eglise Chrétienne étoit composée alors, comme aujourd'hui de toutes sortes de gens, parmi lesquels il y avoit sans doute des fourbes et des credules. Il paroit par l'aigreur que l'on voit dans leurs écrits, et par leurs querelles qu'ils n'étoient pas plus honêtes gens qu'on n'est aujourdhui. Ils embrassent aveuglement tout ce qui peut servir à leur cause, vrai ou non, comme ce que Tertullien rapporte de Tibere, qui voulut ranger J.C. dans le nombre des Dieux, ce qu'il dit de Semo Sangus, qu'il prend pour Simon etc.†5 2. L'interêt faisoit parler les Prêtres, car plus ils attiroient de gens, plus les offrandes étoient grosses, et leur part meilleure,†6 et qui doute qu'en disant qu'ils chassoient les Démons etc. ils n'attirassent de la populace, pour qui the pleasure is as great to be cheat'd as to cheat.†7 Plusieurs autres raisons, comme celles-là, leur ont fait perdre créance dans mon esprit; et
― 473 ―
quoi que je n'osasses pas dire que tout ce qu'ils ont dit est faux, je ne saurois me fier à rien.
Je garderai fidelement les deux Diss: que j'ai, jusqu'à ce que vous me marquiez ce que l'Auteur veut que j'en fasse.†1 Je puis bien dire que ni cela, ni autre chose qui seroit publié ici ne feroit aucune affaire à personne, pourvu qu'on n'en sût rien d'ailleurs delà la mer. Il faut hazarder quelque chose, pour décrasser beaucoup d'honêtes gens, qui ne pechent que par ignorance, et qui desabuseroient les autres, s'ils etoient desabusez. Je ne croi pas qu'il fût bien de dire rien à Mr. Johnston en mon nom, parce que je ne sai pas comme il le recevroit; excepté qu'on ne lui fît mes civilitez, et qu'à cette occasion on ne l'entretint de moi, et de ce que je pourrois faire, si j'avois plus de repos. Je lui traduisis en Latin la harangue qu'il devoit faire à l'Elect. de Brandebourg, en lui donnant la jartiére, et je la lui envoiai à Zell, d'où il me récrivit avec mille offres de services.†2 Depuis je ne lui ai point écrit, mais il m'étoit venu voir auparavant plus d'une fois à Amsterdam. Je suis faché, Monsieur, de vous entretenir de ces bagatelles, et encore plus de vous donner la peine de parler à d'autres pour moi. Soit que cela réüssisse, ou non, je vous en aurai une égale obligation, et je vous prie d'être persuadé qu'il n'y a rien que je ne fisses pour vous faire connoître que je suis très-sincerement
Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
J'ai changé de logis depuis le mois de Mai, et je demeure op de Keiser gracht, by de Leytse Straat.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in Dorset Court, in channel row Westminster
Postmark: IY 11
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 15° Jul 92 Answered 30

1512. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 7 July [1692] (1482, 1560)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 102-3. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 291-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Richmond. 7° Jul.
Mr Lock
The giving Charachters of People is in my opinion not onely a very Dangerouse Undertaking, but a Task too of some Labour and Hardship; when besides the Strict Consideration of the Person spoken of, so much must be had in relation to the Persons address'd to, and that, after one has form'd ones one judgment with much Pains, there is still so much remaining in the Nicety that there must be in delivering of Itt to Others who perhaps have such different Notions, and Understand even the same Things so differently from what ones Self does: But I have not this part of the Trouble with You, which I should have with Others: and since You desire of mee to write you of Mr La Treille's Charachter; I can say well enough what is necessary in the Little time that I have here allow'd mee; since 'tis You that Enquire.
You well know what it is that reconciles mee to the Acquaintance and Freindship of such as I chance to meet with in the world: When I find in any one a Concern for somewhat more in Nature then what is meerly calld Ones self or has immediat relation to itt: and that They carry their Reason Free and Open with no excepted Places, which endure no Examination, and that will not bear the calling in Question: The first is Good nature, the Other is Good Sence. It being my Luck to find as much as this in the Gentleman now mention'd, with that which I Esteem'd a Good Insight into what should, or did Employ Mankind, and a Good Understanding (as I thought) in what was best and most satisfactory of all that: (by which I understand that which frames and Polishes Society) By this means I grew into his acquaintance and gain'd that Habbitt of Conferring reason with him and looking togather often into those things that molested or benifitted Mankind and our selves; that from this Commerce Hee became to mee one of Those whome I most acceptably saw and Lov'd cheifly to convers with in writing or Discours: which I have almost constantly done with him this Year or two, as hardly with Any so besides. How far this may be a
― 475 ―
Byass in my Judment of him in other parts, and in relation to other things, I cannot say my self; but would wish you too view as narrowly as Possible; that if I deceive my self, I may not att least deceive You, or others by You.
As to his being a Governour for a Young Man, all I can say is that I have thought him so much the fittest of any I knew (and you know what a generall acquaintance I have had occasion to have in that form of Men) that when I expected my Brother should have been left without a Governour by the Loss of Poor Mr Denoun (my long acquaintance, and former Fellow traveller) I then design'd Mr La Treille, if he had been free, for that place: not ballancing att all between him and any Other. Hee is Extreamly well vers'd in Humanity, and is in my opinion an Extream good Judg in all Polite Learning and in the Politer Manners and Customes of the World: though I Understand not by that the Particular way that some men have of setting themselves off, which depends not so much on Experience or Insight, as in a happy Constitution that breeds Assurance, the Possession, or want of which does more then can be imagin'd almost, in the Opinion wee begett of our selves in Others. I know not what disadvantage itt may be reckon'd to Mr La Treille, the having left him the Perfect use but of one Eye: I did not my self reckon upon itt more then as a Danger to himself, the having nothing for reserve and the running double the Risk of becoming blind by any accident that an other Man runs who has both Eyes well and has an other in store if any mischance happen to one, For with what he has att present he does things (and even those that require greatest accuracy of sight as in writing and reading) more perfectly then I can doe with what I have got of sight more then he. Having told you these particulars; You, or indeed any one, may draw my Judgment of what remains as to his Integrity, Temper, and all of that kind: For how should I stand thus with him if I were not perswaded myself that he had of that kind what was Better then was ordinarly mett with? So I need say no more. onely I should add indeed that I never knew any such success above once, or so, in my Life in the Teaching of a Young Body as I have known in Mr La Treille: and for the matter of overcoming that mighty Gyant Language, with Youth, the Latin. nor is there any great Mistery there to wonder att when a man has Diligence and Good humour, and onely dares but to contradict the Precepts of some whose Trade is teaching; by postponing Certain Abstract notions
― 476 ―
those Gentlemen have fram'd on Language, not very aptly calculated, I imagine, to young heads; till such a time as they are a more naturall and speedyer way made Masters of the Language they learn: att which time itt is easy for them in one fortnight to understand (as much as they are ever to be understood) all the Parts of that Science.
I doe not speak this without living instance myself: for This You know was what after 8 years in a Free School†1 (and that one of the best too; Winchester) Recover'd a Brother of mine†2 in 2 Years afterwards from knowing hardly any thing att all of any Language but his Country's; to be master compleatly of more then that one Language, besides other things that took up much time in the while—But I have run on here I know not how. How shall I Excuse my self?
'Tis to Mr Locke I write. That's truly a very naturall Excuse: for 'tis the reall reason: and there is nothing surer then that I should have serv'd nobody elce so. But is not this very Injuriouse? that when you know how little Guilty I am of long Letters to other People; You should be the Single Person for whome I become tediouse. I here say nothing for myself but that I am very much yours
ASHLEY
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 7° Jul. 92

1514. Sir James Rushout to Locke, 9 July 1692
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 47. For the writer see no. 429, etc.
Bath July the 9th 1692.
Sir
I am extreamly well satisfyed with the character given by Mr Popple of Monsr De la Treille and the confirmation you give of it from other hands, I know you will not vouch upon slight authorityes and therefore think it needless to make farther enquiryes of Sir John Huband†1 and Mr Vane tho I am known to both of them. my obligations are very great to you for your trouble in it and your frank offer of farther assistance: It is what I shall depend upon and for that purpose intend to bee in London about a month hence in my way home from Cornwall whether I am engaged to goe in a few dayes upon urgent business. I presume it will not bee difficult to settle the termes with Monsr De la Treille upon our meeting, wee shall then see and know and I hope like one another and for the rest as Mr Popple sayes freinds must govern. I must then likewise take my measures about my project for Italy, wherein I am not determined, but the apprehensions I have of another cold winter
― 478 ―
makes mee overcome many difficultyes I foresee in the undertaking. the warme sunn is a comfortable support to a declining constitution and the meanes to obtain it with most ease and speed is most desirable if it may bee with any tollerable degree of prudence. if there should bee any occasion to write to mee a letter directed to Shillingham†1 nere Saltash in Cornwall by Plymouth post will find
Sir
Your most humble servant
J RUSHOUT

WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
William Molyneux belonged to a Protestant family of English origin. His great-grandfather, the first Sir Thomas Molyneux, settled in Dublin in 1576, and was chancellor of the Irish Exchequer from 1590 to 1597. William was born in Dublin on 17 April 1656; Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux (no. 800) was his younger brother. He was admitted to Trinity College, Dublin, in 1671. Having graduated B.A. in 1674 he came to London, where he spent three years studying law in the Middle Temple. Returning to Dublin in 1678 he married Lucy, daughter of Sir William Domvile, attorney-general of Ireland. In 1680 he published his translation of Descartes's Meditations. Towards the end of 1683 he was the principal man concerned in the foundation of the Dublin Philosophical Society. In the following year he was appointed joint surveyor-general of the king's buildings in Ireland, an office which he held until Tyrconnel dismissed him in 1688. He was elected F.R.S. in 1686. He spent most of 1689 and 1690 near Chester as a fugitive from Tyrconnel's and James II's Ireland. On his return he became more and more concerned with Irish politics. About the beginning of 1692 he published his Dioptrica Nova, which won him Locke's friendship. In the parliament of 1692 he was a member for the University of Dublin, that is, for Trinity College, which conferred on him the degrees of LL.B. and LL.D. in 1693. He was again a member for the college in 1695. Early in 1698 he published The Case of Ireland's being bound by Acts of Parliament in England, stated, an attempt to prove the legislative independence of the Irish parliament. He died on 11 October 1698, a few days after his return from a visit to England. He left one son, Samuel Molyneux, the astronomer (D.N.B.).
Molyneux was the ablest Irish scientist of his day. It was he, more than anyone else, who animated the Dublin Philosophical Society. Starting about
― 479 ―
1683 the Society flourished until 1687, when it fell a victim to the political upheaval of the time. It started again in 1693, but succumbed four years later when Molyneux was preoccupied with politics (it was revived again in 1707 by Samuel Molyneux, but lasted only for a year). Molyneux was interested principally in astronomy and optics. He corresponded for some years with Flamsteed (no. 483) and met Cassini (no. 481) in 1685 when he visited Paris. In 1686 he published Sciothericum Telescopicum, an account of a telescopic dial which he had designed, and in 1692 Dioptrica Nova, a work on the refraction of light in which he was assisted by Halley (no. 453). He contributed fourteen articles on a variety of subjects to the Philosophical Transactions, and a note to the Bibliotheque universelle (iii. 329-34). Translations made by him of works by Galileo and Torricelli have remained unpublished.
Authorities: The article on Molyneux in D.N.B. and the sources listed there, notably the autobiography in Sir C. Molyneux, An Account of the Family of Sir Thomas Molyneux, etc., 1820, pp. 53-78; etc.; for his activities as a scientist K. T. Hoppen, The Common Scientist in the Seventeenth Century: a Study of the Dublin Philosophical Society 1683-1708, 1970.
1515. Locke to William Molyneux, 16 July 1692 (1530)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 1-3. Answered by no. 1530.
London, 16. July, 1692.
Sir,
Though the extraordinary complement you were pleased to make me in the Epistle Dedicatory†1 easily persuaded me from whom that present was likely to come, when at my coming to town I found your book left for me, by Mr. Tooke,†2 at my bookseller's; yet my consciousness how little I could deserve the one or the other from you, made me fear some mistake, till enquiring of Mr. Tooke himself he assured me of the favour you had done me. I will not pretend to return you such thanks as I ought, till I can write
― 480 ―
such a book as yours is. Only give me leave to say, that if my trifle could possibly be an occasion of vanity to me; you have done most to make it so, since I could scarce forbear to applaud my self upon such a testimony from one, who so well understands demonstration, did I not see, that those who can be extreme rigorous and exact in the search of truth, can be as civil and as complaisant in their dealing with those whom they take to be lovers of it. But this cannot keep me from being out of countenance at the receipt of such obligations, without the hopes of making such returns as I ought. Instead of that, give me leave to do what is next to it, and let you see that I am not sorry I am obliged to you. The bearer hereof, Dr. Sibelius, is a friend of mine, who comes to Dublin with a design to settle there, and I beg your assistance of him in what lies in your way. I shall take it as a Favour done to me. And methinks I have reason now to expect it of you, since you have done me, more than one, very great ones, when I had no Reason to expect any at all. Sir, you have made great advances of friendship towards me, and you see they are not lost upon me. I am very sensible of them, and would make such an use of them as might assure you I should take it for a new favour, if you would afford me any occasion wherein I might, by any service, tell you how much I am,
Sir,
Your most humble, and most obliged servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
I had the honour to know one of your name at Leyden, about seven or eight years since.†1 If he be any relation of yours, and now in Dublin, I beg the favour of you to present my humble service to him.

1516. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 19/29 July 1692 (1509, 1518)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 67-8. Answers no. 1509; answered by no. 1518.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Summoperè me tibi devinctum profiteor, quod meâ causâ laborem tantum suscipere volueris, mihique Reverendissimi Archiepiscopi animum conciliaveris, ut Dedicationem operis quod jam brevi proditurum est aspernaturus non sit. Misissem jam illam hebdomade elapsâ, verum inopinato quodam casu aliquot mihi dies elapsi sunt, quos difficili alicui negotio, quod nullam patiebatur moram, expediendo impendere debui. Mitto nunc illam Tibi, licet magis elaboratam mallem; sed quia prælum fervet, et editio celerrimè procedit, non satis elaboratam mittere malui, quam ulterius differre. Tu pro prudentiâ ac eruditione tuâ, ac sincero quo me prosequeris affectu, quicquid mutandum videbitur mutabis; atque ita a Te correctam ac emendatam Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo ostendes, ut tanto magis ipsi placeat. Si quid mutandum, addendum, delendum censeatis, rogo ut pro arbitrio mutes: a tuâ manu correctam cum gratiarum actione recipiam. Pervenimus jam ad quartum librum, in quo maxima mutatio facta est, postquam ad Te capitum indicem misi: ille erit omnium librorum maximus, et
― 482 ―
interiora Inquisitionis deteget. Credo ante†a Augusti finem editionem fore absolutam. Autores quorum scriptis maxime sum usus, præter Bzovium et Rainaldum, sunt, Eymerici Directorium Inquisitorum, cum commentariis Francisci Pegnæ: Illi subjecta sunt Romanorum Pontificum Bullæ et rescripta jussu Cardinalium Inquisitorum Generalium in lucem data. Lucerna Inquisitorum Fr. Bernardi Comensis, cum annot. Franc. Pegnæ. Jacobus Simancas Episcopus Pacensis de Catholicis Institutionibus. Ioannes a Roÿas de hæreticis, eorumque impiâ intentione et credulitate. Zanchini Ugolini tractatus de hæreticis, cum additionibus Camilli Campegii. Conradus Brunus de hæreticis. De forma procedendi contra hæreticos, seu inquisitos de hæresi et in causa hæresis; cujus autor creditur esse Joannes Calderinus. Ludovicus a Paramo de Origine et progressu Officii S.Inquisitionis. Cæsaris Carenæ tractatus de Officio S.Inquisitionis. Franc. Pegnæ praxis Inquisitorum. Antonii de Sousa Aphorismi Inquisitorum. Reginaldi Gonsalvii S. Inquisitionis Hispanicæ artes aliquot detectæ ac palam traductæ.†1 Librum Hispanicum, quem Reverendissimus Archiepiscopus habet in suâ bibliothecâ, non vidi: Et nisi vererer, ne jam editio operis mei fermè absoluta esset, antequam liber ille ad manus meas pervenire posset,
― 483 ―
licet vix novi quicquam præter autores a me nominatos continere credam, tamen humanissimè mihi a reverendissimo D. Archiepiscopo oblatum avidissimè acceptarem: Nunc maximas Rev. illius pro oblato libro gratias ago: spero me omnia vidisse, quæ illo continentur. Omnes Paparum Bullas, quotquot exstant S.Officium spectantes, vidi: Rogo autem, ut si quid in Reverendissimi Domini titulis erratum sit, id corrigas: nolim enim hic quicquam contra decorum peccare. Ubi recepero dedicationem, opus mox in lucem prodibit. Statui ego Historiæ meæ catalogum autorum, ex quibus potissimum ea concinnata est, præmittere: addam, qui et quales fuerint, et quo sæculo vixerint: ex illo constabit plerosque fuisse aut Inquisitores, aut Inquisitionis Consultores, aut Advocatos Fiscales (ut vocant.) Unus Reginaldus Gonsalvius†1 Pontificius non est: Verum ille quæ scribit ipse oculis suis spectasse videtur, aut saltem Hispali vixisse, et quæ ipse non vidit, ex ore fide dignorum accepisse: tutius eo uti possum, quia historiæ quas narrat, consentaneæ sunt illis, quæ alii ab Inquisitoribus fieri posse aut debere docent; eaque historiis illis maxime illustrantur. D.Clericus tuas accepit; quamprimum responsurus est: Literas ad Te nuper dedit,
― 484 ―
quas jam te accepisse nullus dubitat.†1 Plurimam tibi salutem scribi jussit. Venius, Guenellonus, aliique plurimum Te salutant. Rogo Reverendissimum Archiepiscopum quam officiosissime verbis meis salutes, quando dedicationem es prælecturus. Uxor ac liberi te salutant, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I profess myself most deeply obliged to you for being willing to undertake so much trouble on my behalf, and for having procured for me the favour of the Most Reverend the Archbishop, so that he will not disdain the dedication of the work which is shortly to appear. I would already have sent it last week, but through an unforeseen event some days escaped me, which I had to devote to the settling of a difficult business affair that brooked no delay. I now send it to you, though I should have wished that it was more highly finished; but as the press is hard at work and publication rapidly proceeding I preferred to send it in an insufficiently finished state rather than to put it off any longer. You with your prudence and scholarship, and with the sincere affection with which you pursue me, will please alter anything that seems to need to be altered, and then show it so corrected and amended by yourself to the Most Reverend the Archbishop, so that it may please him the more. If you and he consider that anything should be altered, added, or deleted, I beg that you will alter it at your discretion; I shall receive it with gratitude when corrected by your hand. We have now reached the fourth book, in which the largest amount of alteration has been made since I sent you the list of chapters; it will be the largest book of all, and will lay bare the innermost [p. 482] parts of the Inquisition. I believe that publication will be completed before the end of August. The authors whose writings I have chiefly used are, besides Bzovius and Rainaldus, Eymeric's Directorium Inquisitorum, with the notes of Franciscus Pegna; appended to this are the Bulls and Rescripts of the Roman Pontiffs published by order of the Cardinal Inquisitors General. Lucerna Inquisitorum, by Fr. Bernardus of Como, with the annotations of Franc. Pegna. Jacobus Simancas, bishop of Badajoz, De Catholicis Institutionibus. Joannes a Rojas De Hæreticis Eorumque Impiâ Intentione et Credulitate. Zanchinus Ugolinus's Tractatus de Hæreticis, with additions by Camillus Campegius. Conradus Brunus De Hæreticis. De Forma Procedendi contra Hæreticos, seu Inquisitos de Hæresi et in Causa Hæresis, the author of which is believed to be Joannes Calderinus. Ludovicus a Paramo De Origine de Progressu Officii S. Inquisitionis. Caesar Carena's treatise De Officio S. Inquisitionis. Franc. Pegna's Praxis Inquisitorum. Antonius de Sousa's Aphorismi Inquisitorum. Reginaldus Gonsalvius's S. Inquisitionis Hispanicæ Artes aliquot Detectæ ac palam Traductæ.†1 I have not seen the Spanish book which the Most Reverend the Archbishop has in his library; and but for my fear that the publication of my work would have been almost completed before that book could reach my hands—although [p. 483] I scarcely believe that it contains anything new beyond the authors named by me—I should have eagerly accepted the Most Reverend the Archbishop's very kind offer of it. As it is, I thank him most sincerely for offering it to me; I expect I have seen everything that is contained in it. I have seen all the Papal Bulls, as many as are extant, relating to the Holy Office. I ask further that if any mistake has been made in his Most Reverend Lordship's titles you will correct it; for in this I should wish not to offend in any way against propriety. When I have received the dedication my work will soon see the light. I have decided to prefix to my account a list of the authors from whom it has chiefly been put together; I shall add who and what they were and in what century they lived; from this it will be clear that most of them were either Inquisitors or Councillors of the Inquisition or Advocates Fiscal (as they call them). One of them, Reginaldus Gonsalvius,†1 is not a Romanist; what he writes of, however, he seems to have seen with his own eyes, or at any rate to have lived in Seville, and what he himself did not see he seems to have heard from the mouths of trustworthy persons. I can use him the more safely since the stories he tells are consistent with the things that the rest teach can, or should, be done by the Inquisitors, and it is mainly those that are illustrated by those stories. Mr. Le Clerc has received your letter; he will answer it as soon as possible. He sent you a letter recently and has no [p. 484] doubt that you have received it by now.†1 He bade me send you his best wishes. Veen, Guenellon, and the others send you theirs. I beg that you will on my behalf convey my most dutiful respects to the Most Reverend the Archbishop when you read the dedication to him. My wife and children send you their best wishes, as I do myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.

First period
℞ [mercury] lb x cleanse it well with lbj of flowers of [sulphur] in 24 hours. To these lb x take ℥ j of mineral soap u†b 2 Shake it with the [mercury] so as it may first imbody with it and afterwards by
― 486 ―
further agitation be spued out by it, This worke may last 24 hours or more. To the same [mercury] adde ℥ j more of the Soap and worke as before. This doe 7 times. Then before any Durca be added the matter must be kept in agitation as before for at least 7 days. for 'twill be the better (if it be forced in) addeing no soap to it. The soap being to make it throw out any feculency that may lie concealed in [mercury], in the forme of a pouder whereby the [mercury] will remain the purer.
℞ lb j of choice [mercury] and grind with it for 2 or 3 hours or longer if need be ʒ j of our dry soap till it have been [amalgamated?] with it and thrown out again in the forme of an unpromiseing pouder. Then put it to an other dram of the Soap and proceed as before afterwards adde a third dram, and set aside the pouder that will be thrown out as formerly and thus impregnate the liquor with ʒ i after another till you have incorporated with it as far as you can doe it by grinding a whole ounce†1

En Tibi iterum Epistola Tua Dedicatoria lecta. probata et quam cito fieri poterat restituta. Nihil in ea Viro optimo minus placere videbatur nisi quod de se nimis multa dixisse te quereretur sed

(Latin)
London 2 Aug 92
Here is your Epistle Dedicatory once more, read, approved, and returned to you as quickly as possible. Nothing in it seemed to displease the excellent man, except that he complained of your having said too much about him; [p. 487] but such modesty is to be pardoned in so great honour and deserts. You will find two words altered in your epistle; and if publication now imminent had allowed time I should have sent it back for you to see whether you would prefer the beginning of the last paragraph thus slightly altered. I did not venture to offer so great an alteration in another man's work without consulting you; I therefore showed the epistle to the Archbishop just as I had received it from you, except for those two words. Indeed I seem to myself to be acting freely enough with you in proceeding so far as to venture to interpose my opinion at this stage and to give advice to you who are so much more expert in this matter. What my advice is you will see from the attached note; but the whole thing must be left to your prudence. If you think that it should be altered in this fashion (for, whatever you may decide, I consider that my words should be entirely disregarded, as having been carelessly written), and if you have enough time for it to be sent back here, I shall show it to the Archbishop again; for it is not in my power to determine on the one hand what your friends there may approve of, and on the other what his modesty here can bear. Please do what seems best to you and most to the advantage of the Reformed Church.
(Latin) I am glad that the publication of a work I have so long wanted, and which I judge to be most useful to the reformed world at this time, is now imminent. [p. 488] Please give my best wishes to your dear wife and children and to our common friends. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE

1519. Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton to Locke, 2 August 1692 (1517, 1659)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 151-2. Printed in King, pp. 220-2; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 217-19 (no. 391). Answers no. 1517.
Aug. 2d. 1692.
Sir
I beg your pardon that I sent not your papers last week. The carrer went out a quarter of an hour sooner then I was aware of. I am glad you have all the 3 parts of the Recipe†a entire but before you go to work about it I desire you would consider these things. For it may perhaps save your time and expence.
This Recipe I take to be the thing for the sake of which Mr B. procured the repeal of the Act of Parl. against Multipliers, and therefore he had it then in his hands.†1 In the margin of the Recipe was noted that the [Mercury] of the first work would grow hot with [Gold] and thence I gather that this Recipe was the foundation of what he published many years ago about such [Mercuries] as would grow hot with [Gold] and therefore was then known to him, that is sixteen or 20 years ago at least.†2 And yet in all this time
― 489 ―
I cannot find that he has either tried it himself or got it tried with success by any body els. For when I spake doubtingly about it, he confest that he had not seen it tried but added that a certain Gentleman was now about it and it succeeded very well so far as he had gone and that all the signes appeared so that I needed not doubt of it. This satisfied me that [Mercury] by this Recipe may be brought to change its colours and properties: but not that [Gold] may be multiplied thereby.
And I doubt it the more because I heard some years ago of a company who were upon this work in London, and after Mr B. had communicated this Recipe to me so that I knew it was the same with theirs, I enquired after them and learnt that that two of them were since forced to other means of living and a third who was the chief Artist was still at work but was run so far into debt that he had much ado to live, and by these circumstances I understood that these gentlemen could not make the thing succeed. When I told Mr. B.†a of these gentlemen, he acknowledged that the Recipe was gone about among several Chymists, and therefore I intend to to stay till I hear that it succeeds with some of them.
But besides if I woud try this Recipe, I am satisfied that I could not. For Mr B. has reserved a part of it from my knowledge. I know more of it then he has told me,†b and by that and an expression or two which dropt from him I know that what he has told me is imperfect and useless without knowing more then I do. And therefore I intend only to try whether I know enough to make a Mercury which will grow hot with [Gold], if perhaps I shall try that. For Mr B. to offer his secret upon conditions†1 and after I had consented, not to perform his part looks odly; and that the rather because I was averse from medling with his Recipe till he perswaded me to it, and by not performing his part he has voided the obligation†c to the conditions on mine, so that I may reccon my self at my own discretion to say or do what I will about this matter though perhaps I shall be tender of using my liberty. But that I may understand the reason of his reservedness, pray will you be so free
― 490 ―
as to let me know the conditions which he obliged you to in communicating this Recipe and whether he communicated to you any thing more then is written down in the 3 parts of the Recipe. I do not desire to know what he has communicated but rather that you would keep the particulars from me†a (at least in the second and third part of the Recipe) because I have no mind to be concerned with this Recipe any further then just to know the entrance. I suspect his reservedness might proceed from mine. For when I communicated a certain experiment to him he presently by way of requital subjoyned two others, but cumbred them with such circumstances as startled me and made me afraid of any more. For†b he expected that I should presently go to work upon them and desired I would publish them after his death. I have not yet tried either of them nor intend to try them but since you have the inspection of his papers, if you designe to publish any of his remains, You will do me a great favour to let these two be published among the rest. But then I desire that it may not be known that they come through my hands. One of them seems to be a considerable†c Experiment†d and may prove of good use in medicine for analysing bodies, the other is only a knack.
In diswading you from too hasty a trial of this Recipe I have forborn to say any thing against multiplication in general because you seem perswaded of it: tho there is one argument against it which I could never find an answer to, and which, if you will let me have your opinion about it, I will send you in my next.
Address: For John Lock Esqr at Mr Pawlin's in Dorset Court in Channel Row in Kings street Westminster London.
Postmark: AV 3

1521. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 3/13 August 1692 (1494, 1604)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 49-50.
Monsieur
je devois avoir esté plus exact et plus prompt a vous respondre, mais nous sommes depuis ce temps la dans une si grande affliction qu'a peine ay je pu regler mes affaires domestiques. il a pris fantaisie a Monsieur Veen de se marier avec nostre tante Vefve d'Arminius,†3 que vous avez veue parmis nous, et laquelle n'ayant que quarante ans poura luy creer une nouvelle famille dont il na pas besoin; sil songoit a la peine quil a de subsister de son revenu dans ces temps facheux et estant hors d'estat d'en gagner, il a fait ces demarches avec tant d'indignation†4 pour des enfans qui l'ayment,
― 492 ―
et elle s'est servie de tant d'artifice et de surprise que nous aurons peine de revenir du tort quelle nous fait, et de la pouvoir jamais regarder de bon œil; cepandant c'est une affaire conclue, et les espousailles seront en bref. et tout ce qu on luy a pu opposer de la foiblesse de sa poittrine et de son crachement de sangh, tout na pu arrester sa rage quil la m'esme fait sortir de son temperamment ordinaire et nous dire cent duretez.
l'enqueste de vostre amis†1 est fort vaste et il peut mieux scavoir la pluspart de ce quil demande de Londres que d'icy. scavoir si l'on tient notice du nombre de ceux qui meurent a Madrid Paris Venice Rome, Constantinople, Smyrne, Dublin, Edenburgh les Barbadoes et Jamaica. pour Amsterdam toutes les sepmaines ont tient un conte public des morts sans dire pourtant comme je me souviens qu'on fait a Londres de quelle maladie les malades sont decedez.†2
Monsieur Vostre Amis n'ignore pas sur son second Article†3 que nous avons de Bartholin. Medicinam Danorum,†4 de Bontius Medicinam Indorum†5 et dans les descriptions des differents voyages en diverses contrées il poura recueillir ce quil demande.
pour le troisieme article si je l'ay bien compris il demande quel jugement nous faisons icy du kina kina, nous croyons que c'est un fort bon remede mais qu'on s'en peut servir imprudemment dans une fievre intermittente recente ou la nature agit regulierement a expulser la matiere morbifique. et dans les fievres accompagnées de grandes obstructions, mais c'est un grand secours dans les fievres opiniastres et dans celles ou les symptomes donnent a craindre. tousjours il est certain quil est plus en usage icy que jamais.
pour ce qui regarde les ouvrages de Monsieur Sydenham nous en faisons grande estime et il est certain que son plan et sa methode est admirable, cepandant il na pas reussi esgalement et ce quil nous
― 493 ―
dit de la gonorrhea est fort foible, et assurement ont seront tres souvent trompé en suivant sa methode.
enfin nos reglements pour le rang des medecins chirurgiens et apoticaires est icy comme ailleurs, et a leyden il y a tousjours un professeur qui exerce la practique sur quelques malades dc l'hospital pour l'instruction des estudians, on va faire la mesme chose dans nostre hospital icy. Monsieur Bernage a force d'amis a obtenu la chaire de professeur en medicine dans cette escole illustre.
ma femme plus languissante que jamais vous presente ses respects. nos petits heureux de ne participer a nos chagrins se portent bien. et si vous escrivez de deca ne faite pas connoistre sil vous plaist la douleur que nous vous tesmoignons, il semble que cela soulage en le faisant a vous qui nous aimez. adieu mon cher Monsieur celle cy vous sera rendue par le bon Monsieur bouhereau de la Rochelle.†1 je suis avec un profond respect
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
GUENELLON
d'amsterd. ce 13 Aoust 1692.

1522. James Tyrrell to Locke, 9 August [1692] (1477, 1589)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 117-20. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxon: Aug: 9th:
Dear Sir
I have deferred the answering your letter till now, that I could assure you that I have performed the effects of it, in sending away the rest of your things, which I could not doe sooner then last weeke, haveing not bin at okeley to stay there till then, in above 2 monthes all things there haveing been very dirty, and unpleasant; but I have now put up, and sent you to Oxford these particulars following: first in the great pair of boxes are put all your paper bookes, which have no writeing in them; except 2, or 3 smaller ones which I have made use of, and will be answereable to you for. the other pair of boxes are sent up empty; because there were no small bookes left to fill them: all of that sort being either sent up
― 494 ―
allready, or els deliverd to Mr: Thomas; with the rest of those physic bookes you orderd to be deliverd to; him; and which filled allmost 3 ordinary boxes: and He, and I, have taken an exact Catalogue of them;†1 which you will find put in the Japan Ennbassy†2 which is in your box with the lock, the Key of which Mr: Thomas hath likewise sent you in a letter to your self: or Mr: Pawling; wee were forced to have a new key made to it because my daughter had soe mislayed the old one before she went away, that it could not be found; but in that box you will find your 2 Carpets: with oglebyes 2 volumes of his Eng: Atlass†3 which I told you were borrowed by Father and my son, as for your China Embassy†4 you may remember that being a weary of it you were pleased to give it me, but it shall still be as much at your service as if it were your owne; there is allso in that box Kettlewell of Christian obedience,†5 which my Sister had borrowed; and Bellonius;†6 with 4 small bookes of your collections which were before mislayd, and so omitted to be sent you: so that I have now nothing of yours in my hands, except those bookes I have borrowed of you; and which you have my note for; and besides an old Terrestriall Globe which would not goe into the box it was so full, and my son desires the use of it a little longer; I have allso your weather glasse at Shotover, which was too long to goe into any of the boxes, but tho' I have put quite new quicksilver into it the old being so foul that it would not move right; yet you shall have it againe when ever you tell me it may be use full to you; and will bring it with me when I come up, next terme;†7 if you please so to order it: there is likewise a thin boxe, which I bought to keep all your Maps in apart from my owne; all which are carefully put up in it: so that you are to receive 4 boxes in all 3 of which are full: so haveing dispatcht this affair; I have nothing more to trouble you with at present; but to know whether you have received the Dialogues which I orderd to be sent you as fast as they came out;†8 not for your instruction; but as a Testimony of my respect: I allso orderd my bookseller to send
― 495 ―
you my Treatise of the law of nature which I told you long since I had abridged out of Dr: Cumberlands latin treatise on that subject; I hope you will have read it; and be able to give me your free censure of it next Time wee meet if not before; onely I desire you would make Syl: correct the Errata (which are pretty many) before you read it: and I hope that this treatise may give the world sufficient satisfaction, or at†a- least may-†a els excite your self or some other thinking person, to give the world a better account of the Law of nature; and its obligation, then what hath bin allready performed: as allso to confute with better Reasons the Epicurean Principles of Mr: Hobs: for the doeing of which, I know no man more capeable then your self if you please to undertake it; and shall no more resent it then the publishing of the 2 Treatises of Goverment after Patriarcha non†b Monarcha;†1 since if truth can be better represented, and improved: by a greater hand: I shall not value if my small performances, serve for a foyle to set it off; since I have, (I thank God) learnt so far that Master Principle in Dr: Cumberlands booke, as to preferre the common good of mankind, before my owne Fame; and all the small reputation of an Authour: but perhaps I would have alterd somewhat in the Doctors definition of the Law of nature, in placeing it in the endeavour of the Common Good of rational Beings of which I suppose God to be the Head, had†c- the notion bin owne:-†c yet I suppose it may passe well enough with that explication the Authour hath given of it in the preface: however I hope you will not take amisse those passages I have added to this treatise out of your Excellent Essay. etc. I have nothing els to tell you but that all my Relations at Shot;†2 are well, and so are (I hope) my Chil: I received lately a letter from my son Thom: dated from the Canaryes. James is in the Countrey, and tells me he hath still in his hands; a booke; and Cushion of yours; which shall be sent you when he comes up: Mr: King†3 boards in the house with me, and desires to have his service presented to you. I goe this week for the Bath; and
― 496 ―

shall stay there about a fortnight; and from thence shall goe into Wales to see my sister, and daughter, if you please to returne an answere to this you may either direct yours to me at Mr: Bushels, Towne Clerk of Bathe, or els to Mrs: Hobyes at Neath Abbey, to be left at Caerdiffe. Glammorgan: Mr: Thomas is this day gone home haveing first sent all your things together with his owne to Mr: Rushes barge, which I suppose sets out on Thursday Mr: Thom: allso payd for the Carriage of the boxes to Oxford: so praying for your health; and satisfaction I remaine

1523. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, [c. 10/20 August 1692] (1518, 1527)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 69-70. The date in Locke's endorsement is probably that on which he received the letter, and probably old style; he replied on 19 August. The date therefore lies between 6/16 August, when van Limborch received no. 1518, and 13/23 August, the latest possible date for the letter to reach Locke at Oates (for this see no. 1527) on 17/27 August. Answers no. 1518; answered by no. 1527.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Gratissimas tuas 2/12 Augusti datas 16 accepi. Grates habeo maximas, et quantascunque habeam plurimarum me debitorem profiteor, pro recenti beneficio, quo me de novo Tibi obstrictum reddidisti. Gaudeo Reverendissimo Domino non improbatam dedicationem meam: Utinam præter duas voculas et alia correxisses! Jam olim
― 497 ―
Tibi perspectum credidi, nihil mihi gratius esse ac jucundius, quam qualescunque meas lucubrationes a peritissimâ tuâ manu castigatas ac emendatas recipere. Mutationem initii ultimi paragraphi ita totus probo, ut mea verba prorsus deleri, tua substitui statim voluerim. Utinam me inconsulto ea Reverendissimo Domino ostendisses! quoniam illo inconsulto nihil hic facere licet. Unum vereor, ne omnibus pateat, purpureum hunc pannum qui late splendeat†1 aliunde esse assutum. Verum non pudebit me aperte profiteri cujus hic vitula araverim:†2 pars enim honoris mihi erit, tanti viri amicitia posse gloriari. Vides itaque denuo Dedicationem correctam et ornatiorem: verba tua in eâ agnosces, quæ immutata servavi; certus si quid mutarem, etiam de illorum gratia ac venustate periturum. Credo editionem ad finem properaturam quando eam recepero. Pervenimus jam ad terminationem processus contra hæreticum confessum et pœnitentem, per abjurationem, aliasque pœnas ac pœnitentias salutares.†3 Verum licet aliquamdiu exspectandum foret, mora ea contemnenda est; paucorum tantum erit illa dierum. Liber Sententiarum jam absolutus est; restat solummodo
― 498 ―
index illi præfixus.†1 Spero Te intra mensem opus hoc diu desideratum conspecturum. Metuisti nuper D. Veenio ne praxi continuæ jam a multis annis assuetus rure otio intabescat. Ille vero ibi non tantum convalescere cœpit, sed sentire veteris vestigia flammæ.†2 Sponsus jam est, ducturus Jacobi Arminii viduam. Connubium hoc non leves in familia ipsius turbas dedit, prout ex D. Guenelloni literis didicisti: omnem animis perturbatoribus leniendis operam impendi; et jam mitius tolerare velle videntur, quod evitari non potest. Ego judico, prudentius facturum fuisse senem, si in viduitate perstitisset: Verum cum ipse aliter statuerit, liberorum esse, non violenter nec aspere paternæ reluctari voluntati. Nihil intentatum reliqui ut hi motus animorum atque hæc certamina tanta†3 componerentur. Mitius omnia se jam habent: de animis judicare meum non est; verba autem jam sunt molliora. Pater filiarum ac nepotum amans est, et ante contractum nuptialem cavere voluit, ne quid ex hisce nuptiis aliquid detrimenti sui patiantur. Jussit Te plurimum salvere Venius, addique sanitatem sibi jam esse multò confirmatiorem. In describenda dedicatione ultima tua verba paululum immutavi, ut paulo magis ab ultimis totius dedicationis verbis
― 499 ―
differrent: Tu scripseras, quibus olim obtinuit semperque stabit religio vere Christiana.†1 Si mea, quæ restitui, verba minus placent, sine ullo scrupulo dele; et si alia mutanda judices, velim eadem qua ego παῤῥησίᾳ†2 utaris, et me credas eundem esse qui semper fui. Verum hora abrumpere jubet. Vale Vir Amplissime. Uxor liberique Te officiosissime salutant.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH.
(English) Reverendissimo archiepiscopo officiosam rogo dicas a me salutem.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I received your very welcome letter of 2/12 August on the 16th. I thank you very much and, however much I may do so, acknowledge that I owe you very many thanks for your fresh kindness, whereby you have made me anew obliged to you. I am very glad that my dedication was not disallowed by his Most Reverend Lordship. Would that you had corrected not merely [p. 497] two words but other things as well! I think you have this long time been aware that nothing is more welcome and pleasing to me than to receive back my lucubrations, such as they are, chastened and amended by your expert hand. I so wholly approve of the alteration of the beginning of the last paragraph that I wished that my words had been entirely deleted and yours substituted forthwith. Would that you had shown them to his Most Reverend Lordship without consulting me! for without consulting him nothing may be done in this matter. The one thing I fear is that it may be manifest to all that 'this purple patch to shine afar'†1 has been sewn on from another source. However I shall not be ashamed openly to acknowledge whose heifer I have ploughed with†2 in this field; for part of the honour will be mine, to be able to boast of the friendship of so great a man. So here you see the dedication once more, corrected and improved; you will recognize your own words in it, which I have kept unaltered, as I was sure that if I altered anything something also of their grace and beauty would be lost. I believe that the work of publication will hasten to an end as soon as I get it back. We have now reached the conclusion of the proceeding against the heretic confessed and penitent, that is by abjuration and other 'salutary' pains and penances.†3 However, though we shall have to wait a little longer the delay is negligible; it will be only for a few days. The Liber Sententiarum [p. 498] is now completed; there remains only the index prefixed to it.†1 I hope you will see this long-wanted work within a month. You recently expressed a fear that Mr. Veen, having been accustomed now for many years to uninterrupted practice, may be pining away in leisure in the country. In fact he has not only begun to regain health there but also to feel 'traces of the old flame'.†2 He is now engaged to marry the widow of Jacobus Arminius. This marriage has caused no slight disturbances in his family, as you have learnt from Mr. Guenellon's letter; I have exerted myself to soothe these disturbing passions, and they now seem willing to endure more calmly what cannot be avoided. In my opinion, as an elderly man he would have acted more prudently if he had remained a widower; however, as he has decided otherwise, it is proper for the children not to oppose their father's wish violently or harshly. I have left nothing untried in order that 'these outbursts of the passions and these mighty wars'†3 may be settled. Everything is now calmer; it is not for me to judge of their feelings, but their words are now gentler. He is a loving father of his daughters and grandchildren, and he wanted to take care before the marriage contract was made lest his own family should suffer any loss by reason of it. Veen bade me to give you his best wishes and to add that his health is now much more settled. In copying the dedication I have altered your last words slightly, in order that they may differ a little more from the last words of the whole dedication; you had written quibus [p. 499] olim obtinuit semperque stabit religio vere Christiana.†1 If the words I have substituted are unacceptable delete them without scruple; and if you consider that anything else should be altered I should wish you to use the same freedom of speech as I, and to believe that I am the same as I always was. But the hour bids me break off. Good-bye, excellent Sir. My wife and children send you their best respects.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
(Latin) Please give my dutiful respects to the Most Reverend the Archbishop.
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mr. Robbert Pawlings in Dorset Coort in Chanell row Westminster
Endorsed by Locke: P. Limborch 17 Aug. 92 Answered 19
1524. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 11 August 1692 (1121, 1536)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 158-9.
Dr. Francis Turner, as a nonjuror, was deprived of the see of Ely on 1 February 1690. His mother and his daughter Margaret and Mrs. Grigg had evidently been transferred to the house of his brother Dr. Thomas Turner, 1645-1714, President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, from 1688 to 1714 (D.N.B.).
Deare Brother
Sure you will excuse my silence when till last night I knew not how to direct my letters to you, for tho I often by diligent enquirys
― 500 ―
heard of your being well and frequently of your progressing life yet was I still ignorant where my letters should find my old friend, else you had not Escapd all this while hearing how I live; If you have met with any that converse with me here, they will tell you that I am as little vissible as the severest Nun, and that I neither pine at what I dislike nor counterfeit more peace of mind then God gives me. The absence of friends and their misfortuns dos not change my friendship unless it be by hightning my concerne for them. At present I am a new mourner for the death of the good Mother of the family I live in,†1 And now both the dead and living movingly bespeak my continuing in this retired Coll: that your pritty Mistris†2 may not be destitute of a plaine dealing friend till she be less an orphant then she is at present, Your intrest in her affections is very great and tho she be now of an age which makes her admired, so that divers please themselves with the hopes of beguiling you, yet no dazling <Elder Brother>†a has leave to make speeches, so that I expect to be causlessly curst for my severe withstanding a poor childs being too Early embark'd in the greatest difficultys of life, (a fine Mariage if without that solid judgment which must make plenty and every thing else in this world a blessing). I am aware deare brother that my fidelity and gratitude will cost me some thoughtfullness, but I shall have the joy of doing as I would be don by myself. All here salut you and dayly speak of you with just respect. My son is now with me and is I am certain with all his heart at your service. I shall be glad to hear that you are well for I am
Sir
Your obliged sister and humble servant
A G
