1525. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 16/26 August 1692 (1511, 1541)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 58-9. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 56-8.
A Amsterdam le 26 d'Août 1692
Je rendis, Monsieur, vôtre Lettre à Mr. Veryn, le lendemain du jour auquel je l'eus reçuë; depuis je ne l'ai pas vû, pour juger de la disposition où il est. Je ne croi néanmoins pas qu'il fasse imprimer sa version, dans ce temps-ci où les Libraires n'impriment que le moins qu'ils peuvent, à cause de la cherté du papier. Cependant si j'en puis apprendre quelque chose, je ne manquerai pas de vous le mander.
Je vous suis bien obligé de la peine, que vous avez prise pour vous informer de l'exemplaire de ma Logique envoié à Mr. Boyle. Ce n'est pas ma faute, s'il ne la reçu avant sa mort, le livre aiant été envoié des le commencement de Decembre, car quoi que la date soit du premier de Janvier 1692. Il avoit été imprimé plus de six semaines auparavant. Si j'avois sû que quelcun eût dessein en Angleterre d'imprimer ces petits ouvrages,†1 je lui aurois envoié un errata, l'édition de Hollande n'étant pas trop correcte. Il y a quelques mots d'omis dans la Pneumatologie sect. 2. c. V. §. 5. où après audiunt il faut, eodem morbo laborare incipiant. C'est la plus grosse, car pour les autres, il est aisé de les corriger.
Ma Critique†2 est à moitié faite, il y a longtemps, mais je l'ai quitée pour mon ouvrage du Pentateuque. J'y reviendrai au premier loisir, et je la publierai. Je suis bien aise que vous pensiez à la démonstration de la Morale, et je prie Dieu qu'il vous donne de la santé et du loisir pour cela. La plûpart s'imaginent que celle de l'Evangile est contre la nature et la raison, ce que je ne croi point.
Je ne serois pas fâché que l'on réfutât les Lettres de l'Inspiration,†3 pourvu que cela se fît sans passion et sine invidia, quæ est primarium
― 502 ―
Theologorum argumentum.†1 Je doute qu'il y ait des gens bien propres à en user ainsi, et j'ai peur qu'ils ne mêlent mon nom mal à propos là dedans. Je ne croi pas que personne ait vû aucun monument en anciens caracteres Phéniciens. On parle beaucoup de certains sicles†2 Samaritains, mais je ne sai si on s'y peut fier, pouvant être fabriquez à plaisir. Mr. Toinard, à ce qu'on m'a dit, doit traiter de cette matiere, comme vous le verrez, dans l'un des Tomes de la Bibliot. Univ. que je vous envoie.†3 Vous y trouverez joint le petit livre de Scheffer, de la Philosophie Pythagoricienne,†4 qui est devenu assez rare, mais dont Wetstein avoit apporté par hazard quelques examplaires de Francfort, la foire passée.
Pour ce qui regarde la Philosophie Chaldaïque,†5 nous n'en avons que des fragmens par-ci par-là. Je croi que l'on en trouve le plus dans les Commentaires de Proclus sur Platon, et dans Iamblique de Mysteriis. Il y a aussi les Commentaires de Psellus et de Plethon sur les Oracles. Le reste ne sont que pur fragmens. Mais il y a quelque chose de fâcheux dans tout cela, c'est que les Paiens y mêlent la Philosophie des Grecs, sur tout celle de Platon; et que les Chrétiens expliquent bien des choses, à la Chrétienne. Or il n'est pas facile de distinguer ce qu'il y a d'Oriental et d'antique là dedans. Pour moi je me persuade que ce qui n'a pas de rapport aux opinions Greques, ni à celles des Chrétiens, est de ce genre. Pour le reste, quoi qu'il se puisse faire que les Grecs et les Chrétiens aient des opinions communes avec les Chaldéens, en diverses choses, il est difficile de s'assurer de celles qui sont venuës d'Orient. Je croi que l'on peut s'assurer que les vers 281 et suivans des Oracles†6 jusqu'au 292. sont de la premiere espece, car on n'y voit ni Christianisme, ni Platonisme. C'est dommage que nous n'ayions pas biens des vers comme ceux-là. Cependant je croi que le peu de chose, que nous savons de cela, peut nous servir, en plusieurs rencontres, pour entendre le V.Testament, et j en donnerai quelques preuves dans mon Ouvrage sur le Pentateuque, qui sera, avec l'aide de Dieu, bientôt sous la presse. Je me flatte que ce livre ne vous déplaira pas, ma maniére
― 503 ―
d'expliquer l'Ecriture étant, comme je me l'imagine, beaucoup plus conforme aux plus severes regles de la Critique, que quoi que ce soit de cette nature, qui ait paru. Vous en jugerez, lors que vous le verrez, et je ne dois pas prévenir vôtre jugement. Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur tout à vous J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in Dorset Court, in channel row Westminster
Endorsed by Locke: J le Clerc 26° Aug. 92 Answered 9° Sept.
1526. Edward Clarke to Locke, 17 August 1692 (1502, 1532)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 66-7. Printed in Rand, pp. 349-50.
Chipley August the 17th. 1692.
Dear Sir,
I Return you my hearty thankes for your Kind Letter of the 9th., and for the Good Advise you gave the Lord B.†1 in relation to mee; I have (with difficulty) gott good Returns for 200l. on Bylls payable to Mr. Percyvall, but was forced to ride to Exeter on purpose before I could gett it done; 'tis the Return of the Taxes that make's it soe difficult, but I hope to find a Return for the remainder of your money in a short time, I will order That allready in Mr. Percyvalls handes to bee paid where, or in what manner you shall appoynt, and if your occassions require hast I will write to Mr. Percyvall to give mee Creditt for the Remainder due to you untill I can gett Return's for it to Him, in Answere to which pray give mee a Lyne per next, and in the meane time give my humble service to Sir Francis and my Lady, and the rest of your good company at Oates, and bee assured that I am
your most obleiged Faithfull servant

Excellent Sir,
Your last letter has found me in the country, but lest there should be any delay I have sent at once to London to a friend of mine in the Archbishop's household,†1 who, having done what is necessary, will duly send you what you are waiting for, which I trust you will receive at the same time as this letter. You speak too highly of another man's words, when you could have found more graceful and suitable ones yourself. For mine were not sent you as a pattern, but merely to let you see to what I incline.
(Latin) I wish that all may be prosperous and peaceful in our friend Veen's family; I therefore beg you to do all you can to settle things. You write as if our friend Guenellon had written to me recently about that matter; but I have received not a single word from him for a long time. I should be much troubled if his letter was lost. Please give my best wishes to him, as well as to Veen and the rest of that family, and tell them all, so far as you think it may be of use, that I advise above all things peace, concord, friendship.
(Latin) [p. 505] You do not know how great a joy it is to us, to Mrs. Cudworth, that is, and to me, that your work will appear so soon. We are eagerly expecting it. She sends you her best wishes, as I do mine to your wife and all your family. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE

I received two from you since I wrot last, your first came not till Tuesday†2 in the afternoon and I came not in till eight, but the next morning I went up into the City early as I use to do and being near London bridg I went over it and had a fine walk through St Georges fields.†3 I delivered mr Coxes letter in his absence to his wife, who is well and presents her service to you and promised to send the letter to him immediately. I met with mr Mountacue†4 by accident at White hall and delivered your message. he presents his service to you and told me there is no hast of what he desired when he had told me what it was I could have told him I could have don it, but I did not. on Monday morning as I returned from the City I tooke your boxes from Rushes Barge,†5 that was just come in and they are now safe at home; one pair of the boxes, I guess are empty. 1530. William Molyneux to Locke, 27 August 1692 (1515, 1538)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 3-6. Answers no. 1515; answered by no. 1538.
Dublin. Aug. 27. 1692
Sir
Upon the Arrival of Our Lord Lieutenant†2 in this Place (which was on the 25th Inst.) I had the Favour of a Letter from you by the Hands of Dr Sibelius. I cannot easily tell you, How Gratefull it was to me; Having the Highest esteem for him that sent it, from the first Moment that I was so happy, as to see any of his Writings. and therefore it was, that I was so ambitious of Making a Freindship with you, by presenting you One of My Trifles, which I Orderd My Bookseller to lay before you under this Character, As a Mean Testimony of the Great Respect I had for the Author of the Essay of Humane Understanding. And since I find by Yours to Me, that My Ambition is not fallen short of its Designe; But that you are pleased to Incourage me by assuring Me that I have made great Advances of Freindship towards you; Give me leave to Imbrace the Favour
― 508 ―
with all Joy Imaginable. And that you may Judge of my Sincerity by my Open Heart, I wil plainly confess to you, that I have not in my Life read any Book with More Satisfaction, than your Essay; Insomuch that a Repeated perusal of it is still more pleasant to Me.
And I have indeavourd, with Great Success, to Recommend it to the Consideration of the Ingenious in this Place. Dr King Bishop of Derry,†1 when he read it, made some slight Remarks on the formost parts of the Book; but his Busines would not permit him to go through it all. what he did, rough as it was, he gave to me. and they are at your Commands, when you please.
One Thing I must needs insist on to you, which is, that you would think of Obleidging†a the World, with a Treatise of Morals, drawn up according to the Hints you frequently give in Your Essay, Of their Being Demonstrable according to the Mathematical Method.†2 This is Most Certainly True. But then the task must be undertaken only by so Clear and Distinct a Thinker as you are. This were an Attempt worthy your Consideration. And there is Nothing I should More ardently wish for, than to see it. And therefore, Good Sir, Let me Beg of you to turn your thoughts this way. and if so Young a Freindship as mine have any force; Let me prevail upon you.
Upon my Reading your Essay, I was so taken with it, that when I was in London in August 1690 I made enquiry amongst some of My Learned Freinds for any other of your Writings (if perhaps they knew any). I was recommended by some to Two Discourses Concerning Government, and a Little Treatise Concerning Toleration. there is neither of them Carrys your Name. and I wil not venture to ask, whether they are yours or Not.†3 This only I think, No Name need be ashamed of Either.
Dr Sibelius I find is your Freind, and therefore I assure him of all service I can possibly do him. I wil make it my Busines to get him acquaintance in this Place; and I dare promise him some of the Best.
― 509 ―
The Inclosed from My Brother will tell you that he was your Acquaintance in Leyden. I my self have been there, Anno 1685, but had not the Good Fortune of being known to you. But from this time I shall reckon my self Happy in your Freindship and shall ever subscribe My self
Your Most Affectionate and Obleidged Humble Servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
Your Letters Directed to me nigh Ormonds Gate in Dublin will come safe.†a
Endorsed by Locke: W: Molineux 27° Aug. 92. Answered 20 Sept.
1531. Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux to Locke, 27 August 1692 (800, 1556)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 277-8. Enclosed in no. 1530. Answered by no. 1556.
Dubl: Aug: 27. -92
Sir
I'm very sensible of Your great Civility in Remembring me uppon so short an Acquaintance as I had with You in Holland so long time since: and I assure You with out any Complement, I reccon it among the most Fortunate Accidents of my Life, my so luckily faling into Your Conversation, which was so candid, diverting and instructive that I still reap the Benefit and Satisfaction of it.
Some Years after I left You in Holland, uppon my Return for England I contracted no smale Intimacy with Dr. Sydenham, on the account of having been known to You his much estimed Friend, and I found him so accurate an Observer of Diseases, so throughly skilld in all Usefull Knowledge of his Profession, and with all, so communicative, that his Acquaintance was a very great Advantage to me; and all this I cheifly owe to You Sir, besides the Information of many usefull Truths, and a great deale of very pleasing Entertainement I have mett with in the Perusal of Your latly publishd Writings: so that on many accounts I must needs say

there are very few Men in the world, to whom I can with the like Sincerity profess myself to be as I am
Dear Sir
Your most reall Friend and very humble and oblidg'd servant

Address: To Mr John Lock in London
Endorsed by Locke: T: Molineux 27° Aug. 92
1532. Edward Clarke to Locke, 31 August 1692 (1526, 1546)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 68. Printed in Rand, pp. 350-1.
Chipley August the 31th 1692.
Deare Sir,
Yours of the 22th. came not to my handes untill yesterday, or else you should sooner have received my thankes for it, and for your greate kindnesse to mee therein with respect to the Returns of money I mentioned to you in my last, But I have now noe occasion to take the Benifit of your Kind offer in that Particular, For soon after the Writeing my last to you I mett with a Convenient and Good Return for 100l. more to Mr. Percyvall, Soe that I have now between 3. and 4. hundred pounds in his handes, out of which you may Receive the Ballance of my last Accompt with you, when ever you thinke fitt, Presumeing there is more then suffitient (togather with the money you received since I came out of Town at my Lord Bellomonts-Office)†1 to Discharge that Ballance, But I am at a Losse to know the certainty thereof, not haveing the last Accompt here with mee in the Countrey, and therefore in your next, Pray lett me know the certaine summe that will discharge that Ballance, and I will not fayle to send you a Byll on Mr. Percyvall for the Payment thereof to you or your Order, and least you should want it in the meane time, I have inclosed sent you a Byll on Him for three hundred pounds, which you may use if there bee occasion: I am heartily Glad to heare that you and the Good Family at Oates are Well, and that you escaped the High-way-men
― 511 ―
in the Forest,†1 Pray give my humble service to all the Good campany you are with, and bee assured that I am,
Your most affectionate Faithfull servant,
EDW: CLARKE:
Address: These, For Mr. John Lock [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford] Franke: Edw: Clarke:
Postmarks: SE 3; SA
Endorsed by Locke: E: Clarke 31° Aug. 92
1533. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 31 August/10 September 1692, with postscript [7/17? September 1692] (1506, 1534)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 96-7, 100. The contents of f. 100 show that it belongs to September 1692. Furly implies that it was appended to a letter which he had intended to send by private conveyance; as at one time he intended to send the present letter by a servant of his, it is likely that the postscript belongs with it.
[ff. 96-7:]
Rotterdam 10 September 1692
Deare Friend
I am ashamed I have been so long answering your letter of the 6/16th of June, which you were so long awriting and sending away, that part of it was wrote at Oats, and the other part at London. I render you in the first place thanks for your pains in extracting me those 5 verses in Luke out of Beza's Venerable Cantabrigian M:S.†2 by which I see its true enough, that those words, do this in remembrance of me, which are onely to be found in Luke; are wanting in that copy. And that it is written in capital letters, as I had been informed not onely without accents, and distinctions of points, to distinguish the sence, but even without distinguishing the words from one another, so that one line seems to the Ey to be but one word. which I intend so to register at bottom of this letter, in my copy book. If the Autographs of the Apostles were so writ. We have in our bibles, besides the defect of the Transcribers, the varios lections, and translation, a great deal more humane Artifice, than
― 512 ―
men are aware of, so that there will want to render it al infallible divine Truth, infallible inspiration to discern the true reading, and to distinguish the true Apostolicall sense from the fallible conceptions of the first punctators,†1 who have insensibly imposed their sense upon us, as that of the Apostles, whereas it may be vastly different from it, as appears by the five fold punctation of these words, without him was nothing made what was made in him was life.†2
If you can answer my desire as to the other part of my letter of the 22 march last, with respect to the various reading of 1 Peter 3.21. in that M:S. which Dr. Hammond cals the Kings M:S. wrote in Capital letters also. And especially that m:S. in Oxford, in small letters which reads it inline image not ὁ with the vulgar, nor ὧ with the complutensian copy.
For tho I have layd aside the thoughts of publishing what I have writ against that scurrillous fellow, because all men say he is not worthy any answer because of his vile prevarication, and shewing him to be a man of no principles;†3 yet I would leave my thoughts upon that subject to my children; and whatever I can discover upon it, which makes such a noise in the world, and stands upon so slender foundations.
Mr. Leers returns you his thanks for the catalogue given mr. Cunningham,†4 in which he finds Authors, not in his own, tho a very large one, he begs you to continue your request to mr Charleton, about the Catalogue of his medals; to whom pray present my service.
I see you have found what I desired you to do with the Trunk you had of Monsieur Leon because mr. wright has it; I send you by the bearer (a servant of mine, whom I have commanded to wayt upon you, for your commands, at his returne) a small packet received from Monsieur Le clerc,†5 to which I have added 2 small Treatises received yesterday from the Baron, one his own, (of which I wrote you, and now expect your account of it I never having read it) translated into Latin,†6 by an ingenious Switser Doctor
― 513 ―
Amman,†1 Author of the other called Surdus Loquens, who has taught a yong Gentlewoman at harlem, that was born deaf and dumb, to speak as distinctly and audibly, as I do, and to write what she speaks. Dr. Kohlhans has spoke with her severall times, I have been this 12 month agoing to satisfy my curiosity, to see and speak with her, but could never yet break forth; he has there publisht his method, by which he says, that in the space of two months he will teach any sharp witted body to speak, that never spake before. The world wilbe much obliged to him, if others can take up what he writes.
My little Boys were all here this faire time,†2 and have all their humble service presented to you; Arent is the entertainment of all where he comes.
        
Now I come to my concern with Swinton; and humbly thanke you for your care for me, and ingaging mr. Johnson†3 in it, to whom pray present my humble service. Thus it stands, in the yeare 1679, after his fayling to pay my, and other bills of Excha: he came over and the 1 of September 1679 we settled accounts and by ballance of Account he subscribed to ow me 	f 8592: 04: 4

First he saith he left me many assignations at his departure, on people in Town, which is true, but the men for the most part denyed the Transactions, and all correspondence with him, as many as I could prove anything against, I sued and recovered of divers by sentences the sum of f 1812.4. deducting the charges of the suits—f 212: ——I Credit him 	f 1601: 4

Thus things stand truly and honestly betwixt us. If you wilbe pleasd now to represent it to mr Johnson, I shalbe obliged to him and yourself for it. In the meanwhile, when I think upon the man, and his cuntry, and the lamentable account the chancelor of Scotland gave of his cuntrymen, and Law, to the Lord Bacon, which you told me of,†1 I shal looke upon all that I get, as pure gain, and would sel my Action to any body for £500 sterling downe upon the nayle. My Lord Monmouth was pleased upon reading your letter to inquire what that concerne of Swinton was, and to promise his Lordships assistance in the case, which I also now in mine to his Lordship request of him;
For news we have none, but that the mighty men of Goes have taken in soldiers, which they had always the liberty to do, and having so done by consent, their priviledges remain firm, for the stadholder with the consent of the Burgermasters and Goverment (tho not without it) might lodge militia in the Town and Island. The matter lyes before the States of Zealand. They received them in upon conditions, That they should not be lodged upon the Townsmen at their charge. That the Townsmen should keep the Main guard at the stadhouse, and the keys of the gates, and that the new Regiment that was but then arrived in boates should not debark. But having possession, they say, they have in every respect not regarded the conditions.†2 We are now in possession of Dixmuyden
― 516 ―
10 miles from Yper, and of Veurn 10 miles from Dunkirk which we are fortifying that we may fall upon which we please.†1 I wish we have as good success, and scape so well as the french before Namen,†2 Luxenbergh†3 is very quiet hitherto, but I fear when he sees where weel pitch our tents hele be upon our skirts. But your parliament may now see if they be not blind that we have cut out good work for them to assist in, for without mony, whatever preparations we make those Towns, nor Callice†4 neither will not be taken; I would could see them in good English hands, tho it cost us two pence h'apeny more than it has; I am Sir
Your humble Servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

1534. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 8 September 1692 (1533, 1562)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 94-5. Furly generally uses new-style dates when writing to Locke from Rotterdam; the earthquake shows that the date of the present letter is old style.
Rotterdam 8 September 1692
Sir
This comes by Captain Masham,†1 by whom I could not but give you an account of an Earthquake that happend in this Town about 2 aclock when many were sitting at table, But I had dined, my servants retired into my comptoir, and I putting of my upper garments to lye down, and take a nap, as—when they came affrighted into my chamber and askt me if I did not feel the house to shake I said no, but standing still saw it, and found my head grow light and my stomach grow sick, as if I were at sea; I went then into the street, not thinking any thing but that it was some particular defect in my own house, to looke upon the Gable, and outside, as I stood gazing, I saw the people in heaps, and my next neighbour came and askt me, if I felt it also, I askt what, she said the earth quake.†2
My next neighbour on the left-hand of me, one of the Vroedschaaps†3 of this Town, askt me what I thought of it, I said I thought it was an earthquake, and he gravely said he beleevd it to be a discharge of one of those machines provided for the walls of Dunkirk. in which there is 30000 and some 50000 lb of powder; I desire this case may be layd before your Royall Society. Whether it be more probable to have been an earthquake, seing the earth houses, water and ships all were very gently 7 or 8 times tost to and fro from South to North and back again, in a cuntry that have no subterraneous caverns, or sulphureous matter, but what is in
― 518 ―
our mud of which we make our turf, so wel guarded with water from having any effect upon us, till it be sufficiently dryed in the sun.
Or whether any quantity of powder, at such a distance, as we could not heare the least noise in the Ayre, not so much as to make our glass windows rattle, could shake our cuntry; they say the bell in the steeple sounded.
All the files of papers hanging in my counting house shaked too and fro, and the booke the lad was writing in was moved from under his Arme;
This is a strange passage, as ever has been seen—one telling mony, the table was overturnd with the mony, but my clock, or slinger,†1 that in motion was shaked into rest. I wish it be not a presage of a shaking of our fabrick,—I am
Sir
Your most affectionate friend and servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
My service to Sir Fr. M. and my Lady
Just now come to towne, my Lord Pagets†2 Gentleman of the horse from the Hague, that says it was more violent there, than we felt it here, as they sate at table the whole Table shooke.
Address (written by an amanuensis): To Doctor Locke per Ami Q D G
Endorsed by Locke: B. Furly 8 Sept. 92
1535. Charles Mordaunt, earl of Monmouth, later third earl of Peterborough, to Locke, 10 September [1692] (1411, 1540)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 109-10. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Mr Lock.
I was afflicted to the last degree that i was forced out of Town before I heard from you, Mr Hobbes was impatient to have Johny†3 att the Bath, the letter I writt by Mistake and directed to chemsford I conclude came not to your hands, but I would have staid it till I had sent a messenger a purpose, but that my Damsel tould me you had said to her you would not drink the watters, and that she aprehended a journey at this time of the year so far you would only
― 519 ―
engage in out of complaisance. I own I condemne your ingratitude to these watters that have done greater miracles then ever this season. Mr Clark my Lord Bellamont telles me will be here, we all agree Mr Trencherd and Mr Hall in our wishes for you, and if my damsel mistook you as I believe she did let me know the day you will come and I will send my coach to Reading for you that you may come the ill part of the way att ease, the weather is very good and our houses were lesse shook as we heare then those about Town.†1
yours
MONMOUTH
Sep. the 10th.

1536. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 11 September [1692] (1524, 1591)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 160-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Deare Brother
I should not have bin half so well pleas'd with your quick answer had it not very obligingly reproved my hard to be excusd silence, but yet I perceive you doe with a kind severity take no notice of your leaving london and your hiding yourself from your sister; for all your former letter inform'd me was that you were going into the Country; but as soon as Mr Tyril instructed me how to send to you I fail'd not to pay you my respects; Besids my conversation for a good part of my Mute humour was with a dieing friend the good Mother of this family whome we greatly Miss. Your Mistris values the intrest she has in you much and for your comfort her Uncle Mr President†2 says you shall be wellcome if you please to come yourself and make your complements to her, I am sure I should be glad if you could be prevail'd upon to try whither this place could not afford you a Book friends and retirement to. As to myself I never was less vissible in My Empire At Brentwood†3 then here, But indeed I
― 520 ―
never wore a square Cap†1 and unless your old acquaintence be gon or have forgot your way of conversation tis not easy for you to be free from more vissits then are desirable, but for your health and diversion I could allmost wish your fine Young Lady would command you to come and see whither all be true that is said of her. My son is now at Bristoll, I wherever you are I am very fixtly
Deare Brother
Your affectionate sister and humble servant
A G
September the 11
Mr President and Mrs Turner†2 present their service to you the post is going

1537. William Stratton to Locke, 15 September 1692 (1484, 1558)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 76.
Bristoll the 15th Sep 1692
Dear Cosin
I Rec yours dated the th of this Instant and give you this account that William Sledg dyed about 28 days sinc littell before his deth we made even to last our lady day and I abated him but 4l̷ for those bad years I designed to abate him 6l̷ but you left it to me to doe what I would so we agreed and he was well enow pleased and it was with your Cosent when you was In the Countery†3 that I should doe what I thought fit, I was at buckhill lately to treate about securing this years rent and am this day uppon it I dout not but I shall
― 521 ―
secure it and shall Indever to let the estate to a suffisient tenant I shall ackt the best I Can, though substainciall tenants are very scars that will give a good rent, I have noe suffisient answear to what I writ to you about the tax to the king on that Ground that William Gullock doeth rent and that buisnes hangs in suspence betwene me and those that gather the kings mony you may Remember it is disputable whether that Ground belong to the living†a †1 at belton but I am resolved not to pay it In pertecular by it selfe, If posible, for it will be a perpetuall burden to the estate If it belong to belton tenement I desire I may heare from you about it, I have in my hands of yours about 55l̷ which If you draw a bill on sight I shall pay it If not I suppose I shall in a littell time get a safe return, as for my buying further right In buck hill I have don nothing in it yet, but may speake with the Gent:men after micall mas unles the lord†2 be at London and so it be thought fit to speake with him theare, I perceive he will be of age this winter and suppos you have acquaintance with him and it may be my Interest for you to treate with him for two lives I am not very forward In the busnes, the bounds is very ordinary†3 about Buck hill and theare must be charge in repairing if I can get a good tenant for it, but will put you to noe unnesesary Charg. I have bene very unwilling and have soe long defered that I must now doe sum thing for Sledg was displeased becaws noe more was don, and likewise mus digg round the foundation of the hous at belton for the upper side of the house is not suffisient for swine to ly in by reson of the water that sokes in and therfore must be at sum Charge for a mason to secure the house round the upper side at the foundation these things I thought fit to acquaint you with In pertecular that so you might be fully satisfied with what I doe I take leave
Your faithfull Kinsman and humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
Address: For Mr: John Locke Att Mr: Pawlings In Dorset Court in Chanell row Westminster London
Postmark: SE 21
Endorsed by Locke: W: Stratton 15° Sept. 92

1538. Locke to William Molyneux, 20 September 1692 (1530, 1544)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 6-12. Answers no. 1530; answered by nos. 1544 and 1579.
London, Sept. 20. 1692.
Sir,
There being nothing that I think of so much value as the acquaintance and friendship of knowing and worthy men, you may easily guess how much I find my self obliged, I will not say by the offer of, but by the gift you have made me of yours. That which confirms me in the assurance of it is the little pretence I have to it. For, knowing my self, as I do, I cannot think so vainly of my self as to imagine that you should make such overtures and expressions of kindness to me for any other end, but merely as the pledges and exercise of it. I return you therefore my thanks, as for the greatest and most acceptable present you could have made me; and desire you to believe, that since I cannot hope that the returns which I make you of mine should be of any great use to you, I shall endeavour to make it up, as well as I can, with an high esteem, and perfect sincerity. You must therefore expect to have me live with you hereafter, with all the liberty and assurance of a settled friendship. For meeting with but few men in the world whose acquaintance I find much reason to covet, I make more than ordinary haste into the familiarity of a rational enquirer after, and lover of truth, whenever I can light on any such. There are beauties of the mind, as well as of the body, that take and prevail at first sight; and wherever I have met with this, I have readily surrender'd my self, and have never yet been deceived in my expectation. Wonder not therefore, if having been thus wrought on, I begin to converse with you with as much freedom as if we had begun our acquaintance when you were in Holland; and desire your advice and assistance about a second edition of my Essay,†1 the former being now dispersed. You have, I perceive, read it over so carefully, more than once, that I know no body I can more reasonably consult about the mistakes and defects of it. And I expect a great deal more from any objections you should make, who comprehend the whole design and compass of it, than from any one who has read but a part of it, or measures
― 523 ―
it, upon a slight reading, by his own prejudices. You will find, by my epistle to the reader, that I was not insensible of the fault I committed by being too long upon some points, and the repetitions, that by my way of writing of it, had got in, I let it pass with, but not without advice so to do. But now that my notions are got into the world, and have in some measure bustled through the opposition and difficulty they were like to meet with from the receiv'd opinion, and that prepossession which might hinder them from being understood upon a short proposal; I ask you whether it would not be better now to pare off, in a second edition, a great part of that which cannot but appear superfluous to an intelligent and attentive reader. If you are of that mind, I shall beg the favour of you to mark to me these passages which you would think fittest to be left out. If there be any thing wherein you think me mistaken, I beg you to deal freely with me, that either I may clear it up to you, or reform it in the next edition. For I flatter my self that I am so sincere a lover of truth, that it is very indifferent to me, so I am possess'd of it, whether it be by my own, or any other's discovery. For I count any parcel of this gold not the less to be valued, nor not the less enriching, because I wrought it not out of the mine my self. I think every one ought to contribute to the common stock; but to have no other scruple or shyness about the receiving of truth but that he be not impos'd on, and take counterfeit, and what will not bear the touch, for genuine and real truth. I doubt not but, to one of your largeness of thought, that in the reading of my book you miss several things, that perhaps belong to my subject, and you would think belongs to the system: If in this part too you will communicate your thoughts, you will do me a favour. For though I will not so far flatter my self as to undertake to fill up the gaps which you may observe in it, yet it may be of use where mine is at a stand, to suggest to others matter of farther contemplation. This I often find, that what men by thinking have made clear to themselves, they are apt to think, that upon the first suggestion it should be so to others, and so let it go not sufficiently explained; not considering what may be very clear to themselves, may be very obscure to others. Your penetration and quickness hinders me from expecting from you many complaints of this kind. But if you have met with any thing, in your reading of my book, which at first sight you stuck at, I shall think it a sufficient reason, in the next edition, to amend it for the benefit of meaner readers.
― 524 ―
The remarks of that learned gentleman you mention, which you say you have in your hands, I shall receive as a favour from you.
Though by the view I had of moral ideas, whilst I was considering that subject, I thought I saw that morality might be demonstratively made out, yet whether I am able so to make it out is another question. Every one could not have demonstrated what Mr. Newton's book†1 hath shewn to be demonstrable: but to shew my readiness to obey your commands, I shall not decline the first leisure I can get to employ some thoughts that way; unless I find what I have said in my Essay shall have stir'd up some abler man to prevent me, and effectually do that service to the world.
We had here, the 8th instant, a very sensible earthquake, there being scarce an house, wherein it was not by some body or other felt. We have news of it at several places from Cologn, as far as Bristol. Whether it reach'd you I have not heard. If it did, I would be glad to know what was the exact time it was felt, if any body observed it. By the Queen's pendulum at Kensington, which the shake stop'd from going, it was 2 h. post m. At Whitehall, where I observed it, it was by my watch 2 h. 5 m. post m. Which supposing the Queen's pendulum went exact, and adding the æquation of that day,†2 it will fall near the time marked by my watch, or a little later. If there could be found people that in the whole extent of it did, by well adjusted clocks exactly observe the time, one might see whether it were all one shock, or proceeded gradually from one place to another.
I thank you for having taken Dr. Sibelius into your protection. I desire you, with my service, to present my most humble thanks to your brother for the favour of his letter; to which, though I have not time this post, to return an answer, I shall not long delay my acknowledgments.
I hope you will see, by the freedom I have here taken with you, that I begin to reckon my self amongst your acquaintance. Use me
― 525 ―
so, I beseech you. If there be any service I can do you here, employ me, with an assurance that I am,
Sir,
Your most humble, and most faithful servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
1539. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 30 September/10 October 1692 (1527, 1553)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 71-2. Answers no. 1527; answered by no. 1572.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Tandem editioni Historiæ Inquisitionis et Libri Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ finis est impositus. Recepi literas tuas, et post aliquot dies Dedicationem cum involucro, cui nihil erat inscriptum, titulus autem manu tuâ erat exaratus. Inde collegi Dedicationem ita mutatam non displicuisse. Illa itaque excusa est. Jam exspectamus diem, quo navis præsidiaria onerarias in Angliam est deductura, tum mox exemplaria mittentur. Wetstenius aliquatenus diffidit sedulitati Samuelis Smith bibliopolæ, ad quem exemplaria mittentur: metuit ne cunctetur in distribuendis exemplaribus, quæ meo nomine distribuenda sunt. Itaque cum aliis libris mittet quinque exemplaria seorsim fasciculo inclusa, quæ ita distribuentur: Unum destinatum est Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo, alterum Excellentissimo Comiti Pembrokiensi: reliqua Tibi,†1 et duobus Episcopis, Salisburiensi nimirum, et Bathoniensi ac Wellensi.
― 526 ―
Rogamus, si forte Londini tu sis, ut eum fasciculum a Samuele Smith petas, et ut exemplaria illis quibus destinata sunt tradi procures: Sin vero ruri degas, ut per amicum aliquem tuum id fiat. Indecorum enim foret, exemplaria venalia Londini prostare, et Archiepiscopo, cui liber dedicatus est, exemplar suum non esse traditum. Unum doleo, non licere exemplaria compacta in Angliam mittere: Wetstenius adeo severas Angliæ leges esse ait, ut metuat, ne exemplar Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo destinatum, si compactum esse deprehendatur, fisco adjudicetur. Illum tamen Anglicanarum legum rigorem minime mihi persuadere possum: aliud autem nisi compactum ad Reverendissimum Archiepiscopum mittere nequeo. Excellentissimus Comes, et Episcopi, tecum mihi ignoscent, quod incompacta mittam, ne exemplaria a me missa periculo confiscationis exponantur.†1 Adderem alia quædam, de ministro, qui tractatum de dæmonibus paradoxum edidit, quem Synodus Hollandiæ Borealis nuper degradatione verbali†2 punivit, et ministerio abdicavit: Verum historia est prolixior, et nunc temporis angustiâ abrumpere cogor. Vale Vir Amplissime: D. Cudworthæ omnia a me
― 527 ―
fausta precare. Venius jam uxorem duxit: Omnia jam satis pacata sunt. Salutat te uxor mea ac liberi, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 10 Octobris

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
The publication of the Historia Inquisitionis and the Liber Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ is at last completed. I received your letter and a few days later the dedication, with a cover on which nothing was written, though the direction was in your handwriting. Hence I concluded that the dedication so altered was not displeasing. It has accordingly been printed. We are now waiting for the day when the convoying warship is to escort the merchantmen to England; the copies will then be sent soon. Wetstein rather distrusts the diligence of the bookseller Samuel Smith, to whom the copies will be sent; he is afraid he may linger in distributing the copies that are to be distributed on my behalf. Accordingly he will send along with the other books five copies enclosed in a parcel by themselves, which are to be distributed thus: one is designed for the Most Reverend the Archbishop, and another for the most excellent earl of Pembroke; the rest are for you†1 and the two bishops, of Salisbury, that is, and of Bath and Wells. We request [p. 526] you, should you by chance be in London, to ask for this parcel from Samuel Smith, and to arrange for the copies to be delivered to those for whom they are designed; if, however, you are living in the country, that it may be done through some friend of yours. For it would be improper that copies should be offered for sale in London if the copy for the Archbishop, to whom the book is dedicated, had not been delivered to him. I regret one thing, that bound copies are not allowed to be sent into England; Wetstein says that the English laws are so strict that he is afraid that the copy designed for the Archbishop might be adjudged to the public revenue if it were discovered to be bound. I cannot however persuade myself that the English laws are as rigorous as that, and it is impossible for me to send it to the Most Reverend the Archbishop other than bound. The most excellent earl and the bishops as well as yourself will pardon me for sending unbound copies, which I do lest they be exposed to the risk of confiscation.†1 I would have added some further news about the minister who published the paradoxical treatise on daemons; the Synod of North Holland has recently punished him by verbal degradation†2 and has expelled him from the ministry; but it is a rather lengthy story, and now I am compelled by lack of time to break off. Good-bye, excellent Sir; give my best wishes to Mrs. Cudworth. Veen is now married, [p. 527] and everything is peaceful enough. My wife and children send you their greetings, as I do myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.

1541. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 11/21 October 1692 (1525, 1570)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 60-1. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 58-60.
A Amsterdam le 21 d'Octobre 1692.
Il y a trois jours, Monsieur, que j'ai donné au Sieur Wetstein le†a- petit livre de Scheffer de Philos. Italica,-†a†1 pour le mettre dans le paquet de livres, qui doit partir pour Londres à la premiére occasion. Je croi que Mr. Limbourg adresse un exemplaire de ses livres†2 à Mr. le Comte de Pembroke, et ce petit livre y sera joint, ou au moins avec l'exemplaire qu'il vous envoie. Comme le volume de la dédicace à Mylord de Cantorbery y est, il ne manquera pas de chercher la plus prompte et la plus sure occasion. Je n'ai point encore vû les livres dont vous me parlez, mais quelques personnes, qui les ont vus, m'en ont parlé. Je n'ose pourtant pas m'en fier à eux, et je m'imagine toûjours que le Théologien d'Oxford pugnat invidiâ.†3 On m'a dit que les quatre lettres inserées dans les Sentimens de Q.T. de H. et dans la Défense avoient été imprimées à part en François en Angleterre.†4 Si vous en savez quelque chose, aprenez moi, je vous prie, si cela est vrai. J'ai†a- lû ces jours passez quelques endroits de Ciceron dans l'édition de Mr. Gronovius. Je ne voi pas que
― 529 ―
les additions qu'il a faites à celle de Gruter vaillent grand'chose.†1 C'est un Critique présomtueux et mordant, s'il y en eût jamais, et en même temps fort malheureux dans ses conjectures. Si l'on ne savoit d'ailleurs qu'il a lu Ciceron, on ne le pourroit jamais reconnoître à son stile, qui est très-mauvais, ni à ses maniéres qui sont très-emportées. Ainsi si vous avez l'edition in 12°. d'Elzevir†2 ou celle de Blaw,†3 qui pour la caractere sont plus belles que celle-ci, et aussi commodes pour la forme, ce n'est pas la peine de l'acheter, sur tout étant aussi chere qu'elle l'est.†-a Je suis tout occupé à mon Ouvrage sur la Bible, dont une partie verra le jour, si Dieu me donne la santé, dans cinq ou six mois. Après y avoir bien pensé j'ai résolu d'entreprendre d'imprimer cet ouvrage à mes frais, et de le publier par morceaux, pour n'on pas avoir toute la peine et les Libraires tout le profit. Je donnerai d'abord la Genese, qui tiendra cent feuilles d'un papier semblable à celui sur lequel cette Lettre est écrite; en comptant quelques dissertations que j'y joindrai. Un an après, je pourrai donner les quatre autres livres de Moïse, qui ne tiendront pas beaucoup plus; parce qu'aiant remarqué certaines choses, il ne sera pas necessaire que je les répete. Je trouverai ici un nombre considerable de Subscribers,†4 comme vous les appellez en Anglois, et si j'en trouve quelques uns en Angleterre, j'aurai retiré mon argent en peu de mois. Je ferai imprimer pour cela quelques feuilles, avec les conditions, dont je prendrai la liberté de vous envoier quelques exemplaires, pour les faire voir à ceux que vous jugerez à propos. Mon dessein étoit bien d'en envoier deux exemplaires, pour les deux Seigneurs que vous me marquez. Mais si j'entreprenois de dédier l'Ouvrage à l'un, ou à l'autre, croiez vous que je fisses mal? J'avois pensé à l'Archevêque. Marquez moi, s'il vous plait, ce que vous en jugez. Je pourrois lui envoier le Volume imprimé avant que d'y joindre la dédicace, afin qu'il puisse voir ce que c'est. Mais je puis dire par avance qu'il n'y aura aucun sentiment,
― 530 ―
soûtenu d'une maniére positive et déterminée, qui soit contraire à ceux des Protestans en géneral, et de l'Eglise Anglicane en particulier. J'ai évité la Théologie autant que j'ai pu, et je me suis attaché uniquement à la Critique, sans rien dire de trop hardi, ni tirer aucune consequence. Cependant il y a beaucoup de choses nouvelles en matiére de Critique. Un nom illustre, à la tête d'un ouvrage comme celui-ci, fait non seulement de l'honneur à l'Auteur, mais encore sert au débit, et c'est à quoi il faut que j'aie quelque égard. J'attendrai là dessus, Monsieur, vos bons avis, pour qui j'aurai toûjours une très-grande déference. Je me réjouïs de voir que vôtre ouvrage, que j'estime autant qu'aucun livre que j'aie lu, paroîtra une seconde fois. Cela ne servira pas peu à réformer le mauvais goût de bien des gens. Pour moi je ne vois pas ce que vous y pourriez retrancher, et je sai bien que s'il étoit beaucoup plus long, je ne m'ennuierois pas à le lire. Pour ma Critique, elle n'est qu'à moitié faite, et je ne suis pas en état, pour le present, de l'achever. Je n'ai rien aussi à ajoûter à ma Logique et aux autres petits Ouvrages qui y sont joint, parce qu'il faudroit que je la relusses avec soin pour cela, et je n'en ai pas le loisir. Je croi que le Libraire de Hollande,†1 dont je ne suis pas fort content, en fera dans quelques mois une seconde édition, et pour lors je verrai ce que je pourrai faire. Il y a beaucoup d'irregularitez de style, qui meritent d'être corrigées. Quand j'aurai le temps, j'y penserai. Cependant, Monsieur, je suis toûjours de tout mon coeur tout à vous
J LE CLERC
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr Pawlings in Dorset Court in Chanell row Westminster.
Postmark: OC 15

1542. Locke to Thomas Stringer, 15 October 1692 (1046, 1545)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 264. Copy written by an amanuensis. Answered by no. 1545.
Westminster 15 October 92
Sir
The prosecution of the Treasury which now drives me to account for money imprest to me when Secretary and Treasurer to the
― 531 ―
Council of Trade and Plantations†1 has forced me to search how it came about that I was charged in the Exchequer with £250. more than I had ever received or so much as knew of or could tell how to discharge my self of. Which overcharge has been the reason why I have deferd an account which had otherwise been so easy for me to passe as well as it was my interest so to do, and not let it alone till I was driven to it. After many enquirys and long search I at last found in the Exchequer a receit whereof the inclosed is a true copy†2 which lately gave me the first light in the affair and that leading me to you I must desire your assistance further to clear up this account which now presses that I may passe it in the Exchequer and we may be totally discharg'd.
Pray present my most humble service to My Lady†3 and my thanks for her supplying my occasions as she has donne when my need forced me to presse her. Give my very affectionate service to Mrs Stringer and Mrs Percival And beleive that I am
Sir
Your most humble servant
If you direct your Letter to me at Mr Pawlings in Dorset Court in Channell row Westminster it will finde me

In another hand: Bishop of Derry's Short Observations on some few of the First Chapters of Mr Locks Essay.
Further endorsed by the second hand: Bishop of Derry
― 534 ―
[King's remarks:]
1.
The whole 2d chapter seems to me a meer Jangle. by innate notions or principles is understand such truths as arise so immediately in the mind of man upon the first exercise of his faculty of reasoning that people cannot generally tell when they first made use of them and I do believe there are some such principles, and why may they not be called innate in contradiction to those of whose birth and first entrance into the mind we are able to give account.
he seems to confound the observation of a principle with the use of its terms. but many use this principle in reasoning that the same thing cannot be and not be at the same time that never observed the terms.
They that use the word innate ideas tell what they mean by them. 'Tis hard they may not be allowed to make their own dictionary without a chap: written against them.
It is no argument that there are no notions graven in the mind by nature antecedent to all sence because men do not immediately think of them any more than it is an argument that a philosopher never knew any thing in his life because he is hard to be awakened out of sleep
Notions may be said to be innate because God has so framed the nature of man and placed him in such circumstances that he cannot, without violence to his mind, reject or dissent from them or so much as miss them.
Chap 3
Seems a quarrel about words. Some actions bring so great inconveniencys on the actor that as soon as his reason begins to act he will certainly discover the inconveniency and se himself obliged to avoid it. Such actions, as have by nature these inconveniency so annexed to them, that we cannot tell when we first obser'ved it, may be said to be ill from nature. and the principle of avoiding them may be called an innate principle of morality. this may I confess be over ruled by a further consideration of some good that may be obtained by induring the evil immediately consequent to the action. but to argu from thence that this is not from an innate principle because it may be conquered is as good a conclusion as to say the stone doth not naturally tend down wards because a pully may raise it.
― 535 ―
for example; to be drunk brings sickness, therefore nature teachs to avoid it. but a man may have a further prospect of advantage for which he may be content to be sick. but it is absurd to argu from thence that nature doth not teach us to avoid drunkenness. such are all the arguings in this chapter
Chap: 4
This chapter is made up of the same with the former. he will allow no idea innate but such as a man brings coined in his mind like a shilling. So that an innate idea is an actuall thought with him which no body, that I know of, ever said. all that any one means by an innate idea is a thought that the natural frame of the mind and circumstances in which God and nature has placed us. will bring into our minds, if we do not do violence to our minds to keep it out. I woud fain se one good argument to prove that there are no such thoughts in our minds. and what he will make of thinking without supposing some such?
Let him but put the youngest childs finger in the fire, and he will find the child has by nature as good an idea of heat. and is as well principled to avoid it, as he is with all his philosophy and I wou'd fain have him tell whence, if not from nature, the child, the very first time, had idea of heat and the principle to avoid it. I humbly conceive the fire it self has no idea of heat to communicate nor principle of aversion to lend the child
Lib:2: Cap: 1
This chapter gives no reason why the application of fire etc. to the touch begets in us the idea of heat. etc. some will think all ideas preexisting in the soul. and that the application of outward objects only oblige the soul <to>†a attend to them; as letters writen with the juice of <l>emnon†a are in the paper but not visible till fire make them so. If it be not thus Twill be hard to say whence they come at lest he has not explained their origine. To say thus seems to give a better foundation for truth than to make all ideas absolutely adventitious. If they were, we can have no certainty that the idea raised by the application of heat in one man, is not the same idea is raised by a sound in another. or that the notion I have of space is not the notion another has of volition
― 536 ―
What is said against the souls continuall thinking seems not conclusive. for in sleep their seems to be a great sense of pleasure and quiet which is still thought. and the reason, why the mind remembers nothing else, may be, because during sleep tis intirely taken up and intent on this sense of pleasure. and when one awakens, he seems to be conscious of and remember, the quiet pleasure of sleep, but nothing else, except perhaps dreams, which is a deviation of the mind from the quiet pleasure of sleep
Cap 6:
Quere whether volition be any more than an active thought or a thought turned outward
Cap 7
there seems here an incongruity in deriving the reasons of pleasure and pain from the idea of a God which he has not yet introduced. quere whether it be not as reasonable an account of Ideas to say, as Malebranche doth, that they Arise in us upon the presence of such a body because God has appointed that they shall then arise
Cap 8
The main point is here undetermined whether perception be consciousness. If it be, there must be thinking substance, that is a spirit, in beasts, as well as in men.
Cap: 12
To say the mind is only passive in the reception of some ideas is to advance a notion without proof that needs it in the highest degree: perhaps there is not any subject in nature can be altered without its own active concurrence
It seems unreasonable to treat of modes or the appendices of substances before we treat of substances.
All this pompous division of Modes substances and relation is only the good old division of ens into substantia and accidens, which as it is more common so seems likewise more naturall
Chap: 13
he endeavours to shew us how we come to the Idea of immensity before he proves that we have any idea of it. All that continuall addition shews us, is that more may be added than we can adde
― 537 ―
and consequently that number is bigger than ou<r b>ut†a not that it is infinite.
by his description of place it is plain that it has relation to circumjacent body but not at all to space and consequently ought to be considered under the third part of his division, it being a meer relation.
he does not prove that there is any extension that is not solid. neither doth he prove that body is so solid as not to take up less room. Twill be hard to perswade every body (tho descartes supposes it) that a foot of gold might not fill as much space as two foot of air. or that all the matter of a foot of air might not loose its quantity so far as to fill only half a foot. these are question beyond the power of our thoughts to resolve and nothing new can be said of them.
Quere whether space, as distinct from body, can be annihilated or whether it doth not include as necessary an existence as a rose doth a possible
The quarrel against the definition of extension is unjust. for habere partes extra partes divides the idea of extension and presents the distinct parts to the thought with much clearness which is all the use of a definition. 'Tis tru it recurres to this that extension is extension. but that is no fault, if it did not, it were no definition. he has abused it by the translation
his objection against the idea of substance is very trifling. 'Tis plain when I conceive (suppose)†b wax; that I can conceive it either hard or soft. n< conc>eive†a the same thing turned to flame or air and after resolved into dew. then into honey and then into wax and yet there is something that still continues the same in it. now that, which continues still the same, is that I call the substance of it, and the severall appearance are the accidents, and tho these accidents coud not be without the substance yet it is plain the substance coud be without them and perhaps there is not a more clear or a more primary idea in nature. and perhaps space is only the naked idea of substance abstracted from all its appearances. which it is easy for the mind to do since we have often seen the same substance devested of 2 or 3 appearances.
The story therefore of the Indians supposing the earth supported by a elephant is very unphilosophically applyed
There is hardly one line of right reasoning in the whole chapter
― 538 ―
13. to prove a vacuum by motion is very idle; since if the world were never so full, there might be still circular motion of the parts of matter and that will bring in all other motion.
To prove a vacuum from mens disputing about it is a plain fallacy men dispute about ens rationis the nature of which is not to be. when men dispute about a vacuum 'Tis no more than whether we have a reall idea answering that words.
Quere whether extension be any thing in nature more than heat or cold. we se the same body now greater now less. quantity may therefore be only a mode of thinking.
Chap: 15
Quere whether duration be any thing else than the repeted motion or acts of the same thing. suppose existence be the act of a body for an instant. this act repeted suppose 100:000:000: of times makes a second etc. then an hour duration will be nothing but the act of existence repeted as many times as there are instants in an hour. and so of every other duration. and in as much as a body can have but one existence in an instance. the repeting the act of existence must of necessity make succession. that is, the act, by which it exists this instant, must cease before it repet its act the next Instant. therefore no two instants of duration can exist at the same time.
Cap 17 Sect 4
Pray is it possible for a solid wheel to move on its own center, if it be then it is possible for a particle of matter to move and not into an empty space
The is no necessity of making space endless because we cannot imagine where it shoud end. many things may be, that we cannot imagine.
§ 6 the reason we do not enlarge whiteness to infinity is because We actually find an end of it. and meet with many things that are not white. but we extend blu or black to infinity because we meet with nothing beyond these colour. hence he that fancys infinite empty space doth likewise in spite of his heart fancy it either blew or black, which plainly shews that the reason we cannot but fancy space existing to infinity is because we never yet coud get beyond it. as we fancy it all along blew or black because we never saw any space but tinged with some colour and the most remote with these
― 539 ―
Cap: 17
observe the partiallity of men to their own notions. before he proved, that he had an idea of Space because we reasoned and argued about it. but here tho we reason and argu about infinite and can demonstrate severall affections of it yet he will not allow us to have an idea of it. to know what a thing is, is to have some idea of it. now pray Who doth not know what I mean, when I ask, if the world be infinite. If he know not how comes he to answer that it is not infinite. In short; he is not content to conceive infinity except he may pass it over in his thought, which is Just as reasonable as to argu that I do not know what an inch is because I cannot pass throw the number of parts in it.
The design of Ideas is to distinguish as a mark one thing from another. if I have the knowlege of but a mole on a mans face by which I may know him from all others I have idea enough of him. If therefore I have any mark on eternity by which I may know it when I met with it. I have idea enough of it, and since I have this mark for it that how much soever I pass of it there remains still more to be past. I think I have as good an idea and as infallible as of the sun, whom I know by this mark, that he make day. If this notion of an idea be not allowd quere if there be any idea in the world
Cap 21
If matter were nothing but passivity. every active power woud make of it what it pleased for it coud make no resistance
Sec. 4 when a bullet is let drop out of my hand and it fals on the floor with a great force. in as much as here there appears no agent this seems to suggest to the mind an active power of moving it self in a body
§ 6: the same work that others make by the mistake of faculty in the soul, will be made by the mistake of power. the power of preferring one action to another is even as lyable to mislead men as the faculty of willing
§ 14. this is a new discovery that it is as absord to ask if the will be free as if virtu be square. I cannot se why it is an absord question to ask whether the motion of my arm be a free act; that whether I might not have for born it. and then why may not I ask whether my will be not free, that is whether I might not have for born chosing what I did chuse. it is tru that the will is the power of
― 540 ―
doing or for bearing an action. I hope we may ask whether this power determines it self to one of these or is determined by something without. if it be; all its actions are as necessary as the falling of a stone, and it is a passive and consequently a necessary agent. that is, it doth not act but as it is acted upon.
§ 16 the will is one power and freedom another. no Sir will is a power and freedom the modus†a of it. by which one power is distinguished from another. one power acts necessarily and another freely. 'Tis true the will is a power to prefer etc but the question is whether it be necessitated to prefer the thing it doth prefer or doth it freely.
Sect: 18 the power of thinking doth not operate on the power choosing. I durst lay a 1000 lb that it doth a litle operate for all his hast. I fancy if in a morning he thought to get a 1000lb by rising out of bed it woud a litle operate towards his chosing to get up. if he pretend that it is the man not the power that acts. I answer this is perfite trifling. every body when he says the power acts means that the man or agent can act nor do I see the lest absurdity in saying that motion is produced by something that can move.
Sect 21 how can any one be freer than to have the power to do what he will. yes a great deal freer. if that will be not crambed down his throat, but proceed meerly from the active power of the soul. without any thing from without determining it to will or not to will
Sec 23. if this be tru a man is no more free then a milston. whereas he argues that there must be an antecedent will to determin this will and so in infinitum this were tru if the will were a passive power. but 'Tis an active power determines it self in its choice and is not determined by another. and he that doth not understand this understands nothing of liberty. which doth not consist he supposes in a power to act or not to act. but likewise in a power to chuse or not to chuse to prefer or not prefer. every one being conscious that when any thing is proposed to the mind. he can either chuse or reject it. will or not will it. this is the native idea of liberty that no sophistry will ever destroy. and all arguments against are but like Zeno's argument against motion†1 and proceed merely from our ignorance of spirits
― 541 ―
Sec 28. is a man indifferent to be pleased or not pleased. I answer wherever he is free he is indifferent or can make himself indifferent. nor is the preference determined by any thing without it self. other wise it woud be a passive power as much as motion is in matter. 'Tis plain the author has no idea of an active power or he woud never put together so many words to so litle purpose
Sect. 29 good then, greater good, is that alone determines the will. this good is from the idea impressed on the mind, and the idea is impressed on the mind by outward objects and outward objects are ordered by God in an absolutely necesary chain and so God necessitates a man as much to kill his father as the sun to move. and this is the perfection of man that he is as necessarily damned as born.†1
Sect: 31†2 The freedom of the almighty hinders not his being determined by what is best. all things are indifferent to God. nothing better than another therefore his freedom cannot consist in chusing what is best. his power is such that amongst infinite things proposed to him to be done none is better than another in it self. but he can make any of them best. if therefore he stay till the consideration of best determine him. he must never do any thing. it is best of all to act freely. pleasure is the only good. and perhaps the reason one thing pleases†a and not another is because the agent chuses or prefers it, and then good is the object of choice or preferring and not preferring of good. agents then that can prefer one thing to another are capable of pleasure and none else.
Sec

1545. Thomas Stringer to Locke, 19 October 1692 (1542, 1551)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 159-60. Sent by post to Pawling's house; sent to Clarke, who opened and read it: p. 546. Answers no. 1542; answered by no 1551.
October 19th. 1692
Sir
Yours of the 15th instant together with the Copie of a Receipt came to my hands on munday night last, but having been that day at Serjeant Eyres House,†1 and coming home very weary, I was not in a Condition by that post to give you an Answere unto it, neyther is it possible for me now to give such a one as your letter seeme to Expect, tho I shalbe wanting in nothing within my power to serve you; But you may Remember when you Returned from your Travells I delivered with your Accompts, All the Papers Orders and Voutchers that any way Related unto you, or any buisnesse I had transacted in your behalfe into your hands. And not Expecting to be ever againe Examined about it, I did not make such memorandums thereof to helpe a bad memory, as 16 yeares after doth most necessarily Require, that I am Constreyned to Referr you back to those orders and voutchers, without which I am totally unable (by the Copie of the acquitance you sent me) to give you such Particular satisfaction as you doe desire. But in the Generall I doe Remember that as Treasurer you were intrusted to Receive and pay the money in an order for the service of that Councill you mention, And that you told me mr Brunker†2 had gott, or was then endeavouring to gett an order for his share of it, And that both of us thinking it would be best to try if we could prevaile with him to procure yours, It being otherwise impossible for eyther of us at that time (having soe little interest with the Lord Treasurer)†3 to obteyne it, And upon that Consideration you directed him to me, whoe you designed to make your Agent in your absence, And for the same Consideration I delayed him from time to time, for many months, And had many heats and Quarells with him about it, And
― 543 ―
once Particularly at Westminster Hall dore, I upon great provocation was goeing to strike him, And my Lord Culpeper†1 Chopping in between us, went imediatly up to the Lords House (which was then sitting) to Complaine that I was offering to strike his Lordshipp, But they not succeeding in that Contrivance, Brunker afterwards apply by mr Slingsby†2 and others to my Lord†3 (whoe was then in the Tower) And his Lordshipp upon Examining the matter, Finding he had a just Right to 250l of the money in that order, And that according unto the usuall Course of the Treasury, your name therein was used in Trust for mr Brunker as well as for others, whoe had passed all the offices to the Tellers, and wanted nothing but my hand to an acquitance to Receive that money, My Lord thought it an injustice in that case to deny it, And soe bidd me doe what you must have done, if you had been present your selfe, And mr Clarke will tell you, that if you should have Refused it, the Court of Exchequer would eyther have Compelled you to doe it, or forced you to make him satisfaction for a breach of Trust, neyther could this be any prejudice to you, sinc there were Papers and Voutchers for the Clearing of it and passing it in your accompt at the time of your Returne, faithfully delivered unto you, together with an account of this whole transaction. And tho you are pleased to tell me that the over Charge of this 250l hath made you soe long deferr the passing of your accompt, which had been soe easy for you to passe, as it was your interest soe to doe, And not lett it alone untill you were driven unto it, Yett (if I could not putt you in minde of an other Reason which made it more your interest to lett it alone) I should think you have not been soe just to your selfe, nor kinde to your Friend to neglect it soe long untill it was past all Remembrance, before you lett me know any thing of such inclinations, for untill within these 12 days last past, (that mr Clarke mentioned it unto me) I never heard the least intimation that you intended any such thing, And it must be a trouble to us both that by such a Reservednesse you have lost the benefitt, and I the opertunity of serving you; But sinc you were in such difficulty to finde it out and thought it soe much your interest
― 544 ―
then to passe your Accompt, me thinks it would have looked kinder both to your selfe and me if you had at that time used the Freedome to Commande my Assistance, while the matter was Fresh in my memory and you could easily have had full and Cleare Satisfaction therein, Rather then neglect it untill now, you are driven unto it, when it is soe many yeares past, that with the uttermost streach of my memory, it is impossible to serve you as I would. But I hope a Review of your Papers will sett every thing Right, tho in this Particular your long delay hath putt it out of my power to manifest how much I am
Sir
Your very humble servant
THO: STRINGER
My Lady presents her service to you, and my wife and Sister Percivall†1 are much oblieged to you for your kinde Remembrance.
Address: For mr Lock at mr Pawlings House in Dorsett Court in Channell Row Westminster
Postmark: OC 21

Deare Sir,

my Maid asked the young man from whom he brought the letter, he said from a Doctor in the City. she shewed him that the letter was crackt, as she called it, he said that was nothing but desired it might be sent. so I guess by the whole it comes from Norris, and is the letter from my Lady Masham which he hath been peeping into. god deliver me from such proud Clergy men. they are not fit for human Society, unsavory salt etc.

1549. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 22 October [1692] (1547, 1594)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 21-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London oct: 22
I am very uneasy 'till I hear of your safe arivall to oattes, and that you doe find the Change of air as successfull to your recovery, as you at this time did need, and your frends wish it; when you doe Let 'em hear so much from you, I hope youle not forget me. I doe suppose that by this post youle have an acount from Mr Clarke, of what progress he has made in my bussness since you went; so I will not spend any part of the little time I have now, to writ in that matter. and it would take up more then I can well hope to be ever misstris of, to make you half the acknowledgments I owe you for the many repeated instances of your frendship to me, to which tho I must allways remaine your debttor, doe me the justice to belive a Constant will to repay I shall never want.
and the most I can say more to express what I think on this subject, will be to refer you to some of your own thought's (so very much to my purpose, that you Cant miss of finding them out your self) in your dedication to your philosophick Lord:†1 I dont know whither you had so sencear a meaning on that occasion, as I have now, but am pretty sure I have more reason on my side. the K haveing sufficently frighted his frend's, is at Last God be thanked safe ariv'd: he had a very unsafe passage both for stormes, and some unwellcome Convoy's that the french had sent him as the tell us, well fited to take any advantage should have apear'd to 'em, of which god be thank't they are well now dissapoint'd. The king has been receiv'd with the highest expressions of joy imaginable, he Look's well, and well pleas'd; I need not tell you how much more this makes the Queen look so, the citty has highly congrattulated his safe return, in Loyall specehes, and Concluded in an invitation to the Lord Mayor's show;†2 so much must serve by way of newes. the conclusion of My letter is to remember you of your promiss to be my advocatt to my Dear Lady Masham, to whom I am I must own too great an offender to speak for my self. yet if you'le undertake this, I shall not fear succeding. pray with my most humble
― 550 ―
service, let her know that tho I have Extreamly wanted in the agreements†1 of my friendship, yet in the reallitys she shall never have reason to quetion, my being, what by so many obligations she has obliged me to be. may one know your thoughts of Mr Paulings panygerick on Mr Noriss's managment of your letter from My Lady, I realy think they are too severe to him; since I belive what he did, was out of a very good designe, that he might take an occasion to advise you both; as to some matters that he expected to find in it, of which doutless you'le soon have a forther acount from him, in his next advice to the blind lady.†2 in the mean time, I hope good Sir Fr: will have his eyes open, I mean to see the inconveniances of these misstakes among you, and so doe the part of a peace maker. my most humble service to him, my duty to my De husband, and servis to all frend's with you, I am
your most obliged, and Faithfull Servant.
My Cosen Cutts gives her service to you all
Address: For Mr Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

1550. Edward Clarke to Locke, 25 October 1692 (1548, 1552)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 72-3. Printed in Rand, pp. 353-4. Answered by no. 1552.
London October the 25th. 1692.
Deare Sir,
I Rejoyce in the Account you give mee of the visible amendment in your health, and heartily wish the dayly increase of it: I had the Note you left with Mr. Pawlin, and would have strictly and punctually followed your Directions therein, But Mr. Rose being verie Positive in His Opinion, That the unsett-stone, and the Long-Diamond sett in a Silver-Collet, were worth to bee sold to any Jeweller 250l., and that Hee would give soe much for them, I thought them; togather with the Ladyes Bond, an ample security for your 200l, And that the takeing one of the other 4. stones, togather with these, into your security would bee rather an Incumbrance
― 551 ―
then a Conveniency to you; espetially the 4. other stones being valued by Mr. Rose but at 25l. a peice, and by the Lady at double that value, I thought if any Accident should happen, it would bee better for them to bee in Her own handes, then to bee made part of your security; Upon these Considerations I adventured to take the unsett stone, and the Long Diamond, togather with the Lady's Bond for your security, and Delivered the other two payre of stones to the Lady in the Presence of Mrs. Cutts and Mr. Pawlin, And at the same time seal'd up the unsett-stone and the Long Diamond before mentioned in theire Presence, and by the Lady's Direction Mr. Pawlin tooke them into his Custody againe, where they still remaine, for Her Conveniency and your security; If I have err'd in what I have done in this Affayre (haveing not exactly fullfill'd your Direction in your Note by Mr. Pawlin)†a I hope you will Pardon mee, haveing Acted therein for you according to the best of my understanding, and as I would have done for my selfe, had it been my own particular Concern; The inclosed is a Counterpart of the security, which is desiered may bee Executed by you before Wittnesses, and sent up againe to bee Delivered to the Lady concern'd by the first safe hand;
Your Pattern for the New-way of Sealeing Deeds shall bee Delivered Mr. Pawlin, That yours may bee Seal'd in that manner, which I thinke to bee an excellent good way:
Mr. Attorney†1 was with the Gentleman verie opportunely the next day after you went hence, and I hope for Good Effects of it etc:
News I have none to tell you but that the Arch-Bishop was the first-man the King tooke into his Closett after his Arrivall here, and 'tis observ'd the King hath been particularly Kind to Him ever since: I am Commanded by Madam to acquaint you, That shee intendes on Saturday next to send your Wife in the Stage-Coach to waite on my Lady Masham and you at Oates, Ellen†2 is to goe down with Her, and I begg you to thinke of some way or other with the least trouble to gett them from Harloe where they are to bee sett down at the usuall Place; Pray forgive this trouble your selfe, and Excuse it to Sir Francis and my Lady, This is
― 552 ―
Madam's frolick, and you know that Women in her Condition are not to bee Contradicted in any thing: I am
your most obleiged Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:
Pray give my humble service to Sir Francis and my Lady to whome
