1551. Locke to Thomas Stringer, 28 October 1692 (1545, 1563)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 265. Draft or copy. The letter itself was sent to Clarke for his approval: p. 554. Answers no. 1545; answered by no. 1563.
Whether it were in me want of kindenesse to you or my self that I did not suspect you to have receeived the £250 which I thought the Exchequer had by a mistake charged on me And whether you have thereupon reason to blame me as you doe in yours of 19th instant for reservdnesse I will not now examin. This is certain, this overcharge as I tooke it to be in the Chequer made me deferre the passeing my account since I came last to England, which had been otherwise soe easy for me to have done and soe much my interest too and has made it lie soe long a burden uneasie upon me which else long ere this I had got rid off. Those that were skild in it assureing me that the officers of the Exchequer being sworne their charge upon me would be good and soe findeing there would be no remedie against this which I concluded a mistake in the chequer not in the least imagining that you or any of my freinds had received the mony I was at a stand till this somer a summons (which I expected not) to account, driveing me to a narrower search if by any means I could hunt out this matter and comeing from office to Office to the Tellers they at last told me there they had paid the £250 and could shew an acquittance for it, which I was very glad to hear. haveing now hopes I might finde who had received the mony this being the first appearance of light I had got and after some attendance they produced me your acquittance, which I confesse mightily surprised me, it being wholy unexpected and I not being able to recollect that you had ever said any thing
― 553 ―
to me of it. But not to trust to my memory I had recourse immediately to your account where findeing not the least mention of any such mony received, I haveing occasion to write to Mr Clarke upon other businesse, I mentiond that also to him who was then at Salisbury desireing him to speake to you of it. You may easily imagin that had I had the least thought that the businesse had lain between you and me I had not troubled the offices and others about it but had writ immediately to you long ere this and not laine soe long under the perplexity I have been ever since I came last to England concerning this matter nor lost soe advantageous an oportunity as I had not only to passe this account but recover the arrears due to me upon it. And though all the appearances joynd with this my absolute ignorance of this matter gave me reason to be confident that you had not put into my hands those vouchers you speake of. yet to satisfie you in the point I searchd before I came out of towne those places where if I had had any such papers I make sure I should have found them. I grant what you say that there could be noe prejudice to any body, if there were such papers and vouchers for the Clearing this matter and passeing the account as you speak of and therefor I desire you again to recollect where they may be found and to search for them amongst your papers For this I fear that if they cannot be produced to satisfie the auditor somebody or other will be liable to repay this mony again. I shall be ready on my side to doe any thing in my power to cleare it and am
Sir
etc
J L
Oates 28° Oct 92

Oates 28° Oct 92
Dear Sir
Had my desire to you in my note been with other designe than it was I should with satisfaction have submitted to your judgment
― 554 ―
in the affair. But the reason why I resolved to give back some of the stones being only because I would not be clogd with more than was necessary for sufficient security what was enough for that was all I in effect desired whether two or three it matterd not. I thank you for your care and trouble therein. The Counterpart I have not yet executed being in some doubt whether it be reasonable for me to doe it till I have the stones out of Mr Pawlings hand where they lye for her convenience and soe I have them not in my custodie, however I will be governd by you in it. In the meane time I thinke it necessary she should write a letter to me to thanke me that I have consented at her request to let them be deposited in Mr Pawlings hands for her to have them to <wear>†a at Christmas if she has occasion and that if they miscary before they be <res>tored†a to me again it must be at her adventure and losse they being deposited there at her request and for her convenience. let†b- her seale and deliver that letter to you which I desire you to keep. but you must make her write it whilst you are with her or else it will not be done-†b
I hope the inclosed in answer to that you conveyd to me is what you will approve of.†1 if not pray blot out or amend whatever you thinke fit and send it back to me for I desire only to doe the businesse, and to avoid wrangleing and therefor I have forborne to take notice of his wonted rhetorick
You will also inclosed receive another short epistle to a worthy neighbour of his which I desire you to seale and send away.†2 you will finde but few and those I think very civil words in it, but I would fain receive an answer to them. What spell is it that they cannot be like other men?
I am exceeding glad that Mr Attorney did as you tell me and I hope he found him to his satisfaction as I said. pray send me word. and give my humble service to Mr Attorney
I thank you for the news you sent me and if the men of this age were like those of former I should hope for some good of it.

him to your Lodging when you please and then he may there execute both the Mortgage and the declaration of Trust at the same time, without troubleing them. You will excuse this liberty I take with you in giveing you soe much trouble on all occasions But I am perfectly
yours
J LOCKE

1553. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 28 October/7 November 1692 (1539, 1572)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 73-4. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 327-31. Answered by no. 1572.
(English) Amplissime Vir Amice plurimum Honorande
Tandem Wetstenius post diuturnas ac longas cunctationes exemplaria nautæ qui hinc in Angliam abit, concredidit. Nudius tertius
― 556 ―
missa sunt Roterodamum: inde prima occasione nauta solvet, fortasse intra biduum aut triduum; adeo ut jam intra paucos dies, modò ventus faveat, ea habiturus sis. Fasciculus ad Te directus est: continet quinque exemplaria; quatuor incompacta, quia Wetstenius rigidas Angliæ leges veritus compacta mittere ausus non est: quod velim saltem apud Honoratissimum Comitem Pembrociensem excuses; indecorum alias foret, ad talem Virum incompactum mittere. Exemplar autem Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo destinatum compactum est, et capsæ inclusum, eodem tamen fasciculo contentum. Singulis exemplaribus additæ sunt epistolæ, ex quibus cognosces, cui unumquodque exemplar destinatum est. Quintum vero, cui nulla addita est epistola, Tibi destinavi. Vides causam, cur et Tibi incompactum mittere debuerim. Rogo ut ipse, si sis Londini, aut per amicum, si ruri degas, apud bibliopolam Samuelem Smith fasciculum hunc requiras, ut saltem Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo suum exhibeatur exemplar, antequam liber vænum prostet. Nunc candidum tuum ac liberum requiro judicium, et quicquid censurâ dignum judices, pro familiaritate nostrâ rigide censeas. Attulit mihi nuperius ex Brabantiâ Wetstenius tractatum de Inquisitione Bisuntinâ†1 ex illo, si ante quinque aut sex menses eum habuissem, aliqua mutuari potuissem: Verum hoc infiniti
― 557 ―
laboris est: nam et alius posthac quidem mihi ostendetur, qui et alia hoc non contenta, continebit. Ego me hac vice satis defunctum puto. Nunc adhuc sub prælo habeo omnes Episcopii conciones in unum volumen in folio redactas: additæ sunt septemdecim aut octodecim hactenus nunquam editæ: Scribo ego historiam vitæ Episcopii, quæ concionibus præmittetur.†1 Duplici illo labore, concionum harum, et historiæ Inquisitionis, hac æstate fatigatus sum: nunc aliquam desidero requiem: verum restat adhuc non contemnenda pars excudenda, et major longe historiæ vitæ Episcopii pars conficienda: Circa proximum ver laboris illius finem me habiturum spero. Processus contra ministrum qui de diabolis paradoxam edidit sententiam hac ratione terminatus est. Synodus Hollandiæ Borealis præscripsit illi formulam palinodiæ, quâ profiteatur se dolere quod hoc suo libro recesserit a S. Scriptura et formulis unionis Reformatæ Ecclesiæ;†2 quod multis Scripturæ locis sensum alienum et explicationem scandalosam tribuere conatus sit; quod variis locis nimis irreverenter verbum Dei tractaverit: quod nimis irreverenter de Servatoris nostri munere prophetico et doctrina divina scripserit; quod Ecclesiæ Reformatæ absurdam sententiam, de scientia et potentia diaboli, non tantum præter
― 558 ―
veritatem affinxerit; sed et exinde valde odiosis consequentiis eam gravaverit; quod non tantum indiscrete, sed et contra decretum Ordinum et Synodi novæ Belgicæ Versionis†1 interpretes sæpius contumeliose reprehenderit; et de Reformatis ministris nimis contemtim scripserit, qua suâ scriptione ministerium ipsorum suspectum et infructuosum reddi possit; et quod librum suum passim stylo satyrico ac sarcastico scripserit: Quæ cum omnia jam maturius expensa ad animum revocet, quod dolens comperiat, theses suas et loquendi formas libro ipso comprehensas, Consistorio Amstelo-damensi, Classi, et Synodo, justas offensionis, et toti Ecclesiæ gravis scandali dedisse causas: ac propterea a misericorde Deo, Christiana Synodo, omnibusque quos libri sui editione contristavit aut scandalum præbuit, precatur delicti sui veniam: quod ipsorum de suo libro ac persona judicium approbet, et sincere promittat, tanquam coram facie Dei, quod imposterum adhæsurus sit immobilibus fundamentis Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, prout illa in omnibus et per omnia in formulis unionis, videlicet Catechismo, Confessione, et Canonibus Synodi Dordracenæ juxta verbum Dei definita sunt, nec ullum illius dogma in dubium sit revocaturus: et quod hac sua subscriptione simul promittat prædictas sententias a se jam retractatas
― 559 ―
et libro suo contentas, in posterum nec in concionibus, nec catechisationibus, nec scriptis, nec colloquiis, directe nec indirecte, docere aut asserere; et quicquid scripturus aut editurus est non tantum visitationi Classis subjicere; sed et contraria et saniore doctrina eos quos seduxit, quantum in se, in rectam viam reducere. Ille hanc palinodiam non tantum recusavit; sed oblato scripto, contendit causam suam jam a Classe fuisse judicatam ac decisam; ac proinde non posse Synodum denuo sententiam pronuntiare: Tandem Synodus, auditis omnium Classium suffragiis, hanc in ipsum pronuntiavit sententiam: Christiana Synodus omni mansuetudine et æquitate usa, ut Doctorem Balthasarum Bekkerum ad sufficientem retractionem inducat; ipseque Synodum pro judice competente agnoscere, et articulos satisfactionis a Christiana Synodo conceptos recipere recuset, et in hac sua recusatione persistat; auditis Classium sententiis, concordibus suffragiis eundem Doctorem Bekkerum declaravit non posse ut pastorem in Ecclesia Reformata tolerari; ac proinde ipsum a ministerio suo removit, ac hoc suo decreto removet. Hujusque decreti apographum Reverendæ Classi et Consistorio Amstelodamensi mittetur, ut ipsis actionum erga ipsum norma sit. Habes prolixius paulo enarratam hanc sententiam, ut in illa specimen jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ
― 560 ―
videas.†1 Verum hæc hactenus. Rogo venerandam Dominam Cudwortham meis verbis quam officiosissime salutes. Uxor mea liberique plurimam Tibi precantur salutem: imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus

Amstelodami 7 Novembris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir and most honourable friend,
At length after lasting and tedious lingerings Wetstein has entrusted the copies to a mariner who is leaving here for England. They were sent to [p. 556] Rotterdam the day before yesterday. The mariner will set sail from there at the first opportunity, perhaps in two or three days' time; so you will now have them in a few days, provided that the wind is favourable. The parcel is addressed to you; it contains five copies; four are unbound as Wetstein, fearing the rigorous laws of England, has not ventured to send them bound. I should like you to make my excuses for this, at least to the most honourable earl of Pembroke; it would otherwise be improper to send an unbound copy to such a man. On the other hand the copy designed for the Most Reverend the Archbishop is bound and enclosed in a case contained in the same parcel. Letters are attached to the several copies; from them you will know for whom each copy is designed. But the fifth, to which no letter is attached, I design for you. You see the reason why I have had to send it unbound even to you. Please ask for the parcel at the bookseller Samuel Smith's either yourself, if you are in London, or through a friend, if you are in the country, so that at least his copy may be presented to the Most Reverend the Archbishop before the book is offered for sale. Now I ask for your sincere and free judgement and that in accordance with our familiarity you will censure rigorously whatever you deem worthy of censure. Wetstein recently brought me from Brabant a treatise about the Inquisition at Besançon;†1 if I had had this five or six months ago I could have derived some things from it; but [p. 557] this is a matter of endless labour; for hereafter some other will surely be shown me that will contain other things not contained in this one. For my part I think I have done enough for the time being. At present I still have in the press all the sermons of Episcopius, collected in one folio volume; seventeen or eighteen never so far published are added; I myself am writing an account of Episcopius's life, which will be prefixed to the sermons.†1 I have been fatigued this summer by this double task of these sermons and the account of the Inquisition, and now I long for some rest; but a considerable part still remains to be printed, and by far the greater part of the life of Episcopius to be completed; I hope to end this labour about next spring. The proceeding against the minister who published the paradoxical opinion about devils was terminated in this way: the Synod of North Holland ordained for him a form of recantation, in which he would declare that he regrets that in his book he has departed from Holy Writ and the articles of union of the Reformed Church;†2 that he has tried to impart an alien meaning and a scandalous interpretation to many passages of Scripture; that in various places he has treated the word of God too irreverently; that he has written too irreverently about the prophetic office and divine teaching of our Saviour; that he has falsely attributed to the Reformed Church an absurd opinion about the knowledge and power of the Devil, an opinion not only contrary to the truth, but one which he has furthermore aggravated [p. 558] with most detestable consequents; that he has not only promiscuously, but also in opposition to the decree of the States and the Synod, often abusively found fault with the translators of the new Dutch Version,†1 and has written about Reformed ministers too contemptuously, by which writing of his their ministry could be rendered suspect and unfruitful; and that he wrote in many places in his book in a satirical and sarcastic style; that now, when he calls all these things to mind, all more maturely considered, he finds to his sorrow that his theses and forms of expression contained in that book have given just causes of offence to the Consistory of Amsterdam, to the Presbytery, and to the Synod, and of grievous scandal to the whole Church; and therefore begs forgiveness for his fault from merciful God, from the Christian Synod, and from all whom he has grieved or given scandal to by the publication of his book; that he approves their judgement on his book and person, and sincerely promises, as in the presence of God, that he will henceforth cleave to the immovable foundations of the Reformed Church as they are defined in all points and for all purposes according to the word of God in the articles of union, namely in the Catechism, the Confession, and the Canons of the Synod of Dort, nor will he call any of its dogmas in question; and at the same time promises by this his subscription that henceforth he will neither teach nor assert, whether [p. 559] directly or indirectly, the aforesaid opinions now retracted by him and contained in his book, in neither sermons nor catechizings nor writings nor conversations; and that he will not only submit whatever he is about to write or publish to the examination of the Presbytery; but will also by contrary and sounder teaching, so far as in him lies, bring back into the right path those whom he has led astray. He not only rejected this recantation but submitted a written statement in which he contended that his case had already been judged and decided by the Presbytery, and that therefore the Synod could not pronounce sentence afresh. The Synod, after hearing the votes of all the Presbyteries, at length pronounced this sentence: 'The Christian Synod having used all gentleness and moderation to persuade Dr. Balthasar Bekker to a sufficient retraction; and he refusing to acknowledge the Synod as a competent judge and to accept the articles of satisfaction drawn up by the Christian Synod, and persisting in his refusal: the Synod, after hearing the opinions of the Presbyteries, has with concordant votes declared that the same Dr. Bekker cannot be suffered as a pastor in the Reformed Church, and has therefore removed him from its ministry, and by this its decree removes him. And a copy of this decree shall be sent to the Reverend Presbytery and to the Consistory of Amsterdam to be a rule for their actions in regard to him.' You have this sentence recounted rather lengthily for you to see in it an example of ecclesiastical [p. 560] administration of justice.†1 But that is enough about that. Please convey my most dutiful greetings to the respected Mrs. Cudworth. My wife and children send you their best wishes, as first and foremost do I
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 7 November

1554. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke [31?] October 1692 (1490, 1584)
Rand, pp. 356-7. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The letter appears to have been written after the arrival of Betty Clarke at Oates on Saturday 29 October, and shortly before no. 1555.
Oates, 28th October, 1692.
Dear Madam,
It was kind of you to send my wife to me, though I know not how it may prove if she be not very constant. For little master†2 is so mightily in love with her that he professes openly he will get her from me if he can. You need not make use of my interest to recommend her to Mrs. Anne,†3 who is well enough disposed to it
― 561 ―
of herself, besides what my Lady expects of her. However, I shall not fail to desire her care of my wife, which I do not at all doubt of. She shall not want books whilst she is here. And I doubt not, whatever you in your mother's way of talking say of her being troublesome, but she will so behave herself as to get the love and kindness of everybody here, which they have all [expressed] for her. Pray therefore trouble not yourself about us here. Think my wife safe with me, where I shall take care of her, and everybody love her. <My Lady>†a thinks she behaves herself so well and so womanly that she may [need little] of me. But for that we shall do well enough. Look you to yourself [and to the] great belly, which I desire you may lay down with as little danger and [trouble] as may be. As to any other concernment of your health there is nothing else now to be considered or meddled with. I hope I shall now speedily have news that you are well delivered of a lusty boy, and after that we will talk of other matters.
I see my countryman of Taunton Dean†1 is like his neighbours, very fond of fine shows. He would not else have gone to town for my Lord Mayor's on Saturday last, when he might [as easily] have come hither, spent one Sunday well with us at church, and then we could have delivered him back the day after to the hands of his [beloved] brethren.
My Lady presents her service to you, and wishes you a good hour. I am,
Dear Madam,
your most humble ...
....
Sir Francis and all the good company [present their humble service to] Mr. Clarke.
Address: These present to Mrs. Mary Clarke at Mrs. Henman's, over against Little Turnstile in Holborn, London.

1555. Locke to Edward Clarke, 31 October 1692 (1552, 1557)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, f. 61. A passage printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 247; the whole in Ollion, pp. 230-1; Rand, pp. 357-8.
Oates 31° Oct 92
Dear Sir
My wife came safe and well hither on Saturday and you had compleated the kindenesse if you your self had come with. But you could not part it seems with my Lord Mayors shew for your pore country freinds and a sermon to boot this I tell Madam is the reason why you staid in town though I doubt not but you have businesse enough, but yet I know you will not blame me that I desire to see you.
You will receive to day my packet I sent you by the post on Friday last.†1 if my letter to Mr S †2 have any thing in it you approve not of pray correct it and send it me again to be transcribed. I finde that since he talked with you there, he has changed his note, talkes noe more of the vouchers being in the Exchequer but now is come to be infallible that he deliverd them to me, for seeing where the matter pinches, he noe longer desires me to search for the Order and Mr Bronkers receit in the Pells or any where else but is sure he deliverd them to me. I have writ to him as civilly and as gently as is possible to presse him to doe what I thinke is his interest for if he can but finde those vouchers there will be an end of the trouble and my account will be easily passed
My wife I shall take care of as her mother desires And I thinke she need be in noe pain about her whilst she is here where every body is soe disposed to take care and make much of her as she very well deserves. But my Lady intending to write to Mrs Clarke her self I shall say noe more on that subject. I thanke you for your care in my businesse. Excuse the trouble of it and beleive I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray doe me the favour to let Mr Pawling have the inclosed as soon as you can.

1556. Locke to Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux, 1 November 1692 (1531, 1578)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 278-80. Printed from fresh transcript by (Sir) William R. W. Wilde in Dublin University Magazine, xviii, July-December 1841, 611-12. Answers no. 1531; answered by no. 1578.
Oates, 1 Nov. 1692.
Sir,
The indisposition of my health, which drove me out of London, and keeps me still in the country, must be an excuse for my so long silence. The very great civility you express to me in your letter makes me hope your pardon for the slowness of my answer, whereby I hope you will not measure the esteem and respect I have for you. That your own distinguishing merit amongst the rest of my countrymen I met with at Leyden, has so settl'd in me, that before the occasion your brother's favour lately gave me to enquire after you, I often remember'd you, and 'twas not without regret I consider'd you at a distance that allow'd me not the hopes of renewing and improving my acquaintance with you. There being nothing I value so much as ingenuous knowing men, think it not strange that I laid hold on the first opportunity to bring my self again into your thoughts. You must take it as an exercise of your goodness drawn on you by your own merit: For whatever satisfaction I gain to my self in having recover'd you again, I can propose no advantage to you in the offer of a very useless and infirm acquaintance, who can only boast that he very much esteems you.
That which I always thought of Dr. Sydenham living, I find the world allows him now he is dead, and that he deserved all that you say of him. I hope the age has many who will follow his example, and by the way of accurate practical observation, as he has so happily begun, enlarge the history of diseases, and improve the art of physick, and not by speculative hypotheses fill the world with useless, tho' pleasing visions. Something of this kind permit me to promise my self one day from your judicious pen. I know nothing that has so great an encouragement from the good of mankind as this.
I beg you to present my most humble service to your brother, whom I forbear now to interrupt, in the midst of his parliamentary affairs, whereof I know a great part must fall to his share, with my thanks for the favour of his of 15th Oct. which lately found me out
― 564 ―
safe here. Let him know that I am exceedingly sensible of the obligation, and shall at large make my acknowledgments to him as soon as good manners will allow it. I am,
Sir,
Your most humble and, most faithful servant
JOHN LOCKE.

Dear Sir
My wife and I and all here (except Mrs Cudworth who also is much mended are well and according to our respective dutys salute you. I cannot let Sir Francis come to town without telling you this though I have very litle else to say unlesse it be to thank you for your care and trouble in my affairs and that would furnish me with matter enough for more than one letter. I have this farther favour to beg of you that you would send for Mr Awnsham Churchill (to whom I have writ fower or five times to desire him to send me the sheets have been printed since I came out of town but can not receive a word from him) and tell him I would by noe means have him publish it till I have perused all the remaining sheets which I would have him send to me. I desire you would give your self this trouble. For I am concernd to see it before it goe abroad.†1 Pardon me the trouble I give you with my letters and beleive that I am perfectly yours

1558. William Stratton to Locke, 2 November 1692 (1537, 1561)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 77.
Bristoll nov the 2th: 1692
Dear Cosin
I this evening paid mr: Edwards sixty pound for you and have a bill to pay you in London But doe not Intend to send the bill from Bristoll till the begining of the next weake for Mr Edwards design<s>†a to be in London about the middle of next weake, I have let your estate at Buck hill that sledg did rent for two years at the same rent being 25l p Anum and he hath signed a writing with a bond hoe hath taken it his name is John Tayler A Industreous honest man I thinke it being for soe short a time I thinke If I signe a counter part it may be well enow for his satisfacktion for I think thear was noe nead of any for he rents Considerable from Mr Jeferis and others with out any writing but I am willing to doe your buisnes as safe and as plaine as I Can, but heare a great stur about your paying the kings tax for that which William Gullock doeth rent by it selfe as noe part of the tenement at belton If I should pay it it must Continewally pay by it selfe and likewise pay the poore which will be a great burden to your estate and allsoe perpetuall. I have yet stafed of the payment with a promise to write to you that soe they may be satisfied now If the deads of your Land doe mention it all to gether with the tenement at belton I think it will be satisfacktion to those whoe are concerned, for it will be such a perpetuall burden I know not wheare it will end, I desire you will spedily looke ovr the deads that I and they may have satisfacktion, for I have bean very stif with them becaws I know the Consequenc will prove very troblesum and Chargable and doe aprehend that you have wrong, If you should pay it, and further the Justise whoe is Mr Cornelas Loyd†1 I dout doe leane to them becaws it is on the othe side of the high way which is not suffisient argument that†b is not In Stantons Parish: I hope to give you a pertecular account the begining of the weake how accounts stand betwen us and let theare be care taken that you may have the bill for the bill is to you or the bearer now if theare should be a
― 566 ―
miscarriage and cum to a fals hand they may demand the mony soe I will Give you direcktions wheare to find Mr Edwards and the bill in the same letter that goeth out of Bristoll Munday night you know when it will cum to London I take leave
your faithfull freind and humble servant
WILLIAM STRATTON
If you are in London you may be able to give me an answeare by saterday nights pos that will be hear munday befor I wright to you

1559. Robert Pawling to Locke, 3 November 1692 (1529, 1548, 1573)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 10-11.
London Novemb: 3d 1692
Sir
I have bought the Round Cyperus†1 and presume tis the right though I found no root (as you wrot) in the letter, the Tinderbox shalbe bought and both shalbe sent to the Cariers on Saturday though it be the 5th of November. I have not met with Mr Seger†2 as yet but I wilbe mindfull of that busines. I hear nothing of your boxes return from mr Warr†3 though he, when twas delivered, said he would return it to me. I hear nothing of any Books from Hollon and know not who Mr Smith is you order me to call on,†4 I use to call on Mr Wright,†5 it may be you mistooke the name. I know where he lives and intend to call there if I go that way. your letter with the inclosed to Mr Hayter†6 was so ill made up that it cost 4d though
― 567 ―
it came the same day the other came which you sent by Mr Clarke. I caryed him a letter this day for you and left word, for he was not at home, that all the writings are drawn, and that I would meet him at Whitehall when he pleased to see them sealed. Madam Lockhart presents her service to you and bids me tell you that she received your letter which she thinks had not been broke open and this brings me to the last and chief busines I have to write of.
I went this morning to Mr Manships,†1 he being from home I enquired of his man whether Mr Norris were in Town he replyed he had been gon about 3 weeks and as near as he could guess he went out of a friday; this gave me very little satisfaction, by enquiry I found he had not lodged at that house but lodged with his wife at a Wyerdrawers in Vine Court in Spittle fields;†2 so, in hopes of learning there the exat time of his going out of town, I resolved to go presently thither and intended to call again, as I came back, at Mr Manships; but by that time I entered in my book the place etc mr Manship came in. I first did enquire when mr Norrice went out of London he said it was about a fortnight or 3 weeks ago and on a friday: then I enquired by whom the letter was sent that was for you; he then asked me whether I belonged to my Lady Mashams family; I said no, but was acquainted there; he said he himself received the letter from Mr Norris's own hands who told him he should have delivered it himself but had not time, therfore prayed him to take care of it; he says this was the day before Mr Norris went out of Town and the same day being Thursday he himself went to Mr Locks lodgings and delivered the letter to a servant maid and a few days after he cald to know whether you were come to town again and then he enquired whether the letter was sent or not and answer was returnd him that it should be sent to you; all this while he doth conclude that the letter hath miscaried since, which occasions all this enquiry and I did not think fit to undeceive him, for I lead him not into that error. So that here is exactly what you aimed at and desired to know. mr Norris went out of town on Friday Oct: 21th he delivered the letter to Mr
― 568 ―
Manship the Thursday being the day before; that same day mr Manship brought the letter and left it with the maid; which exactly agrees with our account, for Mary received it on Thursday Oct: 20th I delivered it to Mr Clark the day after, and I presume he sent on Saturday by the post; the Tuesday before you went hence†1 I find he hath got a comfortable importance.†2 they can talk of Platonic love but it usually ends thus but his peeping is a crime unpardonable. I am
Sir
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING

1560. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 3 [November 1692] (1512, 1597)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 104-5. Month and year from Locke's endorsement.
London the 3d
It's thought allways cruelty to Punish any One for being meerly Unfortunate: and indeed if this were Just, there should be no degrees left in Ill-Fortune; No body could be once Unhappy, but he must be infinitely so: for by the same Reason he is first Punish'd, (He being then surely more miserable then he was before) 'tis necessary he should be punish'd again, wors then before: and where to stop I know not.
Woe be to mee if this Rule were good! I find itt my own Case; that I am in a manner punish'd, or to be punish'd, for being onely Unfortunate enough not to give my self a happiness that I am the most unwillingly depriv'd in the world: and though I take all the Pains in the world, and use all the Conduct imaginable in
― 569 ―
order to what You Enjoyn mee and I so voluntarily incline to; Yet if I am onely so Unsuccessfull as not to overcome all Opposition instantly, but fail any while in my Attempt, I find You of a most Mahumetan Disposition, ready to give Sentence according to this Success, without Regard to any thing besides.†1 In Earnest, 'tis a hard Case now That I should be putt to make my Defence thus, and to Excuse my self for not doing that which if I had any Power, any Choice, any Liberty, any Self-disposal in that respect left mee, I should not defer to doe, in effect, one Moment. I know not what my Indifference to the rest of the World may subject mee to, and what occasion itt may give of Reproach against Me: but I am sure I am so little Consciouse to myself of any Indifference here, that I can never be reproach'd justly for not answering the Invitation that You have made mee Joyntly with Somebody elce: An Invitation that had even been Superfluouse if through the strongest inclinations and Good-Affection itt could be admitted in any One to make their own: An Invitation that so perfectly drew over all my wishes and carried in itt such pleasingness; that itt left nothing but what was very weak on any other side: so far was I from answering this Ill, or giving preference to any thing elce besides. In short, Mr Lock, (why may I not say itt to you, since 'tis properly so much my own Loss) Itt will be impossible for mee Yet to see you att Oates: but I hope in some time, however, to be able. I acquitt my self as well as I am able according to my instructions, and with a great deal of Satisfaction of my own, to Mr Popple.
I have nothing more to say now but what I'le beg of you to say of mee to my Lady: which is onely what you know of mee or have heard from mee att other times, at all times: and as much my Enemy as you threaten to bee, I cannot distrust you of so horrid an Injury, but that you will Doe mee Justice in this respect. If you will but lett my Lady know what Service and Respect I think I owe Her; I Fear nothing as to your self: for I defye you, if you can, to think otherwise of mee then that I am with Uttmost sincerity
Your Freind and oblig'd humble servant
A ASHLEY
Mr Popple desires mee to make known how sensible he is of the Favour shown him. I doe not question but when he is able he will
― 570 ―
endeavour to prove it by coming to Oates. and By that time I shall be att liberty I hope he will be able to Venture with mee.

1562. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 7/17 November 1692 (1534, 1585)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 98-9.
Rotterdam 17 November 1692
Dear Friend
I received yesterday your acceptable lines adjoynd to the Letter of my Lady Masham of the 24th past, Where I see you are, mr. Popple gave me an account of a Dry Club,†1 and the Rules of it, began amongst you, but withal told me that you had been forc't to quit there to take the fresh aire at Oates. I see nothing wanting in your Rules, but one thing, that is, a too strict binding of every one to speak to every question, even those that shalbe sur le champ propounded, and that from the very first of their admission, without the lest leave to pass any of them tho a man be never so conscious of his inability to speak anything to the purpose upon the subject, which is enough to terrify a modest man from offering himself to your society. My thinks a month or 6 weeks time, till a man has learnd a little confidence might be allowed to a novice, but such it seems you desire not to be troubled with.
As to my affaire in Scotland, I perceive by your saying that you beleeve mr. Johnson†2 would have done me some service in it, that my information came too late. It was the effect of my diffidence of ever seing any thing of it. tho most justly due to me. Is he then come to stay in England? or does he return? If the latter I know not why he may not, do the same service at his return.
The time of the Earthquake†3 by all the account I could collect from letters, and gazets, from severall parts, was the same as with
― 572 ―
you; I received the packet for monsieur Le Clerc last week, and sent it him, and doubt not but he has received it.
There is now come forth P. Simons Histoire Critique des Principaux Commentateurs du N.T. depuis le Commencement du Christianisme jusques a notre Temps; to which is added Dissertation critique sur les principaux actes M.SS. qui ont ete citez dans les 3 parties de cet ouvrage. where he replyes to the objections of Mr. Arnauld upon Bezas Manuscript. The first containing p. 926. the last p. 99.†1
I have also received from the Professor Limborgh my manuscript, (which I call so because I have an obligation for 15 of upon it)†2 and A printed copy. Shall I send you these pieces, or are they there public and to be had, perhaps the Professor has sent you a copy of his work, as well as me. When I know your mind, I shall do as you direct in the meanwhile Leers has sent me one†a- in quires-†a knowing that I had the other parts for a friend.†3
He is mightily desirous to have some account about the meddals of England, if it can be.†4
Were I in London I would, if your society admit of such questions: cause this Question to be proposed. How far a prudent man is to extend those exhortations of the Apostle Rom 14.21.1 cor. 8:10:11. 12 with respect to a whole people with whom a man has for many years walked.†5
You know my sentiment with Respect to all the little singularitys which make a great figure, in many honest mens heads and consciences; And I have in part given broad signs of it to the whole world, yet have to this day forborn to practice the utmost liberty I have in my own mind, as to the Capital in ceremonious Ceremony. Upon the buryall of my wife,†6 I received from the next Generall meeting (about 3/m after) a gentle letter testifying their sorrow to
― 573 ―
see that I did so far decline from the testimony I had born against the customs and manners of the WORLD: and did suffer my children, to be brought up in those vanities, hoping that I should be preserved from a total declension—but this letter being signed by no body. I replyed not, till the meeting came again the next year. I then signifyed that I had received such a disorderly letter, which tho signed by no body in their name, yet I beleevd to come from them. And for as much as I did desire to continue in that brotherly love that had hitherto been betwixt us, I could not omit to thank them for their care, and good wishes for me, but with all to inform them that what alteration I had made in my outward†a appearance in matters of civil conversation amongst men was the effect of due and mature consideration both in my wife, in my absence, and in me at the same time in London, not knowing of each others intentions, and afterwards of both of us jointly, my wife having put me upon a serious examination of all those things whether I could find any thing in any of them that could not (where God did not particularly reveal his wil to the contrary) be practisd with a good conscience towards God. And that I had declared to her, that I found no difficulty at all in any of them, and that she might safely go on in the education of our children in that manner; not knowing any reason, why we should impose a yoak upon their tender necks, which God (tho he might) perhaps never would require of them†1 —
I told them that thus things stood with me, tho I had not with respect to my own person used the utmost liberty I could in those things. And that I signifyed this not out <of>†b a spirit of contention, as desiring to contend with any man about them, but onely to let them know it. Onely because I had formerly used by word, and writing the Term, of the Customs and†c Manners of the World, without any precise determinate sence of those words. I desired them to explain to me what they meant by the word World in that sentence. For as much as I could conceive but two meanings of it. Either, the wicked, ungodly World, which the Apostle saith lyes in wickedness. Or all the world, that is all men and women, good and bad, holy and unholy. And I could not conceive either of these to be their meaning. Not the latter for certainly those practises that
― 574 ―
are so universall that all men good as well as bad, holy as well as unholy men do practise, cannot be blamed by any. Not the former, because that would imply that they did condemne as wicked and ungodly men, and women, all the sober serious christians in the world besides them selvs; which I had more charity than to think them so uncharitably guilty off. I desired them If they had any other distinct notion of the term—to let me know what it was that they meant by it. I shewd them in a P.S. the Irregularity of the proceedings of that person, man or woman that brought that thing before that meeting contrary to the good order established by christ among his disciples (to avoyd that canting term Church which signifyes anything and nothing as its used,) without having ever spake one word to me, (any of them all), concerning the lest offence they had conceived against me for it: which was to forget their dutyes strangely towards me.
To this letter they answerd, and it was signd by 3 in the name of the rest. That they were glad to see that I desired to continue in the same love and good will towards them but sorry to heare the rest. That as to those words The customes and manners of the world they meant by them, the Very same thing that I did, in my book calld The Honour of the World detected and for the unprofitableness thereof rejected. etc.†1 (Whereas I had told them I had used it without any determinate sence, inconsiderately). As to the last they tell me surely that I had forgot, that one of the 3 subscribers had wrote to me about it. And that the meeting had received knowledg of it from without.
But besides that writing, is not what christ enjoyned†2 but going to the person first alone, then with 2 or more, then to the meeting the person belonging to and so further to their quarterly classis, (for so I now call it), and then to their yearly synode, as the last remedy—so from without it cannot be brought before them, for that no man that's not of them is admitted into those meetings:†3
I have lately received letters from Pennsylvania which tel me Its thither wrote from London, that I have forsaken the Truth, and buryed my wife with worldly pomp etc—so that tho none of them would ever speak with me about it: They have in England and so far traduced me with lying Letters.
― 575 ―
A little before last General meeting, in the whitson week, came a Scotchman, (Rachel Sonmans husbands brother)†1 to powre out the plagues, wrath, Judgments and indignation of God upon me for forsaking the Truth and entring into the worlds vain customs. I askt him the same questions but got no answer. Now lately from my onely sister (a goodman)†a and her eldest son (a goodman)†a †2 I have lamentable complaints†b that their coffyhouses are full that I have left off being a Quaker, etc—I desire them to tell me (if they can) what those that so report, or themselvs, do mean by the word Quaker. And then I will tell them whether I have so done or no.
That I know nothing that gives a man, (amongst men generally) that name (and I never assumed it) more than not doffing the hat in a way of honour to men, and that no man had ever seen me do so for above 30 years past. tho I had not for many years past forbore it, but in a way of condescension to the weakness of others, and not out of any scruple of conscience in my self; but that a little more such treatment as I had received might make me use that liberty which otherwise perhaps I never should, have done. And that whatever they might conceive of a Cross in it. It had (for many years) been none to me, I having received from all men, magistrates and courts of Judicature as much honour and respect without that complyance, as if I had observed all the civilities of the Cuntry to a punctilio. And that if ever I did change in that point I should have a greater cross to beare, than in continuing as hetherto, for that no man expected a change in that thing from me.
Whereas if I do, they'l say I do it to shun the +, others that I am an unstable man. Others that I never was so much a fool as to beleeve there was any evill in it, but have done it for some by end. Others that I now act against my conscience for self Interest. Others that I am an Atheist and have no Conscience at all. And thus every bird will sing, according as he is billd, (as the dutch proverb says)†3 or ill willd.
Rebus sic stantibus,†4 I desire your serious consideration of this thing, and if you please, communicate this letter to my Lady with
― 576 ―
my humble service to her, (and to Sir F.) and let me have your thoughts, what is most fit in point of conscience, and prudence, for me to do, after all these demarches by me taken to let these friends know, in what liberty I stand in these things, sincerely as in the sight of God.
And if do take that last step, to deliver my self from the odious name, of a Sectarian, narrow spirited creature, which I never was, not to say of that most particularly odious name, I should publish any thing to the world upon that subject, or no.
Had my wife lived, I had long since publisht some dialogues†1 that she put me upon writing, and prest me, for her childrens sake, to make public, but incognito—tho I know her design was thereby to draw me quite out of that form, and to get quit of the name—
I have I beleeve tired your patience with this long rambling letter, I must now beg your excuse, upon assurance of doing so no more—and so I rest—
Your most affect. Friend and servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Endorsed by Locke: B Furly 17 Nov 92
1563. Thomas Stringer to Locke, 9 November 1692 (1551)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 161-2. Probably forwarded by Clarke: p. 580. Answers no. 1551.
November 9th. 1692
Sir
I have taken some time to Consider whether it was fitt for me to send you an Answere to yours of the 28th of October, sinc what I wrote before, and intended for a satisfaction to you, is by a fitt of the spleen and a new way of arguing streyned to be a Charge upon my selfe, And by Consequence I am given to understand whoe is meant by that some body or other, (in your letter) which wilbe Lyable to pay the money againe; I must Confesse my selfe too little skilled in that sort of Learning, to dresse off what I write with Cunning Florishes or terms of Art, And have been used to soe much plainesse, that I cannot Fashion it unto the tricks of the age, being always sincere in what I pretend unto, without looking one
― 577 ―
way and Rowing another, Soe that to an Expert Fencer, which Lyeth upon the Watch for advantages, it is probable I may Lay my selfe open to many Hitts. but amongst all you think, you have gained, I could not guesse the Inference you make from that letter should be one, as you now Charge upon me; Having as I thought been soe Cleare and Particular as to take away all Suspition of that kinde from any but such as are very unwilling to parte with it. However that you may not want plaine English for an Excuse, I shall in other terms, without streynes of Logick lett you know (though I perceive I am soe low in your Esteeme, that it may signifye as little as the other with you) That the some Body you mean never Received the money you pretend to be soe much puzled about, And that I doe not apprehend such difficulty but that the other Body (if he please to turne his minde that way) may as easily discharge himselfe of it, but then there wilbe noe body to beare the blame of 13 yeares delay before you came last into England, or 8 or 9 yeares before you went last out of it. However I doe thank you for the Caution, And sinc you shew your selfe soe kindly disposed, I'le promise you it shall not be altogether lost upon him, that is
Sir
your most humble servant
THO: STRINGER
Address: For mr Locke at mr Paulins House in Dorsett Court in Channell Row Westminster

1564. John Norris to Locke, 10 November [1692] (1505, 1575)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 165-6. This letter is closely connected with nos. 1548, 1559, and 1606. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 1575.
Sir
I am sorry to see a Person of your real Sense and seeming Civility make such hast to expres a Resentment upon so doubtful an Occasion. I am the lesse Concern'd upon my own account, because I apprehend my self to be in very little, if any Fault. But to satisfy
― 578 ―
you, the truth of the Case in short is this. I did not send you the letter the very next day after my return (which was Saturday)†1 because I intended to wait upon you with it my self on Monday Morning. But then being Call'd upon by some Friends to pay a visit to my Lord the Bishop of B and Wells about 3 miles out of town, and being to go out of town the Wednesday following, and fearing I should not be at liberty the tuesday because of taking my leave of Friends, and providing for my journy, besides a great deal of other busines, upon these Considerations I thought it best to give the letter to my Bookseller,†2 but not without these 2 expres Conditions, that it should be deliver'd the very next day, and that he himself should give it you with his own hand. Both which after he had promised me I made no Scruple of intrusting him with it, at the same time desiring him to excuse me to you for not waiting upon you. And what could I do more or Better? I think there was no Care, nor respect wanting on my part, however it proved in the event; But, unles I could Prophesy, I do not see how I am accountable for that. You cannot think that I designed to affront you. You know I have always thought and spoke honourably of you, upon which single account you might have thought me Worthy of a more favourable Construction, and not look upon your self as affronted by me before you knew what I had to say for my self.
But Mr Lock the short is this. Tho I Court no body's Favour, yet I would not willingly incur any Man's Displeasure; and I am so little sensible of any thing I have don justly to deserve yours, that (to be free with you) I must think you lesse a Philosopher, lesse a Gentleman, and lesse a Christian than I have hitherto taken you for, if upon this account you Continue to have any Resentment against
your very real Friend and servant
J. NORRIS.
Bemerton Novemb. 10.

1566. Edward Clarke to Locke, 12 November 1692 (1565, 1571)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 74-5. Printed in Rand, p. 360.
London November the 12th. 1692.
Deare Sir
The Inclosed†1 came to my hand this day, and pursuant to your direction I opened it, and doe find it to bee of that extraordinary nature, that I am perfectly at a losse what to say to it, there seemes to bee Such a disposition to an open Difference touching the matter in Question, that I dispayre of any opportunity to doe you any Reall Service therein, but I hope there will at last bee Right done you in that Affayre: I have tendred the Byll of Exchange sent up by your Cosen Stratton for sixty pounds to Mr Edwards, who promises payment in a weeke or 10. dayes time, which, when performed, I will pay the same to Sir Stephen Evans, and take his Note as you direct: I have sent to Mr. C.†2 for one of the Bookes, but have not yett received it from Him, when it comes to my handes I will carefully indeavour to Answere your Expectations as opportunity will permitt;
For News I can only tell you that the House of Commons have given Admarall Russell Thankes for his great Courage and Conduct in the Victory obtained at sea this last summer,†3 And this day Sir John Ashby†4 is sent for to give an Account why hee did not pursue the Victory as Hee was Ordered; I have not time to add any thing at present but mine and my Wifes humble services to you and all with you, and to subscribe as I am
your most affectionate Faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE

1567. William Popple to Locke, 12 November 1692 (1590)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 201-2.
November 12th. 1692.
Sir,
However unconcerned your Retirement speaks you in respect of the present general noise of this place, yet I can not think you wholly disinteressed as to the Success of our more particular Undertaking. We have lately admitted two new Bretheren into our Club:†1 Mr Hedworth†2 and Mr Stevens:†3 both I think very Worthy Good Men, but of very different Characters. We have also chosen two others: Dr Foot†4 and Mr White:†5 but they are not yet come amongst us. The subjects we have been upon have been very important. The last was thus. It being supposed that God has given some General and Uniform Rule, or at least one same way of knowing his Will, though in never so different degrees, to all Mankinde, Q: 1. What that Rule is? 2. Of what weight or Authority that general Rule is in comparison with any other particular pretended or real Rule whatsoever? We dispatched the first, and are the next time to go upon the second head. But you must excuse me if I ad, that I do not tell you all this so much to satisfy your curiosity, as to excite you to come and see us. We fall naturally enough into Considerations of Weight: But you that know us, know how unequal our Shoulders are to such Burdens, and therefore I hope you will be so charitable as to let us have your assistance.
Another thing that I can not omit to tell you, though it be of a more public nature, is the most horrible breach of charity amongst the French Refugiez here that ever was heard of. The Occasion was the death of Mr Mainbourg†6 (whose character I suppose you know.) Upon his death-bed being visited by some of the Zealous Orthodox Ministers, and prest by them to declare his opinion in some points that they suspected him to differ from them in, he frankly owned
― 582 ―
his own sentiments and endeavoured to maintain them with great calmness. But They out of their great Zeal endeavoured no less to terrify him with threats of damnation unless he changed his opinion and repented. Some few others more moderate visiting him also, discoursed with him more charitably, and prayed with him. He dyed in all respects like a Christian Philosopher. But after his death the Orthodox have made Enquiries into what past between him and the others, and upon meer suspicion without the least proof have suspended one from his Ministry; and complained to the Bishop of London of all:†1 But not being able to discover any thing that they could take hold of in those discourses with Mr Mainbourg they have animated the whole orthodox Herd, and set them upon Enquiring into any by-past conversation of these men that may be an argument of their Heterodoxy. The cry is Socinianism. They have been assembled upon it in a perfect Court of Inquisition, to the number of fourscore Ministers, and are about making Formularies and Tests to choak all that have not so wide a Swallow as themselves.†2 My Lord G—ay†3 too is at the Head of the Party, and has complained to the King of the Growth of this Heresy: And they say the King answer<ed>†a that he would not suffer any Socinians in his Dominions, but would have the Laws put in execution against them. But what that may signify, or whether these things may tend, I undertake not to determin. Here inclosed I send you a Copy of some Errata that I have observed in the impression of the Letter for Toleration,†4 which I leave to your self to make what use of you think fit. I am
Sir
Your most humble servant
W P.
― 583 ―
Address: To John Locke Esqr [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: NO 12; GC
Endorsed by Locke: W. Popple 12° Nov 92
1568. Charles Mordaunt, earl of Monmouth, later third earl of Peterborough, to LOCKE, 19 November [1692] (1540, 1619)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 113-14. Printed in King, pp. 236-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I am tould that so many of your friends have sent you word how desirous they are you should come to Town, that I am resolved I will not be of the number, concluding that your health oblidges you to stay in the Countrey,†1 I am afraid of mentioning Parsonsgreen to you, for I find you would be importuned (if so near) to come often to Town, and our innocent aire would be accused of the ill effects of London smoack, if your acquaintances would make you visitts and expect no return's I would doe all in my power to tempt you to a Lady would take all possible care of you, she has prepared you a Roome I assure you is very warm, and if you take the resolution which she thinkes you almost oblidged too by your promise, you must send me word of itt, for as your Physishian†a you must refuse none of her prescriptions, and she will not allow you to come up but in a glasse coach, this is no compliment. And you can gaine no admittance except my coach bring you, which I can send without the least inconvenience, my wife desires me to present her service to Lady Massum her Rivall and promises to bring you back her self with Mrs Lockart and Mrs Cutt att Chrismass to Oats, and if (Mr Hampden†2 like) you desing not to have all the Lady's to your self I will make one too, but after all I desire you not to venture coming towards us if it may be prejudiciall to your health. if you stay in the countrey I will send you now and then a news letter. Our revolving government allways affordes us something new every three of fower months, but what would be most new, and
― 584 ―
strange, were to see itt doe any†a Thing that were realy for its interest, there seemes a propensity towards something like itt but often I feare their sullen†b stars, and duller heads will not allow it. Monsieur Blanquert†1 telles us the King is grown in love with English men and Whiggs, it is true he smiles and talkes with us, but Mr Seymour†2 and Trevour†3 come up the Back stairs, Monsieur Dolm†c †4 Telles us my Lord Nottingham is a little Lawyer and no man of businesse, yet the Court have taken all possible paines to prevent the petition against him and my good Lord Mayour to sett it Aside†5 broke up the court as abruptly as my Lord Sidney The Irish parlament.†6 I will engage no farther in politicks, but being very sick, am going by way of physick to eat a good supper and drinke your health in a glasse or too, of my reviving wine.
yours
MONMOUTH
19th Nov.
Address: For Mr Lock att Sir Francis Massum's att Oates In Essex

I deferred answeareing yours entending to doe it from London But finding my selfe a little enclineing to a cough I have sent my
― 585 ―
sonne Will thither to doe what he can of my bussinesse and by him I have sent your transactions†1 to be left with Mr Paulin But have not sent your mony because you write you needed it not however I will doe it next terme†2 when I must be in London my selfe and when I hope your lungs will give you leave to be there also

1570. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 25 November/5 December 1692 (1541, 1600)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 62-3. An excerpt printed in King, p. 232; the whole in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 60-1.
A Amsterdam le 5 de Decembre 1692.
Je reçus, Monsieur, avant hier vôtre Lettre du 8 de Novembre, par laquelle, je vois que le Correspondent de Mr. Furly ne s'est pas trop bien aquité de sa commission. Au moins je n'ai reçu aucunes nouvelles des livres, que vous avez eu la bonté de m'envoier par cette voie. Peut-être aussi n'est-ce pas sa faute. J'avois déja ouï dire que le Docteur d'Oxford†5 n'étoit pas un homme si terrible, que je l'avois crû d'abord. Je n'aurai pas besoin d'Apologie, dans un temps où je suis si occupé. Mon ouvrage s'avance fortement, et il y en a déja vint feuilles d'imprimées.†6 Je suis entiérement dans le dessein de le pousser, par Subscrybers, ou autrement, et la dépense
― 586 ―
en est déja faite. Je n'ai pas peur des Libraires, dont quelques uns m'ont offert d'abord d'être les débiteurs. Si je puis trouver en Angleterre quelque nombre de Subscriptions, ce sera tant mieux pour moi, sinon je ne laisserai pas de continuer, pourvû que cette partie soit bien reçuë. Je croi que le Sieur Vaillant, libraire François, in the Strang, in de Salisbury exchange†1 aura envoié à vôtre adresse un paquet, où il y en a une demifeuille avec les conditions. Je ne demande point d'argent par avance; et ceux qui s'obligeront d'en prendre un exemplaire, l'auront pour le moins à vint-sous à meilleur marché que ceux qui l'acheteront après. Pour ce qui est de la Dédicace, j'attendrai vôtre décision;†2 mais à l'égard du Nouveau Testament, ce seroit une chose trop éloignée, puis qu'il faut quelques années, pour avoir achevé le Vieux. Ainsi je n'ai besoin pour le présent, que d'un Patron; à moins que je ne dédiasses les differens Volumes à plusieurs, ce qui n'est pas de trop bonne grace. Il ne s'imprime rien de considerable ici, et il ne s'y fait rien non plus, que je sâche, qui mérite vôtre attention. Vous aurez ouï parler du dernier Tome de la Critique du P. Simon, sur le N. Testament.†3 Il y a encore quelques éclaircissemens sur le passage de S. Jean, sur lequel Mr. Arnaud avoit fait diverses remarques, dans ses objections à M. Steyaert.†4 Cela mériteroit d'être examiné par l'auteur de la Dissertation.†5 Le Petrone paroit ici entier, comme l'on dit.†6 L'Histoire, que l'on en fait dans la Préface, le peut rendre suspect, quoi que quant à moi, je le croie veritable. Mais il s'en faut beaucoup que tout Petrone y soit. Il paroit, par le commencement et par d'autres fragmens, que cet Auteur s'étoit moqué des superstitieux, dans un Roman semblable à celui-ci, et que je regrette beaucoup. Car pour celui qui nous reste, qui n'est qu'une Satire de la vie de quelques Maîtres de
― 587 ―
Rétorique, et de quelques débauchez, il n'y auroit pas grand' perte quand nous ne l'aurions pas. J'aime pourtant mieux l'avoir entiere qu'imparfaite. Je m'imagine, ou que cette copie a été volée à celui qui l'avoit trouvée, ou qu'il n'a pas voulu que l'on sût qu'il s'en étoit mêlé, je ne sai pourquoi. Mais elle a tous les caracteres de verité. Ubi stylo idiotico opus fuit, servatur scienter; ubi politiori, assurgit eleganter oratio, quamvis, exceptis locis nonnullis qui declamationem sapiunt, ubique sit tenuïs.†1 Si vous ne l'avez pas vu encore, voiez-le. Il y auroit de jolies remarques à faire sur ce style idiotique, sur lequel je ferai un Chapitre dans ma Critique.†2 Si l'on n'a pas porté le paquet, dont je vous ai parlé, chez vous, aiez la bonté de le faire retirer. Je suis de tout mon coeur, Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Si vous n'avez pas encore le Petrone à Londres, et que vous le souhaitiez, vous n'avez qu'à me le marquer.

Dear Sir
I got safe hither I thank god.†3 Well I cannot say I yet am under soe troublesome a cough as I have but my lungs move easier than they did
My wives shoes are too little. We thought at first to send them back but upon consideration that it will be longer much before an
― 588 ―
other pair can come from London and that the sending one and tother pair will cost almost the price of a pair of shoes we thinke to send one of these new ones to day to Bishop Startford and hope on friday to have from thence a pair that will fit her.

Oates 28° Nov 92
Vir Amplissime
<De>†a adventu librorum tuorum certior factus qua potui <festinatione Londinum me contuli>†b †1 ut quæ tu de iis jusseras præsens curarem. <Archie>piscopus†b quam primum acc<ede>rem†a maximas se Tibi gratias habere professus est. Opus sibi perplacere. seque a libri tui lectione hoc etiam tempore negotiis maximis occupatissimo abstinere non posse: sed magnam ejus partem summa cum voluptate ex quo accepit percurrisse. Verum quo animo accepit legit laudavit tum demum rectius intelliges ex ipsius verbis cum ad te destinatas literas scribere vacaverit. Episcopus Salisburiensis multa et his similia mihi dixit et se adeo detentum immersumque esse argumento libri tui, (quo historiam Inquisitionis ultra quam expectari poterat dilucidam accuratamque tradidisti)†c ut ad te scribere donec totum pervolverit non potuerit: se interim gratias Tibi amplissimas reddere. Comes Pembrokiensis multa de Te cum
― 590 ―
laude et pro munere tuo per me gratias agi jussit donecipse sua manu agnoscat acceptissimum a Te beneficium. Bathoniensem et Wellensem Episcopum in Domo Procerum quæsivi, sed non aderat: cumque extra urbem habitet hora una vel altera a meo hospitio eum in tam brevi morâ convenire non poteram. Tuum autem librum illi traditum (ante meum ad urbem adventum) uti reliquis omnibus certo scio. Cæterum curavi ut Dominus Clarke communis noster amicus eum adeat, ut < excu>set†a librum incompactum a Te missum, quod ego reliquis quibus opus fuit feci quanquam non omnino opus fuit. Mireris jam meritò cur ego qui non minus meo quam horum virorum nomine gratias agere deberem tantus Cessator essem ubi fæstinandum potius esset ut neglecta propioris loci commoditate rus huc <commigrarem antequam>†b ad Te darem literas. Dicam quod res est. Sanus urbem adii, sed unius dieculæ morâ adeo mihi mutata est valetudo ut respirare vix potuerim. Ingravescebat quotidie malum, et tam cito me urbe expulit, ut neglecta maxima rerum illic agendarum parte aufugere necesse esset. Librum Tuum huc mecum attuli ut Tuo beneficio Domina Cudwortha et ego habeamus hac hyeme noctes Atticas†1 quas nihil
― 591 ―
tam augere poterat quam authoris præsentia et quos secum semper affert sales Attici. Huc ego die Saturni†1 Reversus sum. Hodie libri tui lectionem inchoandam qua spe qua voluptate facile dejudicare potes sed credas velim quas tibi habeo gratias non esse minores. Ex tuis 10 Oct datis quamprimum mihi innotuit quot et quibus huc destinaveras exemplaria, egi cum hospite meo et Bibliopola Smith ut singula singulis quam ocyssime traderentur antequam liber uspiam apud nos prostaret venalis, quod diligentissime factum est. nec ea in parte <interiit>†a aliqua tam eximii et tam oportuni operis gratia. Sed quid tandem statuendum est de MS codice Autographo†2 quod ego in tutissimo aliquo loco inter archiva reponendum suaderem ut in perpetuu<m que>†b effronte<s>†b adversarios faciat fidem. Quinam vero is sit locus tutiss<imus>†b libenter tecum inquirerem.

(Latin)
Oates 28th Nov 92
Excellent Sir,
When I was informed of the arrival of your books I betook myself to London with what speed I could so as to attend in person to your instructions regarding them. As soon as I came to him the Archbishop declared that he was most grateful to you. The work delighted him, he said, and he could not refrain from reading your book even at this time when he is fully occupied with most important affairs; but since receiving it he had run through a large part of it with the greatest pleasure. But you will better comprehend with what feeling he received, read, commended it from his own words when he will be at leisure to write the letter designed for you. The bishop of Salisbury said many similar things to me; he was so occupied by and immersed in the subject of your book, in which you have delivered a clearer and more exact account of the Inquisition than could have been expected, that he could not write to you until he had read through the whole of it; meanwhile he returns you his warmest thanks. The earl of Pembroke bade [p. 590] me write many things in your praise and thank you for your gift until he acknowledges with his own hand your most acceptable kindness. I sought for the bishop of Bath and Wells in the House of Lords, but he was not present; and as he lives out of town an hour or two from my lodging I could not meet him in so short a stay. But I know for certain that your book was delivered to him before my arrival in the city, as it was to all the rest. Moreover I have arranged for Mr. Clarke, a common friend of ours, to go to him to make your excuse for having sent the book unbound; I have excused you to the rest where there was need, though there was no need at all to do so. You may now be wondering, and with reason, why I, who ought to have thanked you on my own, no less than on these gentlemen's behalf, have been such a sluggard where I ought rather to have hastened, that, neglecting the advantage of a nearer place, I removed here to the country before sending you a letter. I shall state the reason. I went to town in good health, but after a single short day's stay there my health changed so much that I could hardly breathe. The trouble grew worse daily and drove me from town so quickly that, leaving undone a very large part of the business I had to do there, I was compelled to flee away. I have brought your book here with me so that this winter by your kindness Mrs. Cudworth and I may have Attic nights,†1 which nothing could enrich so much as the presence [p. 591] of the author and the Attic salt which he always brings with him. I returned here on Saturday.†1 You can easily judge with what anticipation, what pleasure, the reading of your book will begin today, but I should wish you to believe that my gratitude to you is no less. As soon as I learnt from your letter of 10 October how many copies you were sending and for whom they were designed I arranged with my landlord and the bookseller Smith that they should be delivered, each severally, as quickly as possible, before the book should be offered for sale anywhere in our country; this was done most carefully, nor has any pleasure attaching to such a distinguished and timely work been lost in that respect. But what, pray, should be decided about the manuscript autograph volume? I should recommend that it should be deposited in some very safe place among the archives, so that it may remain in perpetuity to command belief against shameless opponents. But I should gladly investigate with you what may be that very safe place.
(Latin) I am glad that the life of Episcopius is to be immortalized by your hand; but in what language? for since it is to be prefixed, as I apprehend, to his Dutch sermons that are now about to appear, I fear that the account of him may also appear in a language with which I am little conversant. Nevertheless I congratulate the scholarly world on these memorials of so learned, [p. 592] so distinguished a man, all of whose lucubrations should be preserved from loss.
(Latin) John Malelas of Antioch has now appeared in this country. My friend Toinard has long and earnestly asked for him. Please therefore arrange with Wetstein that as soon as any copies of that book come into his hands, which I know will be earlier than if I were minded to send one from here to him at Amsterdam, he will get one sent to Toinard as quickly as possible and enter the price, which I shall pay, on my account. Malelas is a writer of no great name or trustworthiness; but Toinard hoped to derive light from him on some chronological question, and I greatly desire to be of service to him in what he requires; I therefore ask you to attend to this matter as one most acceptable to me.
(Latin) Many thanks for what you wrote in your last letter of 7 November about the recantation. Things go on in the same tenor everywhere. For I have a story about the French in this country which can stand second to yours, indeed surpasses it, all things well weighed; but of this some other time, if you want it, for the page grows full.
(Latin) I wrote to our friend Le Clerc 15 days ago, to Guenellon 10 days ago. I [p. 593] hope that all is now peaceably and amicably settled in that family; I wish it all possible good. Please give my kindest greetings to them and all my other friends, and especially to your excellent wife and children, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
Mrs. Cudworth sends you her friendliest greetings; she is longing to see your book, now that it is in her house.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstranse Kerck op de Kaÿsers Graaft t'Amsterdam
Noted by van Limborch (beneath date): Recepta 21 Decemb. 92.

Oates 9° Dec 92
Dear Sir
I must beg you the first time you see my Lord Bellamont with my humble service to assure his Lordship that his commands will in all cases have that weight and authority with me as to dispose of all the power I have for his service. That therefor to enable me to serve him in the present occasion I desire his Lordship to send me Mr Stanleys†1 name and qualifications and the place he is now in in the Court and what ever he thinks may recommend him to my Lord P.†2 For this is an inviolable rule which I always doe and always shall observe in recommending any person that I say what I know my self of them and what ever is beyond my owne knowledg I always tell upon whose report and credit it is that I say it, soe that I shall be sure to vouch by Lord Bellamonts testimony which cannot but be better than mine for a person whom I am soe litle acquainted with as I have the honour to be with Mr Stanley
The Cheese is come safe hither and my Lady desires me to returne you her thanks. she intends to doe it suddainly her self but the news
― 597 ―
to day of the Death of a Neice†1 and the short stay of the messenger that carys back our letters makes her desire me to excuse it this post
When the imprest role comes to your hand pray be sure before you doe any thing else to get a perfect account of the forme of the Oath though I am apt to thinke it is such as I told you†2
I and we all here are very glad Madame is soe well. As to her costiveness I know not what to say. I should not be forward to medle if I were upon the place, but at this distance it would be more than I dare doe. A litle patience will now put her soe out of danger that she may have the assistance of physick if there be need, but I am apt to thinke that nature will returne to her fair naturall easy course without it
People generally thinke that if one has an interest any where one may use it as one pleases. whereas I thinke one has it and preserves it only by a fair and cautious use of it. If my Lord B would reflect upon what I have said and my way of proceeding, which I never doe nor shall vary from he would see it would be of noe great advantage to the businesse to send his recommendation of the Gent to my Lord P: round about by my hand and therefor if you can put him off from sending me on soe silly an errand. you may minde him that I used the same method and measures in recommending Mr La Treille to Sir James Rushout and that you know I will not nor can an honest man vary from it. I trouble you with a new letter for Holland, but it need give you noe more pain than your owne does Betty is very well and I am
Dear Sir
yours J L
My humble service to Madam. As also my Ladys and every bodys here
