1578. Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux to Locke, 20 December 1692 (1556, 1593)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 280-3. Answers no. 1556; answered by no. 1593.
I'm much concernd to hear You have Your Health no better, and on this occasion cannot but deplore the great Losses the Intellectual World in all ages has sufferd, by the strongest and sound Minds possessing the most infirme and sickly Bodys: certainly there must be some very powerfull Cause for this in Nature, or else we could not have so many Instances, where the Knife cutts the Sheath as the French materialy express it;†1 and if so this must be reckond among the many other inseparable Miserys that attend Humane Affairs.
I could wish the Physitiens Arte were so powerfull and perfect as in some measure to prevent so great an Evill, but we find where once Nature, or the Oeconomia Animalis of the Body is so deprav'd, as not to cooperate with Medicine, all Remedies and the courses of them prove wholy ineffectuall or to very little purpose: but still the more imperfect Physick is, so much the more is owing to those who the least improve so difficult a Province, which certainly has been considerably advanced by some late English Authors; and that putts me in mind to desire of You Your thoughts, or what other learned Physitiens You converse with say, concerning Dr. Morton and his late Exercitations on Fevers:†2 as for his general Theory of them, I estime it as all others of this kind, a sorte of meer Waking Dreame, that Men are strangely aptt to fall into, when they think long of a subject, begining quite at the wrong End; for by framing such Conceipts in their Phansys, they vainly think to give their Understandings light, whilst the Things themselves are still, and perhaps ever must remaine in Darkness.
In his first Exercitation that treats of Agues, I do'nt find he has said any thing very material or worth notice that the world did not sufficiently know before, unless it were some Historys of the irregular shapes and symptomes this Distemper appears under, which I think may be very instructive to the Physitien and of great ease and advantage to the sick.
― 599 ―
But his pracktical Remarks in his second Exercitation about Continuing and Remitting Fevers, if they be judiciously founded uppon many and steddy Observations, so that they may safely pas into a rule; must certainly be of great moment in directing the Management and cure of Fevers. I confess my Experience in this Distemper as Yet, falls something to short for to determine positively whether all his Observations be reall and well grounded, but as far as I can Judge at present, several of them do hold good.
I remember to have heard Dr. Morton was once a Presbyterian Preacher, and tho he were, this dos not make him a jot the less capable in above 20. Years practise to have carefully observ'd the Accidents that naturaly occur in the progress of a Disease; and if he be but a true and Judicious Register 'tis all I desire from him.
You see I have taken great freedom in giving a Caracter according to my apprehensions of this Author, but tis only to encourage You to use the same liberty; for if at Your leasure You would lett me know your own thoughts, or what other Candid Men say concerning him and his Methods of cure, or any other Usefull Tract that comes abrode, You will extremly oblidge
Sir
Your very obedient humble servant
T. MOLYNEUX
Dub: Decem: the 20th. —92.
Address: To Mr. John Locke at Mr. Robert Paulings in Dorset-Courte in Channel-Rowe Westminster London
Postmark: DE 28(?)
Endorsed by Locke: T: Molyneux 20 Dec. 92. Answered 20 Jan.
1579. William Molyneux to Locke, 22 December 1692 (1544, 1583)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 13-18. Answers no. 1538; answered by no. 1592.
Dublin. December 22. 92.
Sir
I now sit down to answer yours of September 20. concerning the second Edition of your Book, wherein you desire my Opinion and Advise. And after so long Consideration of the Matter, as between
― 600 ―
that and this, and Consulting some Ingenious Heads here about It, I can say but Little; Only that the same Judicious Hand, that first form'd it, is best able to reform it, where he sees Convenient. I never quarreld with a Book for being too Prolix, especially where the Prolixity is pleasant and tends to the Illustration of the Matter in hand, as I am sure yours always does. And after I received your Letter on this Subject, I communicated the Contents thereof to two very Ingenious Persons here,†1 and at the same time, I lent them your book desiring them to examine it strictly, and to find out, and Note whatever might be changed, added, or subtracted. And after a Diligent Perusal they agreed with Me in the same Conclusion, viz, that the Work in all its Parts was so wonderfully Curious, and Instructive; that they would not venture to alter anything in it. But however, that I may in some measure answer your Expectations, I shall breifly note to you, what I conceive on this Subject.
And first, The Errata Typographica (besides those mentiond in the Table) are many and Great; These therefore, in your next Edition are <diligently>†a to be Corrected.
(Secondly) Pag. 270.†2 tis asserted that without a Particular Revelation we cannot be certain, that Matter cannot think, Or that Omnipotency may not indow Matter with a Power of Thinking. And Pag. 314.315.†3 The Immateriallity of God is evinced from the Absolute Impossibility of Matters Thinking. These two Places I know have been stumbled at by some as not Consistent. To me indeed they appear, and are, very agreable; and I have clearly evinced their Consistency to those that have scrupled them. But I thought fitt to give you this Hint, that in your next Edition you may Prevent any such Doubt. My sense of these two Places is this, in the first tis said, that we cannot tell (without a Particular revelation to the Contrary) but an Almighty God can Make Matter think. in the other tis asserted that Unthinking Matter cannot be this Almighty God. The Next place I take Notice off as requiring some Farther Explication is Your Discourse about Mans Liberty and Necessity.†4 this Thread seems so wonderfully fine spun in your
― 601 ―
Book, that at last the Great Question of Liberty and Necessity seems to Vanish. and herein you seem to make all Sins to proceed from our Understandings, or to be against Conscience; and not at all from the Depravity of our Wills. Now it seems harsh to say, that a Man shall be Damn'd, because he understands no better than he does. What you say concerning Genera and Species†1 is Unquestionably true, and yet it seems hard to assert, that there is no such sort of Creatures in Nature as Birds; for tho we may be Ignorant of the Particular Essense that makes a Bird to be a Bird, or that Determines and Distinguishes a Bird from a Beast, or the just Limits and boundarys between each; Yet we can no More doubt of a Sparrows being a Bird, and an Horses being a Beast, than we can of this Colour being Black and tother White, tho by Shades they may be made so Gradually to Vanish into each other, that we cannot tell where either Determines.
But all this I write more in Deference to your desires from me, than to satisfy my self that I have given you any material hints, or have offerd any Considerable Objection that is worth your Notice and Removal. Mr Norris's Unfortunate attempts on Your Book†2 sufficiently testify its Validity; and truly I think he trifles so egregiously, that he should forewarn all men how far they venture to Criticise on your Work. But this far after all I'll venture to intimate to you, that if you are for an other Work of this Kind, I should advise you to let this stand as it does; and your next should be of a Model wholy New, and that is by Way of Logick, something accommodated to the Usual Forms, together with the Consideration of Extension, Solidity, Mobility, Thinking, Existence, Duration, Number, etc. and of the Mind of Man, and its Powers, as may make up a Compleat Body of what the Schooles call Logicks and Metaphisicks. This I am the More Inclinable to Advise on two Accounts; First because I have Lately seen Johannis Clerici Logica, Ontologia and Pneumatologia, in all which He has little Extraordinary but what he Borrows from you; and in the Alteration he gives them he robbs them of their Native Beautys; which can only be preserved to them by the same Incomparable Art that first framed them. Secondly, I was the First that recommended and lent to the Reverend Provost of Our University Dr Ashe,†3 a most
― 602 ―
Learned and Ingenious Man, Your Essay, with which he was so wonderfully pleased and satisfyd, that he has Orderd it to be read by the Batchelors in the Colledge, and strictly examines them in their Progres therein. Now a Large Discourse in the way of a Logick would be much more taking in the Universitys, wherein Youths do not satisfy themselves to have the Breeding or Busines of the Place, unles they are ingaged in something that bears the name and Form of Logick.
This Sir is in Short what offers it self to me at present concerning your Work. There Remains only that I again put you in mind of the Second Member of your Division of Sciences, the Ars Practica or Ethicks;†1 you cannot Imagine what an earnest desire and Expectation I have raised in those that are acquainted with your Writings by the Hopes I have given them from your Promise of Indeavouring something on that subject. Good Sir Let me renew my request to you herein, for beleive me Sir twill be one of the Most useful and Glorious undertakings that can Imploy you. The Touches you give in many Places of your Book on this Subject are wonderfully Curious, and do largely testify your Great Abilitys that Way, and I am sure the Pravity of Mens Morals does mightily require the most Powerful Means to Reform them. Be as large as tis possible on this subject, and by all means let it be in English. He that Reads the 45 section in your 129 page†2 will be inflamed to read More of the same kind from the same Incomparable Pen. Look therefore on your self as Obleidged by God Almighty to undertake this task (Pardon me Sir that I am so free with you as to insist to your self on your Duty, who doubtles understand it better than I can tell you) Suffer not therefore your Thoughts to rest till you have finishd it, And God Almighty succeed your Labours, is and shall be the Prayr of
Worthy Sir
Your Intirely affectionate Humble servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
Endorsed by Locke: W Molyneux 22 Dec. 92 Answered 20 Jan.

1581. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 23 December 1692/2 January 1693 (1572, 1601)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 75-6. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 332-5. Answers no. 1572; acknowledged in no. 1601.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Gratissimas tuas eodem die quo D. Guenellonus suas recte accepi, sed plane laceras, et pluvia madefactas: quæ communis omnium ferme epistolarum eodem die huc ex Anglia allatarum sors fuit. Gratias Tibi maximas habeo, pro labore meâ causâ suscepto. Sane non id volui, ut Tu amœnissimo, quod rure frueris, contubernio relicto Londinium te conferres, et negotia mea expedires: sed solummodo, si forte Londini subsisteres, typographum, alias fortasse tardiorem, excitares, ne ulla in officinâ suâ exemplaria Historiæ meæ
― 605 ―
vænalia habeat, antequam Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo, reliquisque exemplaria a me ipsis destinata tradidisset: alias id negotii amico Londini degenti demandares. Nunc agnosco solitam tuam humanitatem ac sedulitatem: qua me de novo Tibi devinxisti. Gaudeo opus ipsum Archiepiscopo non displicuisse; judicium ipsius benignum admodum facit, ut mihi gratuler, quod patronum Historiæ meæ, quæ forte aliorum dentes non evadet, adeo benevolum, tantaque autoritate pollentem, elegerim. Episcopus Salisburiensis benevolum suum erga me affectum declarat. Gratissimum tamen erit, benigna ipsorum judicia, literis expressa, videre; ut contra eos, quibus omnia nostra displicent, si necesse sit, me tueantur. Ab Honoratissimo Comite Pembrokiensi nullas literas sperare ausus sum: Quodcunque tamen scripserit, gratissimum erit. Si viri cordati, præjudiciis non præoccupati, et solam spectantes veritatem, mea non improbent, aliorum judicia non moror. Animo affectibus aut præjudiciis excæcato, ad veritatem aditus minime patet. Gratum omnibus credo fore, Inquisitionem Pontificiam genuinis suis coloribus depictam videre: Multum vero dubito, an eodem quo Pontificiam tyrannidem†a- animo-†a nævos eorum, quos ut Patres maxime orthodoxos venerantur, lecturi sint: Et tamen, si Pontificiorum
― 606 ―
tyrannidem damnamus, illorum excusari minime potest. Vidi quidem multorum me reprehensioni expositum: at veritati sincere litandum statui; nec tyrannidem illam antichristianam exstirpari posse credidi, nisi ipsi radici securis admoveatur. Optas ut hac hyeme vobiscum sim, ut simul habeamus noctes Atticas, et a me sales Atticas exspectas. Ego vero nihil tali contubernio prætulerim, ubi Phœbo ac Minervæ Deæ Atticæ assidens oracula Delphicis certiora ex utriusque ore haurirem, et quid in mea historia jure reprehendi queat cognoscerem. Interim quod præsenti denegatum est, ab absentibus exspecto. Radios suos Phœbus etiam in longissime dissitos ejaculatur. Errata mea corrigi unice opto: illa autem acutissimum vestrum judicium minime fugient. Exemplar Manu-scriptum Libri Sententiarum ipse tecum loco nitidissimo, ut ab omnibus inspici possit, collocari optem: idque satis in fine præfationis meæ indicavi, si forte aliquos ἐν ὑπεροχῃ constitutos excitare possim. Ex Te autem audire velim, quem locum aliis præferendum credas. Episcopii vitam jam ad finem perduxi: quoniam concionibus Belgicis præfigetur, etiam Belgice conscripta est: Verum poterit illa in Latinum verti sermonem. Wetstenium conveni. Joannes Malela nondum hic ad ipsum missus est, neque se brevi ulla illius exemplaria nacturum credit; sed citius a Te, vel ad ipsum, vel rectà in
― 607 ―
Galliam ad Toinardum mitti posse. Historiam Gallorum, quæ palinodiæ a me perscriptæ accenseri posset, libenter audiam. Videntur illi locum in Historia Inquisitionis affectare. Utinam tandem, vel suo malo, sapere discant! In familia tibi amicissima†1 omnia jam pacata sunt. Omnes Te salutant peramanter: uti et D. Quina, qui balsamum Capoyvæ Tibi tanquam astmati sanando aptissimum commendat: ego, ut urbem Tibi infestam quantum potes vites, ac ruri Te oblectes docto otio. Clericus literas tuas accepit, mihique quæ de me scripseras quamprimum acceperat indicavit. Vale Vir Amplissime, ac cum laudatissima D. Cudworthâ plurimum a me, uxore, liberisque salve. Deus vobis, nobisque omnibus hunc quem modo inchoamus annum fœliciter transigere benignus concedat.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBOR H
Amstelodami 2 Januarii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I duly received your very welcome letter on the same day as Mr. Guenellon received his, but it was badly torn and soaked with rain-water, which was the common fate of well-nigh all the letters brought here from England on the same day. I am most grateful to you for the trouble you have undertaken on my behalf. I certainly did not wish that, leaving the delightful company which you enjoy in the country, you should betake yourself to London and dispatch my affairs; but only that, if by chance you were staying in London, you should arouse the printer, otherwise perhaps somewhat dilatory, lest he should have on sale in his shop any copies of my Historia before he had [p. 605] delivered to the Most Reverend the Archbishop and the rest the copies designed by me for them; otherwise you were to entrust the affair to a friend living in London. As it is, I acknowledge your accustomed kindness and diligence, by which you have freshly obliged me to you. I am glad that the work itself has not displeased the Archbishop; his very favourable opinion of it causes me to congratulate myself on having chosen for my Historia, which perhaps will not escape the teeth of others, a defender so kind and possessing such great authority. The bishop of Salisbury declares his kind affection for me. It will, however, be most welcome to see their favourable opinions expressed in letters, so that they may protect me, if need be, against those whom everything of ours displeases. I have not ventured to expect any letter from the most honourable earl of Pembroke; whatever he may write, however, will be most welcome. If judicious men, not preoccupied by prejudices, and looking to the truth alone, do not disapprove of what I write, I do not care about the opinions of others. To a mind that is blinded by affections or prejudices access to the truth is hardly open. I believe that it will be acceptable to all to see the Popish Inquisition painted in its natural colours; but I greatly doubt whether it will be with minds the same as those with which they read of the Popish tyranny that they will read of the blemishes of those whom they venerate as the most orthodox Fathers; and yet, if we condemn the tyranny of the Romanists, theirs can hardly be [p. 606] excused. I saw indeed that I should be exposed to the fault-finding of many; but I determined to make an acceptable sacrifice sincerely to the truth; nor did I believe that that antichristian tyranny can be extirpated unless the axe is laid to the root itself. You wish that this winter I may be with you both, so that we may have Attic nights together, and you look for Attic salt from me. I should indeed prefer nothing to such company, where sitting beside Phoebus and the Attic goddess Minerva, I might imbibe oracles surer than those of Delphi from the mouth of each, and learn what may justly be found fault with in my Historia. Meanwhile what is denied to the present I await from the absent. Phoebus shoots his rays even upon those who are furthest away from him. I wish only that my errors should be corrected; but they are unlikely to escape the penetrating judgement of you two. As to the manuscript copy of the Liber Sententiarum, like you I should wish it to be placed in a well-kept (?) place, where it can be examined by everyone; I have indicated that sufficiently at the end of my preface, if perchance I can arouse some of those set in authority. But I should like to hear from you what place you think should be preferred to the others. I have now finished the life of Episcopius; as it is to be prefixed to Dutch sermons it too is written in Dutch; but it could be translated into Latin. I have been with Wetstein. Joannes Malela has not been sent to him here, and he believes that he is not likely to get any copies of it soon, but that it could be sent more quickly by you, either to him or direct to Toinard in France. I should gladly [p. 607] hear the story of the Frenchmen which might be rated with the recantation that I copied. Those men seem to aspire to a place in the Historia Inquisitionis. Would that they might learn wisdom at last, even through their suffering! All is now peaceful in the family that is so friendly to you.†1 All send you their most affectionate greetings, as also does Mr. Quina, who recommends Capoyva balsam as most suitable for curing your asthma; I, that you should as much as you can avoid the city, which is so detrimental to you, and delight yourself in learned leisure in the country. Le Clerc received your letter and told me what you had written about me as soon as he received it. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and along with the most commendable Mrs. Cudworth accept the good wishes of my wife, my children, and myself. May God in his mercy grant to you and to us all that we may pass in happiness the year we are now entering.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 2 January 1693

1583. Locke to William Molyneux, 26 December 1692 (1579, 1592)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 19-21. Answers no. 1544.
Oates 26 Dec. 1692.
Sir,
What ever has happen'd to give you leisure sooner than was expected†3 I hope to receive some advantage by it. And that now you will be able to send me your own thoughts on my book together with the observations of your friend into whose hands you have put it with that design. I return you my humble thanks for the papers
― 609 ―
you did me the favour to send me in your last. But am apt to think you agree with me that there is very little in those papers wherein either my Sense is not mistaken, or very little wherein the argument is directly against me. I suppose that learned gentleman if he had had the leisure to read my Essay quite through would have found several of his objections might have been spared. And I can easily forgive those who have not been at the pains to read the third book of my Essay, if they make use of expressions that when examined signifie nothing at all, in defence of hypotheses that have long possess'd their minds. I am far from imagining myself infallible: but yet I should be loath to differ from any thinking man, being fully persuaded there are very few things of pure speculation, wherein two thinking men who impartially seek truth can differ if they give themselves the leisure to examin their hypotheses and understand one another. I presuming you to be of this make, whereof so few are to be found (for 'tis not every one that thinks himself a lover or seeker of truth who sincerely does it) took the liberty to desire your objections, that in the next edition I might correct my mistakes. For I am not fond of any thing in my book because I have once thought or said it. And therefore I beg you if you will give your self the Pains to look over my book again with this design to oblige me, that you would use all manner of freedom both as to matter, stile, disposition, and every thing wherein in your own thoughts, any thing appears to you fit in the least to be alter'd, omitted, explain'd or added. I find none so fit nor so fair judges as those whose minds the study of mathematicks has open'd, and disintangl'd from the cheat of words, which has too great an influence in all the other which go for Sciences: And I think (were it not for the doubtful and fallacious use is made of those signs) might be made much more sciences than they are.
I sent order some time since that a posthumous peice of Mr. Boyle's should be given to your bookseller in London to be convey'd to you. It is a general history of the air, which though left by him very imperfect, yet I think the very design of it will please you, and it is cast into a method that any one who pleases may add to it, under any of the several titles, as his reading or observation shall furnish him with matter of fact. If such men as you are, curious and knowing, would join to what Mr. Boyle had collected and prepared, what comes in their way, we might hope in some time to have a considerable history of the air, than which I scarce know any part of natural
― 610 ―
philosophy would yeild more variety and use; but it is a subject too large for the attempts of any one man, and will require the assistance of many hands to make it a history very short of compleat.
Since I did my self the honour to write to your brother I have been very ill, to which you must pardon some part of the length of my silence. But my esteem and respect for you is founded upon something so much beyond complement and ceremony, that I hope you will not think me the less so, though I do not every post importune you with repeated professions that I am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
1584. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, [30?] December 1692 (1554, 1810)
Rand, pp. 364-5. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Probably the letter mentioned on p. 616; the preceding post went probably on 30 December.
... December, 1692.
Madam,
You do me right when you think I am very concerned for you and yours, and therefore you may be sure that I shall always contribute what lies in my way to your services, especially in what you know I have more particularly concerned myself in, which is the education of your children. [For as] you state the matter it is evidently less chargeable, and if you can get a fit man, I am inclined to think it may be better, to have a tutor at home than to send them abroad; especially if you can get one who will more look after the fashioning of their minds than the teaching them languages [or any]thing else. For I must often repeat that, because I see it so generally overlooked, that the setting of children's minds right is the principal and almost the only thing to be taken care of. And when that is done and kept so, all the rest will in time easily follow; and without that, all the rest signifies nothing. My wife, which will now be the eldest at home, is very capable of it, and with very little trouble, if a right course be taken with her. But if that be not done, there are few so excellently good by nature, but they may be spoiled; and in the midst of the ordinary accomplishments be brought up with faults, that will scarce be made amends for or
― 611 ―
counterbalanced by all the acquisitions that gentlemen's children usually learn from masters. She being the eldest and set right will have a great influence by her example and instruction over all the rest, and you need not doubt but she will be a good proficient in anything that is taught her, for she is very capable and apt to learn. But she will have need of some prudent and attentive person to guide her without roughness, for she has wit and parts enough to distinguish between one who is and is not discreet. You cannot, therefore, but think, that I, who have been for it from the beginning, should be for their breeding at home, if you can get a good tutor and all other things concur.
As your strength and vigour returns your sight will recover again, and therefore I would not advise you to be tempted to tamper at all with your eyes. Since I find no complaint of it in your letters I hope your costiveness begins to work off. Be sure to have your legs, feet and lower parts warm, and then I hope there will be no need of anything more to be done, and walk as much as your strength will allow: this and some few other things I writ in my last to Mr. Clarke will I hope make an end to that inconvenience without any use of physic. I wish you a happy new year, and am,
Madam,
your most humble and most obedient servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
Address: For Mrs. Clarke.
1585. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 30 December 1692/9 January 1693 (1562, 1599)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 101-2.
Rotterdam 9 January 1693
Deare Friend
I am obliged to you, for the pains you have taken in giving me your advice, how I should guide my self in that affair. I had before I received yours, committed one mistake in writing a large letter to a particular person in Cork, to whom mr. Neale†1 had, among other Quakers,†a communicated some letters of mine, in which I had
― 612 ―
changed my stile, and giving him my reasons for so doing: which he judging christian and cogent, thought, poor man! would have prevayld with them also to come forth in a larger spirit of christian charity. But, as he saith, he found that, instead of that, the obstinate people laught at what they could not answer, and censure what they do not understand.
And the effect of it I find: for one of them has wrote me a virulent letter, charging me 'with departing from the Lord, and from my first love; with dishonouring the Lords pure truth and name, with being returned with the dog to the Vomit, and with the sow that was Washed to the Wallowing in the mire, with offending the Churches of Christ; telling me, it were better that a Milstone were hung about my neck, and I cast into the Sea, if I repent not, warning me to return, return to repent and humble my self in dust and ashes, before it be too late; if peradventure I may yet find a place of repentance.'
I have returnd him, a large and earnest, but very mild and gentle expostulatory answer: And at the end of my letter, to supply the error in writing to him. I have added that for as much as I do not doubt but the meeting knows of his and my letters I desire him to communicate my answer to them, that if they have anything to say to me upon the subject, I may understand what it is, and give them all the satisfaction that lyes in my power. I have prest him to declare whether he Judges all those outside singularities, which I enumerate to 8 or 9, as of absolute necessity either to Communion with God, or to the being of a Quaker.†a And if he does, That I am so far from being†b a Quaker†a that I never was one in al my life: nor kno' what it is to be one: for I never heard any one of them al ever preach, or, in discourse maintain any such doctrines: And therefore, if he does, I beleeve him therein to stand alone by himself. However, I promise him, if he wil produce his reasons for his belief of either of those positions, I wil examine them, with all the care and candor I can; and if I find them convincing embrace and follow them.
I now entreat your further advice in this case. It cannot in all probability be long hid from the magistrates of this City, because known to divers here, that I have no scruple in my own mind, as to the hat. What shal I do, if I have occasion to appear before them. If I do it not, they may justly be offended at me, and look upon it as contempt of them. If I do it in the chamber together, each will
― 613 ―
expect it in the street, as I meet them. If I do it publikly to any, how can I refuse it to all? What's to be done in this case? I pray your advice.
As to my being satisfyed to join with any other society; my answer is No. I never was joined to any, no not to this, but by a voluntary conversation with them, as a people whose retired conversation and company I had more liking to then any other: and because I found them to require no bundle of Articles to be subscribed, nor any listing of names; as among other sects, nor the use of the things called sacraments. So they have nothing they admit a man to, nor seclude him from. their meetings are open and free for all comers and goers. A man may so converse with them, as long as he please, and abstain when he please.
Amongst all other sects a man must own and subscribe to a sett of Articles and sacraments, and then he is enrolled I suppose; for to say the right of it, I do not wel understand the knack of member-making. Nor do I think it needful, in order to the publike worship of God. It suffises for a man to be present, at any act of publike worship in any party, that he is satisfyed with, tho he being not a member, that is, a slave to any.
And I could heartily wish those that are so, in the respective partys, would so far emancipate themselvs, as at certain times once a month or so to meet in one common place, together to perform, and hold forth together some general acts, and doctrines in which all are agreed, and for that time perfectly lay aside all their particular shibboleths, that no shaddow of them might at those times appeare; to such a meeting I could freely Join myself; if that may pass for joyning. And further I cannot go towards a joyning with any. And therefore I find myself most at ease where I am: and from it they cannot, if they would never so fain disjoyne me, so long as their meetings are open to others.
Whether you understand so much of this Society, if it maybe so called that are under no compact one with another: I know not. But I intreat your thoughts of it, and whether you can conceive that I can be anywhere freer or safer.
Mr. Leers thanks you for the pains you have taken in his affairs about the meddals of mr. Charlton; and says you have both reason. Nor did he ever desire, or at lest, not intend, more than a copy of them, that is, een teyckening, a draught which Syl could do very well, and that if mr. Charlton could give way to he would fain have,
― 614 ―
and pay for. If mr. 1586. Locke to Edward Clarke, 2 January 1693 (1580, 1596)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 53. Printed in Rand, pp. 366-8.
Oates 2° Jan. 92
Dear Sir
I finde by your votes of the 23 Dec that you have resolved†a to continue the Act for printing made in the 14th. Car. 2.†2 I wish you would have some care of Book buyers as well as all of Book sellers and the Company of Stationers who haveing got a Patent for all or most of the Ancient Latin Authors (by what right or pretence I know not) claime the text to be their and soe will not suffer fairer
― 615 ―
and more correct Editions than any thing they print here or with new Comments to be imported without compounding with them whereby these most usefull books are excessively dear to schollers and a monopoly is put into the hands of the company of ignorant and lazy stationers.†1 Mr Smith a bookseller in Pauls Church yard can give you a very fresh instance of this concerning the importation of a new fair correct Edition of Tully.†2 By this monopoly also of these†a ancient authors noe body here, that would publish any of them a new with comments or any other advantage can doe it without the leave of the learned judicious stationers, for if they will not print it themselves nor let any other be your labour about it never soe usefull and you have permission to print it from the ArchBishop†3 and all the other Licencers it is to noe purpose. If the company of Stationers soe please it must not be printed. An instance you have of this in Æsops fables.†4 Pray talke with A Churchill concerning this who I beleive will be able to shew you other great inconveniencys of that act and if they can possibly I wish they could be remedied. And particularly I thinke that clause where printing and importation of any books to which any have a right by Patent is prohibited should be at least thus far restraind, that it should be lawfull for any one to print or import any Latin booke whose author†b lived above a thousand year since. Pray talke with your members about it and I should imagin some of the Bishops too of your acquaintance should be for it, for it is a great oppression upon Schollers and what right can any one pretend to have to the writeings of one who lived a thousand years agoe,†c He that prints them best deserves best and should have the sale of them which our company of Stationers can by noe means pretend to. For if you examin it I beleive it will be found that those of the Classick authors which are of their publishing are the worst printed of any
― 616 ―
Your act of Coinage†1 too I thinke may deserve considering. For as it is now orderd†a and other†b as well as milld mony goes it is but labour in vain and soe much tax thrown away to noe purpose. But whether it be fit to touch on it now when there have been attempts and some men are ready to alter and debase our Coin the consequences whereof will be very ruinous I must leave to you there to weigh. And therefor perhaps it may on that consideration be better to let the Coinage act goe as it is with that inconvenience that is in it than by endeavouring to mend it give occasion to the leting in a deluge.
I long mightily to see you and hope you will either bring down with you the paper-draught of the account stated†2 or send it by the next post that we may talke of it here and you carry it back with you. For I make sure you will come downe not only to the Election†3 but hither. I suppose Sir Francis has told you that his coach will carry Mr Andrews†4 and you from hence to Chensford and back again. pray therefor come to Harlow in the Bishop Startford Coach Saturday next†5 if possible, unlesse Sir Francis thinks comeing hithe Tuesday night will be time enough and goeing wednesday morning to Chelmsford. But if your businesse would permitt I long to have more time with you than one night.
My service to Madam. I sent her a letter inclosed in yours the last post, and I received none from you this. I say it to tell you not to complain and am
yours
J LOCKE
We and all ours to you and all yours greeting and a happy new year

Deare Freind
I hope you will not impute my long delay in answereing your letter to any dislike I might have to your advice about my too much inclination to a cough especially in London where I find the young and healthy people miserably afflicted with it the last terme For I doe assure you I take your advice very kindly as I know you intended it and shall and have so farre observed it as to drinke very little claret or wine which goes under that name and shall drinke lesse of any sort of wine though not perfectly abstaine from it for feare a sudden change may bring a dropsy But I have beene hindred from writeing by my sonne Will who is gone about a weeke since on board for the West Indys not to promote his skill in Physicke but to satisfy an eager and youthfull desire of seeing forreine countrys which might more usefully beene satisfyed at Amsterdam but of that enough. As to your mony when you have the least occasion of it in the time of 2 posts I will returne it. Otherwise I expect a considerable summe at London if I am not playd the knave with a second time. I am sincerely your affectionate Freind and servant
D THOMAS

1589. James Tyrrell to Locke, 7 January [1693] (1522, 1665)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 121-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Jan 7th:
Dear Sir
I have bin much pleased to hear by Sir Fr: Masham; of the recovery of your health by goeing out of Towne; which serves but to confirme that experiment that you have so often tried at your owne cost, that this Towne is no safe place for you in winter: I have received Mr: Boyles booke of Air by the hands of Mr: P.†1 and am highly pleased with it not onely for the matter but the method; it being as a perpetual common place booke to which wee may still adde fresh observations: tho as to the matter a person who pretends to be much better. versed in Mr: Boyles workes then I, tells me there is little new in it, more <then>†a what hath bin publisht already in his discourses about air, or other subjects: to which my replye was; that granting it to be so, yet I had not the worse opinion of the worke since the Authour designing it for a common place booke to which might be referred all that he had written, or which could be well written upon that subject; he was not onely to take in other mens experiments and observations but his owne likewise: as for my owne part I am very glad that I could contribute any thing too so usefull a designe, or which the Authour could think worthy the inserting. and am so far from desireing that my name should be more knowne then by the first letters, that if I had bin by you when you sent the papers to the presse I would have desired you to have put no more then O. for Okeley, that none but such as are already acquainted with me should have guessed who was meant by those letters:†2 and now I give me leave to put you in mind of the promise you made me of looking over the treatise I sent you in those places that concerned your self; that you might see whether I have mistaken your meaning as Mr: N.†3 would possesse the Lady you are with: the places I have mentiond you or quoted your opinions are in the preface about the begining: and in
― 620 ―
the latter end the last leafe save one (a). and in the treatise it self ch: v p. 211. and 217. besides one more I could not find.†1 if I have any ways mistaken your sense (which I am not yet senseible to have done) I will correct my errour in the next edition of the booke if it come out againe: the othe day I carryed home your Oleariuss Travells in french; and I then tooke out of your Study (with Mr: Ps: leave) the little booke of the Bannians Religion I returned you when I saw you last and the new Petronius: the former I will returne to you again before I leave the Towne; and the latter I will give you another booke for; since you have one in 4°. besides.†2 I suppose I shall stay in To<wne>†a about the concernes of my dear brother deceased:†3 till a<fter>†a the Terme; and should be glad if you will returne an ans<were>†a to your servant

1590. William Popple to Locke, 14 January 1693 (1567, 1608)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 203-4.
London January 14th. 1692/93.
Sir,
I received lately a letter from Mr Furly with one inclosed for a Minister in Corke,†4 and in that a great packet for a Quaker there,
― 621 ―
being an answer to some Reproaches that had been made him for leaving Truth (as they call it) and thereupon a Vindication of his own Conduct. He has sent me all open, and desires (if you be in town) that you would please to peruse it. But without considering that If, I confess the thing appears to me of so much weight that I can not but desire absolutely that you should peruse it before it go from hence. I beg the favour of you, therefore, either to let me know when we are like to have the honour of seeing you here: or else (if that will not be soon) to direct me by what Conveyance I may send this Packet to you. The Bulk is onely five sheets of small paper. But I am to blame to make this alternative. Surely, after so long absence, you must have some busyness or other to call you hither. If none else, yet give me leave to say, Your Ofspring, the Dry Club, requires a little of your Care. Nay I am inclined to say, it deservs it. Tis a hopeful Childe, and now grows apace: and, what is more, it is pretty towardly. So that it is a great pity you should let it grow out of your knowledg, and leave it destitute of your further instructions. I am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.

1591. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 17 January [1693] (1536, 2692)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 162-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Jan: the 17
Deare Brother
When I am thoughtfull about what very much concerns my son or myself tis Naturall to me to think of you as my best advisor whose judgment and friendship a long experience has taught me to value very highly; And I am allmost perswaded that what I am now desirous to doe will not only be aproved by you but be most likely to succeed well by your intrest and management. My design is first to purchaz 50 pound a yeare for my own life; and tho my yeares and no strong constetution seemes to make this project too
― 622 ―
late, yet considering the uncertainty of bonds and the many hazards mony runs I am willing as wisely as I can to secure myself from being destitute or troublesome when my strength fails me, for a very few yeares may make a larger income then mine is at present necessary and force me to be as liberall to myself as I have bin to my son and then my smale principall must be at my service if it Escape being lost these pirilous trading times; Nor am I so selfish as to forget my only child, who tho he cannot call 200 pounds his own, I am willing to make it 500 to buy him also an Anuity, and having told him all I now write he thanks me heartyly and wishes my contrivence for enlarging our income speedy good success, If this buisness seeme reasonable to you and you can make it practicable, you will have the pleasure of having don for me what your friend my good husband did advise me to doe, and which I declin'd in pure tenderness to his Children,†1 but now I have but one and he needs more than I can spare I know noe way to gratifie him more and secure myself than by the thing I now mention. Having now told you the thoughts of my own and my sons heart, I am sure not only to have your opinion but assistance if you aprove of our wishes; I am told that the humour of building makes our Nobles desirous of mony upon less gainfull termes than I covet and that my Lord Halefax thrives by such adventures†2 and that I may from him have good security, but I leave you to plot innocently for me, and promis myself as quick a reply to this as your leasur will permit; The last thing this letter is to doe is to assure you that your Mistris†3 is grown a very fine Woman and has the wisdom to prefer you to most of your sex her Uncle†4 also gives you his service, so dos my son most respectfully who is now with me, And for myself I have just left room humblie to subscribe, Sir, Your obliged servant
ANNE GRIGG†a

1592. Locke to William Molyneux, 20 January 1693 (1583, 1609)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 22-31. Answers no. 1579; answered by no. 1609.
Oates, 20 Jan. 9 2/3.
Sir,
Had I known I should within so few days have receiv'd the favour of such a letter as is yours of 22. Dec. I should not have troubled you with mine, that went hence but a little before the receipt of yours. I was afraid, in reading the beginning of yours, that I had not so great an interest in you as I flatter'd my self, and upon a presumption whereof it was that I took the liberty so confidently to ask your advice concerning the second edition of my book. But what follow'd satisfied me, that it was your civility, and not reservedness, made you tell me, that the same hand which first form'd it is best able to reform it. Could I flatter my self so as to think I deserv'd all that you say of me in your obliging letter, I should yet think you a better judge of what is to be reform'd in my book than I my self. You have given the world proofs of your great penetration, and I have received great marks of your candor. But were the inequality between us as much to my advantage as it is on the other side, I should nevertheless beg your opinion. Whatsoever is our own, let us do what we can, stands a little too near us to be view'd as it should: and though we never so sincerely aim at truth, yet our own thoughts, judging still of our own thoughts, may be suspected to overlook errors and mistakes. And I should think he valued himself more than truth, and presum'd too much on his own abilities, who would not be willing to have all the exceptions could be made by any ingenious friend, before he ventur'd any thing into the publick. I therefore heartily thank you for those you have sent me, and for consulting some of your friends to the same purpose: and beg the favour, if any thing more occurs from your own thoughts, or from them, you will be pleased to communicate it to me, if it be but those Errata Typographica you meet with, not taken notice of in the table. I confess, I thought some of the explications in my book, too long, though turn'd several ways, to make those abstract notions the easier sink into minds prejudiced in the ordinary way of education, and therefore I was of a mind to contract it. But finding you, and some other friends of mine, whom I consulted in the case,†1 of a
― 624 ―
contrary opinion, and that you judge the redundancy in it a pardonable fault, I shall take very little pains to reform it.
I confess what I say, page 270, compar'd with p. 314, 315. may, to an unwary reader, seem to contain a contradiction; but you, considering right, perceive that there is none. But it not being reasonable for me to expect that every body should read me with that judgment you do, and observe the design and foundation of what I say, rather than stick barely in the words, 'tis fit, as far as may be, that I accommodate my self to ordinary readers, and avoid the appearances of contradiction, even in their thoughts. P. 314. I suppose matter in its own natural state, void of thought, a supposition I concluded would not be deny'd me, or not hard to be prov'd if it should: and thence I infer'd, matter could not be the first eternal being. But page 270. I thought it no absurdity or contradiction to suppose, That a thinking omnipotent being once granted, such a being might annex to some systems of matter, ordered in a way that he thought fit, a capacity of some degrees of sense and thinking.†1 To avoid this appearance of a contradiction in my two suppositions, and clear it up to less attentive readers, I intend in the second edition to alter it thus, if you think it will do.
P. 270. l. 20. read, For I see no contradiction in it, that the first eternal thinking being, or omnipotent spirit, should, if he pleased, give to certain systems of created senseless matter, put together as he thinks fit, some degrees of sense, perception, and thought; though I judge it no less than a contradiction, to suppose matter (which is evidently, in its own nature, without sense and thought) should be the eternal first thinking being. What certainty of knowledge can any one have, that some perceptions, such as v. g. pleasure and pain, should not be in some bodies themselves after ——†2
P. 315. l. 4. read, Thought can never begin to be: For it is impossible to conceive that matter, either with or without motion, could have originally in and from itself, sense, perception, and knowledge, as is evident from hence, that sense, perception, and knowledge must then be a property eternally inseparable from matter, and every particle of it. Not to add, that though our general or specifick conception of matter makes us speak of it as one thing, yet really all matter is not one individual thing, neither is there any such thing existing as one material being or one body, that we know or can conceive.
― 625 ―
And therefore, if matter were the eternal first cogitative being, there would not be one eternal infinite cogitative being: but an infinite number of finite cogitative beings, independent one of another, of limited force and distinct thoughts, which could never produce that order, harmony, and beauty is to be found in Nature. Since therefore whatsoever is the first eternal being must necessarily be cogitative: And whatsoever is first of all things —— higher degree, it necessarily follows, that the eternal first being cannot be matter.†1 Pray give me your opinion, whether, if I print it thus, it will not remove the appearance of any contradiction.
I do not wonder to find you think my discourse about liberty a little too fine spun, I had so much that thought of it my self, that I said the same thing of it to some of my friends before it was printed, and told them that upon that account I judg'd it best to leave it out, but they persuaded me to the contrary. When the connection of the parts of my subject brought me to the consideration of power, I had no design to meddle with the question of liberty, but barely pursued my thoughts in the contemplation of that power in man of choosing or prefering, which we call the will, as far as they would lead me without any the least byass to one side or other; or if there was any leaning in my mind, it was rather to the contrary side to that where I found my self at the end of my pursuit. But doubting that it bore a little too hard upon man's liberty, I shew'd it to a very ingenious but professed Arminian,†2 and desired him, after he had consider'd it, to tell me his objections if he had any, who frankly confessed he could carry it no farther. I confess, I think there might be something said, which with a great many men would pass for a satisfactory answer to your objection; but it not satisfying me, I neither put it into my book, nor shall now into my letter. If I have put any fallacy on my self in all that deduction, as it may be, and I have been ready to suspect it my self, you will do me a very acceptable kindness to shew it me that I may reform it. But if you will argue for or against liberty, from consequences, I will not undertake to answer you. For I own freely to you the weakness of my understanding, that though it be unquestionable that there is omnipotence and omniscience in God our maker, and I cannot have a clearer perception of any thing than that I am free, yet I cannot make freedom in man consistent with omnipotence and omniscience
― 626 ―
in God, though I am as fully perswaded of both as of any truths I most firmly assent to. And therefore I have long since given off the consideration of that question, resolving all into this short conclusion, That if it be possible for God to make a free agent, then man is free, though I see not the way of it.†1
In the objection you raise about species I fear you are fallen into the same difficulty I often found my self under when I was writing of that subject, where I was very apt to suppose distinct species I could talk of without names. For pray, Sir, consider what it is you mean when you say, that we can no more doubt of a sparrow's being a bird, and an horse's being a beast, than we can of this colour being black, and t'other white, etc. but this, that the combination of simple ideas which the word bird stands for, is to be found in that particular thing we call a sparrow. And therefore I hope I have no where said, there is no such sort of creatures in nature as birds; if I have, it is both contrary to truth and to my opinion. This I do say, that there are real constitutions in things from whence these simple ideas flow, which we observ'd combined in them. And this I farther say, that there are real distinctions and differences in those real constitutions one from another; whereby they are distinguished one from another, whether we think of them or name them or no. But that that whereby we distinguish and rank particular substances into sorts or genera and species, are not those real essences or internal constitutions, but such combinations of simple ideas as we observe in them. This I design'd to shew in l. iii. c. 6. If, upon your perusal of that chapter again, you find any thing contrary to this, I beg the favour of you to mark it to me that I may correct it, for it is not what I think true. Some parts of that third book concerning words, though the thoughts were easy and clear enough, yet cost me more pains to express than all the rest of my Essay. And therefore I shall not much wonder if there be in some places of it obscurity and doubtfulness. It would be a great kindness from my readers to oblige me as you have done, by telling me any thing they find amiss; for the printed book being more for others use than my own, 'tis fit I should accomodate it to that as much as I can; which truly is my intention.
That which you propose of turning my Essay into a body of logick and metaphysicks, accomodated to the usual forms, though I thank you very kindly for it, and plainly see in it the care you have of the education of young scholars, which is a thing of no small moment,
― 627 ―
yet I fear I shall scarce find time to do it; you have cut out other work for me, more to my likeing and I think of more use.†1 Besides that, if they have in this book of mine what you think the matter of these two sciences, or what you will call them, I like the method it is in better than that of the schools, where I think 'tis no small prejudice to knowledge, that predicaments, predicables, etc. being universally in all their systems, come to be looked on as necessary principles or unquestionable parts of knowledge, just as they are set down there. If logick be the first thing to be taught young men, after grammar, as is the usual method, I think yet it should be nothing but proposition and syllogisme. But that being in order to their disputing excercises in the university, perhaps I may think those may be spared too. Disputing being but an ill (not to say the worst) way to knowledge. I say this not as pretending to change or find fault with what publick allowance and establish'd practice has setled in universities, but to excuse my self to you, from whom I cannot allow my self to differ without telling you the true reasons of it. For I see so much knowledge, candor, and the marks of so much good will to mankind in you, that there are few men whose opinion I think ought to have so much authority with me as yours. But as to the method of learning perhaps I may entertain you more at large hereafter;†2 only now let me ask you, since you mention logick and metaphysicks in relation to my book, whether either of those sciences may suggest to you any new heads fit to be inserted into my Essay in a second edition.
You have done too much honour to me in the recommendation I see you have given to my book, and I am the more pleased with it because I think it was not done out of kindness to one so much a stranger to you as I then was. But yet, pray do not think me so vain that I dare assume to my self almost any part of what you say of me in your last letter. Could I find in my self any reason you could have to flatter me, I should suspect you resolved to play the courtier a little. But I know what latitude civil and well-bred men allow themselves with great sincerity where they are pleased and kindness
― 628 ―
warms them. I am sensible of the obligation, and in return shall only tell you, that I shall speedily set my self to obey your commands in the last part of your letter. I beg your pardon for trespassing so much on your patience, and am,
Sir,
Your most humble, and most obliged servant
J. LOCKE.
1593. Locke to Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux, 20 January 1693 (1578, 1670)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 283-6. Printed from fresh transcript by (Sir) William R. W. Wilde in Dublin University Magazine, xviii (July-December 1841), 612-13. Answers no. 1578; answered by no. 1670.
Oates, 20. Jan. 1692/3.
Sir,
I must acknowledge the care you take of my health in a way wherein you so kindly apply to my mind; and if I could persuade my self that my weak constitution was owing to that strength of mind you ascribe to me, or accompany'd with it, I should find therein, if not a remedy, yet a great relief against the infirmities of my body. However, I am not the less oblig'd to you for so friendly an application; and if the cordial you prescribe be not to be had (for I know none equal to a judicious and capacious mind) your kindness is not to be blamed, who I am confident wish me that satisfaction, or any thing else that would contribute to my health.
The doctor, concerning whom you enquire of me,†1 had, I remember, when I liv'd in town and convers'd among the physicians there, a good reputation amongst those of his own faculty. I can say nothing of his late book of Fevers, having not read it my self, nor heard it spoke of by others: But I perfectly agree with you concerning general theories, that they are for the most part but a sort of waking dreams, with which when men have warm'd their own heads, they pass into unquestionable truths, and then the ignorant world must be set right by them. Tho' this be, as you rightly observe, beginning at the wrong end, when men lay the foundation in their own phansies, and then endeavour to sute the phænomena of diseases, and the cure of them, to those phansies. I wonder that, after the pattern
― 629 ―
Dr. Sydenham has set them of a better way, men should return again to that romance way of physick. But I see it is easier and more natural for men to build castles in the air of their own, than to survey well those that are to be found standing. Nicely to observe the history of diseases in all their changes and circumstances, is a work of time, accurateness, attention, and judgment; and wherein if men, thro' prepossession or oscitancy†1 mistake, they may be convinced of their error by unerring nature and matter of fact, which leaves less room for the subtlety and dispute of words, which serves very much instead of knowledge in the learned world, where methinks wit and invention has much the preference to truth. Upon such grounds as are the establish'd history of diseases hypotheses might with less danger be erected, which I think are so far useful, as they serve as an art of memory to direct the physician in particular cases, but not to be rely'd on as foundations of reasoning, or verities to be contended for; they being, I think I may say all of them, suppositions taken up gratis, and will so remain, till we can discover how the natural functions of the body are perform'd, and by what alteration of the humors or defects in the parts they are hinder'd or disorder'd. To which purpose I fear the Galenists four humors, or the chymists sal, sulphur, and mercury,†2 or the late prevailing invention of acid and alcali,†3 or whatever hereafter shall be substituted to these with new applause, will upon examination be found to be but so many learned empty sounds, with no precise determinate signification. What we know of the works of nature, especially in the constitution of health, and the operations of our own bodies, is only by the sensible effects, but not by any certainty we can have of the tools she uses, or the ways she works by. So that there is nothing left for a physician to do, but to observe well, and so by analogy argue to like cases, and thence make to himself rules of practice: and he that is this way most sagacious will, I imagine, make the best physician, tho' he should entertain distinct hypotheses concerning distinct species of diseases, subservient to this
― 630 ―
end, that were inconsistent one with another, they being made use of in those several sorts of diseases but as distinct arts of memory in those cases. And I the rather say this, that they might be rely'd on only as artificial helps to a physician, and not as philosophical truths to a naturalist.†1 But, Sir, I run too far, and must beg your pardon for talking so freely on a subject you understand so much better than I do. I hoped the way of treating diseases, which with so much approbation Dr. Sydenham had introduc'd into the world, would have beaten the other out, and turn'd men from visions and wrangling to observation and endeavouring after settl'd practices in more diseases, such as I think he has given us in some. If my zeal for the saving mens lives and preserving their health (which is infinitely to be prefer'd to any speculations never so fine in physick) has carried me too far, you will excuse it in one who wishes well to the practice of physick, tho' he meddles not with it. I wish you, and your brother, and all yours a very happy new year, and am,
Sir,
Your most humble and faithful servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

Tho my last had the ill luck to be lost†2 I doe againe adventure the fortune of a second to tell you that I have some reason to beleive you are not displeased to be undisturb'd by mine yet intrest that strong principle in Courtiers do's not permit my making court to You this way and therefore having given You respit for some Considerable time (only that I have sent you some inquiry's after a letter) I can't forbear any longer writing to you since I have not much hopes of seing you Except your affairs call you to town for disagreable impediment's of vissiting my frends doe still and are like to Continue, our number†3 remaining as pevish and sickley as ever. B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 106. Year from Locke's endorsement.
My expectations of seeing you in Town Before this has been the reason of my writing nothing ever since my Last Letter, and the
― 633 ―
Hopes I yett have of seeing you quickly here is the reason why I shall write but little in this Place.
I Doe assure you here again, and Doe desire too that you would assure My Lady from mee, that had it been possible for mee; I had seen Oates before this Time, and would then have endeavourd, all I could, to bring with mee the Person desir'd.†1 All I desire now is that I may hear from you, when you will come to Town; because I am made to hope that you will come shortly for a day or 2.
I was desir'd to ask You about Mr Monroe†2 (he that is at Clapham). I remember he has told mee he often wayted on You, and in a manner, so as to receive his Instructions and Method from You. I desire but to know that: and whether ever you found him such a one, as to bestow any advice on him: For You must give mee leave to say, I know who those are that onely Get Advice from You: and since you never give it so as to be given in vain; that It allways imply's a Capacity, and a Good Inclination to receive itt. I could find a way to bring in something, by way of vanity, to My own Advantage, in that Consideration: but I had best be silent on that matter; till, being farther Benifitted by that Advice I mention, I be farther Capable of making a More Perfect Charachter of it, and a better Acknowledgment for it, than I am likely to doe att present.
Pray, Say that to my Lady for mee that you think is All I can Possibly Say to One that I have the Greatest Respect for that I am Capable of and Beleive mee upon my Word (which I have so often heartily pass'd for that One thing) that
I am your sincere Freind and Faithfull servant
A: ASHLEY

1600. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 7/17 February 1693 (1570, 1621)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 64-5. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 62-3.
A Amsterdam le 17. de Fevrier 1693.
J'ai envoié, Monsieur, deux exemplaires des 32 premiéres feuilles de mon Ouvrage†4 à Mr. Furly, à Rotterdam, dès le 10. de ce Mois, le priant de vous les faire tenir au plûtôt. Mais je n'ai reçu aucune
― 636 ―
réponse de lui, et je ne sai s'il n'est point en Angleterre. Je n'ai point non plus vû les livres, que vous croiez que j'aie déja reçus; ce qui me met en peine, pour le paquet que je lui ai adressé. Il y a àpresent 50 feuilles de mon Ouvrage d'imprimées, et il n'y en aura pas 90 en tout, de sorte que plus de la moitié est faite. J'espere qu'il sera achevé au mois de Mai prochain, de sorte qu'il est bon que je me hâte un peu, pour me déterminer sur la dédicace. C'est ce que j'attends de vôtre bonté, dès que vous aurez reçu les deux exemplaires que je vous envoie. Ils sont tout deux de la même sorte de papier, mais les feuilles de l'un sont choisies, comme vous le reconnoîtrez par l'épaisseur du papier, et les autres ne le sont pas.
Vous avez raison pour ce qui regarde l'essai, et je vous prie de mettre dessous, comme vous l'avez jugé, a penny english for every sheet. C'est comme je l'ai entendu, croiant qu'un stuyver de Hollande étoit à peu près la même chose qu'un de vos pennys.†1 Si je trouve quelque nombre de subscrybers, il me dedommagera facilement. J'avois envoié quelques feuilles semblables à Mr. de Salisbury, mais ne m'aiant point répondu, je n'oserois lui écrire davantage; étant occupé, comme il est. On ne comprend rien ici dans l'affaire de son livre.†2 La doctrine de la conquête y paroît fort étrange, mais c'est de quoi il ne nous appartient pas de nous mettre en peine. J'en avois aussi envoié à Mr. Cappel,†3 fils de Louïs, qui demeure à Londres, et je lui donnerai le même avertissement, sur les mots de folium et de stuverus.
Je croiois que je vous avois mandé que le Sieur Wetstein m'avoit dit qu'il n'y avoit pas de moien de rien envoier d'ici à Paris, sans de grandes risques, et de grandes longueurs. Tout ce qu'on peut faire de plus sûr, c'est d'envoier à Geneve et de là à Paris, ce qui est trois cents lieuës pour deux cents.†4 Lors que j'aurai reçu les Livres que vous avez eu la bonté de m'envoier, je ne manquerai pas de les lire, et de vous marquer ce que j'en pense. Je suis, Monsieur,
Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
― 637 ―
Si je savois que Mr. Furly ne fût plus à Rotterdam, je prendrois quelque autre voie, pour vous faire tenir les feuilles de mon Ouvrage. Les Occasions sont rares en cette ville, et les Marchands ont accoûtumé d'envoier le plus souvent à Rotterdam, où je chercherois quelque ami.

Londini 10° Jan 92/3
Vir Amplissime
Quamprimum ad urbem accessi nudius tertius Reverendissimus Archiepiscopus me ad se vocari curavit et ut conveni de Te et Libro tuo multa cum laude præfatus tandem dixit se ad Te scripsisse negotiorum multitudine hactenus impeditus paratamque epistolam sigillo muniens mihi in manus tradidit, ut inscriptione, illo dictante,
― 638 ―
meâ manu exarata, tibi transmittendam curarem quod libens suscepi.†1 Insuper mihi tradidit libellum concionum nuper a se editarum†2 ut etiam ad Te illum transmitterem quod itidem diligenter curabo, et quamprimum hinc ad vos proficiscentem quempiam <invenero>†a ei tradam ad Te perferendum. Hactenus de Archiepiscopi mandatis. Ad me quod attinet multas Tibi et habeo et refero gratias pro ea quam ex Historiæ Tuæ lectione percepi voluptate. Illud credo exhausisti argumentum, certe illud mysterium iniquitatis mundo palam exposuisti e tenebris in lucem protractum. Multarum rerum importuno impeditus interventu nondum integram perlegi: post brevem hac in urbe moram rus reversurus, pergam porro ut satisfaciam ei quod in me excitasti desiderio. Novissimis tuis literis mihi pro more gratissimis responsum hac in Charta expectare non debes. Festinans ad urbem eas rure reliqui, illuc cum rediero ad otii et quietis recessus oportunior dabitur tecum colloquendi occasio, hic vix respirandi mihi conceditur facultas. Interim amicitiam humanitatemque tuam consuetam agnosco. Te maximo cum affectu saluto, Tuosque omnes
― 639 ―
inprimis dilectissimam conjugem Liberosque Veeneos Guenelonesque nostros, omniaque tibi prospera et fælicia precor. Vale et me ut facis ama Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE

(Latin)
London 10 Jan 92/3
Excellent Sir,
As soon as I got to town the day before yesterday the Most Reverend the Archbishop caused me to be bidden to him, and when I was with him, after speaking with great praise about you and your book, he finally said that he had written to you, having been prevented till then by a multitude of affairs; sealing the letter, which he had ready, he delivered it to me, for me [p. 638] to write the direction at his dictation and to attend to its being sent to you, which I readily undertook.†1 He further delivered to me a book of sermons which he had recently published,†2 for me to send to you also, to which I shall attend with equal care, and as soon as I come upon anyone travelling from here to your country I shall deliver it to him to convey to you. So much for the Archbishop's commissions. As for myself, I give you my warmest thanks for the pleasure I have got from reading your Historia. I believe that you have exhausted the subject; you have certainly dragged forth that mystery of iniquity from darkness into light and exposed it openly to the world. Prevented by the unseasonable intervention of many affairs, I have not yet read through the whole of it; after a short stay in this city I shall return to the country and I shall then hasten to satisfy the desire that you have aroused in me. You must not expect in this sheet a reply to your last letter, which was as usual most welcome to me. In my haste to the city I left it in the country; when I return there, to a recess of leisure and quiet, a more suitable opportunity will be given me to talk with you; here the power to breathe is scarcely allowed me. Meanwhile I acknowledge your accustomed friendliness and kindness. I greet you with the greatest affection, and all [p. 639] yours, especially your dear wife and children, as well as our friends the Veens and the Guenellons, and I pray that all may go well and happily with you. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my kind regards to Mr. Le Clerc. I wrote to him recently.

B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 55-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Mark Lane†1 Feb: 10th
Dear Sir
No words can express how much I were disappointed, and Griev'd that you never came to Town last Year, during my whole stay of seven Weeks. I had flatter'd my self that the importunityes of your Friends here could not fail to bring you up once in a Month, or two at least, and I was fed with hopes to the last, that every day would bring me the desir'd Happiness; but to my Sorrow you arrived not till the very day after I were gone, which aggravated my misfortune, but theres no remedy against fate; though I must seldome see you, yet I must ever retain the greatest honour and
― 640 ―
affection for you and a deep and gratfull sense of my innumerable Obligations to You. I am once more unexpectedly got to Town, and have heard that you were comming for a few dayes; be so Charitable as to make me, Mrs Hunt, and your daughter†1 here, a Visit before you leave the Town; I would leave all other concerns to wayt on you at your Lodging, could I have any assurance of finding you there; pray contrive it so that I may once more be so happy as to embrace you either here, or there; my heart is so set upon it, that I cannot bear another disappointment; I beg with the more confidence, because your Charity to me will be recompenced with Mrs Hunts agreable Conversation, which every Body Vallues, and will make you think an hour or two not wholly lost, if you pass it amongst us. pardon the liberty I take with you, and do me the right to believe that none in the World longs to see you with a more pleasing impatience, or can more vallue that favour then Sir
Your Unalterable Freind and most Obedient Servant

1604. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 13/23 February 1693 (1521, 1636)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 51-2.
d'Amsterd. ce 23 feb. 1693.
Monsieur,
Jay bien receu vostre agreable du 28 nov. et j'y aurois respondu plustost si en mesme temps je n'u voulu vous rendre conte que vostre conte reste tousjours comme il estoit. Nous serions bien ayse si cela pouvoit vous attirer icy, et vous ne scauriez croire combien nous parlons de vous et souhaitterions de vous revoir encore une fois. l'orage qui a passé sur nostre famille est bien un peu appaisée, mais elle a laissé tant de marques de sa fureur, que nous nous en ressentons tousjours. il est pourtant vray que nous tachons de nous consoler comme il le faut de tous les malheurs qui nous arrivent et dont nous sommes pas coupables. nous vous remercions des bons conseils que vous nous donnez, et nous voyons bien quil faut s'y
― 642 ―
conformer si nous voulons eviter une plus grande perte pour nos enfans.
Tout ce que je peu joindre a ce que je vous ay desja mandé touchant l'enqueste de Monsieur vostre amis,†1 c'est que toutes les sepmaines on publie en cette ville un billet contenant le nombre des morts de la sepmaine precedente. toute l'annee 1691 dans laquelle nous avons eu une grande epidemie pendant l'automne, le nombre a esté 9202,†a l'année dernieré 6977. auquel la pluspart des annees se rapportent. une chose assez remarquable, c'est que quoy que cette ville soit basse de situation et dans un marets, les gens y vivent plus seinement que dans les parties plus exaucées de ces provinces. et nous avons veu plus d'une fois quand la peste ou quelque epidemie y a regné comme celle de l'an 1691. nous en avons eu la moindre part. la mortalité fut alors a haerlem le quadruple de cette ville, et partout ailleurs le double. je vous ay desja touché que nous avons Monsieur Bernagie professeur en Medicine dans nostre escole illustre.†2 que Monsieur Ruysh†3 enseigne au jardin en flamend la botanie pendant l'esté deux jours de la sepmaine un jour aux maistres chirurgiens et apothicaires, et l'autre aux escoliers. il enseigne la chirurgie deux autres jours de la sepmaine au college des chirurgiens principalement l'hyver et l'automne. Nous avons un hospital ou Monsieur Bernagie visite tous les jours avec ses escoliers douze malades six femmes et autant d'hommes pour les mieux diriger a la practique. les chirurgiens de l'hospital n'admettent que rarement les estrangers a la veue de leur manuel, mais contractent pour cinquante ou soixante florins avec ceux qui demandent cette liberté. et pour cent et quelque fois pour cent et cinquante florins avec ceux qui mettent la main a l'œuvre, sans qu'ils soyent logez chez eux. je vous diray que depuis peu jay excité comme Medecin de l'admirauté une reforme pour nos chirurgiens de la flotte, suivant un catalogue arresté nous les obligeons a garnir leur coffres des medicaments preparez a l'hospital, ou les compositions se font tousjours dans toute l'exactitude possible, et au retour de la campagne leur coffres se degarnissent au mesme hospital, eux
― 643 ―
ne payant que ce quils ont consumé. et l'admirauté un quart du prix pour le reste dont se recharge l'hospital, s'obligant au retour de l'equipage de remplir leur coffres de medicaments fraichement composez: l'Admirauté se dedommage en partie du payement quils fait, en retenant aux chirurgiens un mois de gage quon avoit coustume de leur avancer et donner pour equiper leur coffre, et l'hospital fait credit au chirurgiens (quoy qu'assignez sur leur gage) du payement jusqua leur retour. ma precedente faisoit aussi mention de l'estime que generalement on fait icy des œuvres de Monsieur Sydenham. et que pourtant le Cortex peruvianus n'a pas toute la vogue qu'il s'est acquis en Engleterre et en france. je finis avec les baisemains de toute la famille et suis avec un profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
Endorsed by Locke: P. Guenellon 23° Feb. 93
1605. Locke to Edward Clarke, 24 February [1693] (1598, 1611)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 56. Printed in Rand, p. 370. Year from Clarke's endorsement and contents.
Oates 24° Feb
Dear Sir
Though I know you are ready enough of your self to doe Sir Francis all the service you can, yet I am soe far interested in this last that I must thank you for it as if it were for my self.†1 I fear by yours of yesterday that there is noething more to be don by my Lord C and noe thing to be done in the businesse at all if my Lord P (whom we desired to gain by him) be resolvdly engaged for an other. This I would gladly trye and if possibly gain him powerfully to our side, or at least get him to be indifferently favourable. This I know not any other way how to come at but by Mr Atturny†2 to whom I have here inclosed writ, but soe as to leave to you the whole management of the affair with him in such maner and soe far as you shall finde convenient. I presume he will doe for me what one friend may expect from an other and farther than that I can never desire for
― 644 ―
my self, or in a businesse for an other I wish as well to as if it were for my self. If my Lord P would help or not stand in our way I should then think it worth while to move by other hands, but till I can be assured of that I think it is better sit still than make a bustle and noise to noe purpose. If Mr Atturny thinks fit to speak to my Lord P in it you may furnish him with all those arguments in Sir Francis's behalf which you used to my Lord C. If there be found by Mr Atturny any life in it, the time presseing I must desire you to speake in my name to my Lord Pembroke to move the King in it, and tell my Lord that as soon as I receive your letter I shall come up to town on purpose to wait on his Lordship in it, as certainly I shall if you give me any incouragement to hope any good is to be done in this affair. Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
