1606. John Norris to Locke, 27 February [1693] (1595)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 167. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 1595. For the dispute see p. 547, n. 1.
Bemerton. Feb. 27.
Mr Lock,
I am glad to find you in any tendency towards a Reconciliation, but wonder you should be so strait in the Terms of it as to put it all upon my going out of town precisely on that Wednesday; For my plea was not built (as you will have it) upon my actual going that very day, but upon my being to go, for so the posture of my Affairs stood when I put the Letter into my Friend's hand. Tis true indeed as it fell out I did not go till the Fryday, but that was more than I knew or thought of when I deliver'd him the Letter. I was then resolv'd for Wednesday, and to satisfy you that I was in earnest my wife with one of her sisters was gon to take places in the Coach,
― 645 ―
and had don it, but happening to meet with some new Friends were by them over-intreated to let it alone, but this I knew nothing of till tuesday night. If you ask why, since I did not go on the Wednesday as my First Design was, I did not afterwards bring you the Letter, why truly, partly because I took it for granted that by that time my Bookseller had don it, into whose hands since I had already committed it upon the prospect of my going Wednesday, I thought it needles to go to him any more about it. And partly because my little time was so fill'd up with Busines and Company that I had not leisure enough to do it with any tolerable Convenience. For Considering the distance of your Lodging from mine it would have took up the best part of a day (as the length of a day then was) which truely was more time than I could in those Circumstances spare without putting my self to great inconvenience, and that too needlesly as I thought, having taken sufficient care for the Conveiance of the Letter another way. If this will satisfy you, well and good, but if not, I have no more to say, but that I am
Your humble servant
J. NORRIS
what you mean by saying that I have reason to be sorry to see So much infirmity in human nature, I am not guilty enough to understand. You must explain this Retorsion, or it will be lost.
Address: To Mr Lock at Oates in Essex.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Norris 27° Feb 92/3

1608. William Popple to Locke, 2 March 1693 (1590, 1630)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 205-6.
London March 2d. 1692/93.
Sir
I received your letter the last post, and sent forwards the inclosed to Mr Furly. I would not have failed also at the same time to have writ to you, but that Mr Ashly's condition was so very doubtful that indeed I did not know what to say of it.†1 Yesterday it was yet worse. But since last night both the Doctors begin to hope pretty confidently of his recovery. This at present wholly takes up my Lord Ashley. But after this and the public Busyness of Parliament is over,†2 I believe he dos designe to see you: And I intend to give my self the honour to wait upon him in that visit. In the mean while I am exceedingly obliged to My Lady Masham for her kinde invitation. I shall profit by the journey every way. But I doubt you did not calculate all the Consequences when you put her upon it; I mean the hazard of your own reputation, by my ill company. At your perill be it. I shall be very glad to receive the Papers you mention, and to contribute what care I am capable of towards their publication.†3 I have now also finishd some papers that you have seen by pieces.†4 They wait for an opportunity of undergoing your Judgment: that is whether they shall be committed to the fire or confined to my own Closet: for indeed though I have some times amused my own minde agreably enough in composing them, yet I
― 647 ―
think in many respects they are unfit for the public. My wife†1 and daughter†2 present their services to you. I am
Sir,
Your most humble servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.
We have had little alterations in our Club since you left us. But it continues on alwayes very hopefully. Tomorrow it will be at my house. Some considerable members are chosen, as Lord Carberry,†3 Mr Nevill,†4 and Mr Malines:†5 but whether they will come or no I know not. Sir John Wildman is also nominated.

1609. William Molyneux to Locke, 2 March 1693 (1592, 1620)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed with some omissions in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 32-8. Answers no. 1592; answered by no. 1620.
Dublin. March. 2d. 1692/3
Honoured Sir
Yours of Jan. 20. came to my Hands just as I lay down on a Bed of Sicknes being a Severe Cholick, that held me nigh five weeks and brought me very weak; this was the more Greivous to me, in that it hindred me from giving that ready Answer to your Letters, which I desired; being very Coveteous on all Oppertunitys of Keeping up a Correspondence with One for whom I have so great a Respect. I am now, God be thanked, pretty wel recoverd; but yet weak, and have not yet stird abroad. I know the bare signifying this to you is sufficient in my Excuse; So that Relying on your Pardon, I proceed to Answer your Last.
And first, Sir, beleive me, that whatever Expressions of Honour or Respect, I have at any time used to you, have been the sincere thoughts of my Hart, and not the vain Complements that usually
― 648 ―
pas between Courtiers, and how extravagant soever are lookd upon as the Effects of good Breeding, and pas only as such by License. I think I know a Worthy Man when I meet him and they are so rare in the World, that no Honour is too great for those that are such. and I must plainly say it to your self, that so much Humanity, Candour, Condescention, and Good Nature, joynd with so Great Judgement, Learning, and Parts, I have not mett with in any Man Living as in the Author of the Essay concerning Humane Understanding. You so favourably intertain all Mens Objections, You are so desirous to Hear the sense of Others, you are so Tender in differing from any Man, that you have Captivated me beyond resistance. What you propose to add in those places which I intimated to you as†a- seemingly repugnant to unwary Readers pag. 270 and 314. 315. is abundantly sufficient. Unles you may think it convenient (for the prevention of all manner of Scruple, and to shew your Readers that you are aware of the Objection that may be raised against these Passages) to add in the Margin a little Note to that purpose, specifying the seeming Repugnancy that was in the first Edition, and that for the clearing thereof you have thus farther illustrated it in this.†1 but this, as every thing else, I propose with all submission to your better judgement.-†a Mentioning the Marginal Note to you, minds me to Intimate, that I should think it Convenient in your Next Edition, to Expres the Abstract or Content of each section in the Margin, and to spare (if you think fit) the Table of Contents at the Latter end of the Book, tho I think both may do best.†2 I can assure you for My Own reading and Consulting your Book, I have put the Table of Contents to their Respective Sections throughout the Whole.
As†b- to the Errata Typograph. what I have taken notice of, besides those your Table mentions, are as follows.
pag. 23. Lin. 39. Wrong Parenthesis. p. 34. l. 32. Dele My. p. 36. L. 43.†c surely stand, instead of, easily depend as tis in the Book. p. 52. l. 31. if this were. p. 53. l. 33. enjoyments the Creatures. p. 55. l. Ult. Understandings. p. 97. l. penult. dele Can. p. 156. l. 22. We may
― 649 ―
observe. p. 203. l. 48. Imitation. p. 225. L. 12. there seems some word wanting, I suppose it may be thus supplyd, Disloyalty pas current. p. 281. l. 47. to say.†-b †1 I am fully convinced by the Arguments you give me for not turning your Book into the Scholastick form of a Logick and Metaphysicks; and I had no other reason to advice the other, but meerly to get it promoted the easier in our Universitys; One of the Businesses of which Places is to Learn according to the Old Forms. and this Minds me to Let you know the Great joy and Satisfaction of Mind I conceived On your Promise of the Method of Learning; there could nothing be More acceptable to me than the Hopes thereof, and that On this Account; I have but One Child in the World,†2 who is now nigh four years Old, and promises wel, His Mother Left him to me very Young, and My affections (I must Confes) are Strongly placed on him; It has pleased God by the Liberal provisions of Our Ancestors, to free me from the toiling Cares of providing a fortune for Him, so that my Whole Study shall be to lay up a Treasure of Knowledge in his Mind, for His Happines both in this Life and the next. And I have been often thinking of some Method for His Instruction, that may best obtain the End I propose. And now to my Great joy I hope to be abundantly supplyd by Your Method. And My Brother has sometimes told Me, that whilst he had the Happines of your Acquaintance at Leyden, you were upon such a Work as this I desire, and that too at the Request of a Tender Father for the Use of his Only Son. Wherefore, Good Sir, let me most earnestly intreat you by no means to lay aside this infinitely Useful Work, till you have finishd it; for twil be of Vast advantage to all Mankind, as wel as particularly to Me your intire Freind. And On this Consideration of Usefulnes to Mankind I wil presume again to remind you of your Discourse of Morality; And I shall think my self very Happy, if by putting you on the Thought, I should be the least Occasion of so Great Good to the World. What I have more to say relating to your Book is of Little or no Moment; however; you so readily intertain all Mens thoughts of your Works, that Futile as mine are you shall have a Remark or two more from me.
― 650 ―
But first to your Quæry, whether I know any New heads from Logick or Metaphysicks to be Inserted in the second Edition of your Essay. I answer I know none, unles you think it may not do wel to Insist more particularly and at Large†a- on Æternæ Veritates and the Principium Individuationis. Concerning the first you have some touches pag. 281. sec. 31. p. 323. s. 14. p. 345. s. 14.†1 and concerning the Latter, pag. 28. s. 4. p. 40. s. 12.†2
Pag. 96. sec. 9. you assert what I conceive is an Error in Fact, viz, that a Mans Eye can distinguish a Second of a Circle whereof its self is the Center. whereas tis certain that few Mens Eyes can distinguish les than 30 Seconds, and most not under a Minute or 60 Seconds.†3 as is manifest from what Mr Hook lays down in his Animadversions on the first part of Hevelii Machina Cælestis. pag. 8. 9. etc.†4 but this as I said before is only an Error in Fact, and Affects not the Doctrine laid down in the said section.
Pag. 341. sec. 2. you say, the Existence of all things without us (except only of God) is had by our senses. and pag. 147. sec. 33. 34. 35. 36. you shew how the Idea we have of God is made up of the Ideas we have gotten by our senses.†5 Now this tho no Repugnancy yet to unwary readers may seem One; and therefore perhaps may deserve a fuller Expression.-†a to Me tis plain that in pag 341 you speak barely of the Existence of a God; and in pag 147 you speak of the Ideas that are ingredient in the Complex Idea of God; that is, pag. 147†b- You say that all the Ideas ingredient in the Idea of a God are had from Sense;†c- and pag. 341. you only assert that the Existence of this God, or that realy there are united in One being all these Ideas is had, not from-†c Sense, but Demonstration. This to me seems your sense, yet perhaps every reader may not so readily conceive it, and
― 651 ―
therefore possibly you may think this passage pag. 341. worth your farther Consideration and addition.
I wil conclude my tedious lines with a Jocose Problem, that, upon Discourse with several concerning your Book and Notions, I have proposed to Diverse very Ingenious Men, and could hardly ever Meet with One that at first dash would give me the Answer to it, which I think true; till by hearing My Reasons they were Convinced. tis this. Suppose a Man born blind, and now adult, and taught by his Touch to Distinguish between a Cube and a Sphere (Suppose) of Ivory, nighly of the same Bignes, so as to tel, when he felt One and tother, Which is the Cube which the Sphære. Suppose then, the Cube and Sphære placed on a Table, and the Blind man to be made to see. Quære whether by his sight, before he touchd them, he could now Distinguish and tel which is the Globe which the Cube. I answer, Not; for tho he has obtaind the Experience of How a Globe, how a Cube affects his Touch. Yet he has not yet attaind the Experience, that what affects my Touch so or so, must affect my Sight so or so; or that a Protuberant Angle in the Cube that presd his hand unequally, shall appear to his Eye as it does in the Cube.†-b But of this enough; perhaps you may find some place in your Essay, wherein you may not think it amis, to say something of this Problem.†1
I am extreamly Obleidged to you for Mr Boyles Book of the Air, which lately came to my Hands. tis a Vast Designe and not to be finishd but by the United Labours of Many Heads; and indefatigably prosecuted for Many Years. So that I despair of seing anything Compleat therein; However, if Many would lend the same helping hands that you have done, I should be in Hopes; and certainly there is not a Chapter in all Natural Philosophy of Greater Use to Mankind than what is here proposed. I am
Worthy Sir,
Your Most Humble Servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
My†a- Brother Gives You his Most Humble Service and thanks
― 652 ―
you for your last Letter, to which he will soon return you an Answer.†-a

Dear Sir

I am extremly troubled that your cold sticks soe upon you. Pray drinke water and carefully noe wine and be as litle abroad in the Evenings as you can. 1613. Locke to Edward Clarke, 10 March 1693 (1611, 1625)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 57. Printed in Rand, pp. 371-3.
Oates 10° Mar 92/3
Dear Sir
I am soe accustomed to receive matter of thanks from you in every letter and that if true gratitude lay more in the expression of words than in the true sense and disposition of the minde I should be troubled to finde out a new forme of thankeing you upon every new occasion I have to doe soe. I doubt not yet but you will beleive that I am very much obleigd by the lost labour you have laid out for Sir Francis to which I must intreat you to adde this farther kindenesse, that when you see Mr Attorney you will let him see the great sense I have of his favour in this businesse and that I thinke myself to have the same obligation to him in it as if the thing had been for my self and I had obteined it by his intercession, or which pleases me more than all that I receive it as a great and fresh instance of his Freindship, a place which perhaps one noe better versed or taken with the world than I am may thinke he has reason to prefer to any of the places men soe scramble for. Pray tell him he can bestow his favours upon noe body soe much gratis as he does upon me. for whatever he may lay out this way upon me it is like to bring him noe returne of any greater love or esteeme than what I had for him before And for doeing him any service I may with vanity bid him expect it from me when I am Attorney and he a pore uselesse thing in the Country.
― 655 ―
I thank you also for your care about my pol cirtificate.†1 Put pray in your next to†a me an account of your health or which will be a great deale better bring your self hither to give an account of it. My Lady who returnes you many and hearty thanks for this last favour earnestly presses you to doe soe. Tis very ill husbandry for your country to neglect your health even to serve it to day soe as not to be able to doe it to morrow when probably there will be as much need, leave therefor your wrangleing and voteing and bring your cold hither and you shall see what notable states folke we are here I mean as much as goes to the cureing of a cold: Indeed your last letter has made me uneasy and I shall be soe till you give me a better account of your health. If I could be half soe good a physitian to you in town as I can be in the country I would come up to you But beleive it my skil in cureing colds lies at Oates come hither and you shall find it. If at any time you see the Ladys at Whitehall,†2 neither say nor know any thing to them of Sir Francis's affair. I am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE

1614. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 10/20 March 1693 (1599, 1638)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 104-5.
Rotterdam 20 march 1693
Dear Friend
Yours of the 21 Past I have, and wish I had received it together with mr. P.†1 of the 14th detto. I should then not have ordred the sending forward of my letter†2 as I did, he giving scarce any other reason for its being stopt, but the sharpness of the stile, of which I had quite, (and so had all that have heard it here) other thoughts, nor can I upon another reading of it, find any roughness in it. Yet upon other considerations, as my entring into many particulars, that are never like to be my case etc. I could be content if not sent, to receive it back again. But whatever I shal write, I think I ought to write first to the party, for its out of all order to complain to any else for reparations, til he refuses it me, and then neither can I complain to any meeting, regularly, but to that unto which he belongs; as to my sending it to mr. N.†3 open, it was for himself onely, and I cautiond him, to seale it, and conceal his having seen or read it.
My former letters have informd you, that I have declared to the General meeting here, that in all those external formalities, no one excepted, I have freedom in myself. In all of them save that one single practice, I dayly, publickly and constantly do use my liberty, and no man, nor woman of this meeting, nor any other in this countrey, speaks word to me, tho they looke upon it as a direct destroying of their particular Testimony in these things, for, in all those things they beleeve that they have received a Testimony, as they call it, for God, against them all and every one.
Why I should now look upon myself, as concernd, in point of scandal, or offence, to forbear as to that one thing, while I practice my liberty in all other things, and they themselves expect it of me, and wonder at me for it, and are apt to think, and they think not amiss, that it is upon some other account that I do it not, I know no Reason. If they (whatever this hot headed yong man†4 has done) can bear me in all other things without, contending with me about
― 657 ―
them, why should not I think that they will be as quiet, if I do use the same liberty as to that one other thing? If I ought, as you say, to scruple offending my weak brethren, in this, I ought to doe it in all the rest; for I can see no difference at all in the matter; The reall truth is, what ever they may talk of a crosse in the not doing it. I shal find a greater crosse to do it, after so many years forbearance, unless I prepare mens minds, by previous declaration of my liberty in the case, than in continuing to do, as I doe.
Mythinks, instead of growing larger, you grow narrower. In your former letter, you said, if it were the meer exercise of my own liberty, I was to forbear it, rather then give offence. But if other considerations, of greater weight fell in, that I was not bound to sacrifice all to that. Nor to take that for a cause of true offence, that it displeasd the Ruling Scribes and Pharisees of the party. Now you seem to conclude without restriction—
Ile put you a case or two. Suppose the Goverment would in any thing that might be a support to me and my family, if I wanted it, give me an Imployment. Am I bound to continue in that practice, till I can bring, the Rulers of the party, or the Elders of the synagogue, to use or at least allow this freedome?†a how shal I ever know whether they doe, or wil allow this freedom but by using it myself, and trying how they wil bear it? as one none of the meanest among them in Colchester did nigh 30 years agoe;†b †1 who yet continued at times to frequent meetings, against whom they never gave forth, as they phrase it, any publick Testimony; or as <other>†c sects cal it, never excommunicated him.
or, Suppose I find an absolute necessity of seeking a Gentlewoman to wife, to Govern my family, and take care of my children, whom I do not breed up in those things, and therein, do give offence, and occasion talk, suppose I could find one that is every way fit to do this, and willing, but should scruple the ingageing herself till she saw me also out of that practice—must I want such a considerable convenience or advantage to myself, and children, upon that score? or ought I not rather to take up any Cross, of mens evill tongues,
― 658 ―
in the case, then deprive my self of a thing so necessary, as I really find it to be in my family, to have such a stay in it, I could tell you more upon this subject, than I can think fit to write. Now it is impossible, and ridiculous for me to expect any of the party that will undertake that province of educating my children, as I will have them educated, tho' I should promise never so much, never to change, as to my own practice—which yet I would never promise to any woman in the world. This is the case, if ever, that will make me use my liberty, and makes me take all, convenient, occasions of declareing it, and my reasons for it. But I find it not so easy tho, I thus speak, to doe it.
The packet you sent in September, I received in November, and the 8th of November I sent it by the Amsterdam boat, and so it is (as good luck is) registred in the book, of the Commissaries of the Amsterdam Veer†1 —But, as the professor†2 writes me, he never received it—I have given him advice where he must enquire for it, and hope he will find it. The other packet I have not yet, it is shipt with all my books from mr. Popples—
I have told Leers what you write who presents you his service, and thanks—his friend has but 3 medals, so that if mr. charleton has no good quantity they must be totally waved. And then he would desire your advice, what prints to bring in of these following persons. in the reign of H: VII. The King. Elizabeth his Wife daughter of Ed. 4th. Edward Plantaginet. Lambert Simnel son of a baker. Perkin Warbeck. Catharine Gourdon de Huntley his wife. Margarit sister of Ed. 4. James III of Scotland. James 4. Margaret his wife. Margaret Dutchess of Austria sought in marriage by Hen. 7. under Henry 8 his 4 wives. Elisabeth Blunt his miss. Henry fits Roy his bastard. Mary his sister, wife of Louis XII. and afterwards of Charles Brandon Duke of Suffolk—Charles Brandon himself. James V of Scotland. his 2 wives, Charles V. Thomas Howard Duke of norfol†a John Fisher. Bishop of Winchester; Thomas Seymour Admiral Ridley. Bishop Latimer. Bishop of Winchester, Peter Martyr, Martin Bucer, M. Parker. under the reign of Jane Grey, my Lord Guilford Dudley her husband. my Lord Grey Duke of Suffolk her father. John Dudley Duke of Northumberland
― 659 ―
her father in Law, under the reign of Mary Philip her husband. my Lord Courtney Earl of Devon; Edmund Bonner Bishop of London.
He desires advice which of these persons (besides those in Burnet's History of the Reformation,†1 which they will have) are most necessary to be inserted, and where they may be had—

1616. James Johnstoun to Locke, 14 March [1693] (2099)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 25-6. Year from Locke's endorsement. Johnstoun was one of the two secretaries of state for Scotland from 3 March 1692 until January 1696.
14 March
Sir
I am nou to goe to Scotland after the next week. I have carried my point for the present. The parliament is to meet there and D. Hamilton†2 is to be Commissioner. I know not if I shall be as lucky with you. In a word you know I am a man of noe ceremonye. I have considered that in case I can prevaill with you to goe alongst with me, I shall find my account in it, which is to passe some time so much the more agreably. You will consider if you can hope to doe the same and let me know your mind. I know you value your freedome mightily and so doe I mine. I am sure you will not goe if you shall apprehend that it will be under any restraint, and I am sure I should not desire you to goe did I thinck that either yours or mine would be any manner of way encumbred by it. I know not what nicety you may have as to the putting me to charges, but as to that I shall make you a verry sorry compliment, which is the true state of the matter that your being at noe charges will not put me to any; so that you are to have noe obligation to me on that head. My respects to My Lady Masham, who noe doubt would never
― 661 ―
pardon me if she knew this but nou the parliament is up†1 Sir Francis will keep home. I hope the secretary walk†2 is still in favour. My compliments too to Mrs Masham†3 and Mrs Compton.†4 I have little news but what you hear. affairs abroad looke well. God does his part. farewell.

Shall we pretend more that nothing shall surprise us, and have you heard of our late whiggish promotion†1 without admiration. 1620. Locke to William Molyneux, 28 March 1693 (1609, 1622)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 39-43. Answers no. 1609; answered by no. 1622.
London, 28. Mar. 1693.
Sir,
Your silence that spared me a great deal of fear and uneasiness, by concealing from me your sickness till it was well over, is abundantly made amends for by the joy it brings me in the news of your recovery. You have given me those marks of your kindness to me, that you will not think it strange that I count you amongst my friends, and, with those, desiring to live with the ease and freedom of a perfect confidence, I never accuse them to my self of neglect or coldness, when I fail to hear from them so soon as I expected or
― 664 ―
desired: though had I known you so well before as I do now, since your last letter, I should not have avoided being in pain upon account of your health.
I cannot at all doubt the sincerity of any thing you say to me; but yet give me leave to think, that 'tis an excess of kindness alone could excuse it from looking like complement. But I am convinced you love your friends extremely, where you have made choice of them, and then believe you can never think nor speak too well of them. I know not whether it belongs to a man who gets once in print, to read in his book that it is perfect, and that the author is infallible. Had I had such an opinion of my own sufficiency before I writ, my Essay would have brought me to another, and given me such a sight of the weakness of my understanding, that I could not fail to suspect my self of error and mistake in many things I had writ, and to desire all the light I could get from others to set me right. I have found you one of the likelyest to afford it me, your clearness and candor gave me the confidence to ask your judgment, and I take it for no small assurance of your friendship that you have given it me, and have condescended to advise me of the printer's faults, which gives me hopes you have not concealed any you have observed in the work it self. The marginal summaries you desire, of the paragraphs, I shall take care to have added, were it only for your sake, but I think too it will make the book the more useful.
That request of yours you press so earnestly upon me makes me bemoan the distance you are from me, which deprives me of the assistance I might have from your opinion and judgment, before I ventur'd any thing into the publick. 'Tis so hard to find impartial freedom in ones friends, or an unbyass'd judgment any where, that amongst all the helps of conversation and acquaintance, I know none more wanted, nor more useful, than speaking freely and candidly ones opinion upon the thoughts and compositions of another intended for the press. Experience has taught me that you are a friend of this rank, and therefore I cannot but heartily wish that a sea between us did not hinder me from the advantage of this good office. Had you been within reach I should have beg'd your severe examination of what is now gone to the printer at your instance;†1 I had rather I could have said upon your perusal, and with
― 665 ―
your correction. I am not, in my nature, a lover of novelty nor contradiction; but my notions, in this treatise, have run me so far out of the common road and practice, that I could have been glad to have had them allow'd by so sober a judgment as yours; or stop'd, if they had appear'd impracticable or extravagant, from going any farther. That which your brother tells you, on this occasion, is not wholly besides the matter. The main of what I now publish, is but what was contain'd in several letters to a friend of mine, the greatest part whereof were writ out of Holland. How your brother came to know of it I have clearly forgot, and do not remember that ever I communicated it to any body there. These letters, or at least some of them, have been seen by some of my acquaintance here, who would needs persuade me 'twould be of use to publish them; your impatience to see them, has not, I assure you, slacken'd my hand, or kept me in suspence: and I wish now they were out, that you might the sooner see them, and I the sooner have your opinion of them. I know not yet whether I shall set my name to this discourse, and therefore shall desire you to conceal it. You see I make you my confessor, for you have made your self my friend.
The faults of the press are, I find upon a sedate reading over of my book, infinitely more than I could have thought; those that you have observed I have corrected, and return you my thanks; and, as far as I have gone in my review, have added and alter'd several things, but am not yet got so far as those places you mark for the æternæ veritates, and principium individuationis, which I shall consider when I come to them, and endeavour to satisfie your desire. Malebranche's hypothesis of seeing all things in God being that from whence I find some men would derive our ideas, I have some thoughts of adding a new chapter, wherein I will examine it, having, as I think, something for to say against it, that will shew the weakness of it very clearly.†1 But I have so little love to controversy, that I am not fully resolv'd. Some other additions I have made, I hope will not displease you, but I wish I could shew them you before they are in
― 666 ―
print; for I would not make my book bigger, unless it were to make it better.
I thank you for advising me of the error about sight, for indeed it was a great one in matter of fact, but it was in the expression, for I meant a minute, but, by mistake, call'd 1/60 of a degree a second. Your ingenious problem will deserve to be published to the world.
The seeming contradiction between what is said p. 147. and p. 341. is just as you take it, and I hope so clearly expressed, that it cannot be mistaken, but by a very unwary reader, who cannot distinguish between an idea in the mind, and the real existence of something out of the mind answering that idea. But I heartily thank you for your caution, and shall take care how to prevent any such mistake when I come to that place. My humble service to your brother. I am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
April
1621. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 6/16 April 1693 (1600, 1623)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 66-7. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, p. 63.
A Amsterdam le 16 d'Avril 1693.
J'ai renvoié, Monsieur, d'Ordinaire à autre à vous écrire pour vous remercier des soins que vous prenez pour mon Ouvrage,†1 dans la pensée que j'aurois un autre remerciment à vous faire, pour les Livres que vous m'envoiâtes l'automne dernier. Quoi que le paquet se soit perdu de Rotterdam ici, je ne vous en ai pas moins d'obligation. Mr. Furly ne m'aiant pas écrit en envoiant ici le paquet, il ne m'a point été rendu, et c'est en vain que je m'en suis informé jusqu'à présent. Mais j'en ai reçu un autre, où il y a un livre de feu Mr. Boyle,†2 the 3 Letter for toleration,†3 et a gentleman's religion.†4 J'ai lu ce dernier, et une partie de la Lettre, et je trouve l'une et l'autre extrémement à mon goût. J'ai même résolu de traduire en François
― 667 ―
La Religion d'un honête homme, qui n'est ni pasteur ni docteur, car c'est comme il le faudroit intituler; mais c'est ce que je ne puis faire qu'apres que l'Edition de mon livre sera achevée, ce qui sera dans un mois d'ici. Il y en a 80 feuilles d'imprimées, et le tout ne sera que de 92. Vous pouvez, Monsieur, comprendre par là qu'il est temps de penser tout de bon à la Dédicace, et si vous n'avez pas changé d'avis, je prendrai la liberté de vous prier de demander à Mr. le Comte de Pembroke la permission de le lui dédier, pour moi; et s'il l'agrée de me marquer les endroits principaux, par où je lui puis faire compliment. J'ose vous demander de la promtitude, dans cette commission, de peur que je ne sois obligé d'attendre trop longtemps, ce qui me porteroit du préjudice. Une autre fois j'oserai encore vous prier de me dire un peu au long vôtre sentiment touchant l'Ouvrage même, que vous pourrez assez connoître par les 32 feuilles que vous avez. Je vous demande pardon de la peine que je vous donne, soiez persuadé que je suis, Monsieur, très parfaitement à vous
J LE CLERC.

1622. William Molyneux to Locke, 18 April 1693 (1620, 1643)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 44-6. Answers no. 1620; acknowledged in no. 1643.
Dublin. Apr. 18. 93.
Sir
I have lately received farther testimonys of your kindnes and Freindship to me in your Last of Mar. 28th. which brings withall the Welcome News of your having Committed your Work of Education to the Press: than Which, I know not any thing that I ever expected with a more earnest desire. What my Brother told me relating to that Treatise, he had from your self in Holland. But perhaps you might have forgot what pasd between you on that Occasion. I perceive you fear, the novelty of some Notions therein may seem Extravagant; But if I may venture to judge of the Author,
― 668 ―
I fear no such thing from him. I doubt not, but the Work will be New and Peculiar, as his other Performances; And this 'tis that renders them estimable and Pleasant. He that travels the beaten Roads may chance indeed to have Company; but he that takes his Liberty, and manages it with Judgement, is the Man that makes useful Discoverys, and most beneficial to those that follow him. Had Columbus never ventur'd farther than his Predecessors, we had yet been Ignorant of a Vast Part of our Earth, preferable (as some say) to all the other three; And if none may be allowd to trye the Ocean of Philosophy farther than Our Ancestors, we shall have but little advancements or Discoverys made in the Mundus Intellectualis; wherein I beleive there is much more unknown, than what we have yet found out.
I should very much approve of your Adding a Chapter in your Essay, concerning Malbranches Hypothesis. As there are Enthusiasmes in Divinity, so there are in Philosophy; and as one proceeds from not Consulting, or misapprehending the Book of God; so the other from not reading and Considering the Book of Nature. I look upon Malbranches Notions, or rather Platos, in this particular perfectly unintelligible; And if you will Ingage in a Philosophick Controversy, you cannot do it with more advantage than in this matter. What you lay down concerning Our Ideas and Knowledge is founded and Confirmd by Experiment, and Observation, that any man may make in himself, or the Children he Converses with; wherein he may note the Gradual Steps that we make in Knowledge. But Plato's fancy has no foundation in Nature, but is meerly the Product of his Own brain.
I know tis none of your Busines to ingage in Controversy, or remove Objections; save only such as seem immediately to strike at your Own Positions; and therefore I cannot insist upon what I am now going to mention to you; However I will give you the Hint, and Leave the Considerations thereof to your own Breast. The tenth Chapter of your fourth Book is a Most Exact Demonstration of the Existence of a God. But perhaps it might be more full, by an Addition against the Eternity of the World, and that all things have not been going on, in the same Manner, as we now see them, ab Æterno. I have known a Pack of Philosophical Atheists, that reley much on this Hypothesis; and even Hobbs himself does somewhere alledge (If I am not forgetful tis in his Book de Corpore in the Chapter de Universo) that the same Arguments, which are brought
― 669 ―
against the Æternity of the World, may serve as wel against the Æternity of the Creatour of the World.†1
I am
Honr'd Sir
Your Most Affectionate Devoted Servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
My†a- Brother is your Most Humble Servant.-†a

Sir
I returne you my thanks for yours and beg your pardon for trobleing you with that paper which I suppose to be as much nonsence as I se his practise to be who made it. we have taken the best advice for my son†1 we could think of but a Friend of his, much more likely by his example to bring him to such a desease then by his Judgment to find out a man fit to cure it, commended this man to him the man warants he will effect a perfect cure and we thought it reasonable to satisfie my son with a short tryal but I find he takes a way as unlikely as hitherto unsuccesful for he gives him such things as purg him that wheras he used not to go above 5 times he goes 9 and his Gripes returne with violence and he lays downe this for a Rule that he must purg away the Humore and strengthen his stomach we find in his purges Aloes and in his stomach strengthners wormwood either of which I think very hot and improper for him, and we find his strength and his Appetite much abated since the use

1625. Locke to Edward Clarke, 4 May 1693 (1613, 1628)
Rand, pp. 373-5. 'This letter is in very bad condition, and wholly faded in parts.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand.
Oates, 4th May, 1693.
Dear Sir,
... Your letters [have brought] in my mind all that I know of that trouble,†8 and in consideration my thoughts reduced themselves
― 673 ―
to two: which were Sir Thomas Millington and the gentleman in Queen Street†1 I formerly recommended to you. And though upon account of ability my guesses inclined clearly to Sir Thomas (a late book of the other not having much increased my opinion of him), yet I had some thoughts of mentioning the other with Sir Thomas to him, because his having been a neighbour in the country might satisfy our friend concerning him and make him [acceptable to] him. This I say was my purpose to have proposed these two to him, till thinking again on the matter and considering the access Sir Thomas had at court, whereby our friend might have an easier way of procuring himself recesses, or making his excuses for them when his health required, I concluded in all respects Sir Thomas to be the fittest man, and upon second thoughts remain of the same opinion, adding to the former the convenience of his near neighbourhood.
I wish to your general opinion of his ill state of health you had added some particulars concerning it, but for want of that, taking it to be some remains of that indisposition which made him once go out of the house, I am steadily of opinion that he should wholly leave off wine and wholly come to drinking of water, by gradually diminishing the wine and accustoming himself to the other, for which this is a fit time of the year, but by no means to make this change all at once. Another thing I think necessary for his health is to make himself as many holidays as possibly he can, and to disburthen his head of weighty cares every half-hour of leisure that he can get. I am not ignorant how hard a thing I propose in this, but my meaning is that he should get all the time of relaxation of thought and diversion that he can. A third thing necessary is that whenever he takes physic or a water, that he be sure not to let anyone come near him that has the least business in his mouth or so much as looks; but that he get some company to be with him those days who never had any other thoughts in their heads but to laugh and chat and be merry.
I know him and myself too well to be guilty of so much vanity as to think I can say anything to him where his own thoughts would not give him better views....†a This, however, I cannot but say,
― 674 ―
that I count justice and dispatch are the two greatest businesses of his place. The one I know nothing can divert or [lead] him from. The other I know how much the multiplied forms and artificial perplexities brought into the court will hinder him in. But this, too, if he will make good his own character and the expectation of the world, he must break through. It being little release to a man that the cause is judged at last with justice on his side when he is undone in the length of the suit. I easily grant that inveterate evils cunningly wove into the forms of business are not all to be removed in a day. But this I know, that my Lord Shaftesbury making himself Chancellor, and not letting the Registers be so as they were before by making the Register read the minutes he took from his mouth aloud in court, gave so great hopes of dispatch to all men the first day he sat in the bench that it was thereon said he had cut off one great part of the needless charge and delay of clients, and put that in its right course with so general an approbation that none of his enemies durst so much as find fault with it.†1 You may easily see by this what I wish to be done now even for his sake. For it is in that post and the opinion he gives of himself that way that he must gather the strength which must assist his integrity, steadiness, civility, and admirable parts to make his way through all opposition, and I suppose you will concur with me in this. I sometimes wish myself with you and in his neighbourhood that I might talk with you and our friend J F,†2 and show my readiness and respect to my Lord. But I paid so dear for my last being in town, and have so hardly mastered the ill effects of it, that I cannot yet think of returning. Pray present my humble service to him as one that perfectly partakes in all the good he does, and all the good he receives. And be sure that his taking the sacrament and oaths be not forgotten,†3 which I have known like to happen in a man of great business.
My service to Madam, J. F, and the rest of my friends, and my love to my wife. If you have leisure whilst in town pray spend an hour or two with J F upon the printing act,†4 or at least put him up in it.
When I was in town I desired my Christmas half-year annuity ... from my Lady Shaftesbury, but was told there would be no money
― 675 ―
till John Wheelock came to town, who was soon expected. Pray if he be come speak to him and my Lady of it, and get it if you can, and give my humble service to my Lady....
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Sir Francis, my Lady, Mrs. Cudworth ... present their service to you all.
Since the writing of this I received yours of the 2nd by the post, and thank you for both the one and the other. Pray tell me what you can learn of the affairs of Scotland. Mrs. Lockhart promised me a speech from thence, but Mrs. Cutts I hear has laid it up for me against next year. Pray get it if you can and send it to me. My service to them if you see them. I am very glad you came to town well and found all well. I hope you left all well, too, in the country. I have seen the verses on your mistress's visiting.... on the Thames and admire the heroism of the action, but am not poet enough to [criticise the] verses on it.†1
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke, Esq., Member of Parliament, at Mrs. Henman's, over against Little Turnstile in Holborn, London.
Frank.

1626. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 6 [May 1693] (1597, 1746)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 107. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, p. 294. Year from Locke's endorsement; month from postmark and contents.
London. the 6th
Mr Lock
I have stay'd now, this night, to the Utmost hower of the Post that I might give you, if I could, a positive assurance of my Coming by Tuesday's Coach.†2
― 676 ―
But having had no answer Yet from those whome I expected this night in town to End my buisness; and there being therefore, yet, no places taken; I cannot possibly Conclude as I would.
However that You may see what Concern I take in this affaire; I Resolve to Pronounce it now to you, that I will come; and Unless by a Messenger on purpose You hear on munday that something has made it impossible; Mr Popple and I shall be ready on Tuesday to be taken up by you where the Coach setts us down.
I have no time to say any thing farther. You will have no reason to remind mee more of my Word.†1 I am sure already I have acted beyond It. not onely an Extrordinary Regard and Service for You; But a Zeal somewhere elce inspires me to doe things beyond what I am onely oblig'd to by a Promise. Let that be the Cheif part of the Return you make mee; to Represent that Zeal as well as you think it deserves. and if you Let my Lady Masham know with what Respect I allways think of her; 't will be the way to make mee, if possible, with farther Obligation then I have,
your Sincere Freind and humble servant
A ASHLEY
If Sir Francis be at Oates I beg my very humble service.

1628. Locke to Edward Clarke, 15 May [1693] (1625, 1644)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 64. Printed in Rand, pp. 376-7. Year from Clarke's endorsement.
Oates 15° May
Dear Sir
The footing that our freind†1 must have to support himself and the expectation is of him must be in the character and reputation he must make him self in the minds of all men which noe station gives him soe fair an oportunity to doe as that which he is in both by the universal concernement it is of and the late management of it. If his attention and steady progresse be there directed to publique advantage and dispatch he will be invulnerable, hard to be removd or withstood and equally great in or out of that post. That credit of an†a unbiasedly prosecuteing†b and disintangleing right from intricacys and delays will have such charmes that I know not what it may not produce and be a rise to. I say not this that I at all doubt it will be otherwise, or that a man of soe much sense as well as integrity will subject himself to the goodwill or put himself into the power of those to whom his merit has made him not very acceptable by raiseing him without their consent or assistance: but I mention it to justifie what I writ to you in my last rather as an expression of my concerne and good will than that I thought there was any need of it. I am glad to finde by your letter of the 11 (if I mistake it <n>ot†c ) tha<t>†c he <too>k†c it soe. Perhaps I went†d a litle too far in comeing to any particulars, but that which I mentiond being but one litle thing that noe body could ever except against, but yet of that mighty influence (as I remember well) I could not forbear. Besides the desire I have to see you and Madam, my wife and all of you before you goe into the country I could be very glad I could have some discourse with you and our freind John†2 to debate farther of these matters whilst you are in town, for knowing we aim at the same things I would be glad we might consider and propose them togeather but I consider how few oportunitys your short time and the terme†3 is like to give us with
― 679 ―
him whilst you stay and how hard it is to bring fower ordinary people togeather who have more leisure each than I am sure two of these fower have;†1 and I know not whether what I have proposd already be not if not more, yet as much, as is fit to offer, till it be seen how far it is judgd that the world and present circumstances can bear soe much. The health I have here and the ill impressions it receives in London espetially whilst the weather holds at the rate it does, gives me noe incouragement to venture soe soon again unlesse something you judg worth it makes it adviseable and then you know how readily I always obey your summons
I am very glad to hear the Gent health you mention†2 is in a better state. Ease and air are the best things I know to which if he can but adde water I hope he would need noe physick. this perhaps will seem, as it is, hard: but health cannot be paid to dear for. I dare talk thus because I am sure I wish him as well as any body and soe pray give him my most humble service
Though I shall have use of it noe where soe much as in town, yet I think you were best send me hither Mr Passebons letter because I may possibly desire Mr Pawling to enquire out the person I am directed to before I come to town that I may prepare for the dispatch of that businesse before I come
If it fall not out that I see you and Madam, to whom pray give my service, before your journey I wish you all a very good journey into the country and all that you wish your self there. I thank you for your care of my affair with my Lady Shaftesbury and am
yours J LOCKE,
My service to J F very particularly and my love to my dear wife
Address: For Edward Clarke Esquire Member of Parliament at Mrs Henmans overagainst Litle turnstile in Holborn London
Frank
Postmark: MA 17

1629. William Thomas to Locke, 16 May 1693 (1495, 1677)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 138-9. For Thomas's voyage see pp. 585, 617.
Thomas joined the expedition of Sir Francis Wheeler (D.N.B., as Wheler) to the West Indies; it sailed from Portsmouth on 9 January and returned home on 18 October: Sir W. L. Clowes, The Royal Navy, 1897-1903, ii. 469-71.
Sir,
I cannot be so unmindfull of the many favours and obligations you have been pleased continually to lay upon me, as to neglect this opportunity of acquainting that I have hitherto escaped all the dangers of the sea, of warr and the Climate. I had indeed a verry violent feaver for 28 dayes, betwixt Madera and Barbados, when at last, contrary to all expectation the disease languished and Nature prov'd victorious, tho had I not strictly obcerved Dr Sydenham's method, I had undoubtedly sunk into that grave that many hundreds of our men have since fallen into. The Common method of this Country cure is first sweating, then vomiting and lastly bleeding, by which preposterous way of practice†a it comes to pass that not one in 6 of those that are taken, escapes death, which generally surprizes them in 48 hours. One might reasonbly thinke, that such success†1 should put them upon reflection, and so consequently on trying some other method that might prove less fatall: But I assure you Sir, it has a quite contrary effect, and they attribute the death of their Patients to the malignity of the disease, and not to their own ignorance in the cure. As for my own part, I have, where occasion has offered, run point blanc against this practise, for I first bled, then purg'd, and at night gave a large dose of Laudanum, and on the third day after the invasion the Patient was perfectly recovered. For†b- as Feavers-†b in these parts are generally more violent than in England, soe they are sooner cured, when due and proper means are applyed. Laudanum, which acts greater miracles in these Countryes, than in the more Northern, is allmost wholy unknown, and the use of it so generally abhor'd,†c that verry few here tho they see the wonderfull effects of it, will yett adventure on it, and choose rather to dye by the skill of their own Physicians
― 681 ―
than save their lives by so odious, and as they term it, dangerous a Medicine. This with ill dyet and lodging has been the reason that such numbers of our men have lost their lives in this expedition, and that the feaver and flux are grown more Epidemicall and mortall in our fleet and Army Than ever the plague was in London. As for my own part, I thanke God I can now brag of more health and flesh than I was ever Master of in England, and desighn to return by the Barbados fleet which will sail in less than 2 monthes. We have had a verry scurvy come of from Martinique†1 of which I will give you a more particular account when I return. Sir I desire you to present my humble service to my Lord Ashley, and to accept this testimony of respect and gratitude from your
most obliged humble servant
W THOMAS.
St Christophers 16th May 1693.
Address: These For Mr John Locke at Mr Pawlings in Dorsett-Court in Channell-rowe London.
Postmark: IY 5
Endorsed by Locke: W: Thomas 16° May 93
1630. William Popple to Locke, 18 May 1693 (1608, 1698) enclosing an account of a dream by Mrs. Popple
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 17, ff. 207-8, and c. 31, ff. 107-8. The enclosure is identifiable by its contents and by Locke's endorsement.
London. May: 18th. 1693.
Sir,
Since my return home I have much blamed my self for not propounding a Question in our Club at Oates that I now finde concerns very much my own Conduct. It is about the Behaviour of any person, who understands himself to lye under the Obligation of making acknowledgments for some extraordinary Favour or Honour received, and at the same time feels himself under an utter impossibility to express his true sense thereof. What shall such a one doe? I assure you the Club at London have been the last week, and are like to be tomorrow, taken up with matters
― 682 ―
that seem to me of less importance. The Dilemma lyes, in that all his Endeavours to comply with his Duty, coming short (as needs they must) of what he aimes at, they would serve in strictness onely to make his sense thereof seem less than indeed it is. Now I confess my self not able to resolve this Question without a Distinction. If the person that conferd the Honour do believe the Receiver competently worthy of it (which necessarily implies a grateful and generous minde) in that case I am inclined to believe that all strained acknowledgments are not onely needless, but would even be very burdensom to the person to whom they should be addressed. But in the other Case, if he that findes himself under this Difficulty, have not already a favourable Character of him established in the Other's minde, without any dependance on the manner of his discharging this Duty, truly I must determin such a one to be very unhappy: And if we were to debate again the point of man's relinquishing the Station in which Providence has placed him, I would desire to put this man's Circumstances amongst those Excepted Cases which, you remember, we found so hard to regulate. By this time I suppose you see the importance of the Question. But I hope you will be yet more sensible of it when I tell you that it is no Chimerical Moot-point: But that Adjecto Nomine, de me Fabula narratur.†1 Yes, Sir, this is one Consequence of the Visit in which you ingaged me. And therefore you must suffer me to press you to use your best Rethorick in perswading My Lady Masham to believe that I have in me some true Title to the first Distinction. If you prevail not, you see the Consequence. I will not therefore doubt of your Endeavours. But after all, the Solidity of her Judgment, uncapable to be imposed upon by any Rethorical Colours, if I were not a little sustained by the Poet's Murus aheneus,†2 would make me quit this subject (as I must, for fear of wearying you) in great Anxiety. Yet since I am faln upon talking of this Club, I'll ad another word that is not forrein to that subject. I think one of our last Conversations was about the power of imagination, in some hidden way of communicating thoughts; which I must confess I was not much convinced of. But at my return, the first thing my wife
― 683 ―
entertained me with was a Dream of hers, which has so much affinity with the general subject of our Discourse in the Country, that I can not chuse but send it you here inclosed: And I leave you to philosophise thereupon with my Lady, and examin how our Conversation there could influence my wife's Dreams here.
But if that proposition be foolery, I will recompense it, in the next place, by telling you that the Templers have desired the Minister who preached the bold Sermon that I told you of about Civil Liberty, to print it: And the Gentlemen of Lincoln's Inn have desired him to preach the same Sermon over again next Sunday in their Chappell. I hope this will please you. But humane affaires, you know, consist in a very od mixture. And to allay this pleasure, just whilst I was writing, I have received a visit from a very ingenious and worthy French Minister, who tells me of a little French Catechism that has been lately printed and given about in this City. It is intitled Le Catechisme des Pietistes. The Designe of it is to inculcate several free Principles, and is levy'd strongly against Priestcraft. This being spread abroad, complaint was made of it to the Bishop of London, who thereupon sent for Monsieur Graviset,†1 the supposed Author, and asked if he had writ that Catechisme. Mr Gr: owned the writing of it, but denyed his having given it to be printed. The first was enough. The thing was called Socinianism: And he was told that our Toleration dos not extend to Doctrins of that nature.†2 In the End (I know not by what Authority) he was ordered to be committed to Newgate; but found Bail; and so is at Liberty. And the Judge or Justice that should have committed him, reproved his Accusers as much as the Bishop had blamed him. After all, neither the Man nor the Thing are much commended, but the Subject is like to produce a great ferment. I have onely further to beg of you to acquaint My Lady Masham that the History of the Quakers first Rise†3 is not yet don; But that I will send
― 684 ―
her the little Essay about an European Diet,†1 through Mr Churchill's hands, together with some of your Proofs.†2 I hope you will oblige me also in presenting my most humble service to Sir Francis and to her Ladyship, and the like to Mrs Masham and your young Philosopher.†3 I am
Sir,
Your most humble Servant
W P.
Your letter for Holland was carefully sent forwards.
My Lord A.†4 also desires me to present his due Respects to all the Family.
Endorsed by Locke: W. Popple 18° May 93
[The enclosure; written by Mrs. Popple:]
I thought I was in such a Church as the Temple Church is, and that I was in the midle Ile, in a Pew on the left hand: And the Pulpit stood as in the Temple, where a minister was preaching. And I <thought>,†a even whilst he was preaching, that I saw on the right hand of the Ally, in a pew, a man rise up, in plain, but decent, apparil; who spoak of plain inteligible things, adressing himself to me; and straight I knew him to be, A Philosopher, such a one as mr L. Lord A: Mr Fr: Ben: Fur:†5 in fine one that would preach Morality, Truth, and reason. Immediately stood up another, then a third, and a fourth; all of the same sentiments. All to confirm what the other had undertook to demonstrate. In soe much that I begun to look a bout, to see if their speaking had not caused any disturbance, and to see how the minister took it. I thought he stood a little while still, and the people gave no disturbance. When the Minister had stood a little while silent, he went down, puld of his Gown and Wigg, and came up again into the Pulpit in a very dispicable dress: in a White wascoat†6 without sleeves, and a napking about his head, for a Cap, like a Cook, or a Bakers man; and
― 685 ―
soe despicable he was that none regarded him, nor did he speake. But the others I thought kept to their point, and went on teaching plain Truths, back't with strong Reason. Not soe much teaching as speaking their own sentiments, which I aqueesed with; being extreamly pleased, I waked.
Endorsed by Locke: Ps Dream May 93

1635. Locke to Philippus van Limborch, 3 June 1693 (1601, 1640)

London 3° Jun 93
Vir Spectatissime
Jam diu tibi destinaveram verbosam et grandem epistolam sed hoc inter ruris otia, nunc evocatum in urbem negotiorum vis aut certe aliquid negotiis simile ita occupatum detinet ut vix salutandi tempus conceditur. Scripsi ad te præteritâ hieme, et una inclusas misi Archiepiscopi ad Te literas, ex quo tempore ne verbum quidem a Te accepi. An Tuæ an meæ interciderint literæ ignoro: hoc
― 688 ―
certum est me tam diuturnum ægre ferre silentium etsi de amicitia tua securus. Scribas igitur rogo quam primum ut vales ut memor nostri, moneas insuper an acceperis conciones Anglicas ab Archiepiscopo mihi traditas tibi mittendas. Hæc raptim ne Sibelio ad vos profiscenti nihil ad Te tradam. Vale Vir Optime et ut facis perge me amare tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
Salutes quæso meo nomine optimam tuam fæminam liberosque Tuos.
(Latin)
London 3 Jun 93
Esteemed Sir,
I had long since designed a big long-winded letter for you; but this in the leisure of the country; now, called to town, the compulsion of affairs, or at least something like affairs, keeps me so busy that time to send you a greeting is scarcely allowed me. I wrote to you last winter, enclosing in my letter one from the Archbishop to you, since when I have had not even a word from you. I do not know whether your letter or mine has been lost; [p. 688] this much is certain, that I am distressed by so lengthy a silence though I am assured of your friendship. Please therefore write as soon as possible how you are, how mindful of me, and moreover let me know whether you have received the English sermons delivered to me by the Archbishop to send to you. This much in haste, lest I should deliver nothing for you to Sibelius, who is setting out for your country. Good-bye, best of men, and continue to love me as is your wont
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
Please give my best wishes to your excellent wife and children.

Monsieur,
Il y a longtemps que je vous doibs une lettre de remerciement pour le present du livre de Monsieur Boile touchant l'air que Monsieur furly m'a envoyé de vostre part, et ou je trouve plusieurs de vos remarques qui en augmentent l'estime quon en doibt faire. Monsieur le clerc nous dit quelque fois quil a receu de vos lettres et que vous avez la bonté de vous souvenir de nous, dont nous vous sommes fort redevables, et si vous pouviez derober au temps un moment pour nous escrire ce nous seroit une grande joye et beaucoup plus que vous ne croyez. ma femme entre autre se plaint souvent que vous nous escrivez si rarement et voudroit que je
― 689 ―
vous importunasse plus souvent des miennes. ce que je ferois volontier si elles avoient quelques poids et vous pouvoient porter quelque service; bien loin de cela il faut que je vous importune pour vous demander vostre conseil. mon propre pere et moy aurions bien envie de mettre quatre cent livres sterrlingh a l'exequer pour avoir une rente de corps sur deux de mes neveux et mes deux enfans. on nous dit bien icy que <cel>a†a est fort sur et nous connoissons plusieurs <de nos am>is†a qui y ont†a de faire recevoir les rentes a londres par un cousin jarmin†b de mes neveux. on nous dit que la rente est a quatorze pour cent. mais nous navons rien voulu conclure sans vostre sage advis, aquoy nous attendrons jusqua vostre responce.†1 vous pouvez juger Monsieur si nos enfans se portent bien puisque nous nous disposons a risquer de l'argent sur leur vie. ma femme est aussi mediocrement, et vous assure de ses tres humble respects, et moy je suis comme je le doibs,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON
Amsterd. ce 16 jun. 1693.

1637. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 6/16 June 1693 (1623, 1641)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 70-1. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 64-5.
A Amsterdam le 16 de Juin 1693.
Je vous ai bien de l'obligation, Monsieur, de la peine que vous vous êtes donnée de proposer mon dessein à Mylord de Pembroke, et de le lui faire agréer. Je voudrois bien vous en temoigner ma
― 690 ―
reconnoissance, par quelque service réel, plûtôt que par des paroles. La Dédicace roule sur vos instructions, comme vous le verrez. J'envoiai Samedi passé 13. du Mois une cassete à Mr. Furly, où est renfermé un exemplaire relié, et les feuilles qui manquent aux deux que je vous avois envoiez ci-devant.†1 Je l'ai prié de l'envoier par le Paket-boat, parce qu'on m'a assuré que le Lord Privyseal ne paioit point de port.†2 Si vous êtiez à Londres, quand il arrivera, je vous prierois de le lui offrir. Sinon on aura soin de le porter dans l'hôtel de Mylord Privyseal. Il ne se passe rien ici de nouveau, pour ce qui regarde les Lettres. On imprime les Oraisons de Ciceron par M. Grævius,†3 et l'on va mettre sous la presse les Oeuvres de G. J. Vossius, en plusieurs volumes in folio.†4 Tout cela ira lentement. Les armées du Roi Guillaume et du Roi de France sont très-proches l'une de l'autre, depuis quelques jours. Le bruit court que le Roi de France s'en est retourné, mais il n'y a pas d'apparence. Dieu veuille gouverner le tout, pour la liberté et pour la paix.
J'ai donné ordre au Sieur Samuel Smith Libraire de Londres, à qui j'envoie cent exemplaires en commission, de vous en donner si vous lui en demandiez;†5 dans la pensée que j'aie euë que peutêtre vous jugeriez que j'en devrois donner à quelques uns, outre ceux que je lui ai marquez, savoir, Mylord de Cantorbery et Mylord de Salisbury. Je me fie parfaitement dans l'amitié, que vous me faites l'honneur de me témoigner, et tout ce que vous ferez sera très bien fait. J'ai changé le prix, parce qu'ici le donnant à meilleur marché, il n'est pas juste qu'en Angleterre il coûte plus cher. Le prix est de 3 francs 15 sols par exemplaire, ce qui fait environ sept shelings, si je ne me trompe.†6 On m'a conseillé de le faire, pour le prompt débit, et parce qu'il faut que je suive l'usage de Hollande. Le Sieur Smith passe ici pour un honête homme et fidele dans le commerce, et je n'en envoie qu'à lui, pour le commencement. Il peut trouver son compte à la commission, et s'il en veut acheter, je lui pourrai faire meilleur marché, comme je le lui écris. Lors que vous aurez eu le loisir de parcourir mon Ouvrage, vous m'obligerez infiment de m'en dire vôtre sentiment, avec une liberté philosophique, que j'aime beaucoup mieux que des loüanges. Je suis,
― 691 ―
Monsieur, de tout mon coeur Vôtre très-humble et tres obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.

Ever since yours of the 14/24 April, I have been grievously afflicted with a Cough. I write this by the Baron V. Helmont, by whom I intended to have sent My Arent to Joseph wright, and to have intreated your advice, and direction about his education; he is a lovely and sharp lad, and of a pleasant conversation. My Nephew John Furly was lately here, and perswaded me to let him go with him, but when he should go, came news that 5 capers waylayd the packet,†1 and so I was not willing to hazard him. I was to blame that I tooke not a copy of it when I had it.†3 I am leaving the Town to go to lye at school at Noortwyck with my children to get rid of, business, and my cough, which makes me so faint that I cannot write, salute all my friends. 1640. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 16/26 June 1693 (1635, 1646)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 77-8. Answers no. 1635.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Tuas gratissimas per Sibelium accepi: Ipse me non vidit, quia festinans urbem transiit, literis tuis in manibus D. Guenelloni relictis. Summâ cum admiratione in tuis legi, literas meas, quas jam ante tres menses dedi, ad tuas non pervenisse manus. Ego tuas cum
― 693 ―
inclusis D. Archiepiscopi recte accepi mense Februario: quoniam vero librum a D. Archiepiscopo mihi missum exspectabam, responsum meum tribus aut quatuor hebdomadibus distuli, ut et Gratiæ suæ pro dono illo quas debebam grates agerem. Verum cum frustra exspectarem, ad te rescripsi, et satis copiose; monui etiam, Archiepiscopi librum nondum huc appulisse: quin et hactenus non appulit. Laersius a bibliopola Londinensi†1 catalogum accepit librorum, quos ille jam a duobus mensibus nautæ in Hollandiam abituro concredidit: ille catalogus mentionem facit libri hujus hisce verbis: a little pakket for Mr. Limbourg. Quamprimum appulerit, mihique traditus fuerit, D. Archiepiscopo gratias agam. Interim Tibi maximas ago gratias, quod virum tantum mihi conciliaveris, cujus judicio contra aliorum iniqua judicia, si forte illis petar, tutus ero. Literas accepi ab Episcopis Salisburiensi, et Bathoniensi ac Wellensi: utrasque benevolentissimas:†2 et nuperrime a D. Spencero,†3 qui se audivisse ait, plures sibi Germaniam et Galliam excitasse adversarios, quorum tamen libros hactenus a se neutiquam visos dolet. Ego statui omnium ad ipsum catalogum
― 694 ―
mittere; et si eo conspecto ipsos libros videre cupiat, omnes mittam. Sed virum doctissimum plerosque cum nauseâ lecturum credo: Ex præconceptis opinionibus, tanquam principiis indubitatis, argumentari solent, pro more suo. D. Clerico tuas tradidi: ille se nuperrime Tibi respondisse ait, nullusque dubitat, quin responsum suum jam acceperis. Literas quas mihi prolixas meditatus es, avide exspecto; quo prolixiores eò gratiores erunt.†1 Ad finem jam pervenit liber D. Clerici in Genesin; utinam eodem pede reliqua absolvat! opus hoc foret omnibus solidioris eruditionis amatoribus longe gratissimum ac utilissimum. Acta Lipsiensia hujus anni, nisi solius Januarii, hactenus non vidi. in Actis Januarii indicant Historiam meam Inquisitionis prodiisse:†2 Quale ipsorum de ea sit futurum judicium videre desidero: non quod id magni faciam; sed ut cognoscam, quid de liberiore meo stylo, quo quorundam, qui in maximâ sunt veneratione, patrum actiones ac doctrinam ingenue reprehendo, sentiant. Non displicuit mea παῤῥησία Reverendissimo Episcopo Bathoniensi, qui paucis ad me rescripsit, Agis strenue causam Christi. Verum hi Germani, uti plerique alii solent, strenue agunt causam suam: quare quodcunque illi adversatur
― 695 ―
non possunt non improbare. D. Voldero, non diu post editam meam historiam aderat cum aliis Triglandius Professor.†1 Vidit historiam meam, eaque leviter inspectâ rogat eum Volderus, an eam viderit ac legerit. alter negat; additque: Homines hi credunt se anno hujus sæculi decimo octavo læsos,†2 ideoque istud tempestive intempestive inculcare ac repetere solent. Volderus respondit, nihil horum, imo ne unum quidem verbum, exstare in tota hac historia; nisi fortasse existimet, lectores, qui hic processus Inquisitionis graphice depictos conspiciunt, credituros gesta anni decimi octavi hisce per omnia esse similia, atque eâ ratione gesta hæc libro hoc condemnari. Multi ex Contraremonstrantibus eam emunt ac legunt: hactenus tamen non audivi judicia minus benigna. Pontificiorum ulcera detegi gaudent. Interim quod aliis dictum est, et sibi dictum credant. Ego persecutionem detestor, non quia Pontificia, sed quia Religionis Christianæ genio est adversa. Sive itaque eam Roma instituat, sive Geneva, æque mihi damnatur. Habes denuo verbosam epistolam: eam tamen, etsi prolixitate peccet, mittere malo, quam nullam. Salveat a me
― 696 ―
officiosissime D. Cudwortha. Uxor liberique mei plurimam Tibi dicunt salutem, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have received your very welcome letter by Sibelius; he did not see me himself, as he passed through the city in haste, leaving your letter in Mr. Guenellon's hands. I read in it with the greatest surprise that my letter, which I dispatched now three months ago, had not come to your hands. [p. 693] I duly received yours in February with that from the Lord Archbishop enclosed; but as I was waiting for the book sent me by the Lord Archbishop I put off my reply for three or four weeks, so that I might also thank his Grace as I ought for that gift. As I waited in vain, however, I replied to you, and at some length; I told you, too, that the Archbishop's book had not yet arrived here; in fact it has not so far arrived. Leers has received from the London bookseller†1 a list of the books which he entrusted two months ago to a mariner who was about to depart for Holland; that list mentions this book in these words: 'a little pakket for Mr. Limbourg'. As soon as it arrives and is delivered to me I shall thank the Lord Archbishop. Meanwhile I thank you most heartily for having procured me the favour of so great a man, by whose judgement I shall be safeguarded against the unfair judgements of others, if perchance I am assailed by them. I have received letters from the bishops of Salisbury and of Bath and Wells, both most kindly;†2 also one quite recently from Mr. Spencer,†3 who says he has heard that Germany and France have aroused several adversaries against him; he regrets, however, that so far he has not seen any of their books. I have decided to send him a list of them [p. 694] all; and if after looking through that he wants to see the books themselves I shall send them all. But I believe that that learned man would read most of them with nausea. According to their wont they usually argue from previously adopted opinions as if they were undoubted principles. I delivered your letter to Mr. Le Clerc; he says that he replied to you very recently and does not doubt that you have received his reply by now. I am eagerly awaiting the lengthy letter you have been considering for me; the lengthier the more acceptable it will be.†1 Mr. Le Clerc's book on Genesis is now finished; would that he may complete the rest as he has begun! this work would be most welcome and most useful to all lovers of sounder learning. I have not so far seen the Leipzig Acta for this year except only for January. In the January Acta they announce that my Historia Inquisitionis has appeared.†2 I want to see what sort of judgement of it theirs will be; not that I have great regard for it but in order that I may learn what they feel about my somewhat free style in which I frankly find fault with the actions and teaching of some of the most venerated Fathers. My freedom of speech did not displease the Right Reverend the bishop of Bath, who wrote back to me briefly, 'You plead Christ's cause stoutly.' But these Germans, as is the way with most others, plead their own cause stoutly; hence they cannot but disallow anything that [p. 695] runs counter to it. Not long after the publication of my Historia Professor Trigland†1 among others was in company with Mr. de Volder. He saw my Historia and after he had looked at it a little de Volder asks him whether he has seen and read it. He says no, and adds, 'These men believe that they were wronged in the year '18 of this century,†2 and therefore are wont to insist on it and repeat it in season and out of season.' De Volder replies that nothing of that, not so much as a single word, is to be found in this whole Historia, unless perhaps he supposes that readers who see here the proceedings of the Inquisition painted to the life will believe that the acts of the year '18 are similar to them in all respects, and for that reason these acts are condemned in this book. Many of the Contraremonstrants are buying and reading it; so far however I have not heard any unfavourable opinions. They are glad that the Romanists' sores are uncovered. Meanwhile let them believe that what is said to others is said to themselves also. I detest persecution, not because it is Popish, but because it is contrary to the spirit of the Christian religion; so, whether Rome or Geneva sets it up, for me it is alike condemned. Here you have yet another long-winded epistle; nevertheless, though it may transgress by its length, I prefer to send it rather than none. [p. 696] Please give my respectful greetings to Mrs. Cudworth. My wife and children send you their best wishes, as do I most particularly
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 26 June

1641. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 27 June/7 July 1693 (1637, 1653)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 72-3. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 65-7.
A Amsterdam le 7 de Juillet 1693.
Je suis confus, Monsieur, de toutes les peines, que vous prenez pour moi, et du soin que vous avez de mes interêts. Vôtre Lettre m'a fait un extrême plaisir, en ce qu'elle m'a appris que mes livres étoient arrivez en Angleterre, lors que je commençois à en être en peine. Dieu soit loüé, de ce qu'ils sont en sureté! Le Sieur Smith ne m'a point encore écrit, mais peutêtre qu'il me répondra l'ordinaire prochain.†1 Je lui ai écrit de donner, ou d'envoier un exemplaire de ma Genese à ceux dont vous, et Mr. Cappel†2 lui donneriez les noms, et [[Sic]] es leur mettre seulement aux prix auquel je les lui mets à lui même, savoir trois-francs 15s monoie de Hollande, ce qui est un assez bas prix. Je n'ai pas dessein de me
― 697 ―
fatiguer ni moi, ni mes amis à chercher des subscrybers pour le reste, si ce Tome se vend bien. C'est un embarras grand et assez inutile, à moins que d'en avoir grand nombre, ce qui ne peut être sans peine. Le premier Volume s'etant bien vendu, le reste ira de soi même. J'ai crû devoir l'essaier pour le premier, afin de faire connoître l'ouvrage, et afin que l'on sût qu'il alloit paroître.
Vous m'obligerez infiniment de me communiquer vos remarques, dont je ne manquerai pas de profiter dans la suite. Ces sortes d'ouvrages sont pleins d'une si grande varieté de choses, qu'il est impossible de les digerer toutes également, et qu'il ne s'y glisse même des fautes considerables. Peutêtre que vous trouverez quelques contradictions entre la Paraphrase et le Commentaire, dans quelques endroits, où je ne pourrois pas dire tout ce que je pense propter metum Judæorum.†1 J'ai voulu en quelque sorte me satisfaire moi même et les autres. Il y en a un exemple dans le XLIX Ch. où il est parlé du Schilo.†2 Je serois ravi d'apprendre de vous de quelle maniere MyLord de Pembroke recevra ma dédicace, mais je serois fâché si le sejour, qu'il vous faudroit faire dans Londres, incommodoit vos poumons. J'aimerois mieux vous savoir en bonne santé à la campagne, que malade dans Londres. Le†a- Ciceron, ou plûtôt les Harangues de Ciceron qui s'impriment ici, sont de même que les quatre Tomes des Epîtres qui ont paru.†3 Mr. Grævius a plus de soin de donner le texte correct sur les MSS. et les conjectures des Savans, que de le rendre intelligible à ceux qui ne sont pas versez dans les Antiquitez Romaines. Ce sont des notes, qui sont presque toutes de cette Critique, qui regarde la pureté du Texte, mais qui n'ouvre point le chemin qu'il faut tenir, pour trouver la solution des difficultez.-†a Il y aura, pour les seules Harangues, trois gros volumes in 8°. et qui seront assez chers. A moins que d'avoir déja le reste, je ne croi pas qu'il y ait de l'avantage à acheter ces Volumes. Cette Edition de toutes les Oeuvres de Ciceron ne s'achevera peutêtre jamais; puis qu'il y doit avoir quinze ou seize volumes, dont il n'y <a>†b que cinq d'imprimez, sans compter les Harangues, qui ne paroîtront que l'année prochaine;
― 698 ―
et que M. Grævius est déja assez vieux,†1 et lent en tout ce qu'il fait. Mr. Limbourg vous baise les mains, et a été bien aise d'apprendre que vous avez reçu sa derniere lettre. Il n'y a pas longtemps qu'il a reçu le livre de Mylord de Cantorbery.†2 Quand j'aurai le loisir je le lirai, quoi que j'aie un violent préjugé contre touts les livres de cette nature, où l'on dispute sans poser l'état de la question, ni distinguer les degrez des démonstrations dont on se sert. On m'a dit qu'il y avoit une suite au livre intitulé Gentlemans Religion, que je serois ravi de voir.†3 La premiére fois, que vous me ferez l'honneur de m'écrire, marquez moi jusqu'où vous avez de la Bibliotheque Universelle. Je l'avois écrit, à dessein de continuer à vous envoier le reste, mais je ne saurois le retrouver présentement. Dès que vous m'aurez marqué le dernier Volume, j'aurai soin de vous envoier les autres. Je suis, Monsieur, de tout mon coeur Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in Dorset Court in Channel row Westminster.
Postmark: IV 30
