1643. Locke to William Molyneux, 15 July 1693 (1622, 1652)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 47-9. Acknowledges no. 1622; answered by no. 1652.
London, 15. July. 1693.
Sir,
I had not been so long before I had acknowledg'd the favour of your last, had not I a design to give you at large an account of some alterations I intended to make in the chapter of Power, wherein I should have been very glad you had shewn me any mistake. I myself, not being very well satisfied, by the conclusion I was lead to, that my reasonings were perfectly right, review'd that chapter again with great care, and by observing only the mistake of one word (viz. having put things for actions, which was very easy to be done in the place where it is, viz. p. 123. as I remember,†1 for I have not my book by me here in town) I got into a new view of things, which, if I mistake not, will satisfie you, and give a clearer account of humane freedom than hitherto I have done, as you will perceive by these summaries of the following sections of that chapter:
§ 28. Volition is the ordering of some action by thought.
§ 29. Uneasiness determines the will.
§ 30. Will must be distinguish'd from desire.
§ 31. The greater good in view barely consider'd determines not the will. The joys of heaven are often neglected.
§ 32. Desire determines the will.
§ 33. Desire is an uneasiness.
§ 34. The greatest present uneasiness usually determines the will, as is evident in experience. The reasons,
§ 35. Because uneasiness being a part of unhappiness which is first to be removed in our way to happiness.
§ 36. Because uneasiness alone is present.
― 701 ―
§ 37. The uneasiness of other passions have their share with desire.
§ 38. Happiness alone moves the desire.
§ 39. All absent good not desired, because not necessary to our happiness.
§ 40. The greatest uneasiness does not always determine the will, because we can suspend the execution of our desires.†1
This short scheme may perhaps give you so much light into my present hypothesis, that you will be able to judge of the truth of it, which I beg you to examine by your own mind. I wish you were so near that I could communicate it to you at large, before it goes to the press. But it is so much too long for a letter, and the press will be so ready to stay for it before it is finished, that I fear I shall not be able to have the advantage of your thoughts upon the whole thread of my deduction. For I had much rather have your corrections, whilst they might contribute to make it receive your approbation, than flatter my self before hand that you will be pleased with it.
I hope, e're this, you have received from Mr. that which I promis'd you the beginning of this spring.†2 I must desire your opinion of it without reserve, for I should not have ventur'd, upon any other condition, to have own'd and presented to you such a trifle. I am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.

1645. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 25 July/4 August 1693 (1636, 1648)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 55-6.
Monsieur
Nous avions chargé de nos lettres un cousin de Monsieur Daranda qui malheureusement s'est rencontré dans le packetboot que les francois ont coulé a fond, et qui est du nombre des sousmergez. je vous marquois que Monsieur Sibelius estoit bien arrivé icy, et quil nous avoit delivré vos presents. Ma femme toute confuse des honnestetez que vous luy faitte y avoit joint son compliment. mon fils vous y faisoit une profonde reverence pour l'honneur quil recoit de vostre souvenir. pour moy Monsieur, je ne pouvois pas m'attendre au present que vous me faitte puisque j'avois desja receu de vostre part par la voye de Monsieur Furley le mesme livre, comme je vous le marque dans ma precedente, de sorte Monsieur que vous pouvez encore disposer d'un des deux en faveur de quil vous plaira. un de mes neveux fils de ma seur se prepare pour faire un tour en vos quartiers a l'occasion de son negoce. il ne manquera pas de vous aller saluer de nostre part, et ma femme qui est fort paresseuse a escrire diffaire de vous renouveller ses respects et remerciements jusqu'a son depart qui sera au premier convoy, pour eviter les risques du packetboot. les tristes nouvelles qui nous
― 703 ―
viennent de toutes parts, et particulierement le malheureux et rude choc que nous venons de recevoir au pays bas avec un tres grand risque pour la vie de sa Majesté, desole icy tout le monde, et nous met comme hors despoir que nous sortirons jamais heureusement de cette fatale guerre, qui semble vouloir abysmer toute l'europe.†1 cela nous arreste aussi pour le dessein que nous avions d'engager l'argent dont je vous ay parlé. enfin Monsieur tout n'est qu'affliction et misere, et il ny a icy presque plus aucun moyen de faire valoir son bien sur le pays, ou il n'est pas sans risque et ne rend pas deux pour cent. Ma femme, et mon fils pierot vous presentent leur treshumbles respects; forts sensibles et reconnoissants des presents dont il vous a plus les honnorer. et pour mon particulier je suis comme je le doibs,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
d'Amsterd. ce 4 aoust. 1693

1646. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 25 July/4 August 1693 (1640, 1668)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 79-80. The letter was carried by Toland (p. 705, n. 1). He sailed from Holland about 10/20 August: p. 710, n. 5. He delivered the letter when visiting Locke at Oates; this may have been not long before Locke's answer, 13 January 1694 (no. 1692).
(English) Vir Amplissime
Jam diu literas tuas exspecto, quas Te meditari literis ad D. Clericum significasti. Non dubito de propensissima tuâ erga me voluntate: quare ne quid sequius tibi contigerit, aut cum valetudine
― 704 ―
minus læta conflicteris, male metuo. Tu mihi quantocyus scrupulum hunc eximes. De variis antehac ad Te scripsi, quorum jam vix recordor. Verum literis quibusdam meis (an illis quæ interciderunt dubito) mentionem feci novæ editionis Bibliorum Castellionis, quam hic quidam bibliopolæ meditantur.†1 Characterem mihi ostenderunt eximium; omnes notas adjicere, quin et defensionem suarum translationum, nec non descriptionem Reip. Judaicæ ex Josepho concinnatam subjicere ad operis calcem, decreverunt; ut ita omnia quæ Castellio in Scripturam commentatus est, hoc in volumine conjuncta prodeant. Rogarunt me, ut præfationem addam: quod non abnui. Antequam vero opus, quod sine magnis sumptibus perfici nequit, aggrediantur, per te doceri cupiunt, an existimes hoc opus in Anglia gratum fore, et emptores reperturum. Nam in ejusmodi operum editione solent bibliopolæ nostrates vel maxime Angliam respicere. Lator harum Hibernus est, juvenis sane egregius
― 705 ―
et non indoctus,†1 qui hinc abiturus in Angliam literas ad Te flagitavit, fideliter perferendas. Si forte eum convenias experieris liberalem, ingenuum, ac indolis minime servilis. Conciones Reverendissimi Archiepiscopi tandem nactus sum; video stylum esse valde perspicuum, quod in ejusmodi materia rarum est. Plura adderem, verum qui hasce deferet mox adfuturus est. Credideram post octiduum demum profecturum; nunc subito me monuit se hodie abiturum. Omnes amici nostri hactenus bene valent. Utinam idem de patriæ nostræ statu, quæ nunc cum adversa fortunâ conflictatur, dicere liceat!†2 Dabit, spero, Deus his quoque finem.†3 Uxor ac liberi quam amantissime Te salutant. D. Cudwortham officiosissime verbis meis salutabis.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami prid. Non. Augusti
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have waited a long while now for the letter you are considering, as you intimated in your letter to Mr. Le Clerc. I am in no doubt about your very great affection for me; consequently I am much afraid that something [p. 704] rather unfortunate may have happened to you, or that you may be contending with ill health. Please deliver me from this anxiety as quickly as possible. I wrote to you formerly about various matters, which I can now hardly call to mind. But in some letter of mine (perhaps that which was lost) I mentioned a new edition of Castellion's Bible, which certain booksellers here are considering.†1 They have shown me the distinguished type; they have decided to add all his notes and even his defence of his translations, and further to subjoin at the end of the work his description of the Jewish state, put together from Josephus; so that all that Castellion wrote on Scripture will appear together in this volume. They have asked me to add a preface and I have not refused. But before they set about the work, which cannot be carried out without great expenses, they wish to learn through you whether you think that this work would be welcome in England and would find purchasers; for with the publication of works of this kind our booksellers are accustomed to look chiefly to England. The bearer of this is an Irishman, [p. 705] an excellent and not unlearned young man,†1 who, being about to leave here for England, has solicited a letter to you, to be faithfully conveyed. If perchance you meet him you will find him frank, gentlemanly, and not at all of a servile character. I have at last got the sermons of the Most Reverend the Archbishop; I see that the style is very clear, which is rare in matter of that kind. I would have added more, but the man who is to carry this letter will soon be present. I believed that he would start only a week hence; now he has suddenly warned me that he is leaving today. All our friends are in good health until now. Would that one could say the same about the condition of our country, which is now contending with adverse fortune.†2 God will, I hope, grant an end to these things also.†3 My wife and children send you their most affectionate greetings. Please convey my dutiful respects to Mrs. Cudworth.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 4 August 1693

1647. Edward Clarke to Locke, 2 August 1693 (1644, 1660)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 78. Printed in Rand, pp. 378-9.
Chipley August the 2d. 1693.
Deare Sir,
your kind Letter of the 24th. came but last night to mee, but was verie welcome, bringing mee that which I most earnestly desiered, the Intelligence of your good health, which, I pray God to preserve for your own sake, as well as for the greate Benifitt and Advantage that all your Freinds, and the whole Nation will receive by it; Your Labours for the Publique are a Blessing to us all, and the Particular Honour you have done mee in the Publication of your thoughts concerning Education, is never to bee suffitiently Acknowlidged; But haveing Return'd you my particular thankes upon that occasion in the last Letter I writt to you, I shall trouble you noe further on that subject at present; But begg leave to interrupt the Reviseing your Learned Essay touching humane understanding, which prevayles wonderfully amongst all the men of any sence and understanding that I converse with, with Acquainting you That I thinke my Wife is Breeding againe, I hope of another Boy, her Leggs often swell much, and shee has sometimes frequently the same payn on the lower part of the Right side of her Belly that wee have both formerly complayned to you of, and shee often makes that thick sort of water that you have heretofore seen; Shee is I Blesse God otherwise in perfect health, shee eates, drinks, sleepes, and Lookes well, but I would gladly know your thoughts upon the whole matter, whither Adviseable to drinke the Bathwater, if shee bee desierouse of it, whilst shee is with Child, or what else you thinke proper; I hope you will pardon the Freedome I take with you, and accept the humble services of us all here, particularly of your Wife, and beleive that noe man can be more intirely and affectionately
your freind and servant
then, EDW: CLARKE
Pray make all our services Acceptable to Sir Francis and my Lady, and all the rest of that Family, and the Good Neighbourhood etc.
I just now understand that my Wife hath this day written to you, I desire therefore you will take noe notice in your Answere to her,
― 707 ―
of my haveing Written to you at all on that subject, for shee knows nothing of what I have writt, and perhapps I shall incurr her Displeasure by medling; Shee is full of vapours as usuall when with Child, and soe the more difficult to bee pleased or satisfied, sometimes shee seemes to bee willing to goe to Bath, at other times that shee cannot bee content or satisfied to leave her Children here, and frequently askes if the Bath Waters may not bee dranke here at home with good successe, soe that I know not how to behave my selfe better, then to bee willing to goe thither, or to send for the Waters home as shall bee most adviseable, and shee shall bee most inclyn'd, beleiveing that if shee could bee content and quiet in her own mind, That would bee the best Physick to Her, and the greatest satisfaction to mee and all about Her, Pray write fully to Her, and perswade Her to bee a Philosopher if possible; and that shee may not suspect my haveing written to you, pray complayn a little of my Silence towards you, and forgive mee that I am thus troublesome to my Best Freind, and say nothing to mee in any Letter of yours touching Her, least it should happen to fall into Her handes:
Address: These, For Mr. John Lock at Oates, To bee left with Mr. Joselyn a Shopkeeper in, Bishops-startford Essex:

1650. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 9/19 August 1693 (1638, 1672)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 108-9.
Rotterdam 19 August 1693
Dear Friend
I have yours of the 13 past, with the 4 books, and 3 of them, as desired, I sent to monsieur Le Clerc, as, I doubt not, he will have informd you,†1 I return my hearty thanks for the same, and have made a present of it to a person for whom I have, a more than ordinary, love and respect,†2 as I doubt not but the Baron†3 has informd you; I have wrote for 4 more to Joseph wright to supply myself and some other friends.
I am heartily sorry for the delay in the book for my Lord Pembrooke, which could not be got into England by the packet, by reason of the great strictness of the Captains, who will take nothing: in so much, that by the great Authority of Monsieur Vander Poel the General Postmaster there,†4 I could not get it passed that way; but received it back again yesterday, and have given it to the bearer hereof mr. John Toland, who has a letter to you from monsieur Le clerc.†5 I find him to be a free spirited ingenious man; that quitted the Papacy in Jameses time when al men, of no principles were looking towards it, and having once cast off the yoak
― 711 ―
of Spirituall Authority, that great bugbear, and bane of ingenuity, he could never be perswaded to bow his neck to that yoak again, by whom soever claymed; this has rendred it somewhat difficult to him, to find a way of subsistence in the world, and made him ask my counsell in the case: I told him I know no way for him, but to find out some free ingenuous English Gentleman that might have occasion for a Tutor in his family, who would be as glad of the opportunity as himself, were my circumstances such, that I could entertain him, and he willing to abide with me, he should not be put to the trouble to seek further. But that being not so, I intreat you, Sir, to be assistant to him, wherein you can; not for my sake, but for his own worth; he knows you to be the Author of that smal book,†1 by mr. L. Clerc. For while I was telling mr. Spademan,†2 who brought him to me, that I had received such a book from England, he said mr L. Cl. told him it was yours.
my Cough continues, but I hope is going, and I am going to school to my children till kermis time,†3 that I shal bring them home for a while.
Could my chain extend to Oates, I should be very ready to pay that worthy family and your self therein, a visit, till you were weary of my Company; pray meane while pay my humble service to Sir Fr. and my Lady from
Dear Friend
your humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY

B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 217.

Sir
I had not seen the Book the Earl of Pemb: sent but presumed it had been tyed up in paper, but I find it was sent loose; with a black
― 712 ―
lead pen this is written over it For Mr Locke, the Book hath no other dedication, neither is there a preface to it. It is Commentarius in Genesin and reaches but to the 17 Chapter and 11 ver: and breaks off in the middle of a sentence with—quae omnia quidem facile admi- so that it is but part of a book.†1

I hope I shalbe able to hold out then well enough till my money comes in, which, as I said to you, I hope to have about the next term,†5 it may be sooner. I am troubled that I am forced to be so troublesome to you but I hope you will pardon
Sir
Your humble Servant

1652. William Molyneux to Locke, 12 August 1693 (1643, 1655)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 49-56. Answers no. 1643; answered by no. 1655.
Dublin. Aug. 12. 1693.
Sir
Yours of July. 15th. came to my hands about a fortnight since; and I had, ere this, acknowledged the Favour thereof; but that I waited the Arrival of your much desired Peice, OF EDUCATION. which came not to me till about three days ago. I immediately set my self to read it, as all things from its Author, with the utmost Attention; and I find it answerable to the highest Expectations I had of it. And since, with your usual Modesty, you are pleased to require My thoughts more particularly concerning it; I shall with all freedom, but at the same time with all Deference, propose them to you; Not doubting of your favourable Interpretation and Pardon, where you see it Needfull. And first in General, I think you propose nothing in your whole Book but what is very reasonable, and very Practicable, except only in One Particular, which seems to bear hard on the Tender Spirits of Children, and the Natural Affections of Parents. tis pag. 117. 118. where you advise, That a Child should never be suffer'd to have what he Craves, or so much as Speaks for, much les if he Cries for it.†1 I acknowledge what you say in explaining this Rule sec. 101. in Relation to Natural Wants, especially that of Hunger, may be wel enough allowd. But in sec. 102. where you Come to Apply it to Wants of Fancy and Affectation you seem too strict and severe. You say indeed this wil teach them to stifle their Desires, and to Practise Modesty and Temperance. but for teaching these Vertues I conceive we shall have occasions enough in relation to their Hurtful desires, without abridging them so wholy in matters indifferent and Innocent that tend only to Divert and please their Busy Spirits. You allow indeed that twould be inhumanity to deny them those things One perceives would Delight them. If so, I see no reason why in a Modest way and with submission to the Wills of their Superiours, they may not be allowd to Declare what wil Delight them. No, say you; But in all Wants of Fancy and Affectation, they should Never, if once declared, be harkend to, or
― 714 ―
Complyd with. This I can never agree to, it being to Deny that Liberty between a Child and its Parents, as we desire and have granted Us, between Man and his Creator. and as in this case, Man is allowd to Declare his Wants, and with submission to recommend his Requests to God; so I think Children may be allowd by their Parents or Governours. and as between the Creature and Creator, all manner of Repining upon Denyal or disappointment is forbidden; so in the Case of Children; all frowardness or Discontent upon a Refusal is severely to be reprimanded. But thus far I agree with you in the Whole, that whether it be in Wants Natural or Fanciful that they Expres their Desires in a Froward Humersom Manner, there they should be surely Deny'd them. A Farther Reason for my allowing Children a Liberty of Expressing their Innocent desires is, that the Contrary is impracticable; and you must have the Children almost Moped for want of Diversion and recreation, or else you must have those about them study nothing all day but how to find imployment for them; and how this would Rack the Invention of any Man alive I leave you to judge. and besides, were it an easy task for any adult person to study the Fancy, the unaccountable Fancy and Diversion of Children the whole year round; Yet it would not prove delightful to a Child, being not his own Choise. But this you'll say is what you would have imprinted on them, that they are not to Choose for themselves. But why not, in harmles things and Plays or Sports I see no reason. in all things of Moment let them live by the Conduct of Others Wiser than themselves.
This, Sir, is all that in your Whole Book I stick at; to all the rest I could subscribe; and I am not a little pleased when I consider that My Own Management of My Only little One has hitherto been agreable in the Main to your Rules. save only in What relates to his Hardy Breeding, which I was cautious in; because he is come from a Tender and sickly Mother. But the Child Himself is hitherto (God be thanked) very Healthful, tho not very Strong.
The Rules you give for the Correcting of Children and implanting in their Minds an Early sense of Praise and Dispraise, of Repute and Dishonour, are certainly very Just.
The Contrivances you propose for teaching them to Read and Write are very Ingenious. and because I have practised One much of the same Nature, I'll venture to describe it. Tis by Writing Syllables and Words in Print hand on the Faces of a Pack of Cards, with Figures or Cyphers adjoynd to each Word; by Which I can
― 715 ―
form twenty several sorts of Games, that shall teach Children both to read and Count at the same time; and this with Great Variety. One thing more I shall venture to add to what you direct Concerning Writing; that is; I wil have my Son taught Short-Hand; I do not mean, to that perfection as to Coppy a Speech from the Mouth of a Ready speaker. but to be able to write it readily for his own private Busines. Beleive me, Sir, tis as useful a knack as a Man of Busines or any Scholar can be Master of. and I have found the Want of it my self, and seen the advantage of it in others frequently.
You are Certainly in the Right of it, relating to the manner of acquiring Languages, French, Latin; and in what you lay down concerning Grammar Schooles, Themes, Verses, and other Learning. But above all, what you direct in every particular for the forming of Childrens Minds; and giving them an Early Turn to Morality, Virtue, Religion etc is most Excellent. And I can only say In General, That I can give no better proof of my liking your Book in all these Precepts, than by a strict Observance of them in the Education of My Own. Which I shall pursue (God Willing) as exactly as I can. One thing I fear I shall be at a losse in, that is, a Tutor agreable to the Character you prescribe. But In this neither shall my Indeavours be Wanting, tho I leave him the Worse estate, to leave Him the better Mind.
I could hartily have wishd you had been more particular in naming the Authors you would advise Gentlemen†a to Read and be Conversant in, in the several parts of Learning you recommend to their study. Had you done this, I know no Logick that Deserves to be Named, but the Essay of Humane Understanding. so that I fear you would rather have left that Head open than recommended your Own Work.
The last thing I shall take Notice of is, what mightily pleases Me, it being the very thought of My Own Mind these Many years; Which is, your Recommending a Manual Trade to all Gentlemen. This I have ever been for; and have wonderd how it Comes to pas that tis so generally neglected. but the Lazy effeminate Luxuriousnes that overruns the Nation occasions the neglect hereof. Painting I have ever designed for My Son; but you have raised two Objections against it that are not easily Answerd, especially its taking up so much time to attain a Mastery in it.
I have now given you my Opinion of your Book; and now I am
― 716 ―
obleidged to thank you for sending me a Present which I so highly Value.
As to that part of your Letter relating to the Alterations you have made in your Essay concerning Mans Liberty, I dare not Venture upon those short hints you give me to pas my Opinion. But, now that you have discoverd it to me, I plainly perceive the Mistake of sec. 28. pag. 123. where you Put Thing for Action. And I doubt not, but in your next Edition, you will fully rectify this Matter. And I could advise you to hasten that Edition with what speed you can; lest Forreigners undertake a Translation of Your First without your Second Thoughts. Thus they have served me by translating into Latin, and printing My Dioptricks in Holland.†1 when I have now by Me a Translation of my Own of that Work with Many Amendments and large Additions.
Pray Sir Let me beg the Favour of your Correspondense as frequently as you Can for Nothing is More Acceptable to
Your Most Obleidged Humble Servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
My†a- Brother gives you his Most Humble Service.-†a
Address: To Mr John Locke at Mr Robert Pawlings in Dorset Court. Channel Row. Westminster London
Postmark: AV 19
Endorsed by Locke: W Molineux 12 Aug. 93 Answered†b
1653. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 15/25 August 1693 (1641, 1657)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 74-5. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 67-8.
A Amsterdam le 25 d'Août 1693.
Je me donne l'honneur, Monsieur, de vous écrire par Mr. Wetstein le jeune,†2 qui part pour Londres, quoi que je n'aie pas grand'chose à vous mander de nouveau. Mr. Furly nôtre ami, que je croiois infaillible en matiere des paquets à Londres est cause que je n'ai pas pris la voie que je devois prendre, pour envoier mon livre
― 717 ―
à Mylord Privyseal.†1 Enfin après avoir été renvoié deux fois de la Brille à Roterdam, et y être demeuré trois semaines, à chacune, un Etudiant en Theologie Irlandois qui a demeuré quelque temps en cette ville, la pris avec lui, et a promis de le faire rendre fidelement. Il est parti de Roterdam, avec un vaisseau de guerre, il y a environ huit jours, et je ne doute pas qu'il ne soit arrivé il y a longtemps, le vent aiant été très-bon, pendant plusieurs jours. Il se nomme Toland,†2 et il demeure chez Madame Kery,†3 près de Lambeth, qui est parente ou alliée de Mr. L'Archevêque. Je lui ai fait assez d'amitiez, et il m'a paru assez honête homme, pour croire qu'il aura rendu mon paquet; mais en tout cas, il sera facile de s'en informer. Je n'ai reçu aucune nouvelle de lui, quoi qu'il m'eût promis de m'écrire incessamment dès qu'il seroit arrivé. Je m'imagine qu'il m'écrira bientôt, et que je recevrai aussi quelque réponse de Mylord Privyseal, par laquelle je puisse connoître que ma dédicace ne lui a pas été dèsagreable.
Je n'ai rien répondu au Sieur Churchill, parce que ne me proposant que de prendre mon livre en commission, je n'ai pas crû devoir m'embarrasser de tant de comptes, en aiant déja un avec le Sieur Smith,†4 et avec plusieurs autres ici. S'il en vouloit acheter comptant, et me les faire paier ici, en les livrant, je les lui donnerois au même pris qu'aux libraires de Hollande, c'est à dire, à six shelings d'Angleterre la piece. Il ne paroit rien ici de nouveau, et il ne se passe rien de remarquable, que je s'ache. On dit que l'armée du Roi d'Angleterre est de cinquante à soixante mille hommes, et qu'elle est encore à observer l'ennemi. Je ne sai ce qu'il en sera, mais il y a grande apparence qu'il ne se fera rien. Les François ont acheté cher la victoire, et les autres n'ont pas accoûtumé d'entreprendre beaucoup; reliqua θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται†5 et nous prendrons patience, quoi qu'il arrive. Je suis occupé à achever une seconde revision du Dictionaire de Moreri,†6 qui sera plus exacte que la
― 718 ―
premiére. D'abord que j'en serai dehors, je ne moccuperai que des 4 livres de Moïse qui restent, dont une partie considerable est faite. J'attens avec impatience vos remarques, pour en profiter à l'avenir, et si vous entendez dire de mon Ouvrage quelque autre chose qu'il soit important que je sâche, j'espére de vôtre bonté, que vous ne manquerez pas de m'en avertir, étant parfaitement, comme je le suis, Monsieur, vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Un Ministre refugié a travaillé à traduire a gentlemans Religion, et on m'a remis sa copie pour l'examiner. Je lai reluë, et en ai corrigé quelques endrois qui n'étoient pas fideles. Je croi qu'il n'y aura rien, qui s'éloigne trop de l'Original. En peu de semaines elle sera imprimée,†1 et si vous le souhaitez, je vous en envoieroi un exemplaire.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke at Mr. Pawlings in Dorset Court, in Chanell row Westminster.
In another hand, elsewhere on cover: par votre tres humble†a serviteur J L Wetstein logé at the Crosskeys Inn†2 in Wood street near Cheapside.

1654. Robert Pawling to Locke, 21 August 1693 (1651, 1658)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, f. 218.
London Aug: 21 1693

I recived yours with the bill and have received†b the £17 for which I thank you, when Mr Fox comes I will pay him and will observe your order in mentioning to what time he is paid in the acquittance. 1655. Locke to William Molyneux, 23 August 1693 (1652, 1661)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 56-63. Answers no. 1652; answered by no. 1661.
Oates, 23 Aug. 1693.
Sir,
Yours of August 12. which I received last night, eased me of a great deal of pain your silence had for some time put me in; for you must allow me to be concern'd for your health, as for a friend that I could not think in danger or a disease without a concern and trouble suitable to that great esteem and love I have for you. But you have made me amends plentifully by the length and kindness, and, let me add too, the freedom of your letter. For the approbation you so largely give to my book is the more welcome to me, and gives me the better opinion of my method, because it has joyn'd with it your exception to one rule of it; which I am apt to think you your self, upon second thoughts, will have remov'd, before I say any thing to your objections. It confirms to me that you are the good natur'd man I took you for: and I do not at all wonder that the affection of a kind father should startle at it at first reading,†1- and think it very severe that children should not be suffer'd to express their desires; for so you seem to understand me. And such a restraint, you fear, would be apt to moap them, and hinder their diversion. But if you please to look upon the place, and observe my drift, you will find that they should not be indulged, or complied with, in any thing their conceits have made a want to them, as necessary to be supplied. What you say, that children would be moap'd for want of diversion and recreation, or else we must have those about them study nothing all day, but
― 720 ―
how to find employment for them; and how this would rack the invention of any man living, you leave me to judge, seems to intimate, as if you understood that children should do nothing but by the prescription of their parents or tutors, chalking out each action of the whole day in train to them. I hope my words express no such thing, for it is quite contrary to my sense, and I think would be useless tyranny in their governors, and certain ruin to the children. I am so much for recreation that I would, as much as possible, have all they do be made so. I think recreation as necessary to them as their food, and that nothing can be recreation which does not delight. This, I think, I have so expressed, and when you have put that together, judge whether I would not have them have the greatest part of their time left to them, without restraint, to divert themselves any way they think best, so it be free from vitious actions, or such as may introduce vitious habits. And therefore if they should ask to play, it could be no more interpreted a want of fancy, than if they asked for victuals when hungry; though where the matter is well order'd, they will never need to do that. For when they have either done what their governor thinks enough in any application to what is usually made their business, or are perceiv'd to be tir'd with it, they should of course be dismissed to their innocent diversions, without ever being put to ask for it. So that I am for the full liberty of diversion, as much as you can be, and, upon a second perusal of my book, I do not doubt but you will find me so. But being allow'd that, as one of their natural wants, they should not yet be permitted to let loose their desires in importunities for what they fancy. Children are very apt to covet what they see those above them in age have or do, to have or do the like, especially if it be their elder brothers and sisters. Does one go abroad? the other streight has a mind to it too. Has such an one new or fine cloaths, or play-things? they, if you once allow it them, will be impatient for the like, and think themselves ill dealt with if they have it not. This being indulged when they are little, grows up with their age, and with that enlarges it self to things of greater consequence, and has ruin'd more families than one in the world. This should be suppressed in its very first rise, and the desires you would not have encourag'd you should not permit to be spoken, which is the best way for them to silence them to themselves. Children should, by constant use, learn to be very modest in owning their desires, and careful not to ask any thing of their parents
― 721 ―
but what they have reason to think their parents will approve of. And a reprimand upon their ill bearing a refusal comes too late, the fault is committed and allow'd; and if you allow them to ask, you can scarce think it strange they should be troubl'd to be deny'd; so that you suffer them to engage themselves in the disorder, and then think the fittest time for a cure, and, I think, the surest and easiest way is prevention. For we must take the same nature to be in children, that is in grown men; and how often do we find men take ill to be deny'd what they would not have been concern'd for if they had not asked. But I shall not enlarge any farther in this, believing you and I shall agree in the matter; and indeed it is very hard, and almost impossible to give general rules of education, when there is scarce any one child, which, in some cases, should not be treated differently from another. All that we can do in general, is only to shew what parents and tutors should aim at, and leave to them the ordering of particular circumstances as the case shall require.†-1
One thing give me leave to be importunate with you about: You say your son is not very strong; to make him strong, you must use him hardly, as I have directed; but you must be sure to do it by very insensible degrees, and begin any hardship you would bring him to only in the spring. This is all the caution needs be used. I have an example of it in the house I live in, where the only son of a very tender mother†2 was almost destroy'd by a too tender keeping. He is now, by a contrary usage, come to bear wind and weather, and wet in his feet; and the cough which threatned him, under that warm and cautious management, has left him, and is now no longer his parents constant apprehension as it was.
I am of your mind as to short hand, I my self learn'd it since I was a man, but had forgot to put it in when I writ, as I have, I doubt not, overseen a thousand other things, which might have been said on this subject.†3 But it was only at first a short scheme for a friend, and is publish'd to excite others to treat it more fully.
I know not whether it would be useful to make a catalogue of authors to be read by a young man, or whether it could be done, unless one knew the child's temper, and what he was designed to.†4
― 722 ―
My Essay is now very near ready for another edition, and upon review of my alterations, concerning what determines the will, in my cool thoughts I am apt to think them to be right, as far as my thoughts can reach in so nice a point, and in short is this. Liberty†1- is a power to act or not to act, accordingly as the mind directs. A power to direct the operative faculties to motion or rest in particular instances, is that which we call the will. That which in the train of our voluntary actions determines the will to any change of operation, is some present uneasiness, which is, or at least is always accompanyed with that of desire. Desire is always moved by evil to fly it; because a total freedom from pain always makes a necessary part of our happyness. But every good, nay every greater good, does not constantly move desire, because it may not make, or may not be taken to make any necessary part of our happiness; for all that we desire is only to be happy. But though this general desire of happiness operates constantly and invariably in us, yet the satisfaction of any particular desire can be suspended from determining the will to any subservient action, till we have maturely examin'd whether the particular apparent good we then desire make a part of our real happiness, or be consistent or inconsistent with it. The result of our judgment, upon examination, is what ultimately determines the man, who could not be free, if his will were determin'd by any thing but his own desire, guided by his own judgment.-†1 This, in short, is what I think of this matter, I desire you to examine it by your own thoughts. I think I have so well made out the several particulars where I treat them at large, that they have convinced some I have shewn them to here, who were of another mind; and therefore how much soever contrary to the receiv'd opinion I think I may publish them; but I would first have your judicious and free thoughts, which I much rely on; for you love truth for it self, and me so well as to tell it me without disguise.
You will herewith receive a new chapter Of Identity and Diversity,†2 which, having writ only at your instance, 'tis fit you should see and judge of before it goes to the press. Pray send me your opinion of every part of it. You need not send back the papers, but your remarks on the paragraphs you shall think fit, for I have a copy here.
― 723 ―
You desir'd me too to enlarge more particularly about eternal verities,†1 which, to obey you, I set about, but upon examination find all general truths are eternal verities, and so there is no entring into particulars; though, by mistake, some men have selected some as if they alone were eternal verities. I never, but with regret, reflect on the distance you are from me, and am,
Sir,
Your most humble servant,
J. LOCKE.

1657. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 1/11 September 1693 (1653, 1734)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 76-7. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 69-70.
A Amsterdam le 11 de Septembre 1693.
Je vous avois écrit. Monsieur, il y a dix ou douze jours par le Sieur Wetstein le cadet, qui devoit aller à Londres, mais comme il est tombé malade, je ne sai quand il partira. Cependant j'ai reçu la Lettre que vous m'avez fait l'honneur de m'écrire le 18 d'Août, à laquelle j'ai cru devoir répondre sans attendre son départ. Je vous suis très-obligé des offres que vous me faites pour mon paquet, mais je croi qu'il sera à présent entre les mains de Mylord Privyseal.†1 Il étoit encore en Hollande, lors que je vous écrivis la derniere fois. Mr. Furly l'avoit envoié deux fois à la Brille, où il a demeuré quelque temps à chaque fois, et en suite lui est revenu entre les mains. Enfin il y a plus de trois semaines qu'il la remis à un jeune homme Irlandois de ma connoissance, qui se nomme Mr. Toland, et qui demeure ordinairement à Lambeth chez une Dame, qui se nomme Madame Kery, et qui est parente, ou alliée de Mr. L'Archevêque, à ce qu'il m'a dit. Il partit sur un vaisseau de guerre, qui accompagnoit la flotte marchande de Rotterdam,†2 et il promit de le livrer surement. Comme je l'ai vû ici, et qu'il n'a pas de sujet de se plaindre de ma civilité, je ne doute pas qu'il ne l'ait rendu, quoi qu'il ne m'en ait rien écrit, comme il avoit promis de le faire. Il est non-conformiste, et fort de la connoissance de Mr. Daniel Williams,†3 qui a fait le Gospel Truth. Je marque ces circonstances, pour s'en informer, en cas qu'il ne l'eût pas encore rendu. Je n'ai reçu depuis aucune Lettre, qui me l'apprenne, de la part de Mylord Privyseal, et je crains que le retardement ne l'ait un peu refroidi. Ce n'est pourtant pas ma faute, et je croiois avoir fait le mieux du monde.
Pour ce qui est des Subscrybers, je ne puis pas leur mettre plus l'exemplaire que 3 ff. 15 sols monoie d'Hollande, qui est ce qu'il se vend ici, et qui revient environ à sept shelings. La raison de cela est
― 725 ―
qu'en aiant vendu ici à quelques Libraires, qui, comme je croi, en auront envoié à Londres, je ne le puis pas mettre aux Subscrybers plus haut, de peur que d'autres ne l'eussent au même prix qu'eux.
Les Offices de Ciceron, par Mr. Grævius, sont disposez comme les Epîtres qu'il a données ci-devant, c'est-à-dire, que les notes qui sont sous le texte regardent principalement les varietez de lecture, et les remarques de Critique pour établir la veritable maniere de lire.†1 Celles de Manuces,†a †2 où les endroits difficiles sont expliquez, sont à la fin; méthode qui ne me plait nullement. Car enfin, quoi qu'avant toutes choses il faille établir le texte, il vaudroit mieux que les notes qui regardent cette matiere fussent à la fin, parce qu'il n'y a que peu de gens qui les lisent, et que quand on ne trouve rien dans le texte qui arrête, on ne les regarde jamais. On jette au contraire souvent les yeux sur les autres, et il est trop peinible de les aller chercher à la fin. Les Harangues de Ciceron seront sans doute disposées de même. Mais les Critiques sont les gens qui estiment le plus leur propre mêtier, et qui font néanmoins ce <qu'ils>†b peuvent pour le décrier, en se rendant inutiles à la plus part du monde. J'aurai soin, Monsieur de vous envoier les volumes suivans de la Bibliotheque, quoi que je n'y aiës fait presque que les extraits de mes propres Livres,†3 parce qu'au moins cela sert de Catalogue. Celui qui la fait est un Ministre,†4 qui a peu d'étude, et qui gemit sous l'Inquisition, outre qu'il fait d'autres choses, qui le détournent, de sorte que cet ouvrage n'est pas tel qu'il pourroit être. Il n'y a rien ici de nouveau, que je sâche. On assure que le siege de Pignerol†5 est levé, et je croi que cette nouvelle se trouvera veritable, pour le malheur des Alliez. La disette de bled est si grande à Geneve, que la Seigneurie y fait distribuer une demie-livre de pain par tête au petit peuple, par jour. Je
― 726 ―
crains qu'il n'arrive pis. Dieu veuille nous délivrer de nos craintes. Je suis de tout mon coeur tout à vous
J LE CLERC
Address: A <Monsieur>†a Monsieur Locke
<Row>†a Westminster.
Endorsed by Locke: le Clerc 11 Sept. 93

Sir
The inclosed was sent with a presumption that you was here and a speedy answer was expected by the Messenger; if you answer it you be to direct it to mrs Kilsbey a Baker at the Golden Cradle in Hounsditch near Bishops gate. I did not forget to call at Baron van Helmonts Lodgings but met not with him. I should have told you that I received the £3.10s from Lanham by his Porter but could hardly prevail to have it without an acquittance; but he had 6d for bringing it and the Letter; and he was in the right, for why should he pay money without a discharge? Mrs Lockhart continues ill but mends; when she is pretty well she games with the Maids of honor etc. till 12 or 1 and then is ill anights, you will do well to chide her and let her know I acquainted you with it. she will guess it came from me; if you dont say so. I am
Sir
Your humble Servant

Sir
Being of opinion that you endeavoured to embroil me with weomen and†a by other means I was so much affected with it as that when one told me you were sickly and would not live I answered twere better if you were dead. I desire you to forgive me this uncharitableness. For I am now satisfied that what you have done is just and I beg your pardon for my having hard thoughts of you for it and for representing that you struck at the root of morality in a principle you laid down in your book of Ideas†1 and designed to pursue in another book and that I took you for a Hobbist.†2 I beg your pardon also for†b saying or thinking that there was a designe to sell me an office,†c or to embroile me.†3 I am
Your most humble and most unfortunate servant
IS. NEWTON.
At the Bull in Shoreditch.

1660. Edward Clarke to Locke, 16 September 1693 (1647, 1666)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 79-80. Printed in Rand, p. 380.
Chipley Septembr. the 16th. 1693.
Deare Freind,
Haveing not for a long time hear'd any thing from you, I hope you will forgive my inquiery at present after your Welfare, and because I know you are soe heartily Concern'd for the Safety of mee and mine, I with confidence apply to you in all Difficultyes; Poore Mrs Clarke hath had two severe Fitts of a Quartan-Ague, and to morrow expects a third which togather with the usuall Greivances attending Her in Breeding makes Her looke verie thin; I presume shee will not bee prevayled with to take any thing without your Direction, Shee has now gone about halfe her time with Childe, and did formerly in the like circumstances take the Jesuits-Powder with Good successe, tho it Pass'd through Her without being digested in a remarkeable manner as I have formerly related to you, I begg your direction in this Case, And as for goeing to the Bath, I have hear'd nothing at all of it since your last Letters on that subject, and I dare not perswade in any Case; But shall bee ever sensible of the obligations I have to you on that and all other Accounts: Mrs Clarke, your Wife, and all the rest of the younge folkes here joyne with mee in theire humble services to you, Sir Fran: and my Lady and the Rest of the Good Family at Oates, and I am in hast
your most Affectionate and obleiged faithfull servant
EDW: CLARKE:

1661. William Molyneux to Locke, 16 September 1693 (1655, 1685)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 64-5. Answers no. 1655.
Dublin. Septembr. 16. 1693.
Honoured Sir
I have yours from Oates of Aug. 23d. with your Chapter of Identity and Diversity. and I acknowledge my self extreamly obleidged to you for being at all that Thought on my Account. however, I repent not of the trouble I gave you therein, seing the Effects thereof such Clear Reasoning and profound Judgement, that Convinces and Delights at once. And I protest Sir tis to me the hardest task in the World to add any thing to, or make any remarks upon what you deliver therein; every thing you write thereon is deliverd with such Convincing Reason, that I fully assent to all; and to make remarks where I have no room to say any thing would please neither you nor my self. And to shew you that I would not wholy reley on my Own Examination of your Chapter, I imparted it to others, desiring their Censure of it; but still with the same event, all acknowledged the Clearnes of the Reasoning, and that nothing more was left to be said On the Subject.
The Answer you make to what I writ on your Thoughts of Education doe's fully satisfy me. but I assure you Sir I was not the Only Person shock'd at that Passage. I find several stumble at it, as taking little Play-things, that Children are very apt to Desire and ask for, to be matters of Fancy and Affectation within your Rule. But seing in your last letter you confine Desires of Fancy and affectation to other Matters, I am Satisfyd in this Busines.
I can say no more to the scheme you lay down of Mans Liberty; but that I beleive it very just and wil answer in all things. I long to see the second Edition of your Essay; and then, if any thing offer, I'll give you my thoughts more fully.
I am very sensible how closely you are ingaged till you have discharged this Work off your Hands; and therefore I will not venture, till it be over, to pres you again to what you have promised in the Busines of Mans Life, Morality. But you must Expect that I shall never be forgetful of that from which I propose so great Good to the World and so much satisfaction to
Your most Intirely affectionate Humble servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX

If†a- I am sometimes more Dilatory in my returns to you than I ought. Pray impute it to unavoydable Hindrances, that force me from my Duty in that particular.-†a

1663. Locke to Isaac (later Sir Isaac) Newton, 5 October 1693 (1659, 1664)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 203. Draft. Printed (from this draft) by Dugald Stewart in his 'Dissertation' (as cited in no. 1659 n.); King, pp. 224-5; Newton, Correspondence, iii. 283-4. Answers no. 1659; answered by no. 1664.
Oates 5 Oct 93
Sir
I have ben ever since I first knew you so intirely and sincerly your friend and thought you soe much mine that I could not have beleived what you tell me of your self had I had it from anybody else. And though I cannot but be mightily troubled that you should have had soe many wrong and unjust thoughts of me yet next to the returne of good offices such as from a sincere good will I have ever done you I receive your acknowledgment of the contrary as the kindest thing you could have done me since it gives me hopes that I have not lost a freind I soe much valued. After what your letter expresses I shall not need to say anything to justifie my self to you: I shall always think your own reflection on my cariage both to you and all mankind will sufficiently doe that. Instead of that give me leave to assure you that I am more ready to forgive you than you can be to desire it and I doe it soe freely and fully that I wish for noe thing more than the oportunities to convince you that I truly love and esteem you and that I have still the same goodwill for you as if noe thing of this had happend. To confirme this to you more fully I should be glad to meet you any where and the rather because the conclusion of your letter makes me apprehend it would not be wholy uselesse to you But whether you think it fit or not I leave wholy to you. I shall always be ready to serve you to my utmost in any way you shall like and shall only need your commands or permission to doe it
My book†1 is goeing to the presse for a second edition and though I can answer for the designe with which I writ it yet since you have soe oportunely given me notice of what you have said of it I should take it as a favour if you would point out to me the places that gave occasion to that censure that by explaining my self better I may avoid being mistaken by others, or unawares doeing the least prejudice to truth or virtue. I am sure you are soe much a friend to them both that were you none to me I could expect this from you
― 732 ―
But I cannot doubt but you would doe a great deale more than this for my sake who after all have all the concerne of a friend for you, wish you extremly well, and am without Complement.

The last winter by sleeping too often by my fire I got an ill habit of sleeping and a distemper which this summer has been epidemical put me further out of order, so that when I wrote to you I had not slept an hour a night for a fortnight together and for 5 nights together not a wink. 1665. James Tyrrell to Locke, 26 October [1693] (1589, 1721)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 123-5. Year from Locke's endorsement, etc.
Okeley Oct: 26.†b
Dear Sir
I received yours with the Directions for Cambdens Britannia†1 not long before I began my Journey into Derby shire, and not
― 733 ―
haveing then any thing worth troubleing you with, I deferred my answere untill my returne, when I hoped I should have somewhat to write upon that head: and last week upon my returne from my Journey I met with another from you, which was very wellcome because it brought me the good news of the continuation of your health which is and (I hope) ever will be a great concerne to me. but to give you some answere to your first letter I have in my progresse in several Countyes†a of England made some observations which I thinke may deserve a place among additions in the intended Edition of the Britannia; tho they are not concerneing Coigns, or Inscriptions, it not haveing bin my Fortune to meet with any thing new in that Kind. but what I have collected as to seats of ancient Familyes, and some natural things I shall transcribe, and communicate to the Editor of that usefull worke as soon as I come up, or before, if occasion be; as for what you write in your second letter concerneing the paper of Subscriptions to Mr: Le Clerc's first volume; I can onely tell you that upon the first comeing out of it not long before I went into the north, I transmitted it to my book-seller at London to be delivered to Mr: Smyth the undertaker of that worke as allso my owne subscription to it:†1 in order to have my owne; as well as Mr: Kings†2 and his Freinds copyes deliverd to them; therefore pray if you have any oppertunity of seeing Mr: King or sending to him, let him know what I have done, and that their Copyes are ready for them upon payment of the money. I sent Mr: King word of it before but know not whether my book-seller Mr: Baldwin was so carefull as to let him know it as I desired: I am very sorry to hear of his brother Johns unfortunate distemper†3 which was a thing I have long feard and suspected; from a person who gave his braine so little rest. but I hope the care of a good Physitian, and the benefite of the approaching winter will againe restore him his former senses. as for what you desire to know concerneing Dr: Ms: new Testament†4 all I can tell you of it is that I saw the Doctor on monday, and He tells me that the Text is all quite finisht and printed off, as allso most part of the preface: but
― 734 ―
when it will come out he cannot as yet certainly tell. there is now in the presse at the Theater a Catalogue of all the Manuscripts†a in the Bodleian, as allso all the Colledg Libraryes in Towne.†1 it is about half finisht, and will be a worke of great use to learned men. I suppose you have heard of Dr: Allixes designe of puting out a new edition of the greek and Latine Councils out of the best Copyes, and reduceing them to a much lesser volume in order to which He has bin lately at Oxford to collate the best printed Copyes with the Manuscripts†a there, but when this great work will be finisht I cannot tell.†2 I have read with care the Treatise of Education which goes under your name: which if it had not bin told me who was the Authour I could easily have guest for reasons I can tell you when wee meet; but I cannot blame you for not puting your name to it, for tho the notions, and directions are new, and very instructive; yet you must expect to find all fond Mothers, pedantic School-masters, and Tutors Enemyes to your method, and designe, but I doubt not but the worke will out live all their impotent malice so wishing you all health and hopeing to be so happy as to meet you in Towne when I come up I am
Dear Sir
Your most humble servant
J TYRRELL
I will bring up with me the volume of Josephus;†3 and Lucians Dialogues in French†4 when I come up.

1667. Locke to Edward Clarke, 30 October 1693 (1666, 1686)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 65. Printed in Rand, pp. 381-2.
Oates 30° Oct. 93
Dear Sir
Now that I know that you are at Sutton I venture this in answer to three I have received from you. I am sorry Mrs Clarke remains averse to the Jesuits Barke but in her case there is noe contesting with it but it must be left alone. Her Aversion to the Barke makes her not I beleive in Love with her ague which I wish her well rid of. To that purpose pray tell her there is one here that has a plaister which applied to the wrists seldom fails of cureing agues but they make a great secret of it. I know not whether I shall get it or noe but if she be desirous of it I will trie and either send her the receit or the plaisters For I would not have her lie any longer under the inconvenience of her quartan and I am sorry she has sufferd soe many fits of it already. Pray remember me very kindly to her and tell her she must eat heartily the well days espetialy that after the fit and drinke wine more freely than she used to doe. and let her often remember that I shall neither be pleased with her nor eased in my self till I hear she has got rid of her ague
Pray also give my humble service to Mrs Strachy her son and daughter and the rest of my freinds in that neighbour hood and tell my Cosin Lyde I wish my Cosin his daughter much joy. When you see Mr Cornelius Lyde pray give him my service and thanks for the right he did me about the taxes.†1 and if you see my Cosin Stratton whilst you are in those parts pray talke with him about my litle affairs there and give him order in any thing you think fit to be done as if it were your owne affair. I have writ to him to follow your direction in every thing and the money that he has of mine in his hands pray setle with him the best way of returning it and if you have noe need of it there your self let him give you a bill on somebody in London payable to you. Send me word when you intend to be in town for I will be there by that time. I long to see you and am
Dear Sir your most affectionate humble servant

1668. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 31 October/10 November 1693 (1646, 1671)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 81-2. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 335-7. Answered by nos. 1671 and 1692.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Pertinax tuum silentium oppugnare non desinam, donec expugnavero. Jam ultra quinque menses elapsi sunt, ex quo Sibelius mihi Tuas, brevissimas quidem, attamen gratissimas, tradidit.†2 Promittis mihi prolixiores; sed licet ego mox rescripserim, et postea alteras ad Te dederim literas, nihil literarum exinde a Te accepi. Tantæ dilationis causam occupationibus Tuis, licet gravioribus, imputare nequeo. Rus ex urbe reverso vel unica hora superfuit, etiam occupatissimo, brevem amico scribendi epistolam. Quid itaque aliud concludam, nisi Te adversâ detineri valetudine? Ea cura me plane sollicitum habet: Quare si vivas ac valeas, hac quæso me sollicitudine
― 738 ―
libera. D.Clericus mihi bis terve a Te salutem dixit; verum et jam a pluribus hebdomadibus ille nullas a Te literas habuit, quod non mirabatur: Valde autem mirabatur, nullas ad me pervenisse. Aberrasse tuas literas non credo: non enim quæ ad me ex Angliâ mittuntur aberrare solent. Itaque unice de valetudine Tuâ sollicitus sum. Res est solliciti plena timoris amor.†1 Præsertim cum responsum tuum ad duo flagitaverim: de editione Bibliorum Castellionis, quam hic elegantem et plenam meditantur bibliopolæ quidam; et de obitu Doctissimi Spenceri,†2 ad quem si vivat mihi necessario scribendum est: et inofficiosus sim ac cessator, si falsus de morte illius ad nos rumor perlatus est, quod Viro magno hactenus nihil responderim. Exspectaveram accuratum ac sincerum tuum de Historiâ Inquisitionis, jam procul dubio ad finem a Te perlectâ, judicium. Lipsienses in Actis suis illius jam mentionem fecerunt; generatim quædam dixere in illius laudem, recensent satis prolixe librum primum, nihil autem (quod miratus fui) carpunt. An tamen placeat ipsis παῤῥησία mea, ac liberum de actionibus quorundam Patrum judicium, valde dubito.†3 Mihi satis est, quod reprehendere non audeant. Verum nec ab illorum judicio pendet causa libertatis: aliorum requirit patrocinium, qui nullius addicti jurare in verba
― 739 ―
magistri†1 absque præjudicio ac partium studio omnia æquâ lance ponderant. Quare tuum flagito judicium, quod merito me flagitare posse credo, utpote qui Te hortatore Historiæ illius scriptionem aggressus sum.†2 Amici nostri hactenus bene valent. Venius rure relicto rursus vitam urbanam amplecti velle videtur. Credo otium viro, occupatissimo hactenus, esse molestum: hinc est, quod in civitate se ad quietem componere nequeat, sed de novo praxin exerceat. Vivit ac valet, et post nuptias valetudo ipsi videtur reddita confirmatior. Filia mea jam octiduum febri continuâ, quæ suos habet paroxysmos, laborat: spes tamen blanda nos affulget, ipsam convalituram. Alias omnes jam rectè valemus. Salutant te quam amicissimè omnes mei. Salutem plurimam a me rogo dicas Dominæ Cudworthæ, cui omnia servitia humillimè offero. Vale Vir Amplissime, ac persevera in amore
Tui Amantissimi
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 10 Novembris

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I shall not stop assailing your stubborn silence until I vanquish it. More than five months have now slipped by since Sibelius delivered me your letter, a very short one, certainly, but all the same very welcome.†2 You promise me a lengthier one; but although I wrote back at once, and sent another to you after that, since then I have received no letter from you. I cannot attribute so great a postponement to your employments, important though they may be. For a man returned from the city to the country, even for the busiest, there should have remained at least a single hour in which to write a short letter to a friend. What else am I to conclude then but that you are prevented by ill health? This concern makes me thoroughly anxious; so if you are alive and well please free me from this anxiety. Mr. [p. 738] Le Clerc has given me greetings from you two or three times; but now he too has had no letter from you for several weeks, at which he did not wonder; but he wondered very much that none had come to me. I do not believe that a letter of yours has gone astray; for letters which are sent to me from England are not wont to go astray. And so I am anxious only about your health; 'love is a thing full of anxious fear.'†1 Especially as I solicited your reply to two questions: about the choice and full edition of Castellion's Bible, which certain booksellers here are considering; and about the death of the most learned Spencer,†2 to whom I must needs write if he is alive; and if the report of his death that reached us is false I should be undutiful and a sluggard, because I have not as yet replied to that great man. I had expected your well-considered and sincere opinion of the Historia Inquisitionis, which no doubt you have read to the end by now. The Leipzigers have now noticed it in their Acta; in general they have said some things in its praise, (and) they review the first book at some length, but to my surprise they carp at nothing. I much doubt, however, whether my freedom of speech pleases them, and my free judgement of the actions of certain of the Fathers.†3 It is enough for me that they do not venture to find fault. But indeed the cause of freedom does not depend on their opinion; it needs the support of [p. 739] others who have sworn allegiance to no master,†1 and weigh all things in an even balance, without prejudice and party spirit. I therefore solicit your opinion, which I believe I may rightfully solicit, since it was with your encouragement that I set about the writing of that account.†2 Our friends are well up to now. Veen seems to wish to leave the country and to take up city life again. I believe that leisure is irksome to a man who has hitherto been so busy; hence it is that he will be unable to dispose himself to inactivity in the city, but will carry on his practice anew. He is hale and hearty, and his health seems to have improved since his marriage. My daughter has been suffering for a week from a continual fever with its paroxysms, but there is good hope that she will recover. Otherwise we all are well. All my family send you their best wishes. Please give my best wishes to Mrs. Cudworth, to whom I offer my most humble services. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue in the love of
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 10 November

1670. Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux to Locke, 4 November 1693 (1593, 2336)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 287-8. Answers no. 1593.
Sir
for a while I deferd making any returne for the Favor of Your last Letter, on the account I understood by one of Yours to my Brother, that I was suddenly to expect an other Obligation from You, by the receipt of Your Treatise of Education,†1 which Yesterday first came to my hands; and now I returne You my harty Thanks for both Your Kindnesses together; of which should I express the real Thoughts I have, I should seem to run either into extravagant Complement, or gross Flatery: but thus much I must needs say, that as Your Letter certainly contains in shorte the only true Method for the prosecuting the curing parte of the Practise of Physique, and the sure way of improving it; a Mater of the cheif<e>st†a Good in relation to Mens Bodys; so Your Book of Education, lays down such rules for the breeding of Youth, as if followd must necessarily prove of the greatest advantage to the better parte of Man the Mind; by insensibly disposing it to an habitual Exercise of what is vertuous and laudable, and the acquisition of all such Knowledge as is necessary for one's own good or that of others whome we are to converse with. whence I can't but think had those of our own Country but a thorough Perswasion and a right sence of the great Benefit that redounds from a carefull Education, so as universaly to putt it in practise, with out question we should soon become a Nation as remarkably different from the rest of the world for the inward Endowments of our Minds and the rectitude of our Manners, as the Negros are from the rest of Mankind for their outward shape and color of Body. but this I fear is a Happyness only to be wished for, however he that makes it his Endeavour to promote so great a good, by shewing the certain way to it, if they will follow him, justly deserves the high estime of all that know how to value a truly publique spirit.
I hope Sir you have Your Health better, and that we may suddenly have abrode Your Essay of Humane Understanding with
― 742 ―
those further additions and Alterations You have somewhile since designed for the press: Im confident 'tis impatiently expected by all that are acquainted with Your Writings and that peculiar clear manner of delivering truth you are so much master of, but by none more then
Sir Your most Faithfull humble servant
T. MOLYNEUX

1671. Locke to Philippus van Limborch, 10 November 1693 (1668, 1675)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 257 i. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 347-9; address, in Ollion, p. 207. Answers no. 1668; answered by no. 1675.
(English)
London 10 Nov 93
Vir Amicissime
Justè meum a tè reprehendi silentium libens fateor nec si severiore manu delinquentem correxisses queri possim. Etsi enim pudet me adeo tardum fuisse ad officia ut non nisi bis monitus excitarer Gaudeo tamen me tanti apud te fuisse ut me primis vocibus male respondentem iterum tentandum arbitrareris. Excusatione valetudinis quam ipse tibi pro me suggessisti uti non possum. Gratias enim deo ex quo ad te ultimas dedi recte satis pro more meo valui
― 743 ―
nec tamen sine omni causâ a scribendo abstinui. Maximam partem libri tui summâ cum voluptate perlegeram, progredi mihi in animo erat et ad finem usque pervolvere ut de toto opere a capite ad calcem perspecto eas quas possem gratias laudesque redderem. Non multum aberam a fine libri et pauca illa capita quæ mihi restabant legenda spem quotidie fecerunt intra paucos dies potuisse absolvi. sed†a sic negotiorum et invisentium series, dum nova et inexpectata continuato ordine se invicem exciperent, me de die in diem protraxerunt et adhuc protraxissent nisi novissimæ tuæ tam amicâ objurgatione labentis temporis immemorem, primisque cogitationibus indormientem excitassent. En habes fatentem reum†1 negligentem agnosco, sed eo consilio eo animo, negligentem quem culpare vix possis: aut si qua fuerit culpa, ea spei toties deceptæ forte fuit; amicitiæ certe non fuit; quam eandem quæ erga te semper fuit nec minime dum ego tacerem siluisse profiteri gestio. Historia Tua Inquisitionis, ut de ea parte quam legi libere pronuntiem, mihi maximè placet; Ordine, methodo, perspicuitate, testium fide, mihi plane videtur opus absolutissimum nec video
― 744 ―
quid in eo desiderari possit. Et ab omnibus quotquot consulere contigit maxime laudatur. Clericum nostrum nullas a me jam a pluribus hebdomadis (ut scribis) accepisse doleo, scripsi enim ad eum ante duos circiter menses iis inclusas a Comite Pembrokiensi ad illum misi literas†1 quas intercidisse vereor quandoquidem Dominus Clericus in novissimis suis 11mo Septembris datis de iis ne verbum quidem. Me illum de Spenceri obitu monuisse recte memini et credo ea in epistola quandoquidem tu id hactenus ignorare videris. Bibliorum Castellionis editionem qualem tu narras apud vos designari valde lætor et viris literatis apud nos gratum acceptumque fore opus non dubito. post diuturnam rusticationem nuperus meus in urbem reditus nondum mihi concessit plurimorum doctorum colloquia, prout datur occasio alios consulam, quamvis vix credi potest Elegantem editionem tam elegantis versionis notis etiam aliisque†a- scriptis eò spectantibus-†a tam docti viri ornatam non omnibus non placituram. Filiam tuam dilectissimam quam febre continua laborasse scripseras tibi suisque sanam salvamque restitutam spero, reliquos tuos nostrosque recte valere gaudeo. Eos omnes quotquot sunt meo nomine rogo quam officiosissimè
― 745 ―
salutes, quibus diuturnam sanitatem et prospera omnia largiatur deus optimus maximus Te inprimis sospitet. Vale et ut facis perge me amare
Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin)
London 10 Nov 93
Excellent Sir,
I freely confess that you justly find fault with my silence, nor could I complain if you had corrected the delinquent more severely. For though I am ashamed of being so slow in doing my duties that I was not aroused till I had been twice admonished, yet I am glad that you valued me so much as to deem me worthy to be tried again when I had responded badly to the first call. As for the excuse of poor health which you suggested to yourself on my behalf, I cannot make use of it; for, thanks be to God, ever since I sent [p. 743] you my last letter I have been as well as is usual with me, and yet it is not entirely without cause that I have abstained from writing to you. I had read a very large part of your book with the greatest pleasure, and I intended to proceed with it and read through to the end, so that, having examined the whole work from first to last, I would give you such thanks and praises for it as I could. I was not far from the end of the book, and those few chapters that remained for me to read kept me daily in hope that they could be finished in a few days. But as it was, a succession of affairs and visitors, while fresh and unexpected matters followed one another without intermission, dragged me on from day to day, and would still have dragged me on if your last letter had not aroused me with its friendly rebuke, forgetful as I was of the passage of time and falling asleep over my first intentions. There you have the accused who confesses;†1 I acknowledge negligent; but with such a purpose, such a spirit, a negligent with whom you can scarcely find fault; or if there was any fault it was perhaps that of hope so often deceived; it was certainly not of friendship, which I am most happy to declare is the same as it has always been towards you and was in no wise inactive while I kept silent. Your Historia Inquisitionis, to pronounce freely about that part of it that I have read, pleases me exceedingly; in order, method, perspicuity, trustworthiness of witnesses, it assuredly seems to me a most perfect work, nor do [p. 744] I see anything that can be found wanting in it. It is also highly commended by all whom I have chanced to question. I am sorry that our friend Le Clerc has, as you tell me, received no letter from me for many weeks past, for I wrote to him about two months ago, sending enclosed in my letter one from the earl of Pembroke to him.†1 I fear these may have been lost, since Mr. Le Clerc in his last letter dated 11 September says not a word about them. I well remember that I told him of Spencer's death, and I believe it was in that letter, since you seem not to know about it yet. I am very glad that an edition such as you describe of Castellion's Bible is designed in your country, and do not doubt that the work will be welcome and acceptable to the literati here. My recent return to town after my long sojourn in the country has not yet allowed me conversation with many scholars; I shall consult others as opportunity offers, though it is hard to believe that a choice edition of so choice a translation, furnished in addition with notes and other writings relating thereto by so learned a man, will not be approved by all. I hope that your dear daughter, who you told me had been suffering from a continual fever, has been restored safe and sound to you and her family, and I am glad to hear that the rest of yours, and our common friends are [p. 745] well. Please give them one and all my best wishes; may Almighty God vouchsafe to them prolonged health and all happiness, and you above all may he preserve. Good-bye, and continue to love me as is your wont
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstranse Kirck op de Keÿsars Gracht t'Amsterdam

1672. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 17/27 November 1693 (1650, 1684)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 110.
Rotterdam 27 November 1693
Deare Sir
I have not of late wrote to you, nor heard from you; I doubt not but Monsieur Van Helmont acquainted you, as I desired him, that monsieur Bayle is un-professord, not onely, but even forbid to instruct any man in his own habitation; which way the poore Gentleman, being reduced to streights, will turn himself, I do not know, but I could wish he might find a retreat, and subsistence in our Nation†1 —I have now another piece of news to communicate to you, and that is that last Sunday I had the first proclamation of marriage,†2 with a Gentlewoman of this Town, a widdow of a marchant with a plentifull estate, and onely one son of 15 years old to inherit it, who most intirely loves my Benjohan and Arent. She is also the Daughter of a late English marchant, but of a Dutch
― 746 ―
mother,†1 she is the 1 march next 50 years of age of the Reformed perswasion vertuous and pious, but no superstitious bygot, nor narrow spirited Sectarian in that way, witnesse her espouseing me, whom you know to be so great a Heretic, as the chemarims†2 are wont to speak, who have made all the opposition they could, and raisd all the Hobgoblins, and Bugbears they could muster up, to affright her, but such has been her vertue, courage, and constancy that she has vanquisht them all; and the very men that came but a little before to denounce unto her that in good conscience she neither could nor ought to marry such a one as I, have been the very men that she made choice of to betroth us, If God will we shall finally solemnize our marriage about 10 days hence†3 —If you be still at Sir Francises, and myn Heer H.†4 with you, give my Brides and my most humble service to Sir Fr. and my Lady, and to our old Friend, and accept it your self. If our Parliament can procure a solid, and firm peace,†5 we shall, I beleeve, make a step over to see our friends and relations, and not faile to pay a visit at Oates as we go by; And so with most indeared love I rest
Sir your most affectionate Friend and servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Arent has had an ague this 4m, is now almost gone, he quarters at my brides who makes much of him, he learns bravely, has his service remembred to you as also have his Brothers Benjohan and John, and my brides son.†6

1674. —— De Grassemare to Locke, 21 November [1693]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 48-9. Year from Locke's endorsement. The writer was evidently a tutor in Clarke's household.
Monsieur
J'ay longtems apprehendé de prendre trop de Liberté en me donnant lhonneur de vous ecrire. ou au moins d'interrompre des occupations, qui ne peuvent etre qu'importantes et utiles a tout le monde. Cependant vous prenés tant d'interest a l'Education des Enfants de Monsieur Clarke, Et vous en avez donné des marques publiques il n'y a pas longtemps, que jay passé par dessus toute consideration, pour vous rendre conte du progrez que fait le jeune gentilhomme auprez de qui je suis.†1 Je croi Monsieur que vous scavez bien que son age et des Domestiques a la campagne ne luy avoient inspiré que du dégoût, pour tout ce qui demande un peu d'application. C'est la ce qui l'a arrêté longtems, car il n'a pas eté si facile de luy faire sitôt naitre l'envie d'apprendre. Cependant comme il a de l'esprit et le naturel bon, il a surmonté une bonne partie du degoût quil avoit pour l'Etude. Au moins il ne fait plus guere paroître de repugnance a faire ce qu'on souhaite de luy. S'il eust eu ces bonnes dispositions a mon arrivée, il eust sans doute avancé davantage. Cependant il n'a pas tout a fait perdu son tems. il lit passablement bien et commence a parler et entendre ce qu'on luy dit. il prononce bien, soit qu'il parle; ou qu'il lise. il ecrit assez bien pour le temps quil a appris Et j'espere que dans peu il scaura decliner et conjuguer. car, pour apprendre le latin j'ay crû qu'il etoit necessaire quil sceust l'un Et l'autre; au moins ses conjuguaisons ne luy seront pas inutiles a apprendre le francois. Voila
― 749 ―
Monsieur, l'etat de ses Etudes et le conte que j'ay cru etre obligé de vous rendre. si vous Daigniez me communiquer vos Lumieres sur ce sujet, je les recevrois avec le respect que je dois, et vous serois infiniment obligé. Au verte si je ne vous ai pas eté trop importun, monsieur, je m'estime heureux d'avoir eu cette occasion de vous presenter mes tres humbles respects, Et de me pouvoir dire avec une profonde soumission
Monsieur
Votre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
