1675. Philippus van Limborch to Locke, 24 November/4 December 1693 (1671, 1692)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 83-4. Printed in King, 1830, ii. 338-41. Answers no. 1671; answered by no. 1692.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Ultimæ tuæ, quibus te recte valere scribis, non mediocriter me exhilararunt. Omnino enim sinistra quædam de valetudine tuâ metuebam. De amicitiâ tuâ certus eram, nec in ea vel minimum suboriri posse frigusculum persuasissimus sum. Verum cum D. Clericus negaret, ad se quicquam de Spenceri obitu scriptum, in ejusque literis te brevi ad me scripturum indicares, jamque plures elaberentur hebdomadæ, nullusque amicorum ne tenuem quidem de te rumorem audiret, quid aliud suspicari potui nisi morbum, ipse ignarus plurimarum quæ te detinerent occupationum? Interim
― 750 ―
securum te esse volo de literis tuis ad Clericum datis: postremas tuas cum inclusis Comitis Pembrokiensis recte illi esse traditas certo scio; nam ipse statim literas Comitis mihi ostendit. Gratias tibi maximas ago, quod molestissimum illum laborem, Historiam meam Inquisitionis perlegendi, devoraveris. Encomia tua scutum mihi erunt, quo aliorum, si qui exsurgant, criminationes retundam. Mallem tamen ego legere censuras tuas, quas ab eruditâ et amicâ manu profecturas scio, et per quas multum proficere possem. Ego quidem defectus aliquot historiæ meæ video; sed quos tollere non potui. Aliqua, quæ inserta cuperem, pauca tamen, post editionem in quibusdam autoribus, antea mihi non visis, reperi. Sed illa integritati historiæ nihil obsunt: solummodo circumstantias quasdam exactius enarrant. Sed aliud est majoris momenti. Tota historia contexta est ex aliorum autorum testimoniis: nihil ego ad eam contuli, præter solam methodum: hæc si placet, est quod mihi gratuler. Potuisset historia esse brevior et concinnior, si uno filo et eodem stilo conscripta fuisset. Verum consultius duxi ipsa autorum, quos consului, verba exhibere, licet in majorem historia excresceret molem; quia multa adeo sunt tetra ac atrocia, ut, nisi ipsa Doctorum Pontificorum verba adscripta fuissent, fidem vix invenissent. Malui

― 751 ―
itaque prolixior esse, quam alicui calumniandi ansam præbere, quam, si meis verbis usus fuissem, fortassis aliqui arripuissent, meque criminandi, quod quædam minus vera ipsis adscripsissem. Nunc ipsa autorum verba posui, et in margine autores adscripsi, ut unicuique de fide meâ constare possit. Interim rem mihi longe gratissimam feceris, si quicquid censurâ dignum judicaveris, mihi perscribas, ut id in exemplari meo emendem. Ego, quicquid mihi in autoribus quibusdam a me præteritum occurrit, in eodem exemplari annoto, et singula suis locis insero, si forte aliquando usui esse possit; et si non aliis, mihi saltem usui est. Penultimas meas per juvenem quendam Hibernum, doctum sane, ingeniique admodum moderati, ad te misi, quas illum tibi tradidisse nullus dubito, quia maximo te videndi desiderio flagrabat. Nihil tamen post ejus discessum de ipso audivi. Habuit etiam literas a me ad Reverendissimum Archiepiscopum, quibus pro libro mihi misso gratias ago. Judicium tuum de editione nova Bibliorum Castellionis bibliopolæ Halma†1 indicavi: nunc ipsius est decernere, quod e re sua fore crediderit. Vellem ego novam illam editionem videre. Sed nec minus videre cupiam Harmoniam Evangelicam Doctissimi Toinardi.
― 752 ―
Non possum quin obnixe te orem, ne patiaris tantum thesaurum post obitum tuum neglegi, aut interire; sed illum fideli alicui amico commendes, cujus operâ, si non vivo, saltem morto autore, lucem adspiciat: Autor enim ipse moras sine fine nectit, et citius elephas pareret, quam ipse hunc suum fœtum.†1 Filia mea jam multum convaluit; continua febris desiit; quotidie tamen aliquos sentit paroxysmos, quibus integra sanitatis recuperatio retardatur. Spero et illos brevi cessaturos. Omnes Te Amici salutant, imprimis uxor mea liberique. Salutem rogo dicas D. Cudworthæ, cui, uti et tibi, omnia fausta precor.
Tui Amantissimus
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 4 Decembris

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Your last letter, in which you write that you are quite well, rejoiced me not a little; for I was very much afraid of something untoward regarding your health. Of your friendship I was assured; I am fully convinced that not the least coolness could arise in it. But when Mr. Le Clerc denied that anything had been written to him about Spencer's death and you declared in your letter to him that you would shortly be writing to me, and now several weeks slipped by and none of your friends heard even the slightest report about you, what else could I suspect but illness, knowing nothing myself of the many employments that held you back? Meanwhile let me reassure [p. 750] you about your letters to Le Clerc: I know for certain that your last, with the earl of Pembroke's enclosed, was duly delivered to him, for he at once showed me the earl's letter. I thank you most heartily for bearing patiently that very troublesome task of reading through my Historia Inquisitionis. Your praises will be a shield for me with which to blunt the accusations of others, should any arise. Nevertheless I should prefer to read your censures, which I know will proceed from a scholarly and friendly hand, and by which I could profit much. I perceive indeed some defects in my account, but which I was unable to remove. Since it was published I have found in certain authors whom I had not seen previously, some things, though only a few, that I should have liked to insert. But they are not prejudicial to the completeness of my account; it is only that they describe more exactly certain circumstances. But something else is of greater importance. The whole account is put together from the testimonies of other authors; I have contributed nothing to it apart only from the method; if this is approved it is something on which I may congratulate myself. The account could have been shorter and neater if it had been written in one manner (?) and the same style. But, although the account might grow to a greater bulk, I thought it better advised to display the very words of the authors whom I have consulted; for many things are so foul and cruel that they would hardly have found belief if the very words of the Popish doctors had not been added. And so I [p. 751] preferred to be rather lengthy rather than to afford an opportunity to anyone for misrepresentation, which some would perhaps have seized if I had used my own words, and for accusing me of making some less than true additions to them. As it is, I have set down the very words of the authors and added the authors in the margin, so that everyone can be certain of my trustworthiness. Meanwhile you will do me an extremely welcome service if you will write to me in full whatever you deem worthy of censure, so that I may amend it in my copy. Whatever meets me that I have overlooked in certain authors I record in the same copy, and I insert particular items in their places, if perchance it can at some time be useful; and, if not to others, to me at least it is useful. I sent you my last letter but one by a certain young Irishman, certainly learned and of temperate disposition; I have no doubt that he has delivered it to you since he was fired by a strong desire to see you. I have however heard nothing of him since his departure. He also had a letter from me to the Most Reverend the Archbishop, in which I thank him for the book sent to me. I have informed the bookseller Halma†1 of your opinion about the new edition of Castellion's Bible; it is now his business to decide what he believes will be for his advantage. I should like to see that new edition. But I should no less wish to see the learned Toinard's Harmony [p. 752] of the Gospels. I cannot but most earnestly implore you not to allow so great a treasure to be neglected after your death, or to perish; rather I would have you commit it to some trustworthy friend, by whose exertion it might see the light, if not in the author's lifetime, at any rate after his death; for the author himself contrives endless delays, and an elephant might bring forth more quickly than he this offspring of his.†1 My daughter is now much better; the continual fever has ceased, though she feels some paroxysms daily, by which the complete recovery of her health is retarded. I hope that these too will soon cease. All our friends send you their greetings, and especially my wife and children. Please give my respects to Mrs. Cudworth with whom, as with you, I pray that all may be well.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 4 December 1693
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mr. Robbert Pawlings in Dorset Coort in Chanell row Westminster
Postmark: NO 29

1677. William Thomas to Locke, 2 December 1693 (1629, 1688)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 140-1.
Sir,
Two days since these papers were delivered to me, sealed as you see them, by a friend of mine. He told me he knew nothing of the Contents, for they were not his own, but put into his hands by another Gentleman, who desired they might be transmitted by me to your hands. The Gentleman Author has not the honour of being acquainted with you any otherwise than by your bookes, which he mightily values. His request to you is that you would be pleased to give his papers a serious reading at your leisure, and at last be so kind as to give your opinion in few lines of his Notion and his way of managing it. He will thank you too, if you will show him his errors. He intends from your censure to resolve on printing or not printing.—I am further enjoined to desire you to seal up the papers and your opinion when you have committed it to writing, and deliver it or send it to me, that by me by the way of my friend they may be conveighed to the Author.†1 I beg your pardon for this trouble and am Sir your most
obliged and humble servant
W THOMAS
Dec. 2d 1693
Endorsed by Locke: W. Thomas 2° Dec. 93
1678. Locke to Anonymous, 3 December [1693] (1713)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 17-18. Draft. In view of its irregularities I have occasionally rectified wrong readings. Year from Locke's endorsement.
The draft appears to be a response to the papers forwarded to Locke by William Thomas on 2 December. No. 1713 appears to be the writer's answer to the present letter, and no. 1736 a further letter from him. In view of the mention of the Athanasian creed in no. 1713 and the opening passage of the present letter the writer was probably engaging in the Trinitarian controversy: nos. 1325, 1702.
There was 'originally enclosed' in this draft MS. Locke c. 28, f. 159, comments by Locke on Malebranche's De la recherche de la verité: Long, Summary Catalogue, pp. 29-30. The association of the two pieces appears to be fortuitous.
― 757 ―
Dec. 3d
I have read over the papers you have been pleased with soe great a complement to communicate to me. And I have been engaged with the more satisfaction in an uninterrupted perusal of them, for I received them but yesterday since I found as a fair enquirer after truth you layd just blame on the over warme combatants and both sides. It is a controversy I have been litle conversant in and that for the very reasons you proceed on. Contenting†a- my self in a matter of mere revelation with what I find revealed and easily perswading my self there might be unfathomable depths in the incomprehensible nature of that infinite first being.-†a When I finde in what I am nearest acquainted with, my self, and in the meanest of the creaturs what my reason†b can not account for, nor†c- my knowledg comprehend-†c
I know not whether you will think fit to discover your self to any body much lesse to me who am as I am told a stranger to you. Tis what 'tis not for me to desire and had your treatise fallen into my hands in print I should not soe much as have asked after the author. being obleiged to him for the benefit I reaped from the pains he had taken to instruct me I should not have thought it suitable to the gratitude I owed him nor to the rules of good manners to desire to know more of him than he <thought>†d fit to discover of himself. But since you are pleased to desire my opinion I cannot but wish I might have the oportunity of discourseing with you several things in your treatise, wherein I being not perfectly clear my self, cannot avoid thinkeing (for soe are we made) that other <Readers>†e will stick at.†f This I hope will not give you the least suspition that I have any mean thoughts of your discours I†g- have seldom met with any thing relateing to controversy writ in a way that soe much pleases me. And-†g the value I have for it is
― 758 ―
that which makes me think it worth while to propose to you my thoughts on some passages in it if I have an oportunity. For I looke on it as a duty we owe to one another and to truth to deale frankly in al such cases, and therefor when ever my opinion is asked on such an occasion I count my self obleiged to doe as I would be done by. i e to tell it freely and debate it fairly. Could this be as well done in writeing as by word of mouth (which I thinke it cannot) yet the small stay I am like to make in town, and the multitude of avocations and litle businesses I have to take it up will not allow me leisure to engage in the slow and heavy way of writeing. If I have the honour to see you I shall minutely lay before you my opinion and thinke it noe small advantage to be acquainted with soe ingenious a person. If you thinke not fit to increase your obligation soe far I shall not blame you. The honour you have done me already is much more than comes to my share and the deference you are pleasd to expresse to my judgment is a complement that puts me out of Countenance. I know not after what you have said (for fear I should seem to assume to my self an authority of judgment) whether I ought to say what I am now goeing. viz that I thinke the ground you goe on not only of great but necessary use in the present controversie and almost all others and you have managed it with that strength and evidence that it would be a great losse if the publique should be deprivd of a notion that would doe soe much towards the keeping controversies within their due bound and dispose us rather to pitty and as far as we can help one anothers ignorance. than out of a pretended or real zeale for truth outrage one another and grow insolent in the conceit of new discoverys. All Truths as you have well proved we are not obleiged to know or beleive But this must be confessed that universall charity good will and love we are bound to maintein and promote
Endorsed by Locke: J L 3 Dec 93 to Anonymus

Savernake Dec 4 93
Deare Freind
I am now returneing to Salisbury to try that ayre againe though I find this agrees well enough and if drinkeing no wine will cure me I am sure I have dranke none but canary and that mixed with more water then wine for now about 3 months but yet the cough remaines though not so violent as sometimes it hath beene but I am sure I recover no flesh though my stomack fayles mee not. I knowe not what the next spring grasse†1 may doe
I desire to knowe what interest is due on my mortgage till Michaelmas last that I may pay it and put that affayre in such order that it may not be troublesome to your cousin†2 nor my selfe
I knowe not whether you expect any particulars of my distemper which I cannot nowe write but will satisfy you if you desire it. I am sure it is very like a consumption and such a one as I cured in another by putting him on rideing and I had followed the same course and seene you at Oates if the badnesse of the ways had not deterred me from it
I am glad your lungs are so strong as to endure London this Michaelmas terme. I hope it is other then publicke affayres which cannot deserve it. I am deceaved of the Ks letter for my sonne Henery though more then once promised it by this present secretary†3 and knowe not by what hand to retreive it. My wife is and I am
your your affectionate Freind and humble servant
D THOMAS

I Rec yours this day Dated the 2th of this Instant and have bean with Mr Cutheringtons sonn†1 for he saith his Father is In London and he will wright to him to pay Mr Clarke 46l: 8s: 6½d it being all that is In my hands of Lady day last as Will apear by the Account I have sent mr Clarke, which was your order, pray as sone as the mony is paid let me have a loyne that soe I may Charg it, I was at Mr Cutheringtons soe late that it was not fit to pay mony but shall pay it to his Content he hath writ to his father that the mony is paid Eliza Hopkins will not pay whatsoever was left to pay when you was In the Countery for she saith you was satisfied she hath paid me redyly what was dew sinc ladyday 1691 and would not pay any mony before you came Into the Contery for Refleckted that she was a servant to the famely as for Rich: Kent he at present goeth from his word With Cornelias Abraham but he supposes that he will cum on againe. your Affectionate Cosin and Humble Servant
WILLIAM STRATTON
I thought best to write to you severed from Mr Clarke becas If a miscariage shold be it might be Inquired after

1681. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 11 December 1693 (1679)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 121-2.
Sarum Dec 11 93
Deare Freind
My bussinesse hath brought me hither something sooner then I entended, but as my state of health is I thinke it fit to settle all my affayres so that if I dy it may cause the least disturbance or difficulty to those who shall succeed mee
I found the ayre of Savernake agree very well with mee and my cough growes much lesse but the days being at the shortest I could not use rideing as I designed since my returne hither which was fryday last though the weather be cold and variable I as yet find my selfe not worse I have and shall abstayne from all sorts of wine more then what I take my croc gr in†a and if the weather were not too cold to beginne would make my drinke water and a toast and run the hazard of a dropsy which I doe not without reason thinke my selfe secure from. Pray doe you prescribe the course of treacle and laying in bed for more then one month For though I have seene you in it yet I have not a right notion of it For rideing I thinke I find the reason of that to consist in helpeing expectoration and strengthening the Lungs as well as all the other parts specially the fibers. I heartily thanke you for your advice and will followe one of your methods and if that succeeds not the other
I have often designed to acquaint you that I have your cabinet in which are all those preparations I thinke you made with Stale†1 and what wee with Dr Blunt†2 did to gether I have only opened it aswell as I could without a key but have not tryed the goodnesse of any one of them you may now dispose of them as you thinke fitt. I am
your very affectionate freind and humble servant
D THOMAS
My wife daughter and sonne John present their services to you

1682. J. G. Grævius to Locke, 15/25 December 1693 (1286, 1751)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 37-8. Locke did not receive the letter until May: no. 1751, which answers it.
(English)
Virtute et doctrina praecellenti Viro D. Locke S.P.D.
J. G. Graevius.
Longa scribendi intercapedo non tuum, spero, refrigeravit amorem. Meus sane in te fervet, cujus pignus habes nunc diatriben Rubenianum.†1 Hui! dices ex aliena arca?†2 Liceat mihi per tuam bonitatem versura solvere, cum domi non inveniam unde nomen expediam. Adjeci carmina Huetii,†3 et dissertationem Toinardi, communis amici nostri, de aetate Commodi Imperatoris.†4 Is si audierit te valere, et ex sententia rem gerere, valde gaudebit. Nullam fere ab illo epistolam accipio, accipio autem crebras, quin tui
― 763 ―
meminerit summa cum testificatione perpetui sui in te studii.†1 Multa molitur, quae valde desideramus: inter alia de Samaritanis nummis,†2 ut et de illorum imperatorum nummis, in quibus est duplex tribunicia potestas,†3 de quibus nihil adhuc a quoquam est proditum litteris, dissertationes paratas habet. Opto ut brevi illas videamus. Sed utinam et tuas commentationes in Latinam linguam conversas nobis videre liceat, quas et tui cives et exteri vestra dialecto conscriptas tantopere mirantur! Nobis non licet esse tam beatis, ut his fruamur bonis per nostram ignorantiam, quam deploramus quidem, sed cui mederi haec senilis aetas non permittit. Te valere volumus diutissime, et hunc, quem brevi inibimus, annum sine noxa et molestia transigere. Vale vir excellentissime, et me ama. Trajecti D. XXV Decemb. CIϽ IϽC XCIII.
(Latin)
To the excellent and learned Mr. Locke greeting from J. G. Grævius
The long interruption in writing has not, I hope, chilled your affection. Mine for you certainly keeps warm; you now have a token of it in Rubenius's diatribe.†1 'What!' you will say, 'from another man's chest?'†2 Be so kind, please, as to let me pay by borrowing, as I cannot find anything at home to clear the debt. I have added Huet's poems,†3 and a dissertation by Toinard, our common friend, on the age of the emperor Commodus.†4 If he hears that you are well and that you are managing your affairs to your satisfaction he will be delighted. I hardly ever get a letter from him, and I get them frequently, in which he is not mindful of you, with the warmest attestation of his perpetual [p. 763] regard for you.†1 He is working on many things of which we feel much in want; among others he has dissertations ready on the Samaritan coinage,†2 as well as on the coins of those emperors on which there is a double tribunician power,†3 a subject on which nothing has yet been published by anyone. I hope we may see them soon. But would that we might also see your own thoughts turned into Latin, which foreigners as well as your own countrymen admire so much in your language. I am not permitted to be so fortunate as to enjoy these good things owing to my ignorance, which indeed I deplore, but which this advanced age does not let me remedy. I wish you long life and good health and that you may pass the year that we shall soon be entering upon without harm or trouble. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and keep me in your affections. Utrecht 25 December 1693.
Address: Viro ingenio, doctrina et virtute praestanti D. Locke Londinum.
Endorsed by Locke: J. G: Grævius 25 Dec. 93

1684. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 21/31 December 1693 (1672, 1702)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 111-12. Received by Locke probably not before 8 January 1694: no. 1702.
Rotterdam 31 December 1693
Deare Sir
The bearer hereof mr. Peter Sonmans, who has dwelt with me ever since my return out of England, returning now into England to enjoy the good company of his sisters, I could not omit to let you know that after 21 months strong, and almost continual sollicitations, I am, in spight of all that the parsons and other Ecclesiasticall persons could do, to stave it off, by all the hideous pictures they drew of me, happyly married to a Gentlewoman of this Town, born of an English father and Dutch mother, and so hath the use of both languages. She is the 29 february, or this year the primo march 50 years old, and I the 27 April 58;†2 having a plentifull
― 765 ―
estate and but one son of 15 years old to inherit it. She is of the reformed perswasion, but no narrow spirited sectarian, in that way, but a lover of liberty, and of all good men under whatsoever perswasion; witness her marrying so great a libertist†1 and heretick as I am: for which cause divers of the Chemarims and Elders have attackt her, and indeavoured to perswade her that she could not with a good conscience marry such a one as I. But she told them, she had no Idea of conscience, if it were a thing she must enquire of others about, and not be conscious of in herself: and that she was no ways conscious of any such conscience as they talked of, knowing neither sin nor shame in it; and desireing proofe from scripture, to which she ownd obedience due from her. They then produced Two Texts one limiting marryage to be with such as are in the Lord. The other prohibiting, being unequally yoaked with unbeleevers.
Whereupon she askt, on the one hand, whether they durst say that every One that was of their Church, was in the Lord, so that she might with out any scruple of Conscience marry with any such: And on the other hand whether all that frequented not their church, of which she is a member, are unbeleevers, so that upon that account she could not with a good Conscience marry with any such? to which they replying no, they durst not say so, she askt what they would then say, from those two texts: at which the parson burst out into a rage, and said he saw she was resolved to follow her own head, and to listen to no counsell but her own; and that she might do as she pleased, he would trouble himself no more with her, nor the business—which she was glad to hear, for this Pedant had been at her a year before indeavouring to extort from her a promise that she would not marry me. She tells me that she beleevs she has been assaulted, and warned by nigh 1000 persons; but all of them, being askt what they had against me, spake the same language, that they had nothing against my person that I was an honest man, and a wise man, but a Quaker not onely, but the head of them, here, and in other cuntries; and therefore a very dangerous man to enter into such a relation with, which would hazard, her own, her sons and sisters salvation, by drawing them from the church. there being no hopes in the world of her ever being able to draw me to the church. She added, nor any need that
― 766 ―
she knew of, and that she, as well as I, hated all imposition upon any mans conscience. But that it was to her a very remarkeable thing that all of them, did agree in that character of me that I was an honest, and a wise man; which being qualities that she had loved from her youth, and beg'd of God that she might find in any man that she might chuse for her husband; it was enough, (if she had not herself knowne me) to make her love me, when my opposers did unanimously bear such a Testimony of me.
I am not a whit sorry now that it cost me so much pains, and that she took so much time to deliberate, and to hear all that any could say; Her son soon conceivd great love for me, and for my eldest son; and became as hearty a suiter for me, as I for myself: she has a most entire love for your friend Arent; who, with my dearest and my self with the rest of the children heartily salute you, earnestly desiring, if it might suit with your convenience, to enjoy your company here; we hope, if peace once comes, to see you, and all our good friends in England. When shall we see your explication of the hypothesis by you mentiond concerning the Generall deluge?†1 you have forgot to cause somebody to send me Mr. Biddles works.†2 Where can I get them? Pray convey my utmost respects to Sir Francis Masham and his Lady, when you see, or write to them: you would do me a singular kindness to let me know if my children can inherit my land in England being all borne here.†3 I am Deare Sir
your most humble servant
BENJAMIN FURLY
Address: To mr. John Locke These In London per amicum

1685. William Molyneux to Locke, 23 December 1693 (1661, 1693)
The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library, New York. Transcribed from photostat. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 66-8. Answered by no. 1693.
Dublin. Decembr. 23.93.
Honr'd Sir
I have now read over your Essay of Humane Understanding a third time; and always make New discoverys therein of something Profound. I should sett upon it again, but that I'll wait for your Next Edition; which I hope by this time is almost finished. The usual satisfaction I take in reading all things that come from you made me lately again run over your Chapter of Identity and Diversity; Concerning the Justnes whereof I have yet the same Opinion as formerly. But One Thought suggested it self to me, which on my first reading did not Occur. it relates to sec. 22. wherein the reason you give, Why the law may justly Punish a sober Man for what he did when Drunk, or a waking Man for what he did when walking in his Sleep; tho it be true and full in the Case of the Nightwalker; yet I Conceive it not so full in the Case of the Drunken Man. For Drunkenes is it self a Crime, and therefore no one shall alledge it in excuse of an other Crime. And in the law we find that Killing a Man by Chance-Medly is not Capital; yet if I am doing an unlawfull Act, as shooting at a Deer in a park to steal it, and by Chancemedly I kill a Man unawares, this is Capital. because the Act wherein I was ingaged, and which was the Occasion of this Mischeif, was in it self unlawfull, and I cannot plead it in Excuse. In the Case of the Night-walker your answer is true, full, and satisfactory; but that in the Drunkards Case is somewhat short. The night-walking is a sort of Distemper, not to be helpd or prevented by the Patient. But Drunkenes is a Deliberate Act which a man may easily avoid and Prevent. Moreover, whatever the Law appoint in this Case, I think, were I on the Jury of One who walking in his sleep had killd an other, I should not Violate a Good Conscience, if I acquitted Him; for he is certainly During those fitts non Compos Mentis; and it were easy to Distinguish by Circumstances How far he Counterfitted or Not.†1
You will very much obleidge me by a line or two to Let me know
― 768 ―
how forward your Work is; and what other things you have on the Anvil before you; Amongst which I hope you will not forget your Thoughts on Morallity. For I am obleidged to prosecute this request to you, being the first I presume that Moved you in it.
There is a Gentleman in this town, One Captain Henry Monk,†1 a nigh Relation of the Albemarles, who tells me he has been known to you long ago; and On all Occasions Mentions you with the Highest Respects. He Desired me tother day to give you his most Humble Service. I am
Dear Sir
Your Most Obedient Servant
W: MOLYNEUX

Endorsed by Locke: W: Molineux 23° Dec. 93 Answered 19 Jan.

Dear Sir
You have all the news and I all the leisure which is very ill suited for correspondence when you have not time to write and I noething to say unlesse it be to trouble you with my affairs. Give me leave therefor to minde you here again of the hundred pounds due to me now at Christmas from my Lord Ashley and the increase of my security. These things I desire you to speake to him of in the maner we agreed, and get effected if you can
I desire you also to pay Mr Freke seven pounds for me and to desire of him the receit for the Kings evill
― 769 ―
One thing more I must trouble you with. My brother Commissioners†1 being taxed in London (where they ought not to be taxed but in Westminster where the Execution of our office is) though they had warning of it, yet they neglected it soe as to suffer us all to be returned into the Exchequer. This Major Beake†2 a member of your house told me of the day before I came out of town. I beg you to speake with him or Sir William Honywood†3 another of your members and of my brethren about it and set them in the way what to doe as the case now stands. For I see by this what men of businesse they are. My service to Madam. I wish her an happy hower and her and you all a happy new year. I am
Dear Sir
your most humble and most faithfull servant

1688. William Thomas to Locke, 30 December 1693 (1677, 1695)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 142-3.
Sarum December 30th 1693.
Sir,
I came to this place this evening and by my Fathers direction give you this account of the State of his health. He coughs not soe much as he has done, tho of late more than sometime since his return to Salisbury, which he imputes either to Salisbury Air, or to the cutting of his hair, and wearing a Perewig. His breath is not short but pretty well and soe is†a- his stomach.-†a He has a swelling which†b- pitts deep-†b on his left side from the pitt of his stomach down that side of his belly, down that thigh and leg to his toe. Upon motion it pains him extreamly in the Calfe of his leg, so that in the morning he is not able to put his foot to ground for some time. This pain is extraordinary great, and as if the sinews were contracted. He is verry easy at night. My Father has been thus 4 or 5 days. If I should write you all the particulars, I should mightily exceed the bounds of a letter. I hope this will be sufficient to give you light into the Case. My Father receivd your last this day, and sends his service to you. I am, with all respect Sir your most obliged and humble servant
W THOMAS.
P.S. The swelling in his stomach and belly is hard as if flesh grew there. My Mother gives her service to you and says she should be
― 773 ―
verry glad to see you here if you would be so kind as to visitt my Father. She is verry apprehensive of danger tho she does not lett my Father know it.

1689. Locke to Edward Clarke, 8 January 1694 (1686, 1690)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 60. Printed in Rand, pp. 384-5.
Oates 8 January 9¾
Dear Sir
I have more need to excuse my troubleing of you than you soe carefully excuse your self that you spoke not yet with my Lord Ashley nor knew not when you first writ that he was in town. I am of your minde you should not desire a meeting of him about it, but speak to him when accidentaly you meet him that will looke best. The reason why I desired you to speake to him as soon as you could was because he talkd to me of goeing into the country and soe it be done before he returns to Dorset shire it will be time enough.
I thank you for your assistance to me and my Brethren nottable men†1
I have drawn a bill on you for ten pounds to be paid to my Lady Masham, which Mrs Cudworth who returns it to her desires she may receive as soon as may be after the bill comes to your hands there being present occasion for it. I know writeing a bill does it and soe that will be easily and soon dispatchd. I fear my Cosin Stratton has not yet returnd you that money pray let me know in your next. As I remember you told me I might have more mony of you if I wanted it, when I received the last from you, else I should not have drawn this bill on you soe at sight, but if you need that or more you shall have it again.
The other matters of your letter I shall trouble you with in my
― 774 ―
next. This with the three inclosed being enough for this time. My humble service to Madam I wish her an happy hower and am
Dear Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray let the inclosed goe with your letters to the post

1690. Locke to Edward Clarke [12?] January 1694 (1689, 1706)
Rand, pp. 383-4, and B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, nos. 166, 165 (enclosures). 'The letter is faded and discoloured' and the endorsement was illegible. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Rand dates the letter '2nd January', but if Guissemare is identifiable as De Grassemare, Locke wrote to him on 12 January and not earlier: no. 1674, endorsement. There are two extant letters (nos. 1690, 1728) in which Locke implies or states that he is sending Clarke lists of errata for a book that can be identified only as the second edition of Two Treatises, and there are two extant lists of errata for it (B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, nos. 166, 167). Presupposing that there are no losses, of the two lists no. 167 is presumably the later, as it mentions 'the former part'; for it see no. 1730. All the errata in no. 166 are included in the list of errata in the second edition. Locke appears to have sent two enclosures with no. 1690: the list of errata and a second piece, of which Clarke was to give a copy to Churchill. This was probably the set of queries here printed as the second enclosure.
Oates, 2nd January, 1693-4.
Dear Sir,
He has found all the rest right, i.e. all but what is wrong. Who doubts it, but what becomes of the wrong? To this add the list here enclosed, and he has well mended the matter. Whatever he promised this second time I am out of patience. If you please to give him a copy of the enclosed, and keep the original by you, it is more than he deserves. I hope at the same time you will thank him for his great care and exactness.†1 Pray give my service to Mr. Freke and thanks for the receipt he sent me.†2
I have here enclosed writ to Monsieur <Grassemare>;†a †3 if you like what I have said, you may seal and send it.
― 775 ―
I thank you for the minding of Mr. [Skengle†1 when] you sent him the kind letter two days since. And he was here with me yesterday, and returns you his acknowledgment with great sense of your kindness. [He seeks] to me to render some such services to this country that he seemed uncertain whether he should resolve to remove as far as Somerset, whereof I think he means to write to you himself. I have given him your [address]. But if you hear not from him by Monday's post you may take it for granted that he quits all thoughts of taking your Vicarage in Somersetshire.†2 If then you could get it for Mr. Pawling's son you would do a charitable thing to a deserving father, and a sober young man, his son, who is a good scholar and a master of arts of several years' standing, and though not in orders yet you know that is not hard to be got. I desire you, if Skengle accepts not of it, as I conclude he will not (for he was of that mind when we parted) to call in at Mr. Pawling's as you passed by and talk with the father and son about it. You see what liberty I take with you, but it is for those who I think deserve it. And he that I would speak for has a very peculiar and uncommon merit for he is not yet in orders....
Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. LOCKE.

[Second enclosure:]
1 Aske him whether he thinks it will be for his credit to let it goe with soe many great faults as those he has now writ in the margent, and to correct them only by seting them amongst the Errata
2 You may tell him 'tis a book of thought and requires consideration in the reader, which will be mightily disturbd if he must turne to the Errata for such as are more then literal or verbal faults in the book and if the Reader does not looke in the errata (which few readers are at the pains to doe) he will take it to be as in many places it is, as now printed, nonsense. And if any Reader be soe carefull as to correct his booke according to the errata, yet
― 777 ―
the paper of this second edition is soe bad that it will not bear writeing on it in the margent
3 Aske him whether the copy cost him dear, or any thing: and whether the profit of the booke will not bear the charges of reprinting above 8 leaves if there be occasion for more to make the Edition any way tolerable†1
4 Whether he thinks he that promised him more when this is done will ever send more to a man soe negligent in two editions, that to the omision of the corrections sent him of the first has added an hundred new ones in this second. That how ever he lays the blame on the printer the neglect will be imputed to him, and really is his, for if he had not carelessely given the corrections, were sent him, to the printer. But had but taken care to have them writ into the book it self, the printer would not have omitted them. Or if he had lookd after it ever soe litle him self or had but a tolerable corrector Neither the former edition nor this espetialy had had soe many shamefull faults
5 What satisfaction or amends it will be to the Reader or Author that he will not imploy the printer again for the same Reason, they may think it best he, the bookseller, should never be imploid again. Such a negligent Bookseller and printer may be laid aside togeather
6 That as to the Quæres he has put to severall of the corrections you lately gave him, you have looked over those places again, and find that he that doubted whether they should be put in or noe understood not the Author as particularly that place p. 151 l. 17 is not sense unlesse printed thus Heathens, Philosopher Aristotle,†2 and And therefor you are of opinion they ought all to be put in, except one which haveing your self some doubt about you have blotted out of his paper and another p. 120 which by the addition of a word omitted is made plainer†3
7 That you have looked over the later sheets of the book printed since those he formerly shewd you, which are done with the same care as the former which appears by these additionall corrections you here give him
8 In fine, that whatever he made the world expect, this later is soe intolerable an edition that you leave it to him to doe what he will with it

1691. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 12 January [1694] (1683, 1700)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 29-30. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Kensington Jan: 12th
It is as aukward a thing for an old maid to write a love letter as for an old parliament whig to turne courtier and in all probabillity they will succeed alike for that reason I have after full deliberation laid aside all thoughts of making attempts that way; tho it was some time before I could bring my self to this resolution, so much I was incouraged by Your invitation which if any thing could; had certainly inspire'd me with that tallent. since I saw You my Mistress†1 has taken a fancy to have me read to her Your rule's of Education. most of which she seems very much to aprove of, but more of this when I se You for 'tis now high time to tell You I'me unfeignedly glad to hear You have recover'd Your health so well in the countrey which they tell me is in great measure owing, not only to the good air of Oats but, to the company You carried with You. I was desire'd by Mr Cunningham to let You kno' that Mounsieur Fatio had some hopes of being preffer'd to my Lord Russell†2 and he desires me to tell you 'twould be a kindness never to be forgot if You would doe him the favour to recommend him in a letter to my Lady Russell or (if You think that not convenient) to write to Sir James Forbe's†3 to recommend him to her. thus far I undertook to let You kno' their desire and so I leave it with you you being the best judge whether it be fit for you to doe it or no. I need not give you or my self the trouble to give Mr Fatio any Character to You nor tell you how well he discharg'd his duty to my Cosen Dick Ellis,†4 I wish heartilly for a thaw for severall reasons but Especially to bring Mr Lock to town who as he will be wellcome to all his frends so more perticuliarly to his
Most oblige'd humble servant
M LOCKHART

1692. Locke to Philippus van Limborch, 13 January 1694 (1675, 1708)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 257 j. Printed in part in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 349-53; most of the remainder, in Ollion, pp. 208-9. Answers nos. 1646, 1668, and 1675; answered by no. 1708.
(English)
Oates 13 Jan 94
Qualem te Vir Spectatissime semper crediderim talem re ipsâ experior ad omnia infucatæ <amicitiæ>†a officia natum qui non solum pronus in beneficia nullam benemerendi prætermittis occasionem, sed quod dificilius est eadem facilitate ignoscis amicorum delictis quâ alii offensiones objurgant. Diuturnum meum silentium graviore reprehensione dignum simul ac tardas tandem a me literas acceperis quasi primâ voculâ penitus deletum condonas. Agnosco beneficium, candoremque illum tuum, quo tuis quo omnibus gratus, In quo me tuto repono: Dum non ex literis amicitiam meam æstimes, nec silentio imminutam suspicatus fueris. Id enim tibi <persuasum>†b vellem, tempus mihi et verba deesse posse, amicitiam qua te amplector, qua semper amplexurus sum, mihi deesse vel labefactari nunquam posse
(English) In historiâ tua inquisitionis ex quo novissime ad te dedi literas non magnos progressus feci, quotidianis negotiis hactenus impeditus. Quod si ex duobus primis libris quos summa cum voluptate
― 780 ―
perlegi de duobus reliquis judicare licet, nihil potest esse in eo genere perfectius, nec ad <p>erfectam†a illius tribunalis cognitionem aliquid desiderari potest. Laudo c<urs>um†a tuum quod plerisque in locis ipsa authorum verba citaveris, etsi nihil contineant quod tu breviore et elegantiore stilo exprimere non potuisses, si lectori placere unica esset cura, sed cum quo genere hominum tibi res est recte tecum reputasti, et eorum crimina, fraudes, et sævitia ex eorum ipsorum ore optime discenda, vix enim credi poterant si ab extraneo vel adversario afferrentur. Quæ autem ex aliis hauseris autoribus tam sero ut editioni inseri suis apte in locis non potuissent, tuique marginibus libri adscripseris, ea si nimis longa non sint ut tibi nimiam transcribendi creent molestiam, si mihi per otium excerpta transmittere velis gratissimum mihi facies, ut meum etiam librum iis ornem et†b omnibus numeris perfectum habeam, ut nihil desit huic mysterio iniquitatis revelando. Literas tuas per Hibernum illum†1 transmissas ille suis manibus rus huc ad me profectus mihi tradidit. Talem illum reperio qualem tu descripseris nec desunt hic tantæ spei fautores. Editionem illam Castelionis quam meditantur elegantem libens viderem, et nostratibus gratam fore
― 781 ―
nullus dubito. Quod de Harmonia Evangelica doctissimi mei Toinardi ad me scribis: de editione illius ego quidem nunquam cogitavi nec quod amplius est nunquam cogitabo nisi ut ipsum authorem ad opus suum luce dignissimum edendum quâ datâ occasione et quantum possum impellem et instigem. Non quod ego hunc thesaurum literato orbi inviderem. Ego summâ ope donec commercio literarum uti licuit editionem ejus semper efflagitavi. Sed non eâ (ut mihi visum est) fide mihi concreditum est hoc exemplar ut ego harmoniam hanc illo inscio aut inconsulto typis mandarem. Si mihi integrum esset statim sub prælo mitterem, sed dum ille vivit, aut aliunde a suis spes est prodituram nulla quantivis pretii mercede e meis manibus in publicum elabi patiar. Nuper prodiit hic liber quem Toinardo gratissimum fore scio. si reperire possis viam qua ad illum transmitti potest acceptissimum mihi feceris beneficium. Liber quem ad illum mittere vellem est
(English) Joannes Malela Antiochenus Oxonii non ita pridem editus. Si occasionem mittendi reperias, emptum apud vos librum sive compactum sive incompactum, prout commodissimum erit vecturæ quæso ad illum mittas A Monsieur <Toi>nard†a à Orleans

bibliotheca Bodleianâ, aliis privatis Collegiorum Oxonii Bibliothecis†1 jam credo propediem prostabit venalis in usum doctiorum. Centum circiter paginæ secundæ editionis libri mei de Intellectu humano jam imprimuntur: festinantis præli secundi hi labores lætius aspicerem si eâ essent linguâ ut tuum judicium de novis conatibus expectare possem. Paucula mutavi; plura, ut fit, addidi inter quæ unum integrum caput de Identitate præsertem personali: Naturamque voluntatis humanæ ita explicare conatus sum ut si faventium aliquot amicorum judiciis credere ausim me in perscrutandâ humanæ Libertatis conditione non prorsus frustra laborasse sperarem. Sed amicorum judicia sæpe vel fallunt vel falluntur et hæc ignotorum hominum permittenda censuræ;†a in hoc unico mihimet placeo quod unicæ studui veritati. Gallicorum Theologorum pro Orthodoxia zelus in frigidiore nostro climate quasi antiparistasi†b †2 ardentius deflagrare videtur. Cappellum Virum si quis alius inter Gallos, ut mihi videtur, temperatum et modestum, suspectum hæreseos in cœtu ad id convocato insimularunt, in quo ipse citatus suspitionibus nisi prodirent testes et accusatore præsente crimen objiceretur respondere vel purgare se recusavit.
― 783 ―
Hoc nihil proficiente, alia via aggressi sunt. Minister ecclesiæ parochialis ubi degit cum uno alterove hyerophylacte (Anglicè Churchwardens) eum <adeun>t,†a rogantque ut velit coram ipsis fidem suam palam recensam profiteri. Rogat qua authoritate id exigant; contra morem et instituta ecclesiæ Anglicanæ esse, ut quispiam privato jure ita in alterius mentem inquirat. Respondent se id non jure postulare, sed ut amice et fraterne id agat. Quibus ille Non pudet me inquit fidei quam et animo credo et data occasione palam profiteri non erubescam. Sed cum de eâ jam quæstio facta est idque coram plurimis, ignoscetis mihi si nihil hic respondeam et expectem quid illi accusatores mei vel susurrones habeant quod mihi <objiciant>.†b It<a>†c se res habuit cum Londini discesseram quid deinde factum sit nescio, et forsan totam historiam rectius cognosces a Clerico nostro, cui cum Cappello commercium est literarum. Tota hæc procella adversus Cappellum ut audio inde excitata est quod exequiis Ministri Galli non ad amussim orthodoxi interfuerit.†1 Gaudio Veenium nostrum sanum salvumque in urbem et ad praxin rediisse. Vir qui in artis suæ exercitatione a juventute usque consenuerat, continui tædio otii credo languesceret. Illum et
― 784 ―
Guenelonem nostrum uxoresque cum tota familia quæso meo nomine officiosissime salutes. Pacem concordiam et amicitiam inter eos stabilitam spero, omnia fausta uti par est illis. et Tibi tuisque opto. Salutes etiam rogo optimam fæminam tuam, liberosque quos sanos salvosque tibi deus diu conservet. En tandem quam promiseram verbosa et grandis Epistola nec tamen par aut tuis meritis aut amicitiæ meæ. Vale vir Humanissime et ut facis me ama

(Latin)
Oates 13 Jan 94
What I have always believed you to be, esteemed Sir, such I find you in reality: born to all the offices of unfeigned friendship, you, disposed to acts of kindness, not only let no opportunity of well-deserving go by but, what is more difficult, forgive the faults of your friends as readily as others rebuke stumblings. You pardon my lengthy silence, which was worthy of severer reproof, immediately on receiving, at long last, my tardy letter, as if it was blotted out by the first word. I acknowledge your kindness and that sincerity of yours, dear to those about you, dear to all; on this I can safely reckon, so long as you do not rate my friendship by my letters and have not suspected any diminution in it on account of my silence; for of this I would have you convinced, that time and words can fail me, but that the friendship with which I embrace you, with which I shall always embrace you, can never fail or be shaken.
(Latin) I have made no great progress in your Historia Inquisitionis since I last sent you a letter as I have been hindered until now by daily affairs. But if from the first two books, which I have read through with the greatest [p. 780] pleasure, I may judge the remaining two, nothing in that kind can be more perfect nor can anything be wanting for a perfect knowledge of that tribunal. I commend your course in quoting in most places the very words of the authors, although they may contain nothing that you could not have expressed yourself in a shorter and choicer style if your only care had been to please the reader, but you have rightly considered with what order of men you are concerned and that their crimes, deceits, and cruelty are best learnt from their own mouths, for they could scarcely be believed if they were reported by an outsider or an adversary. As for what things you have drawn from other authors too late to be duly inserted in their places in the published work, and which you have added in the margins of your copy, if they are not so very long as to give you very much trouble in copying them you will do me a very great favour if you will send me the extracts at your leisure, so that I may also furnish my own copy with them and have it perfect in all respects, so that nothing may be wanting to the revelation of this mystery of iniquity. The Irishman†1 by whom you sent your letter, journeying to me here in the country, delivered it to me with his own hands. I find him such as you described him, nor are there wanting here patrons of so great promise. I would gladly see that choice edition of Castellion which they are considering, and I do not doubt that it will be welcome to my countrymen. [p. 781] As to what you write to me about my most learned Toinard's Harmony of the Gospels: I for my part have never thought about its publication and, what is more, I shall never think about it except that, given an opportunity and as much as I can, I shall urge and incite the author himself to publish his work, a work most worthy of the sight of man. Not that I would begrudge this treasure to the learned world. As long as intercourse by letter was permitted I always with my utmost power solicited its publication. But, as it seems to me, this copy was not consigned to me with that trust, that I might commit this Harmony to print, he unaware and unasked. If it was open to me I should send it to the press at once, but while he lives or there is a hope that it will be published from another source by his people I shall not, for however great a reward, suffer it to slip out of my hands into public view. A book was published here recently that I know will be most welcome to Toinard. If you can find a way by which it can be sent to him you will do me a most acceptable service. The book that I should wish to send him is
(Latin) Joannes Malela Antiochenus, published at Oxford not so long ago. If you find an opportunity of sending it please buy it in your country and send it bound or unbound, as may be most convenient for carriage, A Monsieur Toinard à Orleans.
(Latin) At Oxford they are now printing a catalogue of all the manuscript books [p. 782] in the Bodleian Library and in other private libraries of the colleges in Oxford.†1 I now believe that it will shortly be on sale for the use of scholars. About a hundred pages of the second edition of my book on the human understanding are now printed; I should have viewed these second labours of the speeding press more joyfully if they were in a language such that I could expect your judgement of the new endeavours. I have altered very few things; as commonly happens I have added more, among them a whole chapter concerning Identity, especially Personal Identity; and I have tried so to explain the nature of the human will that, if I may venture to believe the opinions of some favouring friends, I may hope in investigating the condition of human liberty to have laboured not entirely in vain. But the opinions of friends often deceive or are deceived, and these things having to be left to the censure of strangers, in this one thing alone I find satisfaction, that I have pursued the truth alone. The French theologians' zeal for orthodoxy seems to be blazing more fiercely in our colder climate as if by force of contrast. In an assembly convoked for that purpose they accused Cappel, a man, if any among the French, as it seems to me temperate and discreet, as suspect of heresy; in it he, being summoned, refused to reply to, or purge himself from, the suspicions unless witnesses came forward and the charge was brought with the accuser present. As this had no effect they attacked [p. 783] in another way. The minister of the parish church where he lives and one or other churchwarden go to him and ask him to make a clear profession of his faith in their presence. He asks by what authority they require it; it is contrary, he says, to the customs and ordinances of the Anglican Church that anyone should by a private right inquire in this way into another person's mind. They reply that they do not require it by a right, but ask that he will do it amicably and fraternally. To this he says: I am not ashamed of a faith in which I heartily believe and which I shall not blush to profess in public when there is occasion. But since question has now been made about it, and that before many persons, you will forgive me if I make no reply here and await what those accusers of mine, or rather tale-bearers, have that they bring against me. So the matter stood when I left London; I do not know what has happened after that, and you will perhaps learn the whole story more correctly from our friend Le Clerc, who has intercourse by letters with Cappel. This whole storm against Cappel was aroused as I hear because he attended the funeral of a French minister who was not orthodox to a hair's breadth.†1 I am glad that our friend Veen has returned sound and safe to the city and to his practice. A man who has spent his life from youth to advanced age in the exercise of his art would, I feel sure, languish with the tedium of uninterrupted leisure. Please give my best wishes to him and to our friend [p. 784] Guenellon and to their wives, with the whole family. I hope that peace, concord, and friendship are established among them, and I wish them all prosperity, as is right, as well as to you and yours. Please also give my greetings to your excellent wife and to your children, whom may God long preserve to you sound and safe. Here at last you have the big long-winded letter I promised you, and for all that not equal either to your deserts or to my friendship. Good-bye, most kind Sir, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE

1693. Locke to William Molyneux, 19 January 1694 (1685, 1712)
Some Familiar Letters, pp. 68-73. Answers no. 1685; answered by no. 1712.
Oates, 19 Jan. 9¾.
Honoured Sir,
I can take it for no other than a great mark of your kindness to me, that you spend so much of your time in the perusal of my thoughts,
― 785 ―
when you have so much better of your own to improve it. To which you add this farther obligation, that you read my book for my instruction, still taking notice to me of what you judge amiss in it. This is a good office, that so few in the world perform in the way that you do, that it deserves my particular acknowledgement. And I own my self no less beholden to you when I differ from you, than when convinced by your better judgment, you give me opportunity to mend what before was amiss; your intention being that to which I equally, in both cases, owe my gratitude.
You doubt whether my answer be full in the case of the drunkard. To try whether it be or no, we must consider what I am there doing. As I remember (for I have not that chapter here by me) I am there shewing that punishment is annexed to personality, and personality to consciousness: How then can a drunkard be punish'd for what he did, whereof he is not conscious? To this I answer, Human judicatures justly punish him, because the fact is proved against him; but want of consciousness cannot be proved for him. This you think not sufficient, but would have me add the common reason, that drunkenness being a crime, one crime cannot be alledged in excuse for another. This reason, how good soever, cannot, I think, be used by me, as not reaching my case; for what has this to do with consciousness? nay, it is an argument against me, for if a man may be punish'd for any crime which he committed when drunk, whereof he is allow'd not to be conscious, it overturns my hypothesis. Your case of shooting a man by chance, when stealing a deer, being made capital, and the like, I allow to be just; but then, pray consider, it concerns not my argument; there being no doubt of consciousness in that case, but only shews, that any criminal action infects the consequences of it. But drunkenness has something peculiar in it when it destroys consciousness; and so the instances you bring justifie not the punishing of a drunken fact, that was totally and irrecoverably forgotten, which the reason that I give being sufficient to do, it well enough removed the objection, without entring into the true foundation of the thing, and shewing how far it was reasonable for humane justice to punish a crime of a drunkard, which he could be suppos'd not conscious of, which would have uselessly engag'd me in a very large discourse, and an impertinent digression. For I ask you, if a man by intemperate drinking should get a fever, and in the frenzy of his disease (which lasted not perhaps above an hour) committed some crime, would
― 786 ―
you punish him for it? If you would not think this just, how can you think it just to punish him for any fact committed in a drunken frenzy, without a fever? Both had the same criminal cause, drunkenness, and both committed without consciousness. I shall not inlarge any farther into other particular instances, that might raise difficulties about the punishing or not punishing the crime of an unconscious drunken man, which would not easily be resolv'd without enquiring into the reason upon which humane justice ought to proceed in such cases, which was beyond my present business to do. Thus, Sir, I have laid before you the reasons why I have let that passage go without any addition made to it. I desire you to lay by your friendship to me, and only to make use of your judgment in considering them. And if you are still of opinion that I need give the reason too, that one crime cannot be alledged in excuse of another, I beg the favour of you to let me know it as soon as I can, that I may add what is necessary in this place amongst the errata, before my book comes out, which advances now apace, and I believe there are, by this time, near 150 pages of it printed. And now, Sir, though I have not agreed with your opinion in this point, yet I beseech you believe I am as much obliged to your kindness in it, as if you had shew'd me what, upon your reason, had appear'd to me the grossest mistake; and I beg the favour of you, whenever you cast your eye upon any of my writings, to continue and communicate to me your remarks.
You write to me, as if ink had the same spell upon me, that mortar, as the Italians say,†1 has upon others, that when I had once got my fingers into it, I could never afterwards keep them out. I grant that methinks I see subjects enough which way ever I cast my eyes, that deserve to be otherwise handled, than I imagine they have been; but they require abler heads, and stronger bodies than I have, to manage them. Besides, when I reflect on what I have done, I wonder at my own bold folly, that has so far exposed me in this nice and critical, as well as quicksighted and learned age. I say not this to excuse a lazy idleness, to which I intend to give up the rest of my few days. I think every one, according to what way providence has placed him in, is bound to labour for the publick good, as far as he is able, or else he has no right to eat. Under this
― 787 ―
obligation of doing something, I cannot have a stronger to determine me what I shall do, than what your desires shall engage me in. I know not whether the attempt will exceed my strength. But there being several here who joyn with you to press me to it; (I received a letter with the same instance, from two of my friends at London, the last post)†1 I think, the first leisure I can get to my self, I shall apply my thoughts to it; and however I may miss my aim, will justifie my self in my obedience to you, and some others of my ingenious friends.
I am exceedingly obliged to Captain Monk for his kind remembrance, and to you for sending it me, and letting me know he is alive. I have, as I ought, all the esteem for him, that you know so modest and good a man deserves. Pray, when you see him, present my humble service to him, and let him know that I am extremely glad to hear that he is well, and that he has not forgot me, and should be much more so to see him here again in England. Pray give my humble service to your brother. I am,
Dear Sir,
Your most humble, and most faithful servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
1694. Robert Pawling to Locke, 20 January 1694 (1658, 1699)

Sir
I had written by the two last posts if I had not been prevented by some busines that unexpectedly kept me out till twas too late. I at last pleased my self in a Stuff for a frock I hope it pleased you too; it cost me 10s and 6d the Buttons.
Mrs Percivall was not at home nor Mr Wheelock. I called there twice, as soon as I meet with them I will do what you desire
Mrs Lockharts Drummond returned safe from Cornwall about new years tide and before he came away had let to one of the old Tenents as much of the worst of the Land with the house etc as will come to above 100 li per annum and there are about 60 or 70 Acres more of the best of it that lyes near Penrin that they

can have severall Tenents for, that will come to about 50 per annum more.†1 he tells me Mr Gwin†2 carrest him exceedingly at his first coming and would have persuaded him to have written to his Lady to have sold the Estate; he said it was not worth above 80 li per annum and he would help her to a Chapman for it and the next day a friend of his came that desired to deal for it; but when he said he came not to sell but to know the value of it and to let it; the Gentle man took occasion to complain of him. Mr Hampden†3 tells Madam that if she will sell it he will help her to 9 per cent as long as he lives
Mr Pearce hath don good service he is the man Mr Drummond took advice and directions from and is imployed now. upon inquiry I find the rents we<re>†a paid but every 6 months, therfore I sent the Executor word that Mrs Lockhart expects the half years rent due at Michaelmas; he is very stubborn but if she leavs that and the repairs to an Attorney I shall direct her to I shall bring him to reason
Mr Seager†4 had received his money so I dated your letter and intended this day to have delivered it to Mr Hayter but he was not at home; on Monday I will go again
Mr Seager is very ill, not likely to live many dayes therfore I do intend to advise with Madam Lockhart and some other friends and if they give me incouragement, I resolve to try for that place that he hath in the Excise office, which you mention in your letter. Mr. Hampden hath lately mentioned me with great kindnes to Mrs Lockhart of his own accord and I remember my Lord Monmouth had a promise from my Lord Godolp:†5 when I thought there had been a vacancy at Bristoll. if you can give me some directions in what method I am to proceed, to whom to apply my self; or think it proper to write to my Lord of Pemb:†6 my Lord Mon: or have so much acquaintance with Mr Mountacue†7 or any others you think
― 789 ―
may assist or serve me in it, I intreat you to do it. Sir Hen: Ashurst†1 promised Dr Wallis in generall to do me any kindnes he could. I knew he was ill before, but this evening I hear he is in a desperate condition. I presume the Treasury have the disposall of it. I was with the Earl of Pemb: yesterday about Greenwich who received me kindly and hath made good progress in contriving the Constitution;†2 the Queen on Tuesday mentioned it to Sir Tho†3 with great zeal and will take an opportunity to mention it to the King and then will wholy leave it to those two. my Lord presents†a his service to you and so doth
Your humble servant
ROB PAWLING

1695. William Thomas to Locke, 24 January 1694 (1688, 1731)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 144-5.
Sarum 24th January
Sir,
My Father has received your last and gives you many thankes for it. He farther ordered me to give you this following Account. About August last his Cough began, and he spitt a great deal of thinn Rheume, Coughing with great violence for sometimes near a quarter of an hour together. In This, neither Crocus Graduatus, nor any pectoralls releived him. About the middle of November he Went to Saveracke, where by use of Crocus and balsalmick Pills the Rheume grew thicker, he spitt less, so as sometimes not above 2 or 3 times in 24 hours, and in a word his Cough and all its symptoms abated verry much. Some time before this his left side
― 790 ―
from the mouth of his stomach to his feet began to swell, and with so much pain in his legg that ever since he has not been able to goe, nor to lye easy in his bed so as to continue there 24 hours together. About the End of December he returned hither, since which the pain in his leg and thigh grew so great that he has not been able to goe out of his chamber. Neither is it any ways possible for to goe out of doors much less to Savernacke. His weakness in that left legg especialy is so great that he is not able to stirr it but by the help of a swath†1 which is fastned to his foot. He makes urine proportionable to what he drinkes. His case is such that he cannot be allways in bed, but must of necessity be up sometimes. His cough is return'd in some measure, but not as it has been. He goes not to stool but by help of Clysters. He is verry willing to follow your directions. He is noe ways able to write himselfe, neither does he know when he shall be able.—To this Account which my Father would have me send to you I shall only add that he is now a mere skeleton, and allmost as helpless as an Infant. It is the worke of 3 or 4 of us to take him out of, or help him into his bed. his pains are not verry great, they remitt a little sometimes, but never wholy intermitt and I beleive that if ever you have a mind to see him, you must doe it here and that quickly too. The obligation I have now to follow our Chancery suit drawes me to London this week. I lodge with T. Davys†2 in Little Lincolns Inn feilds,†3 and should be glad to receive your commands if there is any thing I can serve you in. My Father and All here give their due respects to you and I desire you to Accept this from Sir your most Obliged and humble servant
W THOMAS
P.S. My Father does not understand you when you mention Mr Clarkes and Mr Frekes Interest with Mr Secretary Trenchard, but desires to Inform him more particularly.
Address: These To Mr John Locke At Sir Francis Massum's at Oates. To be left with Mr Robert Pawling in Dorsett Court in Channell-Rowe in Westminster London.

Endorsed by Locke: W: Thomas 24 Jan 9¾

1697. Nicolas Fatio De Duillier to Locke, 25 January 1694 (1468, 1888)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 97-8. For Fatio and Lord Russell see p. 778.
Honoured Sir
Mr Cuningham did ingage some of my friends to speak to Mylady Russel of me, that I might be with her Son in order to take care of his Education: and I see they have prevailed very far with her Ladyship. He told me also Sir that You was acquainted with her, and I know by that She will defer much to Your judgement. Shall I Sir take the liberty to beg your concurrence with such as have recommended me to that place. I know Sir You have allready shewed your self very kind to me in this very matter, and I am much obliged to You for it. You had much sooner heard from me, had it not been that Mr Cuningham did act at first without my consent. The loss of my liberty seemed to me so great that I had much ado to be persuaded into it. Yet I thank God there is no family in England where I could give it up with more ease than that of MyLady Russel. I hope Sir You will be pleased to help me with your good advise, for I think it will be no little task for me to give her Ladyship all the satisfaction she expects. I am with all my heart
Honoured Sir
Your most humble and most obedient servant
N. FATIO DE DUILLIER.
London January the 25th 169¾.
Endorsed by Locke: N: Fatio 25 Jan. 9¾ Answered 29.

1698. William and Mrs. Mary Popple to Locke, 25 January 1694 (1630, 1704; 2513)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 209-10.
[Popple:]
Sir
Your letter is so extreamly obliging, that in my best health both of body and minde I should have been very unable to have express'd my sense of it in any due measure: Indeed, now, I can do it no better, than in saying so: But yesterday, when I received that letter, truly I was not capable of doing it at all. And this a little explained comprehends the full state of my case. My best health at this time is accompanied with a continual purging, insomuch that it is very frequent with me to have eight or ten stooles a day. The matter that I voyd is not firy, or otherwise painful to me in the voyding of it: But at other times, especially in walking, there comes from me insensibly some very thin matter, so thin, and so little of it as not to stain my linnen, to which I know not what quality to ascribe; but the effect of it is that the parts where it touches by the rubbing of one side against the other in a little walking do thereupon become galled and sore as any tender skin would be in riding a long journey. I must ad one word more. After each stoole, I am commonly taken with faintings which last about a quarter of an houre: and in the rest of those intervalls my head is so filld with vapours that I am uncapable so much as of thinking seriously upon any thing. Thus, what with weakness of body, what with stupidity of minde, I know nothing more left in my self that is worth any of my friends concerning themselves for. But it is therefore so much the greater favour in you that do it, and in My Lady Masham that gave you the occasion of so doing. And the advice that you are pleased to promise me, upon this information, will be an effect of your own goodness which I shall ever own with the deepest sense.
[Mrs. Popple:]
Really, Sir, my husband is soe weary with writing this, and soe oppressed with vapors, that I think my selfe oblidged to take the pen out of his hand. Soe that he must tell me what he has to say or let it alone till another time. He tels me then, that the Printer
― 794 ―
has now the end of the second Book of your Essay in his hands,†1 but how farr it is printed off he knows not. As for the advice you give him about printing, he bids me tel you it is vastly deferent from what he beggs of you to write. If he could think the one would be deverting, thats the most can be said of it: but the other will be certainly soe highly usefull to man kind, that he finds himself not onely inclined†a- to begg-†a it of you as a favour, but thinks he has a right to press it upon you as a duty.†2 I am very much oblidged to you for your inquiry after all our familys health. Pray accept of our own and their respects. Dr Paus†3 is now here, and presents his service to you. Pray let me begg the favour of you to present our services to Barron van Helmont.
[Popple:]
Good Sir pardon all the irregularities of this letter. I am
Sir,
Your most obliged humble servant
WILLIAM POPPLE.
London. January 25th 1693/94.
Address: For Mr Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]
Postmarks: (G.P.O., defective); GC
Endorsed by Locke: W: Popple 25 Jan 9¾ Answered 29.
1699. Robert Pawling to Locke, 27 January 1694 (1694, 1715)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 20.
London January 27 1693
Sir
I received both yours and that by the Carier came first and I suppose upon enquiry you will find the Carier was not in fault, you bid me send the Serge to Mr Bonvilles who himself said he was to
― 795 ―
send some things to you; whereupon I sent it thither on Friday was fortnight but I believ he sent the serge by it self and it may be not till the week following; however I am glad you have, and like, it.
though I forgot to write to you of it yet I did not forget to solicite Colonel Austen about your Cousin Veal†1 but I found nothing could be don in it
I have left the box and stand with my Lady Masham and a small pot of the Oyl you desired; I presented your service to my Lord Ashley and he returns the same again to you. Mr Fuller hath no Tube roses, about a fortnight or three weeks hence he expects some from beyond sea, as soon as they come he will furnish you with those that are good. I have not met with Mr Chadwick†2 but will time enough to send the seed by my Lady
my son hath been to seek the Book you desire and on Monday he hopes to get a good one he presents his humble service to you and intreats you to enquire about the free schools thereabout; you was speaking of one Carkas†3 that hath a free school near you, that is much declined. Tom thinks he might be persuaded to resign it he allowing him good part of the salary, I did acquaint Sir Francis with my sons desire to take upon him that employment. I know he will do us what kindnes he can therein, but he knows of none vacant
after I understood Mr Seager had received his money I dated your letter and deliverd it to Mr Hayter, who, according to the old custom, said they had not received it and wrot me a note to you to that purpose; but when I said you sent not till we were well assured others had their money, he praid me not to give you the note till he had enquired farther and the next time I came that way he would give me his answer, though he said it could not be that any were paid because Sir Steph:†4 told him the warrant was signed but on Saturday, and I think this was on Monday. when I came again he acquainted Sir St: therewith, who gave me the same answer I had a day or two before; but when I said I was sure others were paid; he said if Dr Locke had occasion for 50 li he bid mr Haiter
― 796 ―
pay me, when I replyed, I came not for the money but for a note he bid Mr Haiter give me a note bearing date the next day for he believed then he should receive it, so I had a note for 50 li bearing date January 25 1693. Mr Seager <is>†a somewhat mended, and Mr Glanvill†1 thinks he sold that place, however it seems twas but the Porters place. I give you my hearty thanks for your readines to assist me on all occasions I hope the time will come when I shalbe provided for some where or other; though we move but slowly in Greenwich affair. I inclose this long letter but perhaps not so long within as this from
Your humble Servant
ROB PAWLING
Address: For Sir Francis Masham a member of Parliament [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]

1700. Martha Lockhart to Locke, 27 January [1694] (1691, 1757)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 31-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Kensington Jan: 27
Your's of the 10th came safe to my hand and I had made my return sooner but that it was some day's before I Could meett with mr Cuningham†b and I did not think any other way so Fiting as to talke with him about it. which at last I have done but I think first I should tell you that I was perfectly of your opinion about this matter and did when Cuningham spoke to me wonder at it that they should have made use of any other to writ to you but thought that upon second consideration's that they might have had to great a share of my awcward basshffullnes which had oblig'd 'em to it. when I meett with Mr Cun I did tell him that I had at his desire,
― 797 ―
and upon Mr Fatios acount writ to you but that tho I did not question your civillity to me nor your Concern for Mr Fatio: for whom I had offten hard you express your selfe with great Concern yett I thought it would have had a much better effect if he who I understood was well acquanted with you had writ to desier the Favour of you him selfe to this purpose. I spoke to Cuningham and so left the subject to ther better management sence which I have hard noe more of it but talking tother day with Sir James Forbes about that Family he askt me if I had hard your opinion of Mr Fatios which I ventur'd to say I beleiv'd was very good, which he made me the Compliement to say weighed more with him then all he had hard and did make use of it as he since tells me to my lady Russell who did as Sir James tell's me allmost debend upon it, I find they have resoulv'd to make tryall of him before the Finsh any bargin in it and so this matter stand's. I am sorry that nether Chang of whether nor dear Lady Ma: indispositon†1 can draw you one step nearer London tho I cant say that if you had been here I had been able offten to have made one of the number you are so kind to wish for very violent Cold's with which I've been very frequently trobled since I saw you together with the dayly drudgery of my life and some times indeavouring to Console a poor mell<a>ncholly†a sister†2 has made me more a stranger to my Lady Masham then realy at the small disstance we are now at I could have thought possible, and this I shall not need to tell you has been more my missfortune then my fault. I thought to have left the sweetest part of my letter, I mean the love, to the last but I find I have unluckly nether left my self roome nor time, for this undertaking. I hope you will allow it a true Maxim in this case that it is not the greatest passion that is soonest expres't therfore Judg not uncharitably my sillance nor belive me Less your affectionate servant
M L
Endorsed by Locke: M: Lockhart 27° Jan 9¾
