Index of Correspondents in this Volume
This index is by the numbers of the letters, italics being used as in the text to indicate letters not by Locke. A bracketed number is either for a letter between persons other than Locke, in which case it appears under the names of both writer (or writers) and person addressed, or for an item other than a letter. If there is correspondence in earlier or later volumes between Locke and a person in this index it is indicated by the citation of the next volume or volumes in which any of it occurs.
The citation immediately following a name is that of a biographical note on the person. For persons concerned with only one or two letters the citation is omitted sometimes if the biographical note occurs in the headnote and is insignificant.

The Cromwell Kin
The present table shows the relationships of a number of persons who came into Locke's correspondence mainly through the marriage of Damaris Cudworth with Sir Francis Masham. The common ancestor is Sir Henry Cromwell, 'the Golden Knight', who was a great-nephew of Henry VIII's minister and grandfather of the Protector. The kinship is large: Sir Henry had eleven children and at least 59 grandchildren. I have omitted from the table almost everyone except persons mentioned in the correspondence and the persons linking them with Sir Henry; in some cases I have stated the relationship in notes; in view of their intermarriages with the Cromwell kin I have added a table for Trevor.
The principal source is Mark Noble, Memoirs of the Protectoral-house of Cromwell, third edition, 1787. I have checked and supplemented it with further materials, mainly printed, but including Esther Masham's letter-book.

Locke may have been preparing to return to the United Provinces in the coming winter: statements and allusions in letters from Thomas (no. 1323, etc.), Furly (no. 1331, etc.), and Newton (nos. 1332, 1338). †5 This was a constitutional question about the selection of the schepenen (aldermen) of Amsterdam. On 28 January of each year the burgomasters and raaden (councillors) of Amsterdam nominated fourteen men from whom the Stadhouder must choose seven schepenen, who were sworn in on 2 February. In the absence of the Stadhouder abroad in 1689 the procedure was irregular; Amsterdam now claimed that the choice should be made by the hof (council) of the States of Holland. William sent Portland (no. 974) to resist this claim, whereupon Amsterdam objected
― 7 ―


to Portland's sitting with the States on the ground that he was in the service of a foreign power: N. Japikse, Prins Willem III, 1930-3, ii. 294-8, and J. Wagenaar, Vaderlandsche historie, 1790-6, as there cited.

†2 Sanskrit. Locke apparently derived the word from Bernier, Suite des memoires, The Hague, 1671, letter to Chapelain, pp. 84, 96-8 (Locke copied these passages in his Journal, 15 May 1676). Bernier took the word from the headings of two plates, 'Elementa Linguæ (or Lingua) Hanscret' in A. Kircher, S.J., China, 1667, p. 162. The material for the plates was supplied by Heinrich Roth, S.J., a missionary who learnt Sanskrit. How the error arose is not clear; there is a possible explanation in Bernier, Travels, translated, etc., by A. Constable and V. A. Smith, 1914, p. 329 n. Locke adds a further error in treating Hanscrit as the name of a particular book.

†1 Samuel Jocelin, from whom four letters to Locke survive: no. 1491, etc. Bishop's Stortford is in Hertfordshire, close to the Essex border. It was formerly a post town: Strype's Stow, v. 402. It is 31 miles from London on the road to Newmarket; Oates was about 6 miles distant. Harlow is only 25 miles from London by the same road, and is about 4 miles from Oates. Locke occasionally gives a Harlow address, but it was not a post town and the great majority of letters to him at Oates were transmitted by Jocelin. The name Bishop's Stortford is frequently mis-spelt or given in variant forms. From now on the full address will be abbreviated to 'For Mr. John Locke [at Oates, by Joslyn, Bishops Stortford]'.

By the Index Furly means the table of contents. The Jesuits at Dijon were said to have maintained a thesis in 1686, 'Le Peché Philosophique, ou Moral est une action humaine contraire à ce qui convient à la nature raisonnable, et à la droite raison. Mais le peché Theologique mortel est une libre transgression de la Loi de Dieu. Le peché philosophique, quelque grief qu'il puisse être, étant commis par un homme, ou qui n'a point de connoissance de Dieu, ou qui ne pense point actuellement à Dieu, peut être un peché fort grief; mais ce n'est point une offense de Dieu, ni un peché mortel, qui rompe l'amitié de l'homme avec Dieu, ni qui mérite la peine éternelle.' This thesis was attacked by the Jansenists and explained and defended by the Jesuits; the Jansenists attacked the defence: Bibliotheque universelle,xv. 233-7 (which gives the thesis); xvii. 378-86; and xviii. 180-4 (the article seen by Furly).

†1 He was a tax-collector for Westminster: no. 1722. Locke as a Commissioner of Appeals in Excise was liable to poll-tax; as he was presumably paying the monthly assessment on his Somerset property locally, this would be one shilling in the pound on his salary; he was also required to pay £5 as an esquire. The poll-tax was imposed by 1 W. and M., c. 13, which was repeated by 2 W. and M., c. 2. In the next two acts for the tax (3 W. and M., c. 6, and 5 and 6 W. and M., c. 14) the liabilities are altered. On 13 July Locke left with Pawling a note for £15 payable to Fox for the tax: Journal.

†1 Carat is now a proportional measure of one-twenty-fourth used in stating the fineness of gold. In the seventeenth century it was (or was regarded as) a definite weight: 'A Pound Weight Troy of Gold was divided into Twenty four Carats, and every Carat into Four Grains of Gold; and a Pound Weight of the Old Sterling, or Right Standard Gold of England, consisted of Twenty three Carats and Three Grains and an half of Fine Gold, and half a Grain of Allay': Lowndes, Report (no. 1949 n.), pp. 17-18. The carat thus equals half an ounce troy or ten pennyweight.

†1 The book is Dioptrica Nova. A Treatise of Dioptricks, London, 1692. It is dedicated to the Royal Society. The passage concerning Locke relates to logic and runs: 'But to none do we owe for a greater Advancement in this Part of Philosophy, than to the incomparable Mr. Locke, Who, in his Essay concerning Humane Understanding, has rectified more received Mistakes, and delivered more profound Truths, established on Experience and Observations, for the Direction of Man's mind in the Prosecution of knowledge, (which I think may be properly term'd Logick) than are to be met with in all the Volumes of the Antients. He has clearly overthrown all those Metaphysical Whymsies, which infected mens Brains with a Spice of Madness, Whereby they feign'd a Knowledge where they had none, by making a noise with Sounds, without clear and distinct Significations.'

†1 Molyneux understood this to refer to II. xxi. 28: p. 716. It perhaps however refers to § 25, also on p. 123 of the first edition. This paragraph, of which §§ 26-8 are an extension, opens: 'Since then it is plain, a Man is not at liberty, whether he will Will, or no; (for when a thing in his power is proposed to his Thoughts, he cannot forbear Volition, he must determine one way or other).' In the second edition 'a thing' is replaced by 'an action'. § 28 opens: 'In the next place we must remember, that Volition or Willing,regarding only what is in our power, is nothing but the preferring the doing of any thing, to the not doing of it; Action to Rest, et contra.' The paragraph is rewritten in the second edition, opening, 'We must remember, that Volition or Willing is an act of the Mind directing its thought to the production of any Action, and thereby exerting its power to produce it.'

†1 Sébastien Castellion (Chastellion or Chatellion; c. 1509/15-1563; D.B.F.) published his Latin translation of the Bible at Basel in 1551; it was reprinted frequently (Locke owned a copy of the edition of 1554: L.L., no. 326). The present project foundered. A new edition was published at Frankfurt in 1697; it contains the Defensio, the account of the Jewish state, and other matter, but nothing by van Limborch. The Churchills advertised it in 1699: T.C. iii. 110.
Castellion was a precursor of Arminianism, influencing it directly and through Dirck Volckertszoon Coornhert (1522-90; N.N.B.W.); and more generally of liberal Protestantism. His views on religious liberty and his denunciations of persecution were important for the Remonstrants. If Locke did not know his Contra Libellum Calvini (no. 1702 n.) already, van Limborch probably introduced him to it before he wrote the Epistola de Tolerantia. The principal work on him is F. Buisson, Sébastien Castellion, 1892; J. Lindeboom, 'La place de Castellion dans l'histoire de l'esprit', in Autour de Michel Servet et de Sébastien Castellion, ed. B. Becker, 1953 (pp. 158-80), is important also. Locke's holdings include, besides the Bible, L.L., nos. 618-23 (Castalio), 843-4 (Coornhert).

†1 Furly perhaps refers to a lost letter from Locke, but more probably to a passage in Some Thoughts concerning Education, A § 180 (C § 192): 'since the Deluge cannot be well explained without admitting something out of the ordinary course of Nature, I propose it to be considered whether God's altering the Center of gravity in the Earth for a time ... will not more easily account for Noah's Flood, than any Hypothesis yet made use of to solve it ... [Locke reserves] to a fitter opportunity, a fuller explication of this Hypothesis, and the application of it to all the Parts of the Deluge, and any Difficulties can be supposed in the History of the Flood as recorded in the Bible.' Locke does not appear to have elaborated his theory, and I have not found it set out elsewhere. The three leading theories of his time were those of Thomas Burnet, in The Theory of the Earth, vol. i (no. 784); John Woodward, in An Essay towards a Natural History of the Earth, 1695 (no. 1865); and William Whiston, in A New Theory of the Earth, 1696 (nos. 2131, 2202); they are summarized and discussed in D. C. Allen, The Legend of Noah, 1949, pp. 92-112.
